title: What’s new
text:
Version 2.0.0 (2024-10-01)

Summary
Version 2.0 contains several major changes. These include: module-specific timesteps and time-aware parameters (including a day/year unit flag for modules, and ss.dur() and ss.rate() classes for parameters), and changes to module types and integration (e.g. renaming update() and apply() methods to step();).


Time-aware parameters and modules

Added ss.dur(), ss.rate(), and ss.time_prob() classes, for automatic handling of time units in simulations. There are also convenience classes ss.days(), ss.years(), ss.perday(), ss.peryear(), and ss.beta() for special cases of these.
ss.dur() and ss.rate(), along with modules and the sim itself, have a unit parameter which can be 'day', 'week', 'month', or 'year' (default). Modules now also have their own timestep dt. Different units and timesteps can be mixed and matched. Time parameters have a to() method, e.g. ss.dur(1, 'year').to('day') will return ss.dur(365, unit='day').
The ss.Sim parameter n_years has been renamed dur; sim.yearvec is now sim.timevec, which can have units of days (usually starting at 0), dates (e.g. '2020-01-01'), or years (e.g. 2020). sim.abs_tvec is the translation of sim.timevec as a numeric array starting at 0, using the sim’s units (usually 'day' or 'year'). For example, if sim.timevec is a list of daily dates from '2022-01-01' to '2022-12-31', sim.abs_tvec will be np.arange(365).
Each module also has its own mod.timevec; this can be different from the sim if it defines its own time unit and/or timestep. mod.abs_tvec always starts at 0 and always uses the sim’s unit.
There is a new Loop class which handles the integration loop. You can view the integration plan via sim.loop.to_df() or sim.loop.plot(). You can see how long each part of the sim took with sim.loop.plot_cpu().
There are more advanced debugging tools. You can run a single sim timestep with sim.run_one_step() (which in turn calls multiple functions), and you can run a single function from the integration loop with sim.loop.run_one_step().



Module changes

Functionality has been moved from ss.Plugin to ss.Module, and the former has been removed.
ss.Connector functionality has been moved to ss.Module. ss.Module objects can be placed anywhere in the list of modules (e.g., in demographics, networks, diseases, interventions), depending on when you want them to execute. However, ss.Connector objects are applied after Disease.step_state() and before Network.step().
Many of the module methods have been renamed; in particular, all modules now have a step() method, which replaces update() (for demographics and networks), apply() (for interventions and analyzers), and make_new_cases() (for diseases). For both the sim and modules, initialize() has been renamed init().
All modules are treated the same in the integration loop, except for diseases, which have step_state() and step_die() methods.
The Starsim module states.py has been moved to arrays.py, and network.py has been moved to networks.py.



State and array changes

ss.Arr, ss.TimePar, and ss.Result all inherit from the new class ss.BaseArr, which provides functionality similar to a NumPy array, except all values are stored in arr.values (like a pd.Series).
Whereas before, computations on an ss.Arr usually returned a NumPy array, calculations now usually return the same type. To access the NumPy array, use arr.values.
There is a new ss.State class, which is a subtype of ss.BoolArr. Typically, ss.State is used for boolean disease states, such as infected, susceptible, etc., where you want to automatically generate results (e.g. n_infected). You can continue using ss.BoolArr for other agent attributes that you don’t necessarily want to automatically generate results for, e.g. ever_vaccinated.



Results changes

Results are now defined differently. They should be defined in ss.Module.init_results(), not ss.Module.init_pre(). They now take the module name, number of points, and time vector from the parent module. As a result, they are usually initialized via ss.Module.define_results(res1, res2) (as opposed to mod.results += [res1, res2] previously). define_results() automatically adds these properties from the parent module; they can still be defined explicitly if needed however.
Because results now store their own time information, they can be plotted in a self-contained way. Both ss.Result and ss.Results objects now have plot() and to_df() methods.



Demographics changes

Fixed a bug in how results were defined for ss.Births and ss.Deaths.
The ss.Pregnancy module has been significantly rewritten, including: (1) Agents now have a parent which indicates the UID of the parent; (2) Women now track child_uid; (3) On neonatal death, the pregnancy state of the mother is corrected; (4) Pregnancy rates now adjusted for infecund rather than pregnant; (4) Pregnancy now has a burn-in, which defaults to True; (5) Pregnancy has a p_neonatal_death parameter to capture fetal and neonatal death if the mother dies.
Slots now has a minimum, default of 100, to account for small initial population sizes that grow dramatically over time.



Computational changes

There have been several performance improvements. The default float type is now np.float32. Transmission is now handled by a specialized Infection.compute_transmission() method. Several additional functions now use Numba, including fastmath=True, which leverages Intel’s short vector math library.
A new ss.multi_random() distribution class has been added, that allows random numbers to be generated by two (or more) agents. It largely replaces ss.combine_rands() and is 5-10x faster.
A new ss.gamma() distribution has also been added.
Distributions have a new jump_dt method that jumps by much more than a single state update.
ss.parallel() and ss.MultiSim.run() now modify simulations in place by default. Instead of sims = ss.parallel(sim1, sim2).sims; sims[0].plot(), you can now simply do ss.parallel(sim1, sim2); sim1.plot().



Other changes

Data can now be supplied to a simulation; it will be automatically plotted by sim.plot().
ss.Calibration has been significantly reworked, and now includes more flexible parameter setting, plus plotting (calib.plot_sims() and calib.plot_trend()). It also has a debug argument (which runs in serial rather than paralell), which can be helpful for troubleshooting issues.
MultiSim now has display methods brief() (minimal), show() (moderate), and disp (verbose).
sim.export_df() has been renamed sim.to_df().
Most classes now have to_json() methods (which can also export to a dict).
Fixed a bug in how the InfectionLog is added to disease modules.
Sim.gitinfo has been replaced with Sim.metadata (which includes git info).
Infection.validate_beta() is now applied on every timestep, so changes to beta during the simulation are now honored.
sim.get_intervention() and sim.get_analyzer() have been removed; use built-in ndict operations (e.g., the label) to find the object you’re after.
requires has been removed from modules, but ss.check_requires() is still available if needed. Call it manually from init_pre() if desired, e.g. a PMTCT intervention might call ss.check_requires(self.sim, ['hiv', 'maternalnet']).
For networks, contacts has been renamed edges except in cases where it refers to an agent’s contacts. For example, network.contacts has been renamed network.edges, but ss.find_contacts() remains the same.
Networks now have a to_graph() method that exports to NetworkX.
ss.diff_sims() can now handle MultiSim objects.
Sim._orig_pars has been removed.
ss.unique() has been removed.



Regression information

Note: the list here covers major changes only; in general, Starsim v1.0 scripts will not be compatible with Starsim v2.0.
Results from Starsim v2.0 will be stochastically (but not statistically) different from Starsim v1.0.
All duration and rate parameters should now be wrapped with ss.dur() and ss.rate(). Events that represent probabilities over time (i.e. hazard rates) can also be wrapped with ss.time_prob(), although this is similar to ss.rate() unless the value is relatively large.
ss.Plugin has been removed. Use ss.Module instead.
init_results() is now called by init_pre(), and does not need to be called explicitly.
default_pars() has been renamed define_pars().
add_states() has been renamed define_states()
initialize() has been renamed init().
Demographics.update() has been renamed Demographics.step().
Network.update() has been renamed Network.step().
Disease.update_pre() has been renamed Disease.step_state().
Disease.make_new_cases() has been renamed Disease.step().
Disease.update_death() has been renamed Disease.step_die() (which is now called by People.step_die()).
Infection._set_cases() has been renamed Infection.set_outcomes().
Intervention.apply(sim) has been renamed Intervention.step(); ditto for Analyzer.
Module.step() no longer takes sim as an argument (e.g., replace intervention.apply(sim) with intervention.step()).
All modules now have methods for start_step(), finish_step(), init_results(), and update_results().
Network.contacts has been renamed Network.edges.
sim.get_intervention() and sim.get_analyzer() have been removed; simply call directly instead (e.g. replace sim.get_intervention('vaccine') with sim.interventions['vaccine']).
requires is no longer an attribute of modules; call the ss.check_requires() function directly if needed.
People.resolve_deaths() has been renamed People.check_deaths()
ss.unique() has been removed.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 0.5.0 (2024-05-14)

Summary
All inputs to the sim and modules now use a ss.Pars() class, which handles updating and validation. It is now not necessary to ever use pars= (although you still can if you want), so what was previously:
sim = ss.Sim(pars=dict(diseases='sir', networks='random'))
is now just:
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sir', networks='random')
Updates happen recursively, so distributions etc. can be flexibly updated.
This has significantly changed how modules are initialized; what was previously:
def __init__(self, pars=None, **kwargs):

    pars = ss.omergeleft(pars,
        dur_inf = 6,
        init_prev = 0.01,
        p_death = 0.01,
        beta = 0.5,
    )

    par_dists = ss.omergeleft(par_dists,
        dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex,
        init_prev = ss.bernoulli,
        p_death = ss.bernoulli,
    )

    super().__init__(pars=pars, par_dists=par_dists, *args, **kwargs)
is now:
def __init__(self, pars=None, **kwargs):
    super().__init__()
    self.default_pars(
        beta = 0.5,
        init_prev = ss.bernoulli(0.01),
        dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex(6),
        p_death = ss.bernoulli(0.01),
    )
    self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs)


Parameter changes

Added a ss.Pars class (and a ss.SimPars subclass) that handles parameter creation, updates, and validation.
Initialization has been moved from sim.py to parameters.py; ss.Sim.convert_plugins() has been replaced by ss.SimPars.convert_modules().
The key method is ss.Pars.update(), which performs all necessary validation on the parameters being updated.



Initialization changes

Previously, the people were initialized first, then the states were initialized and the values populated, then the modules were initialized, and finally the distributions are initialized. This led to circular logic with the states being initialized based on uninitialized distributions. Now, states and modules are linked to the People and Sim objects, but further initialization is not done at this step. This ensures all distributions are created but not yet used. Next, distributions are initialized. Finally, the initial values are populated, and everything is initialized.
New methods supporting these changes include ss.link_dists(), dist.link_sim(), dist.link_module(), sim.init_vals(), people.init_vals(), module.init_vals(),



Module changes

Whereas modules previously initialized a dict of parameters and then called super().__init__(pars, **kwargs), they now call super().__init__() first, then self.default_pars(par1=x, par2=y), then finally self.update_pars(pars, **kwargs).
What was previously e.g. ss.Module(pars=dict(par=x)) is now ss.Module(par=x).
par_dists has been removed; instead, distributions are specified in the default parameters, and are updated via the Pars object.
Modules now contain a link back to the Sim object. This means that all methods that used to have sim as an argument now do not, e.g. self.update() instead of self.update(sim).
ss.module_map() maps different module types to their location in the sim.
ss.find_modules() finds all available modules (including subclasses) in Starsim.
Removed ss.dictmerge() and ss.dictmergeleft (now handled by ss.Pars.update()).
Removed ss.get_subclasses() and ss.all_subclasses() (now handled by ss.find_modules()).
Modules can no longer be initialized with a name key; it must be type (e.g. dict(type='sir') rather than dict(name='sir').
Added to_json() and plot() methods to Module.
Removed connectors.py; connectors still exist but as an empty subclass of Module.



People and network changes

BasePeople has been removed and merged with People.
Time parameters (ti, dt, etc.) have been removed from People. Use sim.ti, sim.dt etc. instead. One consequence of this is that people.request_death() now requires a sim argument. Another is that network methods (e.g. add_pairs()) now take sim arguments instead of people arguments.
SexualNetwork is now a subclass of DynamicNetwork.
Removed ss.Networks (now just an ss.ndict).
Network connectors have been removed.
Person has been implemented as a slice of sim.people[i].
There is a new parameter use_aging; this defaults to True if demographic modules are supplied, and False otherwise.



Other changes

Boolean arrays have new methods true(), false(), and split(), which return the UIDs for the True values (alias to arr.uids), False values, and both sets of values, respectively. ss.bernoulli.split() has been added as an alias of ss.bernoulli.filter(both=True).
All inputs to a sim are now copied by default. To disable, use ss.Sim(..., copy_inputs=False).
There is a new Plugin class, which contains shared logic for Interventions and Analyzers. It has a from_func(), which will generate an intervention/analyzer from a function.
Diseases no longer have a default value of beta=1 assigned; beta must be defined explicitly if being used.
Individual diseases can now be plotted via either e.g. sim.plot('hiv') or sim.diseases.hiv.plot().
Distributions can be created from dicts via ss.make_dist().
A new function ss.check_sims_match() will check if the results of two or more simulations match.
ndict values can be accessed through a call; e.g. sim.diseases() is equivalent to sim.diseases.values().
Merged test_dcp.py and test_base.py into test_other.py.
Renamed test_simple.py to test_sim.py.
Renamed test_dists.py to test_randomness.py.

title: What’s new
text:
Version 0.4.0 (2024-04-24)

Replace UIDArray, ArrayView, and State with Arr, which has different subclasses for different data types (e.g. FloatArr, BoolArr, and IndexArr). States are usually represented by BoolArr (e.g. sir.infected), while other agent properties are represented by FloatArr (e.g. sir.rel_trans).
Arrays that had previously been represented using an integer data type (e.g. sir.ti_infected) are now also FloatArr, to allow the use of np.nan. Integer arrays are supported via IndexArr, but these are only intended for use for slots and UIDs.
Arr objects automatically skip over dead (or otherwise removed) agents; the “active” UIDs are stored in sim.people.auids, which is updated when agents are born or die. This array is linked to each Arr, so that e.g. sim.people.age.mean() will only calculate the mean over alive agents. To access the underlying Numpy array, use sim.people.age.raw.
FloatArr has isnan, notnan, and notnanvals properties. BoolArr has logical operations defined. For example, ~people.female works, but ~people.ti_dead does not; people.ti_dead.notnan works, but people.female.notnan does not.
UIDs used to be NumPy integer arrays; they are now ss.uids objects (which is a class, but is lowercase for consistency with np.array(), which it is functionally similar to). Indexing a state by an integer array rather than ss.uids() now raises an exception, due to the ambiguity involved. To index the underlying array with an integer array, use Arr.raw[int_arr]; to index only the active/alive agents, use Arr.values[int_arr].
Dead agents are no longer removed, so uid always corresponds to the position in the array. This means that no remapping is necessary, which has a significant performance benefit (roughly 2x faster for large numbers of agents).
Renamed omerge to dictmerge and omergeleft to dictmergeleft.

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
In an SEIR model, people infected first pass through a latent period (E, exposed) before they become infectious. In the simplest SEIR, the time spent in each state is exponentially distributed: many people leave a state almost at once and a few stay a long time, which is rarely realistic. A gamma-distributed (Erlang) period with a few stages is closer to most real infections: each person passes through k stages, each exponential, and the total has the same mean but much less spread. This page compares the two, for the same mean infectious period.
crumbs: SEIR with a realistic infectious period

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection per susceptible person, per unit of the fraction infectious


Latent period
5 days
Mean time in E (exponential)


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I: exponential, or Erlang with 3 stages


R0
3
β × the mean infectious period


Population
100,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

def make_seir(infectious_period):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection = S >> E @ 0.3*I
    latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery  = I >> R @ infectious_period
    return ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='seir')

exponential = make_seir(ss.days(10))
erlang = make_seir(ss.erlang(mean=ss.days(10), k=3))

The infection leads to E, so the people infected at the start are put in I with init=dict(I=0.001). The diagram, from diagram():

erlang.diagram()








As an ODE, the Erlang period is exact: I is split into three stages, each with a mean of a third of the period, as the equations show:

erlang.equations()

dS/dt   = -beta * S * I / N
dE/dt   =  beta * S * I / N - E / dur_E
dI_1/dt =  E / dur_E - 3 * I_1 / mean(dur_I)
dI_2/dt =  3 * I_1 / mean(dur_I) - 3 * I_2 / mean(dur_I)
dI_3/dt =  3 * I_2 / mean(dur_I) - 3 * I_3 / mean(dur_I)
dR/dt   =  3 * I_3 / mean(dur_I)
crumbs: SEIR with a realistic infectious period

title: SEIR with a realistic infectious period
text:
Result

sims = {
    'Exponential': ss.Sim(exponential, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
    'Erlang, 3 stages': ss.Sim(erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('seir')








Both have the same R0 and start the same way, in a closed population, so the same fraction of people is infected in the end (the final size depends only on R0 in an SEIR like this one, whatever the distributions of the periods). But with the Erlang period, people infect others over a narrower window of time after they were infected, so the epidemic grows faster, and peaks earlier and higher. A model fitted to the growth of an epidemic with the wrong distribution of the infectious period gets R0 wrong, which is one reason for the stages.

title: Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Data on an epidemic is rarely the number infected: it is reported cases, hospital admissions, or deaths, each a fraction of infections, some time after infection. In Starsim these are outcomes: results computed from the model’s flows, with a fraction, a delay, and (for a stay in hospital) a stay, that don’t change the epidemic itself. This page adds three outcomes to an SIR, makes weekly data from the model with a known β, and fits β to it.
crumbs: Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data

import starsim as ss

beta = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1.0]) # A parameter to fit, with its starting value and bounds
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
cases     = ss.outcome(0.5*infection, delay=ss.days(5))
hosp      = ss.outcome(0.05*infection, delay=ss.days(7), dur=ss.days(10))
deaths    = ss.outcome(0.2*hosp, delay=ss.lognormal(mean=14, std=5, unit='days'))
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, hosp, deaths, init=dict(I=0.001), name='sir')

pars = dict(total_pop=1e6, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-06-01')

The outcomes are not states, so the diagram, from diagram(), is an SIR’s:

sir.diagram()

title: SIR, four ways
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
The SIR model is the starting point of most epidemic modeling: people are susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R), infection is frequency-dependent (each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the fraction of people who are infectious), and people stay infectious for an exponentially distributed time. This page writes it in each of the ways Starsim accepts, checks that they are the same model, and runs it as a deterministic ODE, as two kinds of stochastic compartmental model, and as agents.

title: SIR, four ways
section: The model: four ways to write it
text:
The model: four ways to write it








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection per susceptible person, per unit of the fraction infectious


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


R0
3
β × the infectious period


Population
10,000



Infected at the start
0.1%
10 people



Each transition says where people move from and to, and at what rate. These four spellings say the same thing:

import starsim as ss

spellings = {}

# Operators: from >> to @ rate (or duration)
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Operators'] = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

# Each transition written out in full
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
spellings['Explicit'] = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3*I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10), name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'sir',
)

# A class, for a disease to reuse or extend
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Class'] = SIR(init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

# The whole flow, β S I / N, as most other frameworks write it: read as written, the fraction infectious, 0.3*I.frac, which is 0.3*I when everyone mixes
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
N = S + I + R
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*S*I/N
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
spellings['Whole flow'] = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

The same states, transitions, and rates give the same results, whatever the spelling:

for label, disease in spellings.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(disease, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0).run()
    print(f'{label:12s} peak infections: {sim.results.sir.I.max():,.0f}')

Operators    peak infections: 3,006
Explicit     peak infections: 3,006
Class        peak infections: 3,006
Whole flow   peak infections: 3,006


The state-transition diagram, from diagram() (the dashed arrow is a transmission):

spellings['Operators'].diagram()

title: SIR, four ways
section: Result: four ways to run it
text:
Result: four ways to run it
The same model can be run in four ways: as an ODE (the default for this model, since nothing in it is about individual people), as a chain binomial (a random number of people move between states each day), with the Gillespie algorithm (each event at its own random time), and as agents.

sir = spellings['Operators']
sims = {}
for solver in ['ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', 'abm']:
    sims[solver] = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), solver=solver, verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sir')








The three stochastic runs follow the ODE closely, each a little differently by chance. With 10,000 people and 10 infected at the start, chance mostly moves the timing of the peak; with fewer people, or fewer infected at the start, the runs differ more (see The chance of a major outbreak). In all of them about 94% of people are infected in the end, as the final-size equation predicts for R0 = 3 (see Final size):

msim.summarize().loc['sir_infection']

title: Cholera with a water reservoir
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Cholera spreads mostly through water rather than from person to person: infected people shed bacteria into the water, the bacteria decay over weeks, and susceptible people are infected by drinking it. A model of it needs a state that is not people at all: the amount of bacteria in the water, W. This page models W as a state of the disease that holds a count rather than people, following the model of Codeço (2001).

title: Cholera with a water reservoir
text:
The model
Infection depends on the bacteria in the water, with a dose-response curve that saturates: the rate is β W / (W + K), where K is the amount of bacteria at which the rate is half its maximum. W and K are amounts; Codeço writes them as concentrations, which is the same model for a fixed volume of water (taken here as one unit).








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.5 per day
Maximum rate of infection, when the water is saturated with bacteria


K
100,000
Amount of bacteria at which the rate is half its maximum


Infectious period
5 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


Shedding
10 per day
Bacteria shed into the water by each infectious person


Survival of bacteria
30 days
Mean time bacteria survive in the water


Population
10,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
W = ss.State(people=False) # Bacteria in the water: a count, not people
K = 1e5                    # Amount of bacteria at which infection is half its maximum

infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(0.5) * W.n / (W.n + K)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)
shedding  = ss.outside >> W @ ss.perday(10) * I.n  # Each infectious person sheds 10 a day
decay     = W >> ss.dead @ ss.days(30)          # Bacteria survive 30 days on average
cholera = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, shedding, decay, init=dict(I=0.001), name='cholera')

W.n and I.n are counts (the amount of bacteria, and the number of people infectious), where a bare I in a rate would be the fraction of people infectious (I.frac). ss.outside and ss.dead are outside the model: shedding adds bacteria from outside it, and decay removes them. The diagram, from diagram(), in which W is slanted since it is not people:

cholera.diagram()









cholera.equations()

dS/dt = -perday(0.5) * W.n / (W.n + 100000) * S
dI/dt =  perday(0.5) * W.n / (W.n + 100000) * S - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I
dW/dt = -W / dur_W + perday(10) * I.n

title: Cholera with a water reservoir
text:
Result

sim = ss.Sim(cholera, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(200))
sim.run()
sim.plot('cholera')

Sim: cholera, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 200
  Done in 0.0026 s









Bacteria build up in the water while people are infectious, and outlast them: the amount in the water peaks after the number infectious does, and keeps infecting people as the epidemic declines. Since W is a count and not people, it is left out of the population, and it stays a count when the people are run as agents (n_agents=).

title: Hospitalization and death
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Two different mechanisms decide what happens to people after a state, and a model needs the right one. In a split on entry, the outcome is decided when people enter the state: here, 10% of infectious people will go to hospital and the rest will recover, each after their infectious period. With competing hazards, two transitions out of a state run at the same time and whichever happens first wins: here, people in hospital are discharged after 10 days on average, but die at a rate of 0.02 per day while they are there, so the fraction who die depends on both rates. This page puts both in one model, a respiratory infection with hospitalization, and checks the fraction who die. Then it makes the chance of hospitalization depend on age, written as a Python function, and runs the model both as compartments and as agents.

title: Hospitalization and death
text:
The model








Parameter

Hospitalized

R0

Population
100,000

The model is written as a function of the chance of hospitalization, so that the same model can be made again with a chance that depends on age, below:

import starsim as ss

def make_covid(hospitalized=0.1):
    """ An SIR with hospitalization and death; hospitalized is the chance of going to hospital """
    S, I, R, H, D = ss.states('S I R H D')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
    course    = ss.Transition(I, {R: None, H: hospitalized}, dur=ss.days(8))  # Split on entry: 10% to H, the rest to R
    discharge = H >> R @ ss.days(10)                                            # Competing hazards: discharge ...
    death     = H >> D @ ss.perday(0.02)                                        # ... and death
    return ss.Disease(infection, course, discharge, death, init=dict(I=0.001), name='covid')

covid = make_covid()

In {R: None, H: 0.1}, None stands for the rest (here, 90%). The diagram, from diagram():

covid.diagram()








And the equations, in which the split appears as the fractions (1 - 0.1) and 0.1 of the flow out of I, and the competing hazards as two flows out of H:

covid.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  (1 - 0.1) * I / dur_I + H / dur_H
dH/dt =  0.1 * I / dur_I - rate_death * H - H / dur_H
dD/dt =  rate_death * H


A rate given as a number is named by its transition, so the rate of death appears as a parameter called rate_death, and a duration by the state it is the time in (dur_I and dur_H). To give it a name of your own, write it as ss.par(ss.perday(0.02), name='mu') (see Parameters).

title: Hospitalization and death
text:
Result

sim = ss.Sim(covid, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200))
sim.run()
sim.plot('covid')

Sim: covid, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 200
  covid: R0 = 2.4, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0025 s; covid: 87,777 infections; at most 21,892 infectious, on day 41









Of the people admitted to hospital, the fraction who die is the rate of death over the sum of the two rates out of H: 0.02 / (0.02 + 1/10) = 1/6. The flow course.H is the number admitted to hospital:

admitted = sim.results.covid['course.H'].sum()
deaths = sim.results.covid.death.sum()
print('Admitted:', round(admitted), 'Died:', round(deaths), 'Fraction:', round(deaths/admitted, 3))

Admitted: 8788 Died: 1465 Fraction: 0.167

title: Hospitalization and death
section: Advanced: severity by age, as a function
text:
Advanced: severity by age, as a function
Some parts of a model are easiest to write as a function. Here the chance that an infection is severe enough for hospital depends on age: 10% under 50, and 40% from 50 up. Rather than stratify the disease by age and give a value for each group, the chance is a Python function of the sim, which reads people’s ages. Starsim tries the function on the model’s age groups, and since it works on them, the model still runs as compartments; run as agents, the same function is evaluated for each person.

def severity(sim):
    """ The chance of hospitalization: 10%, plus 30% from age 50 """
    return 0.1 + 0.3*(sim.people.age >= 50)

covid_age = make_covid(hospitalized=severity)

The sim is split into two age groups at 50 (stratify=dict(age=[0, 50])), so that the function has ages to work on in a compartmental run. The same model is run as an ODE and as agents, in a population of 10,000:

sims = {
    'ODE': ss.Sim(covid_age, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(200), stratify=dict(age=[0, 50]), verbose=0),
    'Agents': ss.Sim(covid_age, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(200), solver='abm', verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('covid')








The two agree, apart from chance in the agent run. Of about 8,800 infections, about 1,500 people are admitted to hospital (covid_course.H): about one in six, between the 10% of those under 50 and the 40% of those over, since about a quarter of people are 50 or over (the population’s ages are guessed as the world’s in 2024, as describe() says). Of those admitted, one in six die, as before, since the competing hazards out of H haven’t changed:

title: Vaccination as a stratification
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
In many compartmental models, vaccination is not part of the disease at all: the population is split into the vaccinated and the unvaccinated, vaccination moves people from one group to the other, and the vaccinated are infected at a lower rate. This is how summer2, Atomica, and many published models write it, and it keeps the disease model the same whatever the vaccination program. This page writes an SIR this way, with a campaign that vaccinates half of the population on day 10, and compares it with no vaccination.

title: Vaccination as a stratification
text:
The model








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
0.3 per day
Rate of infection of the unvaccinated


Vaccine effect
90%
The vaccinated are infected at 10% of the rate of the unvaccinated


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


R0
3
Before vaccination


Campaign
Day 10
Vaccinates 50% of people, whatever their state


Population
10,000



Infectious at the start
0.1%





import starsim as ss

def make_sir():
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3*ss.by(vaccinated=[1.0, 0.1])*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='sir')
    sir.stratify(vaccinated={False: 1, True: 0})
    return sir

campaign = ss.Event(dict(vaccinated=True), when=ss.days(10), p=0.5, name='campaign')

stratify() splits each state in two, with everyone unvaccinated at the start ({False: 1, True: 0}), and ss.by() in the rate of infection multiplies it by 1 for the unvaccinated and 0.1 for the vaccinated. The campaign is a delivery that moves people to the vaccinated group: it needs no vaccine product, since the effect of vaccination is in the stratification. The diagram, from diagram(), is an SIR’s, since the vaccinated and unvaccinated groups split each state:

make_sir().diagram()

title: Vaccination as a stratification
text:
Result

sims = {
    'No vaccination': ss.Sim(make_sir(), total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0),
    'Campaign': ss.Sim(make_sir(), interventions=campaign, total_pop=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sir')








Vaccinating half of the population lowers the reproduction number from 3 to 3 × (0.5 + 0.5 × 0.1) = 1.65: that is R0 weighted by the susceptibility of each group, for a population that is still almost all susceptible. By day 10 some people have already been infected, so the effective reproduction number on the day of the campaign is a little lower. The epidemic infects under half as many people:

title: Checks against theory
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Two classic results of epidemic theory hold for the simplest SIR model, and are good checks of any way of running it. The first is deterministic: the fraction of people ever infected, the final size, depends only on R0. The second is stochastic: an epidemic with R0 above 1 doesn’t always take off, and the chance that it does also depends only on R0. This page sweeps R0 and checks Starsim against each: the final size with the ODE, and the chance of a major outbreak with many stochastic runs.

title: Checks against theory
text:
The model
Both checks use the same SIR, with an infectious period of 10 days and β = R0 / 10 per day for each value of R0, and differ only in the population and how the epidemic starts.








Parameter
Value
Meaning




β
R0 / 10 per day
Rate of infection, for each value of R0


Infectious period
10 days
Mean time in I (exponential)


Population
1,000,000 (final size); 1,000 (major outbreak)



Infectious at the start
One in a million (final size); one person (major outbreak)





import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

def make_sir(R0, **kwargs):
    """ An SIR with an infectious period of 10 days; kwargs say how it starts """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ (R0/10)*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, name='sir', **kwargs)


make_sir(2).diagram()

title: Checks against theory
text:
Final size
In a closed SIR epidemic that starts with almost everyone susceptible, the fraction of people who are ever infected, z, depends only on R0. Kermack and McKendrick (1927) showed that it solves the final-size equation
\[z = 1 - e^{-R_0 z},\]
whatever the infectious period or how fast the epidemic runs. Here the model is run as an ODE for R0 from just above 1 to 4, in a population of a million that starts with one person in a million infectious, so that almost everyone starts susceptible, as the equation assumes. Each run lasts long enough (2,000 days) for even the slowest epidemic, with R0 just above 1, to end. For each R0, the final size from the model is the fraction of people recovered at the end:

R0s = np.arange(1.1, 4.01, 0.3)
model = []
for R0 in R0s:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(R0, init=dict(I=1e-6)), total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(2000), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    model.append(sim.results.sir.R[-1] / 1e6)

The equation has no closed-form solution, but it can be solved by iteration: start from any z between 0 and 1 and apply the right-hand side repeatedly, which converges to the solution when R0 > 1.

R0_curve = np.linspace(1.01, 4, 200)
z = np.ones_like(R0_curve)
for i in range(500):
    z = 1 - np.exp(-R0_curve*z)

plt.plot(R0_curve, z, label='Final-size equation')
plt.plot(R0s, model, 'o', label='Starsim (ODE)')
plt.xlabel('R0')
plt.ylabel('Fraction of people ever infected')
plt.legend()
plt.show()








The model agrees with the equation to within a few parts in a million, for every R0: about the fraction of people infectious at the start, which the equation leaves out. Run as agents or stochastically in a large population, the model gives close to the same final size in the runs in which a major outbreak occurs, the subject of the next check.

title: Checks against theory
section: The chance of a major outbreak
text:
The chance of a major outbreak
Early in an epidemic, when there are only a few cases, each one infects a random number of others, and by chance all of them can recover before passing the infection on. For an SIR model with an exponential infectious period, started by one infectious person, the chance that this happens (that the outbreak is minor) is 1 / R0, so the chance of a major outbreak is 1 − 1 / R0 (Whittle, 1955). A deterministic model can’t show this, since in an ODE an epidemic with R0 above 1 always takes off.
Here the model starts with a single infectious person in a population of 1,000, and is run 300 times for each R0 (1,500 runs in all, which take seconds as compartments) with the Gillespie algorithm, which follows each infection and recovery as an event at its own random time, as the theory does. A run counts as a major outbreak if more than 10% of people are infected. The theory is for an infinite population, and in a finite one the line between minor and major outbreaks is not sharp; but with R0 well above 1 and 1,000 people, minor outbreaks infect at most a few people each, so the exact threshold hardly matters. Close to R0 = 1 it matters more, and the agreement is looser. infection.summarize() gives the infections over the whole of each run:

R0s = [1.25, 1.5, 2, 3, 4]
major = []
for R0 in R0s:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(R0, init_n=dict(I=1)), total_pop=1000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='gillespie', verbose=0)
    msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=300, verbose=0)
    infections = msim.results.sir.infection.summarize() # One total for each run
    major.append(np.mean(infections > 100))

R0_curve = np.linspace(1, 4.2, 100)
plt.plot(R0_curve, 1 - 1/R0_curve, label='Theory: 1 − 1/R0')
plt.plot(R0s, major, 'o', label='Starsim (300 Gillespie runs each)')
plt.xlabel('R0')
plt.ylabel('Fraction of runs with a major outbreak')
plt.legend()
plt.show()








Each point is the fraction of 300 runs with a major outbreak, so it is uncertain by about ±0.05 (two standard errors), and within that the runs agree with the theory.
The theory is for continuous time. A chain binomial model moves people between states in steps of time, and in a step the chance that a person recovers before infecting anyone is lower than in continuous time, so it gives more major outbreaks. How many more depends on the step. With 10,000 runs at R0 = 2 (theory: 0.5), in steps of a day:



Solver
Major outbreaks




'gillespie'
0.49


'binomial' (by default, with substeps as needed)
0.52


ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1) (each day taken whole)
0.55


'binomial' with dt=ss.days(0.1)
0.50



Each is uncertain by about ±0.01. So the default chain binomial is close to the theory here, and taking each day whole, as discrete-time models do, overstates the chance by about a tenth. Agents also take steps of a day, but draw each person’s infectious period from the exponential distribution itself, and come close to the theory too (0.53 ± 0.03 in 1,000 runs).

title: An STI on a sexual network
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This model restricts transmission to sexual partnerships, which form and dissolve over time, so how fast the infection spreads depends on who partners with whom and for how long, not just on the average number of partners. That needs a model of individual people and their partnerships: a network, and so agents. This page models a curable bacterial STI (an SIS model: people become susceptible again when cured) on Starsim’s sexual network of men and women, with a different chance of transmission per sex act from men to women and from women to men. The parameter values are illustrative, not estimates for a particular infection.

title: Age groups and contacts
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
People of different ages mix differently: children have the most contacts, and most of them with other children. An age-structured model splits each state by age group, and a contact matrix says how many contacts a day a person in each group has with people in each other group. With contacts, β is the rate of infection per contact, and the force of infection on group i is β times the sum over groups j of the contacts of i with j times the fraction of j who are infectious. This page builds an age-structured SIR with a contact matrix written by hand, as in the age-structured models of Keeling and Rohani (2008, chapter 3). Then it uses a real country’s population and contact matrices, one for each setting (home, school, work, and the rest of the community), and closes schools by removing one of them.

Advanced: a real population, with contacts by setting
This part is an extension of the example above, with a larger model. Closing schools is one of the first measures considered against a new respiratory infection. It removes the contacts children make at school, but not those at home or elsewhere, so whether it helps depends on how much of the spread happens at school, and on when the schools close and reopen. A model of it needs contacts by setting. This part adapts the school closure example of the Epidemics R package: an SEIR model of an influenza-like infection in the population of the United Kingdom, in three age groups, with the contact matrices of Prem et al. (2021) for each setting.

Rather than writing the fractions of each age group and the matrix by hand, ss.population() gives the country’s population by age, and ss.contacts() its matrix for each setting, for the age groups of the model:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
flu = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> E @ 0.016*I,
    onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(3),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7),
    init      = dict(I=1e-6),
    name      = 'flu',
)
flu.stratify(age=[0, 20, 40])

home, school, work, community = [ss.contacts('United Kingdom', layer=layer) for layer in ['home', 'school', 'work', 'community']]

R0 is about 1.5.

title: Age groups and contacts
text:
Closing schools
The closure is a modifier of the school contacts: from day 200 to day 260 they are multiplied by zero, and when it ends, they are back as they were, since a modifier never changes the contacts themselves.

closure = ss.modify(school, multiply=0, start=ss.days(200), stop=ss.days(260))


pars = dict(people=ss.population('United Kingdom'), networks=[home, school, work, community], stop=ss.days(600))
sims = {
    'Schools open': ss.Sim(flu, **pars),
    'Schools closed for 60 days': ss.Sim(flu, interventions=closure, **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('flu_I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Schools open, Schools closed for 60 days)
  Done in 0.95 s









The closure doesn’t prevent the epidemic. It delays the peak by about six weeks and lowers it by about a fifth, which could matter for hospitals, but most of those it spares are infected after schools reopen, since the epidemic resumes among people who are still susceptible: the number infected in all is only about 3% lower.

The Epidemics package says a closure another way: as a fraction by which the contacts of each age group fall (e.g. by half for those under 20). That works in Starsim too, as a modifier of each group’s susceptibility and transmissibility, e.g. ss.modify(flu.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, who=flu.age < 20, start=..., stop=...). Removing the school contacts says more directly what a closure does, when the contacts by setting are known.

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Starsim declares most models in a few lines: states, transitions, rates, and the data to fit them to. Sooner or later, though, a model needs something none of these say. This page takes a model with several such parts, the measles model of He, Ionides and King (2010), and writes it in Starsim in three ways:
Along the way, it gives a likelihood of its own, compiles the coded model’s loop with @ss.jit, and runs Starsim’s particle filter on the declared model, at the published parameters.
This is an advanced case study, and the longest page in the gallery (it takes about a minute to run). To start from the version to use, read The model, then A likelihood of your own and section 3; sections 1 and 2, and compiling, show the alternatives, and Which to use compares all three.

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
The model
He et al. fitted a stochastic SEIR model to the weekly measles cases reported in London from 1944 to 1965. It is the classic test of methods for fitting stochastic models, and it has four features beyond a plain SEIR model:

Noise on the rate of infection. Besides the chance of who is infected each day, the force of infection itself varies at random from day to day (“extra-demographic” noise, gamma-distributed with variance σ²).
Births that enter school together. Most children (55.7%) enter the susceptible pool all at once, on the day school starts in September; the rest enter through the year. The birth rate and the population follow the census.
School terms. Transmission is higher during the four school terms than in the holidays.
A measurement model whose spread grows with the cases. Each week’s reported cases are normal, with mean ρC and variance ρC(1 − ρ + ψ²ρC), where C is the number who recovered that week.

The parameters are those the paper estimated. The census and the cases are two small tables:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as sps
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss

pars = sc.obj(
    R0=56.8, sigma=28.9/365.25, gamma=30.4/365.25, mu=0.02/365.25, # Latent and infectious periods of about 12 days; deaths per day
    alpha=0.976, iota=2.9, sigma_se=0.0878,  # Mixing, imported infections, and the noise
    amplitude=0.554, cohort=0.557,           # School terms, and the fraction of births entering at school start
    rho=0.488, psi=0.116,                    # Reporting
    s0=0.0297, e0=5.17e-5, i0=5.14e-5,       # Starting fractions
)
start = ss.date('1943-12-31')
stop = start + ss.days(7*1096) # 1,096 weeks of data
terms = [(7, 100), (115, 199), (252, 300), (308, 356)] # School terms, in days of the year

census = pd.read_csv('../tutorials/data/he2010_london_covariates.tsv', sep='\t') # Days from 1944-01-07; the birth rate is per person per year, lagged four years
cases = pd.read_csv('../tutorials/data/he2010_london_cases.tsv', sep='\t')        # Days from the start to the end of each week
data = pd.DataFrame(dict(recovery=cases.weekly_cases.values), index=[start + ss.days(int(t) - 7) for t in cases.time]) # Each week dated by its first day, as Starsim dates a flow

def year(date):
    """ The time as He et al. count it: the year, plus the day of the year over 365.25 """
    return date.year + date.dayofyear/365.25

census_years = year(ss.date('1944-01-07')) + census.t.values/365.25
def lookup(column, date):
    """ The census value in force at a date (each month's value holds until the next) """
    i = np.searchsorted(census_years, year(date), side='right') - 1
    return census[column].values[max(i, 0)]

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
1. Declared, with a little code
The states, transitions and deaths are declared as usual. The rest is written as functions of the sim, which Starsim calls once a step: the force of infection, which reads the calendar for the school terms, and the births, which on day 251 of the year include the cohort entering school. The noise is a value that changes each step, so it is a few lines of a connector, whose step() draws it before the diseases run; the force of infection reads it. It is one number for the whole population, not a draw for each person, so it uses a NumPy generator seeded from the sim rather than a Starsim distribution: common random numbers pair the draws of individuals between scenarios, and there are none here to pair (see Random numbers). (Section 3 declares all of these instead.)

class Noise(ss.Connector):
    """ Gamma noise on the force of infection, with mean 1, drawn once a step """
    def __init__(self, sigma_se):
        super().__init__(name='noise')
        self.var = sigma_se**2*365.25 # The variance of a day's noise
        self.value = 1.0

    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(self.sim.pars.rand_seed)

    def step(self):
        self.value = self.rng.gamma(1/self.var, self.var)

def force(sim):
    """ The force of infection: school terms, mixing that rises a little more slowly than the number infectious, and the noise """
    doy = sim.now.dayofyear
    school = any(lo <= doy <= hi for lo,hi in terms)
    seas = 1 + pars.amplitude*0.2411/0.7589 if school else 1 - pars.amplitude # The same mean over the year
    beta = pars.R0*seas*(1 - np.exp(-(pars.gamma + pars.mu)))
    I = sim.diseases.measles.I.n
    return ss.perday(beta*(I + pars.iota)**pars.alpha/lookup('pop', sim.now)*sim.connectors.noise.value)

def births(sim):
    """ Births per day; on day 251, also the cohort of the year's births entering school """
    yearly = lookup('pop', sim.now)*lookup('birthrate', sim.now)
    entry = sim.now.dayofyear == 251
    return ss.perday(yearly*((1 - pars.cohort)/365.25 + pars.cohort*entry))

def make_measles():
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    N0 = lookup('pop', start)
    return ss.Disease(
        infection = S >> E @ force,
        latency   = E >> I @ ss.perday(pars.sigma),
        recovery  = I >> R @ ss.perday(pars.gamma),
        births    = ss.unborn >> S @ births,
        deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.perday(pars.mu)),
        init_n    = dict(S=round(pars.s0*N0), E=round(pars.e0*N0), I=round(pars.i0*N0)),
        name      = 'measles',
    )

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(), connectors=Noise(pars.sigma_se), solver='binomial', total_pop=lookup('pop', start),
             start=start, stop=stop, dt=ss.days(1), data=data)
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 2,464,805 people, as a stochastic compartmental model (chain binomial), 1943-12-31 to 1965-01-01
  Note: the initial value of S in "measles" is kept, and the other 2,391,346 people start in R, the only state not given one
  Note: run a step at a time, which is much slower than all at once, since noise has a step of its own (a module written as code)


  Done in 5.1 s


Sim(n=2464804; 1943-12-31—1965-01-01; diseases=measles; connectors=noise)


The model runs as a chain binomial, a stochastic compartmental model. To compare it with the data, the weekly recoveries are scaled by the reporting rate ρ:

weekly = sim.results.measles.recovery.values[:-1].reshape(-1, 7).sum(axis=1) # The steps from days 0-6, 7-13, ..., as the data are (the last step, from the stop, is past the data)
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(data.index, data.recovery, label='Reported', alpha=0.6)
plt.plot(data.index, pars.rho*weekly, label='Model × ρ', alpha=0.8)
plt.ylabel('Cases per week')
plt.legend()








The model’s epidemics come every other year, as London’s did, though not always in the same years: a stochastic model’s timing drifts from the data’s unless it is filtered. describe() shows everything that is declared, and says what is code:

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
2. Written as code
The most direct way is to write the model as one module, in NumPy, with nothing declared. This is He et al.’s own algorithm, line for line (an Euler-multinomial step each day). Its states are arrays with one value for each of n runs, so one sim can also run many copies of the model at once:

class He2010(ss.Module):
    """ He et al.'s model, as code: n copies of S, E, I and R, advanced each day by the function euler """
    def __init__(self, n=1, euler=None):
        super().__init__(name='he2010')
        self.n = n
        self.euler = euler

    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(self.sim.pars.rand_seed)
        N0 = lookup('pop', self.sim.t.start)
        self.S, self.E, self.I = [np.full(self.n, np.round(N0*x)) for x in [pars.s0, pars.e0, pars.i0]]
        self.C = np.zeros(self.n) # Recoveries in the last step
        self.recoveries = []

    def step(self):
        p, now = pars, self.now
        pop = lookup('pop', now)
        yearly = pop*lookup('birthrate', now)
        births = np.round(yearly*((1 - p.cohort)/365.25 + p.cohort*(now.dayofyear == 251)))
        seas = 1 + p.amplitude*0.2411/0.7589 if any(lo <= now.dayofyear <= hi for lo,hi in terms) else 1 - p.amplitude
        beta = p.R0*seas*(1 - np.exp(-(p.gamma + p.mu)))
        var = p.sigma_se**2*365.25
        noise = self.rng.gamma(1/var, var, self.n)
        rates = (p.iota, p.alpha, p.sigma, p.gamma, p.mu)
        self.C = self.euler(self.S, self.E, self.I, beta, pop, births, noise, self.rng, rates)
        self.recoveries.append(self.C.mean())

def euler_step(S, E, I, beta, pop, births, noise, rng, rates):
    """ One day for each copy: who leaves S, E and I, and where to (the rest die) """
    iota, alpha, sigma, gamma, mu = rates
    foi = beta*(I + iota)**alpha/pop*noise
    out = []
    for n,rate in [(S, foi), (E, sigma), (I, gamma)]:
        leaving = rng.binomial(n.astype(np.int64), 1 - np.exp(-(rate + mu)))
        out.append((rng.binomial(leaving, rate/(rate + mu)), leaving))
    (inf, nS), (lat, nE), (rec, nI) = out
    S += births - nS
    E += inf - nE
    I += lat - nI
    return rec

def make_coded(n=1, euler=euler_step, **kwargs):
    return ss.Sim(modules=He2010(n, euler), start=start, stop=stop, dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0, **kwargs)

sims = ss.parallel([make_coded(rand_seed=seed) for seed in range(6)]).sims
totals = [pars.rho*np.sum(s.custom.he2010.recoveries) for s in sims]
print(f'Reported cases over 21 years: {np.mean(totals):,.0f} ± {np.std(totals):,.0f}')

Reported cases over 21 years: 539,594 ± 7,455


The module keeps nothing for each person, so the sim has no agents: Starsim calls its step() once a day, and gives it the dates, seeds, and parallel runs. What it can’t do is show what the module does, run it under another solver, or fit it with sim.fit(), since there is nothing declared to fit.

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
A likelihood of your own
He et al.’s measurement model is a normal whose variance grows with the mean, which isn’t one of Starsim’s likelihoods. Any likelihood can be given as a function of the data and the model’s values, returning the log-likelihood of each. Here, as in the paper, it is the chance of the reported number rounded to a whole case:

def reported(observed, recovered):
    """ The log-likelihood of the reported cases, given the recoveries """
    m = pars.rho*recovered
    sd = np.sqrt(m*(1 - pars.rho + pars.psi**2*m)) + 1e-18
    lik = np.where(observed > 0, sps.norm.cdf(observed + 0.5, m, sd) - sps.norm.cdf(observed - 0.5, m, sd), sps.norm.cdf(0.5, m, sd))
    return np.log(lik + 1e-18)

ss.fitting.loglik(sim, likelihood=dict(recovery=reported))

-31485.821261718982


The function can be given wherever a distribution is: on an outcome (ss.outcome(..., likelihood=reported)), to sim.fit(likelihood=...), and to the particle filter. For a single stochastic run, the log-likelihood is low, since its epidemics are not in step with the data; a particle filter (below) measures the fit properly.

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
Compiling the coded model
@ss.jit compiles a function with Numba, with no change to what it does. Here is the step above as a loop over the copies:

@ss.jit
def euler_loop(S, E, I, beta, pop, births, noise, rng, rates):
    """ The same as euler_step(), one copy at a time """
    iota, alpha, sigma, gamma, mu = rates
    rec = np.zeros(len(S))
    for i in range(len(S)):
        foi = beta*(I[i] + iota)**alpha/pop*noise[i]
        nS = rng.binomial(int(S[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(foi + mu)))
        nE = rng.binomial(int(E[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(sigma + mu)))
        nI = rng.binomial(int(I[i]), 1 - np.exp(-(gamma + mu)))
        inf = rng.binomial(nS, foi/(foi + mu))
        lat = rng.binomial(nE, sigma/(sigma + mu))
        rec[i] = rng.binomial(nI, gamma/(gamma + mu))
        S[i] += births - nS
        E[i] += inf - nE
        I[i] += lat - nI
    return rec

make_coded(euler=euler_loop).run() # The first run compiles it
for label,euler in [('NumPy', euler_step), ('Compiled', euler_loop)]:
    T = sc.timer()
    make_coded(euler=euler).run()
    T.toc(f'One run, {label}')

  Compiling euler_loop() with Numba, estimated time: 1-10 s


  Compiled euler_loop() with Numba in 2.2 s


One run, NumPy: 2.43 s
One run, Compiled: 1.39 s


The first call compiles it, once; after that it is loaded from Numba’s cache. Compiling pays off most for loops that NumPy can’t write as whole arrays. A function that Numba can’t compile is an error, which says why; @ss.jit(nopython=False) runs it as Python instead.

title: Measles in London, three ways
text:
3. Declared, with noise
Each of the four features can also be declared, so that nothing in the model is Python run once a step:

The noise is noise= on the transition of infection: gamma white noise on its rate, as pomp’s rgammawn(), drawn for each step by the chain binomial. Its σ is in the square root of the sim’s unit, here a day, so He et al.’s 0.0878 per square root of a year is multiplied by √365.25.
The school terms, the census and the births are known in advance, so they are time series with a value for each day (ss.timeseries()), worked out once from the same tables: the rate of infection, with the school terms and the population folded in, and the births, with the cohort on day 251. The births are an inflow from ss.unborn, so under the chain binomial the cohort is drawn as a random number around its size rather than added exactly, which at London’s size makes no visible difference.
The measurement model is the likelihood reported() above.


dates = [start + ss.days(d) for d in range(7*1096 + 1)] # Every day of the run
days = np.array([date.day_of_year for date in dates])
pop = np.array([lookup('pop', date) for date in dates])
school = np.array([any(lo <= day <= hi for lo,hi in terms) for day in days])
seas = np.where(school, 1 + pars.amplitude*0.2411/0.7589, 1 - pars.amplitude)
beta = pars.R0*seas*(1 - np.exp(-(pars.gamma + pars.mu)))/pop # Per day, per (I + iota)^alpha
daily_births = pop*np.array([lookup('birthrate', date) for date in dates])*((1 - pars.cohort)/365.25 + pars.cohort*(days == 251)) # Per day, with the cohort on day 251

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.Transition(S, E, rate=ss.perday(ss.timeseries(dates, beta))*(I.n + pars.iota)**pars.alpha, noise=pars.sigma_se*np.sqrt(365.25)), # σ per square root of a day
    latency   = E >> I @ ss.perday(pars.sigma),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.perday(pars.gamma),
    births    = ss.unborn >> S @ ss.perday(ss.timeseries(dates, daily_births)),
    deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.perday(pars.mu)),
    init_n    = dict(S=round(pars.s0*pop[0]), E=round(pars.e0*pop[0]), I=round(pars.i0*pop[0])),
    name      = 'measles',
)
declared = ss.Sim(measles, solver=ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1), total_pop=pop[0], start=start, stop=stop, dt=ss.days(1), data=data, verbose=0)
declared.init()
ss.fitting.ParticleFilter.reason(declared) # Why the filter can't run the sim: None, since the kernels run it whole

substeps=1 takes each day whole, with a chance of 1 − exp(−rate·dt) on every exit, as He et al.’s Euler-multinomial step does. declared.describe() shows the noise under the transition of infection. Starsim’s particle filter, ss.fitting.ParticleFilter, takes the sim and the likelihood, and gives an estimate of the log-likelihood for a number of particles and a seed:

filt = ss.fitting.ParticleFilter(declared, likelihood=dict(recovery=reported))
print(f'Log-likelihood: {filt(n_particles=200, rand_seed=0):,.1f}')

Log-likelihood: -5,910.4


The filter runs many copies of the model (the particles) and, at each week of data, weights each by how likely the reported cases are under it, then draws the copies again in proportion to their weights, so that those that have drifted from the data are dropped. That is with 200 particles, to keep this page quick. With so few, the estimate is noisy, and tends to be too low: the filter’s estimate of the likelihood is unbiased, but the log of it is biased downward, more so with fewer particles. With 2,000 particles, ten filters give −5,816.7 ± 11.5, against −5,827.4 from pomp, the R package He et al. used; without the noise, they give about −13,000, so the noise is what lets the published values fit. It is the filter that sim.fit() uses for IF2 (method='if2') and particle MCMC (method='pmcmc'), so the declared model can be fitted with them: give a rate to fit bounds, e.g. I >> R @ ss.par(ss.perday(pars.gamma), bounds=[0.05, 0.12]) (here R0 and the school terms are folded into the time series, so they stay fixed). The noise is drawn only by the chain binomial: the ODE leaves it out (and says so), and the other solvers refuse it.

title: Beyond disease
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
Starsim is built for infectious diseases, but its machinery for agents is general: a population of agents, each with properties kept as arrays over all of them; modules that change those properties at each step; results recorded over time; and random numbers drawn so that runs can be repeated and compared. A module written as code can hold any property of people and any rule for changing it, so Starsim can run agent-based models with no disease at all. This page shows two classic ones: a model of wealth, from economics, and a model of flocking birds, from computer graphics.
Not every model of something other than an infection needs code. States and transitions describe any process in which people move between categories at given rates (smoking, use of contraception, stages of a chronic disease, employment), and a declared model of such a process runs under every solver, with the same interventions as a disease: see Diseases. Some models track things that are not people at all, such as bacteria in water or a population of mosquitoes, as states with people=False in the same model as the people (see Cholera with a water reservoir).

title: Beyond disease
text:
Wealth
This is the “wealth model” of the Mesa tutorial: each person starts with one unit of wealth, and gives one unit at a time to someone chosen at random. Though the rule is fair, wealth ends up very unequal. Here each person who has any gives with a chance of 1 in 10 at each step, so that inequality builds up over steps rather than all in the first.








Parameter
Value
Meaning




People
1,000



Starting wealth
1 unit
The same for everyone


Giving
1 unit
With a chance of 0.1 a step, from each person who has any, to someone chosen at random


Steps
100




Each person’s wealth is a state, and who gives and to whom are drawn from Starsim distributions, so that runs can be repeated and compared (see Random numbers). The Gini coefficient (0 if everyone has the same, near 1 if one person has everything) is a result:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

class Wealth(ss.Module):
    """ Each person starts with 1 unit of wealth; each step, a tenth of those with any give 1 unit to someone chosen at random """

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            p_give = ss.bernoulli(p=0.1), # The chance that a person who has any wealth gives a unit in a step
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('wealth', default=1.0, label='Wealth'),
        )
        self.recipient = ss.randint(low=0, high=lambda self, sim, uids: len(sim.people)) # Whom each giver gives to: a position, the same as a UID only since nobody is born or dies here
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('gini', label='Gini coefficient', kind='ratio'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        givers = self.pars.p_give.filter((self.wealth > 0).uids)
        recipients = self.recipient.rvs(givers)
        self.wealth[givers] = self.wealth[givers] - 1
        self.wealth[:] = self.wealth + np.bincount(recipients, minlength=len(self.wealth)) # Each recipient gets 1 unit for each giver who chose them
        return

    def record_states(self): # The state at the start of each step
        super().record_states()
        w = np.sort(self.wealth.values)
        n = len(w)
        self.results.gini[self.ti] = np.sum((2*np.arange(1, n+1) - n - 1)*w)/(n*w.sum())
        return


sim = ss.Sim(Wealth(), n_agents=1000, stop=100) # 100 steps
sim.run()
sim.results.wealth.gini.plot()

Sim: wealth, as 1,000 agents, steps 0 to 100


  Done in 0.024 s









Inequality rises over the first 10 or so steps, and then stays high, with a Gini coefficient of about 0.65, close to that of the most unequal countries. The final distribution has many people with nothing and a few with several units:

wealth = sim.people.wealth.wealth
plt.figure()
plt.hist(wealth.values, bins=np.arange(wealth.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Wealth')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.show()








Compared with Mesa, where each agent is an object with its own step(), Starsim keeps each property as one array over all people, so a rule is applied to everyone at once, as operations on arrays.

title: Beyond disease
text:
Flocking
Boids are the classic model of flocking, in which each bird follows three simple rules about the birds it can see: alignment (steer towards their average heading), cohesion (steer towards their center), and separation (steer away from any that are too close). No bird leads, and nobody tells the flock where to go, but flocks form and fly together.








Parameter
Value
Meaning




Boids
200



Sight
0.1
How far a boid can see, in a world that is a unit square


Too close
0.03
The distance within which a boid steers away


Alignment, cohesion, separation
0.1, 0.005, 3 × 10⁻⁵
How strongly each rule steers


Speed
0.005 to 0.01
The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step


Steps
200




In Starsim, each boid’s position (x, y) and velocity (vx, vy) are states, starting at random. The world is a unit square whose edges wrap around, so a boid leaving on the right comes back on the left. At each step, the module works out the offset from every boid to every other (the short way round), applies the three rules to all the boids at once, keeps each boid’s speed between a minimum and a maximum, and moves them. How well the flock is aligned is a result: for each boid, the length of the average heading of those it can see (itself included), averaged over all boids, which is 1 when each moves with its neighbors and close to 0 when their headings are random:

class Boids(ss.Module):
    """ Flocking: each boid steers towards the heading and center of the boids it can see, and away from those too close """

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            radius     = 0.1,    # How far a boid can see (the world is a unit square)
            too_close  = 0.03,   # How close is too close
            alignment  = 0.1,    # How strongly a boid steers towards its neighbors' heading
            cohesion   = 0.005,  # ... towards its neighbors' center
            separation = 3e-5,   # ... away from those too close
            speed      = [0.005, 0.01], # The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(
            ss.FloatArr('x',  default=ss.random(), label='Position (x)'),
            ss.FloatArr('y',  default=ss.random(), label='Position (y)'),
            ss.FloatArr('vx', default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (x)'),
            ss.FloatArr('vy', default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (y)'),
        )
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('aligned', label='Alignment with neighbors', kind='ratio'))
        return

    def offsets(self):
        """ The offsets from each boid to every other, the short way round the edges, and the distances """
        x, y = self.x.values, self.y.values
        dx = x[None, :] - x[:, None]
        dy = y[None, :] - y[:, None]
        dx -= np.round(dx)
        dy -= np.round(dy)
        return dx, dy, np.hypot(dx, dy)

    def step(self):
        p = self.pars
        vx, vy = self.vx.values, self.vy.values
        dx, dy, dist = self.offsets()
        np.fill_diagonal(dist, np.inf) # A boid is not its own neighbor
        near = dist < p.radius
        n_near = np.maximum(near.sum(axis=1), 1)
        close = dist < p.too_close

        # The three rules, for all the boids at once
        steer_x = p.alignment*(near @ vx / n_near - vx) + p.cohesion*(near*dx).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dx/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        steer_y = p.alignment*(near @ vy / n_near - vy) + p.cohesion*(near*dy).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dy/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        alone = ~near.any(axis=1) # A boid that sees nobody flies straight on
        vx = vx + np.where(alone, 0, steer_x)
        vy = vy + np.where(alone, 0, steer_y)

        # Keep the speed within limits, then move, wrapping around the edges
        speed = np.hypot(vx, vy)
        factor = np.clip(speed, *p.speed)/speed
        self.vx[:] = vx*factor
        self.vy[:] = vy*factor
        self.x[:] = (self.x + self.vx) % 1
        self.y[:] = (self.y + self.vy) % 1
        return

    def record_states(self): # The state at the start of each step
        super().record_states()
        speed = np.hypot(self.vx.values, self.vy.values)
        hx, hy = self.vx.values/speed, self.vy.values/speed # Each boid's heading
        _, _, dist = self.offsets()
        sees = dist < self.pars.radius # Including itself
        self.results.aligned[self.ti] = (np.hypot(sees @ hx, sees @ hy)/sees.sum(axis=1)).mean()
        return

The rule of alignment is what makes a flock: without it, boids still gather and keep their distance, but each flies its own way. Here 200 boids fly for 200 steps, with and without it:

scenarios = {
    'Flocking': ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200),
    'No alignment': ss.Sim(Boids(alignment=0), n_agents=200, stop=200),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
msim.plot('boids.aligned')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Flocking, No alignment)
  Done in 0.55 s









With alignment, most boids are moving with their neighbors within about 50 steps, and nearly all within 100; without it, their headings stay about as random as at the start.
The positions and velocities are states, so the flock can be drawn at any point in a run. Here the sim runs in stages (run(until=...) runs up to a given step, and the next call carries on from there), keeping the boids’ positions and headings every 3 steps, and then plays them back as an animation, with each boid as an arrow along its heading (the plotting code is folded; click to show it):


The code for the animation
from matplotlib import animation
from IPython.display import HTML

sim = ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200)
sim.init()
boids = sim.custom.boids # The module is given as `custom`: any module that is not a disease, network, demographic module, intervention, analyzer, or connector
frames = []
for step in range(0, 201, 3):
    sim.run(until=step)
    frames.append([state.values.copy() for state in [boids.x, boids.y, boids.vx, boids.vy]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4), dpi=72)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xticks=[], yticks=[], aspect='equal')
arrows = ax.quiver(*frames[0], angles='xy', scale_units='xy', scale=0.25, width=0.005, pivot='mid')

def draw(i):
    x, y, vx, vy = frames[i]
    arrows.set_offsets(np.c_[x, y])
    arrows.set_UVC(vx, vy)
    ax.set_title(f'Step {3*i}')

anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, draw, frames=len(frames), interval=100)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(anim.to_jshtml(default_mode='loop'))

From random headings at the start, groups form within a few dozen steps, and by the end the boids fly as a few large flocks (which wrap around the edges of the square), with space between their members.
As in the wealth model, each rule is applied to every boid at once, as operations on arrays, rather than by looping over the boids. Working out the distance between every pair of boids takes time and memory in proportion to the square of their number, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand; for many more, a spatial index (such as SciPy’s cKDTree) would find each boid’s neighbors faster.
