title: Starsim
text:
Note: Starsim v4 is now available. It’s quite different from v3, with a new and simpler syntax for creating diseases, and support for compartmental and geospatial models. Models written for v3 will need to be migrated; see the changelog for details, or contact us for help. To continue using Starsim v3, use pip install starsim<4; the v3 docs are also still available. But really, please upgrade to v4! You’ll be glad you did!

Starsim is a fast, flexible disease modeling framework, from compartments to agents. It supports modeling multiple co-transmitting diseases, including infectious and non-infectious diseases plus other health states (such as pregnancy and birth), and captures their biological and behavioral interactions. It lets users compare intervention strategies, such as vaccines or treatments, across delivery methods like mass campaigns or targeted outreach. It also includes built-in tools for scenario analyses and calibrating models to real-world data.
Starsim builds on our previous suite of disease-specific models, including Covasim and HPVsim, as well as many other disease modeling frameworks (see below). It can model different levels of detail, including agent-based, metapopulation, and deterministic or stochastic compartmental modeling. It is designed to be simple and fast enough to enable rapid or exploratory analyses (from project start to calibrated model and scenario analyses in hours to days), while also being flexible enough to support complex, long-term research projects (such as intrahost immunity, data-driven spatial network transmission, and health economics optimization).
For more information, see the documentation or the code. For Starsim for R, see r.starsim.org. For Starsim’s AI tools, see ai.starsim.org.


Starsim includes an extensive library of features aimed to support a broad diversity of disease modeling needs. The full set is covered in the documentation. Because the features are modular and written in Python, you can mix-and-match Starsim features with custom-written code, and you only use what you need. Highlights include:

Modeling modalities: Switch between compartmental, stochastic compartmental, metapopulation, and agent-based modeling using a flag (solver='abm') without needing to rewrite any code (solvers);
Performance: Numeric kernels are heavily optimized, with Numba and Rust kernels that give the same numbers, plus GPU support (via JAX) (performance);
Diseases: A large library of already-implemented diseases including COVID, flu, measles, malaria, syphilis, gonorrhea, cholera, Ebola and many others (plus HIV, TB, COVID, HPV, chlamydia, typhoid, and others in the models below); diseases support coinfection between different diseases, as well as multiple strains of a single disease (library diseases, diseases);
Networks: Contact networks including age-stratified contact matrices, sexual (including male-female, male-male, and commercial), respiratory (household/workplace/school); also supports other forms of disease transmission including environmental and vector-borne (networks, library networks);
Interventions: Flexible options for representing interventions, including screening, diagnostics, treatments, vaccination, and care cascades; health system considerations such as prioritization, capacity constraints, and clinic visits (interventions, products);
Costing: Support for intervention- and disease-related costs, health outcomes like disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and budget optimization (costs, optimization);
Time: Unit-aware time and date handling, including natural dates for data and plotting, module-specific timesteps, and timestep-aware conversion of rates and probabilities (time);
Data and places: Extensive built-in data, including population and age structures for 187 countries and territories, contact matrices (Prem et al., 2021), and geospatial boundaries, with maps and animations of results by place (population data, geography);
Fitting: Automatic gradients for compartmental models, plus Bayesian fitting and calibrating algorithms including no-U-turn sampling (NUTS) and the tree-structured Parzen estimator (Optuna) (fitting, methods);
Scientific rigor: Automatic checking of units to prevent common programming errors; common random numbers that allow exact comparison between even stochastic model runs (time, random numbers);
Intercompatibility: Automated import from more than a dozen other disease modeling frameworks, and export to SBML and odin (import and export); interoperable with other disease modeling tools like GeoPops and HubVerse;
AI support: Extensive set of skills and plugins that help implement Starsim models (AI integration), including no-code chat interfaces for policymakers (EpiChat). 

Starsim “stands on the shoulders of giants”, and aims to build on the best aspects of other disease modeling frameworks. It is especially indebted to EpiModel, MEmilio, SimInf, summer2, camdl, epidemics, and epydemix (see the full list). If there’s a feature you think Starsim should support, please get in touch.



Starsim is the basis of several other established disease modeling frameworks. These include:

Covasim, for modeling COVID-19;
HPVsim, for modeling human papillomavirus and cervical cancer;
STIsim, for modeling HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis, and bacterial vaginosis (including co-transmission);
TBsim, for modeling tuberculosis, including drug resistance;
FPsim, for modeling family planning and women’s life courses.
Typhoidsim, for modeling typhoid, including environmental transmission.

A full list of diseases modeled using Starsim is available in the documentation.



If you’re new to Python, check out our getting started guide. You can also use our installer, which will install Python along with all required dependencies. On Linux and macOS, run:
curl -LsSf https://docs.starsim.org/install.sh | sh
On Windows, download install.bat and double-click it.


Python 3.12-3.14 or R.
We recommend, but do not require, installing Starsim in a virtual environment, such as uv or conda.



Starsim is most easily installed via PyPI:
pip install "starsim[jax]"
starsim init
JAX is recommended if you’ll be calibrating compartmental models – otherwise you can skip it, i.e. pip install starsim.
starsim init compiles numeric kernels if needed (usually it’s not). It also asks if you want to install Starsim’s AI skills (so you can type /starsim in your agent to use them). To do either the compile or the AI install, run starsim init compile or starsim init ai.
You can also of course install with uv:
uv init example
cd example
uv add "starsim[jax]"
To work on Starsim itself, clone this repository, then run:
pip install -e .
starsim init dev
This installs the optional dependencies for testing and documentation, and JAX; installs Rust if it is missing; and builds Starsim’s kernels. See the developer guide for details.



R-Starsim can be installed with:
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("starsimhub/rstarsim")
library(starsim)
init_starsim()
See r.starsim.org for more information.




Full documentation, including tutorials and an API reference, is available at docs.starsim.org.



You can run a simple demo via:
import starsim as ss
ss.demo()
Here’s a minimal SIR model, with an infection rate of β = 0.3 per day and an infectious period of 10 days, written much as you’d write it on paper:
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R') # Create the SIR states
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I # From S to I, at a rate of β times the fraction infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10) # From I to R, after 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery) # Create the disease from the transitions

sim = ss.Sim(sir)
sim.run()
sim.sir.plot()
 
The same model, written out in full:
import starsim as ss

S = ss.State(label='Susceptible')
I = ss.State(label='Infectious')
R = ss.State(name='Recovered')
beta = ss.perday(0.3)
dur_inf = ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10))
sir = ss.Disease(
    name = 'SIR',
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=beta*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=dur_inf, name='recovery'),
    ],
)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=sir, solver='ode')
sim.run()
sim.plot()
These run as a compartmental model (an ODE). To run the same model as agents, give the number of agents, e.g. ss.Sim(sir, n_agents=5_000).
You can also run the same example from R:
library(starsim)

states("S I R")
sir <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 0.3 * I), # From S to I, at a rate of β times the fraction infectious
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(10))  # From I to R, after 10 days on average
)

sim <- Sim(sir)
sim$run()
sim$plot()
More usage examples are available in the tutorials and user guide.



Starsim comes with skills for AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, and others), which always match the version installed: how to write, check, and run a model, and how to import a model from another framework or upgrade one from Starsim v3. starsim init ai links them into your project, and starsim ai install --global sets them up for all your projects instead. You can also install them with other standard tools, such as uvx library-skills. starsim ai "how would I model a leaky vaccine?" asks your agent a question about Starsim (-i for an interactive session), and starsim help RandomNet looks a name or term up in the docs, without an agent. For anything else, llms.txt is a map of the docs and the API for agents.



We welcome contributions of all kinds! Questions or comments can be directed to info@starsim.org , or on this project’s GitHub page. Full information about Starsim is provided in the documentation.



We believe in being transparent about AI use. Each page comes with a little note estimating the human vs. AI contribution; hover to get more info. For this page:
Authorship: 🧠90%, 🤖10%

The tour builds one epidemic model, from a first run to a fitted forecast, in ten minutes. The tutorials then teach Starsim step by step, through one measles model.


Look up a topic
The user guide covers each topic in full, from writing models to fitting them; the API has every class and function.

The gallery has complete models, each with its diagram, code, and result, to copy and change.

title: Gradients
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
For a deterministic model, run as an ODE, Starsim can work out the gradient: how each result changes as each parameter changes. It does this by automatic differentiation with JAX, which follows the calculation of the run step by step. Gradients make it possible to fit many parameters quickly, to draw from a posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS), and to see which parts of the epidemic a parameter affects.
This page assumes the basics of Fitting a model. Gradients need JAX (pip install "starsim[jax]") and a model whose whole run JAX can follow: a rate that calls a Python function, a module written as code, or a movement register rules this out. The fit says why when it can’t use gradients, and ss.solvers.why_not(sim, 'jax') says so for any sim (see Solvers). JAX runs on the CPU unless ss.options.jax says otherwise: for these runs, a GPU is several times slower.

title: Gradients
text:
The gradient of a result
The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune, with two unknowns, the transmission rate beta and the fraction of cases reported report, and a Poisson likelihood. The data are a year of weekly cases from a run with beta = 1.9 and report = 0.5:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])  # Transmission rate per day
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1]) # Fraction of cases reported

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson())
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0034 s; measles: 5,858 infections; at most 298 infectious, on 2025-08-05


sim.gradient() gives the derivative of each result, at each time, with respect to each parameter with bounds, at the parameters’ current values. Here, at the true values, for the daily reported cases:

grad = truth.gradient('cases')

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
t = truth.results.timevec
ax.plot(t, grad.beta.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of beta')
ax.plot(t, grad.report.measles.cases, label='Change in daily cases per unit of report')
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
ax.legend();

  Compiling the run with JAX, estimated time: 0.2-5 s
  Compiled the run with JAX in 0.2 s
  Compiling the gradient with JAX, estimated time: 0.2-5 s
  Compiled the gradient with JAX in 1.2 s









The result is indexed by parameter, then module, then result: grad.beta.measles.cases is an array with one value per time step. Two parameters whose gradients have the same shape can only be fitted as a combination (see Fit diagnostics).
sim.gradient() also takes a function of the run sim that returns a number or an array, e.g. a total cost:

total = lambda sim: sim.results.measles.cases.sum()
truth.gradient(total)

sc.obj(beta=3064.6101185993757, report=5827.7149074910985)



Many values
A parameter with a value for each level of a stratification (ss.par(ss.by(patch=[...]), bounds=...)), an array, or a time series has a gradient for each value, named as a fit names them. A time series fitted value by value is a way to estimate a transmission rate that changes in time, with no shape assumed for it. Here the data come from an outbreak whose transmission rate fell by about a third over June (as it might when schools close for the summer), and the rate is fitted as a value every four weeks, with straight lines between them:

start = ss.date(pars['start'])
true_beta = ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-05-31': 1.9, '2025-06-30': 1.2}, 'linear') # 1.9 until the end of May, then falling to 1.2 by the end of June
dates = [start + ss.days(d) for d in range(0, 365, 28)] # A value every four weeks, in between which it changes linearly
beta = ss.par(ss.timeseries(dates, [1.5]*len(dates), 'linear'), bounds=[0.5, 4])

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
onset = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # The fraction reported, taken as known here
measles_t = ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
truth_t = ss.Sim(measles_t, pars=dict(beta=true_beta), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars).run()
data_t = truth_t.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

smooth = lambda pars: 100*np.sum(np.diff(pars['beta'].values)**2) # Large changes from one value to the next are unlikely
fit_t = ss.Sim(measles_t, data=data_t, **pars).fit(penalty=smooth, verbose=False)

days = lambda times: [(ss.date(t) - start).days for t in times] # Days since the start
t = np.arange(365)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, np.interp(t, days(true_beta.times), true_beta.values), 'k--', label='True')
ax.plot(days(fit_t.pars.beta.times), fit_t.pars.beta.values, 'o-', label='Fitted')
ax.set_xlabel('Days since 1 January 2025')
ax.set_ylabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)

The penalty (penalty=) keeps each value close to its neighbors: a larger one gives a smoother curve that is slower to follow a change, and a smaller one a curve that follows the noise. With many values, the gradient takes one pass in reverse mode, whatever their number.

title: Gradients
text:
The log-density
sim.log_density() gives the log of the posterior density of the fitted parameters (the log-likelihood of the data, plus the log of the priors), as a function of their values, together with its gradient. It is what a sampler or optimizer of your own would use. Besides calling it (density(x)) and its gradient (density.grad(x)), density.fn is the function itself, to compose with JAX (jax.vmap, jax.hessian, …), and density.run(x) gives the number in each state at each time at those values:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
density = sim.log_density()
print('Parameters:', density.names)
print('At the starting values:', density.x0)
print('Log-density:', density(density.x0))
print('Its gradient:', density.grad(density.x0))

Parameters: ['beta', 'report']
At the starting values: [1.5 0.3]

  Compiled the log-density with JAX in 0.3 s
Log-density: -4060.865915627085
Its gradient: [17589.42561341  8142.6806164 ]


The same log-density is what L-BFGS-B and NUTS use in a fit with a likelihood. Initial numbers, branching fractions, and inflows that depend on fitted parameters need to be linear in them; if not, building the log-density is an error that names them, and require_jax=False takes the gradients with Python in the loop instead.

title: Gradients
text:
Fitting with gradients

A best fit with gradients
sim.fit() uses the gradient by default ('l-bfgs-b') when a deterministic model has three or more fitted parameters; with one or two, Nelder–Mead is faster. Either can be asked for:

fit = sim.fit(method='l-bfgs-b')
fit.table

With a likelihood for every series, this is the maximum likelihood estimate (with priors, the most probable values).


A posterior with NUTS
A posterior is the whole distribution of values consistent with the data. method='nuts' draws from it, given a likelihood for every data series, with each parameter’s prior=, or a uniform prior over its bounds:

post = sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method('nuts', warmup=100, draws=200)) # Fewer draws than the default, to run quickly
post.summarize();

Each chain starts near one of the best points of a scan, spends warmup= draws tuning itself (these are discarded), and then draws until the chains agree, with enough effective draws of each parameter (see Fitting methods). The table gives each parameter’s median and 95% interval, with R-hat and the effective sample size; Fit diagnostics says how to read them.
The draws themselves are in post.samples, one row for each:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(post.samples.beta, post.samples.report, s=5, alpha=0.5)
ax.scatter(1.9, 0.5, marker='x', s=100, color='red', label='True values')
ax.set_xlabel('beta (per day)')
ax.set_ylabel('report')
ax.legend();








This posterior is narrow because the data were made by this very ODE with Poisson noise. Real counts vary more, and real outbreaks have chance in transmission that an ODE leaves out, so a Poisson likelihood would give a posterior just as narrow, and wrong (see Fitting methods). A negative binomial likelihood with its dispersion fitted widens it to match the data, as in T6; for chance in transmission, use a stochastic model and method='pmcmc'.


Profile likelihoods
A profile likelihood gives a confidence interval for one parameter, without priors: at each value of it, the others are refitted, and the values whose negative log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the lowest form the 95% interval. A profile that stays flat up to a bound means the data don’t determine the parameter.

prof = ss.fitting.profile(sim, 'beta', values=np.linspace(1.86, 1.94, 9))
print('Best value of beta:', round(prof.best, 3))
print('95% confidence interval:', np.round(prof.interval, 3))

Projecting from a posterior
fit.project() runs each scenario once for each of n_runs draws from the posterior, with the same draws in every scenario, so the spread of the runs carries the uncertainty in the fitted values. Here, a catch-up campaign on 1 April, compared with none:

Other samplers
For stochastic models, and models JAX can’t run, the other methods apply: 'pmcmc', 'abc-smc', and 'if2' (see Fitting methods). Starsim’s samplers can also be used directly on a log-density of your own (such as density above): ss.fitting.nuts(), ss.fitting.pmmh(), and ss.fitting.abc_smc(); see ss.fitting. A posterior can also be put together by sampling-importance resampling (SIR, not to be confused with SIR): run draws from the priors (ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=1000)), score each with ss.fitting.loglik(run), and resample in proportion to the likelihoods; it works for any model, but needs many runs, and fails for many parameters.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
sim.fit() always returns values. Whether to trust them has several parts: does the model match the data, did the search find the best values, do the data determine the values, and does the fitted model predict data it hasn’t seen? This page goes through the checks in that order. It assumes the basics of Fitting a model.
The examples use a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000, 90% of whom are immune. The data are a year of weekly reported cases, made from an SEIR model with a latent period of 10 days, beta = 1.9, and half of all cases reported:
import starsim as ss

def make_seir():
    """ Measles with a latent period: infected (E), then infectious (I) about 10 days later """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    onset  = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    cases  = ss.outcome(report*onset)
    return ss.Disease(S >> E @ beta*I, onset, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
truth = ss.Sim(make_seir(), pars=dict(beta=1.9, report=0.5), rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Does the model match the data?
text:
Does the model match the data?
Start by looking: a fit can converge perfectly and still be wrong, if the model can’t produce the pattern in the data. Here the data are fitted with a model that leaves out the latent period, an SIR model:

def make_sir():
    """ Measles without a latent period: infectious as soon as infected """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    beta   = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])
    report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    cases     = ss.outcome(report*infection)
    return ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9), name='measles')

sir_fit = ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars).fit()

Searching on a log scale: report
Fitting by nelder-mead (2 fitted parameters, for which it is faster than gradients; override with method=)
Converged: the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 0.00038 of each other (objective values 0.3834 at beta=1.434, report=1; 0.3834 at beta=1.434, report=1; 0.3834 at beta=1.434, report=1; 199 evaluations)
The loss is 0.3834 at the best values and 0.6956 at the initial values

the best-fit value of "report" (1) is at one of its bounds [0.05, 1]; consider widening them



fit.plot(residuals=True) shows the model against the data, and below it the residuals (data minus model) on the data’s own weeks:

sir_fit.plot(residuals=True)








The residuals have a pattern, and the fraction reported is pushed to its bound of 1: the model is wrong. For the right model, they wander above and below zero at random:

seir_fit = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars).fit(verbose=False)
seir_fit.plot(residuals=True)








A pattern in the residuals points to the structure of the model, or to how the data were defined, and no search will fix it. Some common patterns, and what to look at first:







Pattern
Things to examine




The peak consistently too early or too late
The initial infections and when they are introduced; the latent period; reporting delays


The right shape but the wrong size
The population size; the fraction reported; whether the data count events (a flow) or people at a time (a stock)


A best value at a bound
The bounds; a missing process that the parameter is making up for; weak identification


Different starts giving different answers
Several optima, too short a search, a noisy objective


A good fit but an unstable projection
Parameters the data can’t tell apart; a change in the epidemic the model doesn’t have



Also check that like is compared with like: incidence with case counts over the same interval, prevalence with a survey at a time, admissions with admissions rather than beds occupied, and dates aligned (see The data). fit.objective compares fits to the same data, but the plot shows where a model fails.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Did the search converge?
Every fit says whether it converged, and how it decided, in fit.converged and fit.why, which are also printed:

print(seir_fit.converged)
print(seir_fit.why)

True
the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 9.5e-05 of each other (objective values 0.09543 at beta=1.9, report=0.4832; 0.09543 at beta=1.9, report=0.4832; 0.09544 at beta=1.9, report=0.4833; 275 evaluations)


What “converged” means depends on the method (see the appendix). A fit that has not converged is not necessarily wrong, but can’t be trusted until it has been run longer, or the reason is understood. A fit that has converged has passed its method’s check, which is evidence, not proof, that it found the best fit or the whole posterior: a search can settle on a local best, and chains can agree while all missing the same region.

A best value at a bound
A best value at the edge of its bounds gives an AtBound warning, as for the SIR model above. It means one of three things: the true value is beyond the bound (widen it, if such values are plausible); the data don’t determine the parameter (see below); or the model is missing something, and the parameter is making up for it, as the reporting fraction was above.


The same answer again
A stochastic model is fitted to noisy scores, so a second fit, with another rand_seed=, shows how much the answer depends on chance:

import pandas as pd

stochastic = ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
rows = []
for seed in [1, 2]:
    fit = stochastic.fit(rand_seed=seed, verbose=False, method=ss.fitting.method('optuna', n_trials=100))
    rows.append(dict(rand_seed=seed, beta=fit.pars.beta, report=fit.pars.report, converged=fit.converged))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)

If the fits differ by more than matters, use more trials, more runs per trial (n_runs=), or a likelihood, with which Optuna scores each trial by a particle filter rather than by runs. For a deterministic model, more starting points (scan=) do the same job. Check a stochastic fit against many runs, ss.parallel(fit.sim, n_runs=20), not one, as in Fitting a model.


The time step
A model run as agents, or as a chain binomial with ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1), takes infection a step at a time, and when its rates are fast compared with the step, the step changes the fitted values (the chain binomial’s default substeps keep this small) (see Solvers and backends). fit.sim.check_dt() reruns the fitted sim with half the step and shows how much each result changes; if more than the mismatch of the fit, fit again with the smaller step.


A posterior
For a posterior by NUTS or particle MCMC, fit.summarize() gives two checks for each parameter (ABC-SMC’s has the effective sample size only):

R-hat (rhat) compares the spread within each chain with that between chains. Above 1.01, the chains disagree, and the posterior is not yet reliable.
Effective sample size (ess) is how many independent draws the correlated draws are worth. A few hundred is usually enough for a median and a rough 95% interval; the ends of an interval, or a more precise one, need more.

NUTS also counts divergent draws (fit.diagnostics.divergences), where the sampler’s path went wrong; even a few mean the posterior may be missing a region. If any check fails, the fit warns (ss.errors.NotConverged). More warm-up (warmup=) sometimes fixes it, but a common cause is a ridge (see below): then fix a parameter that is known from elsewhere, or get more data.


Looking at the search
For any method, fit.to_df() has every evaluation, for plots of your own (there is one below). For Optuna, fit.study takes Optuna’s plots (these need Plotly): how the best score improved (has it leveled off?), which parameters mattered most, and the score over a pair of parameters (a long diagonal valley is a ridge):
import optuna
optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(fit.study)
optuna.visualization.plot_contour(fit.study, params=['beta', 'report'])

title: Fit diagnostics
section: Can the data tell the parameters apart?
text:
Can the data tell the parameters apart?
A parameter is identifiable if the data determine its value. This fails in two ways:

Structurally: the model can’t tell two parameters apart, whatever the data, e.g. when transmission depends only on the product of contacts and the chance of infection per contact.
Practically: these data can’t, because there is too little of it, it is too noisy, or it doesn’t cover the part of the epidemic that would show the difference.

A practical check is to fit data made from the model with known values, as this page does. If the fit doesn’t recover them, it is unlikely to recover the truth from real data. If it does, that is evidence for those values and data like these, not a proof of identifiability: other values, or other data, can behave differently. Starsim also notes when two parameters appear in the model only multiplied together (e.g. contacts*p_infect*I), so that the data determine only their product: fit one and fix the other, or make their product one parameter. For a posterior, it notes parameters that are almost perfectly correlated.

Recovering known values
The SEIR model, now with three unknowns, beta, the infectious period dur_inf, and report, and a Poisson likelihood, fitted to data from a run with beta = 1.9, dur_inf = 8 days, and report = 0.5:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta    = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])             # Transmission rate per day
dur_inf = ss.par(ss.days(6), bounds=[3, 15])       # Infectious period, in days
report  = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])            # Fraction of cases reported

infection = S >> E @ beta*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ dur_inf
cases     = ss.outcome(report*onset, likelihood=ss.poisson())
measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, init=dict(I=0.0001, R=0.9))
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

true_values = dict(beta=1.9, dur_inf=ss.days(8), report=0.5)
truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=true_values, rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
weekly = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=weekly, **pars)
fit = sim.fit()
table = fit.table.copy()
table['true'] = [1.9, 8, 0.5]
table

Which combinations the data determine
A best fit is a single point; it doesn’t show how far the values could move and still fit nearly as well. Optuna spreads its trials widely before it narrows down, and each is kept, with its score, in fit.to_df(), so plotting beta against dur_inf for each trial shows the shape of the fit:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

search = sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method('optuna', n_trials=300), rand_seed=1, verbose=False)
trials = search.to_df()

worse = np.log10(1 + trials.objective - trials.objective.min()) # 0 at the best trial
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
points = ax.scatter(trials.beta, trials.dur_inf, c=worse, cmap='viridis_r', s=15)

ax.set_ylabel('dur_inf (days)')

ax.set_ylim(3, 15)

Less data, and fixing what is known

The spread of the estimates is how precisely one outbreak of this size can determine the parameters. An ODE’s posterior is much narrower, and can exclude the truth (see Fitting methods). To run the model at draws from the priors, for a Bayesian workflow of your own, use ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=200); the profile likelihood, which shows how well the data determine one parameter, is in Gradients.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Does the model predict?
A model with more parameters usually fits better without being better. A fairer test is how well a model fitted to the start of the data predicts the rest. ss.fitting.compare_models() fits each model to the data before a cut, runs it forward, and scores it on the part held out (by default the last 25% of each series; here holdout= gives dates two months and one month before the peak):

models = {'SIR': ss.Sim(make_sir(), data=data, **pars), 'SEIR': ss.Sim(make_seir(), data=data, **pars)}
for cut in ['2025-06-01', '2025-07-01']:
    comparison = ss.fitting.compare_models(models, method='nelder-mead', holdout=cut, verbose=False)
    comparison.summarize()

held out: from 2025-06-01 (cases: 2025-06-04 to 2025-12-24)
fit error and prediction error are the normalized absolute error, on the data fitted to and on the held-out data (lower is better)
held out: from 2025-07-01 (cases: 2025-07-02 to 2025-12-24)
fit error and prediction error are the normalized absolute error, on the data fitted to and on the held-out data (lower is better)


A stochastic model is scored over many runs at its best values (n_runs=, 100 by default), which is harsher than on an ODE. folds= repeats the comparison over several cut points, and comparison.plot() shows each model’s fit and prediction.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
A checklist



Check
How
A problem looks like
What to do




The model matches the data
fit.plot(residuals=True)
A pattern in the residuals; a parameter pushed to a bound
Change the model, or how the data are matched to it


The search converged
fit.converged, fit.why
“Not converged”, with the reason
Run longer (see the appendix)


No value is at a bound
The AtBound warning
A best value at the edge
Widen the bounds only if such values are plausible


The answer is stable
Fit again with another rand_seed= or scan=
Different values each time
More trials, runs, or particles; a likelihood


The parameters are identifiable
Recover known values; the notes that parameters appear only together or are correlated
Values far from the truth; a ridge
Fix one parameter from other evidence, or get more data, or data of another kind


The posterior is reliable
rhat, ess, divergences
R-hat above 1.01, few effective draws, any divergences
More warm-up and draws; check identifiability


The model predicts
ss.fitting.compare_models()
A model that fits well but predicts badly
A simpler model, or more data


The fit is plausible
Compare with what is known from elsewhere
A reporting fraction above 1, an infectious period of months
Rethink the model



The last check matters most, and no software can make it: whether the values, and the model, make sense for the disease and the setting is a judgment for the modeler.
When reporting a fit, say what each data series is and how it was matched to the model; the measure of fit or likelihood; the parameters fitted, with bounds and priors, and those fixed and why; the method, its settings, and the seed; the diagnostics above; and the versions of Starsim and the data.

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Further reading

Stan: Posterior predictive checks: checking a fitted model against data it should reproduce
Optuna: Visualization: the plots of a search that fit.study takes
ArviZ: R-hat, effective sample size, and plots for checking a posterior
pomp: Getting started: diagnostics of fits of stochastic models, including iterated filtering and profiles
Stan: Problematic posteriors: ridges and non-identified parameters in a posterior, and what to do about them

title: Fit diagnostics
text:
Appendix

When each method has converged
The rule by which each method sets fit.converged (and says why in fit.why), and what to try if it hasn’t:








Method
Converged when
If not




SciPy optimizers ('nelder-mead', 'powell', 'l-bfgs-b', 'slsqp')
The two best searches, from the best few points of a scan that are apart, end at the same value (with a single search, SciPy’s own stopping rule)
More starting points (scan=) or searches (restarts=), or more iterations (maxiter=); a sign of several local optima, or a ridge


Optuna ('optuna')
The best score improved by less than 1% over the last quarter of the trials, and the best trial is not one of the first 10 (which are random) or the starting values
More trials (n_trials=)


Iterated filtering ('if2')
Chains from different starts end within 2 of the best log-likelihood
More passes (iterations=) or particles (particles=); better bounds, if a chain has wandered off where the outbreak dies out


NUTS ('nuts')
The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01) and no draws diverged
More warm-up (warmup=); a higher max_draws=; check identifiability


Particle MCMC ('pmcmc')
The chains agree (R-hat at most 1.01)
More draws and warm-up; more particles, if the acceptance is low


ABC-SMC ('abc-smc')
Not assessed (fit.converged is None): no rule says when its final tolerance is close enough; fit.why and fit.diagnostics give it
More generations (generations=) or samples (samples=); with a likelihood, 'pmcmc'


A list of methods
Its last stage converged; a stage that doesn’t stops the list, with a warning, and its fit (or the last that converged) is returned
Make that stage converge, by its own rule



A best fit of a stochastic model is also marked as not converged if, rerun with the same seeds, its best values score worse than the starting values.


Other warnings and notes
The messages a fit can give that are not covered above. Warnings are Python warnings (some of a class of their own, which warnings.filterwarnings() can select); notes are printed, and are silenced with verbose=False.









Message
Kind
Means
What to do




The profile stays within the threshold up to a bound
Warning, ss.errors.AtBound
A profile likelihood’s interval may extend beyond the bounds
Wider bounds, or more values


The scan tries fewer than 10 points for each parameter
Note
With more than 10 parameters, the scan is capped at 100 points
scan= to change it


The fit would take the gradients (or the posterior) with Python in the loop
Error, ss.CapabilityError
A method with gradients was asked for, but something in the model or likelihood can’t be run in JAX (e.g. a likelihood given as a function, or an initial value that is not linear in the fitted parameters)
A method without gradients (e.g. 'nelder-mead', or no method=), or require_jax=False to accept the slower way


A data column matches no result
Note when the sim is initialized, and an error when it is fitted
A typo in a header, or a result that doesn’t exist
Rename the column (ss.SimData(aliases=...))

title: People and demographics
text:
🧠8% 🤖92%
Every model has a population: its size, the ages and sex of its people, and anything else about them the model needs. Over years, births, deaths, and aging change it.
This page covers the population at the start, births and deaths, pregnancy, and, for a model run as agents, the People object. How agents are kept in arrays and indexed is in Array indexing, who meets whom in Mixing, and the data by place that comes with Starsim in Places and data.
The examples use the measles model from the tutorials:
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I # β = 1.9 per day (typed, beside annual demographics)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

title: People and demographics
text:
The population at the start

How many people
total_pop= is the number of people in the population. A model run as compartments needs nothing else:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0029 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


As agents, n_agents= is the number of agents. Given both, each agent stands for total_pop/n_agents people, here 10, and results are given in people, not agents:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.046 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 77,040 infectious, on day 9









Without either, a model has 10,000 people. Fewer agents than people make a model faster, but add noise from chance; see Branching and rescaling.


Ages and sex
As agents, each person has an age and a sex. By default, agents have the ages of the world’s population in 2024, and an even chance of being female (ss.People(n_agents, p_female=0.49) for another fraction). A compartmental model split into age groups without a fraction for each takes the fractions from the same ages, and describe() marks them as guessed.
The population of a country is ss.population(): its size, its ages, and the fraction of women, from the UN World Population Prospects (see Places and data). The sim takes its size from it, under any solver:

kenya = ss.population('Kenya', year=2024)
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(kenya.named.total))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.population('Kenya', year=2024, n_agents=5000), stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();

Population of Kenya in 2024: 56571298
Sim: measles, as 5,000 agents, each 11,300 people, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: people were given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters









In a compartmental model, ages matter only once the model is split into age groups (measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]); see Stratification), which then take their fractions from the named population.
Ages can also come from data of your own, with ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...): a table (or CSV file) with a column age (the lower edge of each age group) and a column value (the number or fraction of people in it):

ppl = ss.People(5000, age_data='test_data/nigeria_age.csv')
sim = ss.Sim(measles, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.init()
sim.people.plot_ages();

Sim: measles, as 5,000 agents, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: people were given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters









A sim copies the people it is given when it is built, so look at sim.people afterwards, not at ppl.


Properties of people
A model refers to a property of people with ss.person: ss.person.age, ss.person.female, or a property of your own. ss.person.age < 5 is a condition, which picks out people, for example to say who an intervention reaches:
ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, who=ss.person.age < 5, when=ss.days(10), coverage=0.8) # Vaccinates children under 5
A property of your own is given to ss.People as a state, with a value for each agent, which can be drawn from a distribution, and can be used in a rate as well as in a condition. Here 30% of people live in towns, where the rate of infection is doubled; two campaigns give the same number of doses, one to anyone and one to people in towns:

urban = ss.BoolState('urban', default=ss.bernoulli(p=0.3))
ppl = ss.People(10_000, extra_states=urban)

infection = S >> I @ 1.9*(1 + ss.person.urban)*I # Twice the rate in towns
measles_towns = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.92), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

anyone = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, when=ss.days(1), coverage=0.27, name='campaign')
towns = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, who=ss.person.urban, when=ss.days(1), coverage=0.9, name='campaign')
base = ss.Sim(measles_towns, people=ppl, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No campaign': base,
    'Campaign, anyone': base.new(interventions=anyone),
    'Campaign, towns': base.new(interventions=towns),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
for sim in msim.sims:
    print(sim.label, '- infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))








No campaign - infections: 367
Campaign, anyone - infections: 35
Campaign, towns - infections: 30


ss.person is read when the sim is built, so the property can be given after the model is written. In a compartmental model, people have no properties of their own; the same property is a stratification (measles_towns.stratify(urban={False: 0.7, True: 0.3})), and the same rates and conditions then work on groups.

title: People and demographics
text:
Births and deaths
Births and deaths for the whole population go in demographics=. ss.birth(rate=r) adds people at a crude birth rate r into the first state of each disease (here S); ss.death(rate=r) removes people from every state at rate r. Here is measles over 30 years, with 30 births and 10 deaths per 1,000 people a year. The “Explicit” tab declares the same births and deaths in the disease itself, as transitions, which is what demographics= does with them:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I # β = 1.9 per day (typed, beside annual demographics)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births per 1,000 people per year
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01)), # 10 deaths per 1,000 people per year
]
pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **pars)
msim = ss.parallel({'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **pars), 'Births and deaths': sim})
fig = msim.plot('measles.I', log=True, do_show=False) # A log scale shows the later epidemics, which are far smaller than the first
fig.axes[0].set_ylim(0.1, 200_000)
fig

















library(starsim)

states("S I R")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = ss$perday(1.9) * I) # β = 1.9 per day (typed, beside annual demographics)
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))  # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles <- Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev = 0.001)

demographics <- list(
  ss$birth(rate = ss$peryear(0.03)), # 30 births per 1,000 people per year
  ss$death(rate = ss$peryear(0.01))  # 10 deaths per 1,000 people per year
)
make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2000", stop = "2030", dt = days(1), verbose = 0, ...)
}
msim <- parallel(list("No births or deaths" = make_sim(), "Births and deaths" = make_sim(demographics = demographics)))
fig <- msim$plot("measles.I", log = TRUE, do_show = FALSE) # A log scale shows the later epidemics, which are far smaller than the first
fig$axes[[1]]$set_ylim(0.1, 200000) # The first axes (R counts from 1)
fig



S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles_demog = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8),
    births    = ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # Births into S, the first state, as a transition of the disease
    deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01)),    # Deaths from every state
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'measles',
)
sim_explicit = ss.Sim(measles_demog, **pars) # No demographics= needed: the disease has them
msim_explicit = ss.parallel({'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **pars), 'Births and deaths': sim_explicit})
fig = msim_explicit.plot('measles.I', log=True, do_show=False)
fig.axes[0].set_ylim(0.1, 200_000)
fig


















The births and deaths are transitions of the disease, so they are among its results (sim.results.measles.births) and in describe(). In an ODE, a fraction of an infectious person is enough for the epidemics to recur, and the sim warns when the number infectious falls below one; a stochastic solver shows whether the infection would have died out (see Solvers and backends).
A death from a disease alone is a transition of the disease: ss.death(I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1)) (see Diseases). demographics=True adds births and deaths at default rates (20 and 10 per 1,000 people a year). Instead of a rate, ss.birth() can take when=, a transition whose flow drives the births: ss.birth(when=pregnancy.delivery, children=2) gives twins at each delivery.
A birth or death rate can change over time, with ss.timeseries() (see Parameters). Here the birth rate falls from 40 to 20 per 1,000 a year over 30 years:

PythonR



deaths = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01))
constant = ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.04))
falling = ss.birth(rate=ss.timeseries({'2000-01-01': ss.peryear(0.04), '2030-01-01': ss.peryear(0.02)}, interpolation='linear'))

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'Constant birth rate': ss.Sim(measles, demographics=[constant, deaths], **pars),
    'Falling birth rate': ss.Sim(measles, demographics=[falling, deaths], **pars),
})
msim.plot(['alive', 'measles.I'])










library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = ss$perday(1.9) * I), # β = 1.9 per day (typed, beside annual demographics)
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)

deaths   <- ss$death(rate = ss$peryear(0.01))
constant <- ss$birth(rate = ss$peryear(0.04))
falling  <- ss$birth(rate = ss$timeseries(list("2000-01-01" = ss$peryear(0.04), "2030-01-01" = ss$peryear(0.02)), interpolation = "linear"))

make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2000", stop = "2030", dt = ss$months(1), verbose = 0, ...)
}
msim <- parallel(list(
  "Constant birth rate" = make_sim(demographics = list(constant, deaths)),
  "Falling birth rate"  = make_sim(demographics = list(falling, deaths))
))
msim$plot(c("alive", "measles.I"))




Rates from data
Birth and death rates usually come as data: crude birth rates by year, and death rates by year, sex, and age. The modules ss.Births and ss.Deaths take these, or a country by name for the UN’s rates. Here is the population of Kenya from 2000, checked against the UN’s own estimates:

kenya = dict(
    people = ss.population('Kenya', year=2000, n_agents=20_000),
    demographics = [ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya')],
    start = 2000,
    stop = 2030,
    dt = ss.years(1),
)
sim = ss.Sim(**kenya)
sim.run()
sim.results.alive.plot()
for year in [2010, 2020, 2030]:
    print(year, 'model:', round(sim.results.alive[year - 2000]), 'UN:', round(ss.population('Kenya', year=year).named.total))

Sim: births, deaths, as 20,000 agents, each 1,530 people, years 2000 to 2030
  Note: unit='year' (from dt)


  Done in 0.12 s









2010 model: 40915919 UN: 41598566
2020 model: 52293624 UN: 52217334
2030 model: 63538032 UN: 63102246


These modules run as agents. They give each newborn a mother (people.parent), and can run on a step of their own (e.g. dt=ss.years(1) in a model whose diseases step daily). rel_birth= and rel_death= multiply all the rates. The UN’s totals include migration, which this model leaves out (see Migration).


Data of your own
Rates of your own are given as a table: crude birth rates with columns Year and CBR (ss.Births(birth_rate=df)), and death rates with columns Time, Sex (Male or Female), AgeGrpStart, and mx (ss.Deaths(death_rate=df)). For other column names, give columns=. Each rate holds from its year until the next.
Per person or per 1,000. For births, deaths, conceptions, and migration, a rate’s size says what it is per: a rate above 1 a year is per 1,000 people, and one of 1 or below is per person (for a table, judged by its median). So ss.Births(birth_rate=35) and ss.peryear(0.035) are both 35 per 1,000 people a year. rate_per=1000 or rate_per=1 says which, for rates whose size could mislead (such as net migration of under 1 per 1,000).


Life tables
A life table says how many of a cohort die at each age. ss.death(lifetable=ss.lifetable(ages=ages, deaths=dx)) takes one and runs under every solver, as a death rate for each of its age bands; ss.Deaths(lifetable=...) also takes a table for each sex and year. The UN’s complete life tables come from starsim_data (ssd.download('Kenya', which='life_table')). Death rates by age, or a life table, keep the population from growing implausibly old, as it does with a constant death rate.


Migration
Net migration (arrivals less departures) is ss.migration(rate=r), a rate of either sign: a positive rate brings people in, at the population’s ages, and a negative one takes them out (as agents, recorded as emigrated, not as dead). ss.migration(rate='Albania') takes the UN’s rates for a country. Arrivals and departures can also be given alone, as ss.immigration(n=n) (people per unit time) and ss.emigration(rate=r); in a disease, they can be for one state, e.g. ss.immigration(I, n=ss.peryear(2)) for two imported infections a year.
Here is Albania from 2000, with and without the UN’s rates of net migration:

def make_albania(migration):
    """ Albania's population from 2000, with or without migration """
    demographics = [ss.Births(birth_rate='Albania'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Albania')] + migration
    return ss.Sim(people=ss.population('Albania', year=2000, n_agents=10_000), demographics=demographics, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.years(1), verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel({'Births and deaths': make_albania([]), 'With emigration': make_albania([ss.migration(rate='Albania')])})
for year in [2010, 2020, 2030]:
    model = [round(sim.results.alive[year - 2000]/1e6, 2) for sim in msim.sims]
    print(year, '- millions without emigration:', model[0], 'with:', model[1], 'UN:', round(ss.population('Albania', year=year).named.total/1e6, 2))

2010 - millions without emigration: 3.47 with: 2.89 UN: 2.93
2020 - millions without emigration: 3.65 with: 2.68 UN: 2.87
2030 - millions without emigration: 3.73 with: 2.55 UN: 2.67


The UN’s rates are net, so emigrants are chosen at random. For movement between places within a model, see Movement between places.


Aging
People age if the model has births or deaths (or with aging=True in the sim). In a compartmental model stratified by age, people move from each age group to the next, at a rate set by its width (or, for a named population, by its age pyramid).

title: People and demographics
text:
Pregnancy
ss.Pregnancy models pregnancy itself, for models where it matters: mother-to-child transmission, maternal health, or contraception. Women conceive at age-specific fertility rates; a pregnancy ends in a delivery, a loss, or a maternal death; and each delivery adds a child, whose mother is known. It runs as agents, and takes the place of ss.Births (given both, their births add up, with a warning). Fertility rates come from the UN for a place by name (fertility_rate='Nigeria'), or as a table (columns Time, AgeGrp or AgeGrpStart, and ASFR):

import pandas as pd

fertility = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_asfr.csv') # Age-specific fertility rates by year and single year of age
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=fertility) # Per 1,000 women per year, as the UN's; or fertility_rate='Nigeria'

nigeria = dict(
    people = ss.population('Nigeria', year=2000, n_agents=5000),
    demographics = [pregnancy, ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria')],
    start = 2000,
    stop = 2020,
    dt = ss.months(1),
    verbose = 0,
)
sim = ss.Sim(**nigeria)
sim.run()
sim.results.pregnancy.plot()








Pregnancy is declared, with states NP (not pregnant) and P (pregnant, with P.time_in the gestational age), so its transitions, such as conception, delivery, and birth (listed in the appendix), are events and results that other modules can use. Contraception, for example, is a modifier of conception, and an intervention can reach pregnant women (who=pregnancy.P) or newborns (when=pregnancy.birth; see Interventions):

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(0.08)) # 80 conceptions per 1,000 women a year, at ages 15-49
contraception = ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.5, when=ss.schedule(start='2005')) # Halves conception from 2005

pars = dict(demographics=pregnancy, n_agents=5000, start='2000', stop='2010', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'No contraception': ss.Sim(**pars),
    'Contraception': ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=contraception),
}
for label, sim in scenarios.items():
    sim.run()
    print(label, 'births:', sim.results.pregnancy.birth.sum())

No contraception births: 1053.0
Contraception births: 821.0


Mother-to-child transmission uses the networks that pregnancy makes between mother and child; see Mixing. The other parameters of ss.Pregnancy (losses, maternal and infant deaths, twins, preterm birth, breastfeeding, and more) are in the appendix. Each woman’s parity, n_pregnancies, lactating (breastfeeding), infertile, and the time since her last live birth (pregnancy.since_birth) can be read in conditions, e.g. for lactational amenorrhea:
lam = ss.modify(pregnancy.conception, multiply=0.1, who=pregnancy.lactating & (pregnancy.since_birth < ss.months(6)))
pregnancy.attr(name, dist, when='conception') draws a value for each woman at each pregnancy (e.g. the gestational age of her first antenatal visit), for conditions such as pregnancy.P & (pregnancy.P.time_in >= visit), and pregnancy.add_callback(pregnancy.birth, fn) calls code of your own at each event.

title: People and demographics
text:
People as agents
As agents, sim.people holds every agent: its properties, and the states of every module in the sim, in arrays with one value per agent (see Array indexing). These are the most useful (see People for all of them):







Name
What it is




people.alive, people.dead, people.female, people.male
Who is alive, has died, is female, or is male, as states (.uids for their UIDs)


people.age
Each agent’s age, in years


people.ti_dead, people.ti_removed
The step on which the agent died, or left for another reason such as emigration (NaN otherwise)


people.parent
The UID of each agent’s mother, for agents born in the run (-1 for none)


people.scale
The number of people the agent stands for, relative to the others (1 unless set)


people.causes, people.cause_of_death
The causes of death by name, and the cause of each agent’s death (its position in causes; -1 for none)


people.n
The number of people alive, under every solver: as agents, the people the agents stand for


len(people), people.auids
The number of agents taking part (alive and not removed), and their UIDs


people.died_of(module)
The agents who died of a module in the step just finished, for code in a module


people.keys(), people.brief()
The names of the states, and a one-line summary


people.to_df(), people.get_person(uid)
A table with a row for each agent and a column for each state; everything about one agent


people.plot(), people.plot_ages()
A histogram of each state (key= for some of them); the age pyramid (absolute=True for numbers rather than fractions)



Each module adds its own states, under its name, when the sim is initialized: a declared disease adds each of its states (sim.people.measles.I), and each person’s relative susceptibility and transmissibility (rel_sus and rel_trans). A property that belongs to one module is best defined in that module, with define_states() (see Custom modules); one that several modules use (such as urban) is best given to ss.People with extra_states=.

Looking at people
A sim keeps its people after it has run, and so do the runs of ss.parallel() (msim.sims['label'][0].people), unless they were shrunk to save memory (sim.shrink(), ss.parallel(..., shrink=True), or a finished sim saved to a file). Of each declared disease, agents keep only the times and histories the model reads: the time each agent entered a state (ti_I) is kept when something in the sim reads it, such as a duration of the state, and ss.Sim(keep_times=True) keeps them all (reading one that wasn’t kept raises an error that says so). For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays (e.g. np.mean(sim.diseases.measles.I.stays)).
sim.people.to_df() gives a table, e.g. for the mean age of women and of men:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=1000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()
df = sim.people.to_df()
df.groupby('female').age.mean()

female
False    33.327446
True     34.606384
Name: age, dtype: float32


sim.people.get_person(10) gives everything about the agent with UID 10:

sim.people.get_person(10)

Person({
    'uid':               10,
    'slot':              10,
    'alive':             True,
    'age':               27.815662,
    'female':            False,
    'ti_dead':           nan,
    'ti_removed':        nan,
    'scale':             1.0,
    'cause_of_death':    -1,
    'measles.rel_sus':   1.0,
    'measles.rel_trans': 1.0,
    'measles.S':         False,
    'measles.I':         False,
    'measles.ti_I':      8.0,
    'measles.shift_I':   -1,
    'measles.ti_left_I': 10.0,
    'measles.ti_exit_I': nan,
    'measles.exit_I':    0,
    'measles.R':         True,
})




Deaths by cause
Each agent who dies has one cause, the module whose death it was: its name is in people.causes, and its position in that list in people.cause_of_death:

measles_deaths = ss.Disease(S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), ss.death(I, rate=ss.perday(0.002)), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(0.01), name='other') # Deaths from other causes, 10 per 1,000 people a year
sim = ss.Sim(measles_deaths, demographics=deaths, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()

ppl = sim.people
codes = ppl.cause_of_death[ppl.dead.uids] # The cause of each death
for code, cause in enumerate(ppl.causes):
    print('Deaths from', cause, '-', (codes == code).sum())

Deaths from other - 13
Deaths from measles - 159




In a compartmental run
In a compartmental run there are no agents: sim.people has one row for each group the model is split into. Results, describe(), sim.people.n, and conditions such as who=ss.person.age < 5 (in a model stratified by age) work the same either way; a property of each person, such as sim.people.age, raises an error saying to stratify by it or run as agents.

Appendix: pregnancy
The parameters of ss.Pregnancy (ss.Pregnancy().pars gives them with their defaults), each given by name, e.g. ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Kenya', p_abortion=0.1):



Parameter
What it is
Default

Age-specific fertility rates: a table, a place by name, or one rate; or the hazard of conception itself, as a function of (sim, uids)
ss.peryear(0.1): 100 per 1,000 women a year

How many women the rates are per: 1000 or 1
None: from their size

A multiplier on the fertility rates
1

The ages at which women can conceive
15 and 50

The fraction of women with primary infertility
0


dur_pregnancy
The duration of pregnancy (a number is in weeks)
32 to 42 weeks, mostly 39 to 42

The chance a pregnancy ends in an abortion, at conception
0

The hazard of a spontaneous loss
0

The gestational age that separates a miscarriage from a stillbirth
20 weeks


maternal_death_rate
The hazard of a maternal death while pregnant (e.g. ss.peryear(0.002))
0

The chance of a maternal death at delivery (agents only); with maternal_death_rate, both happen
0

The hazard of death before the age of 1
0

The number of children of each delivery (a distribution, for twins)
1

The chance a child is born female
0.5


preterm

37 and 32 weeks; 1 (varying by 10% between women); 1.2 at the youngest and oldest ages


p_breastfeed
The chance a mother breastfeeds a newborn
1


dur_breastfeed
The duration of breastfeeding
9 months on average


burnin
Whether some women are already pregnant at the start
True



Its events, for when=, ss.modify(), and add_callback():







Event
Who it happens to




conception
A woman, as she becomes pregnant (NP to P)


abortion, miscarriage, stillbirth
A woman whose pregnancy ends without a birth


antepartum
A woman who dies while pregnant


delivery
A woman as she gives birth (and her fetuses, if they are agents)

Each newborn

A child who dies before the age of 1

Its results include a count for each event and state, the crude birth rate (cbr), the total fertility rate (tfr), the maternal mortality ratio (mmr), and the fraction of births that are preterm (preterm_rate):

title: What can be declared
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A Starsim model is made of two kinds of part. A declared part is a description that Starsim reads: states, transitions and their rates, conditions, interventions, and results. A part written as code is a Python function or class that Starsim calls as the model runs. This page lists what can be declared, how to mix the two, and what each costs in speed.
For how to write a declared model, see Writing models; for modules written as code, Custom modules. For questions such as “can people die” or “can I double a rate”, and whether each runs under every solver, see Will my model run as an ODE?.

title: What can be declared
text:
Why the difference matters
A declared part can be read, so Starsim can do more with it:

It runs under every solver: as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents (as long as nothing in it is about individuals; see below).
It can be shown: describe(), equations(), diagram(), and R0() include it.
It is fast: a compartmental model that is all declared runs in compiled code, the whole run in one call, and can be differentiated for fitting.

Code can do anything, but Starsim can only call it. A model with code in it still runs, and runs well, but the code is opaque: it is called at each step, it isn’t in the equations, and in a compartmental run it takes the run out of compiled code a step at a time.

title: What can be declared
text:
Conditions
A condition says who something applies to: who= on ss.modify(), transitions, events, and deliveries; and an event, or a condition that moves people as soon as it holds, says when, in when= (or ss.on()). Conditions are built from:








A condition on
Example
Runs as compartments?




A state
who=hiv.I
Yes


The number in a state, or the fraction
who=sir.I.n >= 20_000, who=sir.I.frac >= 0.02
Yes, in compiled code


The incidence over a period
who=infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7)) > 0.01
Yes, a step at a time


How incidence is changing
who=weekly > infection.incidence(over=ss.days(14)) - weekly (this week more than last)
Yes, a step at a time


Dates
start=, stop=, when=
Yes, in compiled code


A person’s traits
who=ss.person.age < 5, who=ss.person.female
Only if the model is stratified by them; otherwise as agents


Any of these combined
& (and), \| (or), ~ (not)
As the least of its parts



A condition can also be a function of the sim that returns true or false (for a whole compartmental population) or an array (one value for each person or group). That is for what the list above can’t say, such as “while weekly incidence is above half its highest so far”, which needs a memory of the highest so far.
Here are three measures that cut transmission by 30% while a condition holds, for an influenza-like infection with waning immunity:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(180)
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, waning, init_n=dict(I=100), name='flu')

weekly = infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7)) # The fraction of people infected in the last 7 days
last_week = infection.incidence(over=ss.days(14)) - weekly
measures = {
    'No measures':                    None,
    'While 20,000 are infectious':    ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, who=flu.I.n >= 20_000),
    'While 1% are infected a week':   ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, who=weekly > 0.01),
    'While infections are rising':    ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, who=weekly > last_week),
}
pars = dict(total_pop=1_000_000, start='2026-01-01', stop='2027-12-31', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({label: ss.Sim(flu, interventions=measure, **pars) for label, measure in measures.items()})
msim.plot('flu.I')








All four run as ODEs. With waning immunity, the measures lower the first peak and spread out the later ones.

title: What can be declared
section: What makes a model run as agents
text:
What makes a model run as agents
A declared model runs as compartments unless something in it needs individuals. The common reasons are:

A network of individual contacts (ss.RandomNet, ss.SexualNet)
A condition or rate on a person’s traits (ss.person.age) that the model is not stratified by
A value that varies between people (a distribution, or ss.attr())
How long ago, or how often, something happened to each person (.since, .n_times)
A module written as code that keeps a value for each person
n_agents=, or solver='abm'

The sim prints which solver it chose and why (sim.solver_reason), and the full list is in Solvers and backends.

title: What can be declared
text:
Mixing declared and coded parts
Declared and coded parts sit in the same sim, and each can read the other: code reads the declared model’s states, transitions, and parameters by name, and a declared modifier can take its amount from a function. Custom modules combines a declared disease with an antibody level written as code.
A function can also stand in for one value in a declared model: a rate (S >> I @ my_rate), the amount of a modifier, or a condition. The rest of the model stays declared, and is still shown by describe(), with the function by name; in a compartmental run, the run is then taken a step at a time rather than in one call to compiled code. Here is the first measure above, with its condition written as a function:

def many_infectious(sim):
    """ True while 20,000 or more are infectious """
    return sim.diseases.flu.I.n >= 20_000

measure = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, who=many_infectious)
sim = ss.Sim(flu, interventions=measure, **pars)
sim.describe()

title: What can be declared
text:
Performance
A compartmental model that is all declared runs in compiled code, the whole run in one call; a function, a module written as code, or a condition that needs a memory of past steps takes it a step at a time, with the same results but slower, for a small model many times so (how much depends on the model). For one run this doesn’t matter, but for a fit of thousands of runs it does, so where a declared form can say the same thing, it is worth using. As agents, the model is taken a step at a time anyway, and code of your own costs what its own work costs: written with NumPy on whole arrays, or as a loop compiled with @ss.jit, it adds little; as a loop in Python, a lot. Speed and scale gives figures for both.

title: Optimization
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Calibration asks which values of a model’s parameters fit the data. Optimization asks a different question of a model whose parameters are set, usually by calibration: given a budget, how should it be divided between programs to do the most good? With diminishing returns on each program, the best division is rarely all to the program that looks best on its own. sim.optimize() finds it with the same machinery as fitting: the spending on each program is a parameter of the model, and the search runs the model at each allocation it tries. Where costs come from is in Health economics.

title: Optimization
text:
Spending as parameters
sim.optimize() needs the spending on each program as a named parameter of the model (ss.par), and the model has to say what the spending buys. In this SIR model of a respiratory infection with R0 = 2, the fraction of people a program reaches rises as 1 − exp(−spend / (cost per person × population)), with diminishing returns. Testing costs $10 a person and at full reach cuts transmission by 60%; masks cost $5 a person and cut it by 30%. The current budget is $100,000, split evenly:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
tests = ss.par(50e3, name='tests') # Spending on testing, in dollars
masks = ss.par(50e3, name='masks') # Spending on masks

N = (S + I + R).total
reach = lambda spend, cost: 1 - np.exp(-spend/cost/N) # The fraction of people reached, at a cost per person
beta = ss.perday(0.2)*(1 - 0.6*reach(tests, 10))*(1 - 0.3*reach(masks, 5))
sir = ss.Disease(S >> I @ beta*I.frac, I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_prev=0.001, name='sir')

sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10_000, start=2025, stop=2026, verbose=0) # One year, in daily steps

A change in spending is a change in the model like any other: sim.new(pars=dict(tests=100e3, masks=0)) is the sim with everything spent on testing. Before optimizing, check that spending changes the result, with a few allocations by hand (sir.R at the end is the number ever infected):

allocations = {
    'No spending':  dict(tests=0,     masks=0),
    'All testing':  dict(tests=100e3, masks=0),
    'All masks':    dict(tests=0,     masks=100e3),
    'Even split':   dict(tests=50e3,  masks=50e3),
}
for label, spend in allocations.items():
    run = sim.new(pars=spend).run()
    print(label, round(run.results.sir.R[-1]))

No spending 7972
All testing 3575
All masks 5715
Even split 3533

title: Optimization
text:
Finding the best allocation
sim.optimize() keeps the total fixed (by default, the total of the current values, $100,000 here) and searches over its division between the programs, to reach its goal: ss.fitting.minimize() the result to make as small as possible (or ss.fitting.maximize() one to make as large as possible), with at= the time of the result (by default, the end):

best = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize('sir.R'), spend=['tests', 'masks'])
best.summarize()

Optimized sir.R: 3,533.42 to 3,094.7, in 15 runs (0.0 s)
sir.R: 3,533.42 before, 3,094.7 after (15 runs)









before
after




tests
50000.0
75231.626748


masks
50000.0
24768.373252







The best allocation’s run is best.sim, which can be compared with the others:

compare = ss.MultiSim([
    sim.new(pars=allocations['No spending'], label='No spending').run(),
    sim.new(pars=allocations['Even split'], label='Even split').run(),
    best.sim.new(label='Best allocation').run(),
])
compare.plot('sir.I')








The search (SciPy’s SLSQP) is over the fractions of the total, and each point it tries is a run of the model. It is local, and assumes that the result changes smoothly with the spending, so:

Use a deterministic model. With a stochastic model, the search can’t tell a better allocation from a lucky run. Optimize the ODE form of the model (solver='ode'), or give a goal function that averages many runs.
Make returns diminish. If every program’s effect grows in proportion to its spending, the answer is often to put everything into one program, though not always: the epidemic itself responds to the programs nonlinearly, so even linear effects on transmission need not give a result that is linear in the spending. The answer is only as good as the curves that say what spending buys, so try the plausible range of costs and effects.
Check that the answer is not one of several. With more than a few programs, start from another allocation and compare. If the search stops before it has settled (converged is False), maxiter= (50 by default) lets it run longer.
Parameterize the epidemic first, usually by fitting it to data (see Fitting a model), or with values justified from elsewhere: an allocation optimized on the wrong epidemic is optimized for the wrong question.


What to optimize, and when
The goal, ss.fitting.minimize(...) or ss.fitting.maximize(...), takes the name of a result, as a disease’s ('sir.R', or 'R' for the first disease), whose value at the end of the run is used, or at the time given by at= (a date, or a year): ss.fitting.maximize('sir.S', at=2030). For anything else, it takes a function of the run sim, which returns the number to make small or large: here, the height of the peak, for a health system that must not be overwhelmed:

def peak_infectious(sim):
    """ The most people infectious at once """
    return sim.results.sir.I.max()

peak = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize(peak_infectious), spend=['tests', 'masks'], verbose=False)
peak.summarize()

peak_infectious: 206.143 before, 162.629 after (12 runs)

start= says when the new allocation takes effect: before it, each program keeps its current spending, and from then on, the allocation being tried. This is the usual question for a program that is already running: given what has been spent until now, how should next year’s budget be divided?

from_april = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize('sir.R'), spend=['tests', 'masks'], start='2025-04-01', verbose=False)
from_april.summarize()

Limits on each program
bounds= gives the least and most each program can have, in dollars, by name, with None for no limit (a program not named has none beyond 0 and the total):

limited = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize('sir.R'), spend=['tests', 'masks'], bounds=dict(tests=(None, 60e3)), verbose=False)

A single pair, bounds=(10e3, None), applies to every program.


A different total
total= sets the total to divide, for the question “what if the budget were larger (or smaller)?”, starting from the current fractions scaled to the total. Run at a range of totals, it gives a curve of the best result against the budget:

double = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize('sir.R'), spend=['tests', 'masks'], total=200e3, verbose=False)
double.summarize()

The least total that reaches a target
The reverse question, how much money is needed to reach a target, is answered with target=: the least total whose best allocation brings the result to the target (at most the target with ss.fitting.minimize(), at least with ss.fitting.maximize()). The search doubles the total until it reaches the target, then halves the gap between a total that does and one that doesn’t, to within 1%:

needed = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.minimize('sir.R'), spend=['tests', 'masks'], target=1000, verbose=False)
needed.summarize()
