title: Optimization
text:
Reading the result
sim.optimize() returns an ss.fitting.Optimization, which holds:



Attribute
What it is




alloc
The best allocation, by program


value
The result with it


total
Its total (with target=, the least total that reaches the target)


alloc_before, value_before
The current allocation, and the result with it


sim
The sim run with the best allocation


n_runs
The number of runs the search took


converged, why
Whether the search reached its own stopping rule, and its message




best.alloc

{'tests': 75231.6267480361, 'masks': 24768.373251963912}


If the search ends at an allocation worse than the one it started from, the starting allocation is returned. By default (verbose=True, unless ss.options.verbose says otherwise) it prints a line at the end, as in the first example, and with target=, each total it tried.

title: Optimization
text:
Program books from Atomica
An optimization in Atomica starts from a program book: a spreadsheet of programs, their costs, and the coverage and effects they buy. A model imported from Atomica with its program book (see Conversion: Atomica) has a spending parameter for each program, so spend= is not needed, and the same calls work:
sim = ss.import_from('hiv_framework.xlsx', format='atomica', databook='hiv_databook.xlsx', progbook='hiv_progbook.xlsx', programs_start=2020)
best = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.maximize('all_vs', at=2030), start=2020)
least = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.maximize('all_vs', at=2030), start=2020, target=1.1*best.value) # The least money that reaches 10% more

title: FAQ
text:
🧠50% 🤖50%
Short answers to common questions, each with a link to the page that covers it in full.

title: FAQ
text:
Getting started

Do I need to understand all of Starsim to use it?
No! Starsim covers a lot (compartmental and agent-based models, networks, demographics, geography, calibration, and more), but you only need the parts your model uses, and the rest stays out of the way. (By analogy: you probably use pandas, but you’ve probably never used extractall.) A simple SIR model is a few lines, and needs nothing from the pages on networks or custom modules.
To get started, follow T1–T3, then the tutorials your model needs (the tutorials page helps you choose), and look things up in this user guide as you go. Agent-based models are written the same way; the “Advanced” sections of the tutorials show what changes as agents. No model needs the Architecture pages.


Can I use Starsim with an AI coding agent?
Yes. Run starsim init ai in your project: it gives your agent (Claude Code, Codex, and others) Starsim’s skills, which match the installed version, for writing, checking, running, and converting models. See ai.starsim.org.


Why is Starsim built this way?
We were fed up with the limitations of existing disease models (especially our own!), and asked: “Can we build a disease modeling framework that functions as a ‘lingua franca’, that pays homage to the best aspects of all the other disease models that have come before?” The answer is of course “lol no”, but we did our best! For an (extremely) detailed explanation of the design, see the Lingua Franca docs.


Where can I get help?
Email us! Profiling and debugging covers common pitfalls. To report a bug, open an issue on GitHub with the smallest script that shows it (see Contributing).

title: FAQ
text:
Building models

Should I build a compartmental model or an agent-based model?
You don’t have to decide up front. A model written as states and transitions can run either way: by default it runs as an ODE, and as agents once something in it needs individuals, such as a contact network or a value kept for each person. You can also ask for a solver by name (ss.Sim(..., solver='abm')), and run the same model both ways to see what the individual detail changes. Solvers and backends has a table of which to use for which question.


Can I write parts of a model as Python code?
Yes. A model can be fully declared (states, transitions, and rates), fully written as code, or a mix of the two, e.g. a declared disease with an intervention written as a function. Declared parts get diagrams, equations, every solver, and fast fitting without any more work; coded parts can do anything Python can. See What can be declared for how to mix them, and Custom modules for writing modules as code.


Are the models in the library ready to use?
They are starting points, not models of a particular setting. The library of diseases, networks, and maternal-child health modules is illustrative rather than validated: some parameter values are placeholders, and interfaces may change between versions. Copy one and adapt it, with parameters from the evidence for your setting and checks against data. The same goes for any runnable example in these docs.


I have a model in Starsim 3 or another framework. Can I bring it over?
In almost all cases, yes. Starsim imports models from more than a dozen frameworks, including EpiModel, odin, and epydemix, and Starsim 3 code can be rewritten with python -m starsim.converters.migrate. See Import/export and the migration guide. If a model doesn’t translate, email us or open an issue.

title: FAQ
text:
Running and fitting

Why is my first run slow?
The first run after installing Starsim may compile its kernels with Numba, which takes a few minutes, once; they are then kept on disk. (The wheels from pip install starsim include a Rust copy of the kernels, compiled ahead of time, which avoids this.) To compile everything up front, e.g. when building a Docker image or before a batch of runs on a cluster, run ss.compile(), or starsim init compile from the command line. See Solvers and backends.


How large a population can Starsim model?
As compartments, any size: a compartmental run takes the same time for a thousand people as for a billion (except with Gillespie’s method, which takes one event at a time). As agents, the time grows with the number of agents, so a large population is usually represented by having each agent stand for several people. See Branching and rescaling and Speed and scale.


How do I fit a model to data?
Give the parameters you want fitted bounds, give the sim data whose columns are named like its results, and call sim.fit(). There is no function to write that puts the values into the model or pulls out the results to compare. See T6 – Data and calibration to start, and Fitting a model for the details.


Why do two runs give different results, and how do I make them match?
A stochastic run (agents, or a stochastic compartmental solver) depends on its random seed, rand_seed: the same seed gives the same results, and different seeds give different ones. One stochastic run is not a result, so run several seeds and look at the spread. When comparing scenarios, Starsim uses common random numbers, so that two runs with the same seed differ much less by chance, and more of their difference comes from what was changed. See Scenarios and Random numbers.

title: Architecture
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This section explains how Starsim is put together and why, for contributors and for modelers who want to know what happens when they call sim.run(); no model needs it. This page gives the idea, the principles, and a map of the package, and then looks at modules, the pieces a sim is made of. From declaration to run follows a model from its declaration to a run, and Engines and transmission looks at the engines that run it. Random numbers are in Random numbers, and how the design is tested in the developer guide.

title: Architecture
text:
The idea and the principles
A model in Starsim is written once, as data: states (S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')), transitions between them (S >> I @ beta * I), and parameters, with the mixing, demography and interventions around them. Each disease checks its own structure when it is made (unknown names, rates of the wrong shape). When the sim is initialized, Starsim reads those objects, fills in what was left out (and records each guess), checks them against each other, and chooses how to run them: as a deterministic ODE or integro-differential model, as one of three stochastic compartmental solvers, or as agents. Because the model is data rather than code, everything else is derived from the same objects: the printed description, the equations, the diagram, and the exports to other frameworks. One declared model, several ways to run it, and one source of truth for all of them.
A model can also be written as code, as classes with their own step() methods: these run through the same loop, as agents if they keep a value for each person and otherwise with no agents at all (an ODE of your own runs as just that), and can sit beside declared models in one sim. Declared modules and modules written as code, below, covers how the two kinds fit together.
Every design choice is checked against a short constitution. In order of weight:

Simplicity. Writing and changing a model should be easy for an epidemiologist, not just an engineer. A model ported to Starsim should get shorter.
Performance. As close to custom compiled code as is feasible. This is why compartmental runs go through kernels (small compiled functions that step the compartments) and why agents use compiled passes over their arrays.
Flexibility. Every major modeling feature should be expressible, even if not every one is built in. When a declaration can’t say something, a module’s step() can.
Correctness. The machinery is validated by tests, but over-correctness should not cost simplicity or speed: Euler steps, Erlang stages and other standard approximations are fine, as long as they are announced.

After these come understandability (few concepts, no brittle subsystems), maintainability (solvers should not each reimplement the same thing), composability (use as much or as little of Starsim as you want), short startup (no long compilation before a small run), and being easy for AI tools to work with. The development principles add: no legacy shims, avoid bloat, and think about the whole system before adding a special path for one case.
For example, solver='auto' picks the simplest representation that runs the model faithfully (simplicity, performance); every approximation prints one line saying what was done (correctness without refusing); and the compiled kernels are optional, with a plain-Python path for short runs (short startup).

title: Architecture
text:
The map
Starsim has five layers. Broadly, each builds on the ones before it, and a contributor can usually work in one layer at a time.






flowchart TD
    D["<b>1. Declaration</b><br/>states, transitions, rates,<br/>parameters, dimensions"]
    G["<b>The graph</b><br/>resolved, completed, checked"]
    O["<b>2. Build and orchestration</b><br/>sim.init(), the loop, modules,<br/>people, networks, results"]
    C{"choose a solver"}
    K["<b>3. Compartmental engine</b><br/>ode, binomial, gillespie, tau"]
    A["<b>3. Agent engine</b><br/>abm"]
    J["<b>4. Speed and alternate backends</b><br/>Numba and Rust kernels, JAX, compiled draws"]
    E["<b>5. Edges</b><br/>fitting, import and export,<br/>presentation, library, geography"]
    D --> G --> O --> C
    C --> K
    C --> A
    K -.-> J
    A -.-> J
    O --- E









Layer
Files in starsim/
What they do




1. Declaration
internals/transitions.py, internals/expressions.py, internals/graph.py, internals/parameters.py, internals/time.py, internals/dimensions.py, and others
The words a model is written in: states and transitions, rates as expressions (beta * I), parameters (ss.par, ss.by), durations and rates with units, conditions for who=, stratifications and strains. internals/graph.py collects one module’s declarations into an ss.graph.Graph, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them.


2. Build and orchestration
sim.py, internals/loop.py, internals/modules.py, people.py, internals/arrays.py, and a file for each kind of module, results.py, run.py
The runtime objects. sim.init() builds the population, the modules and the results, and chooses the solver; the loop then calls each module in a fixed, printable order each step. ss.Module is the one base class for diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, connectors and analyzers. run.py runs many sims (ss.MultiSim, ss.parallel).


3. Engines
solvers/ (choose.py, compartmental.py, agents.py, joint_states.py, and others)
How a graph is run. choose.py picks the solver and says why. Each declared module gets one engine: Compartmental (which flattens the model into a program of flows that the kernels step) or Agents (boolean arrays over agents). joint_states.py tracks several diseases jointly when one refers to another’s states.


4. Speed and alternate backends
solvers/backends/, internals/gradients.py, and the Rust crate in solvers/rust/
The same runs, faster or differentiable: the Numba kernels that step a compartmental program, the compiled passes over agents and edges, the exact random draws everything shares, the Rust copy of all of these, ss.jit for users’ own code, and the ODE in JAX for gradients. See Engines and transmission.


5. Edges
fit.py, internals/display.py, internals/errors.py, geo.py, data.py, converters/, library/
What builds on a run model. Fitting (sim.fit()); describe(), diagram() and equations(); errors, warnings, and notes; places, mobility and data by place name; importers and exporters for other frameworks; and example diseases and networks (import starsim.library as ssl).



Helpers that every layer uses are in settings.py (ss.options), utils.py, internals/debugtools.py (profiling, debugging, and mock objects for tests) and starsim_cli/ beside the package (the starsim command, apart so that it starts without importing Starsim). Everything in internals/ is also at the top level: ss.graph, ss.expressions, ss.gradients, ss.errors, and so on.
A few things to notice in the map:

A declaration doesn’t say how it will run. The states, transitions and parameters of layer 1 are the same objects whether the model runs as an ODE or as agents; only when they are evaluated (a rate, a condition) do they see one value per group or one per agent. That is what makes the solver a choice rather than part of the model.
Every compartmental solver steps the same program. The ODE, the chain binomial, Gillespie and tau-leaping all run the flat list of flows that Compartmental builds. The ODE in JAX, the Rust kernels and the particle filter run that same program too, so a fix in one place is a fix for all of them.
Code is never analyzed in advance. A function in a rate, or a module’s step(), is simply called with what the solver has (one value per agent, or one per group). If it asks for something that only agents have, the run stops and says so.

title: Architecture
text:
What a module is
Everything a sim runs, apart from the people themselves, is a module: each disease, network, demographic process, intervention, connector and analyzer. The rest of this page is the view from inside a module; for how to write one of your own, see Custom modules and the tutorial T8.
A module is an instance of ss.Module (starsim/internals/modules.py), or of a subclass. Every module has the same parts:

a name (sir, randomnet), unique in the sim, and a label for plots;
its parameters, mod.pars (an ss.Pars), given with define_pars() and set from the user’s arguments with update_pars(), which raises an error for one that wasn’t defined;
its timeline, mod.t (an ss.Timeline), which is the sim’s unless the module is given a dt, start or stop of its own;
its distributions, each with a random number stream of its own, found by searching the module when the sim is initialized (Random numbers);
its states, arrays with one value per agent (define_states()), which the people grow and shrink with the population;
its results, mod.results, one ss.Result per quantity per time point; every ss.BoolState gets a count of the same name without being declared;
a link to the sim, mod.sim, set when the sim is initialized.

A few attributes are locked (pars, t, sim, dists, results, and each state), so that self.I = ... in a step raises an error instead of quietly replacing the array: the error suggests self.I[:] = ....
What kind of module it is decides only where in each step it is called, and where the sim keeps it. The kinds are the subclasses in ss.modules.module_map(), which is the one place that says what they are:



Kind
Base class
Kept in
Examples




Diseases
ss.Disease
sim.diseases
a declared ss.Disease, ss.SIR, ss.AgentDisease and its subclasses, ssl.HIV


Networks
ss.networks.Route
sim.networks
ss.RandomNet, ss.SexualNet, ss.MixingPool


Demographics
ss.Demographics
sim.demographics
ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.Pregnancy


Interventions
ss.Intervention
sim.interventions
ss.vaccinate, ss.screen, ss.treat (deliveries, which hold products)


Connectors
ss.Connector
sim.connectors
ss.modify


Analyzers
ss.Analyzer
sim.analyzers
ss.infection_log, or a function of the sim


Custom
ss.Module, or anything that is none of the above
sim.custom
a module of your own



A module can be more than one kind: ss.Pregnancy is both a demographic module and a declared disease, so it adds people and has states and transitions; a delivery such as ss.screen is an intervention that is also a source of events (the people it reached, screening, and its outcomes, screening.positive), which other deliveries can be triggered by. A product (ss.Vaccine) is a module too, but it has no step of its own: it is held by the delivery that gives it, and listed by sim.products().
Modules can be given to a sim by keyword (diseases=, networks=, …), as positional arguments, which the sim sorts by kind (simpars.py), or by name as strings (diseases='sis'), which ss.modules.find_modules() looks up among Starsim’s classes and any registered with ss.register_modules(). A module given no name is named after its class in lower case, and numbered if two would clash (randomnet, randomnet_1).

import starsim as ss

def make_sir():
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    return ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ ss.perday(0.3) * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_prev=0.01, name='sir')

full = ss.Sim(
    make_sir(),
    networks      = ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4),
    demographics  = [ss.Births(), ss.Deaths()],
    interventions = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, when=ss.days(20), coverage=0.5),
    analyzers     = ss.infection_log(),
    n_agents = 2000,
    unit     = 'day',
    stop     = ss.days(60),
    verbose  = 0,
)
full.init()
for mod in full.modules:
    print(f'{mod.name:15} {type(mod).__name__}')

births          Births
deaths          Deaths
randomnet       RandomNet
vaccinate       vaccinate
vaccine         Vaccine
sir             Disease
infection_log   infection_log


sim.modules lists every module of the sim in the order they are initialized: demographics, connectors, networks, interventions, products, diseases, custom modules, and analyzers. (The vaccine is there because the delivery made it.)

How modules find each other
Modules don’t hold references to each other: a module reaches the rest of the sim through self.sim, at run time, which is always the sim’s own copy. The sim offers several ways in, all to the same objects:



To reach
Write
Notes




A module, by kind and name
self.sim.diseases.sir, self.sim.networks.randomnet
the usual way; each kind is an ss.ndict, so sim.diseases[0] works too


A module, by name alone
self.sim.sir
if the name is unique and isn’t an attribute of the sim


A module through the people
self.sim.people.sir
the people hold every module with states


A state by its full name
self.sim.people.states['sir.I']
every module’s states, flat, as <module>.<state>


A property of people
self.sim.people.age, or ss.person.age in a condition written before the sim exists
ss.person is a lazy reference, evaluated when it is needed


A result
self.sim.results.sir.I, self.sim.diseases.sir.results.I
the same object: a module’s results are nested in the sim’s


The time
self.ti, self.now, self.t.dt
the module’s own; with a timeline of its own, self.ti counts its own steps



States are shared by reading them: any module can read sir.I or another module’s array, and the arrays always have one value per agent alive, in the same order, since the people grow and shrink them all together. Writing is a different matter. A module can write into another’s arrays (an intervention that cures people sets sir.I[uids] = False), and for a declared disease the write is tracked so its counts stay right, but Starsim can’t see what was changed or why. The declared alternative is ss.modify, which never overwrites anything: it keeps the quantity’s base value and applies itself on top, so modifiers can’t clobber each other, and sim.what_modifies() can list them (Engines and transmission). To move people between a declared disease’s states, ss.move() does it the same way under every solver.

title: Architecture
text:
The lifecycle
A module goes through four stages: it is made, initialized with the sim, stepped, and finalized. Every stage is a method that a subclass can override, calling super() to keep what the base class does.
Made. __init__() stores what the module was given: its parameters, states, and, for a declared disease, its states and transitions, which are built into its graph (From declaration to run). Nothing is linked to a sim yet. When a module is given to a sim, the sim copies it, so one module can go into several sims; the copy is the one that runs, which is why a change to the original after the sim is made (adding a callback, say) raises an error saying to make it on sim.diseases.<name> instead.
Initialized. sim.init() (From declaration to run) chooses the solver first, since that decides which objects exist, and then initializes the modules in two passes:

init_pre(sim), for each module in turn: link it to the sim, set up its timeline, link its time parameters to its dt (so that self.pars.dur.to_dt() works without arguments), check its bare numbers against the sim’s unit, add its parameters to sim.pars and its results to sim.results, add it and its states to the people (sim.people.add_module()), and make its results (init_results()). A declared disease first makes its engine, the object that will run its transitions under the chosen solver.
Then the sim initializes every distribution, gives the people their starting values, and calls init_post() on each module, which gives each state its initial values (and, for a declared disease, its initial conditions: who starts infected).

After that, the loop is built, and the parameters are locked, so setting one that doesn’t exist raises an error.
Stepped. Each step, the loop calls the module’s methods at its kind’s place in the order: start_step(), record_states(), step() (and step_state() for a disease written as code), on_death(uids), record_events(), and finish_step(). The order, and what each kind does in it, is in From declaration to run; a method that is sure to do nothing in this sim is left out of the plan (below).
Finalized. After the last step, finalize() calls finalize_results() on each module, which scales the results that count people by the number of people each agent stands for. A module can override finalize_results() to work out results from others; it calls super().finalize_results() first. A module that has been finalized can’t be stepped again: running it again raises ss.AlreadyRunError, which says to copy it first.
Forgetting to call super() is the commonest mistake in writing a module, so the base class’s methods that must be called are marked with @ss.required(). After a run, sim.run() warns about any that weren’t, naming the method and the module.

title: Architecture
section: Declared modules and modules written as code
text:
Declared modules and modules written as code
A disease can be declared (states and transitions), written as code (arrays and a step_state() and step() of its own), or both. The difference is in what the module hands to its engine:

A declared disease’s graph is run by its engine, ss.solvers.Agents or ss.solvers.Compartmental, made by ss.solvers.make_engine(). ss.Disease.step() is three calls to the engine: the transitions that are not contact-mediated, then those that are, then any functions of the model. No method of ss.Disease asks which solver it has.
A disease written as code (an ss.AgentDisease subclass, or an ss.Disease that declares nothing) gets an engine that has nothing to run (ss.solvers.Undeclared), so super().step() is harmless, and its own code does the work. An ss.AgentDisease transmits through the same code a declared disease uses as agents (ss.solvers.Transmission), so modifiers and products act on it in the same way.
A class can be both: declared states and transitions, plus code in step() after super().step() has taken them, reading or writing arrays of its own.

Every other kind of module is written as code (apart from the deliveries and modifiers, which are declared in their own way, by keywords). So a sim is often a mixture, and Starsim has to decide whether it can run as compartments. It never runs code to find out. Instead it looks at what each module written as code keeps (init_capabilities() in starsim/solvers/choose.py):

A module that keeps a value for each person (any array given with define_states()) needs agents, since only agents have one value per person.
So does one that adds and removes agents (ss.Births, ss.Deaths; a declared disease’s ss.birth() and ss.death() are their compartmental form), and an individual-level network.
A module can say for itself: compartmental = True on the class says its code works on groups too, and compartmental = False that it needs agents.
Anything else (code that keeps nothing per person, whatever its kind) runs beside the compartments, called at its place in the loop like any other module. If its code then asks for something only agents have (people.age in a model not stratified by age, say), it raises an ss.CapabilityError that says so.

A sim made only of such modules has no agents at all, so an ODE written by hand in NumPy, as a custom module, runs as just that. Here are two small custom modules beside the same declared SIR: one keeps a single number for the whole population, the other a number for each person:

class Alarm(ss.Module):
    """ Count the days on which more than 5% of people are infectious: nothing per person """
    def __init__(self, threshold=0.05, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(threshold=threshold)
        self.days_over = 0

    def step(self):
        sir = self.sim.diseases.sir
        if sir.I.n > self.pars.threshold*self.sim.people.n:
            self.days_over += 1

class Exposure(ss.Module):
    """ Count each person's days infectious: one value per person """
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.FloatArr('days_infectious', default=0))

    def step(self):
        infectious = self.sim.diseases.sir.I.uids
        self.days_infectious[infectious] += 1

for mod in [None, Alarm(), Exposure()]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_sir(), modules=mod, unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
    sim.init()
    label = type(mod).__name__ if mod else 'No module'
    print(f'{label}: {sim.solver}, since {sim.solver_reason}')

No module: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Alarm: ode, since every part of the model has a compartmental form
Exposure: abm, since "exposure" (Exposure) keeps a value for each person (days_infectious), which only agents have; if its code works on groups, set compartmental = True on it


The SIR alone and the SIR with Alarm run as an ODE; Exposure makes the sim run as agents, and the reason names it and says how to change that. Alarm still costs something: a compartmental run is usually taken by the kernels in one call, but a module with a step of its own makes it go step by step (the plan line of sim.describe() says so). The same Alarm runs as agents unchanged, since sir.I.n is the number infectious either way.

title: Architecture
text:
Reading the loop
The loop (sim.loop, an ss.loop.Loop in starsim/internals/loop.py) is built at the end of sim.init() by Loop.collect_funcs(), which walks the sim’s modules in the order above and collects each method to call. Its plan is every (time, method) pair, sorted by time and then by that order; a module with a timeline of its own appears only at its own times. sim.loop.to_df() gives the plan as a table, so the order can always be checked rather than remembered. Each row is one call. The rows that are missing are the ones left out because they would do nothing: the analyzer’s (ss.infection_log records infections as they happen), and the finish_step() of the modules that don’t override it. The first step (ti == 0) has the same rows but sim.advance(), since the time is already at the first time point.
The same plan is what sim.loop.insert() adds to (a function, or a module’s step() moved to another point), and what sim.profile(kind='loop') and sim.loop.plot() show; see Profiling and debugging. A compartmental run that is taken by the kernels in one call doesn’t use the plan at all, which is why it is made only when it is first needed.

title: Architecture
text:
Limits

The order between kinds is fixed. There are no priorities or phases; within a kind, modules run in the order given. A module that must run at another point is moved there with sim.loop.insert().
What code does to another module isn’t recorded. describe() and what_modifies() see declarations, not the writes of a step().
Whether code needs agents is decided by what it keeps, not what it does. A module with no states that still reads per-agent values in a compartmental run is caught only when it first asks for them, part way into the run.

title: Outcomes
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
What a model tracks is not what is observed: a model of measles tracks who is susceptible, latent, infectious, and immune, while surveillance sees some of the cases, some days after infection. This page covers declaring more results (such as prevalence), declaring outcomes (reported quantities worked out from the model’s flows: cases, hospital admissions, deaths), and attaching data to results by name, so that it can be plotted and fitted. For a step-by-step introduction, see T6 – Data and calibration.

title: Outcomes
text:
Declaring more results
Every declared disease already has a result for each state (a stock: the number in it at each time point) and each transition (a flow: the number who made it during each step), named after it; see Results for working with them. A sum or ratio of states, given to the disease, is a result like any other. Nobody is “in” a sum of states, so it makes no new state; as a result, it is the combined count, and a ratio of two is a proportion:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
N = S + E + I + R
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

prevalence = (E + I)/N # The fraction of people infected, latent or infectious
immune     = R/N       # The fraction immune, as a serosurvey would measure it

measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, prevalence, immune, init=dict(I=0.001))
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.measles.plot('prevalence', 'immune')








In rates and conditions, a state gives its number and fraction directly: I.n is the number in I, and I.frac the fraction of people in it. Flows can be used the same way: infection/S is the incidence per susceptible person. A ratio is a ratio of sums: by group or over a longer period, its numerator and denominator are each summed, and then divided, never averaged.
A result needs a name of its own. A parameter over time is a result of an expression of it under another name, eir_now = 1*eir; giving the parameter itself (eir=eir) raises an error. In a class, an expression with a value for each person, such as age = ss.person.age or duration = affected.time_in, is a helper for the rates, not a result.

title: Outcomes
text:
Outcomes
An outcome is a reported quantity: a flow worked out from the model’s other flows, which moves nobody. It is how a model says what a surveillance system would see. For measles, the rash appears about 4 days after people become infectious, and suppose half of cases are reported, a tenth of reported cases are admitted to hospital (for 5 days on average), and 2% of those admitted die:

PythonR



S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
onset     = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)

cases  = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, delay=ss.days(4))                       # Half of cases reported, at the rash
hosp   = ss.outcome(0.1*cases, delay=ss.days(2), dur=ss.days(5))  # A tenth of those admitted to hospital
deaths = ss.outcome(0.02*hosp, delay=ss.days(5))                       # 2% of those admitted die

measles = ss.Disease(infection, onset, recovery, cases, hosp, deaths, init=dict(I=0.001))
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
print('Reported cases:', round(res.cases.sum()))
print('Hospital admissions:', round(res.hosp.sum()))
print('Most in hospital at once:', round(res.n_hosp.max()))
print('Deaths:', round(res.deaths.sum()))
sim.diseases.measles.plot('cases', 'n_hosp')

Reported cases: 49947
Hospital admissions: 4995
Most in hospital at once: 1163
Deaths: 100











library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
infection <- Transition(S, E, rate = 1.9 * I)
onset     <- Transition(E, I, dur = days(10))
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))

cases  <- outcome(0.5 * onset, delay = days(4))                # Half of cases reported, at the rash
hosp   <- outcome(0.1 * cases, delay = days(2), dur = days(5)) # A tenth of those admitted to hospital
deaths <- outcome(0.02 * hosp, delay = days(5))                # 2% of those admitted die

measles <- Disease(
  infection = infection, onset = onset, recovery = recovery,
  cases = cases, hosp = hosp, deaths = deaths,
  init = list(I = 0.001)
)
sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-05-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
res <- sim$results$measles
cat("Reported cases:", round(sum(res$cases$values)), "\n")
cat("Hospital admissions:", round(sum(res$hosp$values)), "\n")
cat("Most in hospital at once:", round(max(res$n_hosp$values)), "\n")
cat("Deaths:", round(sum(res$deaths$values)), "\n")
sim$diseases$measles$plot("cases", "n_hosp")




The source is a fraction of a flow, or a sum of fractions of several: 0.5*onset is half of those who become infectious. The fraction is the probability of being counted. Reporting that depends on severity is a sum: ss.outcome(0.1*mild + 0.6*severe), where mild and severe are transitions.
Outcomes can follow from outcomes: hosp is a fraction of cases, and deaths a fraction of hosp, so a chain of events is a line for each.
delay= is the time from the source event to this one: a duration (exponentially distributed, as for any duration), a distribution such as ss.constant(ss.days(4)) or ss.lognormal(...), or a function of the sim.
dur= is how long each event counted stays in the outcome (here, a stay in hospital), and gives a second result, n_<name>: the number currently in it, here the number in hospital.
A fraction can be a parameter: ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 0.9]) makes the reporting rate fittable, and ss.by(age=[...]) gives a fraction for each age group, as for any value (Parameters).

An outcome is worked out from the counts of its source flows, in each group, so it never records which people were counted. In a deterministic run, the fraction multiplies the flow and the delay spreads it over the following steps; in a stochastic or agent-based run, those counted are a binomial draw, and their delays are drawn too. Define what the data measures (cases dated by onset, or by report) before choosing the source and delay, and note that a delay moves events past the end of the run, so the last weeks of an outcome are lower than they will be.
describe() gives each outcome’s definition, under the disease’s transitions, e.g. cases   outcome: 0.5 × onset, after 4 days (exponential).

An outcome, an intervention, or a state
An outcome stands for an observation process that the model doesn’t represent. Which to use depends on what the model contains:



The situation
Use




Testing and reporting aren’t in the model: “about half of cases are reported, four days after onset”
An outcome


Testing is modeled, by interventions
The interventions’ own results: each test reports the diagnoses it made (Products)


Being counted changes what happens to the person (people in hospital are isolated and stop transmitting)
A state, with transitions in and out (Diseases)



An outcome is a result, so anything can read it: an intervention can be triggered when n_hosp passes a threshold. What it can’t do is single out individuals. An outcome belongs to one disease; a total over several diseases is arithmetic on their results after the run (sim.results.measles.cases + sim.results.rubella.cases), which is a result but not a declared one, so data can’t be attached to it.

title: Outcomes
text:
Data attached by name
Data is attached to a sim with data=: a table with a time column (date, year, t, or time) and a column for each result there is data for, named like the result. A column called cases is compared with the result cases, and plotted with it. To try this where the answer is known, make data from the model: to_synthetic_data() draws weekly counts of reported cases from a run, with Poisson noise as in real reporting (noise=None gives the model’s values themselves), from a sim with its own random seed:

truth = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01', rand_seed=2, verbose=0)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

sim.run()
sim.plot('cases')








The plot shows the model’s cases summed over each week of the data, as they are compared in a fit, and its title says so.

Data need not be on the model’s time step. A flow, such as weekly reported cases, is compared with the model’s total over each week of the data, from the data’s date to the next (so a week is dated by its first day); a stock or a ratio, such as the fraction immune in a serosurvey, with the model’s value on the date of the data. The result already knows which it is.
With several diseases, a column is matched to the one that has a result of that name, or is named with its disease, measles.cases.
Data by group is given in long form: extra columns named after dimensions (age) say which group each row is for, and each row is compared with cases.select(age=...).
A missing value is not a zero. Leave weeks with no report empty (NaN) rather than 0, so that they are left out of the comparison rather than compared with a count of none.
A column that matches no result gets a note that lists the closest names, so a misspelled header is noticed; in a fit, it is an error.

Data is usually read from a file: data='measles_cases.csv' reads it. A file whose headers are not the names of results is read with ss.SimData(), which renames the columns and can drop those that match nothing:
data = ss.SimData('measles_cases.csv', aliases=dict(date='Week starting', cases='Reported measles cases'), ignore_extra=True)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-05-01')
Data attached this way is what calibration fits to: sim.fit() fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data.

Likelihoods
Nothing needs a likelihood to be compared with data or fitted to it: by default, a fit compares each result with its data by their normalized absolute difference, and sim.fit(loss=...) takes another measure, or a function of your own (Measuring the fit); a fit uses likelihoods for every data series or for none, so loss= with an outcome that has a likelihood is an error. Where a likelihood is wanted, for example for Bayesian methods, it is given with the outcome, as the distribution of the data around the model’s value:
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*onset, delay=ss.days(4), likelihood=ss.nbinom(n=ss.par(10, bounds=[1, 100])))
The model’s value is the mean of the distribution, and the rest (here the dispersion of a negative binomial) is given, or fitted as a parameter. Use ss.poisson() for counts with no more spread than chance gives, ss.nbinom() for overdispersed counts (most surveillance data), and ss.binom() for the positives among those tested; Fitting a model lists every likelihood and the data each suits.

title: Outcomes
text:
Pitfalls and further reading

A daily result against weekly data. Compare like with like: res.cases.resample('week') is the model’s weekly cases.
An outcome where a state is needed. If being counted changes what happens to a person, it is a state, not an outcome.
A misspelled data column. A column that matches no result is only noted when the sim is made; read the notes, or use ss.SimData(..., aliases=...) to rename it.

Further reading:

EpiNow2: estimating epidemic growth from delayed and partly reported cases, with delay distributions, in R
Practical considerations for measuring the effective reproductive number, Rt: why the delays between infection and observation matter, and how to account for them
pomp: stochastic models with an explicit measurement model linking the process to the data, in R
Simulation-based inference for epidemiological dynamics: course notes on measurement models and likelihoods for epidemic data

title: Interventions
text:
🧠5% 🤖95%
An intervention is anything done to change the course of an epidemic. Most are one of two kinds. Some deliver a product (a vaccine, a test, or a drug) to the people who are eligible, at given times or when something happens to them. Others change a quantity in the model, giving nothing to anyone: masks, distancing, and school closures change transmission. Anything else is an intervention written as code.
What a product does is on Products, how one module changes another on Connectors, and what interventions cost on Health economics. The tutorial T5 – Interventions and scenarios compares interventions against measles, and Scenarios covers running the comparison.
Here are the two kinds side by side, against measles in a town of 100,000 people, 90% of whom are immune (an SEIR model with an R0 of about 15, latent for 10 days and infectious for 8): a vaccination campaign that reaches 80% of people on 1 May, and distancing that halves transmission from 1 May to 1 July:

title: Interventions
text:
Delivering products
A delivery says who receives the product, when, and how many. There is one for each kind of product, ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat(); each takes the product as its first argument (ss.vaccinate(vaccine, ...)), or the product’s own keywords. A delivery takes its name from the variable it is assigned to, and has results of its own: the number delivered on each step, the number eligible, and the coverage reached. Its keywords are the same for every product:







Keyword
Meaning




who=
Who can receive it: a condition (ss.person.age < 15), people as they reach an age (ss.at_age(ss.months(9))), or a function of the sim


when=
When: at times ('2025-05-01'), this far apart (ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1))), or on an event (screening.positive); with none, routinely


start=, stop=
A window it is delivered in, with any when=


coverage=
The fraction of eligible people reached


capacity=
The number that can be delivered (per round, per step, or as a rate), or ss.capacity(n, priority=..., queue=...) to say who is served first and whether the rest wait


skip_reached_within=
Skip those this delivery reached less than this long ago, e.g. ss.years(1) (agents only)


trace=
Deliver to the contacts of those selected, on a network (agents only)


disease=
The disease the product acts on, if there is more than one



The appendix lists every delivery, and every form of who= and when=. The examples in this section use a curable infection with no lasting immunity, as an SIS model run as agents:

PythonR



S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.1)

kw = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)



states("S I")
sis <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = ss$peryear(2) * I), # β = 2 per year
  recovery  = Transition(I, S, dur = years(1)),           # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
  init_prev = 0.1
)

make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(sis, n_agents = 5000, start = 2000, stop = 2020, dt = ss$months(1), verbose = 0, ...)
}




Rounds and routine delivery
With times or how often (ss.schedule(every=...)) as when=, delivery is in rounds: in each round, every eligible person is offered the product once. With no when= (with or without start= and stop=), delivery is routine: each person is offered it once, at the first step on which they are eligible, such as children as they reach an age (who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9))). Routine delivery needs people to become eligible over time, so this example adds births and deaths:

PythonR



kw_births = dict(kw, demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.03))])

routine  = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, who=ss.at_age(ss.years(1)), start='2005', coverage=0.8)     # Once per child, as they turn one
yearly   = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2005'), coverage=0.2)   # A round every year
campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, when=['2005', '2010'], coverage=0.6)                  # Two rounds

scenarios = {
    'No vaccination':             ss.Sim(sis, **kw_births),
    'Routine at age one, 80%':    ss.Sim(sis, interventions=routine, **kw_births),
    'Yearly rounds, 20%':         ss.Sim(sis, interventions=yearly, **kw_births),
    'Two campaigns, 60%':         ss.Sim(sis, interventions=campaign, **kw_births),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')










births_deaths <- list(ss$birth(rate = ss$peryear(0.03)), ss$death(rate = ss$peryear(0.03)))

routine  <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.8, who = ss$at_age(years(1)), start = "2005", coverage = 0.8)                  # Once per child, as they turn one
yearly   <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.8, when = ss$schedule(every = years(1), start = "2005"), coverage = 0.2) # A round every year
campaign <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.8, when = c("2005", "2010"), coverage = 0.6)                            # Two rounds

scenarios <- list(
  "No vaccination"          = make_sim(demographics = births_deaths),
  "Routine at age one, 80%" = make_sim(demographics = births_deaths, interventions = routine),
  "Yearly rounds, 20%"      = make_sim(demographics = births_deaths, interventions = yearly),
  "Two campaigns, 60%"      = make_sim(demographics = births_deaths, interventions = campaign)
)
msim <- parallel(scenarios)
msim$plot("sis.I")



ss.schedule() makes a list of times; a plain list, when=list(range(2005, 2021)), works too.
As compartments, ss.at_age() needs age groups with an edge at that age (e.g. measles.stratify(age=[0, 0.75, 1, 5, 15]) for 9 months).


Coverage and capacity
coverage=0.7 is a fraction of the eligible people. A typed rate, such as coverage=ss.perday(0.1), is the chance of being reached over the step, which routine delivery offers at every step to those eligible (a rate of seeking care, for example). capacity= is the number available: a bare number is per round (or per step, for delivery on events), and a rate, such as ss.peryear(500), is per unit time, which routine delivery needs. Coverage is applied first, and capacity caps the result (an example is below). When there is too little capacity, those served are chosen at random, unless ss.capacity(n, priority=...) says who comes first: a condition, or a list of them served in order ([sis.I, ss.person.age >= 65]), or a score, highest first (-hiv.cd4). With ss.capacity(n, queue=True), those not served wait, longest first; a duration (queue=ss.months(6)) limits the wait, and those still waiting at its end are the delivery’s outcome never_ran.


Who is eligible
who= is a condition on people or on the states of modules, written before the sim exists: ss.person.age < 15, sis.I, or a combination with &, |, and ~ (and, or, not), such as (ss.person.age >= 65) & ~sis.I. It can also be a condition on the whole population (sis.I.n > 1000), or a function of the sim returning a boolean array, the UIDs of people, or True or False for everyone. A condition on a property of people, such as age, runs as compartments only if the model is stratified by it; otherwise the model runs as agents. The who= of ss.modify() below works the same way.
Here children are vaccinated, and the 200 oldest people who are infected are treated each year, chosen by a function, which is called on each step the delivery happens:

def oldest_infected(sim):
    """ The 200 oldest people who are infected """
    infected = sim.diseases.sis.I.uids
    order = np.argsort(sim.people.age[infected])
    return infected[order[-200:]]

children = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, who=ss.person.age < 15, when=['2005'], coverage=0.9)
targeted = ss.treat(cure=0.9, who=oldest_infected, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2005'))
sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[children, targeted], **kw)
sim.run()
print('Children vaccinated:', sim.results.children.delivered.sum())
print('Treated:', sim.results.targeted.delivered.sum())

Children vaccinated: 1067.0
Treated: 3200.0


A function in when= is a function of the date, true on the steps it is delivered (e.g. when=lambda now: now.month == 1).


Delivery when something happens
An event as when= delivers to the people something has just happened to: a transition (sis.infection, or by its path, 'sis.infection'), or the outcome of another delivery. who= then says which of them are eligible. Here half of people are treated when they are infected, with no limit, or with up to 30 treatments a month:

unlimited = ss.treat(cure=0.9, when=sis.infection, coverage=0.5, name='on_infection')
limited   = ss.treat(cure=0.9, when=sis.infection, coverage=0.5, capacity=30, name='on_infection')
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No treatment':                    ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Treatment on infection':          ss.Sim(sis, interventions=unlimited, **kw),
    'Treatment, at most 30 a month':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=limited, **kw),
})
msim.plot('sis.I')








A delivery triggered by a transition acts on the next step; an outcome of another delivery triggers its follow-up in the same step. For a step that must happen at once, declare it as a transition of the disease, e.g. T >> D @ ss.on(care) (see Diseases).
Each event remembers, per person, whether it ever happened (.ever), how often (.n_times), and how long ago (.since), and ss.mother(cond, include_born=True) holds for a person whose mother meets cond. Here newborns are tested if their mother tested positive at antenatal care within the past year:

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(0.1)) # Conceptions a year per woman: 100 per 1,000
anc = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, who=pregnancy.P, coverage=0.5)
newborn = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, who=ss.mother(anc.positive.since <= ss.years(1), include_born=True), when=pregnancy.birth)
sim = ss.Sim(sis, demographics=pregnancy, interventions=[anc, newborn], **kw)
sim.run()
print('Newborns tested:', sim.results.newborn.delivered.sum())

Newborns tested: 1273.0


As agents, these can be read after a run (sim.interventions.screening.ever.uids), and delivery.reached() gives the UIDs reached on this step. trace= is contact tracing: it delivers to the contacts, on a network, of the people the event in when= selects; a network with memory= reaches recent past partners too (see Contact networks).


Events: moves without a product
ss.Event() is what the deliveries are made from: something that happens to people, here a move between states, with no product. It takes who= and when= as a delivery does, and says how many it reaches with n= (at most that many each time) and p= (the chance for each person); a delivery takes a move as its first argument too, when it needs a delivery’s keywords, such as coverage=. It runs under every solver. Here measles is brought into the town of the first example by two infections a month, and the campaign is a move of the people it protects (80% reached, 93% of them protected) to the recovered state:

PythonR



S, E, I, R = measles.S, measles.E, measles.I, measles.R # The states of the first example's measles
imports  = ss.Event(S >> E, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(30)), n=2) # Two susceptible people infected each month
campaign = ss.Event(S >> R, when='2025-05-01', p=0.8*0.93)            # Protection as a move between states

sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=[imports, campaign], total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.I')










states("S E I R") # The states of the first example's measles
imports  <- ss$Event(Transition(S, E), when = ss$schedule(every = days(30)), n = 2) # Two susceptible people infected each month
campaign <- ss$Event(Transition(S, R), when = "2025-05-01", p = 0.8 * 0.93)       # Protection as a move between states

sim <- Sim(measles, interventions = list(imports, campaign), total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
sim$plot("measles.I")



The other forms of an event:

dict(vaccinated=True) moves people to a level of a stratification, and dict(risk=('low', 'high')) from one level to another (see Stratification).
strain= gives the strain people arrive with in a move into an infected state: ss.Event(S >> E, when=['2021-01-01'], n=20, strain='alpha') brings a new strain in on a date; DS >> RIF changes the strain people carry, e.g. to a drug-resistant one (see Diseases).
increment='doses' adds one to a counter for each person reached (with the model stratified by doses=[0, 1, 2, 3]), and dict(doses=2) adds two.
With no move or increment, an event is a step people attend, such as a clinic visit, which several deliveries can follow with when=visit.

title: Interventions
text:
Changing parameters
ss.modify() changes a quantity in the model for as long as it applies, as distancing does in the first example. The examples in this section use a flu-like epidemic (β = 0.4 per day, infectious for 5 days, so R0 = 2), here with masks that cut transmission by 40% from day 20 to day 60, and distancing that halves it from day 20 and eases to 80% of its usual level from day 60:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)   # Infectious for 5 days on average
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

masks = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start=ss.days(20), stop=ss.days(60))
distancing = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=ss.timeseries({ss.days(20): 0.5, ss.days(60): 0.8}), start=ss.days(20))

kw = dict(total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(flu, **kw),
    'Masks':           ss.Sim(flu, interventions=masks, **kw),
    'Distancing':      ss.Sim(flu, interventions=distancing, **kw),
})
msim.plot('flu.I')








flu.pars.beta is the β of the transmission, which a declared disease names beta.

What a modifier takes
ss.modify(target, multiply=...) applies always, between a start and a stop, at the times when= gives, or where a condition holds (who=). It takes exactly one of:







Keyword
What it does




multiply=
Multiplies the quantity


efficacy=
Removes a fraction of the risk: the same as multiply=1 - efficacy, for protection such as condoms


add=
Adds to the quantity (parameters only), or to an inflow from outside the model (ss.modify(typhoid.shedding, add=ss.perday(4e6)))


set=
Replaces the quantity (parameters only)



and any of:







Keyword
Meaning




who=
Who it applies to: a condition, or a function of the sim (by default, everyone)


start=, stop=
When it starts and stops applying (by default, always): dates, years, or durations after the start


when=
When it applies, on time alone (by default, always): a schedule of times or how often, or a function of the date that returns True on the steps it applies (lambda now: now.month in [6, 7, 8])


until=
Once who= (or when=) selects someone, it stays on for them: for at least this long (a duration), or until this condition holds


frac=
With multiply= or efficacy=, the fraction of acts (or contacts) it applies to, e.g. condom use in 30% of acts; with network=, as agents, a function of the network giving a fraction for each partnership, e.g. frac=lambda net: net.edges.condoms


network=
For a change to transmission, the network or networks it applies on, by name (by default, all)



The amount can itself vary: multiply= takes anything a parameter takes, such as ss.seasonal() or ss.timeseries() (see Parameters). multiply=ss.timeseries({t1: x1, t2: x2}) multiplies the quantity by each value from its time until the next, each relative to the quantity’s own value, not to the one before; set= gives values instead. The times are dates or years in a sim with a calendar, numbers in the sim’s unit in one without, and in either a duration is that long after the start (ss.days(20)).
The target of a modifier is any named quantity in the model:








Target
Example
What it changes




A parameter
flu.pars.beta
The parameter, for everyone it applies to


A transition
flu.recovery
The transition’s rate (or its probability, for a branch with p=)


Susceptibility or infectiousness
flu.rel_sus, flu.rel_trans
Each person’s relative chance of infection, or of infecting others (multiply only)


A network or contact layer
school, from ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=[...])
The contacts on it


Any of these by name
'flu.pars.beta', 'school.pars.n_contacts'
The same, written as a path



Here faster diagnosis from day 30 halves the time that people stay infectious, by doubling the rate of recovery, and susceptibility is halved for people aged 65 and over in an age-structured version of the model:

faster = ss.modify(flu.recovery, multiply=2, start=ss.days(30))
sim = ss.Sim(flu, interventions=faster, **kw)
sim.run()
print('Infections with faster diagnosis:', round(sim.results.flu.infection.sum()))

flu_age = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
flu_age.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
older = ss.modify(flu_age.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, who=ss.person.age >= 65)

sim = ss.Sim(flu_age, interventions=older, **kw)
sim.run()
sim.results.flu_age.I.by('age').plot()

Infections with faster diagnosis: 53684









Closing schools is a modifier on the school layer of a contact matrix: see Population data.


Changes triggered by the epidemic
A rule such as “close schools when cases pass a threshold” is a who= that is a condition on the population, or a function of the sim, which can read the stocks at the start of the step (sim.results.flu.I[sim.ti]) and the flows of the steps before ([sim.ti - 1]). A bare threshold switches on and off as the epidemic crosses it; until= adds memory: once on, the modifier stays on for at least a duration, or until a condition holds. Here transmission is halved for at least 30 days whenever more than 5,000 people are infectious, or from when 2,000 are until 1,000 are:

def many_infectious(sim):
    return sim.results.flu.I[sim.ti] > 5000 # The number infectious at the start of this step

reactive = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, who=many_infectious, until=ss.days(30))
lockdown = ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, who=flu.I.n >= 2000, until=flu.I.n <= 1000)
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention':              ss.Sim(flu, **kw),
    'For 30 days, above 5,000':     ss.Sim(flu, interventions=reactive, **kw),
    'From 2,000 down to 1,000':     ss.Sim(flu, interventions=lockdown, **kw),
})
msim.plot('flu.I')








A condition on a result can be worked out for each place (or other group) on its own: who=flu.infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7), by='patch') > 200e-5 applies in each place whose cases over a week pass 200 per 100,000 people.
Any other rule that remembers what it did is an intervention written as code (see below).


How changes combine
A modifier never overwrites the quantity it changes. The quantity keeps its own base value, and the modifiers active now are applied on top of it to give the effective value, which the model uses:
effective = (the set value, if any, otherwise the base) × every multiplier + every addition
whatever order the modifiers were given in: two 40% reductions give a 64% reduction (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36), and the efficacies of products are multipliers of the same kind. As agents, the effective value of each person is dis.current_value(), e.g. sim.diseases.flu_age.current_value('rel_sus') (rel_sus itself gives the base values), and sim.what_modifies(sim.diseases.flu_age.rel_sus) lists the modifiers on a quantity, with their conditions.
A modifier can be given to the sim with interventions= or connectors=; the two differ only in where they run in each step. By convention, policies go in interventions=, and interactions that are part of the biology in connectors= (see Connectors).
As agents, a change to contacts (such as multiply=0.5 on a layer) means each contact happens with that probability in a step; in a compartmental run, the contacts are scaled.

title: Interventions
text:
Writing an intervention as code
Anything deliveries and modifiers can’t say is a subclass of ss.Intervention with a step() method, which runs on every step and can read and change anything in the sim (see Custom modules, and the tutorial T8 – Custom modules).
An intervention written as code is best kept to deciding, leaving the change itself to ss.modify(), so that the base value is never overwritten and the change combines with others: e.g. an intervention lockdown whose step() sets self.active, and ss.modify(flu.pars.beta, multiply=0.5, who=lambda sim: sim.interventions.lockdown.active). A product whose effect needs code is a subclass of ss.Product instead: see Products.
An intervention that acts on people can be given who=, as a delivery is (including a state by its path, 'flu.I'). Its step() then gets the UIDs of those eligible now, and alive, from self.check_eligibility(), which a subclass can override for a rule of its own:

class Isolate(ss.Intervention):
    """ Each day, a fraction of the people eligible are isolated, which ends their infectiousness """
    def __init__(self, p=0.2, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs) # Including who=
        self.define_pars(p=p)
        return

    def step(self):
        uids = self.check_eligibility()
        self.sim.diseases.flu.move(uids, 'R', p=self.pars.p) # A fraction of those eligible (here the infectious)
        return

isolate = Isolate(who='flu.I')
sim = ss.Sim(flu, interventions=isolate, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0).run()
print('Peak infectious:', sim.results.flu.I.max())

Peak infectious: 10.0

title: Interventions
text:
Pitfalls

Infections delayed, not averted. A change that ends can mostly delay infections rather than avert them: in the first example, distancing for two months pushes the peak months later but averts fewer than a tenth of the infections over the 18 months, while vaccination averts most. How much a temporary change averts depends on the epidemic and on the horizon, so run long enough to count what happens after it ends (see Scenarios).
Routine is once per person. For a fraction of people reached every year, use yearly rounds, or routine delivery with a typed coverage (coverage=ss.probperyear(0.5)), a chance at every step for as long as people are eligible.
A function made in a loop sees the loop’s last value. Every who=lambda sim: sim.people.age >= lower made in for lower in [0, 15]: uses 15. Use a condition (who=ss.person.age >= lower), which keeps the value it was written with.

The API reference for this page: Interventions, Connectors (for ss.modify()).

title: Interventions
text:
Further reading

Covasim: Interventions: changing transmission, testing, tracing, and vaccination in an agent-based model
epydemix: Modeling interventions: changing contacts over time in a compartmental model
EMOD: Creating campaigns: another framework’s approach to events, eligibility, and coverage of interventions

title: Interventions
text:
Appendix: reference

Every delivery



Delivery
What it delivers
Use it for




ss.vaccinate()
A vaccine (ss.Vaccine): protection for as long as it is held
Vaccination, prophylaxis such as PrEP, bed nets


ss.screen()
A test (ss.Diagnostic), whose outcomes trigger what follows
Screening, diagnosis, triage


ss.treat()
A treatment (ss.Treatment): a cure or other move when given, effects while held, or both
Cures, and treatment that suppresses infection, such as ART


ss.Delivery()
Any product, including one written as code
A product of your own, with its own administer()


ss.Event()
No product: a move between states or levels, a counter, or a visit
Importations, protection as states of a disease, changes of risk group


ss.modify()
Nothing: a change to a quantity of the model
Distancing, masks, school closures, condoms


An ss.Intervention written as code
Anything
Anything else (above)



The library has interventions for its own diseases: ssl.ART (see Diseases in the library) and ssl.mnch.treat_pregnant (see Maternal, newborn, and child health).


Who and when
What when= and who= (and a capacity’s priority=) can be:



Kind
Examples
Who it is




A transition
sis.infection, 'sis.infection', a branch tb.progression.to(tb.active)
The people who went through it on this step


Entering or leaving a set of states
(sis.I \| sis.R).enter, ss.ref('ng.C').enter
The people who entered (or left) it from outside it on this step


A delivery, or its outcomes
screening, screening.positive, treatment.failed
The people it reached, or with that outcome, on this step (see Products)


An event of pregnancy
pregnancy.birth, pregnancy.conception, pregnancy.delivery
The children born; the women who conceived, or delivered


The memory of an event
screening.positive.ever, .n_times >= 2, .since <= ss.years(1)
Whether, how often, and how long ago it happened to each person


A state
sis.I, ~sis.I, ss.ref('hpv18.X')
The people in it now


The time in a set of states
(sis.I \| sis.R).time_in > ss.years(1)
The time since each person entered it


A property of people
ss.person.age < 15, ss.person.female, any stratification, e.g. measles.age < 15
The people with it


A product held
vaccine.held, ss.Vaccine.held
The people who hold it (or any vaccine) now


Someone’s mother
ss.mother(anc.positive.ever, include_born=True)
The people whose mother meets the condition (agents only)


A count, or a fraction
sis.I.n > 1000, sis.I.frac > 0.02
Everyone, on the steps when it holds


Recent incidence
flu.infection.incidence(over=ss.days(7), by='patch') > 200e-5
Everyone in the groups where it holds, on the steps when it does


A function of the sim
lambda sim: sim.people.age >= 15
Whatever it returns: a boolean array, UIDs, or one value for everyone


A function of the date (when=)
lambda now: now.month == 1
Everyone, on the steps when it returns True



The ways to time an event or a delivery:







when=
Means




None
Routinely: each person once, at the first step they are eligible


'2025-05-01', 2025, [5, 30]
In rounds, at these times


ss.days(30)
In a round 30 days after the start


ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1))
In rounds, this far apart, from the start


sis.infection, screening.positive
When the event happens, to the people it happened to


ss.on(screening.positive, delay=ss.months(3))
That long after the event (agents only)


ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start=2025, stop=2030)
Times or how often, between a start and a stop; with only start= and stop=, routinely between them


start=2025, stop=2030 (beside when=)
Any of these within that window, e.g. when=screening.positive, start=2025



Reaching people as they reach an age is who, not when: who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9)).


What needs agents
A model with any of these runs as agents, unless a solver is asked for, when it is an error that names the reason (see Solvers):



Feature
Why it needs agents




ss.on(event, delay=...), or a delay on a test
People wait


ss.capacity(..., queue=...)
People wait


trace=
Only agents have contacts


.since and .n_times of an event (not .ever)
Only agents keep them per person


ss.mother()
Only agents know who someone’s mother is


disease=[...] with several diseases (not a product keyed by disease)
Each person is tested or treated for each


A function of (sim, uids) in who=, coverage=, or priority=
It reads particular people


Waning by a function of time (not ss.boxcar())
Only agents keep the time since delivery


A product written as code, or an intervention that acts on particular people
It acts on agents


A condition on a property the model is not stratified by (e.g. age)
Only agents have it

title: Health economics
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Every product in Starsim takes a cost=, the cost of each delivery, and each delivery then records what it spent as a result, cost, next to the number it delivered. With the results of a scenario without the program, that gives the cost of a program and the cost per outcome averted. The tools for adding costs up, discounting them, counting DALYs, and comparing scenarios are in the Starsim library, in ssl.econ: ssl.Costs, ssl.DALYs, ssl.discount(), and ssl.ICER. They are short, so they can be copied and changed for an evaluation that needs something else. What each product does is on Products, and how they are delivered on Interventions.

title: Health economics
text:
Costing a vaccination program
Here is measles in a population of a million people over 30 years, with births and deaths, so that it stays endemic. From 2010, a program vaccinates 80% of infants, in yearly rounds, and each dose costs $5, the cost of the vaccine and of giving it. The model is stratified by age, so that infants can be picked out, and runs as an ODE:

import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day, for an R0 of about 15
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 1, 5, 15, 65])

demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.01))]
pars = dict(demographics=demographics, total_pop=1_000_000, start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)

routine = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, leaky=False, who=ss.person.age < 1, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2010'), coverage=0.8, cost=5.0)

base = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
msim = ss.parallel({'No vaccination': base, 'Routine vaccination': base.new(interventions=routine)})

The delivery’s result cost is the amount spent on each step; over a year, it is the cost of that year’s round:

vx = msim.sims['Routine vaccination']
vx.results.routine.cost.resample('year').plot()








The cost of the program, and the infections it averts, are the totals of these results, and their ratio is the cost per infection averted:

no_vx = msim.sims['No vaccination']
cost = vx.results.routine.cost.sum()
doses = vx.results.routine.delivered.sum()
averted = no_vx.results.measles.infection.sum() - vx.results.measles.infection.sum()

print('Doses given:', round(doses))
print('Total cost ($):', round(cost))
print('Infections averted:', round(averted))
print('Cost per infection averted ($):', round(cost/averted, 2))

Doses given: 526384
Total cost ($): 2631922
Infections averted: 436355
Cost per infection averted ($): 6.03


The same count works for any outcome a model has, such as deaths or cases needing treatment, if the model declares them (see Outcomes).
Costs work the same under every solver. In a compartmental run, the number delivered on a step is a number of people; as agents, the cost is counted per agent and scaled, like any count, by the number of people each agent stands for. A delivery that offers a product but doesn’t give it (to someone not eligible, or beyond its capacity) costs nothing.

title: Health economics
text:
Comparing programs
When there are several programs, the question is usually what each one adds over the next cheapest: its incremental cost per outcome averted (an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, or ICER). Here the routine program is compared with the same program plus a campaign every four years for children under five, at $8 a dose:

campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, leaky=False, who=ss.person.age < 5, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(4), start='2010'), coverage=0.9, cost=8.0)

costed = base.new(analyzers=ssl.Costs()) # Adds up the cost of every delivery, as the result costs.total
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No vaccination':         costed,
    'Routine':                costed.new(interventions=routine),
    'Routine and campaigns':  costed.new(interventions=[routine, campaign]),
})

icer = ssl.ICER(msim, outcome='measles.infection')
icer.df.round()

ssl.Costs gives each sim a result for the cost of each delivery, and their total, costs.total. ssl.ICER orders the scenarios by cost, and compares each with the next cheaper one that is not dominated: the incremental cost over the incremental outcome averted (here infections; by default, DALYs). Outcomes averted are counted from the first scenario, unless baseline= names another.
Here routine vaccination costs about $6 per infection averted, and adding the campaigns about $22 for each further infection averted. Neither program is dominated: a program is dominated (dominated) if a cheaper one averts as much, and extendedly dominated (extended) if a mix of two others would avert more for the same cost; neither kind gets a ratio. ssl.ICER takes any number of scenarios, and with several runs of each compares their means; its columns and methods (such as icer.best(wtp=1000), the best scenario at a willingness to pay) are in the appendix.
ssl.ICER can also be an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs: the sim is then compared at each step with the finished sims it is given, so that an intervention can act on the result (e.g. follow sim.analyzers.icer.best(wtp=1000)); window=ss.years(1) compares the latest year alone. How best to divide a budget between programs is an optimization: see Optimization.

title: Health economics
text:
Disability-adjusted life years
ssl.DALYs counts disability-adjusted life years as results: the time people spend in a state, multiplied by its disability weight (yld, years lived with disability), plus the years of life lost to deaths (yll). ssl.ICER compares these by default, so the outcome doesn’t need naming. Here is a curable infection that kills 1% a year of those infected and has a disability weight of 0.05, and a test-and-treat program that costs $4 a test and $20 a treatment, as 5,000 agents standing for 100,000 people:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, deaths=ss.death(I, rate=ss.peryear(0.01)), init_prev=0.1, name='sis')

screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2010'), coverage=0.5, cost=4.0)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8, cost=20.0)

analyzers = [ssl.Costs(), ssl.DALYs(weights={'sis.I': 0.05})]
base = ss.Sim(sis, analyzers=analyzers, n_agents=5000, total_pop=100_000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({'No program': base, 'Test and treat': base.new(interventions=[screening, treatment])})

for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results.dalys
    print(sim.label, '- YLD:', round(res.yld.sum()), '- YLL:', round(res.yll.sum()), '- DALYs:', round(res.dalys.sum()))
ssl.ICER(msim).df.round()
