With agents, the years of life lost come from each person’s age at death and a standard life table (from the Global Burden of Disease 2019 study). Compartmental runs don’t record ages at death, so they take a number: ssl.DALYs(weights=..., life_lost=30).

Costs with uncertainty
A model run as agents gives different costs and effects in each run, so a cost per outcome averted needs several runs, paired by seed (as n_runs= does). Here the test-and-treat program is run 8 times for each scenario:

msim = ss.parallel({'No program': base, 'Test and treat': base.new(interventions=[screening, treatment])}, n_runs=8)

res = msim.results
program = 'Test and treat'
cost = sum(res[name].cost.select(scenario=program).values.sum(axis=1) for name in ['screening', 'treatment']) # The cost of each run of the program
averted = -res.sis.infection.diff('No program')[program].values.sum(axis=1) # The infections it averted, run by run (paired by seed)
print('Infections averted, fewest:', round(averted.min()))
ratio = cost / averted

print('Cost per infection averted ($), median and range:', np.round(np.median(ratio), 1), np.round([ratio.min(), ratio.max()], 1))

Infections averted, fewest: 77380
Cost per infection averted ($), median and range: 62.5 [52.9 64.8]


A ratio is only meaningful when the program averted something: here every run averts many thousands of infections, but a small program can avert none, or fewer than none, in a run by chance, giving an infinite or negative ratio. Check the outcomes averted before dividing, or compare mean costs and outcomes (as ssl.ICER does). The uncertainty here is only from chance: uncertainty in the parameters needs runs with values drawn from their priors as well (ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=...); see Scenarios).

title: Health economics
text:
Discounting and other costs
Economic evaluations usually discount costs and outcomes in later years, at 3% a year for example. ssl.discount() weights each time point of a result by (1 + rate)**-(t - start), for a time t in years, and gives back a result. Here the two runs of the first example (vx and no_vx), discounted at 3% a year from 2010:

cost = ssl.discount(vx.results.routine.cost, 0.03, start=2010).sum()
averted = ssl.discount(no_vx.results.measles.infection - vx.results.measles.infection, 0.03, start=2010).sum()
print('Discounted cost ($):', round(cost))
print('Discounted infections averted:', round(averted))
print('Discounted cost per infection averted ($):', round(cost/averted, 2))

Discounted cost ($): 1959273
Discounted infections averted: 327287
Discounted cost per infection averted ($): 5.99


A cost that does not depend on deliveries, such as running a program (staff, cold chain, training), is an amount per year; the cost of the disease itself, such as care for each case, is a cost per infection, which the infections averted then save. ssl.Costs takes both: fixed=, a cost per unit time from start= (e.g. ss.peryear(20_000)), and unit_costs=, the cost of each event of any result, by its path (and deliveries=False leaves out the costs of the deliveries, for a table of the other costs alone). Here the program costs $20,000 a year to run from 2010, and each infection $50 of care, in both scenarios, so that the difference between them is the net cost:

care = {'measles.infection': 50} # $50 of care for each infection
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No vaccination': ss.Sim(measles, analyzers=ssl.Costs(unit_costs=care), **pars),
    'Routine':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=routine, analyzers=ssl.Costs(unit_costs=care, fixed=ss.peryear(20_000), start=2010), **pars),
})
df = ssl.ICER(msim, outcome='measles.infection', discount=0.03, discount_start=2010).df # Discounted, as above
print(df[['cost', 'averted']].round())
net = df.cost['Routine'] - df.cost['No vaccination']
print('Net cost per infection averted ($):', round(net/df.averted['Routine'], 2))

                      cost   averted
scenario                            
Routine         79313061.0  327287.0
No vaccination  93415774.0       0.0
Net cost per infection averted ($): -43.09


A net cost below zero means a program saves more than it costs; ssl.ICER then marks the scenario without it as dominated.

title: Health economics
text:
Pitfalls

The cost is per delivery. cost= is the cost of each product given, including what it takes to give it; costs that don’t grow with the number delivered are added separately, as above.
Count every delivery. A program of several steps (a test, then treatment) has a cost for each; add them up.
Compare like with like. Take costs and outcomes from the same runs, over the same period (see Scenarios).
The horizon matters. Infections averted after the end of the run are not counted, and a program that starts late in a run has had little time to avert any.

The API reference for this page: Products, Economics.

title: Health economics
text:
Further reading

WHO: Making choices in health, a guide to cost-effectiveness analysis: the methods behind cost per outcome averted
Atomica: Optimization: allocating spending between programs in a compartmental framework built around program costs
Optima HIV: allocation of HIV budgets with program costs and coverage

title: Health economics
text:
Appendix: the economic tools
The tools in ssl.econ, with the first line of each one’s documentation (see the API reference, Economics):

import inspect

for module in [ssl.econ.costs, ssl.econ.dalys]:
    for name in module.__all__:
        print(f'ssl.{name}: {inspect.getdoc(getattr(module, name)).splitlines()[0]}')

ssl.Costs: The costs of a sim, from its results, with their total
ssl.discount: Discount values over time at a yearly rate
ssl.DALYs: The disability-adjusted life years of a sim: the years lived with disability, plus the years of life lost
ssl.ICER: Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios


The columns of ssl.ICER(...).df, one row for each scenario:







Column
Meaning




cost
The total cost (discounted, with discount=), from ssl.Costs unless cost= names another result


outcome
The total of the outcome, from ssl.DALYs unless outcome= names another result


averted
The outcome of the baseline less the scenario’s


incremental cost
The cost more than the next cheaper scenario that is not dominated


incremental averted
The outcome averted more than that scenario


ICER
Their ratio, the incremental cost per outcome averted (none for a dominated scenario)


dominated
Whether a cheaper scenario averts as much or more


extended
Whether a mix of two other scenarios would avert more for the same cost (extended dominance)



And its methods: icer.plot() (each run on the cost-effectiveness plane), icer.plot_ceac() (the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve: how often each scenario is best at each willingness to pay), and icer.best(wtp=...) (the best scenario at a willingness to pay).

title: Parameters
text:
🧠9% 🤖91%
The parameters of a model are the numbers in it: transmission rates, durations, fractions, and the like. This page covers where they live, their units, how to name and change them, and the forms a value can take.

title: Parameters
text:
Values live in the model
In a declared disease, a value lives where it is used. There is no separate block of parameters to fill in: each number becomes a parameter, named after its role. The “Explicit” tab gives each parameter its name outright, with ss.par(..., name=...), and β its unit; the parameters, and the results, are the same:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars

Pars(init_prev=par(0.001), beta=par(1.9), dur_I=par(days(8)))




library(starsim)

states("S I R")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I)
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))
measles <- Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev = 0.001)

measles$pars



beta  = ss.par(ss.perday(1.9), name='beta') # Named for what it multiplies: the fraction infectious
dur_I = ss.par(ss.days(8), name='dur_I')    # Named for the state it is the time in

S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=beta*I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=dur_I, name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'measles',
)

measles_explicit.pars

Pars(init_prev=par(0.001), beta=par(perday(1.9)), dur_I=par(days(8)))





The number that multiplies a source of infection is beta, a duration is named by the state it is the time in (dur_I), and a rate by its transition (rate_death); the full rules cover the rest.

Units of time
A typed value says its unit: ss.days(8) is a duration, and ss.perday(1.9), ss.peryear(0.02) are rates. A bare number is in the sim’s unit, here days, from ss.days(8), so β = 1.9 is per day. Time says how the unit is chosen; to depend on none of it, type every rate or give the sim unit=.
Values are converted to the time step of the sim, whatever it is, so the same model can be run with a step of a day or a week. A rate (ss.perday) is a rate, converted exactly. A probability over a period, such as a 10% chance of recovering each day, is written ss.prob(0.1, 'day'), and is converted as a probability: over a week it is 1 − 0.9^7, not 0.7. See Time for durations, rates, and dates.

title: Parameters
text:
Named parameters
When a parameter is to be documented, reused, or fitted, give it a name with ss.par(). It behaves like its value in a rate, so it can be used anywhere a number can:

PythonR



beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day', source='Chosen to give R0 of about 15')
dur  = ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[ss.days(6), ss.days(10)], doc='Infectious period', source='About 4 days either side of the rash')

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

measles.pars

Pars(
    init_prev = par(0.001),
    beta      = par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day'),
    dur       = par(days(8), bounds=[days(6), days(10)], doc='Infectious period'),
)




library(starsim)

beta <- par(1.9, bounds = c(1, 3), doc = "Transmission rate per day", source = "Chosen to give R0 of about 15")
dur  <- par(days(8), bounds = c(days(6), days(10)), doc = "Infectious period", source = "About 4 days either side of the rash")

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = beta * I),
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = dur),
  init_prev = 0.001
)

measles$pars




The name is taken from the variable (beta), or given with name=.
bounds is the range of plausible values. A parameter with bounds can be fitted: sim.fit() fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data (Fitting a model). A value outside its bounds is an error.
doc (what it means) and source (where the value came from) are free text. describe() shows them under the transition that uses the parameter, and they are kept when the model is saved.
prior= gives a distribution of belief about the value: its uncertainty, not variation between people. It is used in calibration (Fitting a model), and to carry that uncertainty into projections, with runs that draw the value from its prior (ss.parallel(sim, priors=True, n_runs=...); Scenarios).
label= is a human-readable name, for plots and tables.

ss.pars(defaults, **kwargs) makes several named parameters at once, for a disease declared in __init__() (Diseases). A module written as code gives its parameters with define_pars() (Custom modules).

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.describe()

Changing a parameter
A parameter can be changed when the sim is made, by name, without changing the model, e.g. to use a fitted set of values:

PythonR



sim = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
print('R0 with beta = 1.5:', round(sim.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 12, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0016 s; measles: 99,899 infections; at most 70,922 infectious, on day 7
R0 with beta = 1.5: 12.0




sim <- Sim(measles, pars = list(beta = 1.5), total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50))
sim$run()
cat("R0 with beta = 1.5:", round(sim$diseases$measles$R0(), 1), "\n")



With several modules, a parameter’s name is given with its module’s, e.g. pars={'measles.beta': 1.5}. A name that matches no parameter is an error, which lists the names there are, so a misspelled parameter is never silently ignored:

try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=1.5)).init()
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

KeyNotFoundError pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are measles.init_prev, measles.beta, measles.dur; did you mean measles.beta?


A parameter can also be changed during a run, from a date or when a condition holds, with ss.modify(); see Interventions.

title: Parameters
section: The forms a value can take
text:
The forms a value can take
Where a value is given decides what it means; the form it takes is free. Each of these can be a rate, a duration, a fraction, or a starting value:








Form
Example
Means




A number
1.9
The same for everyone, always (in the model’s unit of time)


A typed value
ss.perday(1.9), ss.days(8)
The same, in its own unit


A value for each group
ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0])
One value for each age group (or other group)


A time series
ss.timeseries({'2025-01-01': 1.9, '2025-03-01': 1.2})
Changes over time, from given values


A seasonal cycle
ss.seasonal(mean=1.9, amplitude=0.2, peak='March')
A yearly cycle around a mean


A function of the sim
lambda sim: 1.9 if sim.now < ss.date('2025-03-01') else 1.2
Worked out at each step


A distribution
ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2))
Varies between people


A function of the sim and the people
lambda sim, uids: ...
One value for each person (agents only)



A function takes any of self (the module whose value it is), sim, and uids (the people it is for), by those names, in any order: lambda sim: ..., lambda self, sim: ..., and lambda self, sim, uids: ... all work. One that takes uids gives a value for each person, so runs as agents only; one that doesn’t means the same under every solver.
Any of these can be wrapped in ss.par() to give it a name, bounds, or a source.

Values for each group
ss.by() gives a value for each level of a stratification. Here β is higher for children than for older adults, and each scenario reports the fraction of each age group’s susceptible people infected in a year. The “Explicit” tab gives β by age as a function of each person’s age instead, so it runs as agents:

PythonRExplicit



import pandas as pd

def make_measles(beta):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction in each
    return measles

betas = {
    'The same for everyone': 1.9,
    'By age':                ss.by(age=[2.5, 1.9, 1.0]),
}
attack = {}
for label, beta in betas.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    attack[label] = {age: round(res.infection.select(age=age).sum() / res.S.select(age=age)[0], 2) for age in ['0-14', '15-64', '65+']}
pd.DataFrame(attack) # The fraction of each group's susceptible people infected

make_measles <- function(beta) {
  states("S I R")
  infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = beta * I)
  recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))
  measles <- Disease(infection, recovery, init = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))), init_n = list(I = 10), name = "measles")
  measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction in each
  measles
}

betas <- list(
  "The same for everyone" = 1.9,
  "By age"                = ss$by(age = c(2.5, 1.9, 1.0))
)
attack <- sapply(betas, function(beta) {
  sim <- Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", verbose = 0)
  sim$run()
  res <- sim$results$measles
  sapply(c("0-14", "15-64", "65+"), function(age) {
    round(sum(res$infection$select(age = age)$values) / res$S$select(age = age)$values[1], 2)
  })
})
attack # The fraction of each group's susceptible people infected



import numpy as np

def beta_by_age(sim, uids):
    """ β for each person: 2.5 per day under 15, 1.9 from 15 to 64, and 1.0 from 65 """
    age = sim.people.age[uids]
    return ss.perday(np.where(age < 15, 2.5, np.where(age < 65, 1.9, 1.0)))

betas_explicit = {
    'The same for everyone': 1.9,
    'By age':                ss.par(beta_by_age),
}
attack_explicit = {}
for label, beta in betas_explicit.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(beta), total_pop=100_000, n_agents=20_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    attack_explicit[label] = {age: round(res.infection.select(age=age).sum() / res.S.select(age=age)[0], 2) for age in ['0-14', '15-64', '65+']}

The values can also be given by label (ss.by(age={'0-14': 2.5, ...})), as a table, or for several dimensions at once. See Stratification. They can also come from code, as a function of the sim that gives one value per level, worked out at each step: ss.by(patch=fn), e.g. a biting rate in each place from mosquitoes written as code, whatever other dimensions the sim has.


Values that change over time
Contact patterns, reporting, and treatment change over time, and so do the parameters that stand for them. A value can be a time series (ss.timeseries()), held or interpolated between given dates; a smooth yearly cycle (ss.seasonal()); or a function of the sim, worked out at each step. Each goes wherever a number would, in a rate, a fraction, or a starting value. Time covers them, with examples of measles with and without school terms. A change made by an intervention, from a date or when a condition holds (ss.modify()), is covered in Interventions.


Values that vary between people
A distribution, given as a value, gives each person their own value: recovery = I >> R @ ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(8), std=ss.days(2)) gives each person their own infectious period. For durations, a compartmental run represents the distribution with stages; see Durations and Distributions.
A function of the sim and the people, fn(sim, uids), returns one value for each person it is given, and can use anything about them. Here the infectious period is longer for children under 5:

def dur_fn(sim, uids):
    age = sim.people.age[uids]
    return ss.days(8 + 4*(age < 5)) # 12 days for children under 5, 8 for everyone else

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(dur_fn)) # Each person's own duration, as given
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
same = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.constant(ss.days(8))), init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), verbose=0) # A quarter-day step, short enough for measles as agents
msim = ss.parallel({
    '8 days for everyone': ss.Sim(same, **pars),
    '12 days under 5':     ss.Sim(measles, **pars),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')








A function in a rate is called each step for the people in its source state; multiplied by a condition, only for those it holds for (with ss.par(fn, name='infant')*(ss.person.age < 1), fn is given only the children under 1). A function about individual people needs agents; where the same thing can be said by group (ss.by(age=...)), it runs under every solver.
A distribution in a rate gives each person their own rate: in S >> I @ ss.gamma(shape=0.5, scale=3.8)*I, each person has their own transmission rate (the same as ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.gamma(shape=0.5, scale=3.8)*I)). A distribution on its own after @ is a dwell time; times a state, it is a rate.

title: Parameters
text:
Pitfalls

A bare number in the wrong unit. A bare number is in the model’s unit of time: in a model whose unit is years, I >> R @ 0.125 is 0.125 per year. Typed values (ss.perday(0.125), ss.days(8)) don’t depend on it.
Changing the disease after the sim is made. A sim runs its own copy of each module, made when the sim is made, so changing measles afterwards doesn’t change that sim, and changing sim.diseases.measles doesn’t change measles. To try another value, give it by name to a new sim (ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5)), or sim.new(pars=dict(beta=1.5))), and read a run’s values from the sim’s copy (Writing models).
A distribution as a value or as a prior. A distribution as a value is variation between people. Uncertainty about a single value is a prior, ss.par(1.9, prior=...), used in calibration and in runs with priors=True.
A function where a time series would do. A function can’t be printed by describe(), exported to another framework, or written out as equations.

title: Parameters
text:
Further reading

epiparameter: a library of epidemiological parameters (incubation periods, serial intervals, and the like) from the literature, in R
Rates and probabilities in economic modelling: converting between rates and probabilities over different periods
pomp: estimating the parameters of stochastic dynamic models, in R

title: From declaration to run
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A disease written as code, as a class whose step() method changes arrays of agents, can be run but not read: Starsim can’t describe the model, draw it, or run it any other way. A declared disease is instead a set of objects (states, transitions, parameters) that describe the model without running it. Everything else is derived from them: the description, the diagram and equations, the stratified model, the exports to other frameworks, and the engines that run it as an ODE, a stochastic compartmental model, or agents.
This page follows a model from those objects to a run: the objects, how they are resolved and checked, what sim.init() does, how time and the order of a step work, and how Starsim reports what it assumed. For how to write a disease as a modeler, see Diseases and Writing models.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Declaring a model

States and transitions
A state (ss.State) is something a person can be in: a compartment in an ODE, a boolean array over agents in an agent-based run. A transition (ss.Transition) moves people between states, driven by a rate, a dwell time, a branch probability, or a trigger. The ways of writing a model (operators, ss.Transition(), a class body, or define_states() and define_transitions() in __init__(); see Writing models) all build the same objects, and give the same results. This is a rule of the design: a keyword means the same thing in every form, and subclassing adds behavior, not vocabulary. A transition takes the state objects themselves, never their names as strings, so nothing is inferred from a name. What is declared in __init__() is collected as it is given and built once, when the outermost __init__() returns (BuiltAfterInit in starsim/diseases.py), so a subclass can add to its parent’s states before anything is built; after that, declaring more raises an error.


Rates are expressions
When you write 0.3 * I, nothing is computed. I is a state, so the result is an expression (ss.expressions.Expr, in starsim/internals/expressions.py): a small tree whose leaves are parameters, states, counts (I.n), and properties of people (ss.person.age), joined by arithmetic and NumPy functions. Each engine evaluates the same tree in its own terms (a value for each group, for each agent, or as JAX arrays for gradients), which is what lets one model run under any solver.
Two kinds of leaf differ. I.n is the number of people in I, used literally (or, in an acquisition’s rate with a contact matrix, the number met through it). A bare I means contact with people in I: with no network that’s I.n / N, so beta * I is the textbook beta * S * I / N, and with a network each engine works it out from who actually meets whom, which no single formula can say. Since that is a sum over contacts, a rate must be linear in its bare states (beta * I * I raises a ValueError that suggests the two ways to say what was probably meant). Engines and transmission covers how each engine turns a bare state into a force of infection.
The kind of a transition is derived from its rate, not declared: if the rate mentions a bare state, the transition is contact-mediated and that state is a source of infection; otherwise it is spontaneous. For sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10)):
sir.infection.contact     # True: its rate mentions I
sir.infection.terms       # {I: par(0.3)}: the coefficient of each source of infection
sir.recovery.contact      # False


Parameters
A number written inline becomes a parameter of the module, named after its slot (beta for the coefficient of I, dur_I for the time in I; the rules are in the appendix of Writing models). The slot decides what a value means, and the form is free: a value may be a number, an ss.par() with bounds or a source, or vary by group, in time, or between people. See Parameters.


Dimensions
Age, sex, place, and risk group are all handled by one operation, stratify(), which divides a finished model by a property of people. It doesn’t copy the states: the dimension becomes an axis, with one row per group in a compartmental run, and an array on the people as agents. The base model and the stratification don’t refer to each other, so one disease can be reused with different structures, and a stratified result is still one result (res.I.by('age')). The code is in starsim/internals/dimensions.py (ss.dimensions.Strat), and the groups a sim ends up with are sim.groups. See Stratification.


The vocabulary
The design record lists every public name in one place (The complete vocabulary), and a name is added only after asking whether Starsim already has one, whether it can be written with what exists (a bednet is an ss.modify), whether more than one kind of model would use it, and whether a keyword is enough. Modules, containers, and base classes are CamelCase (ss.Sim, ss.Vaccine); the pieces put inside them are lowercase (ss.days, ss.modify, ss.vaccinate). Importers write only names a person would write by hand.

title: From declaration to run
text:
The graph: resolve, complete, check
When ss.Disease(...) is called, it builds the module’s graph (ss.graph.Graph, in starsim/internals/graph.py). The graph is where the objects you wrote become a model:

Collect and name. It gathers the states, transitions, parameters, and results, and names any that have no name: from the keyword they were passed under, then a name= argument, then the variable they’re bound to in the calling code. A transition with none of these is named infection if it is the disease’s only transmission (as in ss.SIR), and otherwise gets a name built from its endpoints (I_to_R); a state with none raises a ValueError, since a made-up state name would leak into results. Names are picked up from variables in this one place; it can miss (a transition written inline in the call gets the fallback name), and describe() shows the names used.
Resolve. It finds which states are people and which are plain counts (a water reservoir, a mosquito population), derives the kind of each transition from its rate, marks the sources of infection, works out which transitions are acquisitions of the disease, and finds the first state (where people start and are born into).
Complete. It turns inline values into named parameters, and groups the exits of each state into those that compete (rates, resolved together in one draw; see below) and those that split on entry (p=).
Check. It checks what can be checked without a sim: the time dimension of every rate, that branch probabilities add up, that exposure is linear, and that keywords name real parameters.

So mistakes in the model’s structure are errors when the disease is built, at the line that made it. What needs the sim (the unit of bare numbers, values against their bounds, the shapes of values by group, the choice of solver) is checked at sim.init().

Guessed defaults
Short models leave a lot unsaid: how a dwell time is distributed, how people mix, how many there are. Starsim fills each gap with a guessed default, and describe() marks every guess:

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(bounds=[0.1, 1.0], source='to be fitted')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(3)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=100)
sim.describe()

Every [guessed: ...] is a choice you didn’t make: 10,000 people, the ODE solver, homogeneous mixing, 11 Erlang stages for the lognormal dwell time, and beta starting at the geometric middle of its bounds. Each guess is tested both ways: a model that makes it has it marked, and one that doesn’t, doesn’t.
Because the model is data, its other views (equations(), diagram(), and the table of transitions, all in starsim/internals/display.py; see Writing models) and its exports (below) are read from the same graph.

title: From declaration to run
text:
What sim.init() does
Creating a sim only stores what it was given (as copies, so one sir can go into several sims). The rest happens at sim.init(), which sim.run() and sim.describe() call if needed. In order (Sim.init() in starsim/sim.py, and choose_solver() and the steps that build a declared model in starsim/solvers/choose.py):

Values. Values given by name (pars=dict(beta=0.1)) are set, and each parameter is checked against its bounds (a ValueError).
Groups. The stratifications of the sim and its modules are collected into sim.groups.
Unit. The unit of bare numbers is chosen (below).
Solver. Starsim lays the model out as compartments (which runs none of its code) and, under solver='auto', chooses an ODE if every part has a compartmental form, agents otherwise; a compartmental run reuses that layout. See Engines and transmission.
Objects. The timeline, the people, and for each declared disease an engine, the object that runs its transitions under the chosen solver. This is the one place where the solver changes which objects exist.
Starting values. Random number streams (Random numbers), people’s attributes, then each state’s initial conditions.
Results and the loop. Results are allocated, data is attached to them by name, and the loop’s functions are collected. Parameters are locked, so setting one that doesn’t exist raises an error.
Report. One line saying what will run and how, a note for each inference or approximation (kept in sim.notes), and for a compartmental model with transmission, R0 and the number infectious at the start. The reason for the solver is in sim.solver_reason, and in describe().


S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01')
sim.init()

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, 2020-01-01 to 2020-07-01
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start


Sim(n=10000; 2020-01-01—2020-07-01; diseases=sir)


Errors are raised at the earliest point that can detect them: a mistake in the model’s structure when the module is built, a value out of bounds at step 1, and a function that asks for something the solver can’t give when it is first called. After sim.init() the sim’s settings are frozen: a changed copy is made with sim.new().

The runtime objects
The engines and modules are covered in Architecture and Engines and transmission. The other objects a module written as code reads and writes are:

People. As agents, sim.people (starsim/people.py) has one entry per agent: age, sex, whether alive, and every module’s states. In a compartmental run it has one row per group, so people.age in a model not stratified by age raises an ss.CapabilityError saying to stratify or run as agents.
Arrays. As agents, a declared state is an ss.BoolState over agents (starsim/internals/arrays.py), beside the ss.FloatArr and others that code adds. Arrays grow as agents are born; the dead leave at the end of the step. Writes by code to a declared state (sir.I[uids] = True) are tracked, so counts see them; writes through .raw, the NumPy array underneath, are not. See Array indexing.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Units, time points, and steps
Durations, hazard rates, probabilities per period, and frequencies are types of their own (starsim/internals/time.py, with dates in internals/dates.py): converting one to a timestep is the type’s job (a hazard r becomes the probability 1 − exp(−r·dt), a frequency the expected count f·dt), and arithmetic that mixes them wrongly raises a TypeError. A bare number is typed by its slot (after @, a rate; for dur=, a duration), in the sim’s unit, which is taken from unit= or inferred from the typed values and dates (Time lists the order). The unit is never guessed from the size of a number (0.05 is plausible per day and per year); Time says when inferring it prints a note.
A sim has time points 0, 1, ..., N, from start to stop. Step k runs from time point k to time point k + 1:
time point   0         1         2               N
             |--step 0-|--step 1-|--  ...  --|--step N-|
stocks       I[0]      I[1]      I[2]        I[N]
flows        inf[0]    inf[1]    inf[2]      inf[N]
A step is taken from every time point, the last one included, so every time point is a period:

A stock at time point k (e.g. I[k], the number infectious) is the state at the start of step k. I[0] is the initial condition.
A flow at time point k (e.g. infection[k], the new infections) is the total during step k.

So with yearly steps, the row for 2020 holds the prevalence on 1 January 2020 and the infections during 2020, which is how data labeled “2020” are usually meant. The state after the last step isn’t recorded, so after a run sim.people is one step past the last time point.
Throughout step k, in every module, sim.ti is k (the index, where results go) and sim.now is time point k as a date or a duration (the value, at which values that vary in time are read).
Because a stock is the state at the start of a step and a flow is the total over it, each stock is the one before it plus the flows of the step between them:

import numpy as np

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=ss.SIR(), total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=60, solver='binomial', verbose=0)
sim.run()
r = sim.results.sir
print('I[0], the initial condition:', r.I[0])
print('S[k+1] - S[k] == -infection[k] at every step:', np.array_equal(np.diff(r.S), -r.infection[:-1]))

I[0], the initial condition: 100.0
S[k+1] - S[k] == -infection[k] at every step: True



Why stocks and flows are recorded separately
A stock is a snapshot and a flow is a sum over an interval, so they are ready at different times. The stocks are ready at the start of a step, before anything has changed. The flows are ready only at its end, after every module has run and the deaths have happened. One call to record both can get only one of them right. Hence two methods:

record_states() runs at the start of each step, before any module steps.
record_events() runs at the end, after the deaths and before the analyzers.

Starsim 3 had one method, update_results(), called after the step, so its stocks were the state at the end of the step: Starsim 3’s n_infected[k] is Starsim 4’s I[k + 1] (see Migrating from v3). How a module written as code fills each is in Custom modules.

title: From declaration to run
text:
The order of a step
Each step, the loop calls the modules in Starsim’s long-standing order (starsim/internals/loop.py):








Order
Who
What happens




1
sim, then every module
advance() (from the second step on) and start_step(): move time and the random number streams on


2
people, then every module
record_states(): the state at the start of the step


3
custom modules, then demographics
step(): custom modules; births add agents, and deaths are requested


4
diseases
step_state(): state updates of a disease written as code


5
connectors, networks, interventions
step(): cross-module code, then edges, then deliveries


6
diseases
step(): transmission, and every transition of a declared disease


7
people
step_die(): requested deaths take effect, and every module’s on_death() is called


8
people, then every module
record_events(): what happened in the step


9
analyzers
step(), reading the finished step


10
every module, people, sim
finish_step(): dead agents are removed



This is the same order as in Starsim 3. New agents exist before diseases see them, so a child born during a step can be infected in it. The progression of a disease written as code comes before the networks, so that a change of state can change who is eligible for contact (a declared disease takes all its transitions at row 6, so that a delivery sees the same people under every solver). Networks update before interventions, so an intervention sees the final network, and interventions run before transmission, so someone vaccinated today is protected today. Within a kind, modules run in the order given. Three rules follow:

Each module sees what the modules before it did. Infection, testing, and treatment can happen in one step. HIV and syphilis can each change the other’s transmission: the order decides who goes first, and its effect shrinks with the step.
Order inside a declared disease matters little. Transitions out of one state compete in one draw: the total hazard decides who leaves, and each one’s fraction of the total decides where they go, so declaring recovery before death favors neither on average. The few places where declaration order does decide are below.
Nobody is removed mid-step. A death is a request that takes effect at step_die(), so someone who dies during a step can still transmit in it, and arrays never change length partway through.

The plan can be printed, changed, and profiled (Reading the loop). In a compartmental run with nothing that needs a step of its own, the whole run is one call to the kernels (Engines and transmission); sim.describe() says why a run is stepped instead, and require_kernels=True makes that an error.

Per-module timesteps
A module can have its own dt. The loop’s plan is every (time, function) pair of every module on its own timeline, sorted by time and then by the order above, so on the days yearly demographics are due they run at their usual place in a daily sim. Rates and durations are converted with the dt of the module that uses them. describe() shows the schedule; for a daily disease with ss.Births(dt=ss.years(1)) and ss.Deaths(dt=ss.years(1)):
schedule     every day: sir
             every 365 days: births, deaths


How the state is updated within a step
This section is the reference for what happens inside one step; other pages link here. Four questions have separate answers.
1. Competing exits. Exits out of one state that are driven by rates compete: the total rate decides who leaves, and each exit’s share of it decides where they go. In the ODE the flows simply add. The stochastic compartmental solvers draw how many leave a compartment and then split them by share, taking the flows in order of the names of their states and transitions, so the order they are declared in doesn’t change the draws. As agents, each person takes one draw, and the order of declaration sets which part of it goes to which exit: with the same seed, reordering can change which agents take each exit, but not how many do on average. Declaration order does decide a few things as agents: an exact tie between timed exits (two fixed delays of the same length) goes to the one declared first, as does someone reached by two triggers in the same step, and a loop of states is broken at the transition declared first. Exits with p= are decided when people arrive in the state.
2. When the rates are read. The compartmental solvers work out every rate from the state at the start of each substep: the ODE’s own substeps, the chain binomial’s substeps (or the whole step, with ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1)), tau-leaping’s leaps, or each event under Gillespie. As agents, a declared disease takes its step in two parts:

first the transitions that are not transmission (progression, recovery, death), whose rates all read the counts at the start of the step, so these are simultaneous;
then transmission, which reads who is infectious after those moves, so someone who recovers during a step doesn’t transmit in it.

To first order, the second part is balanced: someone who arrives in a state that transmits has only half a step of its exit rates at their first draw, so each stay counts in transmission for as long as it lasts. Likewise, people who arrive in a state during the first part get half a step of its rates in that step. Both half steps are those of the default, ss.solvers.abm(step='midstep'); with step='wholestep', each rate acts only over whole steps, and with step='events', agents move in continuous time within the step.
3. Cascades. As agents, moves with no wait happen in the step that caused them. After the transitions are taken, anyone who has reached a state whose exit is already due (a trigger whose event has just happened, or a wait that rounds to no steps) moves on, in an order worked out from the graph, until nobody moves (Engines and transmission describes this sweep). The step’s infections are dated at its end and then cascade the same way, so with a zero wait from E to I, someone infected in a step is in I at the next time point. A loop back to the same state waits at least a step. In a compartmental run, a branch with dur=0 goes straight to its destination, and other arrivals leave from the next substep.
4. Between modules. Modules run one after another, in the order of a step, and each sees what the modules before it did, under every solver. A declared disease takes all its transitions in its step() (row 6), so connectors, networks, and interventions see it as it was at the start of the step, and it sees what they changed. A move made from code (an intervention’s move, ss.move(), disease.infect()) is a round of its own, taken when it is made, with its own random draws. A disease written as code does what its code says, changing its states in place in step_state() (row 4) and step() (row 6), as in Starsim 3.
A small example, as agents, of an SEIR with a zero wait from E to I, in one step: the people due to recover leave I (read from the start-of-step counts); transmission then reads who is in I, and infects some people in S; those infections are dated at the end of the step, move to E, and, with no wait, on to I, so they are counted in I at the next time point; then an analyzer (row 9) sees the finished step.

Why it matters: accuracy and the size of the step
Every scheme that takes whole steps is an approximation, with an error that shrinks as the step shrinks. Updating states one after another within a disease, without the half-step balance above, would be the worst choice: someone infected and then recovered in the same step would never transmit, which lowers the effective R0 by a fraction of order γ·dt. This is why the agent engine reads its rates at the start of the step and balances what transmission sees. Between modules, the error is of order dt, like the rest of the step. sim.check_dt() measures every effect of order dt at once; see Solvers for how big it is under each solver, and what to do about it.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Errors, warnings, and notes
The policy is: prefer guessing a default and printing it to raising an error. An error is for when there is no sensible guess: a name that doesn’t exist, lengths that don’t match, a request the solver can’t meet. Every message is meant to be read once, by an epidemiologist or by an AI writing a model for one, so it uses the user’s own names, says what exists instead, and says what to do:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.05 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(betta=0.2), verbose=0)
try:
    sim.init()
except KeyError as e:
    print(f'{type(e).__name__}: {e}')

KeyNotFoundError: pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are sir.init_prev, sir.beta, sir.dur_I; did you mean sir.beta?


There are three levels:








Level
Type
What happens




Error
a built-in exception: a KeyError for a name that is not found, a TypeError for a value of the wrong kind, a ValueError for the rest
raises; caught by type, e.g. except KeyError


Warning
a RuntimeWarning
issued through Python’s warnings, so filters (and ss.options.warnings='error') apply; the run continues


Note
ss.note()
a line about something assumed or approximated; kept in sim.notes whatever the verbosity, and printed as one line when verbose is 1 or more



A note is said once: the same note isn’t kept twice, and notes made while a sim is being initialized are held and printed after the line that starts the run, so they read as part of it. Since the notes are kept, they survive into a saved sim, and a test can check for them.
The few errors and warnings that code catches or filters by kind (ss.CapabilityError, ss.AlreadyRunError, ss.errors.AtBound, and others) are classes of their own, in starsim/internals/errors.py, listed in Profiling and debugging. The tests check each error, warning, and note by its message (tests/devtests/test_errors.py), so a change to a message is a deliberate one.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Advanced: importers and exporters
Every importer reads another framework’s model into one intermediate object, ss.converters.Source: its states, parameters, flows as rate expressions, stratifications, outcomes, and what it couldn’t translate. One function, ss.converters.write(), writes a Source as Starsim code (a declared ss.Disease, with its parameters, states, and transitions as variables, ending with sim = ss.Sim(...)), by the same rules for every format, and ss.converters.build() runs that code to make the sim. So there is one path, from a foreign model to code to a sim, and never from a sim back to code; each framework needs only a reader, and there are no framework-to-framework converters. The code is kept as sim.imported.code, for the user to keep and change. A value the writer can’t write as code, such as a network, is given by the importer as ss.converters.Code('...'), the Python that makes it.






flowchart LR
  F["odin, SBML, EMULSION, SimInf,<br>flepiMoP, summer2, Atomica, camdl,<br>EpiModel, epipack, epydemix, epymorph, MEmilio"] --> R[reader] --> S["ss.converters.Source"] --> W["ss.converters.write()"] --> C["Starsim code"] --> Sim[sim]
  Sim --> E["SBML, odin"]






The hardest part of importing is reading rates. Most frameworks write a flow as a total, such as beta * S * I / N; the importer turns it into a per-person rate on a transition, and says how it read each one. A rate divided by the population total is exposure through the routes (beta * I); one without the division is density-dependent and is kept as a count (beta * I.n); anything else is kept literally, as an expression of counts, which is exact under every solver.
An importer keeps the source’s names, marks what it guessed (as [guessed] in describe()), keeps going when something doesn’t map onto a built-in piece, and lists what it couldn’t translate (ss.errors.ImportIncomplete, also in sim.imported.incomplete). Exporters write SBML and odin from the built model’s compartmental form, and list what they left out or changed (ss.errors.LossyExport); a network, a module written as code, and a function are always left out. A sim made in Starsim is never written back out as Starsim code: its code is the script that made it.
The code is in starsim/converters/: core.py holds Source, write(), and build(), there is one file per framework, and export.py has the exporters. The files for epipack, epydemix, epymorph, MEmilio, and summer2 also run as scripts in those frameworks’ own environments, writing the model as JSON for the importer (EpiModel’s equivalent is dump_epimodel.R). Each importer is tested against its framework’s own examples (tests/devtests/io/). For the modeler’s view, with worked examples, see Import and export.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Limits

A disease written as code is not data. It runs in the same loop, but describe() shows only its class, arrays, and parameters, and it can’t be exported. See Declared modules and modules written as code.
Order between modules is a modeling choice that Starsim won’t make for you. By convention, the module whose accuracy matters most runs last, since it sees the most up-to-date state.

title: From declaration to run
text:
Further reading

Execution: the design record’s account of the loop, deferred removals, and per-module timesteps
States and transitions: the design record’s account of declared models
odin: Introduction: a domain-specific language in which a compartmental model is declared as equations and compiled, the closest relative of Starsim’s declared models
Vivarium: the simulation lifecycle: setup, initialization, main loop, and cleanup, for comparison with Starsim’s init() and loop
Wikipedia: Euler method (the simplest scheme that takes whole steps, and why its error is of order dt) and Stock and flow

title: Mixing
text:
🧠8% 🤖92%
A disease model says how infectious people are; the mixing says who meets whom, and how often. This page goes from the simplest mixing to the most detailed: homogeneous mixing, mixing pools, contact matrices between groups (such as age groups), and networks of individual contacts. Everything but networks runs as written as compartments or as agents; networks are about particular people, so only agents run them as written, and a compartmental solver approximates them (below). Movement between places is in Places and data, and the tutorial T4 – Mixing builds up the same material as a single worked path.

title: Mixing
text:
Choosing how people mix
The disease and the mixing are separate: changing from homogeneous mixing to a network does not change the disease. Each way of mixing is a route (a path by which infection can pass), given to the sim with networks=, which takes networks and mixing pools alike, singly or as a list:

No route given: homogeneous mixing, the assumption of the standard ODE models. The transmission rate β (beta) is a rate per unit time: in S >> I @ beta*I, each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the fraction of people who are infectious.
A mixing pool, ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10): homogeneous mixing with 10 contacts per unit time. β is then per contact, so β × the number of contacts is the transmission rate.
A contact matrix, ss.contacts(...): mixing between groups, such as age groups, with a number of contacts for each pair of groups (see below).
A network, such as ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10) or ss.SexualNet(): contacts between particular people, with β per contact (or per sex act, on a network with acts).

Which to choose depends on how people meet:



How people meet
Use
Runs as




Many brief contacts, at random
No route (homogeneous mixing), or ss.MixingPool()
Compartments or agents


At random, but more within some groups (e.g. by age)
ss.contacts() with a stratified disease
Compartments or agents


The same few people, again and again (households, partners)
A network: ss.RandomNet(dynamic=False), ss.SexualNet(), or the library’s household networks
Agents (a compartmental solver approximates it: see below)


From mother to child
ss.PrenatalNet(), with ss.Pregnancy()
Agents



Here is the same disease under three kinds of mixing. With no route, β = 0.05 per day and an infectious period of 10 days give R0 = 0.5; with 10 contacts a day, R0 = 5, and the mixing pool and the random network give nearly the same epidemic:

PythonR



import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I       # β = 0.05: per day with no route, per contact with one
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

kw = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'Homogeneous mixing':    ss.Sim(sir, **kw),
    'Mixing pool (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10), **kw),
    'Random network (10 contacts a day)': ss.Sim(sir, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sir.I')










library(starsim)

states("S I R")
sir <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 0.05 * I), # β = 0.05: per day with no route, per contact with one
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(10)),  # Infectious for 10 days on average
  init_prev = 0.01
)

make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(sir, n_agents = 10000, stop = days(120), verbose = 0, ...)
}
msim <- parallel(list(
  "Homogeneous mixing"                 = make_sim(),
  "Mixing pool (10 contacts a day)"    = make_sim(networks = ss$MixingPool(n_contacts = 10)),
  "Random network (10 contacts a day)" = make_sim(networks = ss$RandomNet(n_contacts = 10))
))
msim$plot("sir.I")



Transmission along every route is frequency-dependent: what matters is the fraction of a person’s contacts who are infectious (a density-dependent rate is written with the count, ss.perday(3e-5)*I.n; see Diseases). β belongs to the disease, not to the route, and a disease transmits over every route unless given a β of 0 for it (see Transmission that differs by route).

Which solver runs it
A model whose mixing has a compartmental form (no route, a mixing pool, or a contact matrix) runs as an ODE unless it is given agents. A model with a network runs as agents. A compartmental solver can still be asked for (solver='ode'); it then approximates the network, and says so in one line:



Route
As agents
As compartments




none given
exact
exact


ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=c)
exact
exact


ss.networks.MixingPools(...), ss.contacts(...)
exact
exact


ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=c)
exact
homogeneous mixing with c contacts per unit time


ssl.StaticNet(graph=...)
exact
homogeneous mixing with the graph’s mean number of contacts


ss.DegreeNet(), ss.SexualNet(), and other partnership networks
exact
the partner-change model (partnerships formed at a rate, each with the chance it transmits over its whole length), which needs the model stratified by sex for ss.SexualNet



The approximations are rough where the network matters most; see Solvers and backends. Contact tracing, partner notification, and the transmission tree need a network, and so agents.


Numbers of contacts
n_contacts= is a mean on every route, and a distribution gives its shape. For a count of contacts (ss.RandomNet, mixing pools), a number gives everyone that many; for a target number of partners (ss.DegreeNet, ss.SexualNet) or a size (ssl.ClusterNet’s cluster_size), it is the mean of a Poisson. A distribution says otherwise: ss.poisson(10) for contacts that vary between people, ss.constant(1) for exactly one partner each. A compartmental run uses only the mean.

title: Mixing
text:
Mixing pools
A mixing pool is homogeneous mixing among a group of people: no individual contacts, but each person has an effective number of contacts in the pool (n_contacts; a distribution is drawn once for each person). With no groups, a pool is everyone. source= and target= restrict it to the people who can infect and the people who can be infected, so a pool can be one group, or one-way between two; each is a condition on people (e.g. ss.person.age < 15), a function of the sim, or UIDs. Each susceptible person in the pool has a hazard of β × the mean infectiousness of the sources × their number of contacts × their rel_sus: the term β × S × I/N of the ODE, applied to each person. Here a flu-like infection spreads through a school, in which children aged 5 to 14 have 10 contacts a day with each other, and the community, in which everyone has 3:

school = ss.MixingPool(
    name = 'school',
    source = (ss.person.age >= 5) & (ss.person.age < 15), # Children aged 5-14 infect ...
    target = (ss.person.age >= 5) & (ss.person.age < 15), # ... each other
    n_contacts = ss.poisson(mean=10),    # 10 contacts a day on average
)
community = ss.MixingPool(name='community', n_contacts=ss.poisson(mean=3))

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.03*I       # Per contact
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
flu.stratify(age=[0, 5, 15]) # Ages 0-4, 5-14, and 15+, for the results
sim = ss.Sim(flu, networks=[school, community], n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.flu.infection.by('age').plot()








ss.networks.MixingPools (plural) is a set of pools between groups, with source and target as dicts of groups and n_contacts as a matrix read as a contact survey is: row i is the contacts of a person in target group i, with each source group by column. For mixing by age, the usual case, ss.contacts() makes it from a contact matrix, as below.

title: Mixing
text:
Contact matrices

A contact matrix by age
A contact matrix needs groups to act between, so the model is stratified by age first (see Stratification), here with the fraction of the population in each group. ss.contacts() takes the matrix and the lower edge of each of its age groups, and β is per contact:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.03*I       # β = 0.03 per contact
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)   # Infectious for 5 days on average
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
flu.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 4, 0.5], [2, 8, 0.5], [1.5, 3, 2]]) # Contacts a day
sim = ss.Sim(flu, networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
sim.results.flu.I.by('age').plot()

Sim: flu, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  flu: R0 = 1.83, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0059 s; flu: 67,902 infections; at most 10,741 infectious, on day 40











library(starsim)

states("S I R")
flu <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 0.03 * I), # β = 0.03 per contact
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(5)),   # Infectious for 5 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)
flu$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction of people in each

age_contacts <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(10, 4, 0.5), c(2, 8, 0.5), c(1.5, 3, 2))) # Contacts a day
sim <- Sim(flu, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(150))
sim$run()
sim$results$flu$I$by("age")$plot()



With a contact matrix, the R0 that the sim prints is β × the infectious period × the largest eigenvalue of the matrix (about 12.2 here, so R0 ≈ 1.8).
Reciprocity. Each contact between two groups is counted from both sides, so Ni × Cij = Nj × Cji. Starsim uses a matrix as given, with each row as the contacts of a person in that group, and says so in a note when it is not reciprocal for the sizes of the model’s groups.


The forms of a matrix
ss.contacts() takes a matrix and what it is over:



Form
Example
The groups




A matrix with its own age groups
ss.contacts(matrix, ages=[0, 15, 65])
The matrix’s own, given by their lower edges; they need not be the model’s


A matrix over the model’s groups
ss.contacts(matrix) (its age groups), ss.contacts(risk=matrix)
The levels of the model’s stratification by that name, in order


One matrix over several stratifications together
ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk']), with an axis for each, rows before columns (e.g. shape 2 × 2 × 2 × 2)
Every combination of their levels


Everyone with everyone
ss.contacts(10): 10 contacts per person per unit time (an ss.MixingPool of everyone)
None


A matrix for each of several stratifications
ss.contacts(age=..., risk=...)
Every combination of their levels, with the product of the entries for each


A country’s matrix, by name
ss.contacts('Kenya')
5-year age groups, from a published study



A matrix with its own age groups suits data from a study. In a compartmental run it is aggregated to the model’s age groups, weighted by population; as agents, each person is counted in the matrix’s group for their age. Groups need not be ages: here 20% of people are at high risk, with four times as many contacts with each other as people at low risk have:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ 0.05*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.days(10) # No lasting immunity
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)
sis.stratify(risk={'low': 0.8, 'high': 0.2})

mixing = ss.contacts(risk=[[2, 1], [4, 8]]) # Reciprocal: 80% × 1 = 20% × 4
sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=mixing, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(200))
sim.run()
sim.results.sis.I.by('risk').plot()

Sim: sis, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 200
  sis: R0 = 4.3, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0026 s; sis: 1,028,384 infections; at most 53,280 infectious, on day 200









The entries of a matrix are contacts per unit time, in the sim’s unit unless unit= says otherwise (e.g. unit='day', so that in a sim in years, 10 is not taken as 10 contacts a year). A country’s matrix is always contacts a day.


What a matrix acts on
The rate of the infection says what the matrix multiplies: the fraction of each group who are infectious, their number, or their number as a fraction of everyone. With C the matrix, Ij and Nj the number infectious and the number of people in group j, and N everyone:









The rate
The force of infection on group i
The matrix is
As in




beta*I
β Σj Cij Ij / Nj
Contacts per person with each group, and β is per contact
Contact surveys and the matrices of countries; frequency-dependent models


beta*I.n
β Σj Cij Ij
A rate for each pair of people (density-dependent)
Lloyd & Jansen (2004), and metapopulation models in densities


beta*I.frac, or beta*I.n/N
β Σj Cij Ij / N
A rate on the fraction of everyone who are infectious in each group
Keeling & Rohani (2008), chapter 3; the WAIFW (who acquires infection from whom) matrices of Bjørnstad (2018)



So a matrix from a textbook goes in as given, with the rate written as the textbook writes it. Keeling & Rohani’s Program 3.1, an SIS in a high- and a low-risk group whose β acts on fractions of the whole population, is:

import numpy as np
beta = np.array([[10, 0.1], [0.1, 1]]) # Per year: row i is the group infected, column j the group infecting
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(S >> I @ I.frac, I >> S @ ss.peryear(1), init=dict(I=ss.by(risk=[1e-5/0.2, 1e-3/0.8])), name='sis')
sis.stratify(risk={'high': 0.2, 'low': 0.8})
sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ss.contacts(risk=beta), total_pop=1, stop=15, unit='year')
sim.run()
print('Infectious at year 15, as fractions of everyone:', sim.results.sis.I.by('risk').values[-1].round(6)) # The book's 0.100132 and 0.026810

Sim: sis, in proportions (total_pop=1), as an ODE, years 0 to 15
  sis: R0 = 2, with 0.00101 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0044 s; sis: 1.06 infections; at most 0.127 infectious, on year 15
Infectious at year 15, as fractions of everyone: [0.100136 0.02681 ]


equations() says what a matrix acts on in each rate. In a model with places, N is everyone in the same place. A weighted count works the same way: beta*I.n_infectious weights each group by its infectiousness (rel_trans).


Contact matrices by setting
A country’s contact matrix can be split by setting: ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school', 'work', 'community']) gives a matrix for each, named after it, which together make up the whole (layer='all', the default). study= picks the study they come from (see Places and data). Each layer can then be changed on its own with ss.modify() (see Interventions); here schools close from day 10:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.03*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5)
flu = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
flu.stratify(age=[0, 5, 15, 65]) # The fractions in each come from the population

layers = ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school', 'work', 'community'])
home, school, work, community = layers
closure = ss.modify(school, multiply=0, start=ss.days(10)) # No school contacts from day 10

kw = dict(people=ss.population('Kenya'), networks=layers, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
scenarios = {
    'Schools open': ss.Sim(flu, **kw),
    'Schools closed from day 10': ss.Sim(flu, interventions=closure, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('flu.I')








Each layer’s matrix is also a table by age group (ss.data.contacts('Kenya', layer='school')), which ss.contacts() also takes, e.g. after changing it.


Contact matrices as agents
Everything above runs as agents too: given n_agents, the matrix works as a set of mixing pools, one for each pair of groups (ss.networks.MixingPools), not as a network of particular contacts. Everyone in an age group then has the mean number of contacts; for contacts that differ between people, give a distribution whose parameters are the matrix, here a lognormal with a standard deviation of half the mean:

C = ss.data.contacts('Kenya') # The mean contacts a day, by 5-year age group
mixing = ss.contacts(ss.lognormal(mean=C, std=C*0.5))

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
flu = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.03*I, I >> R @ ss.days(5), init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(flu, people=ss.population('Kenya', n_agents=10_000), networks=mixing, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0).run()
sim.results.flu.I.plot()








Each person draws their contacts when they enter an age group, and keeps them while they are in it. Any distribution of values that are not negative will do (e.g. ss.poisson(C)); a compartmental run uses the means.

title: Mixing
text:
Networks

Random networks
ss.RandomNet pairs people at random, with n_contacts contacts per person. By default the contacts are redrawn every step; with dynamic=False, they are made once at the start and kept, and with dur=, each lasts that long and is then replaced. who= restricts the network to some people. Several networks can be given together, each with its own name, as a layered population: here households (fully connected clusters of about three people, ssl.ClusterNet) and contacts at work among adults:

households = ssl.ClusterNet(name='households', cluster_size=ss.poisson(3))
work = ss.RandomNet(name='work', n_contacts=10, who=(ss.person.age >= 20) & (ss.person.age < 65), dynamic=False)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ 0.02*I       # Per contact, per day
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.days(10)  # No lasting immunity
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)

def make_sim(networks):
    return ss.Sim(sis, networks=networks, n_agents=2000, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0)

msim = ss.parallel({'Work only': make_sim(work), 'Households and work': make_sim([households, work])})
msim.plot('sis.I')
print('Number of households:', msim.sims[1].networks.households.n_clusters)








Number of households: 669


The same β applies on every layer unless it is given by route. ssl.HybridNet gives the four layers of Covasim in one: households (h), schools (s), workplaces (w), and the community (c); once in a sim, it becomes four networks, each reached on its own, e.g. sim.networks.s.


Sexual networks
ss.SexualNet is a network of partnerships between two groups of people: by default a man and a woman, or two men (between='mm'), or any two groups by name, such as female sex workers and their clients (between=('fsw', 'client')). A partnership lasts dur (a duration is a mean; a distribution gives any other spread), and has acts sex acts per unit time, for a probability of transmission per act.
By default, people with no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one partner at a time. With n_contacts=, the mean number of partners at a time is a target instead, and so are concurrency= (the fraction with two or more), max_contacts=, and match= (the fraction of partnerships within the same level of a property, e.g. match=dict(risk=0.8)). net.check() runs the sim again and compares the network it makes with each target:

net = ss.SexualNet(n_contacts=1.2, concurrency=0.1, dur=ss.years(2))
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, networks=net, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.networks.sexualnet.check(output=True)

the network "sexualnet" has concurrency 0.0806, against a target of 0.1

ss.SexualNet is ss.DegreeNet between men and women, with an age of debut and participation. Partnerships that are not sexual, such as needle sharing, are ss.DegreeNet itself, which takes the same targets among anyone (or the people that who= gives, or between two groups with between=).


Mother-to-child networks
Transmission from mother to child needs pregnancy (ss.Pregnancy; see People and demographics), which adds and removes the one-way edges from mother to child: ss.PrenatalNet while the child is in the womb, ss.BreastfeedingNet while the mother breastfeeds, and ss.PostnatalNet for a period after birth (dur=). Here a chronic infection passes through partnerships, to children before birth, and through breastfeeding:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(
    sexualnet        = ss.peract(m2f=0.002, f2m=0.001), # Chance of infection per sex act
    prenatalnet      = ss.permonth(0.03),               # Rate of infection per month of pregnancy
    breastfeedingnet = ss.permonth(0.008),              # Rate of infection per month of breastfeeding
)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
chronic = ss.Disease(infection, init_prev=ss.by(age=[0, 0.1])) # 10% of adults, and no children, at the start
chronic.stratify(age=[0, 15]) # Children (0-14) and adults (15+)

pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(0.1)) # 100 conceptions per 1,000 women a year
deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(0.01))          # 10 deaths per 1,000 people a year
sim = ss.Sim(chronic, networks=[ss.SexualNet(), ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.BreastfeedingNet()], demographics=[pregnancy, deaths],
             analyzers='infection_log', n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.chronic.I.select(age='0-14').plot()
print(sim.analyzers.infection_log.log.to_df().network.value_counts())








network
sexualnet           420
prenatalnet          85
breastfeedingnet     18
Name: count, dtype: int64




Working with edges
A network keeps its edges as arrays: p1 (the first person in each edge), p2 (the second), and weight (a multiplier on the chance each edge transmits, 1 by default), reached as net.edges or as net['p1']. net.find_contacts(uids) gives the contacts of some people, net.to_df() the edges as a table, and a network can be made from a table of edges with from_df():

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), stop=ss.days(10), verbose=0)
sim.run()
net = sim.networks.randomnet
print('Edges:', len(net))
print('Contacts of person 0:', net.find_contacts([0]))

custom = ss.Network(name='custom').from_df(dict(p1=[0, 1, 2], p2=[1, 2, 3]))
custom.to_df()

net.remove_edges() removes edges by a condition on them (e.g. net['p1'] < 100), net.to_graph() gives the network as a NetworkX graph, and net.plot() draws it. For a network of partnerships, net.degrees(uids) gives the number of partners each person has now, and memory= (e.g. ss.SexualNet(memory=ss.years(1))) keeps partnerships that ended within that time, so that contact tracing (the trace= of a delivery: see Interventions) also reaches recent past partners.


Writing a network
A network written as code is a subclass of one of the networks in the appendix (usually ss.DynamicNetwork, for partnerships that form and end, or ss.SexualNet) that overrides how edges are made. The methods it can override:



Method
What it does




add_pairs()
Makes new edges; the main method to override


remove_pairs()
Ends edges, e.g. those whose duration is over


step()
Called every step; by default removes, then adds, pairs


init_post()
Sets the network up once the people exist


find_contacts()
Gives the contacts of some people



Custom modules has the general pattern, and the tutorial T8 – Custom modules writes a network step by step.

title: Mixing
text:
Transmission that differs by route
How infectious someone is can depend on the route: HIV, for example, passes far more readily through a shared needle than through sex. The disease then gives one β for each route, as a dict keyed by the route’s name (the network’s class in lowercase, unless it was given a name=), with a value for every route. On a network with directions, β takes a value for each: ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...) is a probability per act from men to women and from women to men. On a network without acts, β is a rate for each contact with an infectious person, e.g. ss.peryear(0.2). The infection log (ss.infection_log; see Analyzers) records the route of each infection:

S, I = ss.states('S I')
beta = dict(randomnet=ss.peryear(0.2), sexualnet=ss.peract(m2f=0.01, f2m=0.005))
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=[ss.RandomNet(), ss.SexualNet()], analyzers='infection_log', n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
log = sim.analyzers.infection_log.log.to_df()
print('Infections by route:')
print(log.network.value_counts()) # The seeds at the start have no route

Infections by route:
network
randomnet    17584
sexualnet     2724
Name: count, dtype: int64

title: Mixing
text:
Pitfalls

β changes meaning when a route is added. With no route, β is a rate per unit time; with a mixing pool, contact matrix, or network, it is a rate per contact, so a contact with an infectious person infects with probability 1 − e^−β·dt over a step (give ss.probperweek() and the like for a chance per contact over a time; ss.peract() for one per act). Adding networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10) to a model fitted with homogeneous mixing multiplies its R0 by 10. Check the R0 that the sim prints.
A probability per act needs acts. ss.peract() on a route without acts (a random network, a mixing pool, a mother-to-child network) raises an error; give a rate per contact instead.
A contact matrix needs groups. A matrix with its own age groups, on a model with no age groups, stratifies it by the matrix’s groups, with the fraction in each from the world’s population, a guess that describe() marks; give the fractions (or a named population) if they matter.

text:
Further reading

The API reference: Networks
EpiModel: Network models: stochastic network models of HIV and other STIs, estimated with exponential random graph models
Covasim: Population structures: the households, schools, workplaces, and community that ssl.HybridNet copies
Prem et al. 2021: Projecting contact matrices in 177 geographical regions: the source of the contact matrices by country
socialmixr: Contact matrices from surveys: an R package for making contact matrices from the POLYMOD and other contact surveys

see The forms of a matrix
