The base classes, for a network of your own (see above) or one made from a table of edges (from_df())




The library (import starsim.library as ssl) has more:



Network
What it is
Main parameters




ssl.ClusterNet
Fully connected clusters, such as households
cluster_size, dynamic, who


ssl.HouseholdNet
Households from survey data (such as the DHS), which also sets each person’s age and sex to match; with ss.Pregnancy, newborns join their mother’s household
dhs_data, dynamic


ssl.HybridNet
Households, schools, workplaces, and community, as in Covasim
household_size, n_contacts, school_ages, work_ages, clustered


ssl.StaticNet
A fixed network from a NetworkX graph (such as one of its generators), by default an Erdős–Rényi graph (each pair of people connected with a probability)
graph, p, n_contacts


ssl.GeoNet
People in real places, with contacts falling off with distance
places, local, c, n_contacts


ssl.GridNet
People on a square grid
diagonal, periodic


ssl.SmallWorldNet, ssl.ScaleFreeNet
The classic small-world and scale-free graphs
n_contacts, rewire; n_contacts


ssl.DiskNet
People who move in a plane, in contact within a radius
r, v


ssl.NullNet
No contacts, for testing
none

title: Places and data
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
A model of a particular setting needs data about its people and its places: how many people there are and of what ages, how fast they are born and die, who has contact with whom, and where they live. Starsim has these for 187 countries and territories, by name, and takes data of your own in the same forms. This page covers that data, and then places: geographies of towns or of a country’s administrative units, movement between them, and maps of results.
How a population, its births, and its deaths are used is in People and demographics, and contact matrices in Mixing. The tutorial T4 – Mixing builds up a model of several towns step by step, and T6 – Data and calibration uses real places and populations.

title: Places and data
text:
Data by place
The data by place comes from the package starsim_data: populations by age and sex, rates of birth, death, fertility, and migration, contact matrices, and administrative units (counties, provinces, and states). The common data is bundled; the rest is downloaded on first use and kept (see the appendix). The model objects that use a place take its name, and ss.data gives the data itself:



What
In a model
The data itself




Population by age and sex (UN World Population Prospects)
ss.population('Kenya') (Ages and sex)
ss.data.population('Kenya'), ss.data.age('Kenya')


Contact matrix by 5-year age group (Prem et al. 2021)
ss.contacts('Kenya') (Contact matrices by setting)
ss.data.contacts('Kenya')


Birth and death rates by year (and by age and sex, for deaths)
ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya') (Rates from data)
ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births'), ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'deaths')


Fertility rates by year and 5-year age group of the mother
ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Kenya')
ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'fertility')


Net migration rates by year (per 1,000 people a year)
ss.migration(rate='Kenya') (Migration)
ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'migration')


Administrative units, with their populations and positions
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1) (below)
ss.data.geography('Kenya', level=1)



ss.population() takes a year (from 1950 to 2100), and ss.contacts() a study, e.g. ss.contacts('Japan', study='mistry2021'). A US state is named with its country, ss.population('United States:Massachusetts'). The data is given as tables, with age groups labeled as a stratification labels them ('0-4', '5-9', …) and the source in .attrs['ref'], which describe() also shows:

import starsim as ss

births = ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'births') # Crude birth rates per 1,000 people, by year
print(births.head())

pop = ss.data.population('Kenya', year=2024) # Women and men by 5-year age group
print('Population of Kenya in 2024:', round(pop.values.sum()))
print('Source:', pop.attrs['ref']['study'])

   Time        CBR
0  1950  49.337002
1  1960  55.183998
2  1970  52.540001
3  1980  48.210999
4  1990  43.930000
Population of Kenya in 2024: 56571298
Source: UN World Population Prospects



Looking up a place
A place can be named by its name ('Kenya'), its ISO code ('KE' or 'KEN'), its official name, or a common alias ('Czechia'), without regard to case or accents. starsim_data can say what it has for a place, and plot it as a check (an age pyramid, the crude birth rate, death rates by age, and the contact matrix):

import starsim_data as ssd

info = ssd.location_info('KEN') # The name, codes, aliases, and sources of the contact matrices
print(info.location, info.iso3, info.official_name, '- contact matrices:', info.contact_sources)
ssd.plot('Kenya');

Kenya KEN Republic of Kenya - contact matrices: prem2021|prem2017









ssd.list_locations(dataset) lists the places in a dataset, and ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True) the datasets, as in the appendix. ssd.cache_info() lists what has been downloaded.


Data of your own
Data of your own takes the same forms. Ages are a table of counts or fractions by age group, for ss.People(n_agents, age_data=...), and ss.data.age() gives a country’s in that form, to change before use:

ppl = ss.People(10_000, age_data=ss.data.age('Kenya', year=2000))

ss.data.age_split(edges, ages, counts) gives the fraction of people in each of the model’s age groups from data in other age groups, and ss.data.age_labels(edges) labels groups as Starsim does ('0-14', '15-64', '65+'). Birth and death rates are tables by year (see Data of your own); a contact matrix is an array or a table by age group (see The forms of a matrix); and places are a table of names, populations, and positions (see Geographies). Data on the disease itself (cases, deaths, prevalence) is given to the sim with data= (see Fitting a model).

title: Places and data
text:
Places

Towns linked by commuting
A geography (ss.geo.geography) is a set of named places, with the population of each and where they are. Stratifying a disease by it makes a copy of each state for each place, and mobility= says how people move between them (see Movement between places), as stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=...)). Here are three towns of measles, with 10 infectious people in Riverton at the start, and people spending 0.1% of their time in the other towns, split between them by a gravity model:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

towns = ss.geo.geography(
    names       = ['Riverton', 'Hillside', 'Lakeside'],
    populations = [60_000, 30_000, 10_000],
    x           = [0, 20, 50], # Positions in km
    y           = [0, 0, 10],
)

S, R = ss.states('S R')
I = ss.State('I', infected=True) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0]))) # 10 infectious people in Riverton
measles.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, stop=ss.days(60))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('patch').plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 60
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0047 s; measles: 99,990 infections; at most 68,065 infectious, on day 8











library(starsim)

towns <- ss$geo$geography(
  names       = c("Riverton", "Hillside", "Lakeside"),
  populations = c(60000, 30000, 10000),
  x           = c(0, 20, 50), # Positions in km
  y           = c(0, 0, 10)
)

states("S R")
states("I", infected = TRUE) # Infected: counted in the results infected and prevalence
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # β = 1.9 per day
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init_n    = list(I = ss$by(patch = c(10, 0, 0)))  # 10 infectious people in Riverton
)
measles$stratify(patch = ss$levels(towns, mobility = ss$geo$gravity(away = 0.001)))

sim <- Sim(measles, stop = days(60))
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$I$by("patch")$plot()



The sim takes its population from the geography. Without mobility=, people mix only within their own town. Places run under every solver, and so does movement between them, except as agents stepped by events (ss.solvers.abm(step='events')); as agents, each agent has a home place.


Geographies
A geography can be given by hand, read from a file, or looked up by country:
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], x=[0, 30], y=[0, 0])  # Positions in any unit of distance
ss.geo.geography(names=['a', 'b'], populations=[10_000, 20_000], lat=[-1.3, -0.1], lon=[36.8, 34.8]) # Latitudes and longitudes; distances in km
ss.geo.geography('districts.csv')               # A table with columns name, pop, and x and y (or lat and lon)
ss.geo.geography('districts.shp')               # Shapes (.shp, .geojson, or .gpkg, read with geopandas); each place at the center of its shape
ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)              # Kenya's 47 counties, with populations and positions
ss.geo.geography(['Kenya', 'Uganda'], level=1)  # Several countries, with places named e.g. 'Kenya:Busia'
It also takes distances=, places= (some of a country’s units), level=0 or level=2, and year= (populations for another year than 2020); level 2 needs geopandas (pip install starsim_data[spatial]). Each of a country’s units comes with its population, position, area, and p-code (kenya.codes, e.g. 'KE047' for Nairobi), the standard code for joining surveillance data by unit to the places of a model; the rest is in the appendix.
Here measles starts in Nairobi and spreads across Kenya’s counties, in a population that is 90% immune:

kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)

measles_kenya = ss.Disease(infection, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=0.9),                         # 90% immune at the start
    init_n = dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})), # 10 infectious people in Nairobi, and none in the other 46 counties
)
measles_kenya.stratify(patch=ss.levels(kenya, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.001)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles_kenya, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles_kenya
for county in ['Nairobi', 'Kiambu', 'Mombasa', 'Turkana']:
    peak = res.I.select(patch=county).values.argmax()
    print(county, '- infectious people peak on', res.timevec[peak])

Nairobi - infectious people peak on 2025-06-01
Kiambu - infectious people peak on 2025-07-17
Mombasa - infectious people peak on 2025-09-12
Turkana - infectious people peak on 2025-09-07




Values by place
Anything that can vary by level of a stratification can vary by place, with ss.by(patch=...): a value for each place, in order, or a dict by name. In a starting value (init, init_n, or init_prev), a place left out of a dict starts with 0, while a rate or other parameter by name needs every place; a transmission rate by place is S >> I @ ss.by(patch=[1.9, 1.9, 1.0])*I. Results are by place too: by('patch') splits a result into one column for each place, and select() picks one, e.g. sim.results.measles.I.select(patch='Hillside'). Contact matrices act within each place, so a model can be stratified by age and by place together.

title: Places and data
text:
Maps
A result of a model stratified by place can be drawn on a map with the result’s map(). Each place is colored by the result there, and drawn as its shape, if the geography has shapes, or else as a point sized by its population. Here is the outbreak above, on three dates:

res.prevalence.map(t=['2025-05-01', '2025-07-01', '2025-09-01'], shapes=True)

Using cached /home/cliffk/.cache/starsim_data/boundaries/UNOCHA-KEN-ADM1.gpkg.zstd (789.495 KB)
















Call
What it draws




res.map()
One map of the result’s summary in each place over the run, as summarize() gives it


res.map(n=6)
Six maps, evenly spaced from the start of the outbreak to its end


res.map(t='2025-02-01')
The map on one date, or on each of a list of dates (or times, e.g. t=[15, 25], for a sim without dates)


res.map(animate=True)
An animation, shown in a notebook with controls to play it; elsewhere, a Matplotlib animation


res.map(animate=True, filename='spread.gif')
The same, saved to a file (a GIF, or an MP4, which needs ffmpeg)


res.map(shapes=True)
For a country, its units’ boundaries, downloaded the first time (needs geopandas); a geography read from shapes always draws them


geo.plot()
The places of a geography, with their populations


geo.plot(values=..., label=...)
The places colored by a value for each one, e.g. kenya.plot(values=res.infection.by('patch').summarize()/kenya.populations, label='Fraction infected')



Both take cmap=, vmin= and vmax=, and names= (whether to label the places, by default when there are 15 or fewer). A result of agents is mapped the same way; for the runs of a MultiSim, map one run (res.select(run=0)).

title: Places and data
text:
Movement between places
Movement between places makes a metapopulation model: each place mixes within itself (homogeneously, or with a contact matrix) and is linked to the others by movement. Movement is given with the places, as stratify(patch=ss.levels(places, mobility=...)), and has three parts: its shape, its amount, and its kind.
The shape (which places people go to):

ss.geo.gravity(source_power=1, dest_power=1, distance_power=2): movement from place i to place j proportional to popis−1 × popjd / distanceijr, so people go more to bigger and nearer places.
ss.geo.radiation(): the radiation model (Simini et al. 2012), with no parameters to fit: the fraction who go to each place depends on the populations of the places nearer to it.
ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=M): a matrix you already have, with the movement from each place (rows) to each place (columns), e.g. from commuting data; a SciPy sparse array suits many places.
ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=kenya.adjacency): movement only between places that share a border, split evenly between each place’s neighbors (adjacency is there for a country’s units, or given to ss.geo.geography(adjacency=...)): the classic model of spread from district to district.

The amount is away=, the fraction of their time that people spend away from home, split between the other places by the shape (10% if not given, which describe() marks as guessed). scale= instead gives the amount as a constant in the gravity formula, for an amount fitted to data; with it, movement from a small place to a large one can exceed all of people’s time, which Starsim caps with a warning. The amount can be fitted like any other parameter: ss.geo.gravity(away=ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1])) (see Fitting a model).
The kind is kind=, on the movement model or the matrix; by default it is commuting. The numbers of a matrix mean different things under each kind:








Kind
What it means
Used for




'commute' (default)
People keep their home, and spend a fraction of their time in other places, where they can be infected and infect others
Daily travel to work, school, and markets


'visit'
As for commuting, but visitors can only be infected away from home, and infect nobody there
Short trips; flepiMoP’s form


'migrate'
People move home, at the rates the movement gives (per person per unit time)
Migration and relocation; needs scale= as the rate


'force'
Nobody moves; a fraction of each place’s force of infection goes to the others
LASER’s form



Under commuting, with Tik the fraction of their time that people from place i spend in place k (each row of T sums to 1), the force of infection on people from place i takes the standard form for time spent between places:
\[\lambda_i = \sum_k T_{ik} \, \beta \, \frac{\sum_j T_{jk} I_j}{\sum_j T_{jk} N_j}\]
ss.geo.gravity(away=0.2)                    # Commuting, 20% of time away
ss.geo.gravity(away=0.2, kind='visit')      # Visiting
ss.geo.gravity(scale=2e-5, kind='migrate')  # Migration, at rates from the gravity model
ss.geo.radiation(away=0.1, kind='force')    # A moving force of infection, as in LASER

Movement between neighbors
Here is the Kenya outbreak above, with the same amount of movement but only between counties that share a border, so that infection spreads as a wave from county to county:

measles_borders = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})), name='measles')
measles_borders.stratify(patch=ss.levels(kenya, mobility=ss.geo.Mobility(matrix=kenya.adjacency, away=0.001)))
borders = ss.Sim(measles_borders, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', verbose=0).run()
borders.results.measles.prevalence.map(t=['2025-05-01', '2025-07-01', '2025-09-01'], shapes=True)

Using cached /home/cliffk/.cache/starsim_data/boundaries/UNOCHA-KEN-ADM1.gpkg.zstd (789.495 KB)











A movement register
A table of moves on given dates (a movement register, such as livestock sales between farms) is ss.geo.register(...), a file name or a DataFrame with columns date, from, to, and n, and optionally states (who can move, or which state people added go into). A row with no from adds people, and one with no to removes them. Here, in the three towns, 100 people move from Riverton to Lakeside on day 5, and 50 people join Hillside:

import pandas as pd

register = pd.DataFrame({
    'date': [5, 5],
    'from': ['Riverton', None],
    'to':   ['Lakeside', 'Hillside'],
    'n':    [100, 50],
})
measles_moves = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])))
measles_moves.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.register(register)))

sim = ss.Sim(measles_moves, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles_moves.infection.by('patch').plot()










Under compartments and agents
In an ODE, a tiny fraction of an infected person in a town starts its epidemic growing at once; with agents, a whole person there has to be infected first, which takes longer, and by chance may not happen at all. For whether, or when, an outbreak reaches a small place, use agents or a stochastic solver (see Solvers and backends):

measles_slow = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=[10, 0, 0])))
measles_slow.stratify(patch=ss.levels(towns, mobility=ss.geo.gravity(away=0.0001)))

kw = dict(stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0)
for label, sim in {'As an ODE': ss.Sim(measles_slow, **kw), 'As agents': ss.Sim(measles_slow, n_agents=10_000, **kw)}.items():
    sim.run()
    peaks = sim.results.measles_slow.I.by('patch').values.argmax(axis=0)
    print(label, '- day of the peak in Riverton, Hillside, and Lakeside:', peaks)

As an ODE - day of the peak in Riverton, Hillside, and Lakeside: [ 7 10 11]
As agents - day of the peak in Riverton, Hillside, and Lakeside: [11 18 22]

title: Places and data
text:
Pitfalls

A name does not make a place. A stratification is spatial when it is given a geography (patch=towns) or kind='space' (stratify(patch=ss.levels(['a', 'b'], kind='space'))). A list of names alone makes ordinary groups, whose people mix with each other; a stratification named like places (patch, region, district, and so on) given only names says so in a note. describe() gives the kind of each stratification.
Start the outbreak somewhere. init_prev=0.01 infects 1% of people in every place; to start it in one place, give init_n (or init) by place, e.g. init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch={'Nairobi': 10})).
A movement model needs a geography. ss.geo.gravity() and ss.geo.radiation() work out the movement from the places’ populations and distances, so on a stratification with no geography they raise an error; give a geography, or the movement itself as a matrix.
Check the links. Before trusting a spatial model, seed one place and check that the others stay free of infection with no movement.

title: Places and data
text:
Further reading

The API reference: ss.data, ss.geo
UN World Population Prospects: the populations, birth rates, and death rates that come with Starsim
epydemix: Populations: populations and contact matrices by place, for compartmental models
flepiMoP: Model description: metapopulation models of US states and counties, with mobility between them
LASER: Migration: movement between places in an agent-based model, with gravity and radiation models

title: Places and data
text:
Appendix: what a geography has
The attributes of a geography (kenya = ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)), for making maps, movement matrices of your own, or joining data by place:







Attribute
What it is




names
The name of each place, in order: the levels of the stratification


populations
The population of each place (None if not given)


lat, lon
The latitude and longitude of each place, in degrees (for a country’s units, the center of each unit)


x, y
The positions of the places, for a geography given by hand with x= and y=


distances
The distance between each pair of places (in km, from latitudes and longitudes)


adjacency
Whether each pair of places shares a border (for a country’s units at level 1 or below, or as given)


area
The area of each place, in km² (for a country’s units)


codes
The p-code of each place (for a country’s units), e.g. 'KE047'


shapes
The shapes of the places, for a geography read from shapes (None otherwise; res.map(shapes=True) downloads a country’s)


ref
Where a country’s units came from, which describe() shows



len(kenya) is the number of places, and kenya.plot() draws them (see Maps).

The contact matrices (prem2021, prem2017, prem, mistry2021, and, for US states, mistry2021_us) are the study= of ss.contacts() and ss.data.contacts(). Those of Prem et al. are by 5-year age group, from 0-4 to 75+; those of Mistry et al. by single year of age, from 0 to 84+. Each has the settings 'home', 'school', 'work', and 'community' (layer=), and their sum, 'all'. The administrative units at level 2 and below are not in a dataset of their own: ss.geo.geography(place, level=2) downloads the boundaries (from geoBoundaries or UN OCHA) and the populations. indicators and life_table are the UN’s other tables, which ssd.download(place, which='life_table') gives.


Every place and its data
Every place that has data, with its ISO code, the contact matrices it has, and its number of first-level administrative units (blank where there are none bundled). Every place listed has the UN’s population, birth, death, fertility, and migration data:

import pandas as pd

places = ssd.list_all_locations()
sources = ['prem2021', 'prem2017', 'mistry2021']
has = {source: set(ssd.list_locations(source)) for source in sources}
with_units = set(ssd.list_locations('nodes'))
un_data = all(set(ssd.list_locations(ds)) == set(places) for ds in ['population', 'births', 'deaths', 'fertility', 'migration'])
print('Every place has all the UN data:', un_data)

rows = []
for place in places:
    row = dict(place=place.replace('_', ' '), code=ssd.location_info(place).iso3)
    row['contact matrices'] = ', '.join(source for source in sources if place in has[source])
    row['level-1 units'] = len(ssd.load_nodes(place, level=1)) if place in with_units else None
    rows.append(row)
table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('place')
table['level-1 units'] = table['level-1 units'].astype('Int64')
print(len(table), 'places')

title: Running sims
text:
🧠19% 🤖81%
A sim (ss.Sim) is one model put together with everything needed to run it: the diseases, the population, the time span, how people mix, and any births and deaths, interventions, and analyzers. It runs them in the right order, and holds the results afterwards. T1 – Getting started and T2 – Building a model build and run the measles model used here; running many sims and comparing them is in Scenarios.

title: Running sims
text:
The smallest sim
A sim needs a model and, usually, a population and a time span. Here is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, run for 50 days:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)                    # Transmission rate per day
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0031 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6











library(starsim)

states("S I R")
beta <- par(1.9) # Transmission rate per day
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = beta * I),
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)), # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50))
sim$run()
sim$plot()



S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
beta_explicit = ss.par(ss.perday(1.9), name='beta') # Transmission rate per day
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=beta_explicit*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery'), # Infectious for an exponentially distributed time of 8 days on average
    ],
    init_prev = 0.001,
    name = 'measles',
)

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = ss.contacts(1), # Everyone mixes with everyone, with one contact per person per day
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = ss.days(0),
    stop      = ss.days(50),
    dt        = ss.days(1),     # Steps of a day
    unit      = 'day',          # The unit of bare numbers
    solver    = 'ode',          # Run as an ODE
    rand_seed = 1,              # The random seed (it matters only for a stochastic run)
    verbose   = 1,              # Print a line for what it runs, and one when it is done
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.006 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6












A run prints:

What it runs, and how: the diseases, the population, the solver (here an ODE, since nothing in the model needs individual people; see Solvers and backends), and the time span.
R0 of each disease with the number infectious at the start, as a check that the model is the one you meant (here 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15); if some people start immune, the reproduction number at the start too.
Notes, if any: something Starsim assumed, approximated, or wants you to check, such as a step that is long for the rates in the model. Notes are kept in sim.notes too.
Progress, for a run that goes a step at a time (as agents, say), rather than all at once.
A closing line: how long it took, the total number of infections, and the size and timing of the peak.

How much is printed is set by verbose, given to the sim or to sim.run(): 0 prints nothing (the usual choice inside loops and fits), 1 the lines above (the default), 2 everything, and a fraction such as 0.1 the progress every 10% of the run.

title: Running sims
text:
What a sim takes
The settings of a sim are its keywords. Most models use only a few: the diseases (the first argument), total_pop, start and stop (or dur), dt, and the modules that say how people mix (networks) and what else happens (demographics, interventions, analyzers, connectors). Every setting, with its default, is in the appendix; sim.pars holds them all once the sim is made, and sim.describe() shows the whole model as Starsim has built it, with each value it chose itself marked (see Writing models).
total_pop and n_agents are separate on purpose. total_pop is the number of people the model stands for, and is the same under every solver; n_agents is how many individuals are followed when the sim runs as agents. Given both, each agent stands for total_pop/n_agents people, which saves time at the cost of coarser random events (see Branching and rescaling):

agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
agents.run()

Sim: measles, as 10,000 agents, each 10 people, days 0 to 50
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.053 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 77,040 infectious, on day 9


Sim(n=100000 (10000 agents); 0—50; diseases=measles)


The first line now says “as 10,000 agents, each 10 people”.

Settings in a dict
The settings can also be collected in a dict and passed together, which is handy when several sims share them:

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', verbose=0)

town = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
city = ss.Sim(pars, diseases=measles, total_pop=1_000_000) # The same settings, with one changed

A dict given as the first argument is read as settings, and a keyword given as well overrides the same setting in the dict, as total_pop does for city. In such a dict, a module from Starsim’s library can be given by name (diseases='sir', with its default parameters) or as a dict of its parameters with its name as type (diseases=dict(type='sir', beta=ss.perday(0.1)), the same as diseases=ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(0.1))), a shorthand found in many existing scripts.

title: Running sims
section: What happens when a sim runs
text:
What happens when a sim runs

What happens before the first step
Nothing is computed when a sim is made. sim.init(), which sim.run() calls if it hasn’t been called, builds the sim:

It fills in whatever was left out (the unit of time from the values in the model, how long each state lasts beyond its average, how people mix, where people start) and records each choice, so that describe() can show it.
It checks the model: unknown parameter names, values outside their bounds, and shapes that don’t match the model’s groups are errors here, before the run.
It chooses the solver, makes the people (with a default age and sex structure, unless a population is given; see People and demographics), adds each module’s states, parameters, and results, sets up the time steps, and starts the random number generators.

Calling sim.init() yourself is useful for looking at the people or the model before a long run, or for finding an error without waiting for one.
A sim copies the modules it is given, so the same disease can be given to several sims. After a run, use the sim’s own copy: sim.diseases.measles, not the variable measles, which is never run.


The order of each step
For a declared model, Starsim works out the order of everything in a step from the model itself. Modules written as code run at fixed points in the step: demographics, then disease progression, connectors, networks, interventions, transmission, and analyzers, so a child born in a step can be infected in it, and a new partnership can transmit in the step it forms. Take a woman with pre-symptomatic COVID who, in one busy day, develops symptoms, gets tested, moves out of her parents’ house into her husband’s, and becomes pregnant. Starsim orders her day: she (1) becomes pregnant, (2) develops symptoms, (3) moves house, (4) gets tested, and (5) transmits COVID to her contacts, who by now include her husband but not her parents. (That is for a disease written as code; a declared disease takes all its transitions at step 5.) sim.loop.to_df(), after sim.init(), lists every function called in every step, and sim.loop.plot() draws it; Steps and time points explains the order in full.

title: Running sims
text:
Running again, and variants
sim.run() on a sim that has already run runs it again from the start. To run it again with something changed, use sim.new(), which makes a new sim as this one was before it was run, with whatever is given changed. Here the same outbreak with a lower transmission rate, as if contacts were fewer:

PythonR



sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), label='Original', verbose=0)
sim.run()
slower = sim.new(pars=dict(beta=1.2), label='Fewer contacts')
slower.run()

msim = ss.MultiSim([sim, slower])
msim.plot('measles.I')










sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50), label = "Original", verbose = 0)
sim$run()
slower <- sim$new(pars = list(beta = 1.2), label = "Fewer contacts")
slower$run()

msim <- MultiSim(list(sim, slower))
msim$plot("measles.I")



What sim.new() changes can be settings (sim.new(total_pop=1_000_000), sim.new(solver='abm')), parameters of the model by name (sim.new(pars=dict(beta=1.2)), for a parameter made with ss.par(); see Parameters), or modules (sim.new(interventions=campaign)). This is the usual way to make the scenarios of a comparison (see Scenarios). sim.run() itself takes only until= and verbose=; two other ways of running again are sim.copy(), an exact copy, including the state of a sim part of the way through a run (below), and sim.restart(pars=dict(beta=1.2)).run(), which runs a sim again from its start with new parameter values (or rand_seed=), without building a compartmental model again, so many times faster.

Running part of the way
sim.run(until=...) runs up to a given time and stops, after the step that starts at that time; a later sim.run() carries on from there. This is useful for looking at a sim in the middle of a run, for changing it before going on, and for running a shared start once and then branching into scenarios, which in a stochastic run then share the chance events up to the branch point. Here measles, run as agents, reaches a town in which 90% are immune, and a month in, each scenario is a copy of the sim with contacts reduced by an ss.modify():

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)
measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ beta*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=10)) # 90% immune, 10 infectious

base = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, solver='abm', dt=ss.days(0.25), start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
base.run(until='2025-02-01')

reductions = {'No change': 0, 'Contacts down by 20%': 0.2, 'Contacts down by 40%': 0.4}
sims = {}
for label, reduction in reductions.items():
    sim = base.copy()
    sim.add_module(ss.modify('measles.pars.beta', multiply=1-reduction))
    sims[label] = sim

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')








A module added with sim.add_module() acts from the time it is added. Only modules that leave the layout of the model as it is can be added part of the way: a vaccine adds a state for the people who hold it, so ss.vaccinate() is given when the sim is made (with a start date). A parameter of the copy can also be set directly before it carries on (sim.diseases.measles.pars.beta = 1.9*0.6).
A shared start also saves time when it is long, such as a burn-in of decades before a few years of scenarios. For an ODE, it is simpler to run each scenario in full with sim.new() and an intervention that starts on the date.

title: Running sims
text:
Saving and loading
sim.save() saves a sim to a file, and ss.load() loads it again:

sim.save('my-measles.sim')
loaded = ss.load('my-measles.sim')
loaded.plot('measles')








By default a saved sim that has finished keeps its results but not the people, which makes the file much smaller; a sim saved part of the way through keeps everything, so that it can be loaded and run on (shrink=False keeps everything in either case). sim.shrink() does the same in memory, and ss.parallel(..., shrink=True) does it to each run (by default, runs keep their people). A sim that keeps its people can be looked at person by person (sim.people.to_df(); see People and demographics), but a declared disease run as agents keeps only the times and histories the model reads (such as ti_I, when a duration needs it): make the sim with keep_times=True to read any other. A saved sim is a Python pickle, so it needs the same version of Starsim (and of any modules written as code) to load. For the results alone, sim.to_df() gives them as a table and sim.to_json() as JSON (see Results); to write the model itself in another format (SBML, odin), see Import and export.

title: Running sims
text:
Larger projects: make_sim()
A project with more than a few scenarios is usually built around one function that makes the sim, with an argument for each thing that varies, so that every scenario, seed, and calibration run is made the same way. It can get long: this is, after all, where most of the science happens. A sketch of the pattern, as an HIV project might have it:
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
import pandas as pd

def make_sim(seed=1, n_agents=10_000, start=1990, stop=2030, scenario='baseline', debug=False):
    """ Make the sim for one scenario and seed """
    if debug: # A quick version for testing the code
        n_agents, stop = 1_000, 2000

    # Population and demography, from data
    people = ss.People(n_agents, age_data=pd.read_csv('data/age_dist_1990.csv'))
    pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=pd.read_csv('data/asfr.csv'))
    deaths = ss.Deaths(death_rate=pd.read_csv('data/deaths.csv'))

    # Networks, disease, and interventions
    sexual = ss.SexualNet()
    prenatal = ss.PrenatalNet()
    hiv = ssl.HIV(beta={'sexualnet': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004), 'prenatalnet': 0.2})
    interventions = []
    if scenario == 'treat':
        interventions.append(ssl.ART(coverage=ss.timeseries({2004: 0.1, 2020: 0.8}, 'linear')))

    sim = ss.Sim(
        people = people,
        diseases = hiv,
        networks = [sexual, prenatal],
        demographics = [pregnancy, deaths],
        interventions = interventions,
        start = start,
        stop = stop,
        total_pop = 9.98e6,
        rand_seed = seed,
        label = scenario,
    )
    return sim
The scenarios and seeds are then a loop over its arguments, run together with ss.parallel() (see Scenarios); if making each sim is slow, they can be made in parallel too (see Speed and scale). Keep anything that differs between scenarios as an argument rather than editing the sim afterwards, and keep debug=True as a quick way to check the code end to end. For running such a project from a script or on a cluster, see Speed and scale.

title: Running sims
text:
Pitfalls

Reading a variable rather than the sim. A function given to a sim should read what it needs from the sim it is given (lambda sim: sim.diseases.measles.I.n), not from the measles you made, which is never run.
Changing a setting after the sim is built. Once a sim is initialized its settings belong to that run, and setting one (sim.pars.stop = 30) raises an error; give it to sim.new(stop=30) instead.
A sim that isn’t what you meant. Read the first lines a run prints, and sim.describe(): R0, the unit of time, and the solver catch most mistakes (see Profiling and debugging).

Every keyword of ss.Sim(), by what it is for; sim.pars (an ss.SimPars) holds them all once the sim is made, and the API pages for ss.Sim and ss.SimPars give the details.



Setting
Default
What it is




The model




first argument

The model: a module, transitions, or a list of them; or a dict of settings


diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, analyzers, connectors
none
Modules of each kind: a module, a name ('sir'), a dict with type, or a list. networks default to everyone mixing with everyone (Mixing); demographics=True gives births and deaths at 20 and 10 per 1,000 people per year


modules
none
Modules of any kind together, sorted by kind; those of your own of no standard kind are in sim.custom


step_order
‘type’
The order the modules step in: 'type', each kind at its place in the step, or 'given', in the order they were given (the model and modules= first)


pars
none
Values of the model’s parameters by name, e.g. pars=dict(beta=0.1) or pars=fit.pars; it can hold settings too (pars=dict(start=2000, beta=0.1)), told apart by name, or be a whole ss.SimPars


data
none
Data to plot with the results and to fit to, with a time column and columns named like measles.infection


people
none
An ss.People to use, rather than making one (see People and demographics)


The population




total_pop
10,000
The size of the population modeled


n_agents
as total_pop, up to 10,000
The number of agents, for a run as agents; giving it makes the sim run as agents (and without total_pop, it is an error for a compartmental run). Each agent then stands for sim.pop_scale = total_pop/n_agents people


rescale
False
Dynamic rescaling, for agents: start at one person per agent, and grow by at least a factor whenever more than a given fraction of agents are no longer naive; True, or a dict of its options, e.g. dict(threshold=0.05, factor=1.2) (the defaults) (see Branching and rescaling)


aging
with demographics
Whether agents age; by default, only if there are births or deaths


stratify
none
Groups by a property of people for every module, e.g. dict(age=[0, 15, 65]) (see Stratification)


Time




start, stop
50 of the sim’s unit, from 0 (or from 2000 for a model in years)
The time span: dates, years, or, with no calendar, durations from 0. A date or a year as the start gives the sim a calendar, and every bare number given as a time is then a year


dur
none
The length of the run: the stop is the start plus it, or with a stop and no start, the start is the stop minus it; all three must agree if given


dt
1
The step, in the unit of time


unit
the model’s
The unit of time, and of bare numbers in declared transitions ('day', 'week', 'year', …)


How it is run




solver
'auto'
'ode', 'binomial', 'gillespie', 'tau', or 'abm'; or with options: ss.solvers.ode(integrator=, substeps=, dwells=), ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=), or ss.solvers.abm(step=) (see Solvers and backends)


branching
False
Run as a branching process: infection takes no one from the uninfected (see Branching and rescaling)


approximations
‘note’
What to do with each approximation a solver makes: ‘note’ notes it, ‘allow’ keeps the note in sim.notes without printing it, ‘error’ makes it an error


require_kernels
False
Raise an error, rather than run in Python, if a compartmental run can’t be taken whole in the kernels (see sim.describe())


rand_seed
1
The random seed, from which each module’s seeds are made


even_draws
False
For agents (an error for a compartmental run): space each call’s random numbers evenly, which reduces the variance between runs, but makes outbreaks die out less often than they should


Output




group_results
all
The results to keep by group (e.g. ['I', 'cases']); the others keep only their totals, which saves memory in a model with many groups (by default all are kept, but only every few steps if every step would take more than about 100 MB)


keep_times
False
For a declared disease run as agents, keep the time each agent entered every state (ti_S) and the history of every transition, to read after the run; by default only those the model reads are kept


record_people
True
Whether to record the people’s results (alive, female, died, emigrated) each step; False saves a little time in a light sim that doesn’t need them, though demographics read alive


label
none
A name for the sim, used in plots and comparisons


verbose
1
How much to print: 0 nothing, 1 the solver, notes, and progress, 2 everything; a fraction gives progress at each such fraction of the run

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Introduction
Starsim is a framework for modeling the spread of diseases: as deterministic or stochastic compartmental models, as metapopulation models across places, or as agents with dynamic transmission networks. A disease is written as its states and the transitions between them, as in a textbook model, and the same model then runs in any of these ways. Starsim also models several diseases at once and how they interact, non-infectious diseases, pregnancy and birth, interventions and how they are delivered, and fitting to data.
Starsim is available for both Python and R (see R-Starsim), and is fully open-source under the MIT license.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Kinds of model and tool
Mechanistic models of transmission differ in how they represent the population. Deterministic compartmental models follow the number of people in each compartment (susceptible, infectious, recovered, often stratified by age, sex, or place) as an ordinary differential equation (ODE): fast, smooth, and easy to fit, but with no chance in them. Stochastic compartmental models move whole numbers of people between the same compartments at random (a chain binomial, or the Gillespie algorithm), which captures fade-out and the variation between runs. Metapopulation models link compartmental models in many places by movement. Network and agent-based models (ABMs) follow individuals, with their own states, contacts, and histories: the most flexible, and the most costly to run and to check. The choice depends on the question: an ODE for the expected course of a large epidemic, a stochastic or agent-based model where chance, heterogeneity, or individual histories matter. For example, “Are vaccinated people less likely to be infected?” is a question for a statistical model; “What will prevalence be in 5 years with 100% vaccine uptake?” for a compartmental model; and “What will prevalence be in 5 years given realistic screening and vaccine coverage?” for agents.



Types of model


Tools differ as much in how a model is written: by hand in a general-purpose language (NumPy, deSolve), in a model language (odin), in configuration files (flepiMoP, Atomica), as a library of compartmental models (summer2, epydemix, MEmilio, SimInf), as a network or agent-based framework (EpiModel, LASER, EMOD, Mesa), or with statistical tools that fit mechanistic models to data (pomp, Stan). Models from many of these can be read into Starsim, and Starsim models written out to several (see Import and export); the lingua_franca repo has a model from each written both ways, with how their results and speed compare. If you are coming from Starsim 3, see the migration guide.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Where Starsim fits
Starsim’s distinctive feature is that one model runs in more than one of these ways. A disease declared as states and transitions (S >> I @ beta*I; see Writing models) is data that Starsim can read, so the same declaration runs as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents, in one place or across several as a metapopulation. Starsim runs it as compartments unless something in it needs individuals, such as a contact network, and says which it chose; one argument overrides it (see Solvers and backends). So a model can start as an ODE, be fitted fast, and then run as agents to add a network or an intervention that targets individuals, without being written twice. What the declaration can’t express is added by a module written as code (Custom modules). The conceptual overview explains how this works.
Starsim’s design follows two principles: common tasks (defining parameters, running a sim, plotting results) should be simple, and custom tasks (a new vaccine, a new disease, a calibration function of your own) can’t always be simple, but should still be possible. If you’re modeling a complicated disease, some of that complexity is irreducible: Starsim’s job is to help where it can, then get out of the way and let you write your code. See Architecture for the full set.

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Why use a framework?
A disease model is a few equations, so why not write them in Python or R yourself? For many models that is the right answer.

When your own code is enough
A single deterministic SIR model is about 15 lines of Python with SciPy. Here is the measles outbreak used throughout these docs, with β = 1.9 per day and 8 days infectious, in a town of 100,000 people:

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

beta, gamma, N = 1.9, 1/8, 100_000

def deriv(t, y):
    S, I, R = y
    infection = beta*S*I/N
    recovery = gamma*I
    return [-infection, infection - recovery, recovery]

days = np.arange(51)
out = solve_ivp(deriv, [0, 50], [N - 100, 100, 0], t_eval=days, rtol=1e-8)
print('Most infectious at once:', round(out.y[1].max()))

Most infectious at once: 74112


And here is the same model in Starsim:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
measles = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_n=dict(I=100))
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=N, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0).run()
print('Most infectious at once:', round(sim.results.measles.I.max()))

Most infectious at once: 74112




library(starsim)

N <- 100000
states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)), init_n = list(I = 100))
sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = N, stop = days(50), verbose = 0)$run()
cat("Most infectious at once:", round(max(sim$results$measles$I$values)), "\n")



S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
measles = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection'),       # β S I / N
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery'), # γ I, with γ = 1/8
    ],
    init_n = dict(I=100), # 100 infectious at the start, and the rest susceptible
    name   = 'measles',
)
sim = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles,
    networks  = ss.contacts(1), # Everyone mixes with everyone, with one contact per person per day
    total_pop = N,
    start     = ss.days(0),
    stop      = ss.days(50),
    dt        = ss.days(1),
    unit      = 'day',
    solver    = 'ode',
    verbose   = 0,
)
sim.run()
print('Most infectious at once:', round(sim.results.measles.I.max()))

Most infectious at once: 74112





The two agree to within a couple of people. If this is the whole job (one model, run deterministically, read by you), the plain version is fine, as is deSolve or odin in R; Starsim is not faster than good code of your own for a model like this.


Where your own code starts to strain
A model rarely stays that small. These are the changes that tend to turn a short script into a long one, and what each takes in Starsim:



The model grows to need
In code of your own
In Starsim




Age groups with a contact matrix
Rewrite every equation as a vector, and the force of infection as a matrix product
sim.stratify(age=[0, 5, 15, 65]) and ss.contacts('Kenya') (Stratification)


A latent period that isn’t exponential
Add the right number of stages, and keep their rates consistent
ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10)) (Diseases)


A stochastic version, or agents
A second model, written and tested again
solver='binomial', or n_agents= (Solvers)


Rates in different units (daily transmission, yearly births)
Convert each by hand, and again whenever the step changes
Each value carries its unit (ss.peryear(0.02)) (Time)


Vaccination campaigns and routine immunization
Code for eligibility, coverage, timing, and waning
ss.vaccinate() with a product (Products)


Reported cases, with delays and under-reporting
A second set of results worked out from the first
ss.outcome(0.5*onset, delay=ss.days(4)) (Outcomes)


Fitting to data
A likelihood, an optimizer or sampler, and code tying parameters to the model
ss.par(bounds=...) and sim.fit() (Fitting)


Comparing scenarios fairly
Seeds managed so the scenarios differ by the intervention, not by chance
Common random numbers, on by default (Random numbers)


A second disease that interacts with the first
Combined states, or two models coupled step by step
Two diseases in one sim, and ss.modify() between them (Connectors)


Someone else checking the model
Reading the code
describe(), equations(), diagram(), and R0() (Writing models)



None of these is hard on its own, but each touches the others (age groups change the force of infection, which changes what the vaccine acts on, which changes what the fit compares with data), and the bookkeeping is where the mistakes are. A rough guide: once a script is past about 100 lines, or needs calibration, more than one unit of time, or both a deterministic and a stochastic version, a framework is likely to save time.
Speed matters less for one small model than for many runs (fitting, uncertainty, scenario sweeps), for agents, and for large populations. Starsim runs compartmental models in compiled code, at the same cost whatever the size of the population, and steps agents with compiled passes over arrays; see Speed and scale.


Problems that are easy to miss
The hardest mistakes in a model are the ones that give plausible numbers. Each of the problems below was found while building Starsim, sometimes in Starsim itself, and each is now handled and tested:



The problem
How big it can be
What Starsim does




Competing exits drawn one after the other. Deaths are drawn among those infectious, and then recovery among the survivors, so whichever comes first in the code gets more people
Of the order of the rates times the step
Draws who leaves a state once, from the total rate, and then which way each person goes, in proportion to the rates


People infected during a step are given a whole step to recover at their first chance, rather than the half step they have on average
An SIR with 8 days infectious, in 8-day steps: an attack rate of 7% instead of 77% (the ODE gives 80%)
People who arrive in a state during a step face half a step of its exits


A step that is long for the disease. Someone infected in a step can’t infect anyone until the next one
Measles in daily steps peaks about 3 days late (see the conceptual overview)
Compartmental solvers take as many substeps as they need; agents get a note when the step is long, and sim.check_dt() measures the effect


Converting a probability between periods by dividing. An annual probability of 0.5 is not 0.5/12 a month
0.042 a month instead of 0.056; scaling the other way gives probabilities above 1
Probabilities, rates, and durations are typed, and converted through the rate


Losing the unit of time. A rate or duration becomes a bare number, and the unit is forgotten
A country’s contact matrix, in contacts a day, used 365 times too low in a model in years
Values carry their units, and arithmetic that mixes them wrongly raises an error


Scenarios that differ by chance. With one stream of random numbers, one extra draw in a scenario changes every draw after it
Differences between scenarios that the intervention didn’t cause, which need many more runs to average out
Common random numbers: each person’s draws stay the same between scenarios unless the scenario changes them


Compartments that go negative when the outflows in a step are larger than the compartment
Negative numbers of people, or runs that stop
In steps that are taken whole, outflows that would take more than everyone in a compartment are scaled down together; the stochastic solvers draw no more people than there are



Most of these errors are of the order of the rates times the step, so a model checked in daily steps can go wrong when run in weeks.
A framework is not a guarantee of correctness: the model’s structure, assumptions, and evidence are still yours to get right. Starsim takes the bookkeeping off your hands, and says what it assumed (sim.describe() lists every value it filled in itself).

title: What is Starsim?
text:
Should I use Starsim?
Starsim suits modelers who write code (or are willing to), and is a good fit:

If your agent-based model is too slow, inflexible, or hard to use for your questions (a single run takes 14 hours, and every year you worry that your computing grant won’t be renewed).
If you model with compartments and want to try agents without months of learning a new tool: an mpox model asked to evaluate an individually targeted intervention can run as an ODE and as agents, and the two can be compared.
If you want to prototype a disease or network before adding it to your full model (you know and love your HIV model, but want to see what syphilis co-transmission, or a different MSM network, would do).

It may not be the best choice:

For one run of a simple SIR or SEIR model, where plain Python or R is enough (above).
If your team has a working model, highly specialized to its context, in another tool: the cost of switching may not be worth it. Starsim can import models from several frameworks (Import and export), so get in touch if this interests you.
For networks estimated from survey data with exponential random graph models (nodemix, gwesp): EpiModel. Starsim’s networks target degrees and matching.
For the fastest agent-based runs at national scale (tens of millions of agents): LASER, which is about 4 times faster on the England and Wales model.
For many small stochastic runs: odin and its companions, whose compiled models start slower but run faster.
For livestock in thousands of herds driven by a register of movements: SimInf.
For models built and used in spreadsheets, with budget optimization: Atomica.
For a full pipeline of hub scenario projections on a cluster: flepiMoP, which has the batch jobs and post-processing Starsim lacks.
For teaching with a graphical interface: NetLogo.
For estimating the reproduction number or forecasting from surveillance data, or for statistical models not about transmission: EpiNow2, the Epiverse packages, Stan, or PyMC.

These models are inter-compatible: an HIV-TB coinfection model can combine the HIV module from STIsim and the TB module from TBsim.


The built-in library
Starsim also comes with a library of example diseases, networks, maternal-child health modules, and health economics, imported with import starsim.library as ssl. They are illustrative rather than validated, and meant to be copied and adapted.
The core of Starsim also includes the classic compartmental structures, ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR (see Diseases).


Choosing a starting model
Start from the smallest model that represents the mechanism your question depends on. These pages are good starting points:



Question
Starting point




How does a closed outbreak progress?
SIR, four ways


How many people are infected in the end? Will a single imported case start an epidemic?
Checks against theory


Does the distribution of the latent or infectious period affect the timing?
SEIR with a realistic infectious period


How many hospital beds will be occupied, and how many people die? Does severity depend on age?
Hospitalization and death


Does an environmental reservoir matter?
Cholera with a water reservoir


Which age groups are most affected? Does closing schools help?
Age groups and contacts, T4 – Mixing


What is the effect of vaccination?
Vaccination as a stratification, T5 – Interventions and scenarios


How does infection move between towns?
T4 – Mixing


What do surveillance data say about the parameters?
Cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, fitted to data, T6 – Data and calibration


What drives recurring epidemics, such as those of measles?
Measles in London


Do individual partnerships matter?
An STI on a sexual network, T4 – Mixing



A runnable example is a starting point, not a calibrated model of a particular population.

title: Time
text:
🧠30% 🤖70%
Every rate in a model is per some unit of time, every duration is in some unit, and a sim runs over a span of time in steps. Give rates and durations with their units (ss.perday(1.9), ss.days(8)), give the span as dates or durations, and Starsim converts between them. Starsim’s choices where reasonable conventions differ come first, below. Units, dates, and steps are introduced in T2 – Building a model.

title: Time
text:
On the philosophy of time
Starsim’s implementation of time is complex, because, well, time is complex. Some questions we’ve had to wrestle with:

If you run a simulation from 2000 to 2020, does it include 2020?
With monthly steps, would you expect the same average number of infections in 2004 (a leap year) as in 2005? What about February 2012 vs. March 2012?
Is a year 365 days, 365.25 days, or either 365 or 366 days depending on the year?
Usually years and dates are interchangeable: start=2000 is start='2000-01-01'. But what if someone simply wants to run for a number of years, start=0, stop=20, given that there is no year 0?
If an event is scheduled for year 2025.7, is that the nearest day (2025-09-14) or that exact moment (2025-09-13 12:00)? Will users ever want to worry about hours and minutes? What about microseconds?
Should units be strict (ss.days(5) != 5) or permissive (ss.days(5) == 5)?
If a death rate is “100 deaths per 1,000 people per year”, should 100 of 1,000 people die in a year, or 95 (since the dead stop accruing person-years)?
What does it mean to multiply a probability? Is ss.prob(0.1)*2 == ss.prob(0.2)? If so, what is ss.prob(0.5)*2, or ss.prob(0.9)*2?

Although time seems intuitive, there are many corners where intuition breaks down (and, worse, it might not seem like it has, leading you astray!). So, more than anywhere else in Starsim, check your assumptions about time. Here are our answers, though we recognize that other answers would also be valid:

The stop is included. start=2000, stop=2020 runs to 1 January 2020 (as np.linspace(0, 20) includes 20), so that a plot ends at 2020 and stop and dur are interchangeable. Since a step is taken from each time point, the last included, the row for 2020 is the state at the start of 2020 and the infections during 2020.
A month is exactly 1/12 of a year, so a monthly rate gives the same number of events in February as in March, and in 2004 as in 2005.
A year is 365 days (with some stretching where needed to make whole years and calendar dates line up).
Whether a sim has a calendar is decided once, from its start. A start that is a date ('2025-01-01') or a year (a number from 1800 on) gives it one; then every bare number given as a time (stop=2030, when=2030) is a calendar year. Any other start (0, or none in a model not in years) means no calendar: a bare time is in the sim’s unit from 0. A duration given as a time is that long after the start (when=ss.days(10)), which is how a reusable intervention says “5 years into the run”.
Dates are whole days, unless a smaller step is asked for explicitly (dt=ss.days(0.25)).
Units are loose when compared with plain numbers (ss.days(5) == 5 is true), and compared by value between units (ss.years(1) == ss.days(365) is true, and ss.years(1) == 1 is true too).
A rate is per person-time: of 1,000 people with a death rate of ss.peryear(0.1), about 95 die in a year (1,000 × (1 − exp(−0.1))), since the dead stop contributing person-years. If 100 is what the data means, it is a probability, ss.prob(0.1, 'year'). (Starsim 2 chose 100; by Starsim 3 we had decided that was wrong.)
A probability stays between 0 and 1: ss.prob(0.5)*2 is 0.75 (the chance of at least one of two events), which also means that ss.prob(0.1)*2 is 0.19, not 0.2.

More information about the philosophy of time is available here.

title: Time
section: The time span, the step, and units
text:
The time span, the step, and units
A sim runs from start to stop (or for dur), in steps of dt. The start and the stop are times, read the same way; dur is the length of the run instead of the stop. The span can be given in these ways:








Given as
Example
Time is




Dates
start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01'
Calendar dates; results are dated


A date and a length
start='2025-01-01', dur=ss.days(180)
The same


Years
start=2025, stop=2030
Years, as numbers with dates behind them


A length
dur=ss.days(50)
Time from 0 (day 0, day 1, …)



Here is the measles model over the first two months of 2025:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(1.9)*I # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01')
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0039 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on 2025-01-07











library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = ss$perday(1.9) * I), # β = 1.9 per day
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),             # Infectious for 8 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-03-01")
sim$run()
sim$plot("measles")



The step, dt, is one unit of the model by default (here a day). Results are recorded at every time point, from the start to the stop inclusive, and a step is taken from each, the last included, so this run has 60 time points and 60 daily steps, the last of them 1 March. Each time point is a period: a stock, such as the number infectious, at a time point is the state at its start, and a flow, such as infections, the number during the step that starts there. The state after the last step is not recorded, so after a run sim.people is one step past the last time point.
Any two of the start, the stop, and the length define the third: start=2000, dur=20 (or dur=ss.years(20)) is the same as start=2000, stop=2020, and stop=2020, dur=20 starts in 2000. A run shorter than one step is an error. With no stop, the run is 50 of the sim’s unit (50 years for a model in years, 50 days for one in days), whatever the step. The final time point is the last one at or before stop (see On the philosophy of time for why the stop is included).

Choosing the step
The ODE takes as many substeps as it needs, Gillespie and tau-leaping work in continuous time, and the chain binomial splits each step into substeps by default, so for these the step mostly sets how often results are recorded (and how often anything worked out once a step, such as a module written as code or a function of the sim, is updated). Agents, and the chain binomial with ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1), take each step whole, so a step that is long compared with the time people spend in a state changes the results. sim.check_dt() measures this by running the sim again with half the step and comparing each result:

agents = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', verbose=0)
agents.check_dt()

Change in each result when the timestep goes from 1 to 0.5 days (largest difference, as a fraction of the largest value):
  measles.infection             60.8%   (peak 29030 → 31540)
  measles.recovery              56.1%   (peak 8570 → 8830)
  measles.prevalence            43.2%   (peak 0.7704 → 0.769)
  measles.I                     43.2%   (peak 77040 → 76900)
  measles.infected              43.2%   (peak 77040 → 76900)
  measles.S                     38.5%   (peak 99900 → 99900)
  measles.R                     14.6%   (peak 99820 → 99860)


For measles as agents, a day is too long a step (dt=ss.days(0.25) is closer to right); slower infections can take much longer steps. Twenty years of daily steps is 7,300 steps; Starsim warns when a sim has very many, since a longer step (dt=ss.weeks(1)) is often enough. See Solvers and backends.
A module can have a step of its own, such as yearly births in a model with weekly transmission (ss.Births(..., dt=ss.years(1))), and the modules are run in order of time.


Units
A typed value carries its own unit (ss.perday(1.9), ss.days(8)) and is converted to the sim’s step, so a model can mix units freely.
A bare number is also accepted. The slot says what it is (after @, it is a rate, not a duration: I >> R @ 8 is 8 per unit of time; for dur=, it is a duration), and the sim’s unit says its unit. This page is the reference for how that unit is chosen; other pages link here. It is the first of these that applies:

unit= given to the sim, e.g. unit='day'.
The typed values in the model’s diseases, declared or written as code (ss.days(8) makes it days). The rates of births and deaths declared in a disease (ss.birth(), ss.death()) don’t count, unless they are its only typed values.
start or stop given as dates: days.
A typed dt (dt=ss.weeks(1)), or else a typed start, stop, or dur (dur=ss.days(50)).
start or stop given as years: years.
The typed values of the networks, demographics, and interventions given to the sim, such as the yearly rates of ss.Births() or of ss.birth() given as demographics=. These never decide the unit when anything above does.
None of these: time is counted in steps (below).

So in S >> I @ 1.9*I beside I >> R @ ss.days(8), the 1.9 is per day, and adding ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)) to the disease, or ss.Births() to the sim, leaves it per day. The unit is never guessed from the size of a number, since 0.05 is plausible per day and per year. sim.describe() says where the unit came from, and the sim says so in a note when it came from anything other than the diseases’ typed values or dates.
When the typed values of rule 2 have different units (days in one disease, years in another, say):

if the diseases that have bare numbers all have their typed values in one and the same unit, that is the unit (e.g. a daily disease with a bare β, beside a yearly one with none);
otherwise, if there are any bare numbers, which unit they are in can’t be known, and the sim raises an error that asks for unit=;
with no bare numbers, nothing depends on the unit: it is the shortest, and the sim warns that it steps by one of it, unless dt= is given.

In a model that mixes daily disease dynamics with yearly demographics, type the disease’s rates (ss.perday(1.9)) or give unit='day', so that nothing depends on these rules.

Time in steps
If nothing has a unit, time is counted in steps: a rate is per step, a duration is in steps, and stop=50 is 50 steps. This is what a textbook model in discrete time means:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
textbook = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, ss.Transition(I, R, dur=8), init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(textbook, total_pop=100_000, stop=50)
sim.run();

Sim: textbook, 100,000 people, as an ODE, steps 0 to 50
  textbook: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0014 s; textbook: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on step 6


Such a sim has no calendar, so dated data, dated interventions, and seasonal parameters (which are yearly cycles) are errors until it is given a unit (unit='day') or dates.

title: Time
text:
Rates, probabilities, and durations
Dates say when things happen, but disease modeling is mostly about durations and rates: how many days from infection to recovery? What is the chance of transmission per week? Starsim calls unit-aware quantities time parameters, and has four kinds, each with constructors for days, weeks, months, and years (a week is exactly 7 days, and a month exactly 1/12 of a year):








Kind
Means
Constructors




Duration
A length of time
ss.days(8), ss.weeks, ss.months, ss.years


Rate
A hazard: events per person per unit of time, happening continuously
ss.perday(1.9), ss.perweek, ss.permonth, ss.peryear


Probability
The chance of an event within a period
ss.prob(0.1, 'day'), and 'week', 'month', 'year'


Frequency
An expected number of events per unit of time, such as sex acts per year
ss.freqperyear(80), or ss.freq(80, 'year')



Converting each to a step is Starsim’s job. Over a step of length Δt, a rate r becomes the probability 1 − exp(−r Δt) of at least one event, a probability p per period T becomes 1 − (1 − p)^(Δt/T), a frequency f becomes f Δt events, and a duration d is used through its rate 1/d. As the rate of a declared transition, a frequency is a hazard, the same as a rate of the same value. The ODE, Gillespie, and tau-leaping use the rates themselves, with no conversion.
Every class is listed in the API reference; a unit given as a string, wherever one is (unit='day', ss.prob(0.1, 'week'), .to('years'), resample('month')), is 'day', 'week', 'month', or 'year', in the singular or the plural. ss.prob(0.1, 'day') and ss.probperday(0.1) are the same, as are ss.freq(80, 'year') and ss.freqperyear(80). Each unit also has a one-unit instance, ss.day, ss.week, ss.month, and ss.year (e.g. ss.prob(0.1, ss.year)). Durations add with the left-hand unit taking precedence, and can be converted: ss.years(2) + ss.days(3) is years(2.00822), and ss.years(10).to('days') is days(3650).
The kinds differ in what multiplying by a duration means, which is how each is converted to a step:

A rate times a duration is a probability: ss.peryear(0.8) * ss.years(1) is 1 − exp(−0.8) ≈ 0.55, the chance of the event happening at least once in a year. A rate times a number is a scaled rate (ss.peryear(0.8) * 2 is 1.6 per year), which is how relative risks are applied. A rate need not be below 1: ss.perday(2) is valid.
A probability times a duration is the probability over that duration, worked out through the rate behind it: ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) * ss.years(2) is 0.96, not 1.6 (which is not a probability).
A frequency times a duration is an expected number of events: ss.freqperyear(80) * ss.years(0.5) is 40, where ss.peryear(80) * ss.years(0.5) is the chance of at least one, almost 1 (for either, .to_events() is the number). Adding a frequency to a rate is an error, since they are converted differently.

The kinds combine where the result has a meaning:

print(ss.perday(0.1) * ss.days(3))               # The chance of at least one event in 3 days
print(ss.prob(0.1, 'day') + ss.prob(0.1, 'day')) # Two competing risks of 0.1 a day: 0.19 a day
print(1 / ss.days(10))                           # A rate: 0.1 per day
print(2 / ss.perday(0.1))                        # A duration: 20 days

0.2591817793182822
probperday(0.19)
perday(0.1)
days(20)


Where they don’t, such as adding a rate to a probability, it is an error that says why.

Which to use

A rate (ss.peryear(0.01)) for anything that happens to a person once, at some rate: infection, recovery, death. This is what most models use, and what an ODE means by a rate.
A duration (ss.days(8)) for the average time spent in a state; it is the same as the rate 1/duration, and usually easier to read.
A probability per period (ss.prob(0.01, 'year')) when the data is a fraction of people in a period: for example, 10 deaths in a year among 1,000 people.
A frequency (ss.freqperyear(80)) for a number of events that can each happen many times, such as contacts or acts.

ss.prob is a number, a time-aware value you can multiply and convert; ss.bernoulli is a distribution sampled for each agent (dist.filter(uids) gives the agents for whom the trial succeeded), which is what a module written as code uses to decide who is infected, dies, or is vaccinated. See Distributions.
Confused? That’s OK. As we said, time is complex.


In modules written as code
A module written as code works with time a step at a time. Each time quantity in its parameters knows the module’s step after sim.init(), so:

rate.to_prob() is the probability of an event in one step;
dur.to_dt() is a duration as a number of steps, for comparing with the step numbers that states such as a time of infection hold;
freq.to_events() (or freq*dt) is the expected number of events in one step.

Convert a rate to a probability as the last step of a calculation, after multiplying it by any relative risks, so that the result is a valid probability:
death_rate = ss.peryear(0.1)
rel_death_age = 3.4 # Older age, higher risk
rel_death_ses = 5.7 # Lower socioeconomic status, higher risk

# Right: multiply first, then convert to a probability
p_death = (death_rate * rel_death_age * rel_death_ses).to_prob()

# Wrong: gives an invalid probability
p_death = death_rate.to_prob() * rel_death_age * rel_death_ses
States such as ti_infected or ti_recovered hold step numbers, not times, so a duration has to be converted to steps before it is added to one:
# Right: the duration as a number of steps (from the step after the infection, which is dated at the end of its step)
self.ti_clearance[uids] = self.ti_infected[uids] + 1 + self.pars.dur_persist.to_dt()

# Wrong: ss.years(100), ss.months(100), and ss.days(100) would all mean "100 steps"
self.ti_clearance[uids] = self.ti_infected[uids] + 1 + self.pars.dur_persist
Declare such a state as an ss.TimeArr, and take the move when self.ti_clearance.due(), which rounds a time between steps up or down at random in proportion, so the duration keeps its mean, as a declared disease’s does (see ss.AgentDisease).
.to_dt() also takes a step, to convert to: ss.years(100).to_dt(ss.months(1)) is 1,200 monthly steps. A duration or rate is never silently a plain number: float(ss.peryear(0.1)) is an error, since ss.peryear(1) and ss.perday(1) would both give 1. Use .to_dt(), .to_prob(), .to('year') (or .years), or .value (the number in its own unit). Durations also work on arrays: ss.years(sim.people.age[uids]).days gives ages in days. Values drawn from a distribution of durations (self.pars.dur_inf.rvs(uids)) are already in steps. See Custom modules.

title: Time
text:
Dates and the timeline
ss.date is a calendar date, based on pd.Timestamp, and can be made from many things:

import datetime as dt
import pandas as pd

d1 = ss.date(2025)
d2 = ss.date(2025, 1, 1)
d3 = ss.date('2025-01-01')
d4 = ss.date(pd.Timestamp('2025-01-01'))
d5 = ss.date(dt.datetime(2025, 1, 1))
print(d1 == d2 == d3 == d4 == d5)

d = ss.date('2025-01-01')
print(d.years)            # As a year
print(d + ss.days(10))    # Ten days later

True
2025.0
2025-01-11


Dates are interchangeable with years as numbers (float(d) is the same as d.years, and ss.date(2025.5) is the middle of 2025), although some rounding can occur. A whole number of months or years added to a date follows the calendar, which is what “six months later” usually means; any other duration counts time exactly, with a year as 365 days and a month as 1/12 of a year:

print(d + ss.months(6))             # Six calendar months later
print(d + ss.years(0.5))            # Half of 365 days later
print(ss.date('2025-07-01') - d)    # The time between two dates, in days

2025-07-01
2025-07-02
days(181)


Six months later is 1 July, but half a year later is 2 July, since 2025.5 is closer to 2 July: a month is 1/12 of a year, and 6/12 is certainly 0.5, but calendars don’t care. Likewise dt=ss.months(1) steps a dated sim by calendar months. A sequence of dates is made with ss.date.arange(start='2025-07-01', stop='2025-09-18', step='week'). ss.years(2000) is not ss.date(2000): the first is a duration of 2,000 years of 365 days with no calendar, the second is 1 January 2000.
sim.t (an ss.Timeline) holds the sim’s time points as datevec (dates), yearvec (years as numbers), relvec (time since the start, in the unit of the step), and tivec (step numbers); timevec, which results use, is dates for a dated sim and time since the start otherwise:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-03-01', dt=ss.weeks(1), verbose=0).init()
print(sim.t.datevec[:4])
print(sim.t.yearvec[:4])
print(sim.t.relvec[:4]) # Weeks since the start

[<2025-01-01> <2025-01-08> <2025-01-15> <2025-01-22>]
[2025.         2025.01917808 2025.03835616 2025.05753425]
[0. 1. 2. 3.]
