title: Scenarios
text:
🧠9% 🤖91%
Let’s be honest: there isn’t much you can do with a single sim run. A scenario is a sim with something changed (an intervention added, a parameter set to another value, a different population), and 99.9% of the time you’ll want to compare several, each run many times, since one stochastic run is just one draw of what could happen. T5 – Interventions and scenarios teaches the same through one example; Running sims covers single sims.

title: Scenarios
text:
Scenarios by label
Here, measles has reached a town of 20,000 people in which 90% are immune, with 50 infectious people on 1 January. The question is what a vaccination campaign that reaches half the town, with a vaccine that cuts each recipient’s chance of infection by 95% (a leaky vaccine, the default; leaky=False would instead fully protect 95% of recipients and leave the rest unprotected: see Products), would avert, and whether it matters if it happens in February or March:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(1.9)                    # Transmission rate per day
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)       # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=50)) # 90% immune, 50 infectious

base = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01')
february = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when='2025-02-01', coverage=0.5)
march    = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when='2025-03-01', coverage=0.5)



library(starsim)

states("S I R")
beta <- par(1.9)              # Transmission rate per day
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = beta * I)
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)) # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles <- Disease(infection = infection, recovery = recovery, init = list(R = 0.9), init_n = list(I = 50)) # 90% immune, 50 infectious

base <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 20000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01")
february <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.95, when = "2025-02-01", coverage = 0.5)
march    <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.95, when = "2025-03-01", coverage = 0.5)



sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed, so each scenario is the base sim with its intervention. ss.parallel() runs a dict of sims by label, at the same time on the computer’s cores:

PythonR



scenarios = {
    'No campaign': base.new(),
    'Campaign in February': base.new(interventions=february),
    'Campaign in March': base.new(interventions=march),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No campaign, Campaign in February, Campaign in March)
  Done in 0.33 s











scenarios <- list(
  "No campaign"          = base$new(),
  "Campaign in February" = base$new(interventions = february),
  "Campaign in March"    = base$new(interventions = march)
)
msim <- parallel(scenarios)
msim$plot("measles.I")



The result is an ss.MultiSim: the runs of every scenario, with each result holding a row for each run. msim.summarize() gives each result over the whole run for each scenario: the total of each flow (measles_infection is the number of infections) and the final value of each state:

Without each=True, t= gives the statistics across the runs of each scenario at that time point instead. ss.parallel() also takes a list of sims (each labeled by its own label), or several sims as arguments; its keywords say how to run them (see the appendix). It runs the sims it is given in place (inplace=False runs copies), which is why the scenarios above are made with base.new().
The sims that ran keep their people, so a run can be looked at person by person afterwards (msim.sims['Campaign in March'][0].people.to_df(), for a run of agents). Of each declared disease, agents keep only the times and histories the model reads (such as ti_I, when a duration needs it); make the sim with keep_times=True to read any other (see People and demographics). For many runs of a large population, shrink=True removes the people from each sim once it has run, keeping the results, to save memory.

title: Scenarios
text:
Many runs of one model
These runs are ODEs, so each scenario has one answer: what happens on average. To see the outbreaks that could happen, run the model stochastically, many times. Here is measles introduced into the same town by only five infectious people: first the ODE, then 50 runs as an exact stochastic compartmental model (solver='gillespie'; see Solvers and backends for the choices):

PythonR



measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5)) # Now 5 infectious
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180))
sim.run();

Sim: measles, 20,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 180
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 5 infectious at the start
  Note: "measles" starts with 5 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does
  Done in 0.0047 s; measles: 1,188 infections; at most 137 infectious, on day 74




measles <- Disease(infection = infection, recovery = recovery, init = list(R = 0.9), init_n = list(I = 5)) # Now 5 infectious
sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 20000, stop = days(180))
sim$run()




PythonR



msim = ss.parallel(sim.new(solver='gillespie'), n_runs=50)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 50 runs
  Done in 0.033 s











msim <- parallel(sim$new(solver = "gillespie"), n_runs = 50)
msim$plot("measles.I")



ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=50) runs it 50 times, each with its own random seed (with no n_runs=, it is one run). The plot shows the median at each time point, and the range that holds 95% of the runs (rather than the mean ± 2 standard deviations, which would happily let deaths go negative); lines=True shows each run instead, which shows what the median hides:

msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)









Reading many runs
msim.summarize() gives each result over the whole of each run (the total of a flow, such as infections; the final value of a state), and then the median, a 95% interval (low to high), the mean, and the standard deviation over the runs:

interval=0.5 gives the interquartile range instead. The band in the plot is different: it is the spread at each time point, taken separately. The median curve is not a typical epidemic, since the runs peak at different times, and its peak is lower than the peak of most runs:

peaks = msim.summarize(how={'measles_I': 'max'}).loc['measles_I'] # The peak of each run, summarized
print('Median of the peaks:', peaks['median'])
print('Peak of the median curve:', msim.results.measles.I.median().max())

Median of the peaks: 137.5
Peak of the median curve: 109.0


So for the size or timing of the peak, summarize the peak of each run, not the median curve; for how many people are infected on a given date, use the band. The usual summaries of a result over the runs are built in:
res = msim.results.measles.I
res.values                       # Every run: one row per run, one column per time point
res.median()                     # The median at each time point
low, mid, high = res.quantiles() # The 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% quantiles at each time point
res.quantiles([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]) # Other quantiles
res.mean()                       # The mean at each time point
res.take(3)                      # One run, as the result of a single sim
Each summary is over the runs of each scenario separately (select(scenario='Campaign in February') picks one). msim.to_df() gives every result as quantiles over the runs at each time, as one long table.
As a rough guide to how many runs, 20 to 50 are enough for a median and the shape of the spread, and a few hundred for the ends of a 95% interval, which rest on the most extreme one run in 40.


Seeds
Every stochastic run starts from a random seed (rand_seed, 1 by default), and the same seed gives the same run, on any computer. n_runs=k uses the seeds rand_seed, rand_seed + 1, …, rand_seed + k − 1, so the first of many runs is the same as a single run, and msim.runs, the table of runs, gives the seed of each, so a run that stands out can be made again on its own. To run particular seeds, give them as a sweep (below): ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(rand_seed=[1, 5, 9])) gives three runs of the sim’s scenario (not three scenarios). An ODE has no random numbers, so its seed changes nothing. To compare two runs, see Profiling and debugging.

title: Scenarios
text:
Comparing scenarios with many runs
Comparing two scenarios run many times, the question is whether the difference between them is larger than chance alone would make. The runs of each scenario use the same seeds in the same order, so the first run of the baseline and the first run of the campaign share their random numbers: the same chains of transmission, until the campaign changes them (common random numbers; see Random numbers). The difference between paired runs is then mostly the effect of the intervention, not noise. msim.diff() gives the difference of each scenario from a baseline, run by run, and msim.summarize(baseline=...) summarizes those differences. Here are the February campaign and the baseline, each run 20 times with the chain binomial (the “Explicit” tab makes the 20 runs of each with the seeds that n_runs=20 gives them):

PythonRExplicit



scenarios = {
    'No campaign': base.new(solver='binomial', verbose=0),

title: Scenarios
text:
Parameter sweeps and uncertainty

Parameter sweeps
To see how a result depends on a parameter, run the sim with each of a set of values. pars= takes a list of values for each parameter, and each value is a scenario of its own, labeled with it. Here the outbreak with β from 1.5 to 2.3 per day (R0 from 12 to 18):

PythonR



sim = base.new(verbose=0) # Back to the base sim, with 50 infectious at the start
msim = ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(beta=[1.5, 1.9, 2.3]))
msim.plot('measles.I')










sim <- base$new(verbose = 0) # Back to the base sim, with 50 infectious at the start
msim <- parallel(sim, pars = list(beta = c(1.5, 1.9, 2.3)))
msim$plot("measles.I")




msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

scenario

The parameter is named as it is in the model: here beta, the name of the ss.par() it was given (describe() lists the names); with more than one disease, give the disease too (pars={'measles.beta': [1.5, 2.3]}). The values become columns of msim.runs, the table of runs, and a result can be picked by value: msim.results.measles.I.select(beta=2.3). Several parameters given together are taken value by value, so each needs the same number of values; for other sets, such as a full grid, give a list of dicts ([dict(beta=b, dur=d) for b in betas for d in durs]). n_runs= runs each set that many times, with the same seeds for each set. A seed given in pars= is a run of its scenario, not a scenario of its own.


Uncertainty in parameter values
A sweep gives each value equal space, but that does not say they are equally likely. A parameter declared with ss.par() and bounds (or a prior) can be drawn afresh for each run with priors=True: each run takes a value drawn uniformly between the bounds (or from the prior), on a Latin hypercube so that few runs cover the range evenly, and a seed of its own, so the spread of the runs includes both. Here β is between 1.5 and 2.3 per day (R0 between 12 and 18), with the five initial cases from before, compared with the same runs with β fixed:

beta = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1.5, 2.3]) # β, known to lie between these values
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='gillespie', verbose=0)
fixed = ss.parallel(sim.new(label='Beta fixed at 1.9'), n_runs=50)
drawn = ss.parallel(sim.new(label='Beta drawn between 1.5 and 2.3'), priors=True, n_runs=50)

title: Scenarios
text:
Pitfalls

Scenarios that differ in more than the intervention. Make each scenario from the same base with sim.new(), so that everything else, including the seed, is the same.
Comparing medians instead of differences. The difference between the medians of two scenarios is not the median difference; use msim.diff() for the effect of an intervention, run by run.
Runs that die out pull the summary down. If the question is about outbreaks that take off, look at those runs, and report the chance of dying out separately.
Running in parallel from a script. On Windows and macOS, put the code that runs the sims under if __name__ == '__main__': (see Speed and scale); where processes can’t be started, use workers=1.
Reading a band as a confidence interval for a parameter. The band over runs with fixed values is the spread due to chance alone; it says nothing about how well β is known unless the runs drew β too (priors=True).

Further reading

Covasim: Running scenarios: multisims, scenarios, and uncertainty in Starsim’s predecessor
EpiModel: Training materials: stochastic network models and their simulation-based uncertainty in R
Epiverse epidemics: Modelling scenarios: comparing intervention scenarios, with parameter uncertainty, in an R package
Epiverse epidemics: Parameter uncertainty: drawing parameter values for each run, as priors=True does here

title: Scenarios
text:
Appendix: MultiSims and ss.parallel()

What a MultiSim has
The methods of an ss.MultiSim that a modeler uses, each with the first line of its docstring (see ss.MultiSim for the rest). combine() adds the runs together into one sim, as if they were one population (counts summed, other results averaged by population), and ss.MultiSim.merge() and split() put the runs of several MultiSims together and apart again:

import inspect
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None) # Show each entry in full

names = ['plot', 'plot_each', 'summarize', 'diff', 'to_df', 'combine', 'merge', 'split', 'shrink', 'copy', 'branching', 'run_pars']
docs = {name: inspect.getdoc(getattr(ss.MultiSim, name)).split('\n')[0] for name in names}
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(docs, orient='index', columns=['What it gives'])








What it gives




plot
Plot the results across the runs: the median and a 95% interval of each scenario, or every run if `lines=True`


plot_each
Plot each run on its own time axis, for sims with different time points (see `plot()`): each scenario in a color of its own


summarize
A table of each result over the whole of each run, across the runs: the median, an interval, the mean, and the standard deviation


diff
The difference of each scenario from a baseline, for every result they share, run by run


to_df
Every result across the runs; see `ss.run.MultiResults.to_df()` for the arguments


combine
Combine the sims into a single sim, whose results are those of one population made of all of them, e.g. to treat several smaller sims as one larger population


merge
Merge several MultiSims into one, with the runs of each, one after the other; `msim.split()` separates them again.


split
Split one MultiSim into several, each with some of its runs; the reverse of `ss.MultiSim.merge()`.


shrink
Shrink each sim, to save memory (e.g. before saving the MultiSim), keeping the results across runs; see `sim.shrink()`


copy
A deep copy of the MultiSim, its sims included


branching
For the runs of a branching process (`ss.Sim(branching=True)`): what came of them together, as an `ss.run.Branching`; None if the runs are not branching processes (see `sim.branching` for one run)


run_pars
The values of the parameters swept (or drawn) in each run, as a dataframe (or None if there are none)







Its attributes are msim.results (every result with a run axis first), msim.runs (one row per run: its scenario, the values swept or drawn, and its seed), and msim.sims (the sims that were run, by position or by scenario). For many thousands of runs, keep only what you need from each (msim.summarize(), msim.to_df()) rather than the MultiSim itself; ss.converters.to_hub() writes runs as the quantile tables that forecasting hubs take. A result across runs has these methods of its own:

names = ['median', 'mean', 'quantiles', 'take', 'select', 'cum', 'plot']
docs = {name: inspect.getdoc(getattr(ss.Result, name)).split('\n')[0] for name in names}
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(docs, orient='index', columns=['What it gives'])








What it gives




median
For a result across runs, the median over the runs of each scenario (as a result of one run, if there is one scenario); otherwise the median of the values


mean
For a result across runs, the mean over the runs of each scenario (as a result of one run, if there is one scenario); otherwise the mean of the values


quantiles
Quantiles over the runs of each scenario, for a result across the runs of a MultiSim


take
Some of the runs of a result across runs: a result of one run for a position, or across runs for a list of them


select
Select groups of a stratified result by name: keeps the given levels of each dimension, and sums over the rest


cum
The cumulative total of a flow over time, e.g. `sim.results.sir.infection.cum` (a stock; computed when asked for)


plot
Plot the result, with one line per column for a 2D result









The keywords of ss.parallel()
ss.parallel() and ss.MultiSim() take the same keywords (ss.parallel() is ss.MultiSim(...).run()), and msim.run() takes them again to change them:








Keyword
Default
What it does




the sims

One sim, a list of sims, several sims as arguments, or a dict of them by label (ss.parallel({'baseline': s1, 'vaccine': s2}))


n_runs
1
Run each sim this many times, with the seeds rand_seed, rand_seed + 1, …


pars
none
Sets of values of the model’s parameters, each a scenario of its own: a dict of lists, taken value by value, or a list of dicts


priors
False
Draw n_runs sets of values from the parameters’ priors (or bounds), on a Latin hypercube; or the draws themselves, e.g. from a posterior


workers
one per CPU
The number of processes; 1 runs the sims one after the other in this process


shrink
False
Remove the people from each sim once it has run, keeping the results


inplace
True
Update the sims given (with no n_runs or pars) with their results; False runs copies


verbose
the sims’ own
How much each run prints; by default the MultiSim shows the progress of the runs


until
none
As for sim.run(), for each run: a time, or a condition that stops it


run_args
none
Passed to each sim.run()


par_args
none
Passed to sc.Parallel(), which runs the processes


label
none
A name for the MultiSim

title: Diseases
text:
🧠45% 🤖55%
The Starsim library (import starsim.library as ssl; see Library for what it is) has ready-made diseases: outbreak diseases such as measles, Ebola, and cholera, HIV with its treatment, short versions of published models of others, and SIR, SIS, and SEIR written as code. Most are declared as states and transitions, so they run as compartments or as agents (see Diseases); the rest are written as code, so they run as agents (see Custom modules).
Library classes are available both at the top level and through their submodule (ssl.Measles is ssl.diseases.Measles), and can be mixed freely with core modules, here a library disease on a core network:
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

outbreak = dict(start='2000', dur=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.Measles(beta=ss.perday(0.3)), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak) # On a network, beta is the rate per contact
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles')

Sim: measles, as 2,000 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2001-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (per infectious contact), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters
  Note: init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a fraction) or init_n= (a number)


  Done in 0.28 s; measles: 1,990 infections; at most 1,482 infectious, on 2000-02-05
The outbreak diseases, and those written as code (the rest are further down; the API reference has every class, with its parameters and defaults):

title: Diseases
section: Outbreak diseases: measles, Ebola, and cholera
text:
Outbreak diseases: measles, Ebola, and cholera
The three outbreak diseases are declared, so they run as compartments or as agents, with or without a network. Measles is an SEIR with deaths: a latent period of about 8 days, an infectious period of about 11, an R0 of about 15, and a probability of death of 0.5%. Ebola and Cholera have fuller natural histories (severe disease and burial; symptoms and shedding into the water), each written as states and transitions. Their beta is a rate of transmission per day mixing homogeneously; on a network, it is the rate per contact, so give one suited to the network.
Ebola gives each case a chance of severe disease (p_sev) and of death (p_death); severe cases (Sev) transmit more (sev_factor), and so do the bodies of those who have died (D) until they are buried (unburied_factor), unless they are buried safely, at once, which happens with probability p_safe_bury. Here a quarter of burials are safe (the default), or all of them, with each scenario run 5 times, since chance matters near the epidemic threshold:

ebola = lambda p_safe_bury: ssl.Ebola(beta=ss.perday(0.008), p_safe_bury=p_safe_bury)
scenarios = {
    'A quarter of burials safe': ss.Sim(diseases=ebola(0.25), networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
    'Every burial safe':         ss.Sim(diseases=ebola(1.0),  networks=ss.RandomNet(), **outbreak),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=5, workers=1)
msim.plot(['ebola.infected', 'ebola.infection.cum'])

MultiSim: 10 runs of 2 scenarios (A quarter of burials safe, Every burial safe)
  Done in 7.5 s









Cholera adds environmental transmission to the usual transmission from person to person, with a state that is a count of bacteria rather than people (W, ss.State(people=False)): infectious people shed bacteria into it (at shedding_rate, asymptomatic people much less), the bacteria die off (at decay_rate), and susceptible people are infected by the water at a rate that rises with the concentration, reaching half of beta_env at half_sat_rate. This is the pattern to follow for any indirectly transmitted disease (see also Cholera with a water reservoir). Here it is with and without the environmental route (beta_env=0):

town = dict(start='2000', dur=ss.years(1), total_pop=10_000)
scenarios = {
    'Person to person and water': ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.Cholera(), **town),
    'Person to person only':      ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.Cholera(beta_env=ss.perday(0)), **town),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
msim.plot(['cholera.infected', 'cholera.infection.cum', 'cholera.env_conc'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Person to person and water, Person to person only)
  Done in 0.072 s









The results W (the bacteria in the water) and env_conc (their concentration, as a fraction of the maximum rate of infection from the water) track the reservoir.

title: Diseases
text:
HIV, treatment, and CD4 counts
ssl.HIV comes with two companion modules that show how a disease, an intervention, and an analyzer fit together:

ssl.ART is a delivery, as ss.treat() is, that offers treatment once to each person infected for a year (art_delay), with the chance coverage (here an ss.timeseries, scaled up over the years), reducing transmission by art_efficacy and raising CD4 counts back towards cd4_max. who= and when= restrict who is offered it and when, as for any delivery.
ssl.CD4_analyzer is an analyzer that records every agent’s CD4 count at every step, as an array of steps by agents (sim.analyzers.cd4_analyzer.cd4), so it suits small sims.

HIV plays out over years, so steps of a year suit it. It runs on ss.SexualNet, where beta is a probability per act, from men to women and from women to men (ss.peract):

endemic = dict(start='2000', stop='2030', dt=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000)
hiv = lambda: ssl.HIV(beta=ss.peract(m2f=0.004, f2m=0.002), init_prev=0.05)
net = lambda: ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(2))
art = ssl.ART(coverage=ss.timeseries({2005: 0, 2015: 0.9}, 'linear')) # Coverage rising from 0 in 2005 to 90% in 2015

scenarios = {
    'No ART':   ss.Sim(diseases=hiv(), networks=net(), analyzers=ssl.CD4_analyzer(), **endemic),
    'With ART': ss.Sim(diseases=hiv(), networks=net(), analyzers=ssl.CD4_analyzer(), interventions=art, **endemic),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
msim.plot(['hiv.prevalence', 'hiv.death'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No ART, With ART)
  Done in 0.3 s















Note



ART offers treatment once to each agent, when they have been infected for art_delay (or when it starts, for those infected longer ago), with the coverage at that time: someone offered it while coverage was low is not offered it again. If the number on treatment (n_art) stays at zero, check the coverage and that people are still being infected when treatment starts.

title: Diseases
text:
Other diseases written as code
ssl.NCD is a non-communicable disease, so it needs no network. Each agent starts at risk with probability initial_risk; those at risk develop the condition after a time drawn from dur_risk, and die of it after a time drawn from prognosis. Its results are the number at risk, the prevalence of the condition, and the deaths from it. Here a treatment doubles the time people survive with the condition (prognosis, a Weibull distribution whose scale is the typical survival):

chronic = dict(start='2000', stop='2040', dt=ss.years(1), n_agents=2000, demographics=[ss.Births(), ss.Deaths()])
scenarios = {
    'Current care':                ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.NCD(), **chronic),
    'Treatment doubling survival': ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.NCD(prognosis=ss.weibull(shape=2, scale=ss.years(10))), **chronic),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
msim.plot(['ncd.prevalence', 'ncd.death'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Current care, Treatment doubling survival)
  Done in 0.21 s









Only the starting population is ever at risk here; a model of a real risk factor would put newborns and others at risk too, which is a change of init_post() and step() (see Adapting a library module).
The core ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are declared, with exponential durations and no deaths unless p_death is given. ssl.AgentSIR, ssl.AgentSIS, and ssl.AgentSEIR are Starsim 3’s versions of the same models, written as code, with Starsim 3’s defaults (in years, where those of ss.SIR are of a respiratory infection, in days): durations are lognormal (dur_inf=ss.lognormal(mean=ss.years(6)) by default), and AgentSIR and AgentSEIR have p_death=0.01. They schedule each course in whole steps as the agent engine does a declared disease’s, so each case, seeds included, is infectious for dur_inf on average. AgentSIS also has a level of immunity for each agent, boosted by each infection (imm_boost) and waning exponentially (waning), which lowers that agent’s susceptibility. They are the classes to build on for a disease that changes how infection, progression, or recovery happens for each agent, as the outbreak diseases above do; a Starsim 3 subclass of ss.SIR that replaces its methods can build on ssl.AgentSIR instead, unchanged (see Starsim v3).
With the same mean duration and no deaths, the epidemic of AgentSIR peaks higher and ends more sharply than that of ss.SIR, whose exponential durations give many short infections and a few very long ones. Their results are named differently: the declared model’s after its states (I) and transitions (infection), and the version written as code with Starsim 3’s names (infected, and the same infection).

title: Diseases
text:
Declared diseases
The rest of the library’s diseases are declared, as states and transitions (Diseases), so each runs as a compartmental model or as agents. Each is a short version of a published model, with its default parameters from that source, named for the disease rather than for the model, so the source is given here and in each class’s docstring. They are still illustrative: each is the simplest version of its model that shows what makes it interesting, and none has been fitted to a particular place.








Class
What it shows
The model, and where the parameters come from




ssl.Malaria
A vector: people and mosquitoes in one model, the mosquitoes as counts rather than people
The Ross-Macdonald model, in the form of Keeling MJ, Rohani P, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals, Princeton University Press, 2008, Program 4.4, which gives every parameter


ssl.MalariaImmunity
Immunity that builds with exposure: inoculation that saturates, superinfection, and a faster recovery once immune
The Garki model of Dietz K, Molineaux L, Thomas A, Bull World Health Organ 1974;50:347-357, as given in Molineaux L, Gramiccia G, The Garki Project, WHO, 1980, ch. 10, Table 31


ssl.TB
A spectrum of disease, with movement back and forth between states and reinfection
The LSHTM model of Schwalb A et al., PLOS Glob Public Health 2025;5(1):e0005050, in the form of TBsim’s reference ODE (lshtm_ode.R), which gives every parameter


ssl.COVID
A chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering, by age
MEmilio’s values for Germany by age (Kühn MJ et al., Mathematical Biosciences 2021), which give every parameter; ages=False gives MEmilio’s simple example, in one group


ssl.Influenza
A yearly cycle in transmission (ss.seasonal) with waning immunity
Natural history from Carrat F et al., Am J Epidemiol 2008;167:775-785; R0 of 1.3 from Biggerstaff M et al., BMC Infect Dis 2014;14:480; the cycle is illustrative


ssl.RSV
Maternal immunity: babies born protected, in a seasonal MSEIRS model
Weber A, Weber M, Milligan P, Math Biosci 2001;172:95-113, for the infectious period, the seasonal form, and R0


ssl.Pertussis
Immunity that wanes over decades, giving epidemics that return every few years
Wearing HJ, Rohani P, PLoS Pathogens 2009;5(10):e1000647, for the natural history, R0, and duration of immunity


ssl.Dengue
Several serotypes, each a disease with its own vector, and partial cross-protection between them
The Ross-Macdonald structure above, with indicative dengue values; cross-protection as found by Reich NG et al., J R Soc Interface 2013;10:20130414


ssl.Typhoid
Chronic carriers: a few people shed for life, at a hundredth of the infectiousness of an acute case
Pitzer VE et al., PLoS Negl Trop Dis 2014;8(1):e2642, for the carriers, waning, and R0 of 2.8


ssl.Polio
A rare outcome as a branch: about 1 infection in 200 causes paralysis
US CDC Pink Book for the paralytic fraction; Fine PEM, Carneiro IAM, Am J Epidemiol 1999;150:1001-1021, for R0


ssl.Syphilis
Stages, with infectiousness that falls with the time each person has spent in the latent stage, which needs agents
STIsim’s syphilis module, which cites its own sources


ssl.Gonorrhea
An SIS infection on a sexual network
STIsim’s gonorrhea module



Malaria is the clearest example of what declaring buys: mosquitoes are states like any other, declared with people=False so that they are counts rather than people, and R0() works out the reproduction number from the model itself:

malaria = ssl.Malaria()
print('R0:', round(malaria.R0(), 1))

sim = ss.Sim(malaria, total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=600, verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.malaria.plot('Ih', 'Iv')

R0: 14.6









Starsim’s R0() counts each passage through a mosquito as a generation, so it is the square root of the classical Ross-Macdonald value, m·a²·b·c/(γ·μ_v) = 213.
The Garki model adds immunity, and with it the result the source is known for: malaria dies out below a critical vectorial capacity, (α₁ + δ)/g, which is 0.022 contacts per person per day with these parameters:

critical = 0.022
for C in [0.5*critical, 2*critical, 0.2]:
    sim = ss.Sim(ssl.MalariaImmunity(C=C), total_pop=10_000, unit='day', dt=ss.days(5), stop=ss.days(365*30), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.malariaimmunity
    print('Vectorial capacity', round(C, 3), '- parasite rate', round(res.prevalence[-1], 3), '- detected', round(res.detected[-1], 3))

Vectorial capacity 0.011 - parasite rate 0.0 - detected 0.0
Vectorial capacity 0.044 - parasite rate 0.313 - detected 0.311
Vectorial capacity 0.2 - parasite rate 0.509 - detected 0.491


The same declaration runs as agents (n_agents= instead of total_pop=), where the prevalence is the same but each run differs by chance.
Since these are declared, describe(), diagram(), and equations() work on any of them, which is the quickest way to see what a model does (ssl.Dengue is a set of serotypes, each an ssl.DengueSerotype, so each is shown in its own right, e.g. sim.diseases.den1.diagram()):

ssl.Typhoid().equations()

dS/dt = -birth_rate * S - (beta * S * I / N + beta * rel_carrier * S * C / N) + R / dur_imm + birth_rate * (S + I + C + R).n
dI/dt =  (beta * S * I / N + beta * rel_carrier * S * C / N) - birth_rate * I - I / dur_inf
dC/dt =  p_carrier * I / dur_inf - birth_rate * C
dR/dt =  (1 - p_carrier) * I / dur_inf - birth_rate * R - R / dur_imm


One of them needs agents rather than compartments: ssl.Syphilis, because the falling infectiousness of latent syphilis depends on the time each person has spent in that stage (El.time_in, in two modifiers of rel_trans declared in the class), a clock that is kept for each person. The two sexually transmitted infections, ssl.Syphilis and ssl.Gonorrhea, also take a probability of transmission per act (ss.peract), so they need a sexual network such as ss.SexualNet, whose partnerships run as agents. The rest run under any solver.

title: Diseases
text:
Adapting a library module
Library modules are ordinary Starsim modules, so they can be changed in the usual ways. The simplest is to change their parameters:

measles = ssl.Measles(beta=ss.perday(1.2), dur_exp=ss.normal(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2)), p_death=0.01)


Advanced: building on a class
For a change to how the disease works, build on the class. Here ssl.AgentSEIR gets immunity that wanes, after a time drawn for each person from dur_immune, and a small daily chance of infection from outside the population (p_import). The new class adds two parameters and a state in __init__(), schedules the loss of immunity when each agent is infected (set_prognoses()), and at each step makes the agents whose time has come susceptible again and infects the imported cases (step_state()):

class WaningSEIR(ssl.AgentSEIR):
    def __init__(self, dur_immune=ss.expon(mean=ss.years(1)), p_import=ss.bernoulli(p=1e-4), **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.define_pars(dur_immune=dur_immune, p_import=p_import)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.TimeArr('ti_susceptible', label='Time of losing immunity'))
        return

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.ti_susceptible[uids] = self.ti_recovered[uids] + self.pars.dur_immune.rvs(uids)
        return

    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()
        waned = (self.recovered & self.ti_susceptible.due()).uids
        self.recovered[waned] = False
        self.susceptible[waned] = True
        self.infect(self.pars.p_import.filter(self.susceptible.uids)) # Infections from outside, counted in the result infection
        return

cold = dict( # A cold: a latent period of 3 days, infectious for a week, and an R0 of about 2
    beta = ss.perday(0.03),
    dur_exp = ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(3)),
    dur_inf = ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(7)),
    p_death = 0,
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name = 'cold',
)
pars = dict(start='2000', dur=ss.years(4), n_agents=5000, networks=ss.RandomNet())
scenarios = {
    'Lifelong immunity':              ss.Sim(diseases=WaningSEIR(dur_immune=ss.constant(ss.years(100)), **cold), **pars),
    'Immunity for a year on average': ss.Sim(diseases=WaningSEIR(**cold), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
msim.plot(['cold.infectious', 'cold.susceptible'])

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Lifelong immunity, Immunity for a year on average)
  Done in 6.3 s









Copying a library module and editing it is also a good way to use it; that is what these modules are for. See Custom modules for writing modules from scratch, and the tutorial T8 – Custom modules for a worked example.

title: Products
text:
🧠9% 🤖91%
Vaccination, screening, and treatment programs have two parts: what is given (a vaccine, a test, or a drug: a product), and the delivery, which says who gets it, when, and how many. Starsim keeps the two apart, so the same vaccine can be given routinely in one scenario and in a campaign in another. This page covers products; deliveries, and changes to parameters that need no product, are on Interventions, and costs on Health economics. The tutorial T5 – Interventions and scenarios uses a vaccine for measles, and then tests and treatment (Advanced: interventions as agents).
Each delivery (ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), ss.treat()) takes the product’s own keywords and makes the product, or takes a product made explicitly, as where one product is given by several deliveries (see below). Name a delivery after the activity (vaccination, screening), since the product takes the name of the thing (vaccine, test). Every keyword of each product is in the appendix.
Products run under every solver, but what follows each person’s own history needs agents, and a compartmental run approximates some waning shapes (see What needs agents); for any waning shape under every solver, write the protection as states of the disease, and move people into them with an event (see Interventions).
The examples on this page use a curable infection with no lasting immunity, as an SIS model run as agents:
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(2)*I  # β = 2 per year
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.years(1)      # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.1)

kw = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2020, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)

title: Products
text:
Vaccines
A vaccine’s efficacy is its protection against infection: the chance of infection of everyone who holds it is multiplied by 1 − efficacy. A dict gives efficacy against infectiousness, death, any transition, several diseases, or each strain (see the appendix).
By default a vaccine is leaky: everyone vaccinated is partly protected. With leaky=False it is all or nothing: a fraction efficacy of those vaccinated are fully protected, and the rest not at all. waning= is how protection fades: a duration means it is lost after an exponentially distributed time with that mean. Here are all three, given to half of people in 2010:

kw_vx = dict(coverage=0.5, when='2010')
scenarios = {
    'No vaccine':                     ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Leaky (80%)':                    ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, **kw_vx), **kw),
    'All or nothing (80%)':           ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, leaky=False, **kw_vx), **kw),
    'Leaky, waning after 3 years':    ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=ss.years(3), **kw_vx), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








doses=[0.85, 1.0] gives a vaccine in doses, with the fraction of the full protection after each; each delivery to someone who already holds the vaccine gives the next dose.
Protection can also fade by its own shape. ss.boxcar(plateau=..., decay=...) is full protection for plateau, then (with decay=) an exponential decline with that mean. Agents follow it exactly; a compartmental run approximates the plateau by a series of levels, each left at a rate, so its end is spread out (stages= sets how many), and says so in a note. Any other shape is a function of the time since delivery, t (a duration, so t.years works in any sim), returning the fraction of protection left; a function of (t, sim, uids) also gets the sim and the people who hold it. A function runs as agents only.

scenarios = {
    'Plateau of 2 years, then a decline': ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=ss.boxcar(plateau=ss.years(2), decay=ss.years(3)), **kw_vx), **kw),
    'Fading linearly over 5 years':   ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, waning=lambda t: np.clip(1 - t.years/5, 0, 1), **kw_vx), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








during= holds a product only while people are in some states: ss.Treatment(efficacy=dict(transmission=0.5), during=sis.I) makes people half as infectious while they are infected, and they stop holding it when they recover.
The fraction of people holding a product is also a quantity a rate can read: itn.held_frac is the fraction of the people in the same place who hold it, each counted by the protection they have left, and itn.held_frac(fn) counts each by a function of the time since delivery (e.g. the fraction of mosquitoes a net kills). A disease made with the product can use it in any rate, e.g. Sv >> ss.dead @ 1/life + a*kill*itn.held_frac.

One product, several deliveries
A product made on its own can be given by several deliveries, which then share it: a person vaccinated by either holds the same vaccine, and is not protected twice, and a delivery skips people who already hold its product (unless the product fades by a shape or a function, when a new dose restarts it). Here a vaccine is given routinely to children as they turn one, and in a campaign in 2010, either of the same vaccine or of a vaccine of its own, so that a child reached by both holds two:

kw_births = dict(kw, demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.03))])

vaccine  = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8)
routine  = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, who=ss.at_age(ss.years(1)), start='2005', coverage=0.8)
campaign = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, when=['2010'], coverage=0.5)
separate = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.8, when=['2010'], coverage=0.5, name='campaign') # Makes a second vaccine

scenarios = {
    'No vaccination':                     ss.Sim(sis, **kw_births),
    'Routine':                            ss.Sim(sis, interventions=routine, **kw_births),
    'Routine and campaign, one vaccine':  ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[routine, campaign], **kw_births),
    'Routine and campaign, two vaccines': ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[routine, separate], **kw_births),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')
for sim in msim.sims[2:]:
    print(sim.label, '- doses in the campaign:', round(sim.results.campaign.delivered.sum()), '- routine doses:', round(sim.results.routine.delivered.sum()))








Routine and campaign, one vaccine - doses in the campaign: 2183 - routine doses: 1693
Routine and campaign, two vaccines - doses in the campaign: 2456 - routine doses: 1751

title: Products
text:
Tests and what follows them
A test (ss.Diagnostic) has a sensitivity, the chance that someone infected tests positive, and a specificity, the chance that someone not infected tests negative. ss.screen() delivers it, and its positive and negative are the people with each result on that step. What happens to them is another delivery, triggered by when=screening.positive, with its own coverage, so loss to follow-up is explicit. Here half of people are screened each year from 2010, and 80% of those who test positive are treated with a drug that cures 95%. The “Explicit” tab makes the test and the drug as products first, and gives them to the deliveries, which is what the keywords do:

PythonRExplicit



screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2010'), coverage=0.5)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[screening, treatment], **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')
print('Positive tests:', sim.results.screening.positive.sum())
print('Treated:', sim.results.treatment.delivered.sum())








Positive tests: 9654.0
Treated: 7665.0




library(starsim)

# The SIS model above
states("S I")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = ss$peryear(2) * I) # β = 2 per year
recovery  <- Transition(I, S, dur = years(1))           # Infected for a year on average, then susceptible again
sis <- Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev = 0.1)

screening <- ss$screen(sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.98, when = ss$schedule(every = years(1), start = "2010"), coverage = 0.5)
treatment <- ss$treat(cure = 0.95, when = screening$positive, coverage = 0.8)

sim <- Sim(sis, interventions = list(screening, treatment), n_agents = 5000, start = 2000, stop = 2020, dt = ss$months(1), verbose = 0)
sim$run()
sim$plot("sis")
cat("Positive tests:", sum(sim$results$screening$positive$values), "\n")
cat("Treated:", sum(sim$results$treatment$delivered$values), "\n")



test = ss.Diagnostic(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98) # The product: what the test does
drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.95)

screening = ss.screen(test, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2010'), coverage=0.5, name='screening') # The delivery: who gets it, and when
treatment = ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8, name='treatment')

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[screening, treatment], **kw)
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')
print('Positive tests:', sim.results.screening.positive.sum())
print('Treated:', sim.results.treatment.delivered.sum())








Positive tests: 9654.0
Treated: 7665.0





A follow-up can have follow-ups of its own, to any depth. By default a test detects infection with the disease it is given for; detects= takes a condition for anything else. result_delay= is the time from the test to its result. A test’s values can be by the states of several diseases ({hpv16.I: 0.9, 'hpv18.CIN': 0.95}); with disease=[...], someone is tested once, in the most severe state they are in.
A test can have more than two outcomes: outcomes= gives them, most severe first, each with its chance for people in each state (None for people in none of them), and the last is everyone the others don’t take. Each outcome is a result of the delivery and an event that can trigger what follows:

cytology = ss.Diagnostic(outcomes=dict(high=dict(I=0.9), low={'I': 0.05, None: 0.02}, normal=None)) # Low grade for 2% of those not infected
screening = ss.screen(cytology, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1), start='2010'), coverage=0.5)
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.8, when=screening.high)

sim = ss.Sim(sis, interventions=[screening, treatment], **kw)
sim.run()
print('High grade:', sim.results.screening.high.sum())
print('Low grade:', sim.results.screening.low.sum())

High grade: 9080.0
Low grade: 829.0

title: Products
text:
Treatments
A treatment’s cure is the chance that it clears the infection, once, when it is given: the person leaves the infected states for the state the disease’s recovery leads to. Its efficacy is what it does for as long as it is held, as for a vaccine: antiretroviral therapy for HIV is efficacy=dict(transmission=0.96, mortality=0.9). A treatment is given to the people who are infected, unless the delivery says otherwise. cure= can be a number (everyone infected), a dict by state (cure=dict(cin=0.9), only those in these states; a disease written as code is cured by its clear_infection()), or a dict by what cured people move along: a transition (cure={tb.cure: 0.9}), or a move written with the states (cure={I + CIN >> S: 0.9}).
Here are the two kinds, each given to infected people at a rate of 50% a year: a cure, and a treatment that cuts how infectious people are by 90% while they are infected:

cure = ss.treat(cure=0.9, coverage=ss.peryear(0.5))
suppress = ss.treat(efficacy=dict(transmission=0.9), during=sis.I, coverage=ss.peryear(0.5))

scenarios = {
    'No treatment':                ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Cure':                        ss.Sim(sis, interventions=cure, **kw),
    'Less infectious while held':  ss.Sim(sis, interventions=suppress, **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')









Treatment outcomes and resistance
A treatment that cures has three outcomes on each step, which are results of its delivery and events that can trigger what follows, as a test’s results are: cured, failed (infected, and not cured), and unneeded (given to someone not infected, e.g. after a false positive). ss.treat(..., when=treatment.failed) gives a second-line drug to those the first failed.
A cure keyed by transitions usually names transitions with a rate of 0 (cure = I >> S @ 0), which only treatment drives, each with its own probability: ss.Treatment(cure={syph.cure_early: 0.98, syph.cure_late: 0.95}) cures each stage of syphilis with its own chance, and ss.Treatment(cure={ng.cure: 0.95, ct.cure: 0.95}) is one kit that cures two diseases. moves= names transitions the same way for a treatment that is not a cure, such as starting care (ss.Treatment(moves=hiv.start_art)).
Resistance to a drug is then a transition of the disease, triggered by the drug’s failures. Here a gonorrhea-like infection has a resistant strain (Ir), which arises in 20% of the people the drug fails, and which the drug doesn’t cure:

S, I, Ir = ss.states('S I Ir')
infection     = S >> I  @ ss.peryear(2)*I   # Sensitive infections
infection_res = S >> Ir @ ss.peryear(2)*Ir  # Resistant infections, as transmissible
recovery      = I  >> S @ ss.years(1)
recovery_res  = Ir >> S @ ss.years(1)
cure          = I  >> S @ 0                 # A rate of 0: only treatment moves people along it
drug = ss.Treatment(cure={cure: 0.95})
resistance = ss.Transition(I, Ir, when=drug.failed, p=0.2) # Resistance arises in 20% of failures
ng = ss.Disease(infection, infection_res, recovery, recovery_res, cure, resistance, init_n=dict(I=500), name='ng') # 500 sensitive infections at the start

treatment = ss.treat(drug, start='2005', coverage=ss.peryear(0.5)) # Given to the people in the source of cure, I
sim = ss.Sim(ng, interventions=treatment, n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.plot(['ng.I', 'ng.Ir'])
res = sim.results.treatment
print('Cured:', round(res.cured.sum()), '- failed:', round(res.failed.sum()), '- resistant infections in 2030:', round(sim.results.ng.Ir[-1]))








Cured: 8054 - failed: 440 - resistant infections in 2030: 2597


A second-line drug (cure={cure_res: 0.9}, triggered by treatment.failed or given to those with Ir) is a second product. Resistance as one of several strains of a disease is on Diseases.
Every product takes cost=, the cost of each delivery, which is then a result of the delivery (cost); see Health economics.

title: Products
text:
Writing a product as code
A product whose effect needs code of its own is a subclass of ss.Product (or of ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment) with an administer(uids) method, which is called with the people a delivery gave it to on each step. Like any module, it can have parameters of its own (with define_pars()), states, and results. Here is a vaccine that protects younger people more: 90% at birth, falling to none at 80:

class AgeVaccine(ss.Product):
    """ A vaccine whose protection falls with the age at which it is given """
    def __init__(self, efficacy=0.9, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(efficacy=efficacy)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        return

    def administer(self, uids):
        age = self.sim.people.age[uids]
        protection = self.pars.efficacy * np.clip(1 - age/80, 0, 1)
        self.sim.diseases.sis.rel_sus[uids] *= 1 - protection
        return

scenarios = {
    'No vaccine':                    ss.Sim(sis, **kw),
    'Vaccine, 90% at every age':     ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, when=['2010'], coverage=0.5), **kw),
    'Vaccine, falling with age':     ss.Sim(sis, interventions=ss.vaccinate(AgeVaccine(), when=['2010'], coverage=0.5), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('sis.I')








A product written as code runs as agents. This one changes susceptibility for good; a protection that should wane, or combine with other effects, is better given as efficacy= with waning=. administer() can also return outcomes, as a test does (dict(positive=uids)), which are then results and events of the delivery. An intervention whose logic is not a product at all is a subclass of ss.Intervention: see Interventions.
The API reference for this page: Products.

title: Products
text:
Appendix: reference

Every product and its keywords
From each product’s documentation (the full text is in the API reference, Products):

import inspect, re
import pandas as pd

def keywords(cls):
    """ Each keyword in the Args of a class's docstring (and its bases'), with its meaning up to the first semicolon outside brackets """
    rows = {}
    for base in inspect.getmro(cls):
        if base in [ss.Module, ss.Product, ss.Intervention, ss.Connector]:
            break
        args = (inspect.getdoc(base) or '').partition('Args:\n')[2].split('\n\n')[0]
        for key, desc in re.findall(r'^    (\w+) \([^)]*\): (.*(?:\n {8,}.*)*)', args, flags=re.M):
            desc = ' '.join(desc.split())
            depth = 0
            for i, char in enumerate(desc):
                depth += (char in '([') - (char in ')]')
                if char == ';' and depth == 0:
                    desc = desc[:i]
                    break
            if key != 'kwargs':
                rows.setdefault(key, desc)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows.items(), columns=['Keyword', 'Meaning']).set_index('Keyword')

pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None)
pd.concat({f'ss.{product.__name__}': keywords(product) for product in [ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, ss.Treatment, ss.boxcar]})









Meaning



Keyword





ss.Vaccine
efficacy
protection against acquisition (required)


waning
how protection is lost, as above


doses
for a vaccine given in doses, the relative efficacy after each (e.g. `[0.85, 1.0]`)


leaky
if True (the default), everyone who receives it is partly protected (by `efficacy`)


during
if given, it is held only while people are in these states (e.g. `during=sir.I`): they stop holding it when they leave them


cost
the cost of each delivery


name
the name


label
the label, for plots and printing


ss.Diagnostic
sensitivity
the probability that someone with the condition tests positive


specificity
the probability that someone without it tests negative


outcomes
instead of sensitivity and specificity, the outcomes in order of severity, most severe first, each with its probability for people in each state (a dict by state, of any disease, as for `sensitivity`; a number is for those with what `detects=` says)


result_delay
the time from the test to its result (agents only)


detects
the condition the test detects (default: being in an infected state of the disease)


cost
the cost of each delivery


name
the name


label
the label, for plots and printing


ss.Treatment
cure
the probability that treatment cures (1 if neither `cure` nor `efficacy` is given)


efficacy
the effects while it is held, as for `ss.Vaccine` (e.g. `dict(transmission=0.96, mortality=0.9)`)


moves
what it moves people along, instead of a cure by the disease's recovery: transitions of the disease (by name too), or a move written with the states (e.g. `I + CIN >> S`)


waning
as for `ss.Vaccine`, for the effects while held


during
as for `ss.Vaccine`: held (and its effects acting) only while people are in these states, e.g. `during=typhoid.acute`


cost
the cost of each delivery


name
the name


doses
the relative efficacy after each dose


label
the label, for plots and printing


ss.boxcar
plateau
how long protection is full


decay
then, the e-folding time of its exponential decline (the mean time it lasts after the plateau)


stages
the number of levels of the plateau in a compartmental run









The outcomes of products and deliveries
Each of these is an event, which can trigger a delivery (when=), and a result of the delivery (the number on each step). Each also remembers, for each person, whether it happened (.ever), how often (.n_times), and how long ago (.since, agents only). An outcome of a product (test.positive) is for any delivery of it, and one of a delivery (screening.positive) for that delivery only.

cured, failed, unneeded
A treatment that cures or moves people (cure= or moves=)
Those cured; infected and not cured; not infected (or in no source of the transitions it cures along)


never_ran

Those still waiting when their time in the queue ran out

A product, e.g. who=vaccine.held, or every product of a kind, ss.Vaccine.held
Those who hold it now



The transitions of a disease (measles.infection, or a branch, tr.to(state)) and the events of pregnancy (pregnancy.birth) are events in the same way; see Interventions.

title: Maternal-child health
text:
🧠40% 🤖60%
Transmission from mother to child, and the outcomes of a pregnancy (stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight, neonatal death), are harder to model than a standard disease: they depend on the timing of pregnancy, on which module acts first in a step, and on how deaths around birth are counted. The ssl.mnch submodule of the Starsim library (import starsim.library as ssl; see Library for what the library is) has worked examples of these patterns. All of them build on pregnancy (ss.Pregnancy, which gives each pregnancy as states and transitions, with conception, delivery, and the unborn child as an agent) and on ss.PrenatalNet, the network between a pregnant woman and her unborn child; both are described on Demographics.
Like the rest of the library, these are illustrative: the probabilities and effect sizes are placeholders, chosen to make the effects easy to see. The examples below use a step of a week, since pregnancy outcomes are timed in weeks, and a high fertility rate, so that a small population gives enough births:
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

mnch_pars = dict(start='2000', stop='2005', n_agents=2000, dt=ss.weeks(1))
demographics = lambda: [ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=ss.peryear(0.1), burnin=True), ss.Deaths()]
networks = lambda: [ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.RandomNet()]

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Congenital outcomes
CongenitalDisease is an SIR that is passed from an infected mother to her unborn child through ss.PrenatalNet. For each child infected before birth, it draws an outcome from birth_outcomes (by default stillbirth, congenital infection, or a normal birth, with probabilities 0.3, 0.4, and 0.3), and schedules it for around the time of delivery. An outcome that kills (a stillbirth or miscarriage) is scheduled one step before delivery, so that it happens before birth; otherwise ss.Pregnancy, which runs earlier in each step, would already have delivered the baby, and the loss would be counted as a live birth followed by a neonatal death. Compared with the same population without transmission (beta=0), the extra stillbirths are those the disease causes (and are no longer counted as births):

def congenital(beta):
    disease = ssl.mnch.CongenitalDisease(beta=beta, init_prev=0.2)
    return ss.Sim(diseases=disease, demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars)

for label, beta in {'No transmission': 0, 'Transmission': ss.peryear(20)}.items():
    sim = congenital(beta).run()
    preg = sim.results.pregnancy
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', int(preg.birth.sum()))
    print('  Stillbirths:', int(preg.stillbirth.sum()))
    print('  Congenital infections:', sim.diseases.congenitaldisease.congenital.sum())

Sim: congenitaldisease, as 2,033 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.6 s


No transmission
  Births: 231
  Stillbirths: 1
  Congenital infections: 0
Sim: congenitaldisease, as 2,033 agents, 2000-01-01 to 2005-01-01
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.4 s


Transmission
  Births: 157
  Stillbirths: 75
  Congenital infections: 84


To use this in a disease of your own, build on ssl.mnch.CongenitalDisease, or copy its methods into any ss.AgentDisease:

set_congenital(), called instead of set_prognoses() for each child infected before birth (the mother is people.parent), draws and schedules the outcome;
step_congenital(), called from step_state(), applies the outcomes that are due;
the parameters birth_outcome_keys and birth_outcomes, and a ti_<key> state for each outcome (plus a true/false state for each that doesn’t kill), say what the outcomes are. Outcomes named 'stillborn' or 'miscarriage' are deaths before delivery, and 'neonatal_death' after it.

ssl.HIV (see Library: diseases) instead infects a fetus over ss.PrenatalNet as it infects anyone else.

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Neonatal deaths
NeonatalSepsis infects a fraction of newborns at birth (p_at_birth, by default 30%), and kills half of them (p_death) within about a week. It shows that neonatal deaths need no special handling: ss.Pregnancy counts any death of a baby aged 0 to 28 days, from any cause, as a neonatal death. The results are therefore in the pregnancy module, not the disease, and comparing with a sim without sepsis gives the deaths it causes:

scenarios = {
    'No sepsis': ss.Sim(demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars),
    'Sepsis':    ss.Sim(diseases=ssl.mnch.NeonatalSepsis(), demographics=demographics(), networks=networks(), **mnch_pars),
}
for label, sim in scenarios.items():
    sim.run()
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', int(sim.results.pregnancy.birth.sum()))
    print('  Neonatal deaths:', int(sim.results.pregnancy.neonatal_death.sum()))

  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: pregnancy: women pregnant at the start, conceived over the 40 steps before it (burnin=True)


  Done in 1.1 s


No sepsis

title: Maternal-child health
text:
Fetal health
FetalHealth doesn’t depend on any particular disease: it tracks a baseline fetal weight percentile for each pregnancy, and has two levers that other modules can pull: bringing delivery forward (the risk of a preterm birth) and adding growth restriction (the risk of a low birth weight). At delivery, it works out the birth weight from the gestational age, the percentile, and the growth restriction, and classifies newborns as of low birth weight (under 2,500 g), very low birth weight (under 1,500 g), small for gestational age, or small vulnerable newborns (any of these, or preterm). Its results are the numbers of each on each step, and the means and rates over each step’s births (e.g. mean_birth_weight, lbw_rate), which are NaN on a step with no births and are left out of a mean over time (res.mean_birth_weight.resample('year')).
The fetal_infection connector pulls those levers when a pregnant woman is infected: each infection brings delivery forward by about 3 weeks (timing_shift) and restricts growth by 15% (growth_penalty). The treat_pregnant delivery treats infected pregnant women (90% of them, coverage), as ss.treat() would, and reverses 70% of the damage (growth_reversal, timing_reversal). Both are written as code for an SIR written as code, so the disease here is ssl.AgentSIR, named 'sir'. FetalHealth is given in modules, since it is not a disease, network, demographic module, or intervention. Here are the baseline, infection, and infection with treatment from 2001:

def fetal(beta, treat=False):
    treatment = ssl.mnch.treat_pregnant(disease='sir', start=2001) if treat else None
    return ss.Sim(
        diseases      = ssl.AgentSIR(beta=beta, name='sir'),
        demographics  = demographics(),
        connectors    = ssl.mnch.fetal_infection(),
        interventions = treatment,
        modules       = ssl.mnch.FetalHealth(),
        networks      = networks(),
        **mnch_pars,
    )

scenarios = {
    'No infection': fetal(beta=0),
    'Infection, untreated': fetal(beta=ss.peryear(20)),
    'Infection, treated from 2001': fetal(beta=ss.peryear(20), treat=True),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, workers=1)
for label, sim in zip(scenarios, msim.sims):
    res = sim.results.fetal_health
    births = int(res.birth.sum())
    print(label)
    print('  Births:', births)
    print('  Low birth weight (%):', round(100*res.lbw.sum()/births))
    print('  Small vulnerable newborns (%):', round(100*res.svn.sum()/births))

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No infection, Infection, untreated, Infection, treated from 2001)
  Done in 4.5 s


No infection
  Births: 231
  Low birth weight (%): 4
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 15
Infection, untreated
  Births: 233
  Low birth weight (%): 44
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 69
Infection, treated from 2001
  Births: 232
  Low birth weight (%): 11
  Small vulnerable newborns (%): 33


To adapt this to another disease, build on fetal_infection and replace _apply_damage() with the disease’s own effects: for example, a larger growth penalty for severe infections than for mild ones.
