Here the importer guessed the names of the transitions (such as S_to_E, since odin doesn’t name flows) and the total population N. The solver is an ODE, as odin uses, so that the results can be checked against odin’s. Matching results is a validation check, not a proof that two models are the same: two models can agree on one trajectory and differ at other parameter values, starting conditions, or solvers. So compare their structure as well (each one’s describe()), and their results in more than one setting where it matters. Here is the import against the same model written in Starsim (see T3 – Building a disease):

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10, R=90_000), name='measles')
mine = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', dur=ss.days(365))
mine.run()

theirs = sim.results[sim.diseases[0].name]
print('Largest difference in I:', abs(theirs.I.values - mine.results.measles.I.values).max())

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0018 s; measles: 5,858 infections; at most 298 infectious, on 2025-08-05
Largest difference in I: 0.0


Where two models differ, the describe() of each, side by side, shows how. For a framework installed alongside Starsim, the best check is against its own results; each framework’s page (linked from the formats) does this.
The import can then be run in any of the ways Starsim runs a model. sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed; here it is run as agents, which odin can’t do (see Solvers and backends):

agents = sim.new(solver='abm', n_agents=100_000) # One agent per person
agents.run()
print('Peak infectious, ODE:', round(theirs.I.max()), '; agents:', round(agents.results[agents.diseases[0].name].I.max()))

Sim: measles, as 100,000 agents, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and S_to_E transmits at up to 1.9 per day (with everyone infectious), 85% in a step (and I is fast too). Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.56 s; measles: 5,924 infections; at most 329 infectious, on 2025-07-07


Peak infectious, ODE: 298 ; agents: 329



Keeping the code
An import gives Starsim code: the importer writes the model as Python, and the sim is that code run. The code is kept as sim.imported.code, to be kept, read, and changed like a model written by hand. It says where the model came from and how each rate was read, and ends with anything that wasn’t translated:

print(sim.imported.code)

# Imported from odin (measles.R) by ss.import_from()
#
# How each rate was read:
#   S -> E           beta * S * I / N : S taken out of the flow; N taken as the total [guessed: N = 100000, the number of people at the start]; exposure to I (divided by the total: frequency-dependent) => beta * I
#   E -> I           sigma * E : E taken out of the flow; spontaneous => sigma
#   I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma

import starsim as ss

# Parameters
N = ss.par(100000.0)
beta = ss.par(1.9)
gamma = ss.par(0.125)
sigma = ss.par(0.1)

# States
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')

# Transitions and outcomes
S_to_E = S >> E @ (beta * I)
E_to_I = E >> I @ sigma
I_to_R = I >> R @ gamma

measles = ss.Disease(
    S, E, I, R, S_to_E, E_to_I, I_to_R,
    init_n = dict(S=9990, I=10, R=90000),
    default_state = 'S',
    name = 'measles',
)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=[measles], solver='ode', unit='day', start='2025-01-01', dur=ss.days(365), total_pop=100000.0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sim.run()
    sim.plot()



The code is yours to edit: give transitions better names, write rates as the durations they stand for, and add what Starsim has that the original doesn’t (age groups, interventions, a fit to data). sc.savetext('measles.py', sim.imported.code) writes it to a file, and ss.converters.convert(filename) imports a model and saves its code in one step (beside the original, with the extension .py, unless filename= is given); the saved code also runs faster than reading a slow format again.


Finishing an incomplete import
An importer translates what it can, and lists the rest by name rather than guessing (such as code written in the original language, or a formula it can’t read): the sim runs without those parts, and lists them in a warning (ss.errors.ImportIncomplete) and in sim.imported.incomplete (empty for the import above, whose sim.imported.format is 'odin'). Here is the measles model over 20 years, with births, deaths, and seasonal transmission:

seasonal_code = '''
deriv(S) <- mu * N - beta * S * I / N - mu * S
deriv(E) <- beta * S * I / N - sigma * E - mu * E
deriv(I) <- sigma * E - gamma * I - mu * I
deriv(R) <- gamma * I - mu * R

N <- S + E + I + R
beta <- beta0 * (1 + amp * cos(2 * 3.141593 * t / 365)) # Highest at the start of each year

initial(S) <- 7000
initial(E) <- 30
initial(I) <- 30
initial(R) <- 92940

beta0 <- user(1.9)   # Mean transmission rate, per day
amp <- user(0.2)     # Size of the seasonal cycle, relative to the mean
sigma <- user(0.1)   # 1 / latent period (10 days)
gamma <- user(0.125) # 1 / infectious period (8 days)
mu <- user(0.00008)  # Birth and death rate, per day (about 3% a year)
'''
seasonal_file = os.path.join(folder, 'measles_seasonal.R')
sc.savetext(seasonal_file, seasonal_code)

seasonal = ss.import_from(seasonal_file, stop=ss.days(20*365), dt=7) # A step of a week is plenty over 20 years
seasonal.imported.incomplete

Imported "measles_seasonal" from odin: 4 states, 8 transitions, 5 parameters
  -> S             mu * N : an inflow, from counts => mu * (S.n + E.n + I.n + R.n)
  S ->             mu * S : S taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  E -> I           sigma * E : E taken out of the flow; spontaneous => sigma
  E ->             mu * E : E taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  I -> R           gamma * I : I taken out of the flow; spontaneous => gamma
  I ->             mu * I : I taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu
  R ->             mu * R : R taken out of the flow; an outflow => mu


/home/cliffk/idm/ssv4/starsim/converters/core.py:943: ImportIncomplete:


2 part(s) of the model were not translated:
  time: an equation uses the time (t, time, or step); a value that changes in time could be an ss.timeseries
  S -> E: the rate "beta * S * I / N" could not be translated ("t" is not a state or parameter of the model)
The sim runs without them. To finish it, run "starsim import /tmp/tmp1ttxy20z/measles_seasonal.R odin --ai": an AI coding agent, with Starsim's convert-model skill, translates the rest and checks the result against the original.



[('time',
  'an equation uses the time (t, time, or step); a value that changes in time could be an ss.timeseries'),
 ('S -> E',
  'the rate "beta * S * I / N" could not be translated ("t" is not a state or parameter of the model)')]


β now depends on the time, t, in a formula the importer doesn’t translate, so β and the transmission that uses it are listed; the rest is translated. The code of the import lists what wasn’t translated at the end, as comments, to be added by hand. Here β is written as ss.seasonal() (see Time), and births and deaths as ss.birth() and ss.death() (see People and demographics):

beta = ss.seasonal(mean=ss.perday(1.9), amplitude=0.2, peak=0) # Added: β, highest at the start of the year

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I # Added: the transmission
progression = E >> I @ ss.perday(0.1)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.perday(0.125)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(S=7000, E=30, I=30, R=92940), name='measles')

demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.perday(8e-05)), ss.death(rate=ss.perday(8e-05))]
finished = ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(20*365), dt=ss.days(7))
finished.run()
finished.plot('measles.I')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 7294 (the last whole step before 7300)
  measles: R0 = 18.2 at the start (beta varies in time) (R = 1.28 at the start, with 7% susceptible), with 30 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0087 s; measles: 55,090 infections; at most 263 infectious, on day 1176









For a longer model, sim.imported.prompt is a prompt for an AI assistant with Starsim’s convert-model skill (installed with starsim ai install), to translate what is listed and check the result against the original.

title: Import/export
text:
The formats
ss.import_from() reads these formats, and tells which one a file is from by its contents (or give format=); ss.converters.importers lists them:



Framework
Reads
Notes




Atomica
A framework and databook (.xlsx), and a program book
Programs become parameters of spending, for sim.optimize()


camdl
A .camdl file (compiled with camdlc), or its JSON form
Parameters keep their bounds and priors; observations become outcomes with their likelihoods


EMULSION
A model file (.yaml)
Each state machine becomes a disease


EpiModel
An R script, run first in R by dump_epimodel.R
A fitted network becomes ss.DegreeNet


epipack
A live model, or the JSON written by epipack.py
Each reaction process becomes a flow; a network is read at its mean degree


epydemix
A live model, or the JSON written by epydemix.py
Runs as a chain binomial in daily steps, as epydemix does


epymorph
The JSON written by epymorph.py
Nodes become places; movement clauses are run and averaged into commuting


flepiMoP
A configuration file (.yml), with the files it names
Places become a stratification with commuting between them


MEmilio
The JSON written by memilio.py
Contact matrices with their changes over time; a graph of places


odin
An R file in odin’s language (read without R)
odin 1 and odin2 syntax; arrays become stratifications


SBML
An SBML file (.xml)
Species become states, reactions transitions


SimInf
An R file (read without R), with its initial state and events
Nodes become places; events a movement register


summer2
A live model, or the JSON written by summer2.py
Each stratification, with its mixing matrix



For epipack, epydemix, epymorph, MEmilio, and summer2, Starsim’s importer for that framework (e.g. starsim/converters/memilio.py) also runs as a script in the framework’s own environment, needing neither Starsim nor Sciris there, and writes what it built as JSON for Starsim to read; for EpiModel, starsim/converters/dump_epimodel.R does the same in R. The others are read directly. Each importer is tested against its framework’s own examples. A Starsim 3 script is not imported, but rewritten: see the migration guide.
Every importer reads its format into the same object, ss.converters.Source (states, parameters, flows, stratifications, outcomes, and what it couldn’t translate), which ss.converters.write() writes as Starsim code and ss.converters.build() runs to make the sim. A Source can also be filled in by hand (add_state(), add_par(), add_flow()), to bring in a model from a framework with no importer, such as one from a paper. See Architecture.

title: Import/export
text:
Exporting a model
A Starsim model is written as Python, and that code is the model: it is what is kept, shared, and compared. There are other ways to write a model, or its results, out:



What
How
Holds
Read back?




The code
the script itself; for an import, sim.imported.code
the model, as Python
yes, by running it


The model as JSON
ss.export_to(sim, 'json')
the declared model as plain data, stratifications and all
yes, with ss.import_from()


Results as JSON
sim.to_json()
parameters, summary, and results, for use elsewhere
no


A saved sim
ss.save('run.sim', sim)
the sim itself (a pickle), including partway through a run
yes, with ss.load()


Another framework’s format
ss.export_to(sim, 'odin')
the compartmental form of the declared diseases
yes, with ss.import_from()



ss.export_to() writes a model in SBML (for tools such as COPASI) or odin. Each is written from the model’s compartmental form:

print(ss.export_to(sim, 'odin'))

exported to odin: 4 states, 3 transitions, as 4 compartments and 3 flows (time in days)
## measles, exported from Starsim 4.0.0rc4 (tested with odin 1.2.7); time is in days

deriv(S) <- -S_to_E
deriv(E) <- S_to_E - E_to_I
deriv(I) <- E_to_I - I_to_R
deriv(R) <- I_to_R

initial(S) <- 9990
initial(E) <- 0
initial(I) <- 10
initial(R) <- 90000

S_to_E <- beta * S * I / N
E_to_I <- sigma * E
I_to_R <- gamma * I
N <- S + E + I + R

beta <- user(1.9)
sigma <- user(0.1)
gamma <- user(0.125)



filename= writes it to a file too. A format that can’t carry part of the model (such as a network, a module written as code, or a function) leaves it out, and lists what it left out or changed in a warning (ss.errors.LossyExport). An exported model can be read back in:

sbml_file = os.path.join(folder, 'measles.xml')
ss.export_to(sim, 'sbml', filename=sbml_file)
again = ss.import_from(sbml_file, start='2025-01-01', dur=ss.days(365), verbose=False)
again.run()
print('Infections, imported from odin:', round(sim.results.measles.S_to_E.values.sum()))
print('Infections, after a round trip through SBML:', round(again.results.measles.S_to_E.values.sum()))

A sim made in Starsim is not written back out as Starsim code: its code is the script that made it. Only an import is written as code.

Starsim’s JSON form
ss.export_to(sim, 'json') writes a declared model as plain data, to move it between programs or people without Python. Unlike the other formats, it keeps the model as it was declared, with its stratifications, values by group, units, and bounds, and each value and rate is written as in Python without the ss.:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
gamma = ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 1.0])
R0 = ss.par(ss.by(patch=dict(urban=2.5, rural=1.8)), bounds=[0.5, 10])
infection = S >> I @ R0*gamma*I
recovery = I >> R @ gamma
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=ss.by(patch=dict(urban=10, rural=1))), name='sir')
sir.stratify(patch=['urban', 'rural'])
two_patch = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=2000, unit='day', stop=200)

json_file = os.path.join(folder, 'two_patch.json')
print(ss.export_to(two_patch, 'json', filename=json_file))

Exported to Starsim's JSON form: 1 disease

        "R0": {"value": {"by": {"patch": {"urban": 2.5, "rural": 1.8}}}, "bounds": [0.5, 10]},
        "gamma": {"value": 0.1, "bounds": [0.01, 1.0]}
      },

A transition with a split or a minimum stay is written as the arguments of ss.Transition(), and a network, an intervention, or a disease written as code as its type and the parameters that differ from its defaults ({"type": "RandomNet", "n_contacts": 5}). ss.import_from(json_file) reads it back, as for any import. Reading a file runs no code from it: each expression is checked, and only the model’s own names and Starsim’s and NumPy’s functions are allowed. What the form does not carry yet, such as outcomes, modifiers (ss.modify()), strains, and functions, is listed as ss.errors.LossyExport, as for any export.

Appendix: every importer and exporter
Every format that ss.import_from() reads and ss.export_to() writes, generated from their registries, ss.converters.importers and ss.converters.exporters, with the first line of each function’s documentation, and the version of the framework it was tested with (ss.converters.tested; another version may work too, and importing from or exporting to one installed alongside Starsim notes the difference) (the table in The formats says what each reads and how). ss.converters.sniff(filename) tells which format a file is in, if it can. title: Fitting a model
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
Calibration is fitting a model’s parameters to data: finding the values for which the model’s results match what was observed. A model of a measles outbreak may know from the literature how long people are infectious, but not how fast measles spreads in this particular town, or what fraction of cases were reported: those are the parameters to estimate. A best fit (the single set of values that fits best) is usually enough for a first exploration; when the uncertainty in the values matters too, a posterior (the distribution of values consistent with the data) can be fitted instead.
In Starsim, calibration needs two things: which parameters are unknown, as parameters with bounds (ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])), and the data, attached to the sim in columns named like the results they measure. sim.fit() then fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data, with no function to write that puts values into the model or pulls results out.
The calibration tutorial goes through one fit step by step. Fitting methods compares the methods, Fit diagnostics covers what to check afterwards, Gradients covers posteriors and profile likelihoods of ODEs, and Optimization uses the same machinery to allocate a budget.

title: Fitting a model
text:
A first fit
The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, 90% of whom are immune, using the library’s measles model, ssl.Measles (S to E to I to R). The latent and infectious periods are exponential here, which keeps each fit quick. Reported cases, report times the onsets, are added to the library’s model as an outcome. Three things are unknown: the transmission rate beta, the fraction reported report, and the fraction infectious at the start, I0:

PythonR



import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

beta   = ss.par(1.0, bounds=[0.3, 3])        # Transmission rate per day: unknown
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])       # Fraction of cases reported: unknown
I0     = ss.par(0.0001, bounds=[1e-5, 1e-3]) # Fraction infectious at the start (10 people): unknown

cases = ss.outcome(report*ssl.Measles.onset) # Reported cases: a fraction of the onsets, added to the library's model
measles = ssl.Measles(beta=beta, dur_exp=ss.expon(ss.days(8)), dur_inf=ss.expon(ss.days(11)), cases=cases, init=dict(I=I0, R=0.9))

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')



library(starsim) # Also gives ssl, Starsim's library, as in Python's import starsim.library as ssl

beta   <- par(1.0, bounds = c(0.3, 3), name = "beta")      # Transmission rate per day: unknown
report <- par(0.3, bounds = c(0.05, 1), name = "report")   # Fraction of cases reported: unknown
I0     <- par(0.0001, bounds = c(1e-5, 1e-3), name = "I0") # Fraction infectious at the start (10 people): unknown

cases <- outcome(report * ssl$Measles$onset) # Reported cases: a fraction of the onsets, added to the library's model
measles <- ssl$Measles(beta = beta, dur_exp = ss$expon(days(8)), dur_inf = ss$expon(days(11)), cases = cases, init = list(I = I0, R = 0.9))

make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", ...)
}



The value given to each parameter is where the search starts, and the bounds are the range it searches. A parameter is named by its variable (I0 here), or by name=.
The data here are weekly reported cases made from an agent-based run of the same disease, with beta = 1.4, half of cases reported, 30 people infectious at the start, and counts that vary more than Poisson counts. Real data would be read from a file instead (see below):

PythonR

title: Fitting a model
text:
Parameters and data
Every parameter with bounds is fitted, wherever it is: a rate, a fraction, a duration (with bounds in its own unit, e.g. ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[5, 12])), an initial condition, a parameter of a network or intervention, a value for each level of a stratification, an array, a time series, or a setting of the sim. Each kind, and how it is named in fit.pars, is in the appendix. In addition:

pars= fits only the parameters named, keeping the others at their values: sim.fit(pars=['beta']).
Wide positive bounds (the high end 10 or more times the low end) are searched on a log scale, since going from 0.01 to 0.02 doubles transmission, but going from 0.11 to 0.12 hardly changes it. The fit says which.
A prior, ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4], prior=ss.normal(2, 0.3)), is used by the methods that use likelihoods; without one, the prior is uniform over the bounds.
penalty= adds a function of the values to what a best fit minimizes, e.g. to keep a curve smooth: sim.fit(penalty=lambda pars: 10*np.sum(np.diff(pars['curve'], 2)**2)).


A value that isn’t a parameter
A value set in code, such as a setting of an intervention that its constructor doesn’t take, is fitted by writing a function that sets it, with the value as a keyword argument given as ss.par, and giving the function as a module (a function given as an intervention is called at every step):
def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])):
    sim.interventions.testing.symp_prob = symp_prob
    sim.interventions.testing.asymp_prob = symp_prob/10

sim = ss.Sim(..., interventions=[set_testing, testing], data=data)
fit = sim.fit() # Fits symp_prob, with the others
The value is then a parameter like any other: fit.pars.symp_prob, ss.Sim(pars=dict(symp_prob=0.2)), sim.sensitivity(), and ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(symp_prob=[0.1, 0.2])) all find it by name.


The data
The data have a time column (date, year, t, or time; an integer year is a calendar year), or dates as the index, and one column for each data series, named like the result it is compared with, here cases. A column that could match results of more than one module is named with the module, e.g. measles.cases. Any result can have data, including an analyzer’s (by_age.cancers_0_15), a nested one (hpv.genotype.cancers), or a column of a result (sis.infection.alpha).
The data need not be on the model’s time step, since each result knows what kind of quantity it is:

A flow, like reported cases, is summed over each interval of the data, from its date to the next: each week is dated by its first day. Data dated by the end of each period (“week ending”) need their dates moved back by one period first, e.g. data['date'] -= pd.Timedelta(days=7); Starsim warns if the last row starts a period that ends after the run, as end-labeled data often does.
A stock (like the number infectious) or a ratio (like prevalence) is compared with the model’s value at the data’s time.
Data by calendar year are compared over the year: a flow summed, and a stock or ratio averaged.

data= takes a dataframe or a file name. ss.SimData() renames columns on the way in, and can ignore the rest:
data = ss.SimData('town_cases.csv', aliases=dict(cases='Reported cases (weekly)', date='Week starting'), ignore_extra=True)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
A column that matches no result gets a note listing the closest result names when the sim is initialized, and is an error when fitted. weights= weighs series differently, e.g. sim.fit(weights=dict(cases=1, deaths=5)); in a posterior, a weight of 5 counts the data five times over and makes the posterior too narrow, so use weights for best fits.


Which parameters matter
A parameter that the results don’t depend on can’t be fitted. sim.sensitivity() needs no data: it samples the parameters over their bounds, runs the model at each, and gives the partial rank correlation of each parameter with a summary of each result (near 1 or -1, the result moves with the parameter; near 0, it doesn’t):

sens = sim.sensitivity(n=50, verbose=False)
sens[['measles.I peak', 'measles.cases total']]

title: Fitting a model
text:
Measuring the fit
Without a likelihood, the measure of fit is the normalized absolute error: for each data series, the mean absolute difference between model and data, divided by the mean of the data, which puts series of different sizes on one scale. loss='rmse' uses the root mean squared error instead, and loss= can be a function of the sim that returns the mismatch to minimize:
def peak_error(sim):
    """ How far the model's peak week is from the observed peak, in weeks """
    weekly = sim.results.measles.cases.resample('week')
    return abs(weekly.values.argmax() - data.cases.values.argmax())

fit = sim.fit(loss=peak_error)
A likelihood says how the data vary around the model’s value, which is the mean. It can be declared on the outcome, for every fit, or given to the fit:
cases = ss.outcome(report*ssl.Measles.onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # On the outcome
fit = sim.fit(likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=10)))     # Or for one fit, by series
fit = sim.fit(likelihood=ss.nbinom(n=10))                  # Or the same for every series
The appendix lists the likelihoods, with the data each suits. A likelihood can also be a function fn(observed, model) that returns the log-likelihood of each value; it can’t be differentiated in JAX, so the default fit then uses Nelder-Mead.
With a likelihood for every series, the fit maximizes their summed log-likelihood (for a stochastic model, an estimate of it; see below), and the methods that give a posterior can be used. A fit uses likelihoods for every series or for none: a mix, or likelihoods with loss=, is an error. A negative binomial suits reported cases, and its dispersion n (smaller is more variable) can be fitted too:

dispersion = ss.par(5, bounds=[1, 100], name='dispersion')
fit_lik = sim.fit(method='nelder-mead', likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=dispersion)), verbose=False)

title: Fitting a model
text:
How the fit is found
By default a fit is a best fit, by a method that suits the model, which sim.fit() prints with its reason. A posterior is always asked for by name:








The model
The default method (a best fit)
A posterior, by name




Deterministic (an ODE)
'l-bfgs-b' (gradients from JAX, or by finite differences); 'nelder-mead' for one or two parameters, or when JAX can’t take the log-likelihood
'nuts', given a likelihood for every series; 'pmcmc' if JAX can’t run the model


Stochastic compartmental
'optuna'
'pmcmc' (particle MCMC), given a likelihood for every series


Agent-based
'optuna'
'abc-smc', which needs no likelihood



'powell', 'slsqp', and 'if2' can also be named; Fitting methods compares them all. A method’s settings are given with it: method=ss.fitting.method('nuts', draws=1000, chains=2), and a setting the method does not take is an error. A list, such as method=['optuna', 'nelder-mead'], runs each method in turn from the best values of the one before.

A stochastic model
A stochastic model gives a different result on each run, so each set of values gets a noisy score. Starsim fits it with Optuna, which tries values, scores them by running the model, and uses the scores to choose where to try next. Here is the same model as a chain binomial:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
fit = sim.fit(method='optuna', rand_seed=5)
fit.summarize()

Searching on a log scale: beta, report, I0
Scoring each point by the mean of 4 runs, with fresh seeds at each point (override with method=ss.fitting.method("optuna", particles=..., n_runs=..., reseed=...))

The settings that matter most are n_trials= and n_runs= (the runs that score each trial), given as ss.fitting.method('optuna', n_trials=500); all are listed in Fitting methods. rand_seed= of sim.fit() makes the fit reproducible. Agents are fitted the same way, usually with more trials.
ss.Transition(..., noise=sigma) adds gamma white noise to a transition’s rate, for models whose rates vary at random from day to day; the particle filter, IF2, and particle MCMC all see it (see Measles in London).
fit.sim is one run with the best values; for a stochastic model, compare the data with many:

msim = ss.parallel(fit.sim, n_runs=20)


msim.plot('measles.cases')

title: Fitting a model
text:
Using the fit
The calibrated sim is the starting point for scenarios: sim.new() makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed, and from fit.sim that includes the fitted values. Here, a catch-up campaign on 1 April that vaccinates half of those still susceptible, compared with none:

PythonR



vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.97, who=measles.S, when='2025-04-01', coverage=0.5)
scenarios = {
    'No campaign': fit.sim.new(),
    'Campaign':    fit.sim.new(interventions=vaccination),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.cases')










vaccination <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.97, who = measles$S, when = "2025-04-01", coverage = 0.5)
scenarios <- list(
  "No campaign" = fit$sim$new(),
  "Campaign"    = fit$sim$new(interventions = vaccination)
)
msim <- parallel(scenarios, n_runs = 20)
msim$plot("measles.cases")




msim.summarize().loc['measles_cases']








median
low
high
mean
std


scenario









No campaign
2,340
1,898
2,488

Campaign
206

Strictly speaking, this is not the right thing to do: these runs all use the best values, so their spread is the model’s own noise, not uncertainty about the values. fit.project(scenarios, **kwargs) runs scenarios from the fit, passing kwargs to sim.new(), e.g. fit.project({'No campaign': None, 'Campaign': vaccination}, stop='2026-06-01') to forecast past the data; from a posterior, the runs carry the uncertainty in the values too (T6 has an example checked against what happened next).

Projecting from a posterior
fit.project() from a posterior runs once for each of n_runs draws (100 by default), with the same draws and seeds in every scenario:

With 'pmcmc' or 'abc-smc' on a stochastic compartmental model, each draw comes with a run (fit.trajectories) that follows the data, and by default the projection continues it from the last data point, so the scenarios differ only after it. Continued runs are kept as results only (msim.results).
restart=True runs each draw from the start instead, for a scenario that changes something before the last data point. A scenario that can’t be continued (e.g. an intervention with a capacity, or a delivery before the last data point) is run from the start with a warning; restart=False makes that an error.
For an ODE, a run at the same values is always the same, so the two are the same; see Gradients.

Fit diagnostics covers what to check before using a fit: a best value at a bound, parameters the data can’t tell apart, a lucky trial, and too few runs to judge.

title: Fitting a model
text:
Further reading

Covasim: Calibration: fitting with Optuna in Starsim’s predecessor
Optuna: Key features: the library that fits stochastic models here, and its plots of a search
pomp: Getting started: likelihood-based fitting of stochastic models, including iterated filtering, in R
Stan: User’s guide: Bayesian fitting with NUTS, the sampler used here for ODE posteriors

title: Fitting a model
text:
Appendix

What can be fitted
Every kind of value that a fit can take as a parameter, and how it is named in fit.pars (and so in pars=, ss.Sim(pars=...), and sim.sensitivity()):








What
Given as
Named in fit.pars




A rate, fraction, or duration of a declared model
beta = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4]), used in a transition or outcome
By its variable, beta, or its name=; with the module’s name, measles.beta, if several modules have one of that name


An initial condition
init=dict(I=ss.par(...)) (a fraction), or init_n=dict(I=ss.par(10, bounds=[1, 100], name='I0')) (a number); without a variable or name=, an error
By its variable or name=, as I0 on this page


A value for each level of a stratification
ss.par(ss.by(age=[...]), bounds=...)
One for each level, by its label, e.g. beta[0-14] and beta[15+]; whole in fit.pars


An array
ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])
curve[0], curve[1], … (not those whose low and high bounds are equal); whole in fit.pars


A time series
ss.par(ss.timeseries(days, values), bounds=...)
By its times, beta[0], beta[14], …; whole in fit.pars


A parameter of a module written as code
ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]))
beta, or hiv.beta if the name is taken


A value in a dict parameter
cin_fn=dict(k=ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 0.5]))
cin_fn.k


A modifier’s amount
ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, multiply=ss.par(2.7, bounds=[1, 4]))
multiply, or its name as a parameter of a declared disease


A parameter of a network, intervention, or other module
ss.vaccinate(coverage=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.2, 0.9]))
Its name, e.g. coverage, with its module’s name if needed


A keyword argument of a function given as a module
def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(...))
symp_prob


A likelihood’s own parameter
ss.nbinom(n=ss.par(5, bounds=[1, 100], name='dispersion'))
dispersion (fitted only by a fit that uses the likelihood)


A setting of the sim
ss.Sim(n_agents=ss.par(5000, bounds=[1000, 20000])), fitted with a new sim for each value
n_agents





Likelihoods and priors
The likelihoods that likelihood= (or ss.outcome(..., likelihood=)) takes, and the data each suits. “In JAX” means the log-likelihood can be taken in JAX, as gradient-based fits and NUTS need:



Likelihood
The model’s value is
Suits
In JAX




ss.poisson()
The mean count
Counts with no more spread than chance gives: cases or deaths, reported in full or at a steady rate
Yes


ss.nbinom(n=...)
The mean count; n is the dispersion (smaller means more spread), and can be an ss.par with bounds, which is then fitted
Overdispersed counts, as most surveillance data are: reporting that varies from week to week
Yes


ss.binom(n=...)
The probability; n is the number of trials
The positives among n people tested, e.g. a prevalence survey or a serosurvey
Yes


ss.bernoulli()
The probability
Whether something happened, as 0 or 1, e.g. whether an outbreak was reported
Yes


ss.normal(std=...)
The mean; std is the standard deviation
A continuous measure with noise of a known size, e.g. a fraction estimated with a standard error
Yes


ss.lognormal(std=...)
The mean; std is the standard deviation
A positive measure whose noise grows with its size, e.g. a concentration in wastewater
Yes


A function fn(observed, model)
Whatever the function says: it returns the log-likelihood of each value
Anything else, e.g. a beta-binomial from SciPy, or a normal whose variance grows with the mean
No: the default fit uses Nelder-Mead; a method with gradients (or NUTS) needs require_jax=False, and runs with Python in the loop



The priors that ss.par(..., prior=) takes. Without one, the prior is uniform over the bounds, on the value itself, even for a parameter searched on a log scale; give a parameter whose order of magnitude is uncertain a prior such as ss.lognormal():



Prior
In JAX




ss.normal(), ss.lognormal(), ss.gamma(), ss.beta_dist(), ss.expon(), ss.uniform()
Yes


Any other distribution that has a density (e.g. ss.weibull())
No: it works with the methods that run with Python in the loop





What a fit holds
The attributes of the ss.fitting.Fit that sim.fit() returns (see ss.fitting.Fit):



Attribute
What it is




fit.pars
The best values, which can be passed to ss.Sim(pars=...)


fit.sim
The calibrated sim: a copy of the original with the best values, already run


fit.before
The sim with the starting values, already run


fit.table
Each parameter’s starting value, best value, and bounds; with a posterior, also its median, 95% interval (lower, upper), rhat, and ess; with Optuna and IF2, spread_lower and spread_upper (an indication of the uncertainty, not an interval)


fit.method
The method used


fit.objective, fit.objective_before
The loss (or the negative log-likelihood, or log-posterior) at the best and starting values; for a stochastic model, an estimate; fit.measure says which


fit.scores
The score of the best values in each run; their spread is the run-to-run noise of a stochastic fit


fit.converged, fit.why
Whether the method reached its own stopping rule, and how it decided (see Fit diagnostics)


fit.trials, fit.to_df()
Every evaluation: the values tried, and the objective at each


fit.samples
With a posterior, the draws: one row each, with its chain and number


fit.trajectories
With 'pmcmc' or 'abc-smc' on a stochastic compartmental model, the run that goes with each draw, which fit.project() continues; None otherwise


fit.diagnostics
divergences (NUTS), acceptance (particle MCMC and ABC-SMC), tolerance and generations (ABC-SMC), and band (95% of the model’s values over draws from a posterior, which fit.plot() draws)


fit.study
With Optuna, Optuna’s study, for its plots


fit.summarize(), fit.plot(residuals=), fit.project(scenarios, n_runs=, restart=, **kwargs)
The table with the fit before and after; the model against the data (and the residuals); runs of scenarios from the fit

title: Profiling and debugging
text:
🧠8% 🤖92%
A model can go wrong in three ways: it stops with an error, it runs but gives an answer that looks wrong, or it runs too slowly. This page goes through Starsim’s tools for each, and the mistakes that commonly catch people out.
Where to look first, by symptom (the sections below cover each in turn):
The examples on this page use the measles model from the tutorials (β = 1.9 per day, infectious for 8 days, so R0 ≈ 15):
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0025 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)

title: Profiling and debugging
section: Errors and what a run prints
text:
Errors and what a run prints
When Starsim can’t build or run a model, it raises an error that names what is wrong in the terms of the model, and says what to do about it. Here the parameter β is misspelled:

try:
    ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(betta=2.0), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()
except KeyError as error:
    print(error)

pars= has a value for "betta", which matches no parameter. Parameters are measles.init_prev, measles.beta, measles.dur_I; did you mean measles.beta?


Most errors are Python’s own (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError); the few that code may want to catch by kind, such as ss.CapabilityError (the solver asked for can’t run part of the model), are classes of their own, listed in the appendix. Most mistakes are caught when the sim is built (sim.init(), which sim.run() calls first), so an error usually comes at once rather than after a long run.
A run prints what it is running and how, the R0 of each disease, any notes, and a closing line with the size and timing of the peak. Read these first: most surprises are explained there. A note is something Starsim assumed or noticed that is worth knowing, and doesn’t stop the run. For example, in an SEIR model, init_prev puts people in E, where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at first (to start people infectious, give init=dict(I=0.001) or init_n=dict(I=100)):

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
latency   = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
seir = ss.Disease(infection, latency, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(100))
seir_sim.run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 0 infectious at the start
  Note: init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a fraction) or init_n= (a number)
  Done in 0.0034 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,177 infectious, on day 33


Sim(n=100000; 0—100; diseases=measles)


The notes are kept in sim.notes, even when nothing is printed (verbose=0):

seir_sim.notes

["unit='day' (from the typed values in the model)",
 'init_prev seeds E of "measles", where a new infection starts, so nobody is infectious at the start; to seed infectious people, use init=dict(I=...) (a fraction) or init_n= (a number)']


Some messages are warnings rather than notes: the run continues, but something probably needs attention (for example, a fitted parameter that ended at one of its bounds). To stop at the first warning instead, so that a script can’t carry on past one unnoticed, turn warnings into errors:
ss.options(warnings='error')

text:
Checking the model
Starsim fills in whatever a model leaves out: the population size, the distribution of each duration, how people mix, the unit of time, and which solver to use. describe() lists the whole model as it was built, with each value that Starsim chose itself marked as guessed. If a result looks wrong, check here that the model is the one you meant:

sim.describe()

recovery

equations() gives the same model as the equations of an ODE, which is often the quickest way to check that each rate is what you meant (for example, that a transmission is frequency-dependent, β S I / N, and not density-dependent, β S I):

measles.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I



Runs that should match but don’t
When two sims that should agree don’t, compare what each says about itself: describe() gives the text of each (a string), and a diff of the two shows only the lines where their states, transitions, parameters, and settings differ. Here a second sim has a lower β and a shorter step:

import difflib

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.5*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
other = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='measles')
other_sim = ss.Sim(other, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), dt=ss.days(0.5), verbose=0)

before = sim.describe().splitlines()
after = other_sim.describe().splitlines()
print('\n'.join(difflib.unified_diff(before, after, 'sim', 'other_sim', lineterm='', n=0)))

--- sim
+++ other_sim
@@ -11,2 +11,2 @@
-               beta = 1.9 per day
-               rate = 1.9 × I.n / N                            [homogeneous mixing]
+               beta = 1.5 per day
+               rate = 1.5 × I.n / N                            [homogeneous mixing]
@@ -22 +22 @@
-  schedule     every day: measles
+  schedule     every 0.5 days: measles
@@ -27,3 +27,3 @@
-Per step of measles: 1 day
-  infection    beta = 1.9 per day → 1.9 per step
-  recovery     rate 0.125 per day → p = 1 - exp(-0.125 × 1) = 0.1175 per step
+Per step of measles: 0.5 days
+  infection    beta = 1.5 per day → 0.75 per step
+  recovery     rate 0.125 per day → p = 1 - exp(-0.125 × 0.5) = 0.0606 per step


The lines marked - are the first sim’s and those marked + the second’s. To compare the results of two runs, ss.debugtools.diff_sims() lists each summary result that differs, with the ratio of the two, and ss.debugtools.check_sims_match() gives True if every result matches (see debugtools):

other_sim.run()
ss.debugtools.diff_sims(sim, other_sim);


The following values differ between the two simulations:
                         sim1       sim2    diff   ratio change
measles_S               0.026      0.642   0.615  24.437   ↑↑↑↑
measles_I             317.166    368.459  51.294   1.162     ↑↑
measles_R           99682.808  99630.899 -51.909   0.999      ≈
measles_recovery    99720.076  99653.223 -66.853   0.999      ≈
measles_infected      317.166    368.459  51.294   1.162     ↑↑
measles_prevalence      0.156      0.158   0.001   1.009      ↑


Where two runs of what should be the same model differ only from some step on (after a change to code written as a module, say), sim.set_diagnostics() before the run records every random draw and every agent’s states at every step, in sim.diagnostics, so the step where the two runs diverge can be found. It slows the run a great deal, so use it on a small sim.


Checking the numbers
A few numbers can be checked by hand. The run prints R0, which for an SIR is β × the infectious period; if it is far from what you expected, a rate or a duration is wrong, often in its units (see Common pitfalls). Another check is to run the same model in another way, such as agents against the ODE: a large difference that doesn’t shrink with more agents points to the time step, or to something only one of them does (Solvers and backends says when to expect them to differ). For the time step, sim.check_dt() runs the model with its step and with one half as long, and shows the largest difference in each result at any time, as a fraction of the result’s largest value:

agent_sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
agent_sim.check_dt()

Change in each result when the timestep goes from 1 to 0.5 days (largest difference, as a fraction of the largest value):
  measles.infection             64.1%   (peak 5365 → 6500)
  measles.recovery              55.5%   (peak 1677 → 1789)
  measles.prevalence            38.7%   (peak 0.7844 → 0.7603)
  measles.I                     38.7%   (peak 15688 → 15206)
  measles.infected              38.7%   (peak 15688 → 15206)
  measles.S                     34.3%   (peak 19980 → 19980)
  measles.R                     14.2%   (peak 19884 → 19909)


If the result you care about changes by more than a few percent, use a smaller step (dt=ss.days(0.5)) and check again. For a stochastic run, part of each change is chance.


Finding what changes a parameter
Interventions and connectors change parameters while the model runs. When a parameter doesn’t seem to have the value you expect, sim.what_modifies() lists everything that changes it:

masks = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start=ss.days(10))
masked = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), interventions=masks, verbose=0)
masked.what_modifies(measles.pars.beta)

measles.pars.beta
  modifiers
    masks            multiply=0.6   when=ss.schedule(start=days(10))

title: Profiling and debugging
text:
Common pitfalls
These are mistakes that have caught people out. Most don’t raise an error: the model runs and gives a wrong answer, though Starsim prints a note for many of them. The commonest is a number after @, which is a rate, not a duration: I >> R @ 8 means leaving I at a rate of 8 per day (after an eighth of a day on average), not after 8 days. Starsim notes a duration shorter than the step, which is almost always this:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
wrong = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 1.9*I, I >> R @ 8, init_prev=0.001, name='measles') # Meant: ss.days(8)
ss.Sim(wrong, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50)).run()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 0.238, with 100 infectious at the start
  Note: unit='day' (from start and stop)
  Note: I_to_R has a mean dwell of 0.12 days, shorter than the step; a duration is written dur=, or ss.days(10)
  Done in 0.0015 s; measles: 31 infections; at most 100 infectious, on day 0


Sim(n=100000; 0—50; diseases=measles)


R0 comes out at 0.24 instead of 15. Give a duration with its unit (ss.days(8)), or as dur= in ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8)). The others, each covered in full on its own page:

A plain number is in the sim’s unit of time. If the model’s unit is days, stop=2, meant as two years, is two days. Give times with their units or as dates (Time).
A number as a time is a calendar year if the sim has a calendar. With start='2025-01-01', when=2026 is the start of 2026, whatever the unit; with start=0, it is 2026 units from 0. A time outside the sim is an error that says how it was read (Time).
A rate times a duration is not a rate. The product itself is fine: ss.peryear(0.1)*ss.days(3) is a plain number, the chance of an event over 3 days. Using it as the rate of a transition raises a TypeError that shows the product and asks for the rate itself (Time).
An ODE always takes off. With R0 above 1 it takes off from any number infected, while a real outbreak started by a few cases often dies out by chance; for the chance of an outbreak, run a stochastic solver many times (Solvers and backends).
The median of many runs can hide that some died out. When some runs die out and the rest take off, the median or mean describes neither; count the runs with an outbreak, and summarize those (Scenarios).
n_agents= runs the model as agents. To set the size of a compartmental model, use total_pop= (Running sims).
With contacts, β is per contact. Adding a network or contact matrix multiplies R0 by about the number of contacts, so scale β down to keep the same R0; the sim prints the new R0 (Mixing).
stratify() changes the disease itself. Stratifying the same disease again in another way is an error; build the disease again each time (Stratification).
Vaccines are leaky unless told otherwise. efficacy=0.9 reduces everyone’s chance of infection by 90%; leaky=False fully protects 90% instead, which for a fast disease such as measles gives far fewer infections (Products).
Data is matched to results by name. A column called reported is not compared with the result cases (Starsim notes it, and sim.fit() stops); rename it, or use ss.SimData(data, aliases=dict(cases='reported')) (Fitting a model).
Counts over a period are compared with totals over the same period. Infections are summed between data points, while the number infectious is compared at each; check which kind each column is (Fitting a model).
A method that forgot to call super(). A module written as code that overrides init_pre(), init_post(), finish_step(), and the like without calling the base class’s version leaves part of it unset; Starsim warns at the end of the run (Custom modules).
len(sim.people) still counts those who died this step. For a fraction worked out in an analyzer, use sim.people.n, the number alive.
A date between two steps never equals sim.now. if sim.now == ss.date('2025-03-01') with weekly steps does nothing; compare with >=, or give the module start=.

More are in the pitfalls of Custom modules and Interventions.

Looking inside a run
To look at a run partway through, sim.run(until=...) stops after the step that starts at that time, with the people and their states as they are at its end (sim.people.to_df()); a later sim.run() carries on (see Running sims).

To see what happens during a run, a function of the sim can be inserted into the loop, after (or, with before=True, before) any call in it. Here it prints the number infectious every ten days, just after the disease has taken its step:

def show_infectious(sim):
    if sim.ti % 10 == 0:
        print('Day', sim.ti, 'infectious:', sim.diseases.measles.I.sum())

probed = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=20_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
probed.init()

text:
Appendix: errors and warnings
Most errors are Python’s own (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError); these are the ones that are classes of their own, in starsim/internals/errors.py, so that code can catch or filter them by kind (see Model execution for the policy behind them):

import inspect
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None) # Show each entry in full

rows = []
for name, cls in inspect.getmembers(ss.errors, inspect.isclass):
    if issubclass(cls, (Exception, Warning)) and cls.__module__ == ss.errors.__name__:
        rows.append(dict(
            name = ('ss.' if name in ss.errors.__all__ else 'ss.errors.') + name,
            kind = 'warning' if issubclass(cls, Warning) else 'error',
            subclass_of = ', '.join(base.__name__ for base in cls.__bases__),
            what = ' '.join(inspect.getdoc(cls).split()),
        ))
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('name')








kind
subclass_of
what

A sim that has already run (or been finalized) is stepped, finalized, or added to again; `sim.run()` runs it again from the start

A best-fit value is at or near one of its bounds

error

The requested solver cannot run part of the model. Three cases: there is no sensible approximation (contact tracing, transmission trees, agent-only custom code); a function or condition asked for something that exists only per agent in a compartmental run; or an approximation would be needed and `approximations="error"`. Names the part, what it asked for, and what would fix it

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
🧠19% 🤖81%
Many questions are about a small part of a large population: the first cases of an outbreak in a city, or an epidemic in a country of tens of millions. Simulating every person is then often unnecessary and slow. While an outbreak is small compared with the population, it can be treated as a branching process: each case infects a random number of others, independently of every other case, and the rest of the population hardly matters. Once an epidemic is large, a run as agents can instead let each agent stand for several people: population rescaling. (A compartmental model holds numbers of people, so it can be any size at no cost.) The two differ in kind: branching changes the model itself, by turning off the depletion of susceptible people, so it is right only while an outbreak is small; rescaling changes only how the same model is represented, and should change the answer by no more than the extra noise of coarser agents.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Branching processes
Early in an outbreak, each case infects a random number of others, its offspring. If the offspring of each case are independent of everyone else’s (as they are while nearly everyone is susceptible), the outbreak is a branching process, and a few of its properties follow from the offspring distribution alone:

The chance that an introduction dies out. Even with R0 above 1, the first few chains of transmission can all end by chance. For an SIR model with an exponentially distributed infectious period, started by one case, the chance is 1/R0; started by n cases, (1/R0)^n.
Chains and generations. Who infected whom, how many generations a chain lasts, and how large it gets before it dies out or takes off.
Overdispersion. If some cases infect many more people than others (superspreading), the offspring distribution has a long tail, and more introductions die out, even at the same R0.

In Starsim, a branching process is not a different model, but the same model run with depletion turned off: ss.Sim(branching=True). Infection then takes no one from the uninfected, and gives no one back, so the susceptible side stays as it would be with no infection, however large the outbreak gets. It works with every solver but agents stepped by events (ss.solvers.abm(step='events')):







Solver
What it gives




'ode'
The expected course: exponential growth at the rate that goes with R0


ss.solvers.ode(dwells='exact')
The same, with each dwell time as it is, which is the renewal equation (below)


'gillespie', 'binomial', 'tau'
A branching process of counts: the chance of extinction, and the distribution of chain sizes


'abm'
A branching process of individuals: who infected whom, and differences between people



With solver='auto', the solver is chosen as it would be without branching. What is held is the uninfected side: the states people can be in without having been infected. The model’s other flows act on it as usual, so vaccination (S >> V) still takes people from S. A flow back to the uninfected side, such as waning immunity, takes people out of the process instead, with a note. In a rate, N is the number of people on the uninfected side, so each case’s offspring average R0 however many cases are seeded.

The chance that an outbreak dies out
Here is an SIR infection with R0 = 2 (β = 0.2 per day, infectious for 10 days), introduced by one case into a city of a million people. An ODE always takes off, so the question needs a stochastic solver and many runs (see Solvers and backends). Gillespie’s algorithm is exact for this model, and as a branching process its cost is the number of events, not the size of the population. Each run stops once 100 people have been infected, by when its chain has taken off:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.2*I        # β = 0.2 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average: R0 = 2
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=1), name='sir') # One imported case

sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(100), solver='gillespie', branching=True, verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=100, until=sir.I.n + sir.R.n >= 100)
b = msim.branching
print(f'Fraction of introductions that died out: {b.p_extinct:.2f} (95% interval {b.p_extinct_ci[0]:.2f} to {b.p_extinct_ci[1]:.2f}; theory: 1/R0 = 0.5)')

Fraction of introductions that died out: 0.55 (95% interval 0.45 to 0.64; theory: 1/R0 = 0.5)


until= stops a run once a condition holds: an expression of the model, as here, or a function of the sim, checked at the end of each step (it works for any run). Without it, a branching process that takes off grows without limit. msim.branching.plot() shows how large the chains got, and the gallery page The chance of a major outbreak does the same over a range of R0.


Chains and offspring, as agents
For chains of transmission, run the same model as agents. A branching process of agents makes agents only for the people infected, so a city of 10 million costs no more than a village: here, 100 imported cases, followed for 60 days:

sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=100), name='sir') # 100 imported cases, for enough chains to count
sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10e6, stop=ss.days(60), solver='abm', branching=True, verbose=0)
sim.run()
b = sim.branching
print(f'{len(sim.people):,} agents for {sim.pars.total_pop:,.0f} people; {b.length} generations')

54,203 agents for 10,000,000 people; 23 generations


sim.branching has, for each agent, its infector (−1 for the imported cases), its generation, the time point it was infected (ti), and the number it infected (offspring). Since the most recent cases are still infecting others, only the offspring of the cases infected long enough before the end are counted in full (complete):

n = b.offspring[b.complete]
print('Cases:', len(n), ' Mean offspring:', n.mean().round(2), ' Variance:', n.var().round(1), ' Fraction with none:', (n == 0).mean().round(2))

Cases: 421  Mean offspring: 2.14  Variance: 6.4  Fraction with none: 0.34


To give the cases different infectiousness, give the disease rel_trans as an attribute drawn for each person, ss.attr(). With a fixed infectious period, a gamma distribution with mean 1 and shape k gives a negative binomial offspring distribution with dispersion k. Here, for a SARS-like infection (R0 = 2, k = 0.2), the offspring with and without it, each over 8 runs of 20 imported cases:

k = 0.2
offspring = {}
for label, extra in [('Same infectiousness', {}), (f'Overdispersed (k = {k})', dict(rel_trans=ss.attr(ss.gamma(shape=k, scale=1/k))))]: # Each person's infectiousness, with mean 1
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    sars = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.2*I, I >> R @ ss.constant(ss.days(10)), init_n=dict(I=20), name='sars', **extra)
    sim = ss.Sim(sars, total_pop=10e6, stop=ss.days(60), solver='abm', branching=True, verbose=0)
    msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=8)
    b = msim.branching
    offspring[label] = b.offspring
    print(f'{label}: R = {b.R:.2f}, k = {b.k:.2g}')

bins = np.arange(0, 16)
plt.hist(list(offspring.values()), bins=bins, density=True, label=list(offspring.keys()))
plt.xlabel('Number of people infected by each case')
plt.ylabel('Fraction of cases')
plt.legend();

Same infectiousness: R = 2.00, k = inf
Overdispersed (k = 0.2): R = 1.85, k = 0.2









msim.branching.R and .k are a negative binomial fitted by maximum likelihood, and are fitted only from runs of a fixed length: a run stopped by until= stops because its chain is large, so its cases had more offspring than most.


The renewal equation
solver=ss.solvers.ode(dwells='exact') takes each dwell time as it is, rather than as the Erlang stages that 'ode' uses. As a branching process, it is the renewal equation that EpiEstim, EpiNow2, and epidemia are built on, with the generation interval that the model’s latent and infectious periods give. Here the latent period is lognormal with a long tail (a mean of 5 days and a standard deviation of 10):

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
latent = ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(5), std=ss.days(10)) # Most become infectious within a few days, a few only after weeks
seir = ss.Disease(S >> E @ 0.4*I, E >> I @ latent, I >> R @ ss.days(5), init_n=dict(I=10), name='seir')
solvers = {'Renewal equation (exact dwells)': ss.solvers.ode(dwells='exact'), 'Erlang stages (ode)': 'ode'}
sims = {label: ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=1e6, branching=True, solver=solver, stop=ss.days(60), verbose=0) for label, solver in solvers.items()}
ss.parallel(sims).plot('seir.I')








Erlang stages can be no more variable than an exponential, so 'ode' keeps the mean but not the long tail (the sim notes this); for a latent period no more variable than an exponential, the two are close. For a reproduction number that varies in time, give beta as an ss.timeseries, which sim.fit() can fit.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Population rescaling

Population size and number of agents
total_pop is the size of the population being modeled, and n_agents is how many agents are simulated: a computational choice, like the time step, and giving it makes the sim run as agents. Think of the agents as a sample, like a survey: simulating all 230 million people in Nigeria one by one would be far too slow, but 50,000 agents, each standing for 4,600 people, will do. If only one is given, the other is the same (up to 10,000 agents). Here is an SIR infection with R0 = 3 (β = 0.3 per day, infectious for 10 days) in a city of a million people, as compartments and as 10,000 agents. (This page uses a slower infection than measles, whose fast rates need short steps when run as agents; see Solvers and backends.)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I        # β = 0.3 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious for 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

ode    = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150)).run()               # A million people, as compartments
agents = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150), solver='abm').run() # The same, as 10,000 agents
print('People per agent:', agents.pop_scale)

Sim: sir, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  sir: R0 = 3, with 1,000 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0029 s; sir: 939,539 infections; at most 300,623 infectious, on day 38
Sim: sir, as 10,000 agents, each 100 people, days 0 to 150
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.12 s; sir: 933,200 infections; at most 305,500 infectious, on day 45


People per agent: 100.0


Each agent stands for 100 people, and the counts in the agents’ results are multiplied by 100.


Static scaling
The number of people each agent stands for is sim.pop_scale, which is total_pop / n_agents: give the number of people and the number of agents, and the scale follows. Results that are counts (such as I) are multiplied by it when the run ends; results that are fractions or averages (such as prevalence) are not.
The cost is resolution. With 5,000 agents for a million people, each agent is 200 people, so an epidemic can’t start from fewer than 200 people, and an outbreak started by 10 people can’t be represented at all:

sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10)) # 10 people infectious at the start
static = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), label='Static')
static.run();

Sim "Static": sir, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters
  Note: "sir" starts with one agent in I (200 people): its initial number is 0.05 agents at 200 people per agent, which rounds to 0. For the number given, give more agents (n_agents=), or rescale=True


  Done in 0.11 s; sir: 934,400 infections; at most 313,600 infectious, on day 48


Starsim notes the problem: 10 people are 0.05 of an agent, so the run starts with one agent infectious, which is 200 people (and here, by chance, it recovers without infecting anyone). With static scaling, a seed is a whole number of agents: to seed 10 agents, give 2,000 people (init_n is a number of people, not of agents):

sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=2000)) # 2,000 people, 10 agents of 200, infectious at the start
static = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), label='Static')
static.run();

Sim "Static": sir, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.087 s; sir: 927,400 infections; at most 300,200 infectious, on day 38




Dynamic rescaling
With rescale=True, each agent starts by standing for one person, and the number grows as the epidemic does, up to sim.pop_scale. When the fraction of agents who are no longer naive (who have left the first state of any disease) passes a threshold (5% by default), the sim multiplies the number of people per agent by at least a factor (1.2 by default), and makes enough of the agents who are not naive naive again to keep the infected people’s numbers the same. So every agent always stands for the same number of people, and agents are freed to stand for the part of the population that has not been infected yet. The 10 people infectious at the start, as in the first static sim, are now 10 agents:

sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10)) # 10 people infectious at the start, as above
dynamic = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=1e6, n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(150), rescale=True, label='Dynamic')
dynamic.run()
dynamic.results.pop_scale.plot()

Sim "Dynamic": sir, as 5,000 agents, each 200 people, days 0 to 150
  Running as agents: n_agents was given
  Note: consider a shorter step (e.g. dt=ss.days(0.25)): each step is 1 day, and infection transmits at up to 0.3 per day (with everyone infectious), 26% in a step. Taking whole steps, agents may differ from the ODE by an amount of that order; sim.check_dt() shows how much it matters


  Done in 0.12 s; sir: 945,800 infections; at most 311,200 infectious, on day 74









The number of people per agent (sim.results.pop_scale) grows from 1 to 200. The threshold and the factor are options: rescale=dict(threshold=0.05, factor=1.2) is the same as rescale=True. Rescaling is for agents only. Here are the three runs:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ten = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10), name='sir') # 10 people infectious, as compartments
ode = ss.Sim(ten, total_pop=1e6, stop=ss.days(150), label='ODE', verbose=0).run()

for sim in [ode, static, dynamic]:
    res = sim.results.sir.I
    plt.plot(res.timevec, res.values, label=sim.label)
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();









Results count the people no agent stands for yet
While each agent stands for fewer people than pop_scale, part of the population is not represented by any agent. The sim counts them as sim.results.unrepresented, which falls at each rescaling. They have never been infected, so a declared disease counts them in its first state (a module written as code doesn’t), and the results are of the whole population from the start:

res = dynamic.results
print('Alive at the start:', res.alive[0])
print('Susceptible at the start:', res.sir.S[0])
print('Infectious at the start:', res.sir.I[0])

Alive at the start: 1000000.0
Susceptible at the start: 999990.0
Infectious at the start: 10.0




Diseases written as code
Dynamic rescaling needs to know which agents are naive, and to make agents naive again. A declared disease does both by itself. A disease written as code that transmits (a subclass of ss.AgentDisease) counts the agents who have ever been infected (ti_infected) as not naive, and its make_naive() puts each of its states back to its default value, except rel_sus and rel_trans, which other modules (such as vaccines) often change. A disease that keeps something else, or that sets rel_sus itself, overrides it:
class MyDisease(ss.AgentDisease):
    def make_naive(self, uids, skip_states=None):
        super().make_naive(uids, skip_states=['rel_trans']) # Reset rel_sus too
        self.my_custom_value[uids] = 0 # And anything not kept as a state
A count that is added up during the run would mix steps with different numbers of people per agent, so work out a running total in finalize_results(), after the results have been scaled; a declared disease’s running totals (res.infection.cum) are worked out from the scaled flows when they are asked for.

title: Branching and rescaling
text:
Pitfalls

Results during a run are in agents. Counts are scaled when the run ends; an analyzer that reads a count during the run sees agents.
Rare events. An event that happens to fewer people than an agent stands for (a rare complication) happens to whole agents or not at all; such a model needs more agents.
Dynamic rescaling with births and deaths. The people no agent stands for are not born and do not die, so with many births or deaths before the scale reaches pop_scale, the population differs from that of a run with each agent standing for pop_scale from the start (and the count of people no agent stands for can even fall below 0).
Treating a depleting run as a branching process. Chains and offspring counted once a sizable fraction of people have been infected are biased down; count them only while the outbreak is small.
Networks in a branching process of agents. It mixes in groups and places; a contact network raises a CapabilityError.
