workers= limits the number of cores used (for a shared computer), and workers=1 runs the sims one after another in this process, which gives an error its full traceback. When the sims differ in more than parameter values, make them with a function (see Running sims) and give the list to ss.parallel(). If making each sim is itself slow (reading large data files, or building a large population), make them in parallel too, with sc.parallelize() from Sciris:

def make_sim(seed, coverage):
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when=ss.days(30), coverage=coverage)
    return ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label='Campaign', verbose=0)

sims = sc.parallelize(make_sim, iterarg=range(1, 9), coverage=0.5) # One sim for each seed, 1 to 8
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')








Making sims in parallel copies each one back to the main process, which takes time for a large sim; sc.parallelize(..., serial=True) makes them one after another, to check whether parallel is faster. A remote computer can be used through SSH, from an editor that connects to a remote Python (such as VS Code or Positron), or with a Jupyter server on it (The Littlest JupyterHub).
Starsim sets NumPy’s linear algebra library (BLAS) to one thread when imported; for large matrix calculations of your own, ss.options.blas_threads gives it more (see the appendix).

title: Speed and scale
text:
On a cluster

With Dask
For more runs than one computer can manage, tools such as Dask spread them across many computers. Each task makes and runs a sim and returns it; sim.shrink() first removes the people, so that only the results are sent back. ss.MultiSim() then collects sims that have already run, without running them again. (This and the next example are not run on this page.)
import dask
import dask.distributed as dd
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(seed, beta):
    """ Make and run one sim, and return it without its people """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=5))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), solver='binomial', rand_seed=seed, label=f'beta={beta}', verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    sim.shrink()
    return sim

if __name__ == '__main__':
    client = dd.Client(n_workers=4)
    tasks = [dask.delayed(run_sim)(seed, beta) for seed in range(1, 11) for beta in [1.5, 1.9, 2.3]]
    sims = list(dask.compute(*tasks))
    msim = ss.MultiSim(sims) # Collects the results of sims that have run
    msim.plot()
Coiled, a paid service built on Dask, runs the same tasks on a cloud cluster that grows and shrinks with the work (coiled.Cluster(n_workers=50).get_client() in place of dd.Client()), and the same pattern works with other tools, such as Joblib.


With a job scheduler
On a high-performance cluster run by a scheduler such as Slurm, the usual pattern is a job array: the same script is run many times, each with its own task number, which picks the seed and the scenario. Each job saves its sim (shrunk) or, better, a table of the results it needs, and a final script collects them:
# run_one.py: run as one task of a job array, e.g. with sbatch --array=0-399
import os
import starsim as ss
from measles_campaign import make_sim

task = int(os.environ['SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID'])
coverages = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
coverage, seed = coverages[task % 4], task // 4 + 1  # 100 seeds of each of 4 scenarios
sim = make_sim(coverage=coverage, seed=seed)
sim.run()
sim.save(f'results/sim_{task}.sim')  # Shrunk by default, since it has finished
# collect.py: once every task has finished
import glob
import starsim as ss

sims = [ss.load(filename) for filename in sorted(glob.glob('results/sim_*.sim'))]
msim = ss.MultiSim(sims)  # Collects sims that have already run; sims with the same label are runs of one scenario
msim.summarize()
Some things matter more on a cluster than on a laptop:

One level of parallelism. When the scheduler already runs many tasks at once, don’t have each task start a pool of its own: use ss.parallel(..., workers=1) within a task, or limit it with workers=. Starsim’s own threads (used only for passes over 200,000 agents or more, and never in the workers of ss.parallel()) are turned off with STARSIM_THREADS=1, and NumPy’s with SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS=1 in the task’s environment.
Compile once, before the runs. With the Numba kernels, run starsim init compile (or ss.compile()) once after installing, in the shared environment or when building a container image, so that hundreds of tasks don’t each compile them; starsim init compile --check says whether it has been done.
Settings from the environment. Every option in ss.options can be set by an environment variable (STARSIM_THREADS=1, STARSIM_VERBOSE=0), the easiest way to set it for every task of a job (see the appendix).
The same code everywhere. Install the same versions of Starsim and of your own modules on every node (a container image, or a shared environment): sims are sent between computers as Python pickles, which need the same code to load.
A seed for each run. Give each run its own rand_seed, or every run of a stochastic model is the same.

title: Speed and scale
text:
Interactive dashboards
A model can be put behind a web page, so that others can change its inputs and see the results, with tools such as Shiny for Python, Voilà, Panel, or Streamlit. This Streamlit app has sliders for the fraction of the town that is immune and the coverage of a vaccination campaign:
import streamlit as st
import starsim as ss

def run_sim(immune, coverage):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=5))
    campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.95, when=ss.days(30), coverage=coverage)
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, total_pop=20_000, stop=ss.days(180), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    return sim

st.title('Measles in a town of 20,000')
immune = st.slider('Fraction immune at the start', 0.5, 0.99, 0.9)
coverage = st.slider('Coverage of the campaign on day 30', 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)

sim = run_sim(immune, coverage)
st.write('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))
st.pyplot(sim.diseases.measles.plot())
Saved as app.py, it runs (after pip install streamlit) with streamlit run app.py, which opens the dashboard in a browser.

title: Speed and scale
text:
Appendix: every option
Starsim’s global options are in ss.options: set one for the session with ss.options(threads=1), for a block with with ss.options(threads=1):, or before Python starts with the environment variable STARSIM_ and the option’s name in capitals (STARSIM_THREADS=1), which is the way to set it for every worker or every task of a cluster job. ss.options.disp() shows the current values, and ss.options.help(detailed=True) each option’s value, default, and variable. Here is each option with its description:

import pandas as pd
pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', None) # Show each entry in full

rows = {key: dict(variable=f'STARSIM_{key.upper()}', description=ss.options.optdesc[key]) for key in ss.options.keys()}
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(rows, orient='index')








variable
description




verbose
STARSIM_VERBOSE
How much a sim prints by default: 0 for nothing (e.g. in a batch of runs or a fit), 1 for the solver chosen, notes, and progress (default), 2 for everything, such as each step (for debugging). A sim's own verbose= overrides it.


warnings
STARSIM_WARNINGS
What to do with a warning: "warn" (default) to show it as a Python warning, "print" to print it as plain text, "error" to raise it as an error (useful in tests, or to find where a warning comes from), or "ignore" to drop it.


max_steps
STARSIM_MAX_STEPS
Warn that a sim may be slow if it has more timesteps than this (0 to never warn); the default is more than a century at a daily step.


max_years
STARSIM_MAX_YEARS
Warn that a run is probably a mistake if it lasts longer than this many years (0 to never warn); a run this long is almost always a stop meant as a year, or a time in the wrong unit.


jupyter
STARSIM_JUPYTER
Whether to use the settings for Jupyter notebooks (sharper "retina" figures): -1 to detect a notebook (default), 0 for never, 1 for always.


style
STARSIM_STYLE
The plotting style: "starsim" (default), "fancy", "simple", or any of Matplotlib's styles. To change it for one plot only, use ss.style() in a with block.


show
STARSIM_SHOW
Whether plots are shown as soon as they are made (with plt.show()); set False to make figures without showing them, e.g. in a script that saves them to files.


reticulate
STARSIM_RETICULATE
Whether a NumPy integer array indexes a state by UIDs, as needed for a module written in R (through reticulate), which cannot keep ss.uids; leave False in Python.


precision
STARSIM_PRECISION
The precision of the numbers kept for each agent: 32 (default) for float32, which takes half the memory, or 64 for float64, for when small differences matter (e.g. comparing against another model to many decimal places).


threads
STARSIM_THREADS
The number of threads that the passes over the agents of a large sim, and the particles of a particle filter, use: 0 (default) for as many as Numba has (by default, one per core), or 1 for no extra threads, e.g. on a shared machine. Each worker of ss.parallel() and of a calibration uses one, since the workers already share the cores.


blas_threads
STARSIM_BLAS_THREADS
The number of threads for BLAS, the linear algebra in NumPy and SciPy: 1 (default), since more threads rarely speed up a sim but do slow down many sims run in parallel; or 0 to leave BLAS as it is. For the threads of Starsim itself, see "threads"; see also the "Deployment" page of the user guide.


kernels
STARSIM_KERNELS
Which compiled code runs the solvers (all give the same results):\n\n- "auto" (default): Rust if it is there (in the wheels, or built: see starsim/solvers/rust/README.md); otherwise Numba, running compartmental sims in plain Python until Numba has compiled (Numba compiles first if a run, or the runs of a session, would take longer in plain Python than compiling takes, about two minutes, once per install; a note says which)\n- "rust": Rust, compiled ahead of time, so a first run takes no compiling\n- "numba": always compile with Numba first (see ss.compile())\n- "python": the compartmental kernels in plain Python (the passes over agents are still Numba), e.g. for debugging\n\nJAX is chosen by the run (see sim.jax), and ss.jit always uses Numba.


jax
STARSIM_JAX
Where JAX runs when Starsim uses it (sim.gradient(), fits, and ODE runs with sim.jax = True): "cpu" (default), "auto" for JAX's own choice (a GPU if it finds one), or another platform, e.g. "cuda". The CPU is the default since Starsim's runs in JAX are long loops of small steps, which a GPU runs several times slower. It sets JAX_PLATFORMS, so it applies to everything in the session that uses JAX; if JAX has already started on other platforms, it is restarted on these the next time Starsim uses it (and "auto" goes back to the platforms it had before).


uncompiled_warning
STARSIM_UNCOMPILED_WARNING
Whether to say on import that Starsim has not been compiled yet (see ss.compile()); True by default. Since it is read on import, it only has an effect as the environment variable STARSIM_UNCOMPILED_WARNING.


crn
STARSIM_CRN
Whether to use common random numbers (default True): each agent gets the same random numbers in every scenario, so the difference between two scenarios is due to what changed rather than to chance. Set False for slightly faster draws (one plain random number per agent or edge), which are statistically valid but differ between scenarios.


keep_times
STARSIM_KEEP_TIMES
Whether a declared disease run as agents keeps the time each agent entered every state (e.g. ti_S) and the history of every transition (e.g. sir.infection.n_times, .since, and .ever). Off by default to save memory: only those that the engine or the model needs are kept (with, for each, the time each agent last left the state, e.g. for I.stays), and reading another raises an error. ss.Sim(keep_times=...) sets it for one sim.


max_joint
STARSIM_MAX_JOINT
The most compartments that diseases tracked jointly in a compartmental run may use (their joint states times the groups of the other dimensions; see ss.solvers.JointStates). Above it, solver="auto" runs as agents instead, and a compartmental solver that was asked for raises an error before anything is made, since so many compartments would take too much memory. 0 for no limit.







Starsim also reads SCIRIS_NUM_THREADS for the threads of linear algebra, and STARSIM_CHECK_COUNTS and STARSIM_CHECK_DRAWS, which turn on checks of the agent engine for testing it, at a cost in speed. The settings of a sim that affect speed or memory (n_agents, dt, solver, require_kernels, group_results, record_people) are in Running sims.

title: Speed and scale
text:
Appendix: the starsim command
Installing Starsim also installs a starsim command, for setting up an environment and converting models (starsim lists these, and starsim <command> --help the options of each):



Command
What it does




starsim init
Once, after installing: starsim init ai if an AI coding agent is installed, then starsim init compile unless the Rust kernels are in use (-y not to ask)


starsim init compile
Compiles the Numba kernels ahead of time, as ss.compile() does (a few minutes, once per install); optional, since they are otherwise compiled on first use. --rust builds the Rust kernels instead, in a clone of Starsim; --check says which kernels are in use and whether they are compiled, exiting with 1 if not


starsim init ai
Links the Starsim skills for AI coding agents into this project, as starsim ai install does; --global installs a short skill for all projects, --to=claude,agents chooses the agents, and --force replaces a skill of the same name


starsim init dev
For a clone of Starsim: also the development dependencies, Rust if it is missing, and both sets of kernels


starsim ai
Where the skills are installed; list, show (the guide, or one skill), install and uninstall, and off and on (whether other commands suggest the skills)


starsim convert model.R
Converts a model to Starsim code (model.py), telling the format from the file (or --from=); --to= another format, --out= the file, --force to replace it. starsim convert lists the formats


starsim convert laser_model.py --ai
Has an AI coding agent do the conversion, with Starsim’s skills (--headless to run it on its own; --ai=claude names the agent, by default the one in STARSIM_AGENT or the only one installed)


starsim import model.camdl
The same as starsim convert model.camdl --to=starsim; a second argument gives the format (starsim import model.json epipack), and other options go to the importer (--databook=data.xlsx)


starsim export model.py sbml
Writes the sim that model.py makes (as sim, or --sim=) in another format


starsim --version
The version of Starsim

title: Writing models
text:
🧠4% 🤖96%
A Starsim model is a sim (ss.Sim) that holds a population and a set of modules: one or more diseases, and whatever else the model needs (contacts, births and deaths, interventions). This page covers how those parts fit together, and how to check that the model Starsim built is the one you meant. For a first walk through a model, see T1 – Getting started and T2 – Building a model.

title: Writing models
text:
A model and its parts
Here is a simplified measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people: an SIR model, in which people are susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R). Each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β = 1.9 per day times the fraction of people who are infectious, and people are infectious for 8 days on average:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0028 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6











library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # From I to R, after 8 days on average
  init_prev = 0.001
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50))
sim$run()
sim$plot()



S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
infection = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection')       # From S to I, at a rate of 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
recovery  = ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery') # From I to R, after an exponentially distributed time of 8 days on average
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(transitions=[infection, recovery], init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = ss.contacts(1), # Everyone mixes with everyone, with one contact per person per day
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = ss.days(0),
    stop      = ss.days(50),
    dt        = ss.days(1),     # Steps of a day
    unit      = 'day',          # The unit of bare numbers
    solver    = 'ode',          # Run as an ODE
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0026 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6












The “Explicit” tab is the same model with nothing left for Starsim to fill in (the transitions in full, the exponential infectious period, homogeneous mixing with one contact a day, the unit, the step, and the solver), and gives the same results (below).
A sim can hold these kinds of modules, each given to it by keyword (a disease can also be given first, as here):



Kind
What it is for
Keyword
See




Diseases
The states people can be in, and how they move between them
diseases=
Diseases


Networks and contacts
Who meets whom: contact matrices, mixing pools, and networks of individual contacts
networks=
Places and data, Mixing


Demographics
Births, deaths, and pregnancy
demographics=
Demographics


Interventions
Vaccination, testing, treatment, and changes to parameters
interventions=
Products, Interventions


Connectors
Links between modules, such as one disease making another more likely
connectors=
Connectors


Analyzers
Extra results, collected as the sim runs
analyzers=
Analyzers



The sim itself holds what applies to the whole model: the population (total_pop=, or n_agents= for a model run as agents), the period (start=, stop=, and the time step dt=), and the random seed, and how the model is run (solver=). See Running sims for these, and its appendix of every sim setting; see Time for the span and the step.
A disease can be declared, as states and transitions, as above, or written as code, for what states and transitions can’t say; both kinds can be in the same sim. See Diseases, Custom modules, and What can be declared.

title: Writing models
text:
Shorthand and its written-out form
This page is the reference for how a declared model is written; Diseases says what each kind of transition means. The operators are a short way to write ss.Transition(), and each form below builds the same objects as its written-out form, with the same results:








Shorthand
Written out
Means




S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
S = ss.State(name='S'), and so on
The states


S >> I @ 1.9*I
ss.Transition(S, I, rate=1.9*I)
A rate (a bare number after @ is a rate)


I >> R @ ss.days(8)
ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8))
A duration, or a distribution of durations


I >> R @ dict(dur=ss.days(8), p=0.99)
ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.99)
Any keywords of the transition


I >> {ss.dead: 0.002, R: None} @ ss.days(8)
ss.Transition(I, {ss.dead: 0.002, R: None}, dur=ss.days(8))
One transition with several destinations


S + V >> I @ 1.9*I
ss.Transition([S, V], I, rate=1.9*I)
From any of several states


U >> A @ ss.on(ss.person.age >= 15)
ss.Transition(U, A, when=ss.on(ss.person.age >= 15))
A trigger


ss.Disease(infection, recovery)
ss.Disease(transitions=[infection, recovery]), or ss.Disease(infection=..., recovery=...)
The disease, named after its variable



A disease can also be a class, with the same lines in its body, or declare them in __init__() with define_states() and define_transitions() (Diseases). Names and values that aren’t given are filled in by the rules in the appendix, and units by those in Time.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')

Equations, diagram, and transitions
equations() writes out the differential equations of a declared disease, with its parameters by name (here beta and dur_I, the mean time in I). They hold whatever the model is run as: as agents, each person moves between states at the same rates.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


diagram() draws the model’s diagram, with each arrow labeled with its transition’s name and value:

measles.diagram()








A dashed arrow is a transmission, and a solid one any other transition; a transition with p= also gives the fraction that takes it. measles.diagram('text') gives it as a Mermaid flowchart instead, for GitHub, wikis, and anything else that draws Mermaid. For every disease of a sim, and how they act on each other, use sim.diagram() and sim.equations().
transitions is a table of the transitions, with what drives each (a rate or a duration) and its kind: a transition is a transmission if people catch it from people in another state (here, “transmission, from I”), and spontaneous otherwise. Printing it also shows which state leads to which:

S  .  infection  .

The reproduction number
R0() works out the basic reproduction number from the next-generation matrix of the model. For a simple SIR model this is β × the infectious period (1.9 × 8 ≈ 15), but R0() works for any declared model, including those with several infectious states, groups with their own contacts, or vectors:

measles.R0()

15.2000000000152


R0() on a disease on its own assumes homogeneous mixing. For a disease in a sim with contacts or groups, use the sim’s copy of it, sim.diseases.measles.R0(), which includes them (see below for why the sim has a copy).






Note



The sim prints R0 when it starts. If some people start immune (e.g. init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9)), it also gives the reproduction number in the population as it starts (often called the effective reproduction number, R): “R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.51 at the start, with 10% susceptible)”.


After a run, Rt() gives the reproduction number at each time point, from the people in each state and the rates as they were then (so it drops while an ss.modify() lowers β). It works for a run of any solver:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0).run()
sim.diseases.measles.Rt().plot()

text:
Where the parts of a sim go
A sim runs a copy of each module it is given, so that the same disease can go into several sims (for example, one for each scenario) without one run changing another. After a sim is initialized (by sim.init(), or by sim.run(), which initializes it if needed), its copy of each module is in sim.diseases, sim.networks, and so on, by name. A disease made with ss.Disease() is named after its variable (here measles), and one made from a class after the class (sir); name= gives it a name of its own (see the appendix).

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), verbose=0)
sim.run()

print(sim.diseases.measles is measles) # The sim's copy, not the original
print(sim.diseases.measles.pars)        # The disease's parameters
print(sim.results.measles.keys())       # Its results

The parameters of each module are in sim.diseases.measles.pars (and sim.pars.measles); see Parameters.
The results are in sim.results, by module: sim.results.measles.I. Every state and every transition has a result of the same name. See Outcomes for declaring more, and Results for working with them.
In a model run as agents, the people are in sim.people, with each person’s age, sex, and the states of each disease; see People and demographics. Each module adds its states to the people, so sim.people.to_df() gives a table with a row for each agent and a column for each of their attributes and states:


sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=1000, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50), dt=ss.days(0.25), verbose=0) # A quarter-day step, short enough for measles as agents

title: Writing models
text:
Checks and pitfalls
A model that runs is not necessarily the model you meant, and a plausible plot is not enough to show that it is. These checks catch most mistakes in a new model:

Read describe() once for each new model, and give any value it guessed that matters to your question.
Check that everyone has a place to start. init_prev starts people in E, not I, in an SEIR model (Starting values).
Check that the states add up. In a closed model (no births or deaths), the people in all the states of a disease add up to the population at every time point.
Match the quantity to the question. New infections are a flow (res.infection), and the number infectious a stock (res.I): summing I over time counts each person once for every day they are infectious.
Check the units of β. Adding a contact matrix or a network changes β from a rate per person to a rate per contact; see Mixing.
Don’t change the original after the sim is made. Since the sim has a copy, changing measles after ss.Sim(measles, ...) has no effect on that sim. Change the sim’s copy, give the new value to the sim by name (ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.5))), or make a new sim.

Appendix: what Starsim names and fills in
From some names and forms, Starsim works out what the model didn’t say. Each value it chooses itself is marked as guessed in describe(), with the rule it used; giving the value removes the guess.
Settings:



What
What Starsim does
To say otherwise

50 units of time

From the diseases’ typed values, then dates, a typed dt, years, or the other modules’ typed values; else time is in steps (Time)

solver=, or n_agents=

Parameters. A number written in a declared disease becomes a parameter, named by where it is, so that it can be given by name (pars=dict(...)) and fitted:

S, E, I, A, R = ss.states('S E I A R')
example = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> E @ 0.5*(I + 0.5*A),                    # beta (the 0.5 on A is not a parameter)

Name or form

To say otherwise

Write the rate you mean

title: Results and plotting
text:
🧠11% 🤖89%
A run produces results: for each disease, the number of people in each state at each time point, the number who made each transition in each step, and any other quantities the model declares. This page covers reading, resampling, grouping, summarizing, exporting, and plotting them. Results know their labels, time points, and kinds, so most plots take one line.

title: Results and plotting
text:
Reading results
After a run, sim.results holds the results of each module by name, and the sim’s own (such as alive, the population size). The examples on this page use a measles outbreak in a town where 90% are immune, written as a function so that scenarios can be compared later:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

def make_measles(immune=0.9):
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection  = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
    recovery   = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
    prevalence = I/(S + I + R)         # The fraction of people infectious
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, prevalence, init=dict(R=immune), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')

sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
sim.run()

res = sim.results.measles
print(res)


Results(Disease)
0. timevec: array(start=2025-01-01, stop=2025-07-01)
1. S: Result(min=4073.5, mean=6842.29, max=9990)
2. I: Result(min=10, mean=259.516, max=672.885)
3. R: Result(min=90000, mean=92898.2, max=95901.9)
4. infection: Result(min=1.8624, mean=32.5185, max=88.2787)
5. recovery: Result(min=1.29139, mean=32.4443, max=84.1136)
6. prevalence: Result(min=0.0001, mean=0.00259516, max=0.00672885)
7. infected: Result(min=10, mean=259.516, max=672.885)






library(starsim)

make_measles <- function(immune = 0.9) {
  states("S I R")
  Disease(
    infection  = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # β = 1.9 per day
    recovery   = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
    prevalence = I / (S + I + R),                  # The fraction of people infectious
    init   = list(R = immune),
    init_n = list(I = 10),
    name = "measles"
  )
}

sim <- Sim(make_measles(), total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", verbose = 0)
sim$run()

res <- sim$results$measles
res



A disease has a result for each state (S, I, R: the number of people in it at each time point) and each transition (infection, recovery: the number who made it during each step), named after the variables they were made from, plus any ratio or outcome declared with it, such as prevalence here. res.I and res['I'] are the same. Names with special meaning lists the results every disease and the sim get, and Outcomes covers declaring more, such as reported cases.
Each result is an ss.Result. It behaves like a NumPy array, one number per time point, but also carries what it is:







Attribute
Meaning




values
The NumPy array of values


timevec
The time point of each value


label
A human-readable label, used in plots


kind
What kind of quantity it is: a stock, a flow, or a ratio (below)


scale
Whether the result is a count that scales with the population (as agents, each agent stands for some number of people); by default, a flow or stock does and a ratio doesn’t


low, high
Bounds, for a result that has them




print('Peak infectious:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Total infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('First time points:', res.I.timevec[:3])

Peak infectious: 673
Total infections: 5918
First time points: [<2025-01-01> <2025-01-02> <2025-01-03>]


A result’s kind decides how it is added up over time (its summarize_by), whether it has a running total, and how it is compared with data:










kind
summarize_by
What it is
Examples
Over a period




'stock'
'last'
A number at each time point
S, I, R
Resampled, the value at the start (a running total, .cum, at the end); over the whole run, the last value


'flow'
'sum'
A number of events during each step
infection, recovery, cases
The total


'ratio'
'mean'
One number divided by another
prevalence
Worked out again from the totals of its parts (the mean, for one with no parts)



A result of your own gives it as ss.Result('protected', kind='stock'), or by its name (appendix). scale= overrides whether it is scaled, and kind=None is for a result with no meaning over time, which isn’t summarized. summarize_by= summarizes it another way without changing what it is: ss.Result('new_cases', kind='flow', summarize_by='mean') is still a flow, whose summary over the run is its mean per step.
A flow’s running total is .cum, so res.infection.cum[-1] is the number of infections over the whole run. Summing a stock over time does not count people (res.I.sum() counts each person once for every step they are infectious), and the people infectious at the start are not in infection.sum(). A result also does what a NumPy array does (indexing, arithmetic, sum(), max()); every method of a result is listed in the API reference.
A result has one value for each time point, from start to stop, and each time point is the step that starts there: I[0] is the number infectious at the start, and infection[0] the infections during the first step (Time).

Changing the time step of a result
resample() gives a result over longer periods ('day', 'week', 'month', 'year', or a duration such as ss.weeks(2)), adding it up by its summarize_by: weekly infections are the total over each week, monthly numbers infectious are the value at the start of each month, and a running total is the value at the end of each period. Each period is labeled by its start. to_series() gives a pandas series with the dates as its index:

res.infection.resample('week').to_series().head()

2025-01-01    16.792770
2025-01-08    26.311677
2025-01-15    41.027284
2025-01-22    63.493564
2025-01-29    97.130268
dtype: float64

title: Results and plotting
text:
Results by group
A disease stratified by age (see Stratification) still has one result for each state and transition; each is the total over the groups, and has the groups inside it. select() picks groups, and by() gives one line for each. Here the model is stratified by age, with the contact matrix of Stratification; with contacts, β is per contact, so it is given by name:

by_age = make_measles().stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, inplace=False)
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
strat = ss.Sim(by_age, networks=contacts, pars=dict(beta=0.14), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0)
strat.run()

sres = strat.results.measles
print('Peak infectious, aged 0-14:', round(sres.I.select(age='0-14').max()))
sres.prevalence.by('age').plot()

Peak infectious, aged 0-14: 264









A ratio such as prevalence is never averaged over groups: its numerator and denominator are each added up over the groups selected, and then divided. A module written as code can keep its results by group too: stratify the sim (stratify=dict(sex=['female', 'male'])), make the result with ss.Result(..., groups=True), and set it at each step with set_groups() from sim.groups.count(), which counts the people in each group for whom a condition holds. As agents, stratifying by a property people already have, such as sex or age, changes nothing in the run, so it can be done for the results alone.

Results with several columns
In a module written as code, a result with several values at each time point, such as new infections by age group, is made with columns=. Here an analyzer counts new infections among children and adults:

import numpy as np

class InfectionsByAge(ss.Analyzer):
    """ Count new infections among children and adults """
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'], label='New infections'),
        )

    def step(self):
        new = self.sim.diseases.sis.infection.uids # Those infected in this step
        children = self.sim.people.age[new] < 15
        self.results.new_infections[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(children), np.count_nonzero(~children)]

cols = ss.Sim(ss.SIS(), networks='random', analyzers=InfectionsByAge(), n_agents=2000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2000-12-31', verbose=0)
cols.run()
infs = cols.results.infectionsbyage.new_infections
infs.resample('month').to_df().head()

The runs of a stochastic model together (see Scenarios) have the same results as one run, with every run inside each:

msim = ss.parallel(sim.new(solver='binomial'), n_runs=20)
mres = msim.results.measles.I

median = mres.median()            # The median of the runs at each time point

take() keeps some runs, scenarios() and axes() say how they are arranged, and diff('baseline') is the difference of each other scenario from the one labeled 'baseline', run by run (msim.diff('baseline') does it for every result). msim.summarize() gives the median and interval of each result over the whole run, which is not the same as the median at each time point: the quantiles at each time point don’t give the quantiles of the peak or of the total size.

title: Results and plotting
text:
Plotting

Plotting a sim
sim.plot() plots every result that is plotted by default, each in axes of its own, labeled and dated from the results, with any data as points (show_data=False leaves it out). The sim’s own results that never change are left out; show_skipped=True includes them.

PythonR



sim.plot()










plot(sim) # The same as sim$plot()



What to plot is given by name, as the first argument:







Argument
Plots




None (the default)
Every result plotted by default, each in its own axes


'measles'
The results of one module


'measles.I' (or 'measles_I')
One result


['measles.I', 'measles.infection']
Exactly these results, each in its own axes


[['measles.S', 'measles.I', 'measles.R'], 'measles.infection']
The results in an inner list together in one axes, with a legend



A name that matches no result is an error that lists the names there are. Put together only results of the same kind on a similar scale, such as the two flows here:

PythonR



sim.plot([['measles.infection', 'measles.recovery'], 'measles.I'], figsize=(8, 6))










sim$plot(list(list("measles.infection", "measles.recovery"), "measles.I"), figsize = c(8, 6)) # A list in a list: together in one axes



A module plots its own results with plot(): 'states' (the default, together in one axes), 'flows', 'all', or the names of results, e.g. sim.diseases.measles.plot('I', 'prevalence'). A model run over years can be plotted as yearly values with annualize=True, which adds up each result by its kind.


Plotting results
A single result plots itself, with its label as the title, and so does anything made from one: a resampled result, one group (select(age='0-14')), or one line per group (by('age')). Each plotting function takes the common Matplotlib settings by name (color, lw, alpha, figsize, and the others of ss.plot_args()), and anything else in a dict: plot_kw= to plt.plot(), fig_kw= to plt.figure(), data_kw= to plt.scatter(). log=True gives a log scale.

res.infection.resample('week').plot(color='k', lw=3, figsize=(6, 3))










Comparing scenarios and runs
Sims run together, with ss.parallel() or ss.MultiSim, plot together: each result is one axes, with a line for each scenario, labeled by the sims’ labels. The runs of a stochastic model are plotted as their median at each time point, with a band holding 95% of the runs; lines=True plots every run instead:

scenarios = {
    '85% immune': ss.Sim(make_measles(0.85), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0),
    '90% immune': ss.Sim(make_measles(0.90), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01', verbose=0),
}
ss.parallel(scenarios).plot('measles.I')
msim.plot('measles.I') # The 20 runs above: the median and the range of 95% of them















Plots mark when interventions act (a dashed line at each round of a delivery, and at the start of an ss.modify() or routine delivery), in gray for marks every scenario shares and in a scenario’s color for its own; show_interventions='fill' shades the span from each one’s start to its stop instead (lightly, so overlapping ones show darker), and show_interventions=False leaves them out. msim.plot_each() plots each run on its own time axis, for sims with different time points.


Styles, saving, and Matplotlib
Plots use Starsim’s style ('starsim', with the Mulish font) by default; style= takes 'simple', 'fancy', or any Matplotlib style such as 'ggplot', and font= another font ('sans-serif' for Matplotlib’s default). ss.options(style='simple') changes every plot.
In Jupyter, a plotting function shows the figure and returns nothing; filename= saves it as well, and do_show=False returns the figure without showing it. In a script, the figure is always returned (and shown as ss.options.show says), so it can be saved with fig.savefig(). A figure or axes given with fig= or ax= is not shown, so more can be plotted into it.
Anything else can be plotted with Matplotlib from the results, since a result is an array with its time points. ss.style() applies Starsim’s style to plots of your own, and sc.commaticks() from Sciris puts commas in large numbers on an axis:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with ss.style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    for label, scenario in scenarios.items():
        sres = scenario.results.measles
        ax.plot(sres.infection.timevec, sres.infection.cum/100_000, label=label) # Infected since the start, as a fraction
    ax.set_title('Fraction of people infected since the start')
    ax.legend()
    plt.show()








msim.to_df(quantiles=[0.025, 0.5, 0.975]) gives the quantiles of every result across runs, in long form, for pandas, seaborn, or any library that works with tables. Besides results over time, Starsim draws maps, diagrams, people and contacts, distributions, fits, and timings; the appendix lists every plotting function.

title: Results and plotting
text:
Pitfalls and further reading

The flow at a time point is the step that starts there. The weekly total dated 3 March is the week from 3 March. Data dated by the end of each period (“week ending”) needs its dates moved back by one period to be compared.
Agents’ results are scaled. With each agent standing for several people, counts are multiplied by that number when the run ends; a count read in the middle of a run is in agents (see Branching and rescaling).

Further reading: 10 minutes to pandas (the tables to_df() gives), Matplotlib style sheets (the styles style= accepts), and Ten simple rules for better figures.

title: Fitting methods

🧠0% 🤖100%
sim.fit() chooses a method that suits the model, so most fits don’t need to name one. This page is for choosing one yourself: what each method gives, needs, and costs, and how their answers compare on the same data. The data, parameters, and measures of fit, which are the same for every method, are in Fitting a model.

title: Fitting methods
text:
Best fits
Every example on this page fits the same SIR model of an outbreak in a town of 10,000 people over four months, with half of infections reported (fixed, since 'if2' can fit only the model’s rates). Two parameters are unknown: the transmission rate beta and the infectious period dur_inf. The data are weekly reported cases from a chain binomial run with beta = 0.3 and an infectious period of 8 days, so each method’s estimate can be compared with the truth. The likelihood, where one is used, is Poisson.

import time
import pandas as pd
import starsim as ss

beta    = ss.par(0.4, bounds=[0.05, 1])      # Transmission rate per day
dur_inf = ss.par(ss.days(5), bounds=[3, 15]) # Infectious period, in days
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
cases = ss.outcome(0.5*infection) # Half of infections are reported
sir = ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ dur_inf, cases, init=dict(I=0.002), name='sir')

pars = dict(total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=120)
truth = dict(beta=0.3, dur_inf=8)
data = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.3, dur_inf=ss.days(8)), solver='binomial', rand_seed=2, verbose=0, **pars).run().to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')

deterministic = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, verbose=0, **pars)
stochastic = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, solver='binomial', verbose=0, **pars)
likelihood = dict(cases=ss.poisson())

fits = {} # Each method's fit and how long it took, for the comparison at the end
def fit_by(method, sim, likelihood=None, **settings):
    """ Fit by one method, with its settings, and keep the fit and its time """
    start = time.time()
    fit = sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method(method, **settings), likelihood=likelihood, verbose=False)
    fits[method] = dict(fit=fit, seconds=time.time() - start)
    return fit

fit_by() is sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method(name, **settings)), timed for the comparison at the end. A method with its default settings is given by name alone, e.g. sim.fit(method='optuna').

SciPy: 'nelder-mead', 'l-bfgs-b', and others
These search from the best few points of a scan over the bounds (scan=, 10 per parameter), with restarts= searches (3 by default) from points that are apart, and take SciPy’s own options too, e.g. maxiter=500. The gradient-based methods take their gradients from JAX (see Gradients), or by finite differences. On a stochastic model, they minimize the mean score of n_runs= runs with the same seeds at every point, which with a likelihood is not the log-likelihood.

fit = fit_by('nelder-mead', deterministic, scan=10, restarts=2, maxiter=200)
fit.pars

sc.obj(beta=0.26716887808599854, dur_inf=days(9.56989))



fit = fit_by('l-bfgs-b', deterministic)
fit.pars

Optuna: 'optuna'
Optuna learns where to look from the scores so far, which suits noisy scores: each trial takes fresh random seeds, so the search averages over chance. With a likelihood for every series on a stochastic compartmental model, each trial is scored by a particle filter’s estimate of the log-likelihood, so the best fit is near the maximum likelihood; otherwise (or with n_runs= given) by the mean of several runs’ scores. fit.measure says which. Its key setting is n_trials=; workers= runs trials in parallel, storage= keeps them so a fit can be resumed, and other keywords go to Optuna’s study.optimize(), e.g. timeout=600.

Iterated filtering: 'if2'
Iterated filtering (IF2; Ionides et al. 2015), the method of the pomp package for R, finds maximum-likelihood values of a stochastic model by running a particle filter many times, with each particle’s values taking small random steps that shrink from one pass to the next. Several chains (chains=, 4) each run iterations= passes (50) with particles= particles (1,000); sd= and cooling= set the size of the steps and how fast they shrink. fit.converged is True if the chains, from different starts, end within 2 of the best log-likelihood: a sign that they agree, not proof that they found the maximum.

title: Fitting methods
text:
Posteriors
A posterior uses each parameter’s prior=, or a uniform prior over its bounds. Its draws are in fit.samples, and fit.table adds the median, the 95% interval, and for chains R-hat and the effective sample size (Fit diagnostics covers reading them). The defaults are in the table above. Each of chains= chains first takes warmup= draws, which tune it and are discarded; with draws='auto' (the default), it then draws in batches until the chains agree (an R-hat of at most rhat=1.01 for every parameter) and every parameter has ess=400 effective draws, or until max_draws= (with a warning). A number, e.g. draws=1000, takes exactly that many. The examples take fewer to run quickly, so they may report that they have not converged.

NUTS: 'nuts'
The No-U-Turn sampler uses gradients to move through the posterior of a deterministic model. It needs JAX and BlackJAX. Its warm-up learns the scale of each parameter and the correlations between them (a dense mass matrix), so that strongly correlated parameters, such as an infection rate and a fraction reported, don’t slow it down. On a GPU, the last digits of the draws can differ from run to run (far inside the posterior’s intervals).

Particle MCMC: 'pmcmc'
Particle MCMC takes a random walk over the parameters, with the likelihood at each point estimated by a particle filter, so it includes the model’s process noise. Its draws are more correlated than those of NUTS, so it needs more. It tunes its steps so that about 15% of proposals are accepted (fit.diagnostics.acceptance), and chooses the number of particles in its warm-up unless particles= is given. Each draw keeps the run the filter drew with it (fit.trajectories), which fit.project() continues (see Projecting from a posterior). For an ODE, it is a random walk on the exact likelihood, with no particles.

title: Fitting methods
text:
Comparing the methods
Each fit above is kept, with how long it took, so their estimates can be put side by side, with the true values:

rows = []
for method, entry in fits.items():
    fit, table = entry['fit'], entry['fit'].table.set_index('par')
    row = dict(method=method, gives='posterior' if fit.samples is not None else 'best fit')
    for par in ['beta', 'dur_inf']:
        row[par] = table.loc[par, 'median'] if fit.samples is not None else table.loc[par, 'best'] # The median of a posterior
        row[f'{par} 95% interval'] = f"{table.loc[par, 'lower']:.3f} to {table.loc[par, 'upper']:.3f}" if fit.samples is not None else ''
    row['seconds'] = entry['seconds']
    rows.append(row)
rows.append(dict(method='(true values)', **truth))
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('method')
comparison.round(3).fillna('')

Every result is relative to the model and the likelihood. The methods that fit the ODE (SciPy and NUTS) agree with each other, but the ODE is not the model that made the data, so its best fit is a little off, and the NUTS posterior is narrow around it: a Poisson likelihood on an ODE counts only the noise in reporting, not the chance in transmission, so its interval for β can exclude the true value. Particle MCMC runs the stochastic model itself, so its posterior includes the process noise. ABC-SMC is only as close to the posterior as its last tolerance. IF2 gives the maximum likelihood of the stochastic model, and Optuna without a likelihood the lowest mean mismatch; neither gives an interval (their spreads show only how flat the score is near the best, and ss.fitting.profile() gives a confidence interval for a deterministic model).
So, for data with much more chance in them than reporting noise, a posterior from an ODE understates the uncertainty. A likelihood that allows more variation (ss.nbinom(n=...), with n fitted) widens it, and 'pmcmc' on a stochastic model counts the chance directly, at a higher cost.

text:
Further reading

Ionides et al. 2015, “Inference for dynamic and latent variable models via iterated filtering”: the IF2 algorithm
pomp: Statistical inference for partially observed Markov processes: the R package for iterated filtering and particle MCMC
Andrieu et al. 2010, “Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods”: particle MCMC

title: Fitting methods
text:
Appendix: settings of each method
The settings each method takes (in ss.fitting.method()), from ss.fitting.method_options(), with the defaults from each method’s signature (a SciPy method also takes SciPy’s own options, and Optuna those of study.optimize(), which are listed too):

import inspect
import optuna

rows = []
for method, func in ss.fitting.methods.items():
    defaults = {key:p.default for key, p in inspect.signature(optuna.Study.optimize).parameters.items()}
    defaults |= {key:p.default for key, p in inspect.signature(func).parameters.items()} | dict(require_jax=True) # n_runs and reseed are chosen by the fit
    settings = [f'{key}={defaults.get(key)}' for key in ss.fitting.method_options(method)]
    rows.append(dict(method=method, settings=', '.join(settings)))
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('method')

A default of None is chosen by the fit: for scan, 10 points per parameter, up to 100; for restarts, 3 searches (1 for one parameter of a deterministic model); for particles, chosen in each chain’s warm-up for 'pmcmc' (none for an ODE), and 200 for Optuna where a particle filter scores each trial; for n_trials, 50 per parameter, at least 100; for n_runs, 4 for a stochastic compartmental model and 1 otherwise; for workers, 1. What each setting means is in the API docs of ss.fitting.method() (see ss.fitting). The samplers are also callable directly, for a log-density of your own (such as sim.log_density(); see Gradients): ss.fitting.nuts(), ss.fitting.pmmh(), and ss.fitting.abc_smc().

title: Starsim v3.0 to v3.1 migration guide
text:
This guide describes the breaking changes introduced in Starsim v3.1.0 and the steps required to migrate code from Starsim v3.0.x. It was mostly written by an LLM, and is mostly written for other LLMs.
Most of the changes are in the Pregnancy module and maternal networks. If your code does not use ss.Pregnancy, ss.MaternalNet, ss.PrenatalNet, or ss.PostnatalNet, you may only need to check the general changes in sections 1-3.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, perform each of the following migrations one at a time and confirm with the user after each step.





Previously, people.sir returned a proxy object that exposed only module states (e.g. people.sir.infected). Now it returns a direct reference to the module itself, so all attributes – including dynamically computed @property values – are accessible.
What to change: In most cases, no change is needed – people.sir.infected still works. However, if your code relied on people.sir being a state-only namespace, be aware that it is now the full module object.
# v3.0 -- worked for states, but not for properties
people.sir.infected      # OK
people.sir.infectious    # AttributeError

# v3.1 -- both work
people.sir.infected      # OK (state)
people.sir.infectious    # OK (property)



These boolean attributes have been removed. Type checking is used instead.
What to change: Replace attribute checks with isinstance() checks.
# v3.0
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if nw.prenatal:
        ...
    if nw.postnatal:
        ...

# v3.1
for nw in sim.networks.values():
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PrenatalNet):
        ...
    if isinstance(nw, ss.PostnatalNet):
        ...



The arguments mother_inds and unborn_inds have been renamed to mother_uids and unborn_uids. The dur, start, and end arguments have been removed – edge lifespans are now managed by the Pregnancy module.
What to change: Update argument names and remove dur/start/end arguments.
# v3.0
net.add_pairs(mother_inds=mothers, unborn_inds=babies, dur=dur_preg, start=ti)

# v3.1
net.add_pairs(mother_uids=mothers, unborn_uids=babies)



PostnatalNet is no longer a subclass of MaternalNet. It is now a DynamicNetwork that accepts an optional dur parameter for the postnatal period. Its add_pairs() method now takes mother_uids and infant_uids (not unborn_uids).
What to change: Update how you construct and interact with PostnatalNet.
# v3.0
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet()
# Pairs were added by Pregnancy with dur/start/end

# v3.1
postnatal = ss.PostnatalNet(dur=ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.5), std=ss.years(0.5)))
# Pairs are automatically added at delivery by Pregnancy



A new ss.BreastfeedingNet is available for modeling breastfeeding transmission. It automatically tracks breastfeeding status from the Pregnancy module. This is additive – no migration is required – but if you were previously using PostnatalNet to model breastfeeding transmission, consider switching.
# v3.1
sim = ss.Sim(
    demographics=ss.Pregnancy(),
    networks=[ss.PrenatalNet(), ss.BreastfeedingNet()],
    diseases=ss.SIR(),
)






Previously fecund was a BoolState that was manually set to True/False. It is now a read-only @property that dynamically computes fecundity based on age and sex.
What to change: Remove any code that sets fecund directly.
# v3.0
pregnancy.fecund[uids] = False  # Manually mark as infecund
pregnancy.fecund[uids] = True   # Manually mark as fecund

# v3.1
# fecund is now read-only, computed from age, sex, and min_age/max_age
# Use pregnancy.infertile to mark agents as unable to conceive
pregnancy.infertile[uids] = True



The postpartum BoolState and associated dur_postpartum / ti_postpartum states have been removed. Breastfeeding is now tracked separately.
What to change: Replace postpartum references with breastfeeding or use PostnatalNet with a dur parameter.
# v3.0
pregnancy.postpartum         # BoolState
pregnancy.dur_postpartum     # FloatArr
pregnancy.ti_postpartum      # FloatArr

# v3.1
pregnancy.breastfeeding      # BoolState (mothers currently breastfeeding)
pregnancy.dur_breastfeed     # FloatArr (duration of breastfeeding)
pregnancy.ti_stop_breastfeed # FloatArr (time breastfeeding stops)
pregnancy.breastfed          # BoolState (newborns who were breastfed)



The child_uid FloatArr has been removed. Unborn children are now found dynamically via people.parent.
What to change: Use pregnancy.find_unborn_children(parent_uids) instead.
# v3.0
child = pregnancy.child_uid[mother_uid]

# v3.1
children = pregnancy.find_unborn_children(mother_uids)



The method and associated distribution have been renamed.
What to change: Rename method calls and references.
# v3.0
p = pregnancy.make_p_fertility(eligible_uids)
pregnancy.pars.p_fertility  # Bernoulli distribution

# v3.1
p = pregnancy.make_p_conceive(eligible_uids)
pregnancy._p_conceive  # Bernoulli distribution (now private)



The semantics have been inverted and the name clarified. Despite its name, p_neonatal_death in v3.0 was only applied when a mother dies during pregnancy – it was the probability that the neonate also dies conditional on maternal death. It was never a general neonatal mortality parameter.
In v3.1, p_survive_maternal_death makes this conditional relationship explicit: it is the probability that an unborn child survives the mother’s death (default 0, meaning unborn children do not survive maternal death).
Note: Neither v3.0 nor v3.1 includes a built-in parameter for general neonatal mortality (e.g. from prematurity or birth complications). To model that, override the process_newborns() hook in a Pregnancy subclass.
What to change: Rename the parameter and invert the probability value.
# v3.0
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(p_neonatal_death=ss.bernoulli(0.8))  # 80% chance neonate dies given maternal death

# v3.1
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(p_survive_maternal_death=ss.bernoulli(0.2))  # 20% chance unborn survives maternal death



Previously, dur_pregnancy was a fixed value (default ss.years(0.75)). It is now an ss.choice distribution that draws from gestational weeks 32-42, and duration is assigned per-agent.
What to change: If you were relying on a fixed pregnancy duration or accessing self.pars.dur_pregnancy.years, update accordingly.
# v3.0
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(dur_pregnancy=ss.years(0.75))
# Internally: self.pars.dur_pregnancy.years was a single float

# v3.1
# Default draws from weeks 32-42; to override with a fixed duration:
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(dur_pregnancy=ss.choice(a=ss.weeks(np.arange(38, 43))))
# Per-agent durations are stored in: pregnancy.dur_pregnancy[uids]  (a FloatArr)



The set_prognoses() method has been removed. Its functionality is now split across make_pregnancies(), process_delivery(), and set_breastfeeding().
What to change: If you had a subclass that overrode set_prognoses(), move the logic to the appropriate new method.
# v3.0
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def set_prognoses(self, uids):
        super().set_prognoses(uids)
        # Custom logic for new pregnancies

# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def make_pregnancies(self, uids):
        embryo_counts = super().make_pregnancies(uids)
        # Custom logic for new pregnancies
        return embryo_counts



The step() method no longer delegates to do_step() and update_states(). The burn-in logic has also been moved from step() to init_post(). The new step() calls a sequence of smaller, overridable methods.
What to change: If you had a subclass that overrode do_step() or update_states(), restructure to override the new methods.
# v3.0 step flow
step() -> do_step() -> update_states() + make_pregnancies() + make_embryos()

# v3.1 step flow
init_post()           # Burn-in happens here now
step():
    updates_pre()           # Set base states, check breastfeeding
    progress_pregnancies()  # Advance gestational clock
    process_delivery()      # Handle births
    set_rel_sus()           # Update susceptibility
    select_conceivers()     # Find who conceives
    make_pregnancies()      # Set pregnancy states
    make_embryos()          # Create embryo agents
    update_maternal_deaths()# Handle maternal deaths
Use the _post_delivery() hook for custom post-delivery logic:
# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def _post_delivery(self, mother_uids, newborn_uids):
        # Custom post-delivery logic here
        pass



make_embryos() now returns a tuple (conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids) instead of just new_uids. The first element accounts for multiple embryos per pregnancy (e.g. twins).
What to change: Update any code that captures the return value.
# v3.0
new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids)

# v3.1
conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids, embryo_counts)



The old make_pregnancies() both selected who conceives and set prognoses. These are now separate: select_conceivers() returns UIDs of women who will conceive, and make_pregnancies() sets pregnancy states and durations for those UIDs.
What to change: If you overrode make_pregnancies() in a subclass, split the logic.
# v3.0
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def make_pregnancies(self):
        # Custom selection + prognosis logic

# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def select_conceivers(self, uids=None):
        # Custom selection logic
        return conceive_uids

    def make_pregnancies(self, uids):
        # Custom prognosis logic
        embryo_counts = super().make_pregnancies(uids)
        return embryo_counts



The following new parameters are available via PregnancyPars. No migration is required, but you may want to use them:








Parameter
Default
Description




p_infertile
ss.bernoulli(p=0)
Primary infertility probability


dur_breastfeed
ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.75), std=ss.years(0.5))
Breastfeeding duration


p_breastfeed
ss.bernoulli(p=1)
Probability of breastfeeding


embryos_per_pregnancy
ss.choice(a=[1,2], p=[1.0, 0.0])
Number of embryos (twins support)


rr_ptb
ss.normal(loc=1, scale=0.1)
Baseline relative risk of pre-term birth


rr_ptb_age
Age-dependent array
Relative risk of pre-term birth by age


p_survive_maternal_death
ss.bernoulli(0)
Probability unborn survives mother’s death


trimesters
[ss.weeks(13), ss.weeks(26)]
Trimester boundaries






The following results are now available. No migration is required.



Result
Description




maternal_deaths
Number of maternal deaths per timestep


mmr
Maternal mortality rate (per 100,000 births)


tfr
Total fertility rate


n_fecund
Number of fecund women


n_fertile
Number of fertile women


n_susceptible
Number of susceptible (non-pregnant fertile) women



Age-specific fertility rates are available via pregnancy.asfr (a 2D array, not a standard Result).

What to change: If you had a subclass that overrode do_step() or update_states(), restructure to override the new methods.
# v3.0 step flow
step() -> do_step() -> update_states() + make_pregnancies() + make_embryos()

# v3.1 step flow
init_post()           # Burn-in happens here now
step():
    updates_pre()           # Set base states, check breastfeeding
    progress_pregnancies()  # Advance gestational clock
    process_delivery()      # Handle births
    set_rel_sus()           # Update susceptibility
    select_conceivers()     # Find who conceives
    make_pregnancies()      # Set pregnancy states
    make_embryos()          # Create embryo agents
    update_maternal_deaths()# Handle maternal deaths
Use the _post_delivery() hook for custom post-delivery logic:
# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def _post_delivery(self, mother_uids, newborn_uids):
        # Custom post-delivery logic here
        pass



make_embryos() now returns a tuple (conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids) instead of just new_uids. The first element accounts for multiple embryos per pregnancy (e.g. twins).
What to change: Update any code that captures the return value.
# v3.0
new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids)

# v3.1
conceive_uids_with_repeats, new_uids = pregnancy.make_embryos(conceive_uids, embryo_counts)



The old make_pregnancies() both selected who conceives and set prognoses. These are now separate: select_conceivers() returns UIDs of women who will conceive, and make_pregnancies() sets pregnancy states and durations for those UIDs.
What to change: If you overrode make_pregnancies() in a subclass, split the logic.
# v3.0
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def make_pregnancies(self):
        # Custom selection + prognosis logic

# v3.1
class MyPregnancy(ss.Pregnancy):
    def select_conceivers(self, uids=None):
        # Custom selection logic
        return conceive_uids

    def make_pregnancies(self, uids):
        # Custom prognosis logic
        embryo_counts = super().make_pregnancies(uids)
        return embryo_counts



The following new parameters are available via PregnancyPars. No migration is required, but you may want to use them:








Parameter
Default
Description




p_infertile
ss.bernoulli(p=0)
Primary infertility probability


dur_breastfeed
ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.years(0.75), std=ss.years(0.5))
Breastfeeding duration


p_breastfeed
ss.bernoulli(p=1)
Probability of breastfeeding


embryos_per_pregnancy
ss.choice(a=[1,2], p=[1.0, 0.0])
Number of embryos (twins support)


rr_ptb
ss.normal(loc=1, scale=0.1)
Baseline relative risk of pre-term birth


rr_ptb_age
Age-dependent array
Relative risk of pre-term birth by age


p_survive_maternal_death
ss.bernoulli(0)
Probability unborn survives mother’s death


trimesters
[ss.weeks(13), ss.weeks(26)]
Trimester boundaries






The following results are now available. No migration is required.



Result
Description




maternal_deaths
Number of maternal deaths per timestep


mmr
Maternal mortality rate (per 100,000 births)


tfr
Total fertility rate


n_fecund
Number of fecund women


n_fertile
Number of fertile women


n_susceptible
Number of susceptible (non-pregnant fertile) women



Age-specific fertility rates are available via pregnancy.asfr (a 2D array, not a standard Result).

title: Starsim v3 to v4 migration guide
text:
Starsim 4 adds a way to write a disease as declared states and transitions, which can then be run as an ODE, as a stochastic compartmental model, or as agents. For a Starsim 3 model (custom ss.Infection subclasses with their own states and step methods, ss.MFNet and ss.RandomNet, ss.Births and ss.Deaths, custom interventions and connectors, and ss.Calibration), Starsim 4 is an upgrade rather than a switch: most of it still runs, and what is declared can then be described (sim.describe()), run as an ODE or a stochastic compartmental model when nothing in the sim needs agents, swept and compared with ss.parallel() and msim.diff(), and fitted with sim.fit(). This guide shows the same model in both, maps Starsim 3 code to Starsim 4 job by job, lists what changes meaning on the way, and ends with what works and what does not yet. It is written for both humans and LLMs.
Starsim 3 code is of two kinds, and they migrate differently:

Modules written as code (ss.Module, ss.Disease and ss.Infection subclasses (ss.Infection is now ss.AgentDisease, which the migration script renames) with define_states(), set_prognoses(), and step_state(), custom networks, ss.Intervention and ss.Analyzer subclasses, ss.Births, ss.Deaths, ss.RandomNet, and ss.MFNet, now ss.SexualNet) are still part of Starsim 4. They run unchanged, as agents, and can sit in the same sim as declared diseases. ss.Disease is the base of every disease, as in Starsim 3, whether it is declared, written as code, or both in one class; ss.Infection adds transmission written as code. Per-agent quantities that change continuously (a CD4 count, a level of immunity, time since an event) have no declared form, and keeping them as code is a supported choice.
Starsim 3 spellings that Starsim 4 replaces (the library ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR as code; ss.routine_vx, ss.campaign_vx, ss.routine_screening, ss.treat_num, and the products ss.Vx, ss.Dx, ss.Tx; ss.seasonality) have been removed, as have ss.Calibration with its components, and ss.Samples and ss.Dataset. Use the table of jobs below to port them.

The migration script makes the mechanical changes for you and lists, by file and line, what needs a person: python -m starsim.converters.migrate mymodel.py --check lists what it would change, and without --check it rewrites the files (or folders) in place. Read its diff afterwards. A removed name raises an AttributeError in Starsim 4; the table of jobs says what replaced it.
Note: If you are an LLM reading this, migrate one module at a time, run the model after each step, compare it with the Starsim 3 results (allowing for the changes in the next section), and confirm with the user before going on.



An SIS on a random network, as Starsim 3 wrote it, with the library disease written as code and a beta for each network:
import starsim as ss # Starsim 3

sis = ss.SIS(beta=dict(randomnet=0.05), dur_inf=ss.years(1), init_prev=0.01)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=sis, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=1/12)
sim.run()
In Starsim 4, the same disease is declared as states and transitions. Two things change meaning on the way (see What changes the numbers). A bare number in a Starsim 3 beta dict was a probability per step, so here it is written ss.prob(0.05, 'month'); copied as a bare number, it would be a rate per year, 12 times too low at monthly steps (item 3). And a duration in a declared transition is exponential with that mean, unless a distribution is given, while Starsim 3’s ss.SIS drew a lognormal dur_inf; dur=ss.lognormal(mean=ss.years(1)) keeps the old shape (item 5). Here the textbook exponential is used:
import starsim as ss

S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=dict(randomnet=ss.prob(0.05, 'month')) * I),
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, S, dur=ss.years(1)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=4), n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.months(1), verbose=0)
sim.run()
print('Infections:', round(sim.results.sis.infection.sum()))
sim.plot()
This gives 22,860 infections with the default seed, against Starsim 3’s 21,557 (two seeds differ by about 6%). The Starsim 3 model itself, run unchanged as ssl.AgentSIS, is in What works and what does not yet.



Most of the changes are mechanical, and a tool makes them: python -m starsim.converters.migrate rewrites Starsim 3 code for Starsim 4, in .py files and in the code cells of notebooks, Quarto, and Markdown files. It renames what was renamed (ss.MFNet is ss.SexualNet, ss.time_prob() is ss.probperyear(), the library’s modules are ssl.X), turns subclasses of Starsim 3’s ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR written as code into subclasses of ssl.AgentSIR and the like, rewrites a beta pair on a sexual network as a probability per act in each direction, and renames the results that count people in a state. Everything else it lists by file and line, as something for a person to check. Give --check to see what it would change without changing anything. For this Starsim 3 script, mymodel.py:
import starsim as ss

class MySIS(ss.SIS):
    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()

sis = MySIS(beta=dict(mf=[0.08, 0.04]), dur_inf=ss.years(1), init_prev=0.01)
net = ss.MFNet()
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=sis, networks=net, n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=1/12, verbose=-1)
sim.run()
print(sim.results.mysis.n_infected[-1])
it says:
python -m starsim.converters.migrate mymodel.py --check
mymodel.py: would change 6 line(s)
  0: added import starsim.library as ssl
  3: Starsim 3's ss.SIS, written as code, is ssl.AgentSIS (ss.SIS is now declared)
  7: a beta pair on ss.MFNet (now ss.SexualNet; [p1 to p2, p2 to p1], with men in p1) is ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...), a probability per act in each direction
  8: ss.MFNet is ss.SexualNet (between='mf' is its default)
  9: verbose=-1 ("brief") is verbose=0
  11: the count of a state is the result named after the state (e.g. results.alive, res.infected, results["sir.infected"])

6 change(s) in 1 file(s); 0 item(s) to do by hand
Without --check, it makes the changes in place (so run it on code that is under version control, and read the diff afterwards); give it folders to upgrade a whole package. What it can’t do mechanically, such as a beta given as a bare number that was a probability per step, is in the next section, and an AI assistant with Starsim’s migrate-starsim3 skill can work through the list it leaves.



Read this first: each of these changes results without an error.


In Starsim 4, each time point is a period: a step is taken from every time point, as in Starsim 3, and row ti of a result is the step from time point ti. A flow at ti (e.g. new_infections[ti], now infection[ti]) is the number during that step, as in Starsim 3. A stock (e.g. infected[ti]) is the number at its start, where Starsim 3 recorded it at the end of the step, in update_results(), but labeled it with the step’s start: Starsim 3’s infected[ti] was the number after step ti, which is Starsim 4’s infected[ti + 1]. So infected[0] is now the number at the start of the run, before any step, which Starsim 3 did not record, and the state after the last step is not recorded. The same script, with Starsim 3’s SIR (ssl.AgentSIR in Starsim 4; see 5), gives:
                  infected[:4]            new_infections[:2]
Starsim 3.7.2     53, 99, 186, 356        26, 46
Starsim 4         31, 64, 128, 240        33, 64
(ss.Sim(n_agents=3000, diseases=ss.SIR(beta=0.1), networks='random'), with ssl.AgentSIR(beta=0.1) in Starsim 4.) The counts of states are one index later, and the random draws differ after that, so results agree statistically (over several seeds), not number for number. For a model with yearly steps, the number infected in a row is the number on 1 January of that year, rather than on 31 December, while the infections in a row are still those during its year. To compare a stock with Starsim 3’s, compare Starsim 4’s x[1:] with Starsim 3’s x[:-1]. To reproduce published Starsim 3 numbers exactly, use pip install starsim==3.7.2.
With coarse steps, a model can also differ by more than one step. In Starsim 3, a person could pass through several states within one step (e.g. infected, then latent, then active, all in the same step), each taken for a whole step. In Starsim 4, people infected in a step are infected at its end, so they face the exits of the state they enter from the next step on (unless the exit is immediate, with no rate= or dur=), as in the compartmental solvers; someone moved by a rate during a step faces half a step of the rates out of the state they arrive in, so may move again in the same step (with agents by midsteps, the default; with solver=ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep'), from the next step). So with long steps, people wait longer in their first state after infection. For tbsim with dt=0.1 years, latent TB is 36% higher and active TB 13% higher than in Starsim 3; at dt=0.005 they agree. If results differ at a coarse step, check them at a smaller dt (sim.check_dt() says whether the step is too long for the model’s rates).
So an agent can still move more than once in a step: through two states by rates, or out of a state by a rate and then infected again by the step’s transmission (e.g. asymptomatic, then recovered, then reinfected). Comparing each agent’s state at the end of one step with the next therefore misses some moves (about 1% of infections in tbsim at monthly steps). For flows, read the results of the transitions, which count every move (sim.results.tb.infection, by group with .by()), or, for who was infected, the infection log (disease.infection_log.to_df(ti=self.ti) in an analyzer; see Analyzers), rather than differences of states.
In a module written as code, split update_results() into record_states(), called at the start of each step, before any module steps, for the results that are the state then (a count of a state, a mean level), and record_events(), called at the end of the step, after the deaths, for those about what happened in it (doses, births, new cases). A class that still defines update_results() raises a TypeError when it is created, saying so. A result that needs both (births over the people alive) goes in record_events(), reading the stock from its result (self.sim.results.alive[self.ti]), or in finalize_results():
# Starsim 3
def update_results(self):
    super().update_results()
    self.results.n_on_art[self.ti] = self.on_art.sum()
    self.results.new_doses[self.ti] = self.n_doses

# Starsim 4
def record_states(self): # At the start of the step
    super().record_states()
    self.results.n_on_art[self.ti] = self.on_art.sum()

def record_events(self): # At the end of the step
    super().record_events()
    self.results.new_doses[self.ti] = self.n_doses
Code that reads a stock during a step now reads the step’s own row: sim.results.sir.I[sim.ti] is the number infectious at the start of this step, which in Starsim 3 was [sim.ti - 1], the end of the last step. A flow of this step is not known until it ends, so [sim.ti - 1] of a flow is still the last step’s.



During the step from time point k to k+1, sim.ti (and self.ti) is k in every module and every phase, from record_states() and step() to record_events() and the analyzers, and self.now is time point k, the time the step starts, at which it reads inputs that change in time, as in Starsim 3. The first step is ti == 0, as in Starsim 3, so code that does something if self.ti == 0 in step() still does it in the first step, and self.results.x[self.ti] = v is right wherever it is written. An analyzer runs at the end of each step, as in Starsim 3; the people it sees are as at the next time point.
A declared disease’s ti_<state> is the index of the step in which each person entered the state (a move is taken at the start of its step, and an infection happens by its end); its clocks (dis.P.time_in) are right, and for how long people stayed in a state, use dis.P.stays.
A disease written as code dates its initial infections by the step before the first (self.ti is -1 while ss.AgentDisease.init_post() calls set_prognoses() for them), as a declared disease dates its seeds, where Starsim 3 dated them by the first step. So in a Starsim 3 disease that schedules recovery at self.ti + dur and takes it when ti_recovered <= self.ti, the seeds are infectious for one step less than in Starsim 3, as long as later cases are. Both are about half a step short of dur on average; to give every case dur steps on average, as a declared disease does, schedule from the step after the infection, since an infection happens at the end of its step, and round as the engine does: ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'), self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + dur, and self.ti_recovered.due() (see ss.Infection; ssl.AgentSIR and the others do this).



In Starsim 3, beta=0.05 is a rate per year, but beta={'randomnet': 0.05} is a probability per step, used as it is. In Starsim 4 both are rates per unit time, so a dict copied verbatim is too low by a factor of about 1/dt: 12 times at monthly steps, 52 times at weekly ones (5 infections instead of 22,000 in an SIS on a random network at monthly steps). Give each value its Starsim 3 meaning explicitly:







Starsim 3 (monthly steps)
Starsim 4




beta={'randomnet': 0.05}
beta={'randomnet': ss.prob(0.05, 'month')}


beta={'mf': [0.008, 0.004]}
beta={'sexual': ss.peract(m2f=0.008, f2m=0.004)}



Use ss.prob(..., 'week') or ss.prob(..., 'day') for weekly or daily steps. Starsim 4 does not warn about a dict of bare numbers; the migration script flags each one, but cannot know your step, so change them by hand.
