Repeat the comparison of contacts per person with a rate of infection of 0.083 per contact per day (so R0 is about 2 with random mixing). How much does it matter now that people meet the same contacts every day, and why?
With a rate of infection of 0.083 per contact per day and 3 contacts a day, R0 is about 0.083 × 3 × 8 ≈ 2 with random mixing:

import starsim.library as ssl

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.083*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
disease = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001, name='disease')

pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(200))
sims = {
    'Well mixed':              ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'New contacts each day':   ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3), **pars),
    'Same contacts every day': ss.Sim(disease, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=3, dynamic=False), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('disease.I')
msim.summarize().loc['disease_infection']

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (Well mixed, New contacts each day, Same contacts every day)
  Done in 0.88 s
















value


scenario





Well mixed
7,916


New contacts each day
7,551


Same contacts every day
836







Now it matters a great deal: with random mixing, most people are infected, but with the same 3 contacts every day, far fewer (how many varies a lot from one run to the next, since the outbreak can stall early or find its way through). Over a contact that lasts for the whole infectious period, the chance of passing the infection on is only about 1 − e^(−0.083 × 8) ≈ 50%, and one of each person’s 3 contacts is usually the person who infected them, so each case infects on average not much more than one new person. Measles passes along nearly every link, so for measles the network changed the timing but not the size of the outbreak.

title: Solutions: T4 – Mixing
text:
Exercise 5
In the sexual network with partnerships that last a year, the infection dies out. Give the network n_contacts=1 and concurrency=0.2, so that 20% of people have more than one partner at a time. Does the infection persist?

S, I = ss.states('S I')
infection = S >> I @ ss.peract(m2f=0.1, f2m=0.05)*I
recovery  = I >> S @ ss.months(6)
sti = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.05)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start=2000, stop=2030, dt=ss.months(1))
sims = {
    'One partner at a time': ss.Sim(sti, networks=ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(1)), **pars),
    '20% with more than one': ss.Sim(sti, networks=ss.SexualNet(dur=ss.years(1), n_contacts=1, concurrency=0.2), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('sti.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (One partner at a time, 20% with more than one)
  Done in 1.9 s









Yes: with 20% of people having more than one partner at a time, the infection persists. Someone with two partners can pass the infection from one partnership to the other without waiting for either to end, which is why concurrency matters so much for sexually transmitted infections.

title: Solutions: T4 – Mixing
text:
Exercise 6
Add households of about 4 people (ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(4)), after import starsim.library as ssl) to measles with a community mixing pool of 2 contacts a day. How much of the epidemic do households add?

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.19*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

households = ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(4))
pars = dict(n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(100))
sims = {
    'Community only': ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=2), **pars),
    'Households and community': ss.Sim(measles, networks=[households, ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=2)], **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Community only, Households and community)
  Done in 0.46 s
















value


scenario





Community only
9,423


Households and community
9,945







The community alone gives an R0 of 0.19 × 2 × 8 ≈ 3, and infects most people. Households make the epidemic faster and infect nearly everyone, but they add less than their number of contacts suggests: once one person in a household is infected, the others are soon infected too, so most household contacts after that are wasted.

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
🧠9% 🤖91%
This tutorial goes through the SIR model of Tutorial 1 in more depth, to answer a question that matters for any outbreak: what decides how many people are infected?
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
What the model says
This is the model from Tutorial 1: measles in a town of 100,000 people, with β = 1.9 per day and an infectious period of 8 days.

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0036 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6









States. ss.states('S I R') makes three states: the compartments (or, as agents, a label each person carries). People start in the first state, S, unless put elsewhere.
Transitions. S >> I @ rate moves people from S to I at a per capita rate: the rate for each person in S. For an infection, this is the force of infection, λ = β I / N, which is what 1.9*I says, since a state in a rate is the fraction of people in it. Times S, it gives β S I / N infections a day. Because I is in the rate, Starsim knows the transition is a transmission, and that I is infectious.
This is frequency-dependent transmission: what matters is the fraction infectious, so a larger town has more infections but not a faster epidemic. For density-dependent transmission (as for some diseases of animals), write the number infectious, beta*I.n, so that β is per infectious person and R0 grows with the population. Diseases has these and the other ways to write a rate, such as the whole flow, S >> I @ 1.9*S*I/N, as many textbooks write it.
Durations. I >> R @ ss.days(8) gives a duration instead of a rate: 8 days in I on average, or a recovery rate of 1/8 per day, exponentially distributed as in the standard SIR model (Tutorial 3 shows other distributions).
The disease. ss.Disease puts the transitions together, with how the outbreak starts. It is named measles after its variable, as the transitions (infection, recovery) are, which names their results.

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
How the outbreak starts
There are three ways to say who starts where:



Argument
Meaning




init_prev=0.001
0.1% of people start infected (the initial prevalence), in the state that an infection leads to: I here, but E in a model with a latent period (Tutorial 3)


init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9)
The fraction of people who start in each state, for any states


init_n=dict(I=10)
The number of people who start in each state



Naming the state (init or init_n) makes clear whether those introduced are already infectious. S, I, R = ss.states(S=0.099, I=0.001, R=0.9) is the same as init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9).
Most people are immune to measles, by vaccination or earlier infection. Suppose 90% of the town is immune. To compare with a town where nobody is, run both for a year with ss.parallel():

PythonRExplicit



measles_immune = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.9), name='measles') # Named measles too, so the two runs' results can be compared
nobody = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365))
immune = ss.Sim(measles_immune, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365))
msim = ss.parallel({'Nobody immune': nobody, '90% immune': immune})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Nobody immune, 90% immune)
  Done in 0.24 s











library(starsim)

states("S I R")
infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I)
recovery  <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))
measles <- Disease(infection = infection, recovery = recovery, init_prev = 0.001)
measles_immune <- Disease(infection = infection, recovery = recovery, init = list(I = 0.001, R = 0.9), name = "measles")

nobody <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(365))
immune <- Sim(measles_immune, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(365))
msim <- parallel(list("Nobody immune" = nobody, "90% immune" = immune))
msim$plot("measles.I")



S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
infection_explicit = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection')
recovery_explicit  = ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery')
transitions = [infection_explicit, recovery_explicit]
nobody_immune = ss.Disease(transitions=transitions, init=dict(S=0.999, I=0.001), name='measles')        # The fraction of people in each state at the start
some_immune   = ss.Disease(transitions=transitions, init=dict(S=0.099, I=0.001, R=0.9), name='measles')

settings = dict(networks=ss.contacts(1), total_pop=100_000, start=ss.days(0), stop=ss.days(365), dt=ss.days(1), unit='day', solver='ode')
msim_explicit = ss.parallel({
    'Nobody immune': ss.Sim(diseases=nobody_immune, **settings),
    '90% immune':    ss.Sim(diseases=some_immune, **settings),
})
msim_explicit.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Nobody immune, 90% immune)
  Done in 0.26 s












With 10% susceptible, each infectious person infects 15 × 0.1 ≈ 1.5 others: the reproduction number at the start, which the run prints after R0 (R = 1.51 at the start, with 10% susceptible). R0, for a fully susceptible population, is still 15.2. The outbreak grows slowly, peaking at about 700 infectious rather than 74,000, and infects about 6,000 people rather than almost everyone. An outbreak grows only when the reproduction number is above 1, so to stop measles, more than 1 − 1/R0 ≈ 93% of people must be immune: the herd immunity threshold. Try R=0.95 to see an outbreak die out.

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
Changing parameters
Starsim takes a disease’s parameters from its transitions: beta from the rate of infection, and dur_I (the mean time in I) from the duration of recovery:

measles.pars

Pars(init_prev=par(0.001), beta=par(1.9), dur_I=par(days(8)))


To run with another value, give the sim pars= by name; this changes that sim only, not measles (sim.new(pars=dict(beta=0.5)) does the same from an existing sim). Here are four values of β over a year. ss.parallel() runs the sims and plots them together, as running and plotting each in turn would:

PythonRExplicit



sims = {}
for beta in [0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.9]:
    sims['beta = ' + str(beta)] = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=beta), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365))
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 4 runs of 4 scenarios (beta = 0.15, beta = 0.25, beta = 0.5, beta = 1.9)
  Done in 0.27 s











sims <- list()
for (beta in c(0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.9)) {
  sims[[paste("beta =", beta)]] <- Sim(measles, pars = list(beta = beta), total_pop = 100000, stop = days(365))
}
msim <- parallel(sims)
msim$plot("measles.I")



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

for beta in [0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.9]:
    one = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=beta), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    one.run()
    plt.plot(one.timevec, one.results.measles.I, label='beta = ' + str(beta))
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Number infectious')
plt.legend();











The lower β, the later and lower the peak. For the fraction infected in the end, read each run’s R0 and number recovered (msim.sims has the sims, in order):

for sim in msim.sims:
    R0 = sim.diseases.measles.R0()
    frac = sim.results.measles.R[-1] / 100_000
    print(sim.label, ' R0 =', round(R0, 1), ' fraction infected =', round(frac, 2))

beta = 0.15  R0 = 1.2  fraction infected = 0.31
beta = 0.25  R0 = 2.0  fraction infected = 0.8
beta = 0.5  R0 = 4.0  fraction infected = 0.98
beta = 1.9  R0 = 15.2  fraction infected = 1.0


The fraction infected rises steeply with R0, then levels off: 80% at an R0 of 2, almost everyone above 4. This is the classic final size relation of an SIR model, z = 1 − exp(−R0 z), for a fraction z infected. Above an R0 of about 5 the final size hardly changes, which is why measles infects almost everyone where nobody is immune. So the answer to this tutorial’s question is R0, and how many people are immune to begin with. β and the infectious period matter only through R0; they decide how fast the outbreak happens, not how big it is.
Tutorial 3 shows how to name parameters yourself, with a range of plausible values for calibration. See also Parameters in the user guide.

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
Results
A run’s results are in sim.results, by module:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
res = sim.results.measles
res

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0017 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


Results(Disease)
0. timevec: array(start=0.0, stop=50.0)
1. S: Result(min=0.0262561, mean=8620.66, max=99900)

There are two kinds of result:

A state (S, I, R) is the number of people in it at each time point (the prevalence, as a count).
A transition (infection, recovery) is the number who made it in each step: a flow. infection is the daily incidence.

Each result is a time series:

print('Peak number infectious:', round(res.I.max()))
print('Total infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('Recovered by the end:', round(res.R[-1]))

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
Time
Units. Every run has a unit of time, here a day, taken from the typed values in the model (ss.days(8)). A bare number, such as β = 1.9, is in the same unit: 1.9 per day, the same as ss.perday(1.9) (and nearly ss.perweek(13.3)). Durations can be in any unit (ss.days(), ss.weeks(), ss.months(), ss.years()), converted to the model’s.
If a model mixes units, such as days and years (Tutorial 3), give its bare numbers units (ss.perday(1.9)), or give the sim its unit (ss.Sim(..., unit='day')); Time has the rules.
Start and stop. stop=ss.days(50) runs from day 0 to day 50 (as does dur=ss.days(50)). A run can also start and stop on dates:

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-02-20')
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-02-20
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0023 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on 2025-01-07









Steps. A run moves in steps, dt, by default one of the unit (a day). Agents move once per step, so for agents, a step that is too long changes the results, as Tutorial 1 showed; Solvers shows how to check. See Time in the user guide for more.

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
Saving and loading
sim.save() saves a sim, and ss.load() loads it:

sim.save('my-measles.sim')
sim2 = ss.load('my-measles.sim')

By default, this keeps the model and results but leaves out the people, so the file is small; shrink=False saves everything, e.g. to continue a run later. To use the results elsewhere, save them as a table:

df = sim.to_df()
df.to_csv('my-measles.csv')

title: T2 – Building a model
text:
Exercises

A town of 2,000 people has had no measles for many years, and 70% of its people are immune. Five people arrive with measles. Using init and init_n, model the outbreak over a year. How many people are infected? Is the reproduction number at the start above or below 1?
Using the final size relation, a model with R0 = 1.5 should infect about 58% of people. Choose β to give R0 = 1.5 with an infectious period of 8 days, run the model for long enough for the outbreak to end, and check.
Change the model to density-dependent transmission (I.n), choosing β so that R0 is still 15 in a town of 100,000. Then run it in a town of 10,000 and of 1,000,000. How does the outbreak change with the size of the town, and how does this differ from the frequency-dependent model?

Solutions · Next: T3 – Building a disease

title: T7 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
Who is the outbreak in, and does it make other infections worse?
T4 split the model by age, but other differences matter too. This tutorial has two parts, each starting from a model of its own:
By the end, you will be able to:

title: T7 – Stratification and co-transmission
section: Part 1: several ways of grouping people
text:
Part 1: several ways of grouping people

The starting point
This is the SEIR model of measles from T5 – Interventions and scenarios: 100,000 people in three age groups, mixing by a contact matrix, with 10 infectious on 1 January. In T5, immunity started in R; here it comes from vaccination, so nobody starts immune. A function makes a new copy of the model for each section:

PythonR



import starsim as ss

def make_measles():
    """ The SEIR model of measles, by age, with nobody immune yet """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I       # β = 0.14 per contact per day
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
    return measles

age_contacts = [[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]] # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')



library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
infection   <- Transition(S, E, rate = 0.14 * I) # β = 0.14 per contact per day
progression <- Transition(E, I, dur = days(10))  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    <- Transition(I, R, dur = days(8))   # Infectious for 8 days on average

make_measles <- function() { # The SEIR model of measles, by age, with nobody immune yet
  measles <- Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init_n = list(I = 10), name = "measles")
  measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
  measles
}

age_contacts <- rbind(c(10, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3)) # Contacts a day, between age groups
make_sim <- function(measles, ...) { # A sim of 100,000 people for a year, with any other settings given
  Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", ...)
}





Vaccination status
To give the population its immunity, stratify by vaccination status. Two doses of measles vaccine protect about 97% of people. Here this is modeled as the vaccinated being 97% less susceptible: everyone vaccinated has 3% of the usual susceptibility (a “leaky” effect), rather than 97% of them being fully protected and 3% not at all (“all or nothing”; see Products). Unlike a vaccination campaign on a date (T5), a dimension gives the immunity a population already has, and splits results by vaccination status.
Coverage often differs by age: here 85% of children, 92% of adults aged 15 to 64, and 95% of people 65 and over. A fraction that differs by another dimension is an ss.by() over both: a row for each age group and a column for each level of vaccination, each row adding up to 1, so each age group keeps its size. Written out, it is a table with a row for each combination:

PythonRExplicit



coverage_by_age = ss.by([[0.15, 0.85],  # 0-14: 15% unvaccinated, 85% vaccinated
                         [0.08, 0.92],  # 15-64
                         [0.05, 0.95]], # 65+
                        dims=['age', 'vaccinated'])



coverage_by_age <- ss$by(rbind(c(0.15, 0.85),  # 0-14: 15% unvaccinated, 85% vaccinated
                               c(0.08, 0.92),  # 15-64
                               c(0.05, 0.95)), # 65+
                         dims = c("age", "vaccinated"))



import pandas as pd

coverage_table = pd.DataFrame(dict(
    age        = ['0-14', '0-14', '15-64', '15-64', '65+', '65+'],
    vaccinated = [False, True, False, True, False, True],
    value      = [0.15, 0.85, 0.08, 0.92, 0.05, 0.95],
))
coverage_by_age = ss.by(coverage_table)




ss.levels() gives the levels of the new dimension with their options: the fractions, and the states the dimension applies to (here only S; see below). ss.modify() then changes a quantity of the disease by level: rel_sus, the relative susceptibility, is 1 for the unvaccinated and 0.03 for the vaccinated:

PythonR



measles = make_measles()
measles.stratify(vaccinated=ss.levels([False, True], fractions=coverage_by_age, states=['S']))
protection = ss.modify('measles.rel_sus', multiply=ss.by(vaccinated=[1, 0.03])) # The vaccinated are 3% as susceptible

sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=age_contacts), connectors=protection, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('vaccinated').plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 2.33, with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0062 s; measles: 15,155 infections; at most 1,301 infectious, on 2025-05-12











measles <- make_measles()
measles$stratify(vaccinated = ss$levels(c(FALSE, TRUE), fractions = coverage_by_age, states = list("S")))
protection <- modify("measles.rel_sus", multiply = ss$by(vaccinated = c(1, 0.03))) # The vaccinated are 3% as susceptible

sim <- make_sim(measles, networks = contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = age_contacts), connectors = protection)
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$infection$by("vaccinated")$plot()



The run prints an R0 of about 2.3, not 16: R0 here is worked out for the whole population, vaccinated included, and most of it is protected. Who is infected?

PythonR



res = sim.results.measles
print('Infections:', round(res.infection.sum()))
print('Among the vaccinated:', round(res.infection.select(vaccinated=True).sum()))
print('Among unvaccinated children:', round(res.infection.select(vaccinated=False, age='0-14').sum()))

Infections: 15155
Among the vaccinated: 6242
Among unvaccinated children: 4362




res <- sim$results$measles
cat("Infections:", round(res$infection$sum()), "\n")
cat("Among the vaccinated:", round(res$infection$select(vaccinated = TRUE)$sum()), "\n")
cat("Among unvaccinated children:", round(res$infection$select(vaccinated = FALSE, age = "0-14")$sum()), "\n")



About two in five of those infected are vaccinated, since there are so many more of them. This is common in real outbreaks, and doesn’t mean the vaccine is failing: each vaccinated person is still far less likely to be infected.
states=['S'] splits only S by vaccination: this is partial stratification. Once infected, a vaccinated person is like anyone else in this model, so splitting E, I, and R would only add compartments that behave the same. So results by vaccination count only S and the flows out of it: res.infection.by('vaccinated') says who was infected, but res.I.by('vaccinated') raises an error. A dimension that people mix by can’t be partial, since everyone needs a level of it to mix as. See Stratification for more.


An under-vaccinated community
Overall coverage says little if the unvaccinated are clustered. Suppose 5% of the town belong to a close-knit community in which 60% are vaccinated (at every age), against 98% of everyone else. Overall, 96% are vaccinated; with their susceptibility 97% lower, it is as if about 93% were immune, close to the 94% needed to stop measles spreading (1 − 1/16). Community members make 70% of their contacts with each other and 30% with the rest of the town.
This is a new dimension, community, with coverage now given by community rather than by age:

PythonR



coverage_by_community = ss.by([[0.02, 0.98],  # General: 2% unvaccinated, 98% vaccinated
                               [0.40, 0.60]], # Close-knit community
                              dims=['community', 'vaccinated'])

def make_community_measles():
    """ The measles model, by age, community, and vaccination """
    measles = make_measles()
    measles.stratify(community={'general': 0.95, 'close-knit': 0.05})
    measles.stratify(vaccinated=ss.levels([False, True], fractions=coverage_by_community, states=['S']))
    return measles



coverage_by_community <- ss$by(rbind(c(0.02, 0.98),  # General: 2% unvaccinated, 98% vaccinated
                                     c(0.40, 0.60)), # Close-knit community
                               dims = c("community", "vaccinated"))

make_community_measles <- function() { # The measles model, by age, community, and vaccination
  measles <- make_measles()
  measles$stratify(community = list("general" = 0.95, "close-knit" = 0.05))
  measles$stratify(vaccinated = ss$levels(c(FALSE, TRUE), fractions = coverage_by_community, states = list("S")))
  measles
}



Contacts are now between groups of two dimensions. With a matrix for each, the contacts between two groups are the product of their entries: a child in the community has 10 contacts a day with children, 70% of them within the community, so 7. To see what the clustering does, compare it with the community mixing like everyone else, with the same coverage:

PythonR



clustered = ss.contacts(age=age_contacts, community=[[0.984, 0.016], [0.3, 0.7]], ages=[0, 15, 65]) # The rest of the town makes 1.6% of its contacts with the community, so that the contacts each way add up
mixed     = ss.contacts(age=age_contacts, community=[[0.95, 0.05], [0.95, 0.05]], ages=[0, 15, 65])

sims = {
    'Mixing with everyone': ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), networks=mixed, connectors=protection, **settings),
    'Close-knit':           ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), networks=clustered, connectors=protection, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.infection')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Mixing with everyone, Close-knit)
  Done in 0.32 s











clustered <- contacts(age = age_contacts, community = rbind(c(0.984, 0.016), c(0.3, 0.7)), ages = c(0, 15, 65)) # The rest of the town makes 1.6% of its contacts with the community, so that the contacts each way add up
mixed     <- contacts(age = age_contacts, community = rbind(c(0.95, 0.05), c(0.95, 0.05)), ages = c(0, 15, 65))

msim <- parallel(list(
  "Mixing with everyone" = make_sim(make_community_measles(), networks = mixed, connectors = protection),
  "Close-knit"           = make_sim(make_community_measles(), networks = clustered, connectors = protection)
))
msim$plot("measles.infection")



Mixed with everyone, unvaccinated community members are surrounded mostly by vaccinated people, and the outbreak smolders. Clustered, the community has a reproduction number of about 7 within itself, against about 0.8 in the rest of the town, so it has an explosive outbreak within weeks, which spills over into the town. select() picks out any combination of groups, summing over the dimensions not named:

PythonR



for sim in msim.sims:
    res = sim.results.measles
    print(sim.label, '- in the community:', round(res.infection.select(community='close-knit').sum()), '- elsewhere:', round(res.infection.select(community='general').sum()))
msim.sims['Close-knit'].results.measles.I.by('community').plot()

Mixing with everyone - in the community: 118 - elsewhere: 270
Close-knit - in the community: 2420 - elsewhere: 1720











for (sim in msim$sims) {
  res <- sim$results$measles
  cat(sim$label, "- in the community:", round(res$infection$select(community = "close-knit")$sum()), "- elsewhere:", round(res$infection$select(community = "general")$sum()), "\n")
}
msim$sims[["Close-knit"]]$results$measles$I$by("community")$plot()



With clustering, there are about ten times as many infections, and the community, 5% of the town, has more than half. A model that averaged coverage over the town would miss this, and with it where vaccination would do the most good.


Moving between groups
So far, nobody changes group. ss.transfer() moves people from one level of a dimension to another at a rate, without changing their disease state. Suppose an outreach program offers catch-up vaccination to unvaccinated community members at a rate of 2 a year (reaching about 85% within a year, if measles doesn’t first), and nobody outside it. A transfer is given to the stratify() call of the dimension it moves people along, by name:

PythonR



catchup = ss.transfer(dict(vaccinated=True), rate=ss.peryear(ss.by(community=[0, 2])), states=['S']) # To vaccinated, at a rate of 0 a year outside the community and 2 in it

measles = make_measles()
measles.stratify(community={'general': 0.95, 'close-knit': 0.05})
measles.stratify(vaccinated=ss.levels([False, True], fractions=coverage_by_community, states=['S']), catchup=catchup)

sims = {
    'No catch-up': ss.Sim(make_community_measles(), networks=clustered, connectors=protection, **settings),
    'Catch-up':    ss.Sim(measles, networks=clustered, connectors=protection, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.infection')
print('Doses given:', round(msim.sims['Catch-up'].results.measles.catchup.sum()))
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No catch-up, Catch-up)
  Done in 0.31 s









Doses given: 606









value


scenario





No catch-up
4,140


Catch-up
3,125









catchup <- ss$transfer(list(vaccinated = TRUE), rate = peryear(ss$by(community = c(0, 2))), states = list("S")) # To vaccinated, at a rate of 0 a year outside the community and 2 in it

measles <- make_measles()
measles$stratify(community = list("general" = 0.95, "close-knit" = 0.05))
measles$stratify(vaccinated = ss$levels(c(FALSE, TRUE), fractions = coverage_by_community, states = list("S")), catchup = catchup)

msim <- parallel(list(
  "No catch-up" = make_sim(make_community_measles(), networks = clustered, connectors = protection),
  "Catch-up"    = make_sim(measles, networks = clustered, connectors = protection)
))
msim$plot("measles.infection")
cat("Doses given:", round(msim$sims[["Catch-up"]]$results$measles$catchup$sum()), "\n")
msim$summarize()$loc["measles_infection"]



A transfer is a transition, so it has a result by its name (catchup). About 600 doses prevent about 1,000 infections, nearly two per dose, since each is given where the outbreak is. Three kinds of movement between groups are easy to confuse:



Movement
What it is
How it is given




A transfer
People move steadily, at a rate (catch-up or routine vaccination, migration, a change of risk group)
ss.transfer(), in stratify()


A delivery
People move at given times, with a coverage (a vaccination campaign)
ss.vaccinate() or ss.Event(...), as an intervention (T5)


Aging
People move up the age groups as they get older
Automatic, when people are born or die



Dimensions multiply: here S has 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 compartments, and E, I, and R 6 each. sim.describe() lists each dimension, its levels, and the states it applies to. Stratification works the same as agents (see T1): each agent has a level of each dimension, and transfers change it.

title: T7 – Stratification and co-transmission
text:
Part 2: two diseases that interact

The starting point
Measles damages the immune system’s memory of other infections. For two to three years after recovering, children are more likely to fall ill from other infections (“immune amnesia”), so a measles outbreak leaves a wake of other infections. Modeling this needs a second disease that interacts with measles.
This part starts again from the measles model of T5, with immunity in R by age, and no vaccination dimension. Measles needs one new state, to remember who has had it recently: in a compartmental model, what a person has been through has to be a state. Recovery now leads to A (recovered, with amnesia), and people leave A for R after two years on average.
The second disease is pneumococcus, a bacterium many children carry in the nose and throat for a few weeks at a time, and a leading cause of pneumonia. It is an SIS model: people acquire it (S to C, for carrying) from carriers, and clear it after a month on average. About a quarter of children and a sixth of adults carry it at any time, so it starts there.
The run is three years long, to show the wake. The durations are in days and years, so unit='day' says that the bare values of β are per day (see Time):

PythonR



import starsim as ss

ages = {0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1} # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2028-01-01', unit='day')

S, E, I, A, R = ss.states('S E I A R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I       # β = 0.14 per contact per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> A @ ss.days(8)   # Recovered, with immune amnesia
restored    = A >> R @ ss.years(2)  # Immune memory of other infections restored after 2 years on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, restored,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The fraction immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age=ages)

S, C = ss.states('S C')
acquisition = S >> C @ 0.003*C     # Acquired through contact with carriers, at a rate of 0.003 per contact per day
clearance   = C >> S @ ss.days(30) # Carried for a month on average
pneumococcus = ss.Disease(acquisition, clearance,
    init = dict(C=ss.by(age=[0.25, 0.17, 0.17])), # The fraction carrying it in each age group
    name = 'pneumococcus',
)
pneumococcus.stratify(age=ages)
measles.diagram()










library(starsim)

ages <- list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+
age_contacts <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(10, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3))) # Contacts a day, between age groups
make_sim <- function(...) { # 100,000 people for three years, with any other settings given
  Sim(networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2028-01-01", unit = "day", ...)
}

states("S E I A R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = Transition(S, E, rate = 0.14 * I), # β = 0.14 per contact per day
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)),  # Latent for 10 days on average
  recovery    = Transition(I, A, dur = days(8)),   # Recovered, with immune amnesia
  restored    = Transition(A, R, dur = years(2)),  # Immune memory of other infections restored after 2 years on average
  init   = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))), # The fraction immune in each age group
  init_n = list(I = 10),
  name   = "measles"
)
measles$stratify(age = ages)

states("S C")
pneumococcus <- Disease(
  acquisition = Transition(S, C, rate = 0.003 * C), # Acquired through contact with carriers, at a rate of 0.003 per contact per day
  clearance   = Transition(C, S, dur = days(30)),   # Carried for a month on average
  init = list(C = ss$by(age = c(0.25, 0.17, 0.17))), # The fraction carrying it in each age group
  name = "pneumococcus"
)
pneumococcus$stratify(age = ages)
measles$diagram()





An interaction
ss.modify() changes a quantity for the people a condition selects. Each disease has a relative susceptibility (rel_sus) and transmissibility (rel_trans), both 1 to begin with, so an interaction is a change to one of these for people in some state of the other disease. Here, people with measles or amnesia are twice as likely to acquire pneumococcus (an illustrative value):

PythonR



amnesia = ss.modify(pneumococcus.rel_sus, multiply=2, who=measles.I | measles.A)



amnesia <- modify(pneumococcus$rel_sus, multiply = 2, who = measles$I | measles$A)



It reads as a sentence: for people infectious with measles or with amnesia, multiply their susceptibility to pneumococcus by 2. The condition is evaluated as the sim runs, so it stops applying when people reach R, and the modifier never overwrites rel_sus, so nothing needs restoring. Interactions that are part of the biology go in connectors=. Run the two diseases with and without it:

PythonR



sims = {
    'Independent': ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], **settings),
    'Interacting': ss.Sim([measles, pneumococcus], connectors=amnesia, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['measles.I', 'pneumococcus.C'])
msim.summarize().loc['pneumococcus_acquisition']

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Independent, Interacting)

msim <- parallel(list(
  "Independent" = make_sim(diseases = list(measles, pneumococcus)),
  "Interacting" = make_sim(diseases = list(measles, pneumococcus), connectors = amnesia)
))
msim$plot(c("measles.I", "pneumococcus.C"))
msim$summarize()$loc["pneumococcus_acquisition"]



The measles outbreak is the same in both, since pneumococcus doesn’t affect it. With the interaction, pneumococcus carriers rise by about a fifth over the outbreak’s year, and stay high for years after, as people with amnesia slowly recover. The effect is larger than the 9% who had measles would suggest: they carry pneumococcus more often, and pass it to more people, including people who never had measles. Since some carriers develop pneumonia, a measles outbreak would cause more pneumonia for years.


Diseases tracked jointly
With the interaction, a compartmental model of pneumococcus needs to know how many of the people susceptible to it have measles amnesia, which separate compartments for each disease can’t say. So Starsim tracks linked diseases jointly, with a compartment for each combination of their states (S and S, A and C, and so on). describe() shows this:

Exercises

In the community model, raise coverage in the community from 60% to 80%. How many fewer infections are there in the rest of the town, where coverage hasn’t changed? Why?
Give the same number of catch-up doses (about 600) to unvaccinated people outside the community instead, using a transfer whose rate is 0 in the community. How many infections do they prevent, compared with the doses given in the community?

title: Solutions: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
Fitting (exercises 1–3)
Exercises 1 to 3 start from the model fitted in the tutorial:

import pandas as pd
import starsim as ss

def make_measles(prior=True):
    """ The model of the tutorial, with or without the prior on the fraction reported """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])
    reported = ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.05, 1], prior=ss.beta_dist(mean=0.35, std=0.1) if prior else None)
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    cases       = ss.outcome(reported*infection)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
        init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
        init_n = dict(I=10),
        name = 'measles',
    )
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

measles = make_measles()
contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-09-01', verbose=0)
data = pd.read_csv('data/measles_cases.csv')

1. Different starting guesses.

for guess in [dict(beta=0.14, reported=0.5), dict(beta=0.3, reported=0.2)]:
    fit = ss.Sim(measles, pars=guess, data=data, **settings).fit(verbose=False)
    print('Starting from', guess, '- beta:', round(fit.pars.beta, 3), '- reported:', round(fit.pars.reported, 3), '- objective:', round(fit.objective, 4))

Starting from {'beta': 0.14, 'reported': 0.5} - beta: 0.169 - reported: 0.256 - objective: 0.1684
Starting from {'beta': 0.3, 'reported': 0.2} - beta: 0.169 - reported: 0.256 - objective: 0.1684


From either starting point, the fit finds the same values (β ≈ 0.169, 26% reported): it first scans the whole range within the bounds, then searches from the best few points, so the starting guesses matter little. Agreement shows that the search found the best fit, not that the data pin the values down. These are not the values the data were made with (β = 0.16, 40% reported): with only the rise of the outbreak, a range of fractions reported fits nearly as well, and the best fit to noisy data need not be the truth. With real data, the truth is unknown, which is why the tutorial’s advanced section finds the range of values consistent with the data.
2. A later or smaller campaign. From the best fit, as in the tutorial’s projection:

fit = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **settings).fit(verbose=False)
scenarios = {
    'No campaign':                 None,
    'Campaign on 1 April':         ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, when='2025-04-01', coverage=0.8),
    'Campaign on 15 April':        ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, when='2025-04-15', coverage=0.8),
    'Campaign on 1 April, 50%':    ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, when='2025-04-01', coverage=0.5),
}
proj = fit.project(scenarios)
proj.summarize().loc['measles_cases']








value


scenario

2,309

A campaign on 15 April prevents less than half as many cases as one on 1 April (about 140, rather than 340), since the outbreak is then near its peak. A campaign on 1 April reaching only half of children prevents more than one at 80% two weeks later: here, speed matters more than coverage.
3. (Advanced) Without the prior.

likelihood = dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=20))
posts = {}
for label, prior in [('With the prior', True), ('Without it', False)]:
    sim = ss.Sim(make_measles(prior=prior), data=data, **settings)
    posts[label] = sim.fit(method='pmcmc', likelihood=likelihood, verbose=False)
    row = posts[label].table.set_index('par').loc['reported']
    proj = posts[label].project(n_runs=100)
    print(label, '- reported:', round(row['median'], 2), f"({round(row['lower'], 2)} to {round(row['upper'], 2)})",
          '- projected cases:', proj.summarize().loc['measles_cases'].round().to_dict())

With the prior - reported: 0.3 (0.18 to 0.45) - projected cases: {'median': 2812.0, 'low': 1812.0, 'high': 4378.0, 'mean': 2919.0, 'std': 650.0}
Without it - reported: 0.28 (0.15 to 0.56) - projected cases: {'median': 2801.0, 'low': 1681.0, 'high': 4854.0, 'mean': 2904.0, 'std': 912.0}


Without the prior, the interval for the fraction reported is a little wider (15% to 56%, rather than 18% to 45%), and the range of the projected outbreak wider (about 1,700 to 4,900 reported cases, rather than 1,800 to 4,400), since a lower fraction reported means a larger outbreak. Much of the tutorial’s narrower range comes from the prior, what was known before this outbreak, not from its data. That is legitimate if the prior is sound, but with a different prior, the projection would differ.

title: Solutions: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
A real population (exercises 4–5)
4. A higher birth rate. Starting from the measles model of the tutorial’s made-up town, by age, mixing by a contact matrix:

def make_measles():
    """ The measles model of the made-up town, by age """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 0.14*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

def demographics(birth_rate):
    """ Births at the rate given, and 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people """
    return [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(birth_rate)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02))]

long = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', dt=ss.weeks(1), start='2025-01-01', stop='2045-01-01', verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel({
    '30 births a year per 1,000': ss.Sim(make_measles(), demographics=demographics(0.03), **long),
    '45 births a year per 1,000': ss.Sim(make_measles(), demographics=demographics(0.045), **long),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')








With more births, the later outbreaks come sooner and closer together, and settle sooner to a higher level, since the susceptible children needed for the next outbreak are born faster. (The population also grows faster, 2.5% a year rather than 1%, which is why infection keeps rising.)
5. Niger’s population. Run one model with these rates, and one with the UN’s:

pars = dict(start=2020, stop=2040)
constant = ss.Sim(people=ss.population('Niger', n_agents=5000), demographics=[ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.045)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.009))], **pars)
un = ss.Sim(people=ss.population('Niger', n_agents=5000), demographics=[ss.Births(birth_rate='Niger'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Niger')], **pars)
msim = ss.parallel({'Constant rates': constant, 'UN rates': un})
msim.plot('alive')

for label, sim in zip(['Constant rates', 'UN rates'], msim.sims):
    print(label, '- population in 2040:', round(sim.results.alive[-1]/1e6, 1), 'million')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Constant rates, UN rates)
  Done in 0.29 s









Constant rates - population in 2040: 47.6 million
UN rates - population in 2040: 42.6 million


With a constant 45 births and 9 deaths per 1,000, the population roughly doubles in 20 years. The UN expects the birth rate to fall (and its death rates differ by age), so the two projections differ.

import starsim as ss

title: Solutions: T2 – Building a model
text:
Exercise 1
A town of 2,000 people has had no measles for many years, and 70% of its people are immune. Five people arrive with measles. Using init and init_n, model the outbreak over a year. How many people are infected? Is the reproduction number at the start above or below 1?
With 30% susceptible, the reproduction number at the start is 15.2 × 0.3 ≈ 4.6 (printed as R = 4.53 at the start), well above 1, and almost all of the 600 susceptible people are infected. The run notes that with only 5 people infected at the start, whether an outbreak takes off is partly chance, which the ODE doesn’t show; running it many times with a stochastic solver (solver='gillespie', with ss.parallel(n_runs=...)) does.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(R=0.7), init_n=dict(I=5))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=2_000, stop=ss.days(365))
sim.run()
print('Infections:', round(sim.results.measles.infection.sum()))

  measles: R0 = 15.2 (R = 4.53 at the start, with 30% susceptible), with 5 infectious at the start
  Note: "measles" starts with 5 infected, so whether it takes off is a matter of chance, which solver="ode" does not show; solver="gillespie" with ss.parallel(n_runs=...) does

title: Solutions: T2 – Building a model
text:
Exercise 2
Using the final size relation, a model with R0 = 1.5 should infect about 58% of people. Choose β to give R0 = 1.5 with an infectious period of 8 days, run the model for long enough for the outbreak to end, and check.
β = R0 / the infectious period = 1.5 / 8 ≈ 0.19 per day. The outbreak is much slower than with R0 = 15, taking about two years to end.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ (1.5/8)*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(730))
sim.run()
print('Fraction infected:', round(sim.results.measles.R[-1] / 100_000, 2))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 730
  measles: R0 = 1.5, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0024 s; measles: 58,292 infections; at most 6,369 infectious, on day 91
Fraction infected: 0.58

title: Solutions: T2 – Building a model
text:
Exercise 3
Change the model to density-dependent transmission (I.n), choosing β so that R0 is still 15 in a town of 100,000. Then run it in a town of 10,000 and of 1,000,000. How does the outbreak change with the size of the town, and how does this differ from the frequency-dependent model?
With density-dependent transmission, R0 = β N × the infectious period, so for R0 = 15.2 in a town of 100,000, β = 15.2 / (100,000 × 8) = 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ per infectious person per day. In a town of 10,000, R0 is then 1.5, and the slow outbreak infects about 60% of people; in a town of 1,000,000, R0 is 152, and almost everyone is infected within days. With frequency-dependent transmission, R0 and the fraction infected would be the same at every size. Each run prints its R0 with verbose=1, and sim.diseases.measles.R0() gives it.

beta = 1.9e-5 # Per infectious person per day
for pop in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ beta*I.n
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10))
    sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=pop, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    res = sim.results.measles
    print('Town of', pop, ' fraction infected:', round(res.R[-1] / pop, 2), ' peak infectious:', round(res.I.max()))

Town of 10000  fraction infected: 0.6  peak infectious: 673
Town of 100000  fraction infected: 1.0  peak infectious: 75229
Town of 1000000  fraction infected: 1.0  peak infectious: 951749

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
🧠8% 🤖92%
Starsim is a framework for modeling the spread of disease. In Starsim, you write a model as an epidemiologist would describe it: the states people can be in, and the transitions between them and their rates. Starsim runs it as a compartmental model (equations for the number of people in each state) or as agents (one simulated person at a time). Starsim is in Python, and can also be used from R with R-Starsim.
These tutorials follow one example: a simplified measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, for teaching rather than of any real outbreak. This tutorial asks: how does an outbreak grow, and why does it stop? Tutorial 2 covers the same model in depth, Tutorial 3 gives the disease a more realistic course, and later tutorials add age groups, vaccination, several towns, and data.
You need only basic Python. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
Installing Starsim
Run pip install starsim in a terminal (or %pip install starsim in a notebook), then import starsim as ss in Python.

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
An SIR model of measles
In an SIR model, each person is susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered and immune (R), and moves along two transitions:

Infection, from S to I, at a rate of β (beta, the transmission rate) times the fraction of people infectious: β S I / N new infections a day, for a population of N.
Recovery, from I to R, at a rate γ (gamma, the recovery rate): γ I recoveries a day. People are infectious for 1/γ on average.

For measles, β is about 1.9 per day, and people are infectious for about 8 days, so γ = 1/8 per day. In a fully susceptible town, an infectious person infects about 1.9 people a day, or 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15 over 8 days. This is the basic reproduction number, R0 = β/γ, and 15 is typical of measles.
Here is that model in Starsim, run for 50 days:

PythonRExplicit



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # From S to I, at a rate of β = 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # From I to R, after 8 days on average (γ = 1/8 per day)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(50))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
sim.measles.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0022 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6


















library(starsim)

states("S I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection = Transition(S, I, rate = 1.9 * I), # From S to I, at a rate of β = 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # From I to R, after 8 days on average (γ = 1/8 per day)
  init_prev = 0.001
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(50))
sim$run()
sim$plot()
sim$measles$plot()



import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
infection = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=I, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection')       # From S to I, at a rate of β = 1.9 per day times the fraction infectious
recovery  = ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery') # From I to R, after an exponentially distributed time of 8 days on average
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(transitions=[infection, recovery], init_prev=0.001, name='measles')

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = ss.contacts(1), # Everyone mixes with everyone, with one contact per person per day
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = ss.days(0),
    stop      = ss.days(50),
    dt        = ss.days(1),     # Steps of a day
    unit      = 'day',          # The unit of bare numbers
    solver    = 'ode',          # Run as an ODE
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.plot()
sim_explicit.measles.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0021 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 74,112 infectious, on day 6



















That is a complete model of a measles outbreak, written, run, and plotted.
In Starsim, compartments are states, and each transition gives where people move from and to, and its rate (after @). Read S >> I @ 1.9*I as “from S to I, at a rate of 1.9 × I”. A state in a rate, like I in 1.9*I, is the fraction of people in it. A duration, like ss.days(8), is the average time in a state, 1/γ. A plain number takes the unit of the duration, so β = 1.9 is per day (ss.perday(1.9)). The shorthand builds an ss.Transition, written out in full in the Explicit tab. ss.Disease puts the transitions into a disease, named measles after its variable; init_prev=0.001 starts with 0.1% of people (100) infectious.
Starsim names the parameters itself: beta for β, and dur_I for the infectious period, 1/γ. equations() gives the standard SIR equations:

measles.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
Running the model
The code above gave the disease to a sim (ss.Sim), with the population size and how long to run (50 days), then ran and plotted it. The run printed what it ran (100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 50), R0 (15.2, as worked out above), and what happened: the number infected, and the size and day of the peak.
Starsim ran the model as an ODE (deterministic equations), since nothing in it needs individual people. sim.plot() shows each state, and each transition as the number of people who made it each day. sim.measles.plot() shows the three states together: the classic picture of an SIR epidemic.
The curves answer our question. At first almost everyone is susceptible, so each infectious person infects about 15 others, and cases grow several-fold in a few days. But each infection uses up a susceptible person. Once most of the town has been infected, an infectious person infects fewer than one other before recovering, so cases fall, though β is unchanged. The outbreak stops because it runs out of susceptible people, not because the disease becomes less contagious.
With R0 = 15 and nobody immune, almost everyone is infected, and the peak comes within a week. Real measles is slower, since people are infected for about 10 days before becoming infectious; Tutorial 3 adds this latent period.

title: T1 – Getting started
text:
The same model as agents
Starsim can also run the model as agents: simulated people who are infected and recover by chance. n_agents= sets how many; here 10,000 agents stand for 100,000 people, 10 each. ss.parallel() runs several labeled sims and plots their results together, here the number infectious:

PythonR



agents = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(50))
msim = ss.parallel({'ODE': sim, 'Agents': agents})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (ODE, Agents)
  Done in 0.43 s











agents <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, n_agents = 10000, stop = days(50))
msim <- parallel(list(ODE = sim, Agents = agents))
msim$plot("measles.I")



The epidemic is much the same, but the peak comes a few days later as agents. Run on its own (agents.run()), the agent sim prints a note saying why: agents move once per step (by default, a day), which is long for an outbreak that grows several-fold in a day. With a shorter step, such as dt=ss.days(0.25), agents follow the ODE closely (Solvers shows this).
Agents are needed when people differ in ways compartments can’t hold, such as their own contacts in a network. Where everyone mixes with everyone, both give the same answer with a short enough step, and the model is written the same way. Most of these tutorials use the ODE, which is fast, and say what changes as agents: chance and differences between people (T3), contacts between particular people (T4), and interventions that reach people because of what has happened to them (T5).
As agents, the sim keeps each person’s state, and when they entered it. people.to_df() gives a row per person (measles.ti_I is the step each was infected):

Ready-made diseases
Starsim also has ready-made diseases: the textbook ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR, and, in its library (import starsim.library as ssl), illustrative models of about twenty diseases, such as ssl.Measles. See Library diseases.

title: T1 – Getting started

Exercises

Suppose people with measles were infectious for only 5 days, with the same β. What would R0 be? Change the model, run it, and check the R0 the run prints. How does the epidemic change?
Run the agent version of the model with 1,000 agents instead of 10,000 (each standing for 100 people). What changes in the plot, and why?
Using the output of describe(), find out how Starsim assumes that people mix, and how long people stay infectious (the distribution as well as the average).

title: T8 – Custom modules
text:
🧠10% 🤖90%
When people hear about an outbreak, some of them go and get vaccinated. How much does that slow the outbreak down, and what limits it?
Most of a Starsim model is declared: its states, transitions, interventions, and results, which run under every solver and which describe() can show. But some things are easier to say in code, such as a rule of behavior, or a quantity with its own dynamics. A module written as code is a Python class with a step() method, which Starsim calls at each step, alongside the declared diseases.
This tutorial first writes a module that keeps numbers for the whole population, vaccine demand, and so still runs as an ODE. It then writes one that has to keep a value for each person, which needs agents, and an analyzer. Advanced sections write a disease and a network as code. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:
Before writing a module, check the table at the top of Custom modules: many things that seem to need code (vaccination, testing, treatment, contact tracing, changes to parameters, and protection that depends on the time since an event) can be declared.

title: T8 – Custom modules
text:
Vaccine demand
This is the measles model from T6 – Data and calibration, in a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, with β = 0.16 and 40% of infections reported. These are the values T6’s illustrative data were made with, not the values its fit found (β ≈ 0.17, and about a quarter reported), which fit those data about as well:

import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 0.16*I         # β = 0.16 per contact per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)   # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)    # Infectious for 8 days on average
cases       = ss.outcome(0.4*infection) # Reported cases: 40% of infections
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The fraction immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                          # 10 people infectious at the start
    name = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.cases')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 18.1 (R = 2.81 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0043 s; measles: 9,358 infections; at most 1,140 infectious, on 2025-04-12









During measles outbreaks, parents who had put off vaccinating hear about cases and go to a clinic. A simple rule: the rate at which susceptible people seek vaccination rises with the cases reported in the last week, reaching half its highest value (10% a week) at 300 cases a week.
The smallest module written as code is a function of the sim, called once each step; given as interventions=, it becomes an intervention. In it, sim.results has the results so far, and sim.ti is the index of the current time point. ss.move() moves people between a declared disease’s states, the same way under every solver: here, those vaccinated and protected from S to R. to_prob() turns a rate into the chance of an event in one step, 1 − exp(−rate × dt). Two simplifications keep this short: everyone in S is taken to be unvaccinated (the model doesn’t record who was vaccinated), and the vaccine is all or nothing (93% of those vaccinated are fully protected), unlike the leaky vaccine of T5:

PythonExplicit



def vaccine_demand(sim):
    """ The unvaccinated seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the cases reported in the last week """
    measles = sim.diseases.measles
    last_week = sim.results.measles.cases[max(sim.ti-7, 0):sim.ti].sum()      # Cases reported in the last 7 steps: a week, since each step here is a day
    frac = last_week/(last_week + 300)                                        # From 0 to 1, a half at 300 cases a week
    seeking = (ss.perweek(0.1)*frac).to_prob(sim.t.dt)                        # The chance of seeking vaccination in this step
    ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, p=seeking*0.93)                             # Those vaccinated and protected become immune
    return




import numpy as np

def vaccine_demand(sim):
    """ The unvaccinated seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the cases reported in the last week """
    measles = sim.diseases.measles
    last_week = sim.results.measles.cases[max(sim.ti-7, 0):sim.ti].sum()      # Cases reported in the last 7 steps: a week, since each step here is a day
    frac = last_week/(last_week + 300)                                        # From 0 to 1, a half at 300 cases a week
    rate = 0.1/7*frac                                                         # The rate of seeking vaccination, per day
    seeking = 1 - np.exp(-rate*sim.t.dt.days)                                 # The chance of seeking vaccination in this step
    ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, p=seeking*0.93)                             # Those vaccinated and protected become immune
    return





sims = {
    'No response': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Vaccine demand': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=vaccine_demand, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
print('Solver:', msim.sims['Vaccine demand'].solver)
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No response, Vaccine demand)
  Done in 0.9 s
Solver: ode









The sim still runs as an ODE, since the function keeps nothing for each person. But the function’s numbers are fixed inside it, it has no results (so how many doses were given?), and it forgets a case abruptly after 7 days.

title: T8 – Custom modules
text:
A module as a class
A module written as a class fixes all three. It inherits from one of Starsim’s module types (here ss.Intervention), so that it runs at the right point in each step:



Base class
Use for
Added to the sim via




ss.Disease, ss.AgentDisease
Disease natural history and transmission
diseases=


ss.Network
Who contacts whom
networks=


ss.Demographics
Births, deaths, migration
demographics=


ss.Intervention
Actions that change the simulation
interventions=


ss.Analyzer
Recording results without changing anything
analyzers=


ss.Connector
Interactions between modules
connectors=


ss.Module
Anything that doesn’t fit the others
modules= (or as a positional argument)



The module has:

Parameters, with defaults in __init__() via define_pars(), changed by name when the module is made. Rates and durations are time parameters, so they mean the same whatever the step length.
A state of its own: here, one number, the cases people remember. Each step adds the new reported cases and forgets a fraction of what is remembered, so a case is remembered for memory (30 days) on average: a small ODE of its own, dM/dt = cases − M/memory.
Results of its own, defined in init_results() and filled in each step at self.ti: the doses given in each step (a flow), and the cases remembered (a stock).
A step() method, which does the work. In it, self.sim is the sim, self.t.dt the step length, and self.pars the parameters.
A limit: clinics can give at most capacity doses a day (no limit by default); people who can’t be served try again the next day.


class VaccineDemand(ss.Intervention):
    """ Unvaccinated people seek vaccination at a rate that rises with the outbreak cases they remember """

    def __init__(self, memory=ss.days(30), half=300, max_rate=ss.perweek(0.1), capacity=None, efficacy=0.93, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            memory   = memory,   # How long a reported case is remembered, on average
            half     = half,     # The number of cases remembered at which demand is half its highest
            max_rate = max_rate, # The highest rate at which unvaccinated people seek vaccination
            capacity = capacity, # The most doses the clinics can give, as a rate (None for no limit)
            efficacy = efficacy, # The fraction of those vaccinated who are fully protected (all or nothing)
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.remembered = 0.0 # The cases that people remember, for the whole population
        return

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('doses', kind='flow', scale=False, label='Doses given'),
            ss.Result('remembered', kind='stock', scale=False, label='Cases remembered'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        measles = self.sim.diseases.measles
        dt = self.t.dt

        # Remember the cases reported in the last step (there is none before the first), and forget a fraction of those remembered
        new_cases = self.sim.results.measles.cases[self.ti-1] if self.ti > 0 else 0
        self.remembered += new_cases - self.remembered*(dt/self.pars.memory)

        # The doses sought by those in S (all taken to be unvaccinated), limited by what the clinics can give
        frac = self.remembered/(self.remembered + self.pars.half)
        seeking = (self.pars.max_rate*frac).to_prob(dt)
        doses = seeking*measles.S.n
        if self.pars.capacity is not None:
            doses = min(doses, self.pars.capacity.to_events(dt))

        # Those protected become immune
        ss.move(measles.S, measles.R, n=doses*self.pars.efficacy)
        self.results.doses[self.ti] = doses
        self.results.remembered[self.ti] = self.remembered # Recorded here, where it changes: the cases remembered in this step
        return

measles.S.n is the number of people in S now (and measles.S.frac the fraction), under every solver, and ss.move(..., n=...) moves a number of people rather than a fraction. A module that is not a disease steps before the diseases, so it reads the last step’s cases (self.ti-1), and what it does applies to this step’s transmission. (A stock is usually recorded in record_states(), at the start of a step; remembered is recorded in step() instead, since that is where it is updated, so each value is the memory that step used.) The sim works on its own copy of each module, so reach other modules through self.sim, not a variable from outside the class. The module’s results are under its class name in lower case, sim.results.vaccinedemand. Custom modules lists when Starsim calls each method.
With parameters, one module serves every scenario: no response (a highest rate of 0), demand met in full, and clinics that can give at most 30 doses a day:

sims = {
    'No response':           ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(max_rate=ss.perweek(0)), **settings),
    'Demand met in full':    ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(), **settings),
    'At most 30 doses a day': ss.Sim(measles, interventions=VaccineDemand(capacity=ss.perday(30)), **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['measles.I', 'vaccinedemand.doses'])
msim.summarize().loc[['measles_infection', 'vaccinedemand_doses']]

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No response, Demand met in full, At most 30 doses a day)
  Done in 1.0 s

















value


result
scenario





measles_infection
No response
9,358


Demand met in full
5,397


At most 30 doses a day
6,579

No response
0
