title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
🧠9% 🤖91%
The SIR model of Tutorial 1 and Tutorial 2 is over within weeks, far faster than real measles. Tutorial 2 found that R0 and prior immunity decide how many people are infected. This tutorial asks: what decides how fast an outbreak spreads? It adds, one at a time, structure that most disease models need: a latent period, the distribution of a duration, waning immunity, and a branch (here, a small fraction die). It then names the parameters, checks the finished disease, and runs it as agents. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
A latent period
People infected with measles become infectious about 10 days later. In an SEIR model, people in this latent period are in their own compartment, E (exposed): infected, but not yet infectious. Infection moves people from S to E, and progression from E to I.
Here are the SIR and SEIR models, both named measles, so their results can be plotted together:

import starsim as ss

# The SIR model of Tutorials 1 and 2
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

# The SEIR model: infection leads to E, not I
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # Infected by contact with infectious people, I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious after a latent period of 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Recovered after 8 days on average
seir = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

sir_sim  = ss.Sim(sir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'SIR': sir_sim, 'SEIR': seir_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (SIR, SEIR)
  Done in 0.28 s









Only I is infectious, since only it appears in the rate of infection. Both outbreaks start with 0.1% infectious (init=dict(I=0.001); init_prev=0.001 would put them in E, Tutorial 2).
R0 is the same in both, 15.2: it depends on how many people each infectious person infects (β = 1.9 a day, for 8 days), not on how soon they become infectious. But with a latent period, the time from one infection to the next (the generation time) is about 18 days instead of 8, so the epidemic peaks later and lower. So the first answer is the generation time: for the same R0, a longer one means a slower, flatter epidemic.

title: T3 – Building a disease
section: How long people stay in a state
text:
How long people stay in a state
A duration such as ss.days(10) is an average; by default, the time in the state is exponentially distributed, as in the standard ODE. That describes most latent periods poorly: with a mean of 10 days, 10% of people become infectious within a day. An Erlang distribution (a gamma with a whole-number shape, k) is the usual alternative in compartmental models. With k=10, the latent period still averages 10 days, with a standard deviation of about 3:

progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))  # 10 days on average; 95% between 5 and 17
seir_erlang = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

erlang_sim = ss.Sim(seir_erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'Exponential latent period': seir_sim, 'Erlang latent period': erlang_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Exponential latent period, Erlang latent period)
  Done in 0.33 s









R0 is the same, but the epidemic peaks two weeks later, and higher. With an exponential latent period, the few who become infectious within a day or two start chains of infection early; with an Erlang one, almost nobody does. So the distribution of a duration, not just its average, sets how fast an epidemic grows.
As an ODE, Starsim runs an Erlang distribution as k exponential stages in a row, each 1/k of the mean, only a way to narrow the time in E. Written out, it is a transition with 10 stages:

PythonRExplicit



progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))



progression <- Transition(E, I, dur = ss$erlang(k = 10, mean = days(10)))



progression = ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.days(10), stages=10) # 10 exponential stages of 1 day each, on average




equations() shows the stages, as E_1 to E_10:

seir_erlang.equations()

dS/dt    = -beta * S * I / N
dE_1/dt  =  beta * S * I / N - 10 * E_1 / mean(dur_E)
dE_2/dt  =  10 * E_1 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_2 / mean(dur_E)
dE_3/dt  =  10 * E_2 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_3 / mean(dur_E)
dE_4/dt  =  10 * E_3 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_4 / mean(dur_E)
dE_5/dt  =  10 * E_4 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_5 / mean(dur_E)
dE_6/dt  =  10 * E_5 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_6 / mean(dur_E)
dE_7/dt  =  10 * E_6 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_7 / mean(dur_E)
dE_8/dt  =  10 * E_7 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_8 / mean(dur_E)
dE_9/dt  =  10 * E_8 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_9 / mean(dur_E)
dE_10/dt =  10 * E_9 / mean(dur_E) - 10 * E_10 / mean(dur_E)
dI/dt    =  10 * E_10 / mean(dur_E) - I / dur_I
dR/dt    =  I / dur_I


As agents, each person draws their own time from the distribution instead. Other distributions, such as ss.lognormal(), are covered in Distributions.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Waning immunity
For many infections, such as pertussis or RSV, immunity wanes: a transition from R back to S, an SEIRS model. Suppose (unlike real measles) that immunity lasted 2 years on average:

progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Back to an exponential latent period
waning      = R >> S @ ss.years(2)  # Susceptible again after 2 years on average
seirs = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, waning, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

lifelong = ss.Sim(seir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
waning_sim = ss.Sim(seirs, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
msim = ss.parallel({'Lifelong immunity': lifelong, 'Immunity lasting 2 years': waning_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Lifelong immunity, Immunity lasting 2 years)
  Done in 0.45 s









unit='day' says which unit the bare β = 1.9 is in (Tutorial 2). With waning immunity, smaller waves follow the first outbreak, and the disease becomes endemic. A supply of new susceptible people, from waning immunity or births (Tutorial 6), is what lets an infection persist, rather than burn through the population once and disappear.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Deaths: a branch
A small fraction of people with measles die: from 1 in 1,000 cases or fewer in high-income countries to several in 100 in some low-income settings. Suppose it is 2 in 1,000. People leaving I then branch: 0.2% die and the rest recover. A branch is a transition with p=, the fraction that take it, and p=None marks the one that takes the rest. After @, a dict gives the transition’s keywords:

PythonRExplicit



S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R       @ dict(dur=ss.days(8), p=None)   # The rest recover...
death       = I >> ss.dead @ dict(dur=ss.days(8), p=0.002)  # ...and 0.2% die
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim.results.measles.death.sum()))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0045 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,216 infectious, on day 28
Deaths: 200




library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = Transition(S, E, rate = 1.9 * I),
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)),
  recovery    = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8), p = 0.998),       # 99.8% recover...
  death       = Transition(I, ss$dead, dur = days(8), p = 0.002), # ...and 0.2% die
  init = list(I = 0.001)
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(150))
sim$run()
cat("Deaths:", round(sum(sim$results$measles$death$values)), "\n")



S, E, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='E'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=E, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10)), name='progression'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), p=0.998, name='recovery'),    # 99.8% recover...
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=ss.dead, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), p=0.002, name='death'), # ...and 0.2% die
    ],
    init = dict(S=0.999, I=0.001), # The fraction of people in each state at the start
    name = 'measles',
)

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(diseases=measles_explicit, networks=ss.contacts(1), total_pop=100_000, start=ss.days(0), stop=ss.days(150), dt=ss.days(1), unit='day', solver='ode')
sim_explicit.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim_explicit.results.measles.death.sum()))

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0031 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 29,216 infectious, on day 28
Deaths: 200





ss.dead is outside the model: people who die leave the population. Each branch has its own result (recovery and death), and could have its own duration. In the equations, who goes which way is decided on entering I, so I is in two parts, I_1 (who will die) and I_2 (who will recover):

measles.equations()

dS/dt   = -beta * S * I / N
dE/dt   =  beta * S * I / N - E / dur_E
dI_1/dt =  p_death * E / dur_E - I_1 / dur_death
dI_2/dt =  (1 - p_death) * E / dur_E - I_2 / dur_recovery
dR/dt   =  I_2 / dur_recovery


The same outcome can be written as one transition with several destinations, outcome = I >> {ss.dead: 0.002, R: None} @ ss.days(8), decided as people leave I; its results are then outcome.dead and outcome.R (see Building diseases). Two transitions out of a state with rates and no p= are instead competing risks: whichever happens first moves each person. A branch gives the fraction directly, which is how the case fatality ratio is usually known.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Naming the parameters
Starsim names parameters itself (beta, dur_E, …), as Tutorial 2 showed. To name them yourself, use ss.par(). Each takes its name from its variable, and can have a description (doc=), a source (source=), and bounds, the range of plausible values:

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta           = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day')
dur_latent     = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[ss.days(7), ss.days(14)], doc='Average latent period', source='Assumed for this tutorial')
dur_infectious = ss.par(ss.days(8), doc='Average infectious period')

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ dur_latent
recovery    = I >> R       @ dict(dur=dur_infectious, p=None)
death       = I >> ss.dead @ dict(dur=dur_infectious, p=0.002)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))

One parameter can be used in several places, as dur_infectious is, by both recovery and death: ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_infectious=ss.days(7)), ...) changes it in both. Calibration uses the bounds. See Parameters for more, including priors.

A disease can also be written as a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body, so that it can be made with other parameter values, like the diseases in Starsim’s library (e.g. Measles(beta=1.5)); see Diseases.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Advanced: diseases as agents
Everything above also runs as agents (with n_agents=, as in Tutorial 1). Each person then has their own state, their own durations (measles.E.stays gives each person’s time in E), and, if you want, their own infectiousness and susceptibility. This shows two things the deterministic ODE can’t: chance when cases are few (which a stochastic compartmental solver can also show), and differences between people.

Chance, and the first case
In a deterministic ODE, an infection with a reproduction number above 1 always takes off. In reality, the first cases may recover before infecting anyone. Suppose 90% of the town is immune and one infectious person arrives. R0 is still 15, but the effective reproduction number at the start is R ≈ 1.9 × 8 × 0.1 ≈ 1.5: each case infects about 1.5 others. Here are 20 runs as agents, each with its own random seed, and the ODE for comparison:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1)) # 90% immune, and 1 case

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(ss.Sim(measles, **pars), n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='ode', verbose=0)
ode.run()
ode.plot('measles.I')















The ODE always gives the same outbreak. As agents, some runs give one about as large, and the rest die out after a handful of cases. Counting runs with fewer than 20 infections:

total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1) # Total infections in each run
print('Fraction of introductions that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))

Fraction of introductions that die out: 0.65


Theory says one case dies out with a chance of 1/R, here about 2 in 3, close to the runs. This holds early in an outbreak in a large, well-mixed population, where each case’s infections are independent and the infectious period is exponentially distributed, as here. This matters for questions about introductions: how likely an imported case is to start an outbreak.


People who differ: superspreading
For many diseases, most cases infect few others or none, and a few infect many (superspreading). This is usually described by giving each person an infectiousness drawn from a gamma distribution with mean 1 and dispersion k: the smaller k, the more concentrated transmission is. A value that each person has is an attribute, ss.attr(), here drawn once for each person; ss.modify() then multiplies each person’s infectiousness (rel_trans) by it:

def make_sim(k=None):
    """ The measles model, with the infectiousness of each person drawn from a gamma distribution with shape k """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    if k is None: # Everyone equally infectious
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
        return ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(shape=k, scale=1/k)) # A mean of 1, and a shape (dispersion) of k
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 1': 1, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=40)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- fraction that die out:', np.mean(total < 20), '- median size of the outbreaks that take off:', np.median(total[total >= 20]))

Everyone equally infectious - fraction that die out: 0.675 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 313.0
k = 1 - fraction that die out: 0.65 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 298.5
k = 0.2 - fraction that die out: 0.75 - median size of the outbreaks that take off: 182.5


Each case infects about 1.5 others on average in all three, but the more concentrated transmission is, the more often an introduction dies out: with k = 0.2, about 3 in 4 do, since the first case is most likely one who infects nobody. ss.attr() can also draw a value when something happens to a person (e.g. a severity at infection, with when=infection); see Diseases. Susceptibility can differ in the same way, with ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, ...).


Counting each person’s infections
With waning immunity, people can be infected again and again. Measles immunity is lifelong, so this example switches to a cold-like respiratory infection: an SIRS model (R0 = 0.4 × 7 = 2.8) with immunity lasting 6 months on average. keep_times=True keeps each person’s history, which only agents have:

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7)   # Infectious for 7 days on average
waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(180) # Immune for 6 months on average
cold = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, waning, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

sirs = ss.Sim(cold, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), keep_times=True, verbose=0)
sirs.run()
sirs.plot('cold.I')








After a first wave, the infection settles into smaller, repeated waves. cold.infection.n_times is the number of times each person has been infected:

counts = sirs.diseases.cold.infection.n_times.values
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');








Most people are infected 3 to 5 times. A model can use a person’s history: e.g. ss.modify(cold.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, who=cold.infection.n_times >= 2) would halve the susceptibility of people infected at least twice. A disease can also be written as Python code, as in Starsim 3: T8 – Custom modules shows how.

title: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercises

Measles has a latent period of 10 to 12 days. Using the model with named parameters, run it with a latent period of 12 days, using pars=. Does R0 change? How do the timing and height of the peak change?
Give the infectious period an Erlang distribution too, with k=4. Using R0() and a plot of I, check whether R0 or the course of the epidemic changes.
About 1 in 10 people with measles in this town are admitted to hospital, after 4 days of being infectious on average, and stay for 7 days. Add a state for people in hospital (assume they don’t transmit), and find the largest number of people in hospital at once.
Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model of the respiratory infection (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
In the town with 90% immune, increase the fraction susceptible to 20% (init=dict(R=0.8)), so that each case infects about 3 others. What fraction of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?

Solutions · Next: T4 – Mixing

title: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
🧠5% 🤖95%
How big will this outbreak get, and would a vaccination campaign now make a difference?
A model of a real outbreak is checked against what was observed. This tutorial fits the measles model to the cases reported in an outbreak, checks the fit, and projects what happens next, with and without a campaign. Advanced sections then find how sure the fit is, and project from that range. A last section gives the model a real population, with births and deaths. By the end, you will be able to:

title: T6 – Data and calibration
section: The model and what the data measure
text:
The model and what the data measure
This is the measles model from T5 – Interventions and scenarios: a town of 100,000 people in three age groups, mixing by a contact matrix, most of them already immune. It is late March. Measles cases have been reported weekly since January, and are still rising. The health office asks how many cases a vaccination campaign for children would prevent, and how much it matters how soon it starts. Some parameters, like the rate of infection per contact or the fraction of cases reported, can’t be measured directly; calibration fits them to data, and the calibrated model then projects what happens next. Here is the model, with two additions explained below:

PythonRExplicit



import pandas as pd
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5])  # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day
reported = ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.05, 1], prior=ss.beta_dist(mean=0.35, std=0.1)) # The fraction of infections that are reported: about a third, from earlier outbreaks

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I         # Infection, at a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)   # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)    # Infectious for 8 days on average
cases       = ss.outcome(reported*infection) # Reported cases: a fraction of new infections
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, cases,
    init = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The fraction immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                          # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-09-01')



library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
beta     <- par(0.14, bounds = c(0.05, 0.5)) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day
reported <- par(0.5, bounds = c(0.05, 1), prior = ss$beta_dist(mean = 0.35, std = 0.1)) # The fraction of infections that are reported

infection <- Transition(S, E, rate = beta * I)
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = infection,
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)), # Latent for 10 days on average
  recovery    = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),  # Infectious for 8 days on average
  cases       = outcome(reported * infection),    # Reported cases: a fraction of new infections
  init        = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))), # The fraction immune in each age group
  init_n      = list(I = 10)
)
measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+

age_contacts <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(10, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3)))
make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-09-01", ...)
}



S, E, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='E'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
beta_explicit     = ss.par(ss.perday(0.14), bounds=[ss.perday(0.05), ss.perday(0.5)], name='beta') # Per contact with an infectious person
reported_explicit = ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.05, 1], prior=ss.beta_dist(mean=0.35, std=0.1), name='reported')

infection_explicit = ss.Transition(source=S, dest=E, rate=beta_explicit*I, name='infection')
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        infection_explicit,
        ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10)), name='progression'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery'),
        ss.outcome(source=reported_explicit*infection_explicit, name='cases'), # Moves nobody: a result worked out from the infections
    ],
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The rest start in S
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name   = 'measles',
)
measles_explicit.stratify(age=ss.levels({0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, kind='age')) # Age groups, which people would age through

contacts_explicit = ss.contacts(matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], ages=[0, 15, 65], name='contacts')
settings_explicit = dict(networks=contacts_explicit, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-09-01', dt=ss.days(1), unit='day', solver='ode', aging=False)




First, data rarely measure a model’s states directly: a health office counts only reported cases. An outcome is a result computed from the model’s states and transitions, to compare with what was observed (see Outcomes). Here, cases is reported times the new infections each day.
Second, neither β nor the fraction reported is known, so each is a parameter with bounds (ss.par(..., bounds=...)): the values a fit may try, starting from the values given.

The data
The file data/measles_cases.csv has the measles cases reported each week, from the week starting 1 January to the week starting 12 March:

data



The counts jump around, as real counts do, by chance and because reporting varies.






NoteWhere this data comes from



This data is illustrative. It was made from an agent-based run of this model (so not the smooth curve of the ODE), with β = 0.16 and 40% of infections reported (the “true” values, which a fit to real data never knows), and its weekly totals were drawn with more variation than Poisson counts, as reported counts usually have. So, as with real data, no parameter values fit it exactly:
truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=0.16, reported=0.4), n_agents=100_000, rand_seed=3, **settings).run()
weekly = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week', noise=ss.nbinom(n=30)) # Weekly reported cases, each dated by the first day of its week, with extra variation (negative binomial counts)
weekly[weekly.date <= ss.date('2025-03-12')].to_csv('data/measles_cases.csv', index=False)
weekly[weekly.date > ss.date('2025-03-12')].to_csv('data/measles_cases_after.csv', index=False) # What happens next


Data is matched to results by name: the column cases is compared with the outcome cases, and each row with the model’s total over the week starting on its date. To attach the data, give it to the sim; plotting the cases then shows the data with the model, here with the starting guesses, which rise too slowly:

PythonR



sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.plot('measles.cases')

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-09-01
  measles: R0 = 15.8 (R = 2.46 at the start, with 11% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0037 s; measles: 8,788 infections; at most 934 infectious, on 2025-04-27











sim <- make_sim(data = data)
sim$run()
sim$plot("measles.cases")

title: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
Fitting and checking the fit
sim.fit() fits every parameter with bounds (β and reported) to every result with data (cases), keeping the values with the smallest mismatch: by default, the average difference between model and data, relative to the data’s size. It reports how it searched, and whether searches from different starting points agreed:

PythonR



fit = sim.fit()

Searching on a log scale: beta, reported
Fitting by nelder-mead (2 fitted parameters, for which it is faster than gradients; override with method=)
Converged: the best two of 3 searches, from points of the scan that are apart, ended within 0.00017 of each other (objective values 0.1684 at beta=0.1689, reported=0.2562; 0.1684 at beta=0.1689, reported=0.2562; 0.185 at beta=0.1446, reported=0.5089; 275 evaluations)
The loss is 0.1684 at the best values and 0.2905 at the initial values




fit <- sim$fit()



The searches agree on the best values, but one ended at β ≈ 0.145 with about half of infections reported, fitting nearly as well: these data can’t tell some combinations of the two apart (more on this below).
The fit holds the values found (fit.pars), the sim with the starting guesses (fit.before), and a sim run with the fitted values (fit.sim). A fit always finds some values, so check that they make sense. First, the values, and how much better they fit than the starting guesses:

PythonR



fit.summarize()

Second, the model against the data, before and after fitting:

Projecting a campaign
The model runs to September, so the fitted model projects the rest of the outbreak. fit.project() runs each scenario with the fitted values. The scenarios are a campaign vaccinating 80% of children under 15 on 1 April, two weeks from now, or on 1 May, if it takes six weeks to organize:

scenarios = {
    'No campaign':         None,
    'Campaign on 1 April': campaign('2025-04-01'),
    'Campaign on 1 May':   campaign('2025-05-01'),
}
proj = fit.project(scenarios)
proj.plot('measles.cases')
proj.summarize().loc['measles_cases']

title: T6 – Data and calibration
section: Advanced: how sure is the fit?
text:
Advanced: how sure is the fit?
The data cover only the rise of the outbreak, and while it grows, a smaller outbreak with more reported looks like a larger one with less reported. When data can’t tell two parameters apart like this, they are not identifiable from it (see Fit diagnostics).
The range of values consistent with the data is a posterior. Finding it takes two more things. A likelihood says how the data vary around the model: here, as counts that vary more than Poisson counts (ss.nbinom(n=20), a negative binomial). A prior says what is known before seeing the data: the fraction reported has one (prior= above), about a third, from earlier outbreaks; β’s is uniform over its bounds. A sampler then draws values in proportion to how probable they are, given both. Here it is 'pmcmc', a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler (for an ODE, a random walk that needs one run of the model per draw); Fitting methods compares it with the others, such as 'nuts':

PythonR



post = sim.fit(method='pmcmc', likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=20))) # 4 chains, each sampled until they agree
post.summarize()

Using the likelihood: the sum of the log-likelihoods of cases, treated as independent
Searching on a log scale: beta, reported

The sampler keeps drawing until it is, and until each parameter has at least 400 effective draws (ess), which takes more draws here than usual, since β and the fraction reported are strongly correlated, which slows a random walk. The interval for the fraction reported, about 18% to 45%, is wide: the data say little more about it than the prior did.

Since this data is illustrative, we can see what came next, with no campaign (project() passes other arguments, here data=, on to its sims):

Starsim labels each row of data on a flow by the start of the period it covers; if these data are labeled by its end (e.g. weeks ending on a date), subtract one period from their times; if not, run the sim to the end of that period.












after <- read.csv("data/measles_cases_after.csv")
everything <- rbind(data, after)
proj <- post$project(list("No campaign" = NULL), n_runs = 100, data = everything)
proj$plot("measles.cases")



The outbreak was within the projection’s range, near its top: about 40% of infections were in fact reported, which the March data couldn’t tell from a smaller fraction. Early data say how fast an outbreak grows, but not how big it will get, so a decision should rest on the projection’s range, not its median. Fitting a model covers fitting stochastic and agent-based models, other measures of mismatch, and the choice of method; Fit diagnostics covers what else to check.

title: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
A real population
The town above is made up. For a real place, the age groups and contacts can come from data. ss.population('Kenya') is Kenya’s population by age and sex (UN World Population Prospects), and ss.contacts('Kenya') a contact matrix by 5-year age group (Prem et al., 2021). stratify() then needs only the age groups, taking their fractions from the population, and Starsim adds up the matrix into them. total_pop keeps the model to a town of 100,000:

PythonR



measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, # The model above, without reported cases
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name   = 'measles',
)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]) # The fraction in each group comes from the population

kenya = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.population('Kenya'), networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
kenya.run()
kenya.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2026-01-01
  measles: R0 = 17.4 (R = 2.44 at the start, with 12% susceptible), with 10 infectious at the start
  Note: contact matrix "contacts" aggregated from 16 age groups to the model's 3 (0-14, 15-64, 65+)
  Note: people do not age between the age groups, since nobody is born or dies; pass aging=True to age them
  Done in 0.0041 s; measles: 10,401 infections; at most 1,125 infectious, on 2025-04-27











measles <- Disease(infection, progression, recovery, # The model above, without reported cases
  init   = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))),
  init_n = list(I = 10),
  name   = "measles"
)
measles$stratify(age = c(0, 15, 65)) # The fraction in each group comes from the population

kenya <- Sim(measles, people = ss$population("Kenya"), networks = contacts("Kenya"), total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01")
kenya$run()
kenya$results$measles$infection$by("age")$plot()



Kenya’s population is young, about 37% under 15, and has more contacts than the made-up matrix, so the outbreak is larger, nearly two thirds of it in children. These data are inputs, not a calibrated model: check the year, age groups, and how the survey defined contacts before relying on them. Places and data explains the data, lists every place there is data for, and shows how to use a country’s regions as places.

Births and deaths
Over decades, children are born susceptible, which is what makes measles come back. Births and deaths go to the sim as demographics: ss.birth() takes a crude birth rate, here 30 a year per 1,000 people, and ss.death() a death rate, here 20 a year per 1,000 at every age. People are born into each disease’s first state (S), die from every state at the same rate, and move up the age groups as they age. Here is the made-up town over 20 years, with and without them:

PythonR



measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), init_n=dict(I=10), name='measles')
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # The made-up town's age groups
demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births a year per 1,000 people
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), # 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people
]
long = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', dt=ss.weeks(1), start='2025-01-01', stop='2045-01-01')

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **long),
    'Births and deaths':   ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **long),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (No births or deaths, Births and deaths)
  Done in 0.32 s











measles <- Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))), init_n = list(I = 10), name = "measles")
measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # The made-up town's age groups
demographics <- list(
  ss$birth(rate = peryear(0.03)), # 30 births a year per 1,000 people
  ss$death(rate = peryear(0.02))  # 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people
)
make_long <- function(...) {
  Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, unit = "day", dt = weeks(1), start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2045-01-01", ...)
}
msim <- parallel(list(
  "No births or deaths" = make_long(),
  "Births and deaths"   = make_long(demographics = demographics)
))
msim$plot("measles.I")



The birth and death rates are per year and β per day, so unit='day' says which unit the bare β is in (see Time). dt=ss.weeks(1) records results weekly; as an ODE, the model is still solved finely in between.
Without births, there is one outbreak, and then measles is gone. With births, smaller outbreaks follow a year or two apart: the classic pattern of measles where too few children are vaccinated. In the troughs, only a handful of people are infectious, and in reality measles would often die out; an ODE can’t show this, but a stochastic run can (Solvers and backends).
Real birth and death rates change from year to year, and death rates differ by age and sex. Starsim includes the UN’s for 187 countries and territories: ss.population('Nigeria') gives the ages, sex ratio, and size of Nigeria’s population in the start year, ss.Births(birth_rate='Nigeria') its births, and ss.Deaths(death_rate='Nigeria') its deaths by year, age, and sex. People and demographics shows how to check such a model against the UN’s estimates.

title: T6 – Data and calibration
text:
Exercises

Start the fit from other guesses, e.g. β = 0.3 and 20% reported (ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=0.3, reported=0.2), data=data, **settings)). Does it find the same values? Are they the values the data were made with?
From the fit, how many reported cases would a campaign on 15 April prevent? And one on 1 April reaching only 50% of children?
(Advanced) Find the posterior without the prior on the fraction reported (remake reported with no prior=, and the disease from it). How do the interval for the fraction reported, and the range of the projection, change? Where did the narrower range come from?
In the model with births and deaths, raise the birth rate to 45 a year per 1,000 people, as in some countries with young populations. How does the time between outbreaks change, and why?
In Niger, the crude birth rate is 45 and the crude death rate is 9. Assuming these rates stay constant, and starting with its population in 2020 (ss.population('Niger', n_agents=5000)), how many people will there be in 2040? (You do not need to include any diseases in your model.) Compare this with its UN birth and death rates.

text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
These are solutions to the exercises at the end of T3 – Building a disease. Many of the exercises are open-ended, so these are examples: there are often other good answers. This page runs on its own, from the setup below.
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss

title: Solutions: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercise 1
Measles has a latent period of 10 to 12 days. Using the model with named parameters, run it with a latent period of 12 days, using pars=. Does R0 change? How do the timing and height of the peak change?
R0 doesn’t change (15.2), since it depends only on β and the infectious period. A longer latent period lengthens the generation time, so the epidemic peaks about 3 days later, and a little lower.

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta           = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day')
dur_latent     = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[ss.days(7), ss.days(14)], doc='Average latent period')
dur_infectious = ss.par(ss.days(8), doc='Average infectious period')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ dur_latent
recovery    = I >> R @ dur_infectious
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

latent10 = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
latent12 = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_latent=ss.days(12)), total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'Latent period of 10 days': latent10, 'Latent period of 12 days': latent12})
msim.plot('measles.I')

MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Latent period of 10 days, Latent period of 12 days)
  Done in 0.23 s

title: Solutions: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercise 2
Give the infectious period an Erlang distribution too, with k=4. Using R0() and a plot of I, check whether R0 or the course of the epidemic changes.
R0 is unchanged, since the average infectious period is still 8 days. The epidemic peaks a few days sooner and higher: with an exponential infectious period, some people stay infectious a long time, spreading their infections out, whereas with an Erlang one most are infectious for close to 8 days.

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))
exponential = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(8)) # An Erlang infectious period
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))
erlang = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
erlang.run()
print('R0:', round(erlang.diseases.measles.R0(), 1))

msim = ss.parallel({'Exponential': exponential, 'Erlang': erlang})
msim.plot('measles.I')

  measles: R0 = 15.2, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0047 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 36,389 infectious, on day 25
R0: 15.2
MultiSim: 2 runs of 2 scenarios (Exponential, Erlang)

title: Solutions: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercise 3
About 1 in 10 people with measles in this town are admitted to hospital, after 4 days of being infectious on average, and stay for 7 days. Add a state for people in hospital (assume they don’t transmit), and find the largest number of people in hospital at once.
People leaving I now branch: 10% go to hospital (H) after 4 days on average, and 90% recover after 8. People in hospital don’t transmit, so R0 falls a little, to 14.4: those admitted are infectious for 4 days instead of 8.

S, E, I, H, R = ss.states('S E I H R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
admission   = ss.Transition(I, H, dur=ss.days(4), p=0.1) # 10% go to hospital...
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.9) # ...and the rest recover
discharge   = H >> R @ ss.days(7)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, admission, recovery, discharge, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
print('Most people in hospital at once:', round(sim.results.measles.H.max()))
sim.results.measles.H.plot()

Sim: measles, 100,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 150
  measles: R0 = 14.4, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0078 s; measles: 99,900 infections; at most 27,872 infectious, on day 28
Most people in hospital at once: 2440

title: Solutions: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercise 4
Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model of the respiratory infection (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
This uses the SIRS model of the respiratory infection from the tutorial, made by a function so that the duration of immunity can change:

def make_cold(dur_imm=ss.days(180)):
    """ The SIRS model of a respiratory infection, with immunity lasting dur_imm on average """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I       # β = 0.4 per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7)
    waning    = R >> S @ dur_imm
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, waning, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), unit='day', keep_times=True, verbose=0)
sims = {
    '1 month':   ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(1)), **pars),
    '6 months':  ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(6)), **pars),
    '24 months': ss.Sim(make_cold(ss.months(24)), **pars),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('cold.I')

for sim in msim.sims:
    print(sim.label, '- mean number of infections per person:', round(sim.diseases.cold.infection.n_times.values.mean(), 1))








1 month - mean number of infections per person: 18.9
6 months - mean number of infections per person: 4.3
24 months - mean number of infections per person: 0.9


The shorter immunity is, the faster the susceptible pool is replenished, so transmission settles at a higher endemic level, and people are infected more often. With long-lasting immunity the model behaves much more like SIR: a single epidemic, followed by a long gap before the next wave.

title: Solutions: T3 – Building a disease
text:
Exercise 5
In the town with 90% immune, increase the fraction susceptible to 20% (init=dict(R=0.8)), so that each case infects about 3 others. What fraction of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?
Without superspreading, a fraction of about 1/R ≈ 1/3 die out. With superspreading, many more do, since most cases still infect nobody:

def make_sim(k=None):
    """ The measles model with 80% immune and 1 case, with the infectiousness of each person drawn from a gamma distribution with shape k """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    init = dict(init=dict(R=0.8), init_n=dict(I=1))
    sim_pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
    if k is None:
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, **init)
        return ss.Sim(measles, **sim_pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(shape=k, scale=1/k))
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, **init)
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **sim_pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=40)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- fraction that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))

Everyone equally infectious - fraction that die out: 0.375
k = 0.2 - fraction that die out: 0.7
