title: internals.transitions
text:
internals.transitions
States, transitions, and the expressions that drive them.
A model is a set of ss.State objects and the ss.Transition objects between them. A transition can be written with operators or in full, which build the same object:
S >> I @ 0.3 * I                                # Operators
ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I)               # In full
The ss.graph.Graph class (in internals/graph.py) collects the states and transitions of one module, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them. The expressions are in ss.expressions, the values that vary (ss.by, ss.timeseries, ss.seasonal) in ss.parameters, how a model is shown in ss.display, and its stratifications in ss.dimensions.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




State
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people


Transition
A movement between states


lifetable
A life table: how many die at each age, which ss.death(lifetable=) and ss.Deaths(lifetable=) take as a death rate for each age band (see hazards());


outcome
A reported quantity: a flow worked out from other flows, which moves nobody





internals.transitions.State(
    label=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,
    people=None,
    rel_sus=1.0,
    rel_trans=1.0,
    infected=False,
    keep_time=False,
    name=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people
A state is a compartment when the model runs as an ODE and a boolean array over agents when it runs as agents; the declaration is the same.











Name
Type
Description
Default




label
str
a human-readable name, for plots (e.g. S = ss.State('Susceptible'))
None


init
float
the fraction of people who start in the state (1.0 is everyone); for a state that is not people, its starting amount
None


init_n
int
instead, the number of people who start in the state
None


people
bool
whether this state holds people (the default), or is a count of something else (people=False: bacteria in the water, mosquitoes); people=True says so explicitly, for a group of people that only an inflow fills
None


rel_sus
float
susceptibility multiplier while in this state (one value; for a value by group, ss.modify(dis.rel_sus, multiply=ss.by(risk=[...])))
1.0


rel_trans
float
infectiousness multiplier while in this state (likewise)
1.0


infected
bool
whether the people in it are infected, which the disease otherwise works out from its force of infection (the states people are infected into, and those that infect them: E and I in S >> E @ beta*I); once any state is said to be, the infected states are exactly those said to be. The disease’s infected states give the results infected, the number in them, and prevalence, their fraction of everyone in its states (unless it defines its own); infected = E + I, given to the disease, says the same for several states
False


keep_time
bool
as agents, keep the time each person entered the state (ti_<name>) for code to read, e.g. the years since onset; by default it is kept only if the model reads it (a clock, a scheduled exit), to save memory
False


name
str
the name, if it is not the variable or keyword the state is given as (which it is taken from); a state that no variable holds takes its label as its name, if that is one word (ss.Disease(ss.State('S'), ...))
None






S, R = ss.states(2)
I = ss.State(init=0.01)     # 1% of people
E = ss.State(init_n=10)     # 10 people
V = ss.State('Vaccinated', rel_sus=0.2)
A = ss.State(keep_time=True) # Code reads mod.ti_A
H = ss.State('Hospitalized', infected=True) # Counted in the results infected and prevalence, though it does not transmit

Description

The event of entering this state: for when= (or ss.on()), or .uids

The event of leaving this state

Whether a starting value is given (init= or init_n=)

The fraction of the scheduled dwell time in this state that has elapsed, from 0 to 1 (NaN outside it)

Time since this person last entered the state, in the sim’s unit (NaN outside it)


total
The number in these states in the whole population: in a model with places, in every place, not only the same one as with .n







internals.transitions.Transition(
    source=None,
    dest=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=notgiven,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    min_stay=None,
    noise=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per_strain=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




source
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.unborn (births) or ss.outside (arrivals) for an inflow
None


dest
State / dict
the destination state; several (a split), as a dict of each and its probability ({D: p_death, R: None}, None for the rest); or ss.dead (deaths) or ss.outside (leaving) for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate)
None


p
float / None
the probability of taking it, for those it applies to (e.g. on an event); a split gives each destination’s in dest. With several transitions out of a state, each a branch with its own p=, p=None marks the one that takes the rest
notgiven


stages
int
the number of stages a dwell time is split into, in a row (an Erlang distribution), under every solver: more stages make the times in the state vary less around the mean
None


who
Cond / func / str
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ss.person.age > 30, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), as for ss.Event(who=); for everyone else its rate is 0
None


when
Event / on / Cond / func / str
what triggers it, instead of a rate (the same as @ ss.on(...)): an event moves the people it happens to (when=preg.delivery), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it (drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it; a condition moves people as soon as it holds (see ss.on); a path (when='preg.delivery', as ss.ref('preg.delivery')) stands for whatever is there, found when the sim is initialized
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


min_stay
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


noise
float / par
random variation of the rate from step to step (see below), for data that vary more than chance alone explains; sigma, which can be fitted (noise=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0, 0.3]))
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per_strain
str
for a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, an outcome for each strain carried: 'each' or 'first' (see below)
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None



Noise. noise= is sigma of gamma white noise (Bretó et al. 2009; pomp’s rgammawn): the chain binomial multiplies the rate, in each substep of length h, by a gamma draw with mean 1 and variance sigma²/h, for each group (and each particle of a filter). Sigma is in the square root of the sim’s unit (0.0878 in He et al.’s model, in years). Tau-leaping draws it for each leap (h its length), and agents once a step for each group (h the step); the ODE leaves it out (its mean), and the exact solver ('gillespie') refuses it.
Strains. With per_strain=:

'each': with a split, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (the first destination’s probability times the strain’s value for the transition, or '<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left; e.g. cure by treatment
'first': with a rate, each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on as the only strain carried (the others are dropped); e.g. one of two strains progressing




S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S, rate=0) # A rate of 0: only treatment moves people along it
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), who=ss.person.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), min_stay=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
infection = ss.Transition(S, E, rate=beta*I, noise=0.0878) # Infection whose rate varies at random from step to step (He et al. 2010)
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, when=ss.on(preg.delivery, delay=ss.months(6))) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact

internals.transitions.move(*args, p=None, n=None, uids=None, who=None)
Move people between states of a declared disease from code, the same way under every solver
A one-off move along no transition (as ss.Event(I >> R) is for a declared one). People can also be moved into the model and out of it: to ss.dead (they die) or ss.outside (they leave), and from ss.unborn (they are born) or ss.outside (they arrive), with n=. Every disease has the same people, so people who die or leave leave every disease, and people added are in each other disease’s first state, under every solver: as agents, they are agents who die or are made (a death happens at the end of the step, as people.request_death() does); in a compartmental run, the diseases tracked jointly lose and gain the same people, and a disease run apart loses them from its states in proportion, in each group, as it has them (it runs apart since its states do not depend on the others’). People added are placed in groups as declared births (ss.unborn) or arrivals (ss.outside) are. A count that is not people (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes) moves the same way. Also disease.move(...), the same with the disease given.

Type
Description

None

None

ss.move(sir.I, sir.R, p=0.5) # Cure half of those infectious

ss.move(sir.I, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of those infectious die
ss.move(ss.outside, sir.I, n=20) # Twenty people arrive infectious
sir.move(uids, ss.dead) # These agents die, whatever their state

internals.transitions.pars(defaults, **kwargs)
Create several parameters at once, from defaults and the values given, as a class’s declared parameters are made
For a disease whose states and transitions depend on its options, and so are made in __init__() rather than declared on the class (e.g. beta = ss.par(...), as ss.SIR does). Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. A name that is not a default is an error.

transitions = [S >> I @ p.beta*I, I >> R @ p.dur] + ([R >> I @ p.relapse] if p.relapse is not None else [])

Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people
A state is a compartment when the model runs as an ODE and a boolean array over agents when it runs as agents; the declaration is the same.

internals.transitions.Transition(
    source=None,
    dest=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=notgiven,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    min_stay=None,
    noise=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per_strain=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




source
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.unborn (births) or ss.outside (arrivals) for an inflow
None


dest
State / dict
the destination state; several (a split), as a dict of each and its probability ({D: p_death, R: None}, None for the rest); or ss.dead (deaths) or ss.outside (leaving) for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate)
None


p
float / None
the probability of taking it, for those it applies to (e.g. on an event); a split gives each destination’s in dest. With several transitions out of a state, each a branch with its own p=, p=None marks the one that takes the rest
notgiven


stages
int
the number of stages a dwell time is split into, in a row (an Erlang distribution), under every solver: more stages make the times in the state vary less around the mean
None


who
Cond / func / str
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ss.person.age > 30, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), as for ss.Event(who=); for everyone else its rate is 0
None


when
Event / on / Cond / func / str
what triggers it, instead of a rate (the same as @ ss.on(...)): an event moves the people it happens to (when=preg.delivery), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it (drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it; a condition moves people as soon as it holds (see ss.on); a path (when='preg.delivery', as ss.ref('preg.delivery')) stands for whatever is there, found when the sim is initialized
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


min_stay
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


noise
float / par
random variation of the rate from step to step (see below), for data that vary more than chance alone explains; sigma, which can be fitted (noise=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0, 0.3]))
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per_strain
str
for a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, an outcome for each strain carried: 'each' or 'first' (see below)
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None



Noise. noise= is sigma of gamma white noise (Bretó et al. 2009; pomp’s rgammawn): the chain binomial multiplies the rate, in each substep of length h, by a gamma draw with mean 1 and variance sigma²/h, for each group (and each particle of a filter). Sigma is in the square root of the sim’s unit (0.0878 in He et al.’s model, in years). Tau-leaping draws it for each leap (h its length), and agents once a step for each group (h the step); the ODE leaves it out (its mean), and the exact solver ('gillespie') refuses it.
Strains. With per_strain=:

'each': with a split, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (the first destination’s probability times the strain’s value for the transition, or '<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left; e.g. cure by treatment
'first': with a rate, each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on as the only strain carried (the others are dropped); e.g. one of two strains progressing




S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S, rate=0) # A rate of 0: only treatment moves people along it
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), who=ss.person.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), min_stay=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
infection = ss.Transition(S, E, rate=beta*I, noise=0.0878) # Infection whose rate varies at random from step to step (He et al. 2010)
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, when=ss.on(preg.delivery, delay=ss.months(6))) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact






Name
Description




dies
Whether everyone who takes it dies (ss.death(), I >> ss.dead); False for a split with ss.dead (see tr.may_die) and for people leaving alive (ss.emigration())


dur
The dwell time, as a parameter (or None, if the transition has a rate)


ever
Whether each person has gone through this transition, as a condition (agents only), e.g. who=~tb.diagnosis.ever


n_times

An inflow of people: at a crude (per-person) birth rate, e.g. ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)); or driven by a flow, e.g. ss.birth(NP, when=preg.delivery, children=2), children for each person who goes through the transition
With when=, as agents the children are made by the module that owns the transition, with parent set to the person who went through it, and placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(when=...) of the same transition, or else its first state. Agents only, for now.
Births of the whole population go in ss.Sim(demographics=[...]), where they are declared once for every disease’s people and run under every solver; births into one disease’s state go in the disease.

internals.transitions.migration(rate=None, rate_per=None, name=None)
Net migration of everyone, at a rate per person of either sign: arrivals less departures, as the UN gives it, e.g. ss.migration(rate='Albania')
A positive rate is arrivals, in proportion to the population (as agents, at the population’s ages: ss.immigration()); a negative one is departures (ss.emigration()). Both go in ss.Sim(demographics=[...]), and run under every solver. Since the rates are net, they say nothing about who migrates: as agents, those who leave are chosen at random.
The rates are read as those of ss.Births and ss.Deaths are (see ss.demographics.rate_per_of()): a bare number (per year) or a typed rate is per 1,000 people if it is above 1 per year (the median of the sizes, for a time series), else per person; rate_per= says which. internals.transitions.move(*args, p=None, n=None, uids=None, who=None)
Move people between states of a declared disease from code, the same way under every solver
A one-off move along no transition (as ss.Event(I >> R) is for a declared one). People can also be moved into the model and out of it: to ss.dead (they die) or ss.outside (they leave), and from ss.unborn (they are born) or ss.outside (they arrive), with n=. Every disease has the same people, so people who die or leave leave every disease, and people added are in each other disease’s first state, under every solver: as agents, they are agents who die or are made (a death happens at the end of the step, as people.request_death() does); in a compartmental run, the diseases tracked jointly lose and gain the same people, and a disease run apart loses them from its states in proportion, in each group, as it has them (it runs apart since its states do not depend on the others’). People added are placed in groups as declared births (ss.unborn) or arrivals (ss.outside) are. A count that is not people (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes) moves the same way. Also disease.move(...), the same with the disease given.





Name
Type
Description
Default




args

in any order, told apart by what they are: a move written with the states (sir.I >> sir.R), or the state (or a list of states) to move people from and the state to move them to, as the code sees them at run time (sir.I) or by name ('I'), the source first; the disease, which is enough to say where they come from (any of its states of people); and the agents to move (ss.uids), as uids=



p
float
the fraction of the people in the source to move, in each group (by default, everyone)
None


n
float
instead, the number of people to move, shared among the groups and states in proportion to who is in them
None


uids
uids
only these agents (those of them in the source), which needs agents; with p= or n=, a fraction or number of them
None


who
Cond / State / func / str
only the people for whom a condition holds (e.g. ss.person.age < 15, a group, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), under every solver; with p= or n=, a fraction or number of them
None














Name
Type
Description






The number of people moved






ss.move(sir.I, sir.R, p=0.5) # Cure half of those infectious
ss.move(sir.I >> sir.R, p=0.5) # The same, written as a move, as for ss.Event()
ss.move(sir.S, sir.I, n=5) # Five susceptible people become infectious
ss.move(sir.S, sir.R, p=0.8, who=ss.person.age < 5) # Protect 80% of the susceptible children under 5
sir.move(uids, sir.R) # These agents, from wherever they are (also ss.move(sir, uids, sir.R), or sir.move(uids, 'R'))
self.move(self.I, self.R, uids=uids) # In a disease's own code: these agents, if they are infectious
ss.move(sir.I, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of those infectious die
ss.move(ss.outside, sir.I, n=20) # Twenty people arrive infectious
sir.move(uids, ss.dead) # These agents die, whatever their state
ss.move(mosq.Sv, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of the mosquitoes die




internals.transitions.pars(defaults, **kwargs)
Create several parameters at once, from defaults and the values given, as a class’s declared parameters are made
For a disease whose states and transitions depend on its options, and so are made in __init__() rather than declared on the class (e.g. beta = ss.par(...), as ss.SIR does). Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. A name that is not a default is an error.











Name
Type
Description
Default




defaults
dict
the default of each parameter: a value, or an ss.par (with bounds, say)
required


kwargs
dict
the values given, e.g. the keywords of the disease’s __init__()




Returns an sc.obj of the parameters, by name.



defaults = dict(beta=ss.par(ss.peryear(2), bounds=[ss.peryear(0.5), ss.peryear(5)]), dur=ss.years(2), relapse=None)
p = ss.pars(defaults, beta=3) # beta is 3 per year, with the default's bounds
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
transitions = [S >> I @ p.beta*I, I >> R @ p.dur] + ([R >> I @ p.relapse] if p.relapse is not None else [])

None

bool / str / list
which of them are infected (see ss.State): all of them (True); some, by name, with names given up front ('E I'); or some, by position, with a number of states ([1, 2], or range(1, 6))
False

bool
also return the sum of the states, after them: the total of the people in them, often called N, for rates written with it: beta*I/N, the fraction of people in I, which is beta*I.frac; or the whole flow, beta*S*I/N, the same

Import models from other frameworks
ss.import_from(filename, format=...) reads another framework’s model into a sim; see v4_design/design/16-interop.md. Each importer reads its format into an ss.io.Source, and ss.io.build() writes that as Starsim code by the same rules for every format (ss.io.write()) and runs the code to make the sim: the code is kept in sim.imported.code, how each rate was read is printed, and what could not be translated is listed as ss.errors.ImportIncomplete and kept in sim.imported.

title: interventions
text:
interventions
Interventions, which change the course of a sim during a run
Interventions typically include things like testing, treatment, and vaccination. An event (ss.Event) moves the people it reaches, on a schedule or when another event happens, e.g. seeding infections; a delivery (ss.Delivery, and ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()) is an event that gives a product. Both exist so that the same intervention can be written once and run under any solver. It also works with a disease written as code, as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Delivery
Deliver a product to people: an ss.Event with what only interventions need; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()


Event
Something that happens to people: a move between states, on a schedule or when another event happens; see ss.Delivery to deliver a product


Intervention
Base class for interventions written as code


at_age
Who an event reaches: people as they reach an age, as its who=; e.g. ss.vaccinate(who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9)))


capacity
How many a delivery can serve, who is served first, and what happens to the rest, as its capacity=


screen
Deliver a diagnostic test; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


treat
Deliver a treatment; see ss.Delivery for the arguments


vaccinate
Deliver a vaccine; see ss.Delivery for the arguments





interventions.Delivery(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    coverage=None,
    capacity=None,
    strain=None,
    increment=None,
    trace=None,
    skip_reached_within=None,
    disease=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Deliver a product to people: an ss.Event with what only interventions need; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()
Who and when are as for ss.Event. What is delivered is a product (an ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment, or one written as code, an ss.Product with an administer(uids) method), or a move, as for an event, which a campaign can make (e.g. dict(vaccinated=True)). How many is said as for services: coverage=, the fraction reached, and capacity=, how many can be served, with ss.capacity() for who is served first and whether the rest wait. With an event as when=, the delivery reaches the people it happened to: an outcome of another delivery (when=screening.positive) on the same step, a transition of a disease (when=tb.care) on the next, since deliveries run before the diseases in each step.
A delivery is an event too, and so is each outcome of its product (a test’s positive and negative, a cure’s cured, failed, and unneeded): a follow-up is a delivery of its own, triggered by one (ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive)), and runs after it in the same step.
Its methods are how it runs as agents; in a compartmental run, what differs is delivery.in_compartments (see ss.solvers.CompartmentalDelivery).
Note: CRN safe as agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




what
Product / Transition / dict
what is delivered: a product, or a move as for ss.Event; ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat() instead take the product’s own keywords and make it, e.g. ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, ...)
None


who
Cond / func / at_age
who is eligible, as for ss.Event
None


when
date / list / dur / event / func / schedule
when it is delivered, as for ss.Event: in rounds (times, or ss.schedule(), e.g. with every=), on an event (with ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it, which is the time from the trigger to delivery, drawn per person if a distribution, agents only), or with none, routinely: each person is offered it once, at the first step they are eligible
None


start
date / float / dur
the start of a window it is delivered in, with any when=, as for ss.Event: e.g. when=onset, start=2001, on an event from 2001
None


stop
date / float / dur
the end of the window, likewise
None


coverage
float / rate / func
the fraction of those eligible who are reached; also ss.by(...), a typed rate or probability (e.g. ss.perday(0.1), ss.probperyear(0.5)): the chance over the step or the round (and, for routine delivery, offered at every step to those eligible); or a function of the sim, called at each step, returning one of these or, as agents, a probability for each person: an array over everyone alive, in the order of sim.people.uid, or an ss.Arr, read by UID; only the values of those eligible are used
None


capacity
float / rate / capacity
how many can be served: a number per round (or per step, for delivery on events), or a rate (e.g. ss.peryear(50_000)), which routine delivery needs; or ss.capacity(n, priority=..., queue=...), also saying who is served first and whether the rest wait. A capacity is for a service limited by supply or staff, rather than by how many come forward
None


strain
str / Strain
with a move into a state where people carry a strain, the strain they arrive with
None


increment
str / dict
instead of a product, a counter that goes up for those reached, as for ss.Event
None


trace
str / Network / list
contact tracing: deliver to the contacts, in this network (or these), of the people the event in when= reaches, instead of to them; who= and coverage= then apply to the contacts. Agents only. A network with memory= also gives the partnerships of that long ago that have ended (e.g. ss.DegreeNet(..., memory=ss.months(12)))
None


skip_reached_within
dur
skip the people this delivery reached less than this long ago (agents only), e.g. ss.years(1) for a re-screening interval; the same as who=~(delivery.since < ss.years(1)), which the delivery cannot name before it exists
None


disease
str / list
the disease the product acts on (default: the only one); or a list of them, for one product that acts on several (e.g. a bivalent vaccine), delivered once
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






# A campaign that leaves a mark, for 70% of the unvaccinated in two rounds
rollout = ss.Delivery(dict(vaccinated=True), coverage=0.7, when=[5, 30], who=~sir.vaccinated)

# A test, and a treatment of those who test positive, as two deliveries
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.95, who=ss.person.age > 30, coverage=0.4, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(7)))
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

# Routine vaccination at nine months, from 2025 (the same as when=ss.schedule(start=2025))
mcv1 = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9)), coverage=0.8, start=2025)

# Testing those with symptoms, from 2001 to 2010
testing = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, when=sir.infection, coverage=0.3, start=2001, stop=2010)




interventions.Event(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    n=None,
    p=None,
    strain=None,
    increment=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something that happens to people: a move between states, on a schedule or when another event happens; see ss.Delivery to deliver a product
An event has three parts, each optional. What happens to those it reaches: a move between two states (S >> I), levels of a stratification (dict(risk=('low', 'high'))), or strains (DS >> RIF), or an increment of a counter; with none, it is only an event, which others trigger on (e.g. a clinic visit). Who it reaches: a condition on people, or on the population (sir.I.n > 1000, which decides for everyone at once), or people as they reach an age (ss.at_age()). And when: at times (when=[2025, 2030], when='2024-03-01', or when=ss.days(30), 30 days after the start), on a schedule (when=ss.schedule(every=ss.months(1), start='2024-01-01', stop='2025-01-01')), when another event happens (when=sir.infection, or when=ss.on(sir.infection, delay=ss.days(5))), or, with no when=, routinely: each person once, at the first step they are eligible. start= and stop= limit any of these to a window (the same as when=ss.schedule(start=..., stop=...) for routine events), e.g. when=screening.positive, start=2001.
n= and p= say how many it reaches each time, as for ss.move(): at most n of those eligible, chosen at random, and each with probability p.
It is an event itself: others trigger on it (when=seeding), and it remembers per person whether (.ever), how often (.n_times), and how long ago (.since) it happened. event.reached() is the UIDs of the people it reached on the step (agents only).
Note: CRN safe as agents.





Name
Type
Description
Default




what
Transition / dict / str
what happens to those it reaches: a move between states (S >> I, from any of several, U + P >> P, or by the paths of the states, 'sir.S >> sir.I'), a move to a level of a stratification (dict(vaccinated=True)) or from one level to another (dict(risk=('low', 'high'))), or a change of strains (DS >> RIF)
None


who
Cond / func / at_age
who it can reach: a condition on people (ss.person.age < 5, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), on the population (sir.I.n > 1000), or both joined with &; people as they reach an age (ss.at_age(ss.months(9))); or a function of the sim returning who is eligible (UIDs, a mask, or True or False for everyone); to reach exactly those it returns at each step, also give when= every step
None


when
date / list / dur / event / func / schedule
when it happens: a time or list of them (dates, years, or durations after the start of the sim: ss.days(10) is 10 days in, and with no calendar day 10); an event that triggers it (sir.infection, screening.positive, or a transition by its path), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it; a function of the date of each step, true when it happens; or ss.schedule(), for how often (every=), or any of these with a start= and stop= (with only those, routinely between them)
None


start
date / float / dur
the start of a window it happens in, with any when= (e.g. on an event, from 2001): a shorthand for when=ss.schedule(start=...) that also goes with an event (default: the start of the sim)
None


stop
date / float / dur
the end of the window, likewise (default: the end of the sim)
None


n
float / rate
the most it reaches each time: a number, or a rate (e.g. ss.peryear(20)), which routine events need, since they have no rounds for a number to be per
None


p
float / rate / func
the probability that each person eligible is reached; also ss.by(...), a typed rate or probability (e.g. ss.perday(0.1)), or a function of the sim returning one, or (as agents) one per person
None


strain
str / Strain
with a move into a state where people carry a strain (e.g. S >> E), the strain they arrive with
None


increment
str / dict
instead of a move, a counter that goes up for those reached: its name, which adds 1, or a dict of the amount for each
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None






# Seeding: three people, chosen from everyone susceptible, infected every 30 days for ten years
seeds = ss.Event(S >> I, n=3, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(30), start=ss.days(30), stop=ss.years(10)))

# A new strain on a date
alpha = ss.Event(S >> E, n=20, when='2021-01-01', strain='alpha')

# Twenty importations a year, for the first five years
imports = ss.Event(S >> I, n=ss.peryear(20), stop=ss.years(5))

# Moving people to high risk, five days after infection, half of them
risky = ss.Event(dict(risk=('low', 'high')), when=ss.on(sir.infection, delay=ss.days(5)), p=0.5)

# Each round of a campaign adds a dose (with sim.stratify(doses=[0, 1, 2, 3]))
campaign = ss.Event(increment='doses', p=0.6, when=[2025, 2026, 2027])






Name
Description




age_years
With at_age=: the age, in years


cost
The cost of each delivery: its product’s


dis
The disease the product acts on: declared, or written as code

interventions.Intervention(*args, who=None, **kwargs)
Base class for interventions written as code
Write one when the built-in events and deliveries cannot say what the intervention does. Its key method is step(), called on each timestep, which can change the states of the diseases (e.g. treating or vaccinating agents). To deliver a product, or to move people between states, use ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), ss.treat(), or ss.Event() instead, which run under every solver.
An intervention written as code can be given who=, who it can reach, as for a delivery: a condition on people (ss.person.age < 5), or a function of the sim (and of the intervention, as self) returning UIDs or a mask. Its step() then reads the people eligible now with check_eligibility().











Name
Type
Description
Default




args
list
passed to ss.Module



who
Cond / func
who it can reach (by default everyone alive), read by check_eligibility()
None


kwargs
dict
passed to ss.Module




Example:
class Discount(ss.Intervention):
    def step(self):
        uids = self.check_eligibility() # Those who= holds for now, alive
        self.sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[uids] = 0.5

sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=Discount(who=ss.person.age < 15)).run()

Deliver a diagnostic test; see ss.Delivery for the arguments
when=ss.on(event, delay=...) is the delivery’s, the time from its trigger to the test, as for any delivery; the time from the test to its result is the test’s (ss.Diagnostic(result_delay=...)).
Its outcomes, positive and negative, are events on the step the result is available (after the test’s result_delay), and results: the number with each result on each step. What happens next is a step of its own, triggered by an outcome (when=screening.positive).
Note: CRN safe as agents.


S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10), init_prev=0.01)
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.98, coverage=0.4, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(7)))
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=[screening, treatment], stop=100).run()

Delivery
Deliver a product to people: an ss.Event with what only interventions need; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()

interventions.Delivery(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    coverage=None,
    capacity=None,
    strain=None,
    increment=None,
    trace=None,
    skip_reached_within=None,
    disease=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Deliver a product to people: an ss.Event with what only interventions need; see ss.vaccinate(), ss.screen(), and ss.treat()
Who and when are as for ss.Event. What is delivered is a product (an ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, or ss.Treatment, or one written as code, an ss.Product with an administer(uids) method), or a move, as for an event, which a campaign can make (e.g. dict(vaccinated=True)). How many is said as for services: coverage=, the fraction reached, and capacity=, how many can be served, with ss.capacity() for who is served first and whether the rest wait. With an event as when=, the delivery reaches the people it happened to: an outcome of another delivery (when=screening.positive) on the same step, a transition of a disease (when=tb.care) on the next, since deliveries run before the diseases in each step.
A delivery is an event too, and so is each outcome of its product (a test’s positive and negative, a cure’s cured, failed, and unneeded): a follow-up is a delivery of its own, triggered by one (ss.treat(drug, when=screening.positive)), and runs after it in the same step.
Its methods are how it runs as agents; in a compartmental run, what differs is delivery.in_compartments (see ss.solvers.CompartmentalDelivery).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

A capacity is for a service limited by supply or staff, rather than by how many come forward

# A campaign that leaves a mark, for 70% of the unvaccinated in two rounds
rollout = ss.Delivery(dict(vaccinated=True), coverage=0.7, when=[5, 30], who=~sir.vaccinated)

# A test, and a treatment of those who test positive, as two deliveries
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, specificity=0.95, who=ss.person.age > 30, coverage=0.4, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(7)))
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, when=screening.positive, coverage=0.8)

# Routine vaccination at nine months, from 2025 (the same as when=ss.schedule(start=2025))
mcv1 = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9)), coverage=0.8, start=2025)

# Testing those with symptoms, from 2001 to 2010
testing = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.9, when=sir.infection, coverage=0.3, start=2001, stop=2010)




interventions.Event(
    what=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    n=None,
    p=None,
    strain=None,
    increment=None,
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something that happens to people: a move between states, on a schedule or when another event happens; see ss.Delivery to deliver a product
An event has three parts, each optional. What happens to those it reaches: a move between two states (S >> I), levels of a stratification (dict(risk=('low', 'high'))), or strains (DS >> RIF), or an increment of a counter; with none, it is only an event, which others trigger on (e.g. a clinic visit). Who it reaches: a condition on people, or on the population (sir.I.n > 1000, which decides for everyone at once), or people as they reach an age (ss.at_age()). And when: at times (when=[2025, 2030], when='2024-03-01', or when=ss.days(30), 30 days after the start), on a schedule (when=ss.schedule(every=ss.months(1), start='2024-01-01', stop='2025-01-01')), when another event happens (when=sir.infection, or when=ss.on(sir.infection, delay=ss.days(5))), or, with no when=, routinely: each person once, at the first step they are eligible. start= and stop= limit any of these to a window (the same as when=ss.schedule(start=..., stop=...) for routine events), e.g. when=screening.positive, start=2001.
n= and p= say how many it reaches each time, as for ss.move(): at most n of those eligible, chosen at random, and each with probability p.
It is an event itself: others trigger on it (when=seeding), and it remembers per person whether (.ever), how often (.n_times), and how long ago (.since) it happened. event.reached() is the UIDs of the people it reached on the step (agents only).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

Type
Description
Default

None

when

when it happens: a time or list of them (dates, years, or durations after the start of the sim: ss.days(10) is 10 days in, and with no calendar day 10); an event that triggers it (sir.infection, screening.positive, or a transition by its path), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it; a function of the date of each step, true when it happens; or ss.schedule(), for how often (every=), or any of these with a start= and stop= (with only those, routinely between them)

the probability that each person eligible is reached; also ss.by(...), a typed rate or probability (e.g. ss.perday(0.1)), or a function of the sim returning one, or (as agents) one per person
None

with a move into a state where people carry a strain (e.g. S >> E), the strain they arrive with
None

# Seeding: three people, chosen from everyone susceptible, infected every 30 days for ten years
seeds = ss.Event(S >> I, n=3, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.days(30), start=ss.days(30), stop=ss.years(10)))

# A new strain on a date
alpha = ss.Event(S >> E, n=20, when='2021-01-01', strain='alpha')

# Twenty importations a year, for the first five years
imports = ss.Event(S >> I, n=ss.peryear(20), stop=ss.years(5))

# Moving people to high risk, five days after infection, half of them
risky = ss.Event(dict(risk=('low', 'high')), when=ss.on(sir.infection, delay=ss.days(5)), p=0.5)

# Each round of a campaign adds a dose (with sim.stratify(doses=[0, 1, 2, 3]))
campaign = ss.Event(increment='doses', p=0.6, when=[2025, 2026, 2027])

Base class for interventions written as code
Write one when the built-in events and deliveries cannot say what the intervention does. Its key method is step(), called on each timestep, which can change the states of the diseases (e.g. treating or vaccinating agents). when=ss.on(event, delay=...) is the delivery’s, the time from its trigger to the test, as for any delivery; the time from the test to its result is the test’s (ss.Diagnostic(result_delay=...)).

solvers.deliveries
Not for the user: deliveries in a compartmental run
ss.Event (and its subclass ss.Delivery) is the one class for events and deliveries, and its methods are how it runs as agents. In a compartmental run, a delivery also makes a CompartmentalDelivery (delivery.in_compartments), which holds what only that needs: a selection is the fraction of the people in each state and group, so who is reached, served, moved, cured, or tested is a fraction of each, and moving them moves fractions of the engine’s compartments between groups, carrying the events of the step along. title: library.econ
text:
library.econ
Health economics: the costs of a sim, disability-adjusted life years, discounting, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules
Costs are not part of every sim, so these live in the library rather than in core Starsim: ssl.Costs adds a sim’s costs up as results, ssl.DALYs does the same for disability-adjusted life years, ssl.discount() discounts a result over time, and ssl.ICER compares the costs and effects of scenarios, after they have run or as a sim runs.





Name
Description




Costs
The costs of a sim, from its results, with their total


DALYs
The disability-adjusted life years of a sim: the years lived with disability, plus the years of life lost


ICER
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios





library.econ.Costs(
    unit_costs=None,
    fixed=None,
    start=None,
    deliveries=True,
    **kwargs,
)
The costs of a sim, from its results, with their total
Each delivery made with a cost= (e.g. ss.vaccinate(..., cost=5)) already has a cost result; this adds them up, along with a cost for each event of any other result (e.g. care for each infection) and a fixed cost per unit time. Every cost is a result of this analyzer, named after where it came from, and total is their sum.

a cost per unit time that does not depend on any result, such as running a program (staff, cold chain, training), e.g. ss.peryear(1000)

import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

vx = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, who=ss.person.age < 5, when=ss.schedule(every=ss.years(1)), coverage=0.5, cost=5)
costs = ssl.Costs(unit_costs={'sir.infection': 50}, fixed=ss.peryear(1000))
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sir', networks='random', interventions=vx, analyzers=costs)
sim.run()
sim.results.costs.plot()
print(sim.results.costs.total.sum())

library.econ.ICER(
    sims=None,
    outcome='dalys.dalys',
    cost='costs.total',
    baseline=None,
    discount=0,
    discount_start=None,
    window=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios
Each scenario’s cost and outcome are totaled (discounted if discount is given), and the outcome averted is that of the baseline less the scenario’s. The scenarios are ordered by cost, and each is compared with the next cheaper one that isn’t dominated. A scenario is dominated if it costs more and averts no more than a cheaper one, and extendedly dominated if a mix of two others would avert more for the same cost. With several runs of each scenario, their means are compared.
This works in two ways. After the scenarios have run, give them to ssl.ICER(), and read icer.df. Or add it to a sim as an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs: the sim then counts as one more scenario, compared at each step with the scenarios given over the same period, so that what runs in the sim can act on the comparison, for example an intervention that follows icer.best(wtp=1000).

    sims=None,
    outcome='dalys.dalys',
    cost='costs.total',
    baseline=None,
    discount=0,
    discount_start=None,
    window=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Compare the costs and effects of scenarios: incremental cost-effectiveness ratios
Each scenario’s cost and outcome are totaled (discounted if discount is given), and the outcome averted is that of the baseline less the scenario’s. The scenarios are ordered by cost, and each is compared with the next cheaper one that isn’t dominated. A scenario is dominated if it costs more and averts no more than a cheaper one, and extendedly dominated if a mix of two others would avert more for the same cost. With several runs of each scenario, their means are compared.
This works in two ways. After the scenarios have run, give them to ssl.ICER(), and read icer.df. Or add it to a sim as an analyzer, after ssl.Costs and ssl.DALYs: the sim then counts as one more scenario, compared at each step with the scenarios given over the same period, so that what runs in the sim can act on the comparison, for example an intervention that follows icer.best(wtp=1000).

title: solvers.compartmental
text:
solvers.compartmental
Not for the user: the compartmental engine: a declared model run as groups of people (ode, ide, binomial, gillespie, and tau)
It exists so that a model with nothing per person can run faster than as agents, from the same declaration.
Used with: compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




Compartmental
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode, ide) or stochastically





solvers.compartmental.Compartmental(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode, ide) or stochastically (binomial, gillespie, or tau)
It exists so that the deterministic and stochastic forms share one engine.
The states are expanded into compartments (one per branch and sub-stage) and the transitions into a flat list of flows, each with a source compartment, a rate, and the compartments it feeds. Every solver steps the same list of flows.





Name
Description




engines
The engines whose people its program holds, as joint states’: this one


owner
What holds the people and the program that runs them: this engine, or the joint states its disease is tracked jointly in (see ss.solvers.JointStates), whose program steps them all


saturates
Whether a term of the mixing is a network whose edges each transmit at most once in a step (see saturation())


shared
Whether this engine moves people in ways that belong to the sim rather than to the module (aging, relocating, the movement register): in joint states, only one does (see ss.solvers.JointStates.lead), since they all see the same people


smooth
Whether any parameter varies smoothly in time (not as a step function), so is taken at the middle of each step


transfer_index
The position of each transfer among the flows of a whole run (after the transitions, with the other movers)









Name
Description




add_per_births
After a step: the children of those who went through a transition with births driven by its flow (ss.birth(when=)), n for each, in the youngest groups of their parents’ place


aging_rates
The rate per year at which people age out of each age group (but the last): the density of people in the year below


apart_fracs
For several non-exponential dwell times out of a state, each for other people (who=): the fraction of each group that enters each one’s track, 1 for the one it has (the first, if none)


arrive
Add an amount to a state, split between its tracks; with before=True, as if they arrived a step before (people infectious at the start, who have been so for the first step, as agents date them), so one slot along a conveyor


as_is
Whether a dwell time runs as it is, as a conveyor of whole steps (see slot_rates()), rather than as Erlang stages: under


at_home
Whether a time fraction between places (a sparse array) keeps everyone at home, as np.allclose(frac, np.eye(P)) would say, without forming either


at_middle
Take values that vary smoothly in time at the middle of the step, which runs from time point ti to the next, as tables() does, so that a stepped run takes the same values as a whole one


attr
An attribute in a compartmental run: a trait is the mean of its distribution, as a parameter that is a distribution is (see trait_mean())


backfill_burnin
A module’s people who start part way through (ss.Pregnancy(burnin=True): see its burnin_plan()): each group’s


binomial_substeps
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())


birth_map
Where the children of the people in each group are born (rows to columns): the youngest group of each dimension, by the split of the others, in their parents’ place


births_of
The engine and inflow of each declared module with an ss.birth(when=) of the same transition as tr (this module’s own first)


branch_where

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.binomial_substeps()
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())
People who arrive in a compartment within a substep leave it from the next, so a compartment holds about x/2 too many, with x its total rate out times the substep, and R is that much too high. So x is kept to binomial_bias (5%), which bounds the bias in each compartment to about 2.5%; and near the epidemic threshold, where the prevalence moves by the bias in R over R0 - 1 (an SIS’s endemic prevalence is 1 - 1/R0), to 0.1 × |R0 - 1|, for a bias of about 5% (a model of TB resistance, +12% at 3 substeps a month, is +3% at 12; an SIS with R0 = 1.05 gave 0.083 for 0.048 at whole steps). A fixed delay doesn’t count, since its people don’t leave at a rate: a model whose only exits are fixed delays takes whole steps, which keeps its final size but lowers its peak (by about 15% for an SIR at a fifth of the delay a step); ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=3) gives about 5%, for about twice the time.

The next-generation matrix at the disease-free state, F V⁻¹, over the infected compartments of every group
The infected compartments are those of the states people are infected into or infect from, of any count (such as a reservoir, or infectious mosquitoes) that the rate of an infection uses, and of the counts that infected people’s numbers move a count into (mosquitoes biting them). A new infection is a flow from any other compartment into one of these. At the disease-free state, nobody is infected (so the infected at the start are not counted), and everyone else is in the first state, or in the state their own chain of states starts from if no transition links it to the first (e.g. S_H2 of a second host species; see chain_start()), so R0 is in a population with no immunity; with start=True, the people not infected are as they start, for the reproduction number at the start. Each group keeps its size, except that the people filled by a constant inflow (births of a number a day) and the counts filled by any inflow (mosquitoes not infected) are at their equilibrium, from the rates at the disease-free state. Given the compartments y (one row per compartment, one column per group), the matrix is instead at that state as it is, for the reproduction number at that time (see ss.Disease.Rt()). The matrices are worked out by perturbing each infected compartment in turn. Returns None if nothing moves people into an infected state. See ss.Disease.R0().

title: solvers.compartmental
text:
Name
Description




Compartmental
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode, ide) or stochastically





solvers.compartmental.Compartmental(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as compartments: deterministically (ode, ide) or stochastically (binomial, gillespie, or tau)
It exists so that the deterministic and stochastic forms share one engine.
The states are expanded into compartments (one per branch and sub-stage) and the transitions into a flat list of flows, each with a source compartment, a rate, and the compartments it feeds. Every solver steps the same list of flows.

Add an amount to a state, split between its tracks; with before=True, as if they arrived a step before (people infectious at the start, who have been so for the first step, as agents date them), so one slot along a conveyor



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.as_is(dwell)
Whether a dwell time runs as it is, as a conveyor of whole steps (see slot_rates()), rather than as Erlang stages: under solver=ss.solvers.ode(dwells=‘exact’), any whose distribution function is known; under every compartmental solver, one that takes only whole numbers of steps (an ss.choice of them, e.g. days with daily steps), which is then exact, as it is for agents



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.at_home(frac)
Whether a time fraction between places (a sparse array) keeps everyone at home, as np.allclose(frac, np.eye(P)) would say, without forming either



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.at_middle()
Take values that vary smoothly in time at the middle of the step, which runs from time point ti to the next, as tables() does, so that a stepped run takes the same values as a whole one



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.attr(a)
An attribute in a compartmental run: a trait is the mean of its distribution, as a parameter that is a distribution is (see trait_mean())



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.backfill_burnin(sp)
A module’s people who start part way through (ss.Pregnancy(burnin=True): see its burnin_plan()): each group’s fraction of the first state (sp.frac()) is moved to the target, spread evenly over its compartments (stages, or the slots of a fixed time), as if they entered uniformly over the steps before the start (the module’s fraction takes off those who would have left on the way)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.binomial_substeps()
The substeps the chain-binomial solver takes in each step, from the fastest total rate out of a compartment of people at the start (see substeps())
People who arrive in a compartment within a substep leave it from the next, so a compartment holds about x/2 too many, with x its total rate out times the substep, and R is that much too high. So x is kept to binomial_bias (5%), which bounds the bias in each compartment to about 2.5%; and near the epidemic threshold, where the prevalence moves by the bias in R over R0 - 1 (an SIS’s endemic prevalence is 1 - 1/R0), to 0.1 × |R0 - 1|, for a bias of about 5% (a model of TB resistance, +12% at 3 substeps a month, is +3% at 12; an SIS with R0 = 1.05 gave 0.083 for 0.048 at whole steps). A fixed delay doesn’t count, since its people don’t leave at a rate: a model whose only exits are fixed delays takes whole steps, which keeps its final size but lowers its peak (by about 15% for an SIR at a fifth of the delay a step); ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=3) gives about 5%, for about twice the time.

Where the children of the people in each group are born (rows to columns): the youngest group of each dimension, by the split of the others, in their parents’ place

The engine and inflow of each declared module with an ss.birth(when=) of the same transition as tr (this module’s own first)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.branch_where(tr)

solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.next_generation(start=False, y=None)
The next-generation matrix at the disease-free state, F V⁻¹, over the infected compartments of every group
The infected compartments are those of the states people are infected into or infect from, of any count (such as a reservoir, or infectious mosquitoes) that the rate of an infection uses, and of the counts that infected people’s numbers move a count into (mosquitoes biting them). A new infection is a flow from any other compartment into one of these. At the disease-free state, nobody is infected (so the infected at the start are not counted), and everyone else is in the first state, or in the state their own chain of states starts from if no transition links it to the first (e.g. S_H2 of a second host species; see chain_start()), so R0 is in a population with no immunity; with start=True, the people not infected are as they start, for the reproduction number at the start. Each group keeps its size, except that the people filled by a constant inflow (births of a number a day) and the counts filled by any inflow (mosquitoes not infected) are at their equilibrium, from the rates at the disease-free state. Given the compartments y (one row per compartment, one column per group), the matrix is instead at that state as it is, for the reproduction number at that time (see ss.Disease.Rt()). The matrices are worked out by perturbing each infected compartment in turn. Returns None if nothing moves people into an infected state. See ss.Disease.R0().

For a step in the kernels: the tables and row to take its values from, or, with these set in the program already, no tables, and a row of -1 if they are as in the last step

Move those a declared disease’s own transmit() gives for each of its transmissions, at the start of the step (see ss.Disease.transmit()): from its source states in proportion, in each group, counted in its flow



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.step_triggers()
The transitions moved by an event of this module (when= one of its transitions), at the end of each step: the fraction of each source state and group the step’s event happened to moves then, as a delivery’s people do (triggers on conditions are passed straight through instead: see update_targets() and sweep_triggers())

Type
Description
Default

iterable

required

Store a result of a whole run: its total at each time point, and its values by group if it keeps them; returns the totals



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.substeps()
The number of substeps to take in each timestep (0 to let the solver choose)
The chain-binomial solver takes enough substeps that its step bias is small, as far as the rates are known at the start (at most max_binomial): see binomial_substeps(). Each substep is off the ODE by an amount of order rate × dt (an acute stage of 1.7 months at monthly steps can take everyone infected from 9% to 51%). It moves people through as many stages of a dwell time as they pass in a substep (see ss.kernels.draw_chain()), so it is the dwell’s mean that counts, not its stages; a fixed delay is a conveyor of whole steps, so its length doesn’t count. ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=1) takes whole steps, as most chain-binomial models (and frameworks’ discrete-time models) do.



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.sweep_triggers()
At each step: move the people a trigger holds for who are still in its source (who arrived by aging, a transfer, or another disease’s move, or for whom a condition on time or counts has come to hold)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.sync_maps(sy)
For a synchronized flow: the map between groups that moves the other module’s coordinate (its dimension in the joint) from the levels of its transition’s source to those of its destination (entry, split by its branches), the fraction of each group that it moves, and where the flow is recorded in the other module’s groups



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.sync_rec(sy, val)
A synchronized flow by this module’s groups (the last axis), as the other module’s



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.synced(dim_map, syn)
The map of a flow along a transition that other modules’ transitions are triggered by: its own, then moving their coordinates



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.syncs_of(tr, dst)
The synchronized flows of a transition (to a destination), with their maps worked out



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.table_years(raw)
The year of each row of the tables, one a step, for a value that varies in time: the middle of the step, or its start for a step function, which is held from there, and for Euler’s method, which reads everything there



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.tables(start=0, stop=None)
The parts of the program that can change over time, at each step (or as a single entry, if nothing varies)
A value that varies in time is worked out for every step at once. Modifiers that depend only on time are applied to the steps between the times they change, each span worked out at once in the same way; only a modifier that could change at any step (e.g. one that follows a smooth time series) is worked out step by step. The tables of a whole run are kept for as long as everything they are worked out from is the same, so a sim that is run again, with the same values, does not work them out again.

Type
Description
Default

int
the first step to give the tables for (for a run taken a part at a time: see run_parts())
0

int

None

Some of the people in a compartment: a fraction, or a draw where the solver keeps whole numbers

After a step: the flow along each transition and mover over it, by group, and the people at its end



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.tape_values()
The value of each expression on the tape, worked out once a step (or again, whenever the values it uses can have changed, as the engine’s other cached values are)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.targets(changes)
The group that each group’s people move to when their level in some dimensions is changed ({dimension index: level})



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.trait_mean(mod, a, sim)
Whether an attribute (ss.attr) has a compartmental form: a trait drawn from a distribution, with no modifier, which a compartmental run takes at its mean (see attr())



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.transmitted(tr)
The number infected in the step in each group by a transmission, as the solver works it out at the start of the step: the people in each of its source compartments times the chance of the flow in the step, 1 − exp(−rate·dt) (the default of a declared disease’s transmit(), see ss.Disease.transmit())



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.trigger_frac(tr)
Where a trigger holds, as the fraction of each state (rows) and group (columns) it selects



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.trigger_mask(tr, name)
The groups of a state where a trigger on states and strata holds (1) or not (0); 0 for one on time or counts, which is applied at each step instead: see sweep_triggers()



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.update_targets()
Work out where each flow’s arrivals go; done once per step, since branch probabilities can change (and only worked out again if they have)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.varying_dwell(name, tr, raw, dw, to_unit)
A dwell time whose distribution has parameters with a value for each group (ss.by)
Each group gets the Erlang stages that match its own mean and standard deviation (ragged stages); a function as well has no compartmental form. (Agents look the parameters up for each agent, and make one draw: see Agents.varying_dwell().)



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.weight(expr, state)
What each group’s people in a state count as in a weighted count: their weight, times their infectiousness for n_infectious (as in exposure())



solvers.compartmental.Compartmental.whole_outcomes(todo, flows, weights, width)
The outcomes drawn all at once, by name: with no delay or stay, an outcome’s only draws are binomials of the flows it comes from, one call in the same order as a step at a time; or None if any has more than that

    what,
    dur,
    lowest,
    nearest=False,

A time as a number of whole steps (up, or to the nearest with nearest=True; at least lowest), with a note if it is not one

title: analyzers
text:
analyzers
Analyzers, which record more than a sim records by default, as it runs
For example, the number infected by age or by sex, or who infected whom (ss.infection_log).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Analyzer
Base class for analyzers, which record more about a sim than it records by default: for


infection_log
Log who infected whom – see ss.diseases.InfectionLog for detail





analyzers.Analyzer(name=None, label=None, **kwargs)
Base class for analyzers, which record more about a sim than it records by default: for example, a state of the people on each step, read before the next step changes it.
An analyzer records results as any module does: those about the state at the start of each step (stocks) in record_states(), and those about what happened in it (flows) in record_events() (both with self.ti the step’s, as in every module). Its step(), if it has one, is called at the end of each step, after the flows are recorded, when the people are as they are at the next time point.


class BySex(ss.Analyzer):
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('infected', columns=['female', 'male'], kind='stock'))

    def record_states(self):
        infected, female = self.sim.diseases.sis.I, self.sim.people.female
        self.results.infected[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(infected & female), np.count_nonzero(infected & ~female)]
An analyzer that reads who infected whom sets needs_infection_log = True: each disease then keeps its infection log (disease.infection_log, see ss.infection_log), as with an ss.infection_log in the sim.






Name
Description




step
Nothing by default: an analyzer usually only records results (see record_states() and record_events())





analyzers.Analyzer.step()
Nothing by default: an analyzer usually only records results (see record_states() and record_events())





analyzers.infection_log(**kwargs)
Log who infected whom – see ss.diseases.InfectionLog for detail
This analyzer turns on the infection log of each disease, rather than recording anything itself, since who infected whom is known only inside the disease’s transmit() step.
Each entry has the time (t), the person infected (target), who infected them (source), and the route (network). The source is known only for transmission over a network, where each infection is drawn along an edge: seeds have a source of -1, and infections by a mixing pool (ss.MixingPool), a contact matrix, or mixing with everyone (no network) have a source and network of NaN, since they come from the fraction infectious in a group rather than from a particular person (by events, solver=ss.solvers.abm(step='events'), each contact is with a particular person, so these have a source and route too). For a disease with strains (ss.Strains), each entry also has the strain transmitted (strain; for seeds, the strains they start with). As agents only.
The log stays on the disease (sim.diseases.sir.infection_log) as well, so several analyzers can read it, during the run or after. To follow transmission as the sim runs, an analyzer reads the entries of each step with disease.infection_log.to_df(ti=self.ti) (see ss.diseases.InfectionLog.to_df()).
Note: CRN safe.


import starsim as ss
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=1000, diseases='sir', networks='random', analyzers='infection_log')
sim.run()
sim.analyzers[0].plot()

Description




log
The infection log, if there is only one disease









Name
Description




animate
Animate the infection log – mostly for amusement!


finalize_results
Collect the infection logs from each of the diseases (the same logs, so several analyzers can share them)


plot
Plot all of the infection logs


to_df
Convert the infection log to a dataframe, if there is only one disease

    framerate=10,
    clear=False,
    cmap='parula',
    **kwargs,
)

run.MultiSim(
    sims=None,
    label=None,
    n_runs=None,
    pars=None,
    priors=False,
    inplace=True,
    **kwargs,
)
The runs of one or more sims: every result of the sims with a run axis first, and the sims that were run
Made and run by ss.parallel(), the way to run many sims; ss.MultiSim(...) with the same arguments, then msim.run(), does the same (and is the class to subclass). Each sim is run once unless n_runs, pars, or priors is given: a single sim, ss.MultiSim(sim), is one run, where in Starsim 3 it was run four times by default (ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=4) for that). To make and initialize the sim of each run without running them, use msim.init_sims().





Name
Type
Description
Default




sims
Sim / list / dict
a single sim, a list/tuple of sims, a dict of sims by label, or another MultiSim (or list of MultiSims); the first is msim.base_sim, whose label and settings the MultiSim shows
None


label
str
the name of the multisim
None


n_runs
int
the number of runs of each sim, each with its own seed (by default, 1)
None


pars
dict / list
sets of values of parameters to run each sim with; see ss.parallel()
None


priors
bool / dict
draw n_runs sets of values from the priors of the parameters, or the draws to run; see ss.parallel()
False


inplace
bool
whether to update sims that are run as they are (with no n_runs or pars) with their results (default True)
True


kwargs
dict
how to run the sims, as for ss.parallel(): workers (the number of worker processes: by default one per CPU; 1 runs them one after another in this process), until and verbose (as for sim.run()), shrink, par_args, and run_args




By default (verbose not given: the sims’ own verbose, if they share one, else ss.options.verbose) the runs print nothing of their own, and the MultiSim shows their progress: nothing for runs that are done within a second, a bar for each run if there are up to 10 that each take more than 10 seconds, and otherwise one bar with the number of runs done (to a file, a line every tenth); then a line on what was run.
Once run, a MultiSim has:

results: every result with a run axis first (see ss.Result), e.g. msim.results.sir.I.quantiles();
runs: one row per run, with its scenario (the label of its sim), the values of any parameters swept or drawn, and its seed (rand_seed);
sims: the sims that were run (for runs restarted from one compartmental sim, that sim, as it was after its last run).

len(msim) is the number of runs.
A subclass changes the sim of each run by overriding make_run(), and can take options of its own for it by adding them to run_options (see the last example).



import starsim as ss

s1 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.02), label='Low transmission')
s2 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), label='High transmission')
msim = ss.parallel(s1, s2, n_runs=5)
msim.plot() # The median and a 95% interval of each scenario
msim.results.sis.prevalence.select(scenario='Low transmission').median()

class NoisyMultiSim(ss.MultiSim): # Each run with its own beta, drawn around 0.05
    run_options = ss.MultiSim.run_options + ['noise']

    def make_run(self, sim, values, seed, noise=0.1):
        beta = 0.05*np.exp(noise*np.random.default_rng(seed).normal())
        return super().make_run(sim, dict(values or {}, beta=beta), seed)

msim = NoisyMultiSim(s1, n_runs=10, noise=0.2).run()

Put the results of the sims together as runs (msim.results), if they have the same time points (msim._same_times)
Sims with different time points (e.g. different steps) are kept as they are: each can be plotted on its own time axis (msim.plot()), but their results can’t be put together, so what combines the runs raises an error.



run.MultiSim.combine()
Combine the sims into a single sim, whose results are those of one population made of all of them, e.g. to treat several smaller sims as one larger population
Only the output is combined. Results that scale with population size (res.scale=True, e.g. counts) are summed; other results (e.g. prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim’s total_pop. The population sizes (n_agents and total_pop) are summed, and pop_scale is updated to match. The people are not joined: the combined sim keeps the people (if any) of the first sim, so it is not a larger population of agents that interact, and cannot be run again as one. To keep the runs as runs, see ss.MultiSim.merge().

Run many sims: different sims, each sim many times with its own seed, or with sets of values of its parameters
This is the one way to run many sims (sim.run() runs one, and returns it). Every way of running ends in the same results: each result with a run axis first.

With pars=, each set of values is run n_runs times (default 1), with the same seeds for every set, and each set is a scenario of its own. The values are in msim.runs (and can be selected, e.g. res.select(beta=0.2)), with each run’s rand_seed. Seeds can be given too, e.g. pars=dict(rand_seed=[1, 5, 9]), as runs of the scenario rather than scenarios.
With priors=True, n_runs sets of values are drawn from the priors of the parameters (ss.par(prior=...), or uniform over its bounds), on a Latin hypercube, and each is run once; draws can also be given, as for pars= (as fit.project() passes those of a posterior). Unlike a sweep with pars=, the draws are runs of their sim’s scenario, each with a seed of its own (the sim’s seed, plus 1, 2, …), so quantiles over a scenario’s runs include both the draws and chance.
How to run them, by keyword (see also ss.MultiSim):

workers: the number of worker processes (by default, one per CPU); 1 runs them one after another in this process, e.g. on a shared machine, or to debug a run
until and verbose: as for sim.run()
shrink: whether to shrink each sim after it runs, to save memory (see sim.shrink())
par_args: passed to sc.Parallel()
run_args: passed to each sim.run()
