Only for sims that are nothing but compartments (see ss.Sim.restart()), where this is many times faster than running copies. Returns None if any of the sims is not. Otherwise returns the sim of each run (RestartedSims, which makes each one when it is asked for), the results of every run (ss.run.MultiResults), and a dataframe of the runs.
With pars= (see ss.parallel()), each set of values is run n_runs times (as runs of their sim’s scenario if they are draws). An ODE with sim.jax = True (and JAX installed) takes them all in one call to JAX (see ss.gradients), which is faster than the kernels for tens of thousands of runs, once JAX has started.

The runs of one or more sims: every result of the sims with a run axis first, and the sims that were run
Made and run by ss.parallel(), the way to run many sims; ss.MultiSim(...) with the same arguments, then msim.run(), does the same (and is the class to subclass). Each sim is run once unless n_runs, pars, or priors is given: a single sim, ss.MultiSim(sim), is one run, where in Starsim 3 it was run four times by default (ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=4) for that). To make and initialize the sim of each run without running them, use msim.init_sims().

Type

Default

None

str

None

By default (verbose not given: the sims’ own verbose, if they share one, else ss.options.verbose) the runs print nothing of their own, and the MultiSim shows their progress: nothing for runs that are done within a second, a bar for each run if there are up to 10 that each take more than 10 seconds, and otherwise one bar with the number of runs done (to a file, a line every tenth); then a line on what was run.
Once run, a MultiSim has:

results: every result with a run axis first (see ss.Result), e.g. msim.results.sir.I.quantiles();
runs: one row per run, with its scenario (the label of its sim), the values of any parameters swept or drawn, and its seed (rand_seed);
sims: the sims that were run (for runs restarted from one compartmental sim, that sim, as it was after its last run).

len(msim) is the number of runs.
A subclass changes the sim of each run by overriding make_run(), and can take options of its own for it by adding them to run_options (see the last example).



import starsim as ss

s1 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.02), label='Low transmission')
s2 = ss.Sim(networks='random', diseases=ss.SIS(beta=0.05), label='High transmission')
msim = ss.parallel(s1, s2, n_runs=5)
msim.plot() # The median and a 95% interval of each scenario
msim.results.sis.prevalence.select(scenario='Low transmission').median()

class NoisyMultiSim(ss.MultiSim): # Each run with its own beta, drawn around 0.05
    run_options = ss.MultiSim.run_options + ['noise']

    def make_run(self, sim, values, seed, noise=0.1):
        beta = 0.05*np.exp(noise*np.random.default_rng(seed).normal())
        return super().make_run(sim, dict(values or {}, beta=beta), seed)

msim = NoisyMultiSim(s1, n_runs=10, noise=0.2).run()

run.MultiSim.combine()
Combine the sims into a single sim, whose results are those of one population made of all of them, e.g. to treat several smaller sims as one larger population
Only the output is combined. Results that scale with population size (res.scale=True, e.g. counts) are summed; other results (e.g. prevalence) are averaged, weighted by each sim’s total_pop. The population sizes (n_agents and total_pop) are summed, and pop_scale is updated to match. The people are not joined: the combined sim keeps the people (if any) of the first sim, so it is not a larger population of agents that interact, and cannot be run again as one. To keep the runs as runs, see ss.MultiSim.merge().

run.parallel(*args, n_runs=None, pars=None, priors=False, **kwargs)
Run many sims: different sims, each sim many times with its own seed, or with sets of values of its parameters
This is the one way to run many sims (sim.run() runs one, and returns it). Every way of running ends in the same results: each result with a run axis first.

With pars=, each set of values is run n_runs times (default 1), with the same seeds for every set, and each set is a scenario of its own. The values are in msim.runs (and can be selected, e.g. res.select(beta=0.2)), with each run’s rand_seed. Seeds can be given too, e.g. pars=dict(rand_seed=[1, 5, 9]), as runs of the scenario rather than scenarios.
With priors=True, n_runs sets of values are drawn from the priors of the parameters (ss.par(prior=...), or uniform over its bounds), on a Latin hypercube, and each is run once; draws can also be given, as for pars= (as fit.project() passes those of a posterior). Unlike a sweep with pars=, the draws are runs of their sim’s scenario, each with a seed of its own (the sim’s seed, plus 1, 2, …), so quantiles over a scenario’s runs include both the draws and chance.
How to run them, by keyword (see also ss.MultiSim):

workers: the number of worker processes (by default, one per CPU); 1 runs them one after another in this process, e.g. on a shared machine, or to debug a run
until and verbose: as for sim.run()
shrink: whether to shrink each sim after it runs, to save memory (see sim.shrink())

pregnancy.Pregnancy(
    pars=None,
    fetus='auto',
    lactation='auto',
    metadata=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus on=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is on=preg.birth.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion.

pregnancy.Pregnancy.burnin_plan(engine)
burnin=True (the default): women pregnant at the start. Each woman who could conceive has the chance of having conceived in the mean duration of a pregnancy before the start, at her conception hazard then (1 - exp(-h*dur)), at a step uniform over it, and is run forward by the pregnancy’s own transitions (abortion, losses, and delivery, with no births), so the start has the gestational ages and the first steps their deliveries. In the compartmental form, the same share of each group, less the abortions and the losses on the way, is spread evenly over gestation (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.backfill_burnin()).



pregnancy.Pregnancy.compartmental_form(sim)
The small compartmental form, used only when a compartmental solver is named (solver='auto' runs a pregnancy as agents): the states NP and P, conception, abortion, maternal deaths, and the delivery at the end of dur_pregnancy (a fixed delay, or Erlang stages for a distribution), with n children per delivery (ss.birth(per=preg.delivery)). The losses do not read the gestational age (P.time): the loss rate is split between miscarriage and stillbirth by the share of the mean gestation below loss_threshold. It has no fetuses, no links between mothers and children, no lactation, no preterm risk, and no deaths at delivery (p_maternal_death). Returns the note that says so



pregnancy.Pregnancy.compute_asfr()
The age-specific fertility rates of the step (per 1000 women: deliveries by the mother’s age, over the women of that age), and the TFR from them. As compartments, by the age of each group, so it needs an age stratification (otherwise NaN)

An override can instead take (sim, uids) and return a rate for each of those agents (as agents only), e.g. ss.peryear(table[self.method[uids]]), rather than one for every slot of the raw arrays.



pregnancy.Pregnancy.link(sim)

As agents, at a delivery: the children of the mothers (see ss.solvers.Agents.step_per()), and the events on the mothers

pregnancy.Pregnancy(
    pars=None,
    fetus='auto',
    lactation='auto',
    metadata=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives embryos_per_pregnancy children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(per=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus on=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is on=preg.birth.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion.

pregnancy.Pregnancy.burnin_plan(engine)
burnin=True (the default): women pregnant at the start. Each woman who could conceive has the chance of having conceived in the mean duration of a pregnancy before the start, at her conception hazard then (1 - exp(-h*dur)), at a step uniform over it, and is run forward by the pregnancy’s own transitions (abortion, losses, and delivery, with no births), so the start has the gestational ages and the first steps their deliveries. pregnancy.Pregnancy.compartmental_form(sim)
The small compartmental form, used only when a compartmental solver is named (solver='auto' runs a pregnancy as agents): the states NP and P, conception, abortion, maternal deaths, and the delivery at the end of dur_pregnancy (a fixed delay, or Erlang stages for a distribution), with n children per delivery (ss.birth(per=preg.delivery)). The losses do not read the gestational age (P.time): the loss rate is split between miscarriage and stillbirth by the share of the mean gestation below loss_threshold. title: geo
text:
geo
Places and the movement between them: a geography (ss.geo.geography), and movement between its places: a movement model (ss.geo.gravity, ss.geo.radiation), a matrix (ss.geo.Mobility), or a register of moves on given dates (ss.geo.register)
These exist so that a model of more than one place can be built from named places and a standard movement model. Movement applies to a model stratified by place (sir.stratify(patch=...)), whose networks then pair people within each place; a geography can also be used by a network (ssl.GeoNet), for a disease of either kind.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Mobility
Movement between the levels of a spatial stratification, given as a matrix


geography
A geography: named places with populations and positions, used as the levels of a spatial stratification


gravity
The gravity model of movement: the fraction of their time that a person from place i spends in place j (or, for migration,


radiation
The radiation model of movement (Simini et al. 2012), which has no parameters to fit: of the people from place i who travel,


register
A movement register: a table of moves between places on given dates, e.g. livestock sales between farms





geo.Mobility(matrix=None, kind=None, away=None, **kwargs)
Movement between the levels of a spatial stratification, given as a matrix
People either commute (they keep their home, and spend a fraction of their time in other places, where they are exposed and expose others), visit (the same, but they are exposed to the residents of the places they go to and do not expose anyone there, as flepiMoP has it), or migrate (they relocate). Or, with kind='force', nobody moves and the force of infection does, as in LASER: with M[i,k] the movement from place i to place k, each place keeps 1 − Σ_k M[i,k] of its own force of infection and receives M[k,i] of each other place’s.
The movement models (ss.geo.gravity(), ss.geo.radiation()) take the same kind= and away= themselves, and a register of moves on given dates is ss.geo.register().
Other forms are written with the general pieces. Commuters who come back at a finite rate (Keeling and Rohani’s model 7.3) are a second spatial dimension of where people are now, with transfers between its levels at rates by home.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

geo.Mobility(matrix=None, kind=None, away=None, **kwargs)
Movement between the levels of a spatial stratification, given as a matrix
People either commute (they keep their home, and spend a fraction of their time in other places, where they are exposed and expose others), visit (the same, but they are exposed to the residents of the places they go to and do not expose anyone there, as flepiMoP has it), or migrate (they relocate). Or, with kind='force', nobody moves and the force of infection does, as in LASER: with M[i,k] the movement from place i to place k, each place keeps 1 − Σ_k M[i,k] of its own force of infection and receives M[k,i] of each other place’s.
The movement models (ss.geo.gravity(), ss.geo.radiation()) take the same kind= and away= themselves, and a register of moves on given dates is ss.geo.register().
Other forms are written with the general pieces. Commuters who come back at a finite rate (Keeling and Rohani’s model 7.3) are a second spatial dimension of where people are now, with transfers between its levels at rates by home.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

The number of people, in all or by group



solvers.engine.Engine.never_taken(tr)
Whether a transition to one destination has a branch probability of 0 everywhere (e.g. death in ss.SIR with p_death=0)



solvers.engine.Engine.note_chance()
For a run with real numbers (ode): say where chance would matter, as a stochastic run would show



solvers.engine.Engine.note_counter(strat, what)
Note a counter whose levels are not one apart, if it matters to this engine



solvers.engine.Engine.note_fast_steps()
See note_steps()



solvers.engine.Engine.note_function_reads()
Say when a parameter that a modifier changes is read inside a function, which sees its own value rather than the changed one



solvers.engine.Engine.note_stages(name, dw)
Say how a dwell time that is not exponential or Erlang is approximated; agents draw it as it is (see Compartmental.note_stages())



solvers.engine.Engine.note_steps()
In a run that takes whole steps, say which transitions are fast compared with the timestep: by the parameters’ own values, without their modifiers, which may read what does not exist until the run (e.g. a property of people another module adds)



solvers.engine.Engine.outcome_frac(flow, weight, draw)
The events of an outcome from those of one of its sources, times its weight: a fraction of whole events is a draw if draw, and the part of an event left over (from agents who stand for a fraction of a person) is kept as its mean



solvers.engine.Engine.own_moves(tr)
The moves of move= and increment=: see moves()



solvers.engine.Engine.per_level(rate)
A birth rate per person given for each level of some dimensions (ss.birth(S, rate=ss.by(species=mu))), as the inflow it is: the number of people counted by the rate at their level (a weighted count, see ss.expressions.Count), born at that level; a newborn is in the youngest age group and of either sex, so those are the sum over their levels (counts are already in the same place). Returns the rate, and the dimensions whose levels the births are at (for describe()).



solvers.engine.Engine.plain_value(val)
A value written inside another (a direction of ss.peract, or a route of a beta dict) as a number, or a value for each group



solvers.engine.Engine.plausible_density(tr)
Whether an acquisition at a rate on counts of people is density-dependent transmission as meant (S >> I @ beta*I.n), rather than a count written for a fraction: whether one infectious person would infect fewer than 10 people a day in a population with no immunity (measles infects about 2). A beta meant for a fraction (0.3 a day) gives 0.3 × N, which is far more in any population but a handful of people



solvers.engine.Engine.product_of(expr)
The sim’s copy of the product of a fraction holding it (itn.held_frac, see ss.expressions.HeldFrac)



solvers.engine.Engine.prop(cond)
The value of a property of people, as an expression reads it



solvers.engine.Engine.protection(state, levels, strain)
The fraction of the force of infection of a strain that reaches people in a state at some levels of the strain dimension, by the strains they carry there (see init_immunity())



solvers.engine.Engine.record_events()
Record the flows of the step, at its index, and the results worked out from them and the states at its start



solvers.engine.Engine.record_states()
Record the number in each state at the start of the step, at its index (so R[ti] has the people recovered by time point ti, before the step from it, whose recoveries are recovery[ti]); they are kept for the results worked out with the flows of the step (see record_events())



solvers.engine.Engine.register_sets()
For a movement register: the sets of states its events name, with the default (None) first, and for each, the states of this module that people are chosen from and that people are added to
A state that the register names must belong to some module of the sim; one that is not in this module is left out, and a module with none of the states of a set uses its default.



solvers.engine.Engine.report_outcome(info, buf, amount, ti, draw)
One step of an outcome: its events in the step (amount, for each group, or each run and group) are reported after its delay, and stay in it for its duration, each drawn for each event if draw. buf keeps the events still to be reported (pending) and to leave (leaving), each a ring over the next steps, and the number in the outcome (n). A step at a time for step_outcomes(), and over the steps of a whole run for Compartmental.derived_outcomes(), so the two draw the same. Returns the events reported in the step.



solvers.engine.Engine.route_value(p, raw)
The value of a transmission’s beta on the route it is being worked out for (self._route, as agents): a beta for each route gives its value for this one; on a network with acts, a probability per act (ss.peract, or a bare number) gives the hazard per act, −ln(1 − p), in each of the network’s directions (see act_hazards())



solvers.engine.Engine.row_stocks(stock_groups, ti)
The states by group at the start of the row of several steps that time point ti is in (see ss.solvers.group_rows()), for the results worked out over the row



solvers.engine.Engine.sample(dist, n)
Draw samples from a distribution of durations, in the sim’s unit (used to build delay kernels, not during the run)



solvers.engine.Engine.seed_dist()
An init_prev that chooses who starts infected one by one, which only agents have (see Agents.seed_dist())



solvers.engine.Engine.seed_reach(trs, uids=None)
For seeding through several transmissions (see seed_transmissions()): the fraction of the seeds of each group (or of each agent, with uids) that each takes, equal among those that can infect them (a coefficient above 0 for them), e.g. a transmission to women only seeds women



solvers.engine.Engine.seed_transmissions()
The transmissions that init_prev seeds through: those out of the first state (e.g. one for each sex), or the first transmission if none is, or if they all lead to the same states; with none, the first acquisition



solvers.engine.Engine.series_over(func, years, key)
The values of something that varies in time at some years, kept under key, as (func, the values of any parameters inside it, which can change between runs, values)



solvers.engine.Engine.set_count(state, value)
Set the number of people in a state



solvers.engine.Engine.shrink()
Drop the sim and the arrays the run worked in, for saving; the results are kept on the module



solvers.engine.Engine.split_events(n, p)
n events over the slots with chances p: whole events are drawn, and the part of an event left over is kept as its mean, so that small amounts from fractional agents aren’t rounded away



solvers.engine.Engine.split_states(states)
Some states split into this disease’s own and other diseases’ (e.g. syph.I in a rate of HIV), by the name of each other disease



solvers.engine.Engine.start_count(name, init, fracs, counts, later)
The starting amount of a state that is not people, read from the numbers in other states (e.g. init=m*N): those in the states of people are their fractions of the population



solvers.engine.Engine.start_step()
Start the step: values held for the last step are worked out again



solvers.engine.Engine.step()
The part of a step after the interventions, including transmission



solvers.engine.Engine.step_funcs()
Call the module’s custom per-step functions, after its transitions



solvers.engine.Engine.step_outcomes()
Work out this step’s value of each outcome, in each group, from the flows it is counted from



solvers.engine.Engine.step_state()
The part of a step before the interventions: what changes with no contact with others



solvers.engine.Engine.stock(state)
The number in a state, as an expression reads it



solvers.engine.Engine.strain_effect(strain, state=None)
The multiplier on the force of infection of one strain from the products that protect against acquiring it (ss.by(strain=...)): for each agent, or for each group of a state



solvers.engine.Engine.strain_levels()
The strains of the module’s strain dimension, if it has one: each has a force of infection of its own



solvers.engine.Engine.strain_rate(tr, rate, strain)
The part of a transmission’s rate that comes from one strain



solvers.engine.Engine.superinfects(tr, state)
Whether a transmission leaves people in the state they are in (so only changes the strains they carry)



solvers.engine.Engine.takes_uids(func)
Whether a user function takes the agents (uids), worked out once for each function (see ss.utils.fn_args())



solvers.engine.Engine.total_count(states)
The number in some states in the whole population, wherever they are (I.total)



solvers.engine.Engine.transfer_dist(tf, per_agent=None)
The distribution of a transfer’s dur= as numbers in the sim’s unit, if it is not exponential (None if it is a rate, a scalar, or exponential): agents draw it for each person (see Agents.step_transfers())



solvers.engine.Engine.undefined(name)
The error for a method this engine does not define



solvers.engine.Engine.value(p)
The value of a parameter, as a number in the sim’s unit



solvers.engine.Engine.varying_dwell(name, tr, raw, dw, to_unit)
A dwell time whose distribution has parameters with a value for each group (ss.by): see each engine’s own



solvers.engine.Engine.weighted_events(key, weight, integer)
An outcome’s amount by group from the people who went through a transition, each with their own weight; None if they are not known (see Agents.weighted_events())



solvers.engine.Engine.where_frac(tr, state, uids=None)
For a branch with who=: 1 for the people it is open to and 0 for the others (agents: for uids; compartments: for each group of state, if the condition is on states and strata), or None



solvers.engine.Engine.where_mults(branches, state, mults, uids=None)
The branches’ multipliers with their who=: a branch is closed to the people (or groups) it does not hold for, so the others share the rest; but if every branch is closed to someone, they are split as before and wait until one opens



solvers.engine.Engine.whole_steps(*args, **kwargs)
A time as a number of whole steps



solvers.engine.Engine.with_unrepresented()
The number in each state (and by group), as the results count them: with dynamic rescaling (rescale=True), including the people no agent stands for yet
Each agent stands for scale people; the people no agent stands for (sim.results.unrepresented, see ss.Sim.rescale()) are like the agents, and are shared out as the agents alive are, in agents (as the other counts are, before they are scaled). For a disease, which rescaling makes naive again, they have never been infected, so their fraction is in its first state; for another module (e.g. ss.Pregnancy), each state has its fraction. The engine’s own stocks (used in the dynamics) are untouched.



solvers.engine.Engine.write_scale()
The scale counts of people are written in, as agents (see ss.results.people_scale()), set on the results that keep values by group

demographics
Births, deaths, migration, and pregnancy
These exist so that the population can change during a run. ss.Births and ss.Deaths are written as code, ss.birth() and the like declare the same flows for the whole population, and ss.Pregnancy is declared, so that conception and delivery are transitions that other modules can modify or respond to.

demographics.Pregnancy(pars=None, fetal_agents='auto', columns=None, **kwargs)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time_in. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum, with maternal_death_rate), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives children children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(when=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_death_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus when=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is when=preg.birth. Code reads a step’s newborns and their mothers in that step, before the diseases’ step, with on_birth(parents, children) in any module (see ss.Module.on_birth()), which is called at the delivery; the mothers delivered in the step are also preg.ti_delivered == sim.ti.
As agents, a live birth starts breastfeeding (lactating, with p_breastfeed), or restarts it for a woman breastfeeding already; it ends after dur_breastfeed, or at once if a child of hers dies before the age of 1. It is a state of each woman rather than one of the module’s exclusive states (NP, P), since it overlaps the next pregnancy. A BreastfeedingNet pairs each newborn with a mother who breastfeeds, and ends the pair when she stops.
As agents, a woman who leaves P (a delivery, a loss, or an abortion) faces conception again in the same step, for what is left of it (half a step); the children and records of a delivery (ti_delivered, since_birth, lactating) are made first, so a rate or a modifier that reads them sees this delivery. A rate given as a function (e.g. an override of conception_rate()) can be called more than once a step, for those who arrive in NP within it, so it should not draw random numbers.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion; as agents, lactating (breastfeeding).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

demographics.Pregnancy(pars=None, fetal_agents='auto', columns=None, **kwargs)
Pregnancy, as declared states and transitions
Everyone is in NP (not pregnant: men and children too) or P (pregnant). Gestational age is P.time_in. Conception is one transition, so contraception, HIV, or LAM are modifiers of it (ss.modify(preg.conception, multiply=...)). A pregnancy ends in an abortion (at once, with p_abortion), a miscarriage or stillbirth (a hazard before or after loss_threshold), a maternal death (antepartum, with maternal_death_rate), or a delivery at the end of a dwell of dur_pregnancy. Each delivery gives children children (birth): as agents, new agents whose parent is the mother, placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(when=preg.delivery) (or else its first state). Children die before the age of 1 at infant_death_rate (infant_mortality; 0 by default). It runs as agents under solver='auto'; a compartmental solver named explicitly runs a small approximate form (see compartmental_form()).
For other modules, preg.delivery happens to the mother, and to her fetuses (if they are agents: see _init_fetus()) before they are born, so a death of a fetus when=preg.delivery is a stillbirth; preg.birth happens to the newborns, so a neonatal death is when=preg.birth. Code reads a step’s newborns and their mothers in that step, before the diseases’ step, with on_birth(parents, children) in any module (see ss.Module.on_birth()), which is called at the delivery; the mothers delivered in the step are also preg.ti_delivered == sim.ti.
As agents, a live birth starts breastfeeding (lactating, with p_breastfeed), or restarts it for a woman breastfeeding already; it ends after dur_breastfeed, or at once if a child of hers dies before the age of 1. It is a state of each woman rather than one of the module’s exclusive states (NP, P), since it overlaps the next pregnancy. A BreastfeedingNet pairs each newborn with a mother who breastfeeds, and ends the pair when she stops.
As agents, a woman who leaves P (a delivery, a loss, or an abortion) faces conception again in the same step, for what is left of it (half a step); the children and records of a delivery (ti_delivered, since_birth, lactating) are made first, so a rate or a modifier that reads them sees this delivery. A rate given as a function (e.g. an override of conception_rate()) can be called more than once a step, for those who arrive in NP within it, so it should not draw random numbers.
Its parameters are listed in __init__(); code reacts to its events with add_callback(), e.g. preg.add_callback(preg.birth, fn). Its states and results are P (pregnant), ti_P, the scheduled delivery ti_exit_P (set_delivery() reschedules it), and the flows conception, birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, and abortion; as agents, lactating (breastfeeding).

title: gradients
text:
gradients
gradients
The ODE run in JAX: gradients of results with respect to parameters, and many runs at once
A compartmental engine flattens its flows into a ss.kernels.Program. The Numba kernels step through it; run() here takes the same program and runs the same fourth-order Runge-Kutta (or Euler) steps in JAX, so that the run can be differentiated (gradient()) and many runs with different values can be taken in one call (run_sets()). JAX is imported only when one of these is used.
What JAX differentiates is the run: the program’s numbers, and the compartments at the start, to the compartments and flows at every step. The steps either side of it are Python (working out those numbers from the parameters, and the results from the run, including outcomes and the goodness of fit), and are differentiated by central differences along the direction the run is differentiated in. They are cheap and smooth, so this is accurate to about 1e-9 of the value.

people.People.request_death(uids, cause=None, hazard=None)
Request that agents die at this step; how a module kills agents
Use this rather than setting People.ti_dead directly, so that modules don’t overwrite each other’s deaths (e.g. a death set for the future overwriting one due now from another module). A module with a future time of death (e.g. after the course of a disease) keeps it itself, and calls this when the time comes, with itself as the cause.
The deaths happen after every module has stepped, but before the analyzers, so that analyzers can see and record the agents who died in this step.
Each person dies once, of one cause: if several modules request the death of the same person in the same step, one of them is chosen at random (whatever the order of the modules, with common random numbers): in proportion to the hazards of the claims if each gave one (hazard=), and otherwise each equally likely. The cause is kept in people.cause_of_death (see people.causes). A module counts its deaths after they are resolved, with people.died_of(module), so a death is counted once.

people.People.request_death(uids, cause=None, hazard=None)
Request that agents die at this step; how a module kills agents
Use this rather than setting People.ti_dead directly, so that modules don’t overwrite each other’s deaths (e.g. a death set for the future overwriting one due now from another module). A module with a future time of death (e.g. after the course of a disease) keeps it itself, and calls this when the time comes, with itself as the cause.
The deaths happen after every module has stepped, but before the analyzers, so that analyzers can see and record the agents who died in this step.
Each person dies once, of one cause: if several modules request the death of the same person in the same step, one of them is chosen at random (whatever the order of the modules, with common random numbers): in proportion to the hazards of the claims if each gave one (hazard=), and otherwise each equally likely. The cause is kept in people.cause_of_death (see people.causes). A module counts its deaths after they are resolved, with people.died_of(module), so a death is counted once.

title: internals.gradients
text:
internals.gradients
Not for the user: the ODE run in JAX: gradients of results with respect to parameters, and many runs at once
A compartmental engine flattens its flows into a ss.kernels.Program. The kernels (Numba or Rust) step through it; run() here takes the same program and runs the same fourth-order Runge-Kutta (or Euler) steps in JAX, so that the run can be differentiated (gradient()) and many runs with different values can be taken in one call (run_sets()). JAX is imported only when one of these is used.
What JAX differentiates is the run: the program’s numbers, and the compartments at the start, to the compartments and flows at every step. The steps either side of it are Python (working out those numbers from the parameters, and the results from the run, including outcomes and the goodness of fit), and are differentiated by central differences along the direction the run is differentiated in. They are cheap and smooth, so this is accurate to about 1e-9 of the value.
Used with: compartments; declared modules

internals.gradients.jax()
Import JAX (imported only when first used, since it takes a few tenths of a second), on the platform that ss.options.jax says
If JAX has not been imported yet, it is given a device for each core of the CPU (as numpyro.set_host_device_count() does), or as many as the threads asked for in the environment (e.g. OMP_NUM_THREADS=1: see ss.settings.thread_limit), so that the chains of a posterior run on cores of their own; everything else runs on the first. XLA’s own threads (most of them compiling) are not limited by it: no flag of XLA’s limits them.
The platform it runs on is ss.options.jax (e.g. “cpu”), if not “auto”. If JAX has started already on others (by Starsim or anything else), it is started again on these: arrays made already stay on their devices, and are moved when used with new ones, and what was compiled is compiled again. “auto” goes back to the platforms JAX had before Starsim first changed them. The first time, its devices are started here, so that a GPU that fails to start (e.g. with a CUDA plugin of another version than jaxlib) says what to do.

internals.gradients.Density(
    sim,
    fitted,
    x0,
    set_pars,
    likelihood=None,
    weights=None,
    external=None,

)
The log of the posterior density of a sim’s fitted parameters, as one function in JAX, so that it can be compiled and differentiated whole (see sim.fit() with method=‘nuts’)
The numbers in the run are worked out from the parameters in JAX: the values in the rates by evaluating the model’s own expressions, and the rest (e.g. the compartments at the start) from the change in them as each parameter changes, which has to be linear (checked at the corners and the middle of the bounds when it is built). The platform it runs on is ss.options.jax (e.g. “cpu”), if not “auto”. If JAX has started already on others (by Starsim or anything else), it is started again on these: arrays made already stay on their devices, and are moved when used with new ones, and what was compiled is compiled again. “auto” goes back to the platforms JAX had before Starsim first changed them. The first time, its devices are started here, so that a GPU that fails to start (e.g. with a CUDA plugin of another version than jaxlib) says what to do.

what the result is, which decides how it behaves: ‘flow’ (a number of events in each step, e.g. new infections; it has a cumulative total, and is summed over each period of data it is compared with), ‘stock’ (a quantity at each time point, e.g. the number infected), ‘ratio’ (one quantity divided by another, e.g. prevalence or a mean; one that keeps its numerator and denominator sums each over a period, then divides), or None for a result with no meaning over time. The kind also sets the default scale and summarize_by. By default (‘auto’) it is guessed from summarize_by if only that is given, or else from the name (new_... is a flow; n_..., cum_..., and cumulative are stocks; and ...prevalence is a ratio), or else from the dtype: an integer is a count, guessed to be a flow, a dtype that is not numbers (e.g. list) has none, and anything else is a ratio; a guess from the dtype is warned about, so give kind= for any other name (e.g. ss.Result('vaccinated', dtype=int, kind='stock')). 'auto'

None

False



In most cases, ss.Result behaves exactly like np.array(), except with the additional fields listed above. To see everything in a result, use result.disp().
For a 2D result, res.alpha, res['alpha'], or res.select(column='alpha') returns a 1D result for that column (which shares data with the 2D result), and res[ti] returns the row for that timestep. The columns of a result split by a dimension (res.by('age')) are selected by it, e.g. res.by('age').select(age=0).



res = ss.Result('infection', kind='flow', columns=['wild', 'alpha'], shape=10)
res[3] = [20, 5] # Set the values for timestep 3
res['alpha'][4] = 8 # Set one value for timestep 4
res['alpha'].label # Returns 'infection (alpha)'
A result across the runs of a MultiSim (msim.results.sir.I) is the same result with a run axis first: select() also takes run= (a position), scenario=, and the parameters swept; quantiles(), median(), and mean() summarize over the runs of each scenario; and plot() draws the median and a 95% interval of each scenario (lines=True draws every run).
```python
msim = ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=10)
I = msim.results.sir.I # Runs by time points
I.select(run=3) # One run, as a result of one sim
low, mid, high = I.quantiles([0.025, 0.5, 0.975])
I.median().plot()
```

results.Result.resample(new_unit=None, summarize_by=None, use_years=False)
Resample the result to a longer time unit, by its summarize_by (which by default follows its kind)
A flow is summed over each period, a stock takes its value at the start of each period (a cumulative total, e.g. res.infection.cum, its value at the end), and a ratio sums its numerator and denominator over each period (by group, if it has them) and divides them (one with no parts is averaged over the period). Periods start at the sim’s start and include their start, as for data, as each time point holds the step that starts there; calendar months and years are used instead for a sim with dates. Each period is labeled by its start: for calendar months and years, the first day of the month or year (so a year of weekly steps is labeled 1 January, not the first week of the year), or the start of the run if later; otherwise its first time point. Only whole periods are kept: a monthly run from 2000 to 2020 has 20 years, as its last step (from 2020) is one month of 2020, while a yearly one has 21 (unless no period is whole, when all are kept). The values by group (select() and by()) are resampled too.

# In a module written as code, in a sim stratified by sex and age
def init_results(self):
    super().init_results()
    self.define_results(ss.Result('n_infected', groups=True), ss.Result('prevalence', scale=False, groups=True))

def record_states(self):
    super().record_states()
    alive, infected = self.sim.groups.count(), self.sim.groups.count(self.infected)
    self.results.n_infected.set_groups(self.ti, infected)
    self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, infected, alive)

what the result is, which decides how it behaves: ‘flow’ (a number of events in each step, e.g. new infections; it has a cumulative total, and is summed over each period of data it is compared with), ‘stock’ (a quantity at each time point, e.g. the number infected), ‘ratio’ (one quantity divided by another, e.g. prevalence or a mean; one that keeps its numerator and denominator sums each over a period, then divides), or None for a result with no meaning over time. The kind also sets the default scale and summarize_by. By default (‘auto’) it is guessed from summarize_by if only that is given, or else from the name (new_... is a flow; n_..., cum_..., and cumulative are stocks; and ...prevalence is a ratio), or else from the dtype: an integer is a count, guessed to be a flow, a dtype that is not numbers (e.g. list) has none, and anything else is a ratio; a guess from the dtype is warned about, so give kind= for any other name (e.g. ss.Result('vaccinated', dtype=int, kind='stock')). The results of a declared module are made with their kind
'auto'

In most cases, ss.Result behaves exactly like np.array(), except with the additional fields listed above. To see everything in a result, use result.disp().
For a 2D result, res.alpha, res['alpha'], or res.select(column='alpha') returns a 1D result for that column (which shares data with the 2D result), and res[ti] returns the row for that timestep. The columns of a result split by a dimension (res.by('age')) are selected by it, e.g. res.by('age').select(age=0).

res['alpha'][4] = 8 # Set one value for timestep 4
res['alpha'].label # Returns 'infection (alpha)'
A result across the runs of a MultiSim (msim.results.sir.I) is the same result with a run axis first: select() also takes run= (a position), scenario=, and the parameters swept; quantiles(), median(), and mean() summarize over the runs of each scenario; and plot() draws the median and a 95% interval of each scenario (lines=True draws every run).

I = msim.results.sir.I # Runs by time points
I.select(run=3) # One run, as a result of one sim
low, mid, high = I.quantiles([0.025, 0.5, 0.975])

results.Result.resample(new_unit=None, summarize_by=None, use_years=False)
Resample the result to a longer time unit, by its summarize_by (which by default follows its kind)
A flow is summed over each period, a stock takes its value at the start of each period (a cumulative total, e.g. res.infection.cum, its value at the end), and a ratio sums its numerator and denominator over each period (by group, if it has them) and divides them (one with no parts is averaged over the period). Periods start at the sim’s start and include their start, as for data, as each time point holds the step that starts there; calendar months and years are used instead for a sim with dates. Each period is labeled by its start: for calendar months and years, the first day of the month or year (so a year of weekly steps is labeled 1 January, not the first week of the year), or the start of the run if later; otherwise its first time point. Only whole periods are kept: a monthly run from 2000 to 2020 has 20 years, as its last step (from 2020) is one month of 2020, while a yearly one has 21 (unless no period is whole, when all are kept). The values by group (select() and by()) are resampled too.

# In a module written as code, in a sim stratified by sex and age
def init_results(self):
    super().init_results()
    self.define_results(ss.Result('n_infected', groups=True), ss.Result('prevalence', scale=False, groups=True))

def record_states(self):
    super().record_states()
    alive, infected = self.sim.groups.count(), self.sim.groups.count(self.infected)
    self.results.n_infected.set_groups(self.ti, infected)
    self.results.prevalence.set_groups(self.ti, infected, alive)

title: internals.time
text:
internals.time
Durations and rates, each with its unit (ss.days, ss.peryear, ss.probperyear, …), and plotting dates and durations with Matplotlib
Units are kept with the values so that a module, whatever its timestep, reads a parameter correctly, and mistakes such as adding a rate to a duration raise an error.
Hierarchy of TimePars:
TimePar  # All time parameters
├── Duration  # All durations, units of *time*
│   ├── days  # Duration with units of days
│   ├── weeks
│   ├── months
│   ├── years
│   └── datedur  # Calendar durations, used inside Starsim (ss.dates.datedur); whole ss.months() and ss.years() added to a date follow the calendar
└── Rate  # All rates, units of *per* (e.g. per time or per event)
    ├── per  # Probability rates over time (e.g., death rate per year)
    │   ├── perday
    │   ├── perweek
    │   ├── permonth
    │   └── peryear
    ├── prob  # Unitless probability (e.g., probability of death per infection)
    │   ├── probperday
    │   ├── probperweek
    │   ├── probpermonth
    │   └── probperyear
    └── freq  # Number of events (e.g., number of acts per year)
        ├── freqperday
        ├── freqperweek
        ├── freqpermonth
        └── freqperyear
A per and a freq have the same dimension, and differ in what they give times a duration: a per is a hazard, so rate*dt is the probability of the event in dt, and a freq is an expected count, so freq*dt is the number of events in dt (as rate.to_events(dt) is for either). In a distribution (e.g. ss.poisson(ss.freqperyear(3))), a rate is the number per step, except as a probability (the p of ss.bernoulli()).
The units have one-unit instances, ss.day, ss.week, ss.month, and ss.year (e.g. ss.prob(0.1, ss.year)).

internals.time.DateConverter()
Starsim date conversion interface for matplotlib
It exists so that Matplotlib can plot ss.date and ss.Duration values directly.
This class gets registered with matplotlib as the converter for Starsim date and DateArray types, allowing them to be used directly as axis values. This achieves two outcomes

When Starsim date or DateArray values are plotted, the x-axis values are automatically converted to float years for plotting. If this class is not used, matplotlib will instead convert them to days since 1970-01-01, which is the default behavior for pd.Timestamp.
If the first plotting command used on an axis has date/DateArray as the x-axis, our standard custom date locators and formatters will be used, so that the float years will automatically be labeled with dates.

Together, this means that users can freely plot both Starsim date/DateArray values and plain float years on the same axis without needing any conversions, and they’ll also automatically get date-based ticks without needing to set the locator, even if they are using custom plotting code rather than ss.Result.plot().

internals.time.per(value, unit=None)
A per represents an instantaneous rate of an event occurring. Rates must be non-negative, but need not be less than 1.
Through multiplication, rate can be modified or converted to a probability, depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When a per is multiplied by a scalar or array, the rate is simply scaled. Such multiplication occurs frequently in epidemiological models, where the base rate is multiplied by “rate ratio” or “relative rate” to represent people experiencing higher (multiplier > 1) or lower (multiplier < 1) event rates.
Alternatively, when a per is multiplied by a duration (type ss.Duration), a probability is calculated. The conversion from rate to probability on multiplication by a duration is 1 - np.exp(-rate*factor), where factor is the ratio of the multiplied duration to the original period (denominator).
For example, consider >>> p = ss.per(0.8, ss.years(1)) When multiplied by a duration of 1 year, the calculated probability is 1 - np.exp(-0.8), which is approximately 55%. >>> p*ss.years(1)
When multiplied by a scalar, the rate is simply scaled. >>> p*2
The difference between prob and per is subtle, but important. per works directly with the instantaneous rate of an event occurring. In contrast, prob starts with a probability and a duration, and the underlying rate is calculated. On multiplication by a duration, * per: rate -> probability * prob: probability -> rate -> probability
The behavior of both classes depends on the data type of the object being multiplied.
ss.per has the same dimension as ss.freq, but by default multiplication returns a probability rather than a number of events. Use ss.per for hazards (e.g., the rate of death per year), and ss.freq for events (e.g., number of acts per year).

A probability per act, for a transmission over a network that defines acts (e.g. ss.SexualNet)
It is not a time value: it has no unit and no conversion, so it means the same at any timestep. A partnership with a acts per unit time transmits over a step dt with probability 1 − (1 − p)^(a·dt). Modifiers, rel_trans, rel_sus, and source weights multiply the per-act hazard −ln(1 − p), so beta=0.03 with rel_trans=10 is 1 − 0.97^10 = 0.263 per act.

internals.time.prob(value=None, unit=None, rate=None)
prob represents the probability of an event occurring during a specified period of time.
The class is designed to allow conversion of a probability from one duration to another through multiplication. However, the behavior of this conversion depends on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When multiplied by a duration (type ss.Duration), the underlying constant rate is calculated as rate = -np.log(1 - self.value). Then, the probability over the new duration is p = 1 - np.exp(-rate*factor), where factor is the ratio of the new duration to the original duration.
For example, >>> p = ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) indicates a 80% chance of an event occurring in one year.



p*ss.years(1) When multiplied by the original denominator, 1 year in this case, the probability remains unchanged, 80%.






p * ss.years(2) Multiplying p by ss.years(2) does not simply double the probability to 160% (which is not possible), but rather returns a new probability of 96% representing the chance of the event occurring at least once over the new duration of two years.



When a prob object is multiplied by a number, the underlying rate is scaled, not the probability, so the result is always a valid probability: >>> p * 2 is ss.prob(0.96, ss.years(1)), the same as p + p (two competing hazards), and p * 0.2 is 0.275, not 0.16. A probability of 1 is an infinite rate, so it stays 1 whatever it is multiplied by; as the rate of a declared transition, it moves everyone in the step (as agents, those who arrive in the step too; in compartments, the whole compartment at the start of each step or substep).
Use per instead of prob if you would prefer to directly specify the instantaneous rate.

internals.time.DateConverter()
Starsim date conversion interface for matplotlib
It exists so that Matplotlib can plot ss.date and ss.Duration values directly.
This class gets registered with matplotlib as the converter for Starsim date and DateArray types, allowing them to be used directly as axis values. This achieves two outcomes

When Starsim date or DateArray values are plotted, the x-axis values are automatically converted to float years for plotting. If this class is not used, matplotlib will instead convert them to days since 1970-01-01, which is the default behavior for pd.Timestamp.
If the first plotting command used on an axis has date/DateArray as the x-axis, our standard custom date locators and formatters will be used, so that the float years will automatically be labeled with dates.

Together, this means that users can freely plot both Starsim date/DateArray values and plain float years on the same axis without needing any conversions, and they’ll also automatically get date-based ticks without needing to set the locator, even if they are using custom plotting code rather than ss.Result.plot().

internals.time.per(value, unit=None)
A per represents an instantaneous rate of an event occurring. Rates must be non-negative, but need not be less than 1.
Through multiplication, rate can be modified or converted to a probability, depending on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When a per is multiplied by a scalar or array, the rate is simply scaled. Such multiplication occurs frequently in epidemiological models, where the base rate is multiplied by “rate ratio” or “relative rate” to represent people experiencing higher (multiplier > 1) or lower (multiplier < 1) event rates.
Alternatively, when a per is multiplied by a duration (type ss.Duration), a probability is calculated. The conversion from rate to probability on multiplication by a duration is 1 - np.exp(-rate*factor), where factor is the ratio of the multiplied duration to the original period (denominator).
For example, consider >>> p = ss.per(0.8, ss.years(1)) When multiplied by a duration of 1 year, the calculated probability is 1 - np.exp(-0.8), which is approximately 55%. >>> p*ss.years(1)
When multiplied by a scalar, the rate is simply scaled. >>> p*2
The difference between prob and per is subtle, but important. per works directly with the instantaneous rate of an event occurring. In contrast, prob starts with a probability and a duration, and the underlying rate is calculated. On multiplication by a duration, * per: rate -> probability * prob: probability -> rate -> probability
The behavior of both classes depends on the data type of the object being multiplied.
ss.per has the same dimension as ss.freq, but by default multiplication returns a probability rather than a number of events. Use ss.per for hazards (e.g., the rate of death per year), and ss.freq for events (e.g., number of acts per year).



internals.time.peract(value=None, **directions)
A probability per act, for a transmission over a network that defines acts (e.g. ss.SexualNet)
It is not a time value: it has no unit and no conversion, so it means the same at any timestep. A partnership with a acts per unit time transmits over a step dt with probability 1 − (1 − p)^(a·dt). Modifiers, rel_trans, rel_sus, and source weights multiply the per-act hazard −ln(1 − p), so beta=0.03 with rel_trans=10 is 1 − 0.97^10 = 0.263 per act.

Each value is a number in [0, 1], an ss.par, an expression of them, an ss.timeseries, or an ss.by over a dimension of the susceptible. A direction can also be written as a pair of sides, {('m', 'f'): 0.3}, which is the same as m2f=0.3. Every direction of the network needs a value (unless one is given for all), and a direction it does not have raises; both are checked when the sim is initialized. internals.time.prob(value=None, unit=None, rate=None)
prob represents the probability of an event occurring during a specified period of time.
The class is designed to allow conversion of a probability from one duration to another through multiplication. However, the behavior of this conversion depends on the data type of the object being multiplied.
When multiplied by a duration (type ss.Duration), the underlying constant rate is calculated as rate = -np.log(1 - self.value). Then, the probability over the new duration is p = 1 - np.exp(-rate*factor), where factor is the ratio of the new duration to the original duration.
For example, >>> p = ss.prob(0.8, ss.years(1)) indicates a 80% chance of an event occurring in one year.



p*ss.years(1) When multiplied by the original denominator, 1 year in this case, the probability remains unchanged, 80%.






p * ss.years(2) Multiplying p by ss.years(2) does not simply double the probability to 160% (which is not possible), but rather returns a new probability of 96% representing the chance of the event occurring at least once over the new duration of two years.



When a prob object is multiplied by a number, the underlying rate is scaled, not the probability, so the result is always a valid probability: >>> p * 2 is ss.prob(0.96, ss.years(1)), the same as p + p (two competing hazards), and p * 0.2 is 0.275, not 0.16. A probability of 1 is an infinite rate, so it stays 1 whatever it is multiplied by; as the rate of a declared transition, it moves everyone in the step (as agents, those who arrive in the step too; in compartments, the whole compartment at the start of each step or substep).
Use per instead of prob if you would prefer to directly specify the instantaneous rate.

title: internals.timeline
text:
internals.timeline
Timelines: the time vectors of a sim and of each of its modules
They exist so that sim.t and module.t give the current step and date, and a module can step at its own rate.
How a time is read is decided once, from the sim’s start: if it is a date or a year (a bare number from 1800 on), the sim has a calendar, and every bare number given as a time (a stop, when=, the times of ss.schedule and ss.timeseries) is a year; otherwise, a bare time is a time in the sim’s unit from 0. With no start, the stop decides, as long as the unit is years (or not given): ss.Sim(unit='day', stop=3650) runs 3,650 days from 0. A duration given as a time (when=ss.days(30)) is that long after the sim’s start in a sim with a calendar (ss.years(5) is five years in), and with none a time on the sim’s own axis, counted from 0 as sim.t.tvec is (which is the same thing when the start is 0). The sim’s own stop= is a time, read as the start is; its length is dur= (the stop is then the start plus it; given both, the start is the stop minus it).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Timeline
Handle time vectors and sequencing (“timelines”) for both simulations and modules.


schedule
When something is due: on a calendar cadence (e.g. every 3 months), at a list of times, whenever a function of the date is true, or at every step between a start and a stop (with neither, at every step)





internals.timeline.Timeline(
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    dt=None,
    dur=None,
    name=None,
    init=None,
    sim=None,
)
Handle time vectors and sequencing (“timelines”) for both simulations and modules.
Each module can have its own time instance, in the case where the time vector is defined by absolute dates, these time vectors are by definition aligned. Otherwise they can be specified using dur objects which express relative times (they can be added to a date to get an absolute time)

Type

when the simulation/module starts. For the sim: a date (e.g. ‘2000-01-01’) or a year (a bare number from 1800 on, e.g. 2000) gives it a calendar; any other number, or a duration, is a time in its unit from 0 (default: 2000 for a model in years, else 0). For a module: a time on the sim’s timeline (a bare number as for the sim’s stop; a duration is that long after the sim’s start, in a sim with a calendar)
None

None

None

The Timeline object, after initialization, has the following time vectors, each representing a different way of representing time:

tvec: ground truth simulation time, either as absolute ss.date instances, or relative ss.Duration instances, e.g. DateArray([<2021-01-01>, <2021-01-03>, <2021-01-05>, <2021-01-07>])
tivec: the vector of time indices (np.arange(len(tvec)))
timevec: the “human-friendly” representation of tvec: same as tvec if using ss.date, else floats if using ss.Duration
yearvec: time represented as floating-point years
datevec: time represented as ss.date instances
relvec: relative time, in the unit of the sim’s step (dt)

The Timeline object also has the following attributes/methods:

ti (int): the current time point, which is also the current step: step ti runs from time point ti to the next, and its results go at ti
npts (int): the total number of time points in the timeline, which is also the number of steps (see note below)
now() (ss.date/float/str): the current time, time point ti, the start of the current step, based on tvec by default or a different vector if specified
calendar (str): ‘dates’, ‘years’, or None (see ss.timeline.calendar_of()), and unit, the class of the sim’s unit (e.g. ss.days)
dur (ss.Duration): the length of the run, from its start to its stop

Note: the time vectors include both the start and stop endpoints, and a step is taken from each of them, so each time point is a period: a stock at it is the state at its start, and a flow at it is the total over the step that starts there. For example, start=0, stop=1, dt=1 produces two time points ([0, 1]) and takes two steps; the state after the last one is not recorded. Giving the length (dur) is the same as giving the stop (start=2000, dur=1 is the same timeline as start=2000, stop=2001). See the time user guide for the rationale behind the inclusive endpoint.



t1 = ss.Timeline(start=2000, stop=2020, dt=1.0)
t2 = ss.Timeline(start='2021-01-01', stop='2021-04-04', dt=ss.days(2))
t3 = ss.Timeline(start='2021-01-01', dur=ss.days(90), dt=ss.days(1)) # 90 days from the start

internals.timeline.Timeline(
    start=None,
    stop=None,
    dt=None,
    dur=None,
    name=None,
    init=None,
    sim=None,
)
Handle time vectors and sequencing (“timelines”) for both simulations and modules.
Each module can have its own time instance, in the case where the time vector is defined by absolute dates, these time vectors are by definition aligned. Otherwise they can be specified using dur objects which express relative times (they can be added to a date to get an absolute time)





Name
Type
Description
Default




start
str/int/float/ss.date/ss.Duration
when the simulation/module starts. For the sim: a date (e.g. ‘2000-01-01’) or a year (a bare number from 1800 on, e.g. 2000) gives it a calendar; any other number, or a duration, is a time in its unit from 0 (default: 2000 for a model in years, else 0). For a module: a time on the sim’s timeline (a bare number as for the sim’s stop; a duration is that long after the sim’s start, in a sim with a calendar)
None


stop
str/int/float/ss.date/ss.Duration
when the simulation/module ends, read as the start is: a date, a bare number (a year if the sim has a calendar, else a time in its unit from 0), or a duration (a time from 0, for a sim with no calendar; ss.years(2030) in a sim of calendar years is the year 2030) (default: a run of 100 days in days, else 50 of the sim’s unit)
None


dur
int/float/ss.Duration
the length of the run, from its start (a bare number is in years in a sim of calendar years, as a bare stop is, else in the sim’s unit): start=2000, dur=10 is the same as start=2000, stop=2010, and so is stop=2010, dur=10 (any two define the third; all three must agree)
None


dt
int/float/ss.Duration
the step (a bare number is in the sim’s unit)
None


name
str
if provided, name the Timeline object
None


init
bool
whether or not to immediately initialize the Timeline object (by default, yes if start and stop are provided; otherwise no)
None


sim
Sim
if provided, initialize the Timeline with this as the parent (i.e. populating missing values)
None



The Timeline object, after initialization, has the following time vectors, each representing a different way of representing time:

tvec: ground truth simulation time, either as absolute ss.date instances, or relative ss.Duration instances, e.g. DateArray([<2021-01-01>, <2021-01-03>, <2021-01-05>, <2021-01-07>])
tivec: the vector of time indices (np.arange(len(tvec)))
timevec: the “human-friendly” representation of tvec: same as tvec if using ss.date, else floats if using ss.Duration
yearvec: time represented as floating-point years
datevec: time represented as ss.date instances
relvec: relative time, in the unit of the sim’s step (dt)

The Timeline object also has the following attributes/methods:

ti (int): the current time point, which is also the current step: step ti runs from time point ti to the next, and its results go at ti
npts (int): the total number of time points in the timeline, which is also the number of steps (see note below)
now() (ss.date/float/str): the current time, time point ti, the start of the current step, based on tvec by default or a different vector if specified
calendar (str): ‘dates’, ‘years’, or None (see ss.timeline.calendar_of()), and unit, the class of the sim’s unit (e.g. ss.days)
dur (ss.Duration): the length of the run, from its start to its stop

Note: the time vectors include both the start and stop endpoints, and a step is taken from each of them, so each time point is a period: a stock at it is the state at its start, and a flow at it is the total over the step that starts there. For example, start=0, stop=1, dt=1 produces two time points ([0, 1]) and takes two steps; the state after the last one is not recorded. Giving the length (dur) is the same as giving the stop (start=2000, dur=1 is the same timeline as start=2000, stop=2001). See the time user guide for the rationale behind the inclusive endpoint.



t1 = ss.Timeline(start=2000, stop=2020, dt=1.0)
t2 = ss.Timeline(start='2021-01-01', stop='2021-04-04', dt=ss.days(2))
t3 = ss.Timeline(start='2021-01-01', dur=ss.days(90), dt=ss.days(1)) # 90 days from the start

errors
Errors, warnings, and notes.
Each error is an exception class, e.g. ss.errors.UnknownState, and each warning a warning class, e.g. ss.errors.ImportIncomplete. A note is a line about something that was assumed or approximated: it is kept in sim.notes and printed when verbose is 1 or more (see ss.note()). The docstring of each class says when it is raised, and is what the catalog in the specification (15-errors.md) is made from: see ss.errors.catalog().

The main base class for all Starsim modules: diseases, networks, interventions, etc.
By convention, keyword arguments to modules are assigned to “_“, which is an alias for None. These are then populated with defaults by mod.define_pars(), which are then updated with mod.update_pars(), which inspects the __init__ function to get these arguments.
Note that there is no functional difference between specifying arguments this way rather than simply via **kwargs, but having the arguments shown in the function signature can make it easier to read, and “_” is a convention to indicate that the default is specified below.

            init_prev = ss.bernoulli(p=0.01),

Define aliases for states, e.g. self.define_aliases(infectious='infected')
An alias is only used if the attribute isn’t otherwise defined, so it acts as a default that a subclass overrides simply by defining a state of the same name. E.g. ss.AgentDisease treats everyone infected as infectious this way, while letting a subclass define infectious as a state (or another alias) in its own right.
Each alias is either the name of another state, or a callable taking the module as its only argument. A callable behaves like a property: it is recomputed on each access, so it can be read but not written to.
Note: a callable alias defined as a lambda can’t be saved with plain pickle (sc.save() and ss.MultiSim are both fine, since they use dill). Use a module-level function, or a property, if plain pickling is required.
A callable alias also generates an automatic result, in the same way a BoolState does: an alias named infected produces the result infected. A string alias does not, since the state it points to is already counted under its own name.

internals.modules.Module.from_func(func)
Create a module from a function
Wraps a plain function into a module of the calling class, so that simple, one-off logic can be used anywhere a module is expected without writing a full class. The function must take the sim as its only argument; it becomes the module’s step() method and is therefore called once on every timestep (so it must do its own time gating, e.g. if sim.now == 2015:). The module’s name is taken from the function’s name.
This is the mechanism behind “function-based” interventions and analyzers: passing a function to interventions=, analyzers=, or modules= automatically calls from_func() on the appropriate class (ss.Intervention, ss.Analyzer, or ss.Module respectively), so usually you don’t need to call this method directly. Call it explicitly when you want to construct the module yourself, e.g. to add it to a sim later.
Keyword arguments of the function with defaults are the module’s parameters, passed to it at each call; one given as ss.par with bounds can be fitted (sim.fit()), sampled (sim.sensitivity()), and set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...), ss.parallel(pars=...)) as any other. This is how to fit a value that is not a parameter of any module, e.g. one set in code (see the second example).
Function-based modules are otherwise minimal: they have no states or results of their own. As soon as you need define_states() or define_results(), write a proper subclass instead.

def knockdown(sim): # Halve transmission for one year starting in 2015
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= 0.5

Define aliases for states, e.g. self.define_aliases(infectious='infected')
An alias is only used if the attribute isn’t otherwise defined, so it acts as a default that a subclass overrides simply by defining a state of the same name. E.g. ss.AgentDisease treats everyone infected as infectious this way, while letting a subclass define infectious as a state (or another alias) in its own right.
Each alias is either the name of another state, or a callable taking the module as its only argument. A callable behaves like a property: it is recomputed on each access, so it can be read but not written to.
Note: a callable alias defined as a lambda can’t be saved with plain pickle (sc.save() and ss.MultiSim are both fine, since they use dill). Use a module-level function, or a property, if plain pickling is required.
A callable alias also generates an automatic result, in the same way a BoolState does: an alias named infected produces the result infected. A string alias does not, since the state it points to is already counted under its own name.

internals.modules.Module.from_func(func)
Create a module from a function
Wraps a plain function into a module of the calling class, so that simple, one-off logic can be used anywhere a module is expected without writing a full class. The function must take the sim as its only argument; it becomes the module’s step() method and is therefore called once on every timestep (so it must do its own time gating, e.g. if sim.now == 2015:). The module’s name is taken from the function’s name.
This is the mechanism behind “function-based” interventions and analyzers: passing a function to interventions=, analyzers=, or modules= automatically calls from_func() on the appropriate class (ss.Intervention, ss.Analyzer, or ss.Module respectively), so usually you don’t need to call this method directly. Call it explicitly when you want to construct the module yourself, e.g. to add it to a sim later.
Keyword arguments of the function with defaults are the module’s parameters, passed to it at each call; one given as ss.par with bounds can be fitted (sim.fit()), sampled (sim.sensitivity()), and set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...), ss.parallel(pars=...)) as any other. This is how to fit a value that is not a parameter of any module, e.g. one set in code (see the second example).
Function-based modules are otherwise minimal: they have no states or results of their own. As soon as you need define_states() or define_results(), write a proper subclass instead.

import starsim as ss

def knockdown(sim): # Halve transmission for one year starting in 2015
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= 0.5

# Explicit construction ...
intv = ss.Intervention.from_func(knockdown)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=intv)

# ... or equivalently, let the sim convert it automatically:
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks='random', interventions=knockdown)

# A value set in code, fitted: the fraction of transmission left in 2015
def knockdown(sim, frac=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.1, 1])):
    if sim.now == 2015:
        sim.diseases.sis.rel_trans[:] *= frac

Decorator to mark module methods as required.
A common gotcha in Starsim is to forget to call super(), or to mistype a method name so it’s never called. This decorator lets you mark methods (of Modules only) to be sure that they are called either on sim initialization or on sim run.


import starsim.library as ssl

class CustomSIS(ssl.AgentSIS):

    def step(self):
        super().step()
        self.custom_step() # Will raise an exception if this line is not here
        return

    @ss.required() # Mark this method as required on run
    def custom_step(self):
        pass

A matrix acts on what the rate says: beta*I is exposure to the fraction of each group (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N_j), beta*I.n to the number in each (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j), and beta*I.frac to that number over everyone in the same place (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N). solvers.mixing.Mixing.edge_dur(net, sim)
How long each edge of a network transmits over before it is drawn again, in units of the sim’s time, for its approximation by homogeneous mixing: the network’s own step (a disease that steps less often uses its own: see ss.solvers.Compartmental.saturation()); None for a network whose edges never change (dynamic=False)
As agents, an edge transmits at most once to its susceptible end over a step D, with probability 1 − e^(−b·D) for a rate b, so the force of infection over K contacts per unit time is K·(1 − e^(−b·D))/D, not the K·b of mass action. The two agree as K → ∞ with K·b held fixed, but on a sparse network with long steps the difference matters, most of all near the epidemic threshold. Edges that last several steps (ss.RandomNet(dur=)) are taken a step at a time: within a lasting edge, the partners’ states change (recovery, reinfection), which is the partner-change model’s concern (ss.DegreeNet).

A matrix acts on what the rate says: beta*I is exposure to the fraction of each group (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N_j), beta*I.n to the number in each (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j), and beta*I.frac to that number over everyone in the same place (beta·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N). How long each edge of a network transmits over before it is drawn again, in units of the sim’s time, for its approximation by homogeneous mixing: the network’s own step (a disease that steps less often uses its own: see ss.solvers.Compartmental.saturation()); None for a network whose edges never change (dynamic=False)
As agents, an edge transmits at most once to its susceptible end over a step D, with probability 1 − e^(−b·D) for a rate b, so the force of infection over K contacts per unit time is K·(1 − e^(−b·D))/D, not the K·b of mass action. The two agree as K → ∞ with K·b held fixed, but on a sparse network with long steps the difference matters, most of all near the epidemic threshold. Edges that last several steps (ss.RandomNet(dur=)) are taken a step at a time: within a lasting edge, the partners’ states change (recovery, reinfection), which is the partner-change model’s concern (ss.DegreeNet).
