title: library.networks
text:
library.networks
Additional network types: household, cluster, spatial, and theoretical.
HouseholdNet builds households from DHS-style survey data; ClusterNet divides agents into fully connected clusters, and HybridNet is Covasim’s population of households, schools, workplaces, and community; DiskNet connects agents that are spatially close, GeoNet connects them across real places, and GridNet puts them on a lattice; NullNet is useful for debugging, SmallWorldNet and ScaleFreeNet are the classic graphs, and StaticNet turns a NetworkX graph into a network (by default, an Erdős–Rényi graph). Core network classes (ss.RandomNet, ss.DegreeNet, ss.SexualNet, etc.) live in starsim.networks.
Most of these networks run as agents only. Those a compartmental run can approximate by a mean number of contacts are marked in their files.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




ClusterNet
Fully connected clusters of agents, e.g. households, schools, or workplaces


DiskNet
Disk graph in which edges are made between agents located within a user-defined radius.


GeoNet
Random contacts between real places


GridNet
Agents on a square grid, in contact with their neighbors


HouseholdNet
A household contact network built from DHS-style survey data.


HybridNet
Covasim v3’s “hybrid” population: households, schools, workplaces, and community


NullNet
A convenience class for a network of size n that only has self-connections with a weight of 0.


ScaleFreeNet
A scale-free (Barabási-Albert) network: a few agents have many contacts, and most have few


SmallWorldNet
A small-world (Watts-Strogatz) network: mostly local contacts, with a few long-range ones


StaticNet
A network class of static partnerships converted from a networkx graph. There’s no formation of new partnerships





library.networks.ClusterNet(
    pars=None,
    cluster_size=_,
    who=_,
    dynamic=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Fully connected clusters of agents, e.g. households, schools, or workplaces
Each agent (optionally, only those within an age range) is assigned to one cluster, with cluster sizes drawn from cluster_size, and every pair of agents within a cluster is connected. Agents are assigned to clusters in a random order (from a CRN-safe random number per agent), so clusters are not correlated with other networks. Based on make_microstructured_contacts() from Covasim v3: as there, clusters of size 0 are skipped, and the last cluster is truncated to fit.
Note: CRN safe, unless dynamic=True and people are born or die.

Type

Default

the size of each cluster; a number is the mean of a Poisson distribution (a size, like a target number of partners in ss.DegreeNet; for clusters all of one size, give ss.constant(n))

if given, who takes part: a condition over people (e.g. (ss.person.age >= 6) & (ss.person.age < 22)), as for ss.RandomNet
_

bool
if True, the clusters are recreated on each timestep; if False (default), they are created once and never change
_

dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None

sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks=households)
sim.run()

Disk graph in which edges are made between agents located within a user-defined radius.
Interactions take place within a square with edge length of 1. Agents are initialized to have a random position and orientation within this square. On each time step, agents advance v*dt in the direction they are pointed. When encountering a wall, agents are reflected.
Edges are formed between two agents if they are within r distance of each other.

    places='Kenya',
    level=1,
    local=0.9,
    c=2.0,
    pars=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Random contacts between real places
Each agent lives in a place, in proportion to its population. Most of an agent’s contacts are in their own place, and the rest are in other places, more of them in places that are large and near, as in a gravity model: the fraction going from place i to place j is in proportion to pop_j/distance_ij**c. Within each place, contacts are paired at random. A country’s places need no download (see ss.geo.geography).
The place of each agent is the state place, an index into geo.names. Like ss.RandomNet, this is not CRN safe when people are born or die.

library.networks.HouseholdNet(
    pars=None,
    dhs_data=None,
    dynamic=None,
    prob_move_out=_,
    **kwargs,
)
A household contact network built from DHS-style survey data.
When initialized, this network overrides the age (and optionally sex) of all agents in the sim and assigns each agent a household ID. Use with caution if other modules depend upon or alter age and sex.
Households are created by selecting a random household from the provided data and setting the age and sex of agents to match, repeating until all agents have been assigned to a household. Ages in the data are typically in integer years; a random fractional year is added so agents don’t share exact ages.
This network assumes only one mother per household. Births are automatically added to their mother’s household network.
Note: not CRN safe unless dynamic=False (the partners who move out are drawn together).





Name
Type
Description
Default




dhs_data
DataFrame / str
A pandas or Sciris dataframe with columns hh_id and ages. Optionally also sexes. The ages column should contain comma-separated age strings (e.g. "72, 17, 30"). If sexes is included, it should contain comma-separated values using DHS convention (1 = male, 2 = female) with the same number of entries as ages. Pass 'default' to use synthetic data (see make_default_data()), e.g. for demos and testing.
None


dynamic
bool
If True, households evolve over time: one female is assigned as head of each household, pregnant non-head females may move out to form new households, and births are added to the mother’s household, which needs ss.Pregnancy. If False, the network is static and step() is a no-op. By default, households evolve if the sim has ss.Pregnancy, and are static otherwise.
None


prob_move_out
float
Probability a non-head female moves out to start her own household, evaluated once at the start of each pregnancy. Default 0.7. Only used when households evolve.
_


pars
dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



To update the households less often than every step of the sim, give the network its own step, e.g. dt=ss.years(1).
The expected dataframe format is::
    hh_id                ages          sexes
0       0          72, 17, 30        1, 1, 2
1       1                  37              2
2       2          13, 55, 36        2, 1, 2
3       3  52, 13, 12, 64, 53     1, 2, 1, 2
4       4              30, 66           1, 1
Data in this format can be obtained from the DHS Program. To prepare a DHS household dataset:

Register and request access at https://dhsprogram.com
Download a Household Recode (HR) dataset in Stata format (e.g. XXHR7xDT.zip)
Use HouseholdNet.load_dhs() to extract the data::
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl dhs_data = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet.load_dhs(‘XXHR7xDT/XXHR7xFL.DTA’) sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data, dynamic=False)) sim.run()

If real data are not available, synthetic data can be constructed::
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl

n = 1000
age_strings = []
for i in range(n):
    household_size = np.random.randint(1, 6)
    ages = np.random.randint(0, 80, household_size)
    age_strings.append(sc.strjoin(ages))
dhs_data = sc.dataframe(hh_id=np.arange(n), ages=age_strings)

household = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data, dynamic=False)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks=household)
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Description

Generate contacts by assigning agents to households sampled from the data.

Find females that are pregnant and not a head of household.

Add the first edges, and add a random fraction of a year to each age

Initialize the network: households evolve if the sim has ss.Pregnancy (unless dynamic says otherwise), which they need

Load a DHS Household Recode (HR) Stata file and return a dataframe

library.networks.HybridNet(
    pars=None,
    household_size=_,
    n_contacts=_,
    school_ages=_,
    work_ages=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    clustered=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Covasim v3’s “hybrid” population: households, schools, workplaces, and community
When added to a sim, this expands into four separate networks: households (h), schools (s), and workplaces (w), each an ssl.ClusterNet, and community (c), an ss.RandomNet with Poisson-distributed contacts. Schools and workplaces are restricted by age. As in Covasim v3, the networks are static; unlike it, schools and workplaces are clusters by default, so that a person’s contacts also know each other (use clustered=False for Covasim v3’s random networks). With the default Poisson sizes, clusters give the same mean number of contacts as a random network. Each network can then be modified separately, e.g. sim.networks.s.
Transmissibility on each network is the disease’s, by network. Covasim v3’s relative transmissibility of the layers is ssl.HybridNet.rel_betas (3 for households, 0.6 for schools and workplaces, and 0.3 for the community), and ssl.HybridNet.betas() gives a disease’s beta for each layer from its beta per contact (by default Covasim’s, 0.016 a day), e.g. ss.SIS(beta=ssl.HybridNet.betas()), which is beta=dict(h=ss.perday(0.048), s=ss.perday(0.0096), w=ss.perday(0.0096), c=ss.perday(0.0048)).

library.networks.HouseholdNet(
    pars=None,
    dhs_data=None,
    dynamic=None,
    prob_move_out=_,
    **kwargs,
)
A household contact network built from DHS-style survey data.
When initialized, this network overrides the age (and optionally sex) of all agents in the sim and assigns each agent a household ID. Use with caution if other modules depend upon or alter age and sex.
Households are created by selecting a random household from the provided data and setting the age and sex of agents to match, repeating until all agents have been assigned to a household. Ages in the data are typically in integer years; a random fractional year is added so agents don’t share exact ages.
This network assumes only one mother per household. Births are automatically added to their mother’s household network.
Note: not CRN safe unless dynamic=False (the partners who move out are drawn together).





Name
Type
Description
Default




dhs_data
DataFrame / str
A pandas or Sciris dataframe with columns hh_id and ages. Optionally also sexes. The ages column should contain comma-separated age strings (e.g. "72, 17, 30"). If sexes is included, it should contain comma-separated values using DHS convention (1 = male, 2 = female) with the same number of entries as ages. Pass 'default' to use synthetic data (see make_default_data()), e.g. for demos and testing.
None


dynamic
bool
If True, households evolve over time: one female is assigned as head of each household, pregnant non-head females may move out to form new households, and births are added to the mother’s household, which needs ss.Pregnancy. If False, the network is static and step() is a no-op. By default, households evolve if the sim has ss.Pregnancy, and are static otherwise.
None


prob_move_out
float
Probability a non-head female moves out to start her own household, evaluated once at the start of each pregnancy. Default 0.7. Only used when households evolve.
_


pars
dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



To update the households less often than every step of the sim, give the network its own step, e.g. dt=ss.years(1).
The expected dataframe format is::
    hh_id                ages          sexes
0       0          72, 17, 30        1, 1, 2
1       1                  37              2
2       2          13, 55, 36        2, 1, 2
3       3  52, 13, 12, 64, 53     1, 2, 1, 2
4       4              30, 66           1, 1
Data in this format can be obtained from the DHS Program. To prepare a DHS household dataset:

Register and request access at https://dhsprogram.com
Download a Household Recode (HR) dataset in Stata format (e.g. XXHR7xDT.zip)
Use HouseholdNet.load_dhs() to extract the data::
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl dhs_data = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet.load_dhs(‘XXHR7xDT/XXHR7xFL.DTA’) sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data, dynamic=False)) sim.run()

If real data are not available, synthetic data can be constructed::
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import starsim as ss; import starsim.library as ssl

n = 1000
age_strings = []
for i in range(n):
    household_size = np.random.randint(1, 6)
    ages = np.random.randint(0, 80, household_size)
    age_strings.append(sc.strjoin(ages))
dhs_data = sc.dataframe(hh_id=np.arange(n), ages=age_strings)

household = ssl.networks.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data, dynamic=False)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases='sis', networks=household)
sim.run()
sim.plot()

title: internals.fitting

internals.fitting
Fitting sims to data: likelihoods, particle filters, samplers, and what sim.fit() runs
These exist so that a model can be fitted, with its uncertainty, in the same way whichever solver runs it. Parameters are chosen by giving them bounds (ss.par), in declared modules or in the parameters of modules written as code. Some methods are for some solvers only: gradients come from JAX, and particle filters need a stochastic compartmental solver.
Imported when it is first used (by ss.fitting.X, sim.fit(), or sim.sensitivity()), not by import starsim.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Fit
The result of fitting a sim to its data; see sim.fit()


ModelComparison
The result of comparing models by how well they predict held-out data; see ss.fitting.compare_models()


Optimization
The result of allocating spending to maximize (or minimize) a result; see sim.optimize()


ParticleFilter
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')


Swarm
The parameter values of each particle of IF2, iterated filtering, and the rates of the run that they give (see sim.fit() with method=‘if2’)


maximize
The goal of sim.optimize(): a result to make as large as possible


method
A fitting method and its settings, for sim.fit(method=...)


minimize
The goal of sim.optimize(): a result to make as small as possible





internals.fitting.Fit(
    sim,
    before,
    pars,
    table,
    trials,
    method,
    objective,
    objective_before,
    measure,
    samples,
    diagnostics,
    converged,
    why,
    scores,
    study=None,
    trajectories=None,
)
The result of fitting a sim to its data; see sim.fit()





Name
Type
Description




sim
ss.Sim
the calibrated sim: a copy of the original with the best-fit values, already run


pars
dict
the best-fit value of each fitted parameter; can be passed to ss.Sim(pars=...)


table
df
parameter, initial value, best fit, and bounds (and with method='if2', the lowest and highest of the chains’ estimates, as spread_lower and spread_upper)


before
ss.Sim
the sim with the initial values, already run


objective
float
what the fit minimized, for the calibrated sim: its loss, or its negative log-likelihood (or log-posterior) if the fit used likelihoods; for a stochastic sim, the particle filter’s estimate of it (with Optuna, where the filter can run the sim), or else the mean over several runs of each run’s


measure
str
what objective measures, e.g. ‘negative log-likelihood’, or for a stochastic sim ‘negative log-likelihood (estimated by a particle filter of 200 particles)’ or ‘negative mean log-likelihood of 4 runs’ (which is not the likelihood: the mean of the logs, not the log of the mean)


objective_before
float
the same, before the fit


converged
bool
whether the searches from the best few points of the scan that are apart end at the same value (for SciPy; with a single search, SciPy’s own stopping rule), stopped improving (for Optuna: by less than 1% over the last quarter of the trials), or has chains that agree (for NUTS and particle MCMC: an R-hat of at most 1.01, and no divergent draws; for IF2: chains from different starts that end within 2 of the best log-likelihood); None for ABC-SMC, whose posterior is approximate, by an amount that depends on the tolerance it reached, with no rule for when it is close enough


why
str
what converged is based on


scores
list
the score of the best-fit values in each run (one for a deterministic sim, and one, the particle filter’s, where it scored the points); objective is their mean, so it is the score that was minimized


trials
df
every evaluation: the values, and the objective that the method minimized (what measure says; with method='if2', also each pass of each chain: the middle of the swarm’s values, and minus the log-likelihood of the pass, whose values were perturbed)


samples
df
with method='nuts', 'pmcmc', or 'abc-smc', the draws from the posterior: one row per draw, with its chain, its number, and a column for each parameter


trajectories
list
for a stochastic compartmental sim with method='pmcmc' or 'abc-smc', the run of the sim that goes with each draw of samples (one per row), so that each pair is a draw from the posterior of the values and the epidemic together: with 'pmcmc', a run drawn from the particle filter, up to the last data point (see ss.fitting.ParticleFilter); with 'abc-smc', the run that was accepted. Each is, by the module that runs the compartments, the time point it ends at (ti), the compartments there (y), and by disease how many were in each state (stocks) and the flow along each transition (flows) at each time point before it; a draw that the chain stayed at shares its run with the draw before. fit.project() continues them. (For a deterministic sim, the run at each draw is its trajectory, so none are kept)


study
optuna.Study
with method='optuna', Optuna’s study, e.g. for its plots (optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(fit.study))


diagnostics
dict
what else the method reports: divergences (with method='nuts', the number of draws that followed a divergent trajectory, which suggests the sampler missed part of the posterior), acceptance (with method='pmcmc', the fraction of proposals that each chain accepted after its warm-up; with 'abc-smc', that of its last generation), tolerance and generations (with 'abc-smc', the tolerance of its last generation, which sets how close its posterior is, and the number of generations run), and band (with a posterior, for each data series, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the model’s value over draws from it, at each step, or for a flow with data at a longer period than the step, of its totals over the data’s periods; with 'pmcmc', each from a run with a seed of its own, so the band includes chance)

internals.fitting.Fit.project(
    scenarios=None,
    n_runs=None,
    rand_seed=None,
    restart=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Run the fitted model forward under each scenario, with the uncertainty in the fitted values: one run per draw from the posterior, each with a seed of its own (or runs of the best fit, each with its own seed, for a method that gives none), with the same draws and seeds in every scenario
With a run kept for each draw (fit.trajectories), each run continues the draw’s own, from where it ends (with a seed of its own for what follows): up to there it is the epidemic that the draw’s values give with the data, and the scenarios differ only after it. With restart=True, each draw is run from the start instead, as for a fit that keeps no runs, so its course is not conditioned on the data, only its values are; this is also what happens, with a warning saying why, when the runs can’t be continued (a scenario the kernels don’t run whole, e.g. an intervention they do not take, or different time points). Either way, for a deterministic sim, the runs are the same.

Runs that continue those of the draws are kept as results only (with no results by group), since a sim cannot start partway through.

internals.fitting.ParticleFilter(sim, likelihood=None, weights=None)
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')
Many runs of the sim (the particles, ss.solvers.Particles) go forward together. At each data point, each is weighted by the likelihood of the data given its results, and when the weights become uneven, the runs are drawn again in proportion to them, so that runs that have strayed from the data are dropped and those that follow it are copied. The product over the data of the mean weight is an unbiased estimate of the likelihood (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), which is what particle MCMC needs.
Each declared disease is filtered on its own, since the diseases of a sim that the kernels run whole do not affect each other, except those tracked jointly (see ss.solvers.JointStates), which are filtered together, as the runs of their program. An outcome is compared with the data as its expected number (rather than drawn, as a run of the sim draws it), as the likelihood would compare it.
After each call, path is one run drawn from the filter: a particle at the last data point, drawn by its weight, and the particles it was copied from back to the start (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), as particle MCMC keeps with each draw (see Fit.trajectories). For each disease filtered (or diseases tracked jointly, by the first’s name), it has the time point after the last step that its data read, ti; the compartments there, y; and, by disease, how many were in each state (stocks) and the flow along each transition (flows) at each time point before it (totals over the groups), as ss.solvers.Compartmental.run_many() takes them to continue the run.
Each particle has random numbers of its own, so the particles are shared between threads (see ss.options.threads; one in the workers of ss.parallel() and of a calibration), and the estimate does not depend on how many there are.

the method’s settings; those of each method, with their defaults:

SciPy methods: scan (the points spread over the bounds to try first: 10 per parameter, at most 100), restarts (the searches from the best of them that are apart: 3, or 1 for one parameter of a deterministic sim), and SciPy’s own options, e.g. maxiter=500 (see scipy.optimize.show_options())
'optuna': n_trials (default: 50 per fitted parameter, at least 100), particles (for a stochastic sim that the particle filter can run, with a likelihood for every data series: the particles of the filter that scores each point, 200; see ss.fitting.ParticleFilter), workers (processes that run trials at once, sharing what they learn: 1), storage (a file name, a database URL, or an Optuna storage, where the trials are kept so that calling the fit again resumes it), and Optuna’s own keywords for study.optimize(), e.g. timeout=600
'nuts': draws='auto' (until the chains agree, with an R-hat of at most 1.01, and every value has 400 effective draws; or a number), warmup=300, chains=4, scan (each chain starts from one of the best points of a scan that are apart), and for draws='auto': ess=400, rhat=1.01, max_draws=5000, batch=100
'pmcmc': draws='auto' (as for NUTS), warmup=1000, chains=4, max_draws=20000, batch=250, particles (of the particle filter: by default chosen by each chain in its warm-up; see ss.fitting.pmmh(); none for a deterministic sim, whose likelihood is exact), scan (each chain starts from one of the best points of a scan that are apart), parallel=True (to run the chains in parallel processes)
'if2': particles=1000 (of the particle filter), iterations=50 (passes of the filter in each chain), cooling=0.5 (the fraction of the first size of the random walk’s steps that is left after 50 passes, as pomp’s cooling.fraction.50), sd=0.05 (that first size, on the scale searched on), chains=4
'abc-smc': samples=200 (the parameter values kept in each generation, which are the draws of the posterior), generations=8, quantile=0.5 (of the distances, which sets the next tolerance), tolerance (the distance to stop at)
for a stochastic sim, how each point is scored (SciPy methods and Optuna; n_runs also for particle MCMC’s start): n_runs (runs per point: 4 for a stochastic compartmental sim, 1 for agents and for a deterministic one; every point is scored by the mean over the same seeds of each run’s score; for Optuna, giving it scores by runs in place of the particle filter), and reseed (whether each point takes fresh seeds: by default only for Optuna, whose search then averages over chance)
for the methods with gradients (‘l-bfgs-b’, ‘slsqp’, ‘nuts’): require_jax=True (whether the gradients have to be taken with the log-likelihood as one function in JAX; with False, something JAX does not cover yet is taken with Python in the loop instead, which is much slower)








import starsim as ss

beta = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 1])
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ beta*I
sir = ss.Disease(infection, I >> R @ ss.days(8), ss.outcome(0.5*infection, name='cases', likelihood=ss.poisson()), init=dict(I=0.01), name='sir')
pars = dict(total_pop=10_000, unit='day', stop=60, solver='binomial')
data = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.5), rand_seed=2, **pars).run().to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, **pars)
fit = sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method('optuna', n_trials=50, n_runs=4))
post = sim.fit(method=ss.fitting.method('pmcmc', draws=200, warmup=200, chains=2, particles=100))

Compare models by how well they predict data they were not fitted to
Each model is fitted (with sim.fit()) to all but the last part of each data series, run forward over that part, and scored on it: by the default goodness of fit, or by the log predictive density if every series of every model has a likelihood; the same measure is used for every model. A model with more parameters usually fits better; the prediction error needs no separate penalty for them.
A stochastic model is run n_runs times at its best-fit values, and scored by the log of the mean over the runs of the likelihood (or by the mean loss), since its predictive probability is the average over the epidemics it could give, and a single run scores worse than that average. The runs start at the beginning and are not conditioned on the data fitted to (as a particle filter would condition them), so a run that drifts early is still scored on the held-out part, which is harsher on a stochastic model than on a deterministic one; and they are at the best-fit values, not averaged over a posterior.

The log-density is given in one of two ways. By default, as a function of NumPy arrays that returns its value and gradient, so it can be anything (here, a run of the sim, differentiated by ss.gradients.gradient()); it is called back from JAX, and the chains are run one after another. Sample from a posterior by particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on a log-density that is estimated by a particle filter (or is exact)
Since the estimate of the likelihood is unbiased, the chains sample from the exact posterior (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), however noisy it is; more noise only makes them move more slowly. In the warm-up, the proposal’s covariance is learned from the chain so far (Haario et al. 2001), and its scale is tuned toward accepting 15% of proposals (about the best when the estimate is noisy; Sherlock et al. 2015; 23.4% for an exact log-density). In the first half of the warm-up, the estimate where the chain is is made again at each step, so that a chain far from the posterior, where the estimate is noisiest, cannot be held by a lucky one. With particles=0, the log-density is exact (e.g. of an ODE), so it is worked out once at each point, and this is an adaptive random-walk Metropolis sampler. With draws='auto' (the default), the chains are taken further in rounds of batch draws until they agree, with enough effective draws (rhat, ess; see enough_draws()), or reach max_draws.

internals.fitting.ParticleFilter(sim, likelihood=None, weights=None)
An estimate of the likelihood of a stochastic sim’s data, from a bootstrap particle filter (see sim.fit() with method='pmcmc')
Many runs of the sim (the particles, ss.solvers.Particles) go forward together. At each data point, each is weighted by the likelihood of the data given its results, and when the weights become uneven, the runs are drawn again in proportion to them, so that runs that have strayed from the data are dropped and those that follow it are copied. The product over the data of the mean weight is an unbiased estimate of the likelihood (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), which is what particle MCMC needs.
Each declared disease is filtered on its own, since the diseases of a sim that the kernels run whole do not affect each other, except those tracked jointly (see ss.solvers.JointStates), which are filtered together, as the runs of their program. An outcome is compared with the data as its expected number (rather than drawn, as a run of the sim draws it), as the likelihood would compare it.
After each call, path is one run drawn from the filter: a particle at the last data point, drawn by its weight, and the particles it was copied from back to the start (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), as particle MCMC keeps with each draw (see Fit.trajectories). For each disease filtered (or diseases tracked jointly, by the first’s name), it has the time point after the last step that its data read, ti; the compartments there, y; and, by disease, how many were in each state (stocks) and the flow along each transition (flows) at each time point before it (totals over the groups), as ss.solvers.Compartmental.run_many() takes them to continue the run.
Each particle has random numbers of its own, so the particles are shared between threads (see ss.options.threads; one in the workers of ss.parallel() and of a calibration), and the estimate does not depend on how many there are.

the method’s settings; those of each method, with their defaults:

SciPy methods: scan (the points spread over the bounds to try first: 10 per parameter, at most 100), restarts (the searches from the best of them that are apart: 3, or 1 for one parameter of a deterministic sim), and SciPy’s own options, e.g. maxiter=500 (see scipy.optimize.show_options())
'optuna': n_trials (default: 50 per fitted parameter, at least 100), particles (for a stochastic sim that the particle filter can run, with a likelihood for every data series: the particles of the filter that scores each point, 200; see ss.fitting.ParticleFilter), workers (processes that run trials at once, sharing what they learn: 1), storage (a file name, a database URL, or an Optuna storage, where the trials are kept so that calling the fit again resumes it), and Optuna’s own keywords for study.optimize(), e.g. timeout=600
'nuts': draws='auto' (until the chains agree, with an R-hat of at most 1.01, and every value has 400 effective draws; or a number), warmup=300, chains=4, scan (each chain starts from one of the best points of a scan that are apart), and for draws='auto': ess=400, rhat=1.01, max_draws=5000, batch=100
'pmcmc': draws='auto' (as for NUTS), warmup=1000, chains=4, max_draws=20000, batch=250, particles (of the particle filter: by default chosen by each chain in its warm-up; see ss.fitting.pmmh(); none for a deterministic sim, whose likelihood is exact), scan (each chain starts from one of the best points of a scan that are apart), parallel=True (to run the chains in parallel processes)
'if2': particles=1000 (of the particle filter), iterations=50 (passes of the filter in each chain), cooling=0.5 (the fraction of the first size of the random walk’s steps that is left after 50 passes, as pomp’s cooling.fraction.50), sd=0.05 (that first size, on the scale searched on), chains=4
'abc-smc': samples=200 (the parameter values kept in each generation, which are the draws of the posterior), generations=8, quantile=0.5 (of the distances, which sets the next tolerance), tolerance (the distance to stop at)
for a stochastic sim, how each point is scored (SciPy methods and Optuna; n_runs also for particle MCMC’s start): n_runs (runs per point: 4 for a stochastic compartmental sim, 1 for agents and for a deterministic one; every point is scored by the mean over the same seeds of each run’s score; for Optuna, giving it scores by runs in place of the particle filter), and reseed (whether each point takes fresh seeds: by default only for Optuna, whose search then averages over chance)
for the methods with gradients (‘l-bfgs-b’, ‘slsqp’, ‘nuts’): require_jax=True (whether the gradients have to be taken with the log-likelihood as one function in JAX; with False, something JAX does not cover yet is taken with Python in the loop instead, which is much slower)

sim = ss.Sim(sir, data=data, **pars)

    distance,
    logprior,
    z0,
    samples=200,
    generations=8,
    quantile=0.5,

    min_acceptance=0.02,
    rand_seed=None,
    verbose=True,
)
Approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo (Beaumont et al. 2009): a posterior without a likelihood
A population of samples (parameter values) is drawn from the prior, and in each generation a new one is drawn from the last (each sample perturbed by a Gaussian kernel twice as wide as the population) and kept only if its run is within the tolerance of the data; the tolerance is the median distance of the last population, so it shrinks as the population moves toward the data. Weights correct for the samples not being drawn from the prior.

internals.fitting.compare_models(

    data=None,
    holdout=0.25,
    folds=None,
    n_runs=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Compare models by how well they predict data they were not fitted to
Each model is fitted (with sim.fit()) to all but the last part of each data series, run forward over that part, and scored on it: by the default goodness of fit, or by the log predictive density if every series of every model has a likelihood; the same measure is used for every model. A model with more parameters usually fits better; the prediction error needs no separate penalty for them.
A stochastic model is run n_runs times at its best-fit values, and scored by the log of the mean over the runs of the likelihood (or by the mean loss), since its predictive probability is the average over the epidemics it could give, and a single run scores worse than that average. The runs start at the beginning and are not conditioned on the data fitted to (as a particle filter would condition them), so a run that drifts early is still scored on the held-out part, which is harsher on a stochastic model than on a deterministic one; and they are at the best-fit values, not averaged over a posterior.

Sample from a posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS, from BlackJAX), with Stan’s warm-up of the step size and the mass matrix
The log-density is given in one of two ways. By default, as a function of NumPy arrays that returns its value and gradient, so it can be anything (here, a run of the sim, differentiated by ss.gradients.gradient()); it is called back from JAX, and the chains are run one after another. With traced=True, as a JAX function (see ss.gradients.Density), so that the whole of the sampling is compiled, with the chains run together (each on cores of its own); its gradient is taken in forward mode (one direction per parameter), which for a few parameters is much cheaper than reverse mode through the steps of an ODE, or with forward=False in reverse mode (one pass whatever their number, for many parameters). Sample from a posterior by particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on a log-density that is estimated by a particle filter (or is exact)
Since the estimate of the likelihood is unbiased, the chains sample from the exact posterior (Andrieu, Doucet & Holenstein 2010), however noisy it is; more noise only makes them move more slowly. In the warm-up, the proposal’s covariance is learned from the chain so far (Haario et al. 2001), and its scale is tuned toward accepting 15% of proposals (about the best when the estimate is noisy; Sherlock et al. 2015; 23.4% for an exact log-density). In the first half of the warm-up, the estimate where the chain is is made again at each step, so that a chain far from the posterior, where the estimate is noisiest, cannot be held by a lucky one. With particles=0, the log-density is exact (e.g. of an ODE), so it is worked out once at each point, and this is an adaptive random-walk Metropolis sampler. With draws='auto' (the default), the chains are taken further in rounds of batch draws until they agree, with enough effective draws (rhat, ess; see enough_draws()), or reach max_draws.

title: products
text:
products
Products: vaccines, treatments, and diagnostics, and the protection people hold from them
A product says what something does (e.g. its efficacy), and a delivery (ss.vaccinate(), ss.treat(), ss.screen()) says who gets it and when. They are kept apart so that one product can be delivered in several ways. A product written as code (administer()) runs as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Diagnostic
A diagnostic test: what ss.screen() delivers


Effect
The effect of a product on one quantity, for the people who hold it: a multiplier of 1 - efficacy


EventSource
What a delivery and a product share as events: the people it reached on the step (screening), its outcomes (screening.positive), and their memory


Held
Base class for products that change rates for the people who hold them


Product
Generic product base class: see ss.Vaccine, ss.Diagnostic, and ss.Treatment


StrainEffect
The effect of a product against acquiring each strain of a disease with shared states, for the people who hold it: on each strain’s force of infection (see ss.solvers.Engine.strain_effect())

A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers


Vaccine
A vaccine: what ss.vaccinate() delivers


boxcar
Protection that is full for a time (a plateau), then lost at once, or (with decay=) fading exponentially: the waning= of a product


held_cond
The condition vx.held (whether each person holds this product), which on a class is whether they hold any product of that kind (who=ss.Vaccine.held), for a model built before its products

A diagnostic test: what ss.screen() delivers
A test gives each person one of its results: by default positive or negative, from sensitivity and specificity; or one of outcomes=, each with its probability given the state a person is in. Each outcome is a result of each delivery of it, and an event (screening.positive for one delivery, hiv_rdt.positive for any delivery of the product), which triggers the steps that follow.

products.Treatment(cure=None, efficacy=None, moves=None, **kwargs)
A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers
A treatment can cure (cure=, once, when it is given), change rates for as long as it is held (efficacy=), or both. By default it is given to the people who are infected. A treatment that cures has the outcomes cured, failed (infected, and not cured), and unneeded (not in a state it cures: not infected, or in no source of the transitions it cures along), which are results and events of its deliveries.
A cure is a probability (cure=0.9): the person leaves whichever infected state they are in for the state the disease’s recovery leads to. It can instead be a dict of probabilities, keyed in one of two ways:

By state (cure=dict(I=0.9), or cure={hpv.CIN: 0.9}): the people in those states are cured, to the state the recovery leads to, and people in other states are not.
By what cured people move along: transitions of the disease, usually ones with a rate of 0 (cure = A + C >> S @ 0), whose flows count the people moved (cure={syph.cure_early: 0.98, syph.cure_late: 0.95}); or a move written with the states (cure={I + CIN >> S: 0.9}), which no flow counts, e.g. for a cure to one of several states that recoveries lead to. Each person treated who is in a source of one of them moves along it with its probability (cured), or does not (failed); one in no source is unneeded. The transitions can be of several diseases (cure={ng.cure: 0.95, ct.cure: 0.95}); a modifier of such a transition (ss.modify(ng.cure, multiply=0.5, who=...)) multiplies the probability for the people it applies to. It is then given to the people in their sources.

A name as a key (cure=dict(cure=0.9)) is a state of the disease, or else one of its transitions (it is an error if it is both); 'ng.cure' is the transition cure of ng. What happens at failure (resistance) is a transition of the disease triggered by the outcome: ss.Transition(I, R_res, when=drug.failed, p=0.05).
Not every move a treatment makes is a cure: moves= names what it moves people along, for a treatment that, say, starts care or protects (moves=hiv.start_art, moves={sir.protect: 0.5}), with the probability cure= (1 by default) or one for each in a dict. It works as a cure by transition does, with the same outcomes.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

A test gives each person one of its results: by default positive or negative, from sensitivity and specificity; or one of outcomes=, each with its probability given the state a person is in. products.Treatment(cure=None, efficacy=None, moves=None, **kwargs)
A treatment: what ss.treat() delivers
A treatment can cure (cure=, once, when it is given), change rates for as long as it is held (efficacy=), or both. By default it is given to the people who are infected. A treatment that cures has the outcomes cured, failed (infected, and not cured), and unneeded (not in a state it cures: not infected, or in no source of the transitions it cures along), which are results and events of its deliveries.
A cure is a probability (cure=0.9): the person leaves whichever infected state they are in for the state the disease’s recovery leads to. It can instead be a dict of probabilities, keyed in one of two ways:

By state (cure=dict(I=0.9), or cure={hpv.CIN: 0.9}): the people in those states are cured, to the state the recovery leads to, and people in other states are not.
By what cured people move along: transitions of the disease, usually ones with a rate of 0 (cure = A + C >> S @ 0), whose flows count the people moved (cure={syph.cure_early: 0.98, syph.cure_late: 0.95}); or a move written with the states (cure={I + CIN >> S: 0.9}), which no flow counts, e.g. for a cure to one of several states that recoveries lead to. Each person treated who is in a source of one of them moves along it with its probability (cured), or does not (failed); one in no source is unneeded. The transitions can be of several diseases (cure={ng.cure: 0.95, ct.cure: 0.95}); a modifier of such a transition (ss.modify(ng.cure, multiply=0.5, who=...)) multiplies the probability for the people it applies to. It is then given to the people in their sources.

A name as a key (cure=dict(cure=0.9)) is a state of the disease, or else one of its transitions (it is an error if it is both); 'ng.cure' is the transition cure of ng. What happens at failure (resistance) is a transition of the disease triggered by the outcome: ss.Transition(I, R_res, when=drug.failed, p=0.05).
Not every move a treatment makes is a cure: moves= names what it moves people along, for a treatment that, say, starts care or protects (moves=hiv.start_art, moves={sir.protect: 0.5}), with the probability cure= (1 by default) or one for each in a dict. It works as a cure by transition does, with the same outcomes.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

title: connectors
text:
connectors
Connectors, which link modules as the sim runs: e.g. one disease making another more likely
Most links between diseases need no connector, since diseases can read each other’s states (e.g. in a rate). A connector is for the rest, e.g. seasonal forcing or the effect of a coinfection. The one most used is ss.modify(), which changes a named quantity while a condition holds, e.g. a seasonal ss.modify(sir.rel_trans, multiply=ss.seasonal(amplitude=0.2, peak='January')).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

title: transitions
text:
transitions
States, transitions, and the expressions that drive them.
A model is a set of ss.State objects and the ss.Transition objects between them. A transition can be written with operators or in full, which build the same object:
S >> I @ 0.3 * I                                # Operators
ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I)               # In full
The ss.graph.Graph class (in internals/graph.py) collects the states and transitions of one module, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them. The expressions are in ss.expressions, the values that vary (ss.by, ss.timeseries, ss.seasonal) in ss.parameters, how a model is shown in ss.display, and its stratifications in ss.dimensions.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared modules





Name
Description




State
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people


Transition
A movement between states


lifetable
A life table: how many die at each age, which ss.death(lifetable=) and ss.Deaths(lifetable=) take as a death rate for each age band (see hazards());


outcome
A reported quantity: a flow worked out from other flows, which moves nobody





transitions.State(
    label=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,
    people=None,
    rel_sus=1.0,
    rel_trans=1.0,
    infected=False,
    keep_time=False,
    name=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people
A state is a compartment when the model runs as an ODE and a boolean array over agents when it runs as agents; the declaration is the same.











Name
Type
Description
Default




label
str
a human-readable name, for plots (e.g. S = ss.State('Susceptible'))
None


init
float
the share of people who start in the state (1.0 is everyone); for a state that is not people, its starting amount
None


init_n
int
instead, the number of people who start in the state
None


people
bool
whether this state holds people (the default), or is a count of something else (people=False: bacteria in the water, mosquitoes); people=True says so explicitly, for a group of people that only an inflow fills
None


rel_sus
float
susceptibility multiplier while in this state (one value; for a value by group, ss.modify(dis.rel_sus, multiply=ss.by(risk=[...])))
1.0


rel_trans
float
infectiousness multiplier while in this state (likewise)
1.0


infected
bool
whether the people in it are infected, which the disease otherwise works out from its force of infection (the states people are infected into, and those that infect them: E and I in S >> E @ beta*I); once any state is said to be, the infected states are exactly those said to be. The disease’s infected states give the results infected, the number in them, and prevalence, their share of everyone in its states (unless it defines its own); infected = E + I, given to the disease, says the same for several states
False


keep_time
bool
as agents, keep the time each person entered the state (ti_<name>) for code to read, e.g. the years since onset; by default it is kept only if the model reads it (a clock, a scheduled exit), to save memory
False


name
str
the name, if it is not the variable or keyword the state is given as (which it is taken from); a state that no variable holds takes its label as its name, if that is one word (ss.Disease(ss.State('S'), ...))
None






S, R = ss.states(2)
I = ss.State(init=0.01)     # 1% of people
E = ss.State(init_n=10)     # 10 people
V = ss.State('Vaccinated', rel_sus=0.2)
A = ss.State(keep_time=True) # Code reads mod.ti_A
H = ss.State('Hospitalized', infected=True) # Counted in the results infected and prevalence, though it does not transmit






Name
Description




enter
The event of entering this state: for when= (or ss.on()), or .uids


exit
The event of leaving this state


given_init
Whether a starting value is given (init= or init_n=)


progress
The share of the scheduled dwell time in this state that has elapsed, from 0 to 1 (NaN outside it)


time_in
Time since this person last entered the state, in the sim’s unit (NaN outside it)


total
The number in these states in the whole population: in a model with places, in every place, not only the same one as with .n







transitions.Transition(
    source=None,
    dest=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=None,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    min_stay=None,
    noise=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per_strain=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




source
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.unborn (births) or ss.outside (arrivals) for an inflow
None


dest
State / dict
the destination state; several (a split), as a dict of each and its probability ({D: p_death, R: None}, None for the rest); or ss.dead (deaths) or ss.outside (leaving) for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate)
None


p
float
the probability of taking it, for those it applies to (e.g. on an event); a split gives each destination’s in dest
None


stages
int
the number of stages a dwell time is split into, in a row (an Erlang distribution), under every solver: more stages make the times in the state vary less around the mean
None


who
Cond / func / str
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ss.person.age > 30, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), as for ss.Event(who=); for everyone else its rate is 0
None


when
Event / on / Cond / func / str
what triggers it, instead of a rate (the same as @ ss.on(...)): an event moves the people it happens to (when=preg.delivery), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it (drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it; a condition moves people as soon as it holds (see ss.on); a path (when='preg.delivery', as ss.ref('preg.delivery')) stands for whatever is there, found when the sim is initialized
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


min_stay
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


noise
float / par
random variation of the rate from step to step (see below), for data that vary more than chance alone explains; sigma, which can be fitted (noise=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0, 0.3]))
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per_strain
str
for a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, an outcome for each strain carried: 'each' or 'first' (see below)
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None



Noise. noise= is sigma of gamma white noise (Bretó et al. 2009; pomp’s rgammawn): the chain binomial multiplies the rate, in each substep of length h, by a gamma draw with mean 1 and variance sigma²/h, for each group (and each particle of a filter). Sigma is in the square root of the sim’s unit (0.0878 in He et al.’s model, in years). Tau-leaping draws it for each leap (h its length), and agents once a step for each group (h the step); the ODE leaves it out (its mean), and the exact solver ('gillespie') refuses it.
Strains. With per_strain=:

'each': with a split, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (the first destination’s probability times the strain’s value for the transition, or '<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left; e.g. cure by treatment
'first': with a rate, each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on as the only strain carried (the others are dropped); e.g. one of two strains progressing




S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S, rate=0) # A rate of 0: only treatment moves people along it
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), who=ss.person.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), min_stay=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
infection = ss.Transition(S, E, rate=beta*I, noise=0.0878) # Infection whose rate varies at random from step to step (He et al. 2010)
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, when=ss.on(preg.delivery, delay=ss.months(6))) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact

transitions.move(*args, p=None, n=None, uids=None, who=None)
Move people between states of a declared disease from code, the same way under every solver
A one-off move along no transition (as ss.Event(I >> R) is for a declared one). People can also be moved into the model and out of it: to ss.dead (they die) or ss.outside (they leave), and from ss.unborn (they are born) or ss.outside (they arrive), with n=. Every disease has the same people, so people who die or leave leave every disease, and people added are in each other disease’s first state, under every solver: as agents, they are agents who die or are made (a death happens at the end of the step, as people.request_death() does); in a compartmental run, the diseases tracked jointly lose and gain the same people, and a disease run apart loses them from its states in proportion, in each group, as it has them (it runs apart since its states do not depend on the others’). People added are placed in groups as declared births (ss.unborn) or arrivals (ss.outside) are. A count that is not people (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes) moves the same way. Also disease.move(...), the same with the disease given.

Type
Description
Default

p
float
the share of the people in the source to move, in each group (by default, everyone)
None


n
float
instead, the number of people to move, shared among the groups and states in proportion to who is in them
None


uids
uids
only these agents (those of them in the source), which needs agents; with p= or n=, a share or number of them
None


who
Cond / State / func / str
only the people for whom a condition holds (e.g. ss.person.age < 15, a group, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), under every solver; with p= or n=, a share or number of them
None














Name
Type
Description






The number of people moved






ss.move(sir.I, sir.R, p=0.5) # Cure half of those infectious
ss.move(sir.I >> sir.R, p=0.5) # The same, written as a move, as for ss.Event()
ss.move(sir.S, sir.I, n=5) # Five susceptible people become infectious
ss.move(sir.S, sir.R, p=0.8, who=ss.person.age < 5) # Protect 80% of the susceptible children under 5
sir.move(uids, sir.R) # These agents, from wherever they are (also ss.move(sir, uids, sir.R), or sir.move(uids, 'R'))
self.move(self.I, self.R, uids=uids) # In a disease's own code: these agents, if they are infectious
ss.move(sir.I, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of those infectious die
ss.move(ss.outside, sir.I, n=20) # Twenty people arrive infectious
sir.move(uids, ss.dead) # These agents die, whatever their state
ss.move(mosq.Sv, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of the mosquitoes die




transitions.pars(defaults, **kwargs)
Create several parameters at once, from defaults and the values given, as a class’s declared parameters are made
For a disease whose states and transitions depend on its options, and so are made in __init__() rather than declared on the class (e.g. beta = ss.par(...), as ss.SIR does). Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. A name that is not a default is an error.

Type
Description
Default

dict
the default of each parameter: a value, or an ss.par (with bounds, say)
required


kwargs
dict
the values given, e.g. the keywords of the disease’s __init__()




Returns an sc.obj of the parameters, by name.



defaults = dict(beta=ss.par(ss.peryear(2), bounds=[ss.peryear(0.5), ss.peryear(5)]), dur=ss.years(2), relapse=None)
p = ss.pars(defaults, beta=3) # beta is 3 per year, with the default's bounds
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
transitions = [S >> I @ p.beta*I, I >> R @ p.dur] + ([R >> I @ p.relapse] if p.relapse is not None else [])

Name
Description

Transition
A movement between states

A reported quantity: a flow worked out from other flows, which moves nobody





transitions.State(
    label=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,
    people=None,
    rel_sus=1.0,
    rel_trans=1.0,
    infected=False,
    keep_time=False,
    name=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Something a person can be in, or a count of something that is not people
A state is a compartment when the model runs as an ODE and a boolean array over agents when it runs as agents; the declaration is the same.











Name
Type
Description
Default

str
a human-readable name, for plots (e.g. S = ss.State('Susceptible'))
None

float
the share of people who start in the state (1.0 is everyone); for a state that is not people, its starting amount
None


init_n
int
instead, the number of people who start in the state
None

bool
whether this state holds people (the default), or is a count of something else (people=False: bacteria in the water, mosquitoes); people=True says so explicitly, for a group of people that only an inflow fills
None


rel_sus
float
susceptibility multiplier while in this state (one value; for a value by group, ss.modify(dis.rel_sus, multiply=ss.by(risk=[...])))
1.0


rel_trans
float
infectiousness multiplier while in this state (likewise)
1.0


infected
bool
whether the people in it are infected, which the disease otherwise works out from its force of infection (the states people are infected into, and those that infect them: E and I in S >> E @ beta*I); once any state is said to be, the infected states are exactly those said to be. The disease’s infected states give the results infected, the number in them, and prevalence, their share of everyone in its states (unless it defines its own); infected = E + I, given to the disease, says the same for several states
False

S, R = ss.states(2)
I = ss.State(init=0.01)     # 1% of people
E = ss.State(init_n=10)     # 10 people
V = ss.State('Vaccinated', rel_sus=0.2)
A = ss.State(keep_time=True) # Code reads mod.ti_A
H = ss.State('Hospitalized', infected=True) # Counted in the results infected and prevalence, though it does not transmit






Name
Description

The event of entering this state: for when= (or ss.on()), or .uids

The event of leaving this state

Whether a starting value is given (init= or init_n=)

The share of the scheduled dwell time in this state that has elapsed, from 0 to 1 (NaN outside it)

Time since this person last entered the state, in the sim’s unit (NaN outside it)

The number in these states in the whole population: in a model with places, in every place, not only the same one as with .n







transitions.Transition(
    source=None,
    dest=None,
    rate=None,
    dur=None,
    p=None,
    stages=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    move=None,
    increment=None,
    min_stay=None,
    noise=None,
    acquisition=None,
    per_strain=False,
)
A movement between states
Usually built with the operators (S >> I @ rate); ss.birth() and ss.death() also return an ss.Transition.





Name
Type
Description
Default




source
State / list
the source state, several states (a list, or a sum I + R), or ss.unborn (births) or ss.outside (arrivals) for an inflow
None


dest
State / dict
the destination state; several (a split), as a dict of each and its probability ({D: p_death, R: None}, None for the rest); or ss.dead (deaths) or ss.outside (leaving) for an outflow
None


rate
any
a hazard: a number, ss.per, ss.prob, an expression of states and parameters, or a function; a transmission is a rate with the source of infection in it (rate=beta * I)
None


dur
any
a dwell time: a duration or a distribution of durations (instead of rate)
None


p
float
the probability of taking it, for those it applies to (e.g. on an event); a split gives each destination’s in dest
None


stages
int
the number of stages a dwell time is split into, in a row (an Erlang distribution), under every solver: more stages make the times in the state vary less around the mean
None


who
Cond / func / str
who it applies to: a condition (e.g. ss.person.age > 30, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), as for ss.Event(who=); for everyone else its rate is 0
None


when
Event / on / Cond / func / str
what triggers it, instead of a rate (the same as @ ss.on(...)): an event moves the people it happens to (when=preg.delivery), or ss.on(event, delay=...) for a time after it (drawn for each person), as agents; joined to a condition with &, those who meet it; a condition moves people as soon as it holds (see ss.on); a path (when='preg.delivery', as ss.ref('preg.delivery')) stands for whatever is there, found when the sim is initialized
None


move
dict / StrainMove
a change of level in a dimension as well as of state: the dimension, and the level people move to, or a pair of levels (e.g. move=dict(risk=('low', 'high')), which applies only to people at the first); or a change of strains (move=DS >> (DS, RIF), see ss.strains.Strain)
None


increment
str / dict
a counter that goes up as well: its name, which adds 1 (increment='parity'), or a dict of the amount for each (increment=dict(parity=2) for twins, dict(doses=-1)); a counter is a dimension with integer levels, whose last level is open-ended
None


min_stay
dur
a minimum stay: nobody leaves by this transition until they have been in its source state this long (a rate applies from then on, and a dwell time starts then)
None


noise
float / par
random variation of the rate from step to step (see below), for data that vary more than chance alone explains; sigma, which can be fitted (noise=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0, 0.3]))
None


acquisition
bool
whether it is an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on. If not given: a contact-mediated transition is, and so is any other transition out of the disease’s first state if none out of it is contact-mediated (an infection by a bite rate or an EIR)
None


per_strain
str
for a disease with strains (ss.Strains) in a state they share, an outcome for each strain carried: 'each' or 'first' (see below)
False


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or the variable it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None



Noise. noise= is sigma of gamma white noise (Bretó et al. 2009; pomp’s rgammawn): the chain binomial multiplies the rate, in each substep of length h, by a gamma draw with mean 1 and variance sigma²/h, for each group (and each particle of a filter). Sigma is in the square root of the sim’s unit (0.0878 in He et al.’s model, in years). Tau-leaping draws it for each leap (h its length), and agents once a step for each group (h the step); the ODE leaves it out (its mean), and the exact solver ('gillespie') refuses it.
Strains. With per_strain=:

'each': with a split, each strain carried takes the first destination with its own probability (the first destination’s probability times the strain’s value for the transition, or '<value>', the strains’ values of that name, with their values for the transition then multiplying its rate), and anyone left with a strain takes the second (or stays), carrying those left; e.g. cure by treatment
'first': with a rate, each strain carried has its own rate (the rate times its value), and the first to happen moves on as the only strain carried (the others are dropped); e.g. one of two strains progressing




S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.05 * I)
cure      = ss.Transition(I, S, rate=0) # A rate of 0: only treatment moves people along it
recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10))
maturing  = ss.Transition(J, A, rate=ss.perday(1), who=ss.person.age > 1) # Only adults
failure   = ss.Transition(Tx, I, rate=ss.peryear(0.1), move=DS >> (DS, RIF)) # Treatment fails, and the strain acquires resistance (DS, RIF = strains)
twins     = ss.Transition(P, PP, dur=ss.months(9), p=0.02, increment=dict(parity=2)) # Parity goes up by 2
weaning   = ss.Transition(NB, W, rate=ss.perday(0.5), min_stay=ss.days(21)) # At least 21 days old first, as EMULSION's duration
infection = ss.Transition(S, E, rate=beta*I, noise=0.0878) # Infection whose rate varies at random from step to step (He et al. 2010)
postpartum = ss.Transition(PP, NP, when=ss.on(preg.delivery, delay=ss.months(6))) # Six months after each woman's own delivery
importation = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.perday(1e-4), acquisition=True) # An infection from outside, alongside one by contact

Whether everyone who takes it dies (ss.death(), I >> ss.dead); False for a split with ss.dead (see tr.may_die) and for people leaving alive (ss.emigration())

Whether each person has gone through this transition, as a condition (agents only), e.g. who=~tb.diagnosis.ever

How many times each person has gone through this transition (agents only), e.g. who=tb.relapse.n_times >= 2

An inflow of people: at a crude (per-person) birth rate, e.g. ss.birth(S, rate=ss.peryear(0.02)); or driven by a flow, e.g. ss.birth(NP, when=preg.delivery, children=2), children for each person who goes through the transition
With when=, as agents the children are made by the module that owns the transition, with parent set to the person who went through it, and placed in each declared module’s state given by its own ss.birth(when=...) of the same transition, or else its first state. Agents only, for now.

transitions.move(*args, p=None, n=None, uids=None, who=None)
Move people between states of a declared disease from code, the same way under every solver
A one-off move along no transition (as ss.Event(I >> R) is for a declared one). People can also be moved into the model and out of it: to ss.dead (they die) or ss.outside (they leave), and from ss.unborn (they are born) or ss.outside (they arrive), with n=. Every disease has the same people, so people who die or leave leave every disease, and people added are in each other disease’s first state, under every solver: as agents, they are agents who die or are made (a death happens at the end of the step, as people.request_death() does); in a compartmental run, the diseases tracked jointly lose and gain the same people, and a disease run apart loses them from its states in proportion, in each group, as it has them (it runs apart since its states do not depend on the others’). People added are placed in groups as declared births (ss.unborn) or arrivals (ss.outside) are. A count that is not people (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes) moves the same way. Also disease.move(...), the same with the disease given.





Name
Type
Description
Default




args

p
float
the share of the people in the source to move, in each group (by default, everyone)
None


n
float
instead, the number of people to move, shared among the groups and states in proportion to who is in them
None


uids
uids
only these agents (those of them in the source), which needs agents; with p= or n=, a share or number of them
None


who
Cond / State / func / str
only the people for whom a condition holds (e.g. ss.person.age < 15, a group, or a state by its path, 'sir.I'), under every solver; with p= or n=, a share or number of them
None














Name
Type
Description






The number of people moved






ss.move(sir.I, sir.R, p=0.5) # Cure half of those infectious
ss.move(sir.I >> sir.R, p=0.5) # The same, written as a move, as for ss.Event()
ss.move(sir.S, sir.I, n=5) # Five susceptible people become infectious
ss.move(sir.S, sir.R, p=0.8, who=ss.person.age < 5) # Protect 80% of the susceptible children under 5
sir.move(uids, sir.R) # These agents, from wherever they are (also ss.move(sir, uids, sir.R), or sir.move(uids, 'R'))
self.move(self.I, self.R, uids=uids) # In a disease's own code: these agents, if they are infectious
ss.move(sir.I, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of those infectious die
ss.move(ss.outside, sir.I, n=20) # Twenty people arrive infectious
sir.move(uids, ss.dead) # These agents die, whatever their state
ss.move(mosq.Sv, ss.dead, p=0.1) # A tenth of the mosquitoes die




transitions.pars(defaults, **kwargs)
Create several parameters at once, from defaults and the values given, as a class’s declared parameters are made
For a disease whose states and transitions depend on its options, and so are made in __init__() rather than declared on the class (e.g. beta = ss.par(...), as ss.SIR does). Each parameter is an ss.par named after its key, so it can be fitted or set by name (ss.Sim(pars=...)). A value given takes the default’s bounds and description unless it has its own; a bare number for a typed default keeps its unit (e.g. 2 for a default of ss.peryear(1) is 2 per year); a default of None is an optional parameter, None unless given. A name that is not a default is an error.

Type
Description
Default

dict
the default of each parameter: a value, or an ss.par (with bounds, say)
required


kwargs
dict
the values given, e.g. the keywords of the disease’s __init__()




Returns an sc.obj of the parameters, by name.



defaults = dict(beta=ss.par(ss.peryear(2), bounds=[ss.peryear(0.5), ss.peryear(5)]), dur=ss.years(2), relapse=None)
p = ss.pars(defaults, beta=3) # beta is 3 per year, with the default's bounds
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
transitions = [S >> I @ p.beta*I, I >> R @ p.dur] + ([R >> I @ p.relapse] if p.relapse is not None else [])

settings
Options for Starsim, and the plotting style
These exist so that behavior that isn’t part of a model (how much to print, how to treat warnings, which kernels to use) is set in one place, e.g.:
ss.options(verbose=0)
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Options
The options for Starsim, as ss.options: settings for everything in a session that aren’t part of a model, such as how much to print and how to treat warnings


OptionsContext
What ss.options(...) returns: at the end of a “with” block, it sets the options it changed back to what they were





settings.Options()
The options for Starsim, as ss.options: settings for everything in a session that aren’t part of a model, such as how much to print and how to treat warnings
Set one with ss.options(verbose=0) (or ss.options.verbose = 0), or for a with block only, with with ss.options(verbose=0):; each can also be set before Python starts, by its environment variable (e.g. STARSIM_VERBOSE=0). ss.options.set('defaults') resets them all, and ss.options.set(verbose='default') one. Use ss.style() to set the plotting style for a block.
The options most often set are:
- verbose:  how much a sim prints (0 for nothing)
- warnings: what to do with warnings ("warn", "print", "error", or "ignore")
See ss.options.help(detailed=True) for all of them, with what each is for.


ss.options(verbose=2) # Print everything
ss.options(warnings='error') # Be more strict about warnings

graph
The graph of one module: its states, transitions, and parameters, collected, named, completed with defaults (each guess recorded), and checked

    members=None,
    init_prev=None,
    init=None,
    init_n=None,

)
The states and transitions of one module
The graph is built when the module is constructed. It names everything, works out which states are people and which transitions are transmissions (from their rates), turns inline values into named parameters, and checks the result. Every guess is recorded, in graph.guessed and in the guessed of each state and transition.
