graph.Graph.add_flow(tr)
Add a birth, death, or migration declared for the whole population (ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.birth(...)])), after the graph is built; see ss.Sim._init_flows()



graph.Graph.all_pars()
Every parameter in the graph, named or inline



graph.Graph.bad_splits(exits)
The groups of branches with constant p= whose shares do not sum to 1: those that apply to the people at each level named by a move= arrow are summed within that level; returns [(branches, total)]



graph.Graph.check()
Checks that do not need the sim



graph.Graph.check_counts()
Refuse a forgotten people=False (MA35): a group of states of people that no transition links to the first state and that only an inflow (not a birth) fills, as mosquitoes are, would otherwise silently become agents



graph.Graph.check_first(why=None)
Raise if the module has states of people but no first state (see resolve_people()), which every solver needs: it is where people start unless they are put elsewhere, and where those added later (born, or seeded from) come from



graph.Graph.check_read(state)
Refuse a state that an earlier module only read in a rate, so took as a state of its own that nothing fills, e.g. Rb.frac in disease a, declared before the disease b that Rb was meant to belong to



graph.Graph.collect(args, members)
Sort the members by what they are, and name them



graph.Graph.destination(name)
For the name of one destination of a transition with several, '<transition>.<state>' (e.g. 'progression.C'): the transition; otherwise None



graph.Graph.destinations()
The names of the destinations of the transitions with several, as destination() takes them



graph.Graph.dwell_not_branch(name, how, modname)
For a multiplier (how, e.g. ‘the modifier “m”’) on a transition with several destinations chosen with p= and a dwell time: a note that it changes the dwell, not a branch (TL16), naming the destinations that would; otherwise None



graph.Graph.expand_rows()
Entries of p= with a to axis (an ss.by over to, whose labels are destination states): one Share of the entry for each destination it covers
Entries without one are one destination each, in order, skipping the destinations that a to axis names; an entry whose to axis gives values by position only covers the destinations left. The entries as given are kept as tr.p_given.



graph.Graph.fill_people(tr)
Fill in what depends on which states are people: the sources of the deaths of everyone (ss.death() with no state), and the people a birth rate is per person of (ss.birth())



graph.Graph.leaves()
The leaves of the rates and branch probabilities of its transitions



graph.Graph.modifier_kind(name)
What a modifier on a transition acts on: its probability if it is one branch of several with p= (chosen on entry) or one destination of a transition with several ('recovery.R'), and otherwise its rate



graph.Graph.resolve_acquisition()
Work out which transitions are an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on
A contact-mediated transition is one. So is any other transition of people out of the first state that is not an outflow, whatever its rate (a bite rate, an EIR, a count of bacteria), unless a transition out of that state is contact-mediated, which is then the acquisition (so S -> V alongside S -> I @ beta * I is a vaccination). acquisition= on the transition says it outright.



graph.Graph.resolve_attrs()
Resolve each attribute: another attribute given by name, the cases of a derived one by state (a state, a sum of states, or a | of them), and its events



graph.Graph.resolve_exits()
Group the transitions out of each state: those with p= split on entry, the rest compete



graph.Graph.resolve_init_prev()
By default, 1% of people start infected, seeded through the transmission (frequency- or density-dependent), unless a state is given a starting value



graph.Graph.resolve_pars()
Turn inline values in the standard slots into named parameters (beta, dur, rate, p)



graph.Graph.resolve_people()
Which states are people: every state, unless it is declared a count (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes or bacteria in the water); and the first state, where people are unless they are put elsewhere: first= if given, else the state named S or susceptible (in any case). Nothing else is guessed: with neither, check_first() raises when the sim is initialized (a birth into a state of its own, ss.birth(X), needs no first state, but the people who start in no state do)



graph.Graph.resolve_rest()
Work out where the people not given an initial state start: the first state, unless it is given an initial value of its own, which is then kept (init=dict(S=0.1, I=1e-4) starts 10% susceptible). Then it is the one state of people with no initial value, with a note in guessed; with none or several, there is no such state, and the initial values must sum to 1 (see Engine.init_fractions())



graph.Graph.resolve_states()
Find the states: the ones declared, and those the transitions use



graph.Graph.resolve_transitions()
Give every transition a name, a source, and a rate or a dwell time



graph.Graph.set_keywords()
A value given as a keyword sets the parameter of that name; there is nothing else for it to be



graph.Graph.set_slots(tr)
Record the kind of value each parameter of a transition is, as par.slot (which describe() and the model spec use): ‘rate’ or ‘dur’, or None for a plain number (e.g. a factor of a rate); returns the standard slots it fills, as (slot name, parameter)



graph.Graph.spread_pars()
The parameters whose value is a distribution across people (e.g. beta=ss.lognorm_ex(0.3, 0.1)), other than dwell times, which are stages or are sampled on entry



graph.Graph.stratify(**kwargs)
Stratify the graph by one or more dimensions; see ss.Disease.stratify()



graph.Graph.unit_values()
All the typed values (durations and rates) in the graph, used to infer the sim’s unit



graph.Graph.unset_default_init_prev()
Remove the default init_prev, e.g. of a strain that its disease seeds

All the typed values (durations and rates) in the graph, used to infer the sim’s unit


unset_default_init_prev
Remove the default init_prev, e.g. of a strain that its disease seeds





graph.Graph.add(container, name, obj)
Add a named member, checking the name



graph.Graph.add_flow(tr)
Add a birth, death, or migration declared for the whole population (ss.Sim(demographics=[ss.birth(...)])), after the graph is built; see ss.Sim._init_flows()



graph.Graph.all_pars()
Every parameter in the graph, named or inline



graph.Graph.bad_splits(exits)
The groups of branches with constant p= whose shares do not sum to 1: those that apply to the people at each level named by a move= arrow are summed within that level; returns [(branches, total)]



graph.Graph.check()
Checks that do not need the sim



graph.Graph.check_counts()
Refuse a forgotten people=False (MA35): a group of states of people that no transition links to the first state and that only an inflow (not a birth) fills, as mosquitoes are, would otherwise silently become agents



graph.Graph.check_first(why=None)
Raise if the module has states of people but no first state (see resolve_people()), which every solver needs: it is where people start unless they are put elsewhere, and where those added later (born, or seeded from) come from



graph.Graph.check_read(state)
Refuse a state that an earlier module only read in a rate, so took as a state of its own that nothing fills, e.g. Rb.frac in disease a, declared before the disease b that Rb was meant to belong to



graph.Graph.collect(args, members)
Sort the members by what they are, and name them



graph.Graph.destination(name)
For the name of one destination of a transition with several, '<transition>.<state>' (e.g. 'progression.C'): the transition; otherwise None



graph.Graph.destinations()
The names of the destinations of the transitions with several, as destination() takes them



graph.Graph.dwell_not_branch(name, how, modname)
For a multiplier (how, e.g. ‘the modifier “m”’) on a transition with several destinations chosen with p= and a dwell time: a note that it changes the dwell, not a branch (TL16), naming the destinations that would; otherwise None



graph.Graph.expand_rows()
Entries of p= with a to axis (an ss.by over to, whose labels are destination states): one Share of the entry for each destination it covers
Entries without one are one destination each, in order, skipping the destinations that a to axis names; an entry whose to axis gives values by position only covers the destinations left. The entries as given are kept as tr.p_given.



graph.Graph.fill_people(tr)
Fill in what depends on which states are people: the sources of the deaths of everyone (ss.death() with no state), and the people a birth rate is per person of (ss.birth())



graph.Graph.leaves()
The leaves of the rates and branch probabilities of its transitions



graph.Graph.modifier_kind(name)
What a modifier on a transition acts on: its probability if it is one branch of several with p= (chosen on entry) or one destination of a transition with several ('recovery.R'), and otherwise its rate



graph.Graph.resolve_acquisition()
Work out which transitions are an acquisition of the disease, which rel_sus, a product’s efficacy against acquisition, and ss.treat act on
A contact-mediated transition is one. So is any other transition of people out of the first state that is not an outflow, whatever its rate (a bite rate, an EIR, a count of bacteria), unless a transition out of that state is contact-mediated, which is then the acquisition (so S -> V alongside S -> I @ beta * I is a vaccination). acquisition= on the transition says it outright.



graph.Graph.resolve_attrs()
Resolve each attribute: another attribute given by name, the cases of a derived one by state (a state, a sum of states, or a | of them), and its events



graph.Graph.resolve_exits()
Group the transitions out of each state: those with p= split on entry, the rest compete



graph.Graph.resolve_init_prev()
By default, 1% of people start infected, seeded through the transmission (frequency- or density-dependent), unless a state is given a starting value



graph.Graph.resolve_pars()
Turn inline values in the standard slots into named parameters (beta, dur, rate, p)



graph.Graph.resolve_people()
Which states are people: every state, unless it is declared a count (ss.State(people=False), e.g. mosquitoes or bacteria in the water); and the first state, where people are unless they are put elsewhere: first= if given, else the state named S or susceptible (in any case). Nothing else is guessed: with neither, check_first() raises when the sim is initialized (a birth into a state of its own, ss.birth(X), needs no first state, but the people who start in no state do)



graph.Graph.resolve_rest()
Work out where the people not given an initial state start: the first state, unless it is given an initial value of its own, which is then kept (init=dict(S=0.1, I=1e-4) starts 10% susceptible). Then it is the one state of people with no initial value, with a note in guessed; with none or several, there is no such state, and the initial values must sum to 1 (see Engine.init_fractions())



graph.Graph.resolve_states()
Find the states: the ones declared, and those the transitions use



graph.Graph.resolve_transitions()
Give every transition a name, a source, and a rate or a dwell time



graph.Graph.set_keywords()
A value given as a keyword sets the parameter of that name; there is nothing else for it to be



graph.Graph.set_slots(tr)
Record the kind of value each parameter of a transition is, as par.slot (which describe() and the model spec use): ‘rate’ or ‘dur’, or None for a plain number (e.g. a factor of a rate); returns the standard slots it fills, as (slot name, parameter)



graph.Graph.spread_pars()
The parameters whose value is a distribution across people (e.g. beta=ss.lognorm_ex(0.3, 0.1)), other than dwell times, which are stages or are sampled on entry



graph.Graph.stratify(**kwargs)
Stratify the graph by one or more dimensions; see ss.Disease.stratify()



graph.Graph.unit_values()
All the typed values (durations and rates) in the graph, used to infer the sim’s unit



graph.Graph.unset_default_init_prev()
Remove the default init_prev, e.g. of a strain that its disease seeds

title: distributions
text:
distributions
The distributions to choose from: ss.uniform, ss.normal, ss.poisson, and so on, each a random-number-safe ss.Dist
These exist so that a model can use any distribution for a parameter or a draw, with the same random numbers for the same agent across scenarios. How they work is in ss.dists. As agents, they are drawn for each agent; in a compartmental run, most are read for what they say about the group, such as their mean.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




bernoulli
Bernoulli distribution: True or False with the given probability (which can be an array, or a function of the agents)


beta_dist
Beta distribution, with values between 0 and 1, given by its shape parameters, or by its mean and standard deviation


binom
Binomial distribution: the number of successes in n trials; as a likelihood (see sim.fit()), the model’s value is the probability and the data are counts, e.g. the positives among n tested (not their fraction)


choice
Random choice between discrete options


choose_n
Choose exactly n agents (without replacement) from a set of candidate UIDs


constant
Constant (delta) distribution: every draw is the same value, e.g. for a parameter that takes a distribution but should not vary


expon
Exponential distribution


gamma
Gamma distribution (specifically, scipy.stats.gamma)


histogram
Draws from a histogram, uniform within each bin, e.g. ages from the number of people in each age group


lognormal
Lognormal distribution, given by its own mean and standard deviation, or by those of its logarithm


multi_random
Random numbers for pairs (or larger groups) of agents, e.g. one for each edge of a network in a transmission


nbinom
Negative binomial distribution, given by n and p, or by n and the mean


normal
Normal distribution


poisson
Poisson distribution


randint
Random integer distribution, on the interval [low, high)


random
Random distribution, with values on the interval (0, 1): the raw uniform draws, for code that uses them directly


truncnorm
Normal distribution truncated to an interval


uniform
Uniform distribution, values on interval (low, high); with one argument, it is the upper bound (ss.uniform(5) is between 0 and 5)


weibull
Weibull distribution (specifically, scipy.stats.weibull_min)

distributions.choice(a=2, p=None, replace=True, **kwargs)
Random choice between discrete options
The probabilities can differ by agent: give p as a 2D array with one row per agent drawn for (or a function returning one), and one column per choice. Each row is normalized to sum to 1. Each agent’s choice is found from their own random number by the inverse CDF of their own row, so the draw is one vectorized call, and keeps common random numbers: an agent’s choice doesn’t depend on who else is drawn for, or on other agents’ probabilities.











Name
Type
Description
Default




a
int or array
the number of choices, or the choices themselves (default 2)
2


p
array / func
if supplied, the probability of each choice (default, 1/a for a choices); or a 2D array (or a function returning one) with a row of probabilities (or weights) for each agent
None


replace
bool
whether an option can be chosen more than once (default True)
True






# Simulate 10 die rolls
ss.choice(6, strict=False)(10) + 1

# Choose between specified options each with a specified probability (must sum to 1)
ss.choice(a=[30, 70], p=[0.3, 0.7], strict=False)(10)

# A row of probabilities per agent: here by age group, from a table of age groups × choices
table = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.4, 0.3]])
def p_by_age(self, sim, uids):
    return table[(sim.people.age[uids] >= 18).astype(int)]
method = ss.choice(a=['none', 'pill', 'iud'], p=p_by_age) # In a module's __init__()
chosen = self.method.rvs(uids) # In its step()
Note: although Bernoulli trials can be generated using a=2, it is much faster to use ss.bernoulli() instead.

distributions.choose_n(n=1, weights=None, die=False, **kwargs)
Choose exactly n agents (without replacement) from a set of candidate UIDs
Like ss.bernoulli, use the filter() method, which returns the chosen UIDs. One random number is drawn per candidate (based on its slot), and the n candidates with the smallest numbers are chosen. This means that if the candidates change slightly (e.g. between two scenarios), most of the same agents are still chosen (unlike e.g. ss.choice(replace=False)).
If weights are supplied, candidates are chosen with probability proportional to their weight, via the Efraimidis–Spirakis key (1-u)**(1/w). This is computed as -log(1-u)/w, so the n smallest are chosen as before, and equal weights give the same agents as no weights. Candidates with zero weight are never chosen, so fewer than n UIDs are returned if fewer than n candidates have nonzero weight.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n
int / func
the number of agents to choose (or a function returning it); if more than the number of candidates, all are chosen
1

array / func
if supplied, the relative weight of each candidate (or a function returning them), matching the UIDs passed to filter()
None


die
bool
if True, raise an exception if fewer than n agents can be chosen (default: False)
False






# Seed exactly 20 infections of a disease written as code
sir = ssl.AgentSIR(init_prev=ss.choose_n(20))

# Choose 5 agents, weighted by age
chooser = ss.choose_n(5, weights=lambda self, sim, uids: sim.people.age[uids])

distributions.choice(a=2, p=None, replace=True, **kwargs)
Random choice between discrete options
The probabilities can differ by agent: give p as a 2D array with one row per agent drawn for (or a function returning one), and one column per choice. Each row is normalized to sum to 1. Each agent’s choice is found from their own random number by the inverse CDF of their own row, so the draw is one vectorized call, and keeps common random numbers: an agent’s choice doesn’t depend on who else is drawn for, or on other agents’ probabilities.

    return table[(sim.people.age[uids] >= 18).astype(int)]

distributions.choose_n(n=1, weights=None, die=False, **kwargs)
Choose exactly n agents (without replacement) from a set of candidate UIDs
Like ss.bernoulli, use the filter() method, which returns the chosen UIDs. One random number is drawn per candidate (based on its slot), and the n candidates with the smallest numbers are chosen. This means that if the candidates change slightly (e.g. between two scenarios), most of the same agents are still chosen (unlike e.g. ss.choice(replace=False)).
If weights are supplied, candidates are chosen with probability proportional to their weight, via the Efraimidis–Spirakis key (1-u)**(1/w). This is computed as -log(1-u)/w, so the n smallest are chosen as before, and equal weights give the same agents as no weights. Candidates with zero weight are never chosen, so fewer than n UIDs are returned if fewer than n candidates have nonzero weight.

sir = ssl.AgentSIR(init_prev=ss.choose_n(20))

chooser = ss.choose_n(5, weights=lambda self, sim, uids: sim.people.age[uids])

distributions.poisson.ppf(rands)
Fast inverse-CDF sampling for the common-random-number (ppf) path.
SciPy’s generic discrete ppf is very slow (it root-finds per element), and for CRN draws it is called every time an ss.poisson is sampled by UID. data
Data by place: ages, populations, birth and death rates, contact matrices, and administrative units
ss.data.age('Kenya')                    # The age_data of ss.People: counts by 5-year age group ('world' needs no download)
ss.data.population('Kenya', year=2020)  # By age and sex (also for a US state, e.g. 'United States:Massachusetts')
ss.data.rates('Kenya', 'deaths')        # Birth, death, fertility, or net migration rates, by year
ss.data.contacts('Kenya', layer='home') # A contact matrix by age
ss.data.geography('Kenya', level=1)     # Administrative units, with populations and positions
These are tables. The model objects that take a place by name read them from here: ss.population('Kenya'), ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1), ss.contacts('Kenya'), ss.Births(birth_rate='Kenya'), ss.Deaths(death_rate='Kenya'), and ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate='Kenya'). The data comes from starsim_data (https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data), which bundles what is small and common and fetches the rest on demand. Each lookup returns the data with a record of where it came from (ref; for a table, in .attrs['ref']), which sim.describe() shows.

title: solvers.choose
text:
solvers.choose
The solvers to choose from (ss.solvers.ode(), binomial(), gillespie(), tau(), and abm(), each with its options), and, not for the user, choosing the solver: which engine runs a declared model, and why (choose_solver()), and the steps that build a declared model before it is run (parameters by name, births and deaths of the population, a named population, the unit, life tables)
It exists so that a model need not say how it runs: the choice is made from what it holds, and the reason is kept. Modules written as code are taken into account, and get an engine too.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Solver
A solver, for ss.Sim(solver=...), with only the options of its own: ss.solvers.ode(), binomial(), gillespie(), tau(), or abm()


Undeclared
The engine of a disease that declares no states or transitions (see ss.Disease): there is nothing for it to run, so the disease’s own


abm

solvers.choose.choose_engine(sim)
Whether JAX takes the sim’s whole run of the ODE, as ss.gradients runs it, rather than the kernels, and why
By sim.jax: True for JAX, and otherwise (False, or None, the default) the kernels. JAX is never chosen for a run by itself: it is chosen where it is needed, for gradients and the fits and log-densities that use them (sim.gradient(), sim.log_density(), sim.fit()), and is worth asking for only for a long run over many groups (it takes about half a second to start in a session, and compiles each model; an ODE run in JAX agrees with the kernels to about 1e-14). The other solvers are run by the kernels, as is a model JAX does not cover (see why_not()), with a note.
Returns whether to use JAX, and the reason, also kept as sim.engine_reason.



solvers.choose.choose_solver(sim)
Work out the sim’s unit and solver; see ss.Disease for declaring a model that can be run with different solvers
Agents are made only when something needs them, whether the model is declared or written as code: a sim of modules written as code with nothing per person (e.g. an ODE of its own in NumPy) has no agents, and one with per-person arrays (e.g. a disease written as code) runs as agents. Which engine then takes a whole compartmental run, the kernels or (with sim.jax = True) JAX, is chosen when the sim is run, by choose_engine().
The steps: the modules are gathered and the declared model is built (init_model()); what matters to the choice is recorded (init_capabilities()), with what the layout of the compartments refuses, found by making it (init_layouts()); the solver is chosen; and the population is made ready for it (init_agents() or init_compartments()), and checked. The layouts are made once: a compartmental run uses them, unless its groups changed since.

solvers.choose.init_capabilities(sim)
One record for each ingredient that changes which solvers can run the model, read by solver='auto', sim.describe(), and the CapabilityError of a compartmental solver that was asked for
Each record has the ingredient; the reason it makes auto run the model as agents (reason); whether it stops a compartmental solver that was asked for (fatal); and whether auto runs as agents for it (switch): see capabilities. Code is never run to find out: setting compartmental = True or False on a module (or its class) says whether it works on groups, and agent_reasons() is what a module says for itself. Any module written as code that says nothing, and the code and functions of a declared module, run beside the compartments (and raise a CapabilityError if they ask for agents). What the layout of the compartments refuses is not predicted here: init_layouts() makes the layout, which runs none of the model’s code, and adds its refusal as a record.

solvers.crossing
Not for the user: diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run
It exists since a condition in one disease on a state of another (e.g. coinfection) needs the people counted by both.
Used with: compartments; declared modules

solvers.crossing.Crossing(sim, names, reasons=None)
Diseases whose states are tracked jointly in a compartmental run, since a condition in one refers to a state of another (e.g. ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=3, who=syph.I))
Each disease in the crossing is a dimension of the sim, named after it, whose levels are its compartments and which applies to the people of the others. Each keeps its own engine, which works out its rates and its results, and sees the people as it has them: by its own compartments, and by groups that include the compartments of the others (with its own dimension at its first level).
They are run by one program: its compartments are the product of the diseases’ compartments of people (and, for a compartment that is not people, such as a reservoir, one for each combination of the others’), and its groups are those of the sim’s other dimensions. Each flow of a disease is a flow of the program for each combination of the others’ compartments, so every rate is worked out from the people as they are at the start of the step (not each disease in turn), and a whole run, many runs, a particle filter, and a run in JAX take a crossing as they take one disease. The solvers that draw whole events in steps draw each disease’s in turn, from those rates, so each disease’s moves (e.g. through the stages of a dwell time) are drawn as they would be for it alone. The program’s compartments (y) are the one copy of the people: each engine’s (engine.y) are a view of them (Joint), so a change made in Python (e.g. by an intervention) is seen by all of them at once. The crossing is run as one engine is (see ss.solvers.Compartmental.step() and run_all(), where it is the engine’s owner): the last disease to step takes the step for all of them, and the first to take a whole run takes it for all of them, and gives each its part. Its size is counted before it is made (see ss.solvers.choose.joint_layout()), and kept within ss.options.max_joint; sim.describe() shows it, with the memory a whole run takes.

title: strains
text:
strains
Strains of a disease (ss.Strains), and protection between them (ss.immunity)
These exist so that one disease can have several strains, with their own values and with protection between them, without being written as several diseases. The strains of a declared disease share its states; a disease written as code (ss.AgentDisease(strains=...)) carries one at a time, as an index for each person (dis.strain), passed on by the same code as a declared disease’s.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Strains
The strains of a disease: ss.Disease(..., strains=ss.Strains(...)), which is then dis.strains


immunity
Protection between strains: what having (or having had) one strain does against each strain





strains.Strains(
    strains,
    immunity=None,
    max_strains=None,
    transmit='one',
    fractions=None,
    name='strain',
    label=None,
    **values,
)
The strains of a disease: ss.Disease(..., strains=ss.Strains(...)), which is then dis.strains
The strains share the disease’s states: a person is in a state once, carrying their strains, with one course. The engine chooses how to run what is declared (one strain at a time, or sets of strains carried together), and describe() says which.
With no immunity=, a person carries one strain at a time, being infected (or recovered) protects against every strain, and a new infection takes its source’s strain. ss.immunity(due_to=...) changes that: protection from a state. With max_strains above 1, people carry sets of strains (the levels of the strain dimension, e.g. ‘DS+RIF’), and a set takes the largest of its strains’ values for a transition; once full, a new strain replaces the oldest (counted in the flow that brought it).
Values for each strain are multipliers on the disease’s transitions (by name: their rate, a duration divided, or a branch’s probability) and on rel_trans. They can be given two ways, which are the same thing: by strain, as a dict of dicts; or by parameter, as lists, one entry per strain.

Protection between strains: what having (or having had) one strain does against each strain
protection= is the protection against being infected: a matrix, with rows from the strain held and columns against the strain (1 is complete), or a single number, the same protection from any strain held against every strain. title: internals.dists
text:
internals.dists
The machinery of random-number-safe distributions: ss.Dist, and how the distributions of a sim are found, seeded, and drawn from
It exists so that each decision in a sim has its own random stream, which keeps two runs comparable (common random numbers). As compartments, a distribution mostly describes a dwell time or a parameter: the engine draws from its own generator.
The distributions themselves are in ss.distributions.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Dist
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution,


Dists
Class for managing a collection of Dist objects


scipy_dist
A distribution of scipy.stats, by name, and its parameters (kwds), as a frozen one holds them





internals.dists.Dist(
    dist=None,
    distname=None,
    name=None,
    unit=None,
    round=False,
    seed=None,
    offset=None,
    strict=True,
    sim=None,
    module=None,
    mock=False,
    **kwargs,
)
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution, i.e. one decision per timestep.
See ss.distributions.dist_list for a full list of supported distributions. Their parameters are named by their moments where they have them (ss.normal(mean, std), ss.expon(mean), ss.poisson(mean)), and otherwise by their usual names (ss.gamma(shape, scale)); each is translated to SciPy’s or NumPy’s names inside (sync_pars()), and a keyword a distribution doesn’t take is a TypeError when it is made.
Distributions scale in different ways, such as converting between time units, given by scaling. Some distributions can’t be scaled at all (e.g. ss.beta_dist(), whose values are fractions). For distributions that can be scaled, some distributions can only be (linearly) scaled before the random numbers are generated (called “predraw”), some can only be scaled after (called “postdraw”), and some can be scaled in either way (both).
For example, a normal distribution is both since 2Normal(a, b) = Normal(2a, 2b). A Poisson distribution is “predraw” since 2Poisson(λ) ≠ Poisson(2λ), and there is no way to get the correct shape of a different Poisson distribution once the numbers have been drawn. Finally, distributions with unitless shape parameters as well as parameter that can have units (e.g. a gamma distribution with shape and scale parameters) are referred to as “postdraw” since scaling all input parameters is invalid (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) ≠ Gamma(2shape, 2scale)), but they can still be scaled (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) = Gamma(1shape, 2*scale)).
So scaling is one of:
- 'postdraw' (after the random numbers are drawn, e.g. `ss.weibull()`)
- 'predraw' (before the draw, e.g. `ss.poisson()`)
- ['predraw', 'postdraw'] (either, e.g. `ss.normal()`)
- None (not at all, e.g. `ss.beta_dist()`)
Note: by default, ss.Dist is initialized with an ss.Sim object to ensure random number reproducibility. You can override this with either ss.Dist(strict=False) on creation, or dist.init(force=True) after creation. A distribution with a unit (e.g. ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))) draws in that unit outside a sim, with neither.
Although it’s possible in theory to define a custom distribution (i.e., not one from NumPy or SciPy), in practice this is difficult. The distribution needs to have both a way to return random variates (easy), as well as the probability point function (inverse CDF). In addition, the distribution must be able to take a NumPy RNG as its bit generator. It’s easier to just use a default Dist (e.g., ss.random()), and then take its output as input (i.e., quantiles) for whatever custom distribution you want to create.

internals.dists.hash_uniforms(seed, ind, slots, dtype=None, even=False)
Generate one uniform random number in (0, 1) per slot via a counter-based (splitmix64) hash keyed by (seed, ind); not for the user.
This is the engine behind Starsim’s common random numbers (CRN). Because each output depends only on its slot (plus the per-draw key), the same slot always yields the same value regardless of how many other agents are drawn – so structural differences between scenarios don’t ripple into unrelated agents. It generates exactly len(slots) numbers.
The result is returned at dtype (default ss.dtypes.float) so the CRN path matches the dtype of the native draw path (Dist.rand). The mantissa width is matched to the float width (24-bit for float32, 53-bit for float64) so every value stays strictly < 1 – a plain float64->float32 cast would round the largest values up to exactly 1.0 and break the [0, 1) contract (e.g. expon.ppf(1.0) is inf). With even, the numbers of the call are evenly spaced (see even_out()).

internals.dists.Dist(
    dist=None,
    distname=None,
    name=None,
    unit=None,
    round=False,
    seed=None,
    offset=None,
    strict=True,
    sim=None,
    module=None,
    mock=False,
    **kwargs,
)
Base class for tracking one random number generator associated with one distribution, i.e. one decision per timestep.
See ss.distributions.dist_list for a full list of supported distributions. Their parameters are named by their moments where they have them (ss.normal(mean, std), ss.expon(mean), ss.poisson(mean)), and otherwise by their usual names (ss.gamma(shape, scale)); each is translated to SciPy’s or NumPy’s names inside (sync_pars()), and a keyword a distribution doesn’t take is a TypeError when it is made.
Distributions scale in different ways, such as converting between time units, given by scaling. Some distributions can’t be scaled at all (e.g. ss.beta_dist(), whose values are fractions). For distributions that can be scaled, some distributions can only be (linearly) scaled before the random numbers are generated (called “predraw”), some can only be scaled after (called “postdraw”), and some can be scaled in either way (both).
For example, a normal distribution is both since 2Normal(a, b) = Normal(2a, 2b). A Poisson distribution is “predraw” since 2Poisson(λ) ≠ Poisson(2λ), and there is no way to get the correct shape of a different Poisson distribution once the numbers have been drawn. Finally, distributions with unitless shape parameters as well as parameter that can have units (e.g. a gamma distribution with shape and scale parameters) are referred to as “postdraw” since scaling all input parameters is invalid (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) ≠ Gamma(2shape, 2scale)), but they can still be scaled (i.e. 2Gamma(shape, scale) = Gamma(1shape, 2*scale)).
So scaling is one of:
- 'postdraw' (after the random numbers are drawn, e.g. `ss.weibull()`)
- 'predraw' (before the draw, e.g. `ss.poisson()`)
- ['predraw', 'postdraw'] (either, e.g. `ss.normal()`)
- None (not at all, e.g. `ss.beta_dist()`)
Note: by default, ss.Dist is initialized with an ss.Sim object to ensure random number reproducibility. You can override this with either ss.Dist(strict=False) on creation, or dist.init(force=True) after creation. A distribution with a unit (e.g. ss.erlang(k=4, mean=ss.days(10))) draws in that unit outside a sim, with neither.
Although it’s possible in theory to define a custom distribution (i.e., not one from NumPy or SciPy), in practice this is difficult. The distribution needs to have both a way to return random variates (easy), as well as the probability point function (inverse CDF). In addition, the distribution must be able to take a NumPy RNG as its bit generator. It’s easier to just use a default Dist (e.g., ss.random()), and then take its output as input (i.e., quantiles) for whatever custom distribution you want to create.

internals.dists.Dist.harmonize_par_units()
Ensure that parameters that share dimensions also share time units
Some distributions have several parameters with the same dimensions (e.g. the mean and standard deviation of ss.lognormal()); these are listed in the distribution’s unit_pars attribute. Supplying units for only some of them is the expected usage, since the units of the others follow from it: for example, ss.lognormal(mean=ss.years(10)) means the same thing as ss.lognormal(mean=ss.years(10), std=ss.years(1)). Any plain numbers are therefore converted to the same timepar as their siblings. (Without this, they would be interpreted as numbers of timesteps, and would give different answers for different values of dt.) Mixing durations and rates cannot be resolved this way, so it raises an exception. Distributions with unit_pars = None are not checked.

The smallest of n uniforms becomes (0 + v)/n, the next (1 + v)/n, and so on, with one offset v for the call. Each number is still exactly uniform, so every distribution keeps its shape, but together they have the mean and spread they should. Each stays close to its original value, so CRN keeps working, though less well (see ss.Sim).

internals.dists.hash_uniforms(seed, ind, slots, dtype=None, even=False)
Generate one uniform random number in (0, 1) per slot via a counter-based (splitmix64) hash keyed by (seed, ind); not for the user.
This is the engine behind Starsim’s common random numbers (CRN). Because each output depends only on its slot (plus the per-draw key), the same slot always yields the same value regardless of how many other agents are drawn – so structural differences between scenarios don’t ripple into unrelated agents. It generates exactly len(slots) numbers.
The result is returned at dtype (default ss.dtypes.float) so the CRN path matches the dtype of the native draw path (Dist.rand). The mantissa width is matched to the float width (24-bit for float32, 53-bit for float64) so every value stays strictly < 1 – a plain float64->float32 cast would round the largest values up to exactly 1.0 and break the [0, 1) contract (e.g. expon.ppf(1.0) is inf). With even, the numbers of the call are evenly spaced (see even_out()).

title: converters
text:
converters
Import models from other frameworks, and export sims to them
ss.import_from(filename, format=...) reads another framework’s model into a sim, and ss.export_to(sim, format) writes a sim in another framework’s format; see docs/design/16-interop.md in the lingua_franca repo. Each importer reads its format into an ss.converters.Source, and ss.converters.build() writes that as Starsim code by the same rules for every format (ss.converters.write()) and runs the code to make the sim: the code is kept in sim.imported.code, how each rate was read is printed, and what could not be translated is listed as ss.errors.ImportIncomplete and kept in sim.imported.

title: sim
text:
sim
The sim (ss.Sim)
This is what a user runs. It exists to gather the people, modules, and settings of a model in one object; to choose how to run it (the solver); and to hold the results. It works the same way for every kind of model.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Sim
The sim: a model, how to run it, and its results





sim.Sim(
    *models,
    label=None,
    people=None,
    demographics=None,
    connectors=None,
    networks=None,
    diseases=None,
    interventions=None,
    analyzers=None,
    modules=None,
    data=None,
    pars=None,
    copy_modules=True,
    **kwargs,
)
The sim: a model, how to run it, and its results
Every Starsim model, whatever its kind, is run with a sim. It gathers the people and the modules (ss.Disease, ss.Network, ss.Intervention, ss.Demographics, and others), runs them step by step (see ss.loop.Loop), or all at once in the compiled kernels when nothing needs to happen between the steps, and holds the results.





Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Module / list / dict
the model: a module or a list of modules, which are sorted by kind as for modules; transitions, alone or in a list (or in diseases=), are one disease, named from its states (e.g. sim.sir). Alternatively, the sim’s settings as an ss.SimPars or a dict, which can include any of the other arguments



pars
dict / SimPars
the values of the model’s parameters by name, e.g. pars=dict(beta=0.1) or pars=fit.pars (see ss.par). sim.Sim.fit(
    pars=None,
    data=None,
    weights=None,
    likelihood=None,
    loss=None,
    penalty=None,
    method=None,
    rand_seed=None,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Fit every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data
Fits every parameter that has bounds (see ss.par) to every result that has data (see ss.Sim(data=...)). The original sim is not changed. The fitting itself is in ss.fitting, which is imported when it is first used.
A parameter can be one of a declared model, of a module written as code (ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(...)), also a value in a dict parameter, fitted as e.g. cin_fn.k, or a setting kept as an attribute), a modifier’s amount (ss.modify(..., multiply=ss.par(...))), or a keyword argument of a function given as a module (def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])), for a value set in code); one named alike in several modules is fitted with its module’s name, e.g. hpv16.rel_beta. A parameter whose value is an array, with bounds for each element (ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])), has each element fitted, as knots[0], …, except those whose bounds are equal. A data column names a result, as sim.results has it: e.g. prevalence, sir.prevalence, an analyzer’s by_age.cancers_0_15, a result nested deeper (hpv.genotype.cancers), or a column of a result with columns (sis.infection.alpha).
The fit uses either likelihoods or a loss: every data series has a likelihood (declared on its outcome, or given here), and the fit maximizes their sum; or none has, and it minimizes the loss. loss= is used in place of likelihoods declared on the outcomes (with a note), and likelihood=False switches them off. Some series with a likelihood and some without is an error, as is loss= with likelihood=.
By default, the fit finds the best values (a point estimate), by the method that suits the sim, and prints which and why:

‘l-bfgs-b’ for a deterministic sim, with gradients from JAX (see ss.gradients), or by finite differences for one that JAX cannot run
‘nelder-mead’ for one whose likelihood or priors JAX does not cover (e.g. a likelihood given as a function), or with one or two fitted parameters (where it is faster than gradients)
‘optuna’ for a stochastic sim, including an agent-based one

Other methods for a best fit are ‘powell’ (no gradients), ‘slsqp’ (with gradients, like ‘l-bfgs-b’), and ‘if2’ (iterated filtering, for the sims that ‘pmcmc’ fits: the maximum-likelihood values, from passes of a particle filter in which each particle’s values are perturbed by a shrinking random walk; see ss.fitting.Swarm). For the uncertainty in the values (a posterior), ask for one by name:

‘nuts’ (the No-U-Turn sampler), for a deterministic sim with gradients whose data series all have a likelihood; each chain starts from a draw near one of the best optima found from a scan over the bounds
‘pmcmc’ (particle MCMC), for a sim whose data series all have a likelihood: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on the likelihood estimated by a particle filter for a stochastic compartmental sim (see ss.fitting.ParticleFilter), or on the exact likelihood for a deterministic sim (e.g. one JAX cannot run); each chain starts from a different one of the best points of a scan, and a run is kept with each draw, fit.trajectories, which fit.project() continues
‘abc-smc’ (approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo), for any stochastic sim, with no likelihood needed; its accuracy depends on the tolerance it reaches, and it gives no posterior for a deterministic sim

The priors are the parameters’ prior=, or uniform over their bounds.

sim.Sim.optimize(
    goal=None,
    total=None,
    start=None,
    spend=None,
    bounds=None,
    target=None,
    maxiter=50,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Allocate spending between programs to reach a goal, keeping the total fixed; or find the least total that reaches a target
The spending of each program is a parameter of the model: one per program of an imported program book (sim.imported.programs), or any parameters, given by name with spend=. The search (SciPy’s SLSQP) is over the fractions of the total, and each point is a run (restarted, if the sim is nothing but compartments). With target=, the total is doubled until its best allocation reaches the target, then found by bisection between a total that reaches it and one that does not (to within 1%), assuming that more money never does worse. The sim itself is not changed. The search is in ss.fitting, which is imported when it is first used.

None

None

None

float

None

int

50


verbose
bool
whether to print progress
None

sim.Sim.rescale()
Dynamically rescale the population; only used if pars.rescale=True
The scale factor starts at 1. Once the fraction of agents who are not naive (i.e. have ever been infected with any disease) exceeds the threshold (rescale=dict(threshold=)), the scale factor is increased by at least rescale=dict(factor=) (up to sim.pop_scale), and the same fraction of non-naive agents are made naive again (via disease.make_naive()), so that each agent now represents more people. Based on Covasim’s dynamic rescaling.
The people no agent stands for yet are counted as one number, results.unrepresented: pop_scale - 1 for each agent at the start, less the people the agents alive take on at each rescaling (from scale s to s', s' - s for each); the deaths and births of agents do not change it. So alive is scale people for each agent alive, plus these.

For a sim that is nothing but compartments (one that the kernels run from start to finish: see sim.describe()), this makes repeated runs many times faster; any other sim (or a change the compartments were not laid out for, such as a new distribution) is built again, as sim.new() would. ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=...) and sim.fit() use it where they can.

title: sim
text:
Name
Description




Sim
The sim: a model, how to run it, and its results





sim.Sim(
    *models,
    label=None,
    people=None,
    demographics=None,
    connectors=None,
    networks=None,
    diseases=None,
    interventions=None,
    analyzers=None,
    modules=None,
    data=None,
    pars=None,
    copy_modules=True,
    **kwargs,
)
The sim: a model, how to run it, and its results
Every Starsim model, whatever its kind, is run with a sim. It gathers the people and the modules (ss.Disease, ss.Network, ss.Intervention, ss.Demographics, and others), runs them step by step (see ss.loop.Loop), or all at once in the compiled kernels when nothing needs to happen between the steps, and holds the results.





Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Module / list / dict
the model: a module or a list of modules, which are sorted by kind as for modules; transitions, alone or in a list (or in diseases=), are one disease, named from its states (e.g. sim.sir). Alternatively, the sim’s settings as an ss.SimPars or a dict, which can include any of the other arguments



pars
dict / SimPars
the values of the model’s parameters by name, e.g. pars=dict(beta=0.1) or pars=fit.pars (see ss.par). As in Starsim 3, it can also hold settings of the sim (e.g. pars=dict(start=2000, dur=10, n_agents=1000, beta=0.1)): a name is a setting if no parameter of the model has it, and a keyword given directly wins over the same setting here. A whole ss.SimPars is taken as if given in place of the model. A name that is neither raises a KeyError when the sim is initialized
None


label
str
a name for the sim, shown in plots and printouts
None


people
People
the people to use (by default, the sim makes them)
None


demographics
str / Demographics / list / bool
births, deaths, and migration: declared (ss.birth(), ss.death(), which run under every solver), or modules (e.g. ss.Births(), ss.Pregnancy()), or a list; True for births and deaths at default rates
None


connectors
str / Connector / list
as above, for connectors
None


networks
str / Network / list
as above, for networks
None


interventions
str / Intervention / list
as above, for interventions
None


diseases
str / Disease / list
as above, for diseases
None


analyzers
str / Analyzer / list
as above, for analyzers
None


modules
Module / list
modules of any kind, sorted among demographics, diseases, etc.; a module of your own that is none of these (an ss.Module, or a function of the sim, which becomes its step()) is kept in sim.custom
None


solver
str / Solver
how a declared model is run: ‘auto’ (the default: chosen from the model; sim.solver_reason says why), ‘ode’ (deterministic and fastest), ‘binomial’ (stochastic compartments, a chain binomial), ‘gillespie’ (stochastic and exact, event by event), ‘tau’ (tau-leaping, a faster approximation to Gillespie), or ‘abm’ (agents, for detail about individuals). A solver can take options, e.g. ss.solvers.ode(integrator=, substeps=, dwells=) (dwells='exact' keeps each dwell time as it is, rather than as a chain of stages), ss.solvers.binomial(substeps=), or ss.solvers.abm(step=) (step='events' for agents in continuous time). A declared module can have its own way of running as agents, ss.Disease(..., solver=ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep')), which the sim’s does not override. sim.solver is the one that runs, e.g. isinstance(sim.solver, ss.solvers.abm)



branching
bool

when the sim starts: a date (e.g. ‘2020-01-01’) or a year (a number from 1800 on, e.g. 2000), which give it a calendar; any other number (or a duration) is a time in the sim’s unit from 0 (default: 2000 for a model in years, else 0). With a calendar, every bare number given as a time (stop=, when=, the times of ss.schedule and ss.timeseries) is a year; without one, a time in the sim’s unit from 0. A duration given as a time (when=ss.days(10), until=, the start= of a module) is that long after the start with a calendar, else a time from 0 (day 10; the same when the start is 0)

the length of the run from its start, e.g. start=2000, dur=10 (a bare number is in years in a sim of calendar years, as a bare stop is, else in the sim’s unit) or start='2020-01-01', dur=ss.days(90); any two of the start, stop, and length define the third (stop=2035, dur=10 starts in 2025), and all three must agree

sim.Sim.fit(
    pars=None,
    data=None,
    weights=None,
    likelihood=None,
    loss=None,
    penalty=None,
    method=None,
    rand_seed=None,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Fit every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data
Fits every parameter that has bounds (see ss.par) to every result that has data (see ss.Sim(data=...)). The original sim is not changed. The fitting itself is in ss.fitting, which is imported when it is first used.
A parameter can be one of a declared model, of a module written as code (ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(...)), also a value in a dict parameter, fitted as e.g. cin_fn.k, or a setting kept as an attribute), a modifier’s amount (ss.modify(..., multiply=ss.par(...))), or a keyword argument of a function given as a module (def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])), for a value set in code); one named alike in several modules is fitted with its module’s name, e.g. hpv16.rel_beta. A parameter whose value is an array, with bounds for each element (ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])), has each element fitted, as knots[0], …, except those whose bounds are equal. A data column names a result, as sim.results has it: e.g. prevalence, sir.prevalence, an analyzer’s by_age.cancers_0_15, a result nested deeper (hpv.genotype.cancers), or a column of a result with columns (sis.infection.alpha).
The fit uses either likelihoods or a loss: every data series has a likelihood (declared on its outcome, or given here), and the fit maximizes their sum; or none has, and it minimizes the loss. loss= is used in place of likelihoods declared on the outcomes (with a note), and likelihood=False switches them off. Some series with a likelihood and some without is an error, as is loss= with likelihood=.
By default, the fit finds the best values (a point estimate), by the method that suits the sim, and prints which and why:

‘l-bfgs-b’ for a deterministic sim, with gradients from JAX (see ss.gradients), or by finite differences for one that JAX cannot run
‘nelder-mead’ for one whose likelihood or priors JAX does not cover (e.g. a likelihood given as a function), or with one or two fitted parameters (where it is faster than gradients)
‘optuna’ for a stochastic sim, including an agent-based one

Other methods for a best fit are ‘powell’ (no gradients), ‘slsqp’ (with gradients, like ‘l-bfgs-b’), and ‘if2’ (iterated filtering, for the sims that ‘pmcmc’ fits: the maximum-likelihood values, from passes of a particle filter in which each particle’s values are perturbed by a shrinking random walk; see ss.fitting.Swarm). For the uncertainty in the values (a posterior), ask for one by name:

‘nuts’ (the No-U-Turn sampler), for a deterministic sim with gradients whose data series all have a likelihood; each chain starts from a draw near one of the best optima found from a scan over the bounds
‘pmcmc’ (particle MCMC), for a sim whose data series all have a likelihood: a random-walk Metropolis sampler on the likelihood estimated by a particle filter for a stochastic compartmental sim (see ss.fitting.ParticleFilter), or on the exact likelihood for a deterministic sim (e.g. one JAX cannot run); each chain starts from a different one of the best points of a scan, and a run is kept with each draw, fit.trajectories, which fit.project() continues
‘abc-smc’ (approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo), for any stochastic sim, with no likelihood needed; its accuracy depends on the tolerance it reaches, and it gives no posterior for a deterministic sim

The priors are the parameters’ prior=, or uniform over their bounds.

Type
Description
Default

The fit then maximizes their sum (plus the log of the priors of the parameters that have one, for the methods that find a best fit: the most probable values)

Once a sim is initialized, its settings are those of its run: setting one (e.g. sim.pars.stop = 30 after sim.run()) raises, so give it here instead (sim.new(stop=30)). Other changes made to it then (e.g. to a module’s parameters) belong to that run only, and are not kept.
To run a finished sim again from the start, sim.run() is enough (and sim.restart(pars=...).run() with other values, which for a sim that is nothing but compartments is much faster than a new sim); sim.new() is for other settings, e.g. sim.new(solver='abm').run(). To copy a sim as it is, including its results, use sim.copy().

None

bool
if True, this sim becomes the new one, rather than a new one being returned
False

A subclass’s own arguments (e.g. FPsim’s location=) are not taken again: make the subclass again for those.








sim.Sim.optimize(
    goal=None,
    total=None,
    start=None,
    spend=None,
    bounds=None,
    target=None,
    maxiter=50,
    verbose=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Allocate spending between programs to reach a goal, keeping the total fixed; or find the least total that reaches a target
The spending of each program is a parameter of the model: one per program of an imported program book (sim.imported.programs), or any parameters, given by name with spend=. The search (SciPy’s SLSQP) is over the fractions of the total, and each point is a run (restarted, if the sim is nothing but compartments). With target=, the total is doubled until its best allocation reaches the target, then found by bisection between a total that reaches it and one that does not (to within 1%), assuming that more money never does worse. The sim itself is not changed. The search is in ss.fitting, which is imported when it is first used.

Type
Description
Default

ss.fitting.maximize/ss.fitting.minimize
what to make as large or as small as possible: a result (e.g. ss.fitting.maximize('all_vs', at=2030), or ss.fitting.minimize('hiv.new_infections')), or a function of the run sim
None


total
float
the total to allocate (default: the current total); with target=, the total the search starts from
None


start
float / date
when the new allocation takes effect (default: the start of the sim), read as any time is (see ss.connectors.to_time(): a bare number is a year if the sim has a calendar)
None


spend
dict / list
the spending parameters: names, or {program: name} (default: the imported programs)
None


bounds
tuple / dict
the least and most a program can have, as amounts (default: 0 and the total); a dict gives them by program, e.g. dict(testing=(1e5, None)) (None for no limit), and a program not in it has the default
None


target
float
the value of the result to reach (at least this with ss.fitting.maximize(), at most with ss.fitting.minimize()) with the least total
None


maxiter
int
the most iterations of the search (of each total’s, with target=)
50


verbose
bool
whether to print progress
None



Returns an ss.fitting.Optimization.



sim = ss.import_from('hiv_framework.xlsx', format='atomica', databook='hiv_databook.xlsx', progbook='hiv_progbook.xlsx', programs_start=2020)
best = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.maximize('all_vs', at=2030), start=2020)
best.summarize()
least = sim.optimize(ss.fitting.maximize('all_vs', at=2030), start=2020, target=1.1*best.value) # The least money that reaches it

sim.Sim.rescale()
Dynamically rescale the population; only used if pars.rescale=True
The scale factor starts at 1. Once the fraction of agents who are not naive (i.e. have ever been infected with any disease) exceeds the threshold (rescale=dict(threshold=)), the scale factor is increased by at least rescale=dict(factor=) (up to sim.pop_scale), and the same fraction of non-naive agents are made naive again (via disease.make_naive()), so that each agent now represents more people. Based on Covasim’s dynamic rescaling.
The people no agent stands for yet are counted as one number, results.unrepresented: pop_scale - 1 for each agent at the start, less the people the agents alive take on at each rescaling (from scale s to s', s' - s for each); the deaths and births of agents do not change it. So alive is scale people for each agent alive, plus these.



sim.Sim.restart(pars=None, rand_seed=None)
Take a sim back to its start, optionally with new values of its parameters or a new seed, without running it
sim.run() does this itself for a finished sim; restart() is for running it again with other values or another seed (sim.restart(pars=dict(beta=0.1), rand_seed=2).run()), for stepping it yourself from the start (sim.restart().run(until=2010)), or for a function that sets the values to try (as for ss.gradients.Density). The values given are kept for later runs (as sim.par_values), until changed again.
For a sim that is nothing but compartments (one that the kernels run from start to finish: see sim.describe()), this makes repeated runs many times faster; any other sim (or a change the compartments were not laid out for, such as a new distribution) is built again, as sim.new() would. ss.parallel(sim, n_runs=...) and sim.fit() use it where they can.

internals.expressions
Expressions: the parameters (ss.par), counts, and arithmetic that rates, results, and conditions are made of, and how they are evaluated and printed
They exist so that a rate or result written once can be read by any solver, printed as an equation, and differentiated. They belong to declared models, and a module written as code can also use ss.par and do arithmetic on such values.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules

Description

Base class for anything that can appear in a rate or a result: states,

A value for each person: drawn at an event, recorded at an event, drawn once when the person is made (a trait), or derived


mother

A named parameter with bounds, a prior, and provenance

internals.expressions.attr(
    value,
    when=None,
    combine='last',
    init=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A value for each person: drawn at an event, recorded at an event, drawn once when the person is made (a trait), or derived
Which it is depends on value and when=: a distribution with when= is drawn when the event happens to someone; an expression (or the name of another attribute) with when= is recorded then, as it was just before the move; a dict of them by event (a transition, tr.to(B), X.enter, …) records each event’s own value, with no when=; a distribution with no when= is a trait; and an expression, or a dict of one by state (states not listed give NaN), with no when= is derived, worked out when it is read. Attributes set on the same event are set in the order they are declared, and each sees the ones before it. As agents only.





Name
Type
Description
Default

Dist / Expr / str / dict
the distribution, the expression, the name of another attribute, a dict of expressions by state (or by a sum of states), or a dict of distributions or expressions by event
required


when
Event / Transition
the event(s) that set it, joined with \|; none for a trait or a derived attribute
None


combine
str / func
how a new value is combined with the one already held: ‘last’ (the default), ‘first’, ‘max’, ‘min’, ‘sum’, or fn(old, new)
'last'


init
float / Dist / Expr
the value before any event (default NaN, or 0 for combine='sum'): a number, or a distribution or an expression (e.g. of ss.person) drawn or worked out for each person when they are made (at the start, once placed in their states, and at birth)
None


name
str
the name; if not given, taken from the keyword or class attribute it is assigned to
None


label
str
a human-readable name
None

cd4_preart = ss.attr('cd4', when=start_art)                               # Recorded, just before starting

cd4        = ss.attr({latent: cd4_latent, falling: cd4_latent*(1 - falling.progress)}) # Derived

nab        = ss.attr(ss.uniform(0.5, 0.95), when=clearance, combine='max', init=0)
n_inf      = ss.attr(1, when=I.enter, combine='sum', init=ss.poisson(mean=ss.person.age/20)) # Past infections at the start

Description

The value before any event, as a number (one drawn for each person, init_value, is NaN, or 0 for combine='sum', until drawn)


init_value
The distribution or expression the value before any event is drawn from or worked out from for each person, if it is one


kind
‘drawn’, ‘recorded’, ‘trait’, or ‘derived’ (a dict by event is ‘recorded’, each event’s value drawn or worked out)

internals.expressions.mother(x, include_born=False)
A condition or expression evaluated on each unborn agent’s mother (1/0 for a condition, or its value), and 0 for anyone born, unless include_born=True
Usable in rates, p=, who=, when=ss.on(), and modifier conditions. Agents only: solver='auto' chooses them, and a compartmental solver stops with a CapabilityError.
With include_born=True it is evaluated on the mother of anyone who has one, born or not, e.g. to reach the newborns of mothers who tested positive. An agent with no mother in the sim gets 0. A mother who has died or left is in none of her states, so a condition on them is false, but what was remembered of her (e.g. anc.positive.since) is still read.

Default

required

title: library.diseases
text:
library.diseases
Example disease models: cholera, COVID, dengue, Ebola, gonorrhea, HIV, influenza, malaria, measles, pertussis, polio, RSV, syphilis, TB, typhoid, and a non-communicable disease (NCD), and Starsim 3’s SIR, SEIR, and SIS written as agent-based code.
These are illustrative, lightly-parameterized models intended as starting points for building your own disease modules, not as validated models for any specific setting. Each one says in its docstring where its structure and its default parameters came from. Core disease base classes (ss.Disease, ss.AgentDisease, ss.SIR, etc.) live in starsim.diseases.





Name
Description




ART
Antiretroviral therapy, delivered as ss.treat() delivers a treatment


AgentSEIR
An SEIR model written as agent-based code rather than declared: Starsim 3’s ss.SEIR


AgentSIR
An SIR model written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SIR


AgentSIS
An SIS model with waning immunity, written as code: Starsim 3’s ss.SIS (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_inf


CD4_analyzer
Record the CD4 count of every agent at every timestep.


COVID
COVID-19, as a SECIR model by age: a chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering


Cholera
Cholera, with both direct and environmental (waterborne) transmission


Dengue
Dengue: several serotypes, each passed on by mosquitoes, with partial cross-protection between them


DengueSerotype
One dengue serotype: people are susceptible, infectious, or recovered, with mosquitoes of its own


Ebola
Ebola, including severe disease and transmission from unburied bodies


Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea, as an SIS model on a sexual network


HIV
Simple HIV model with CD4 count dynamics and ART.


Influenza
Seasonal influenza, as a SEIRS model with a yearly cycle in transmission


Malaria
Malaria as the Ross-Macdonald model of humans and mosquitoes


MalariaImmunity
Malaria with immunity, as the Garki model


Measles
Measles, as an SEIR model with deaths


NCD
Example non-communicable disease


Pertussis
Pertussis (whooping cough), as a SEIRS model with slowly waning immunity


Polio
Poliovirus, with a paralytic fraction


RSV
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), as a seasonal MSEIRS model


Syphilis
Syphilis, as a staged infection, wholly declared


TB
Tuberculosis, as the LSHTM model of the spectrum of TB disease


Typhoid
Typhoid fever, with chronic carriers





library.diseases.ART(
    coverage=1.0,
    who=None,
    when=None,
    art_delay=ss.years(1),
    name=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Antiretroviral therapy, delivered as ss.treat() delivers a treatment
By default, ART is offered once to each person who has been infected with HIV for art_delay and is not on it, with the probability coverage; who= restricts who among them is offered it, and when= when, as for any delivery (see ss.Delivery). The people treated are on ART for good: their CD4 count recovers, and they are less infectious (see HIV). Requires the HIV module.
Note: CRN safe.

Default

who among the people eligible is offered it (e.g. ss.person.female)
None


when
various

None

library.diseases.AgentSEIR(pars=None, dur_exp=_, **kwargs)
An SEIR model written as agent-based code rather than declared: Starsim 3’s ss.SEIR (see ssl.AgentSIR), with its lognormal dur_exp and dur_inf and p_death=0.01.
This class extends AgentSIR with an exposed state: agents who are infected but not yet infectious. exposed and infectious are the literal E and I compartments, and infected is derived from them: an agent is infected from the moment it acquires the infection, whether or not it is yet transmitting. So infected and prevalence count E plus I, while transmission depends on infectious alone.
Correspondingly, ti_exposed is the time of acquisition and ti_infectious is the time of becoming infectious. ti_infected is deliberately not defined, since it is too easily confused with ti_infectious.
Note: CRN safe.





Name
Type
Description
Default




beta
float/ss.prob
the infectiousness

library.diseases.COVID(ages=True, **kwargs)
COVID-19, as a SECIR model by age: a chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering
People who are infected are exposed (E), then infected without symptoms (INS), and then either recover or develop symptoms (ISy); of those, some become severe (ISev, in hospital), then critical (ICr, in intensive care), and some of those die. People without symptoms and with symptoms are both infectious, at rel_ins and rel_sym of the transmission rate.
The disease is stratified by age into MEmilio’s six groups (0-4, 5-14, 15-34, 35-59, 60-79, and 80+), since the severity of COVID-19 rises steeply with age: in the oldest group, a symptomatic case is 30 times as likely to become severe as in a child, and a critical one 12 times as likely to die. The fraction of people in each group is the world’s, unless the sim’s population says otherwise (e.g. people=ss.population('Germany')).
Source: the values for Germany of MEmilio (Kühn MJ et al., Mathematical Biosciences 2021, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mbs.2021.108648; examples/ode_secir_parameter_study_graph.cpp), which gives each as a range, by age; each default here is the middle of its range. MEmilio’s transmission is a contact rate times a chance of infection per contact, which is 0.06 for adults and from 0.03 (under 5) to 0.175 (80 and over), here the relative susceptibility rel_sus (1 for adults). Without contacts given, beta is 1 a day, which with the world’s ages gives an R0 of about 3.2, as for the first strains of COVID-19. With a contact matrix, beta is per contact, and MEmilio’s is 0.06: ssl.COVID(beta=0.06) with networks=ss.contacts('Germany').
With ages=False, the model has one group, with the values of MEmilio’s simple example (ode_secir_simple.cpp), whose beta of 1 a day is one contact a day, each certain to infect; with people infectious at rel_ins for 2 days and at rel_sym for 6, this gives an R0 of about 2.7.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    solver=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Cholera, with both direct and environmental (waterborne) transmission
People infected are latent (E) for dur_exp, then a fraction p_symp become symptomatic (Is), and the rest are asymptomatic (Ia), shedding far less (asymp_trans). Asymptomatic people recover; symptomatic people recover, or die (with probability p_death, sooner). Besides transmission from person to person (beta), infectious people shed bacteria into a well-mixed reservoir of water (W, a count of bacteria, not people) at shedding_rate, the bacteria die off at decay_rate, and susceptible people are infected from the water at a rate that rises with the concentration, beta_env times env_conc = W/(W + half_sat_rate), as in the model of Codeço (2001). It is declared, so it runs under any solver.
Sources: Codeço CT, “Endemic and epidemic dynamics of cholera: the role of the aquatic reservoir”, BMC Infect Dis 2001;1:1 (https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2334-1-1), for the structure; the latent period is from Azman et al. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3677557/), a lognormal; asymptomatic shedding of 1 to 10 days (uniform) from the WHO fact sheet; 5 days of symptoms (a lognormal fit to the range of 2.9 to 14 days) from Fung (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3926264/); a rapid death of severe cases (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5767916/); half of infections symptomatic, mid range of Jackson et al. and Nelson et al.; asymptomatic carriers shedding 100 times less; the dose-response, shedding, and decay from Mukandavire et al. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3102413/). beta (from person to person) and beta_env are illustrative. Since the bacteria are a count, shed by everyone infectious into one reservoir, the water carries more of the epidemic in a larger population: with these values, it sustains an outbreak in a town of 10,000, and transmission from person to person alone does not.

library.diseases.MalariaImmunity(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    solver=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
Malaria with immunity, as the Garki model
The states keep the source’s names: x1 (nonimmune and negative), x2 (nonimmune, incubating), y1 (positive and infectious), y2 (positive, not infectious, recovering slowly), y3 (immune positive, recovering fast), x3 (immune and negative), and x4 (immune, incubating). People lose infectivity before they gain a fast recovery rate, and are detected less often once immune (q3). Everything about the mosquitoes is in one number, the vectorial capacity C: the potentially infective contacts each person makes per day through them. Inoculation saturates as C rises (h = g(1 − exp(−C·y1))), and superinfection slows recovery (R(h) = h/(exp(h/r) − 1)).
Source: the Garki model of Dietz K, Molineaux L, Thomas A, “A malaria model tested in the African savannah”, Bull World Health Organ 1974;50(3-4):347-357, in the form given by Molineaux L, Gramiccia G, The Garki Project, WHO, 1980, chapter 10. The defaults are its Table 31: g, alpha2, and r1 were fitted to the Garki data, and alpha1, delta, dur_inc, ratio (r2/r1), and q3 were assumed. C varied by season and village from below 0.01 to above 2 (its Fig. 77), so the default here is a constant chosen for illustration; give an ss.seasonal() for a seasonal one.
Malaria dies out below the critical vectorial capacity, (alpha1 + delta)/g, which is 0.022 per day with these values, as the source gives.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

Syphilis, as a staged infection, wholly declared
People who are infected incubate (E), then have a primary chancre (P), then secondary syphilis (Se), and then early latent syphilis (El), from which some relapse to secondary syphilis and the rest pass to late latent syphilis (Ll). A fraction of those develop tertiary syphilis (T), which can kill; the rest are no longer infectious (R).
How infectious a person with latent syphilis is falls with the time since their latent stage began, a quantity each person carries: two modifiers of rel_trans, members of the disease. Since it acts on each person, this disease runs as agents.
Source: the natural history and its parameters are those of the syphilis module of STIsim (https://github.com/starsimhub/stisim, stisim/diseases/syphilis.py), whose own sources are cited there: the incubation period, primary and secondary stages from Garnett GP et al. (1997), the definition of early latent syphilis as up to two years after infection from WHO Europe, and the fraction developing tertiary syphilis. The half-life of latent infectiousness is STIsim’s.
Nobody is treated here, and the latent and tertiary stages last for years and count towards prevalence, so the level it settles at is well above what a setting with treatment and screening would show; add ss.screen() and ss.treat() to the sim for that. How far it spreads also depends on the network: the partnerships, how long they last, and the acts in them.

Tuberculosis, as the LSHTM model of the spectrum of TB disease
People who are infected either clear the infection, or develop disease that moves back and forth between non-infectious, asymptomatic (infectious, but at trans_asymp of a symptomatic person), and symptomatic. People who cleared or recovered can be infected again, at their own relative rate. Only symptomatic people die of TB; every death is replaced by a birth, so the population stays the same size, as in the source.
Source: the LSHTM natural history of Schwalb A et al., PLOS Glob Public Health 2025, 5(1):e0005050 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0005050), in the form of the reference ODE of TBsim (tbsim/compartmental/lshtm_ode.R), from which every default here is taken: beta, trans_asymp, the reinfection multipliers, the rates between states, and the background death rate. Treatment is off in that reference, and is left out here; TBsim adds treatment, drug resistance, and preventive therapy.
With the reference’s beta of 9, TB declines slowly over centuries (R0() is 0.23, since most infections are cleared and few reach disease), reproducing that reference exactly; beta is what a model of a particular place fits to its data.
Rates are per year, so a step of a year or a month suits it.

library.diseases.COVID(ages=True, **kwargs)
COVID-19, as a SECIR model by age: a chain of increasingly severe states, each of which some people leave by recovering
People who are infected are exposed (E), then infected without symptoms (INS), and then either recover or develop symptoms (ISy); of those, some become severe (ISev, in hospital), then critical (ICr, in intensive care), and some of those die. People without symptoms and with symptoms are both infectious, at rel_ins and rel_sym of the transmission rate.
The disease is stratified by age into MEmilio’s six groups (0-4, 5-14, 15-34, 35-59, 60-79, and 80+), since the severity of COVID-19 rises steeply with age: in the oldest group, a symptomatic case is 30 times as likely to become severe as in a child, and a critical one 12 times as likely to die. The fraction of people in each group is the world’s, unless the sim’s population says otherwise (e.g. people=ss.population('Germany')).
Source: the values for Germany of MEmilio (Kühn MJ et al., Mathematical Biosciences 2021, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mbs.2021.108648; examples/ode_secir_parameter_study_graph.cpp), which gives each as a range, by age; each default here is the middle of its range. MEmilio’s transmission is a contact rate times a chance of infection per contact, which is 0.06 for adults and from 0.03 (under 5) to 0.175 (80 and over), here the relative susceptibility rel_sus (1 for adults). Without contacts given, beta is 1 a day, which with the world’s ages gives an R0 of about 3.2, as for the first strains of COVID-19. With a contact matrix, beta is per contact, and MEmilio’s is 0.06: ssl.COVID(beta=0.06) with networks=ss.contacts('Germany').
With ages=False, the model has one group, with the values of MEmilio’s simple example (ode_secir_simple.cpp), whose beta of 1 a day is one contact a day, each certain to infect; with people infectious at rel_ins for 2 days and at rel_sym for 6, this gives an R0 of about 2.7.
Note: CRN safe as agents.

Cholera, with both direct and environmental (waterborne) transmission
People infected are latent (E) for dur_exp, then a fraction p_symp become symptomatic (Is), and the rest are asymptomatic (Ia), shedding far less (asymp_trans). Asymptomatic people recover; symptomatic people recover, or die (with probability p_death, sooner). Besides transmission from person to person (beta), infectious people shed bacteria into a well-mixed reservoir of water (W, a count of bacteria, not people) at shedding_rate, the bacteria die off at decay_rate, and susceptible people are infected from the water at a rate that rises with the concentration, beta_env times env_conc = W/(W + half_sat_rate), as in the model of Codeço (2001). It is declared, so it runs under any solver.
