Since the bacteria are a count, shed by everyone infectious into one reservoir, the water carries more of the epidemic in a larger population: with these values, it sustains an outbreak in a town of 10,000, and transmission from person to person alone does not.

People infected are latent (E) for dur_exp, then infectious (I) for dur_inf (each a normal, with a spread of a day or two), after which they recover with lifelong immunity (R) or, with probability p_death, die. Sources: the latent and infectious periods are from the US CDC (about 8 days from infection to being infectious, and infectious for about 11 days, from 4 days before the rash to 4 days after it, rounded up; the standard deviations, 2 days and 1.5 days, are illustrative, since the CDC gives ranges: 7 to 21 days from exposure to the rash); beta gives an R0 of about 15 (beta times dur_inf), within the range of 12 to 18 usually quoted (Guerra FM et al., “The basic reproduction number (R0) of measles: a systematic review”, Lancet Infect Dis 2017;17(12):e420-e428, https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(17)30307-9). The probability of death is illustrative of a setting with good care.

Syphilis, as a staged infection, wholly declared
People who are infected incubate (E), then have a primary chancre (P), then secondary syphilis (Se), and then early latent syphilis (El), from which some relapse to secondary syphilis and the rest pass to late latent syphilis (Ll). A fraction of those develop tertiary syphilis (T), which can kill; the rest are no longer infectious (R).
How infectious a person with latent syphilis is falls with the time since their latent stage began, a quantity each person carries: two modifiers of rel_trans, members of the disease. Since it acts on each person, this disease runs as agents.
Source: the natural history and its parameters are those of the syphilis module of STIsim (https://github.com/starsimhub/stisim, stisim/diseases/syphilis.py), whose own sources are cited there: the incubation period, primary and secondary stages from Garnett GP et al. (1997), the definition of early latent syphilis as up to two years after infection from WHO Europe, and the fraction developing tertiary syphilis. The half-life of latent infectiousness is STIsim’s.
Nobody is treated here, and the latent and tertiary stages last for years and count towards prevalence, so the level it settles at is well above what a setting with treatment and screening would show; add ss.screen() and ss.treat() to the sim for that. How far it spreads also depends on the network: the partnerships, how long they last, and the acts in them.

Tuberculosis, as the LSHTM model of the spectrum of TB disease
People who are infected either clear the infection, or develop disease that moves back and forth between non-infectious, asymptomatic (infectious, but at trans_asymp of a symptomatic person), and symptomatic. People who cleared or recovered can be infected again, at their own relative rate. Only symptomatic people die of TB; every death is replaced by a birth, so the population stays the same size, as in the source.
Source: the LSHTM natural history of Schwalb A et al., PLOS Glob Public Health 2025, 5(1):e0005050 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0005050), in the form of the reference ODE of TBsim (tbsim/compartmental/lshtm_ode.R), from which every default here is taken: beta, trans_asymp, the reinfection multipliers, the rates between states, and the background death rate. Treatment is off in that reference, and is left out here; TBsim adds treatment, drug resistance, and preventive therapy.
With the reference’s beta of 9, TB declines slowly over centuries (R0() is 0.23, since most infections are cleared and few reach disease), reproducing that reference exactly; beta is what a model of a particular place fits to its data.
Rates are per year, so a step of a year or a month suits it.

Simple disease with congenital outcomes, scheduled around delivery
Infected mothers transmit to their unborn via PrenatalNet. At transmission, set_congenital() samples an outcome (stillborn, congenital, normal) and schedules it for delivery time. step_congenital() in step_state() executes those scheduled events.

library.mnch.CongenitalDisease.set_congenital(target_uids, sources=None)
Assign congenital outcomes during in-utero infection (called when transmission occurs via PrenatalNet).
Does nothing unless the disease defines birth_outcome_keys and birth_outcomes in its pars. Diseases that need fully custom logic (e.g. syphilis, which has stage-dependent outcomes) can override this method entirely.
To use it, define in the disease’s __init__:
self.define_pars(
    birth_outcome_keys = ['stillborn', 'congenital', 'normal'],
    birth_outcomes     = sc.obj(default=ss.choice(a=3, p=[0.3, 0.4, 0.3])),  # Illustrative placeholder
)
Each outcome name needs a matching ti_<name> FloatArr state; non-lethal outcomes also need a BoolArr of the same name. Death outcomes (‘miscarriage’, ‘neonatal_death’, ‘stillborn’) fire via request_death; others set a bool state.
Outcomes are scheduled for the mother’s delivery timestep, except for fetal losses (‘miscarriage’, ‘stillborn’), which are scheduled one timestep earlier so that they occur before the fetus is delivered and are classified as fetal losses rather than neonatal deaths. A fetus infected within one timestep of delivery is therefore born alive, and a lethal outcome for it counts as a neonatal death.
For state- or GA-dependent probabilities, provide multiple keyed distributions in birth_outcomes and override _assign_congenital_outcomes.
Call step_congenital from the disease’s step_state() to execute the scheduled events each timestep.

library.mnch.FetalHealth(pars=None, **kwargs)
Track fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Works alongside the Pregnancy module to model birth weight outcomes (low birth weight, small for gestational age) based on fetal growth restriction. Disease-agnostic by design: external modules (connectors, interventions) modify fetal health via the public API methods.
Preterm classification is handled by the Pregnancy module (based on gestational age at birth). This module focuses on the weight/growth axis.
Integrates with Pregnancy via its callbacks (add_callback()): Pregnancy calls on_conception when new pregnancies begin and on_delivery when births occur. External modules (e.g. disease connectors) can register their own on preg.conception, after this module’s, to act on new pregnancies after baseline initialization.
During pregnancy, weight_percentile, growth_restriction, timing_shift, and n_exposures are tracked on the mother. At delivery, birth_weight, lbw, vlbw, and sga are stored on the newborn.
Each pregnancy gets a baseline weight percentile drawn at conception. Two modification levers are available:
1. **Delivery timing**: bring the delivery (`ti_exit_P`) forward (preterm birth risk)
2. **Growth restriction**: accumulate fractional weight reduction
At delivery: birth_weight = baseline_for_GA × percentile × (1 - restriction)
The results are counts of births and outcomes on each step, and means and rates over a step’s births (mean_birth_weight, lbw_rate, …), which are NaN on a step with no births, and are left out of a mean over time (e.g. res.mean_birth_weight.resample('year')).
Note: CRN safe.

library.mnch.fetal_infection(pars=None, **kwargs)
Connect a disease to fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Monitors for infections in pregnant women and applies fetal damage: - Timing shift: brings delivery forward (increases preterm birth risk). Drawn from a lognormal distribution per affected pregnancy. - Growth restriction: reduces birth weight by a fixed fractional penalty.
Damage is applied at two points: 1. At conception, if the mother is already infected (via a conception callback registered with the pregnancy, after FetalHealth’s). 2. During pregnancy, when a new infection occurs (detected in step() by checking ti_infected == self.ti - 1, since transmission happens after connectors).
Requires ssl.mnch.FetalHealth() in modules and an SIR disease written as code (ssl.AgentSIR(name="sir")) in diseases.
Note: CRN safe.

Assign congenital outcomes during in-utero infection (called when transmission occurs via PrenatalNet).
Does nothing unless the disease defines birth_outcome_keys and birth_outcomes in its pars. Diseases that need fully custom logic (e.g. syphilis, which has stage-dependent outcomes) can override this method entirely.
To use it, define in the disease’s __init__:
self.define_pars(
    birth_outcome_keys = ['stillborn', 'congenital', 'normal'],
    birth_outcomes     = sc.obj(default=ss.choice(a=3, p=[0.3, 0.4, 0.3])),  # Illustrative placeholder
)
Each outcome name needs a matching ti_<name> FloatArr state; non-lethal outcomes also need a BoolArr of the same name. Death outcomes (‘miscarriage’, ‘neonatal_death’, ‘stillborn’) fire via request_death; others set a bool state.
Outcomes are scheduled for the mother’s delivery timestep, except for fetal losses (‘miscarriage’, ‘stillborn’), which are scheduled one timestep earlier so that they occur before the fetus is delivered and are classified as fetal losses rather than neonatal deaths. A fetus infected within one timestep of delivery is therefore born alive, and a lethal outcome for it counts as a neonatal death.
For state- or GA-dependent probabilities, provide multiple keyed distributions in birth_outcomes and override _assign_congenital_outcomes.
Call step_congenital from the disease’s step_state() to execute the scheduled events each timestep.

library.mnch.FetalHealth(pars=None, **kwargs)
Track fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Works alongside the Pregnancy module to model birth weight outcomes (low birth weight, small for gestational age) based on fetal growth restriction. Disease-agnostic by design: external modules (connectors, interventions) modify fetal health via the public API methods.
Preterm classification is handled by the Pregnancy module (based on gestational age at birth). This module focuses on the weight/growth axis.
Integrates with Pregnancy via its callbacks (add_callback()): Pregnancy calls on_conception when new pregnancies begin and on_delivery when births occur. External modules (e.g. disease connectors) can register their own on preg.conception, after this module’s, to act on new pregnancies after baseline initialization.
During pregnancy, weight_percentile, growth_restriction, timing_shift, and n_exposures are tracked on the mother. At delivery, birth_weight, lbw, vlbw, and sga are stored on the newborn.
Each pregnancy gets a baseline weight percentile drawn at conception. Two modification levers are available:
1. **Delivery timing**: bring the delivery (`ti_exit_P`) forward (preterm birth risk)
2. **Growth restriction**: accumulate fractional weight reduction
At delivery: birth_weight = baseline_for_GA × percentile × (1 - restriction)
The results are counts of births and outcomes on each step, and means and rates over a step’s births (mean_birth_weight, lbw_rate, …), which are NaN on a step with no births, and are left out of a mean over time (e.g. res.mean_birth_weight.resample('year')).
Note: CRN safe.

Connect a disease to fetal health outcomes during pregnancy.
Monitors for infections in pregnant women and applies fetal damage: - Timing shift: brings delivery forward (increases preterm birth risk). Drawn from a lognormal distribution per affected pregnancy. - Growth restriction: reduces birth weight by a fixed fractional penalty.

A value for each level of one or more stratifications, or of people’s own properties
Use it for a parameter that differs between groups, e.g. a higher transmission rate for children, or a death rate by age and sex.
With several dimensions as keywords, the value of a group is the product of its value in each. A table gives every combination directly: it has a column for each stratification (holding the labels of its levels) and a column of values.
A property of people that is not a dimension of the sim (e.g. sex, read from people.female, or a property such as urban) is read from each person, as agents: give its values by name (sex=dict(female=..., male=...)), or as a table. A column of numbers in a table holds the lower edges of bins (the last one open-ended), so a table by single year of age works as agents whatever the model’s age groups (a compartmental run needs bins whose edges are those of the groups, or coarser: a group split by a bin has no one value, and is refused); a row whose key is None gives the value for people with no value of the property, who otherwise get the mean over the levels.

A value may itself vary in time (ss.timeseries or ss.seasonal), in the keyword and table forms.
Arithmetic with a number, or with another ss.by over the same levels, gives an ss.by; anything else (e.g. tables by different bins, a count, or np.minimum(by, 1)) is an expression, worked out where it is used.

beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03], sex=[1.0, 0.8]) # One per age group and sex: the product

internals.parameters.timeseries(
    data,
    values=None,
    interpolation='step',
    period=None,
)
A value that varies in time, given at some times and interpolated between them
It can be used wherever a value or a function of the sim can: as a rate or a duration, as the amount of ss.modify(), or as the coverage or capacity of a delivery. Before the first time the first value is used, and after the last time the last, so a value that holds from before the sim needs no time of its own: give it at the first time you have. A bare time is read as the sim reads any (see ss.timeline): a calendar year if the sim has a calendar (a start that is a date or a year), however small, else a time in its unit from 0; a duration is a time after the start (e.g. ss.days(91), 91 days in; with no calendar, day 91, the same when the start is 0). A bare value is read in the module’s unit, as any other; to give the values a unit, put the series in a type (ss.peryear(ss.timeseries(...)), a series of rates per year), or give each value one.

Type
Description
Default

the value at each time, as a dict, a dataframe (the first column is the time, the second the value), or the name of a file holding one; or the times, with the values as the second argument (ss.timeseries(times, values)). A time is a date, a bare number (a calendar year in a sim with a calendar, e.g. 2030, and otherwise a time in the sim’s unit from 0), or a duration, that long after the start of the sim
required

list

None

str
how to interpolate: ‘step’ (each value holds until the next, as for a policy that starts on a date), ‘linear’ (a steady change from each value to the next, as for coverage that is scaled up), or ‘cosine’ (a smooth S-shaped change between each value and the next, as MEmilio’s dampings)
'step'


period
dur
if given, the series repeats with this period, measured from its first time (e.g. ss.years(1) for a yearly pattern given over one year); keyed by durations, they are the times within each cycle, from the start of the sim (e.g. {ss.years(k/12): v[k] ...}, one value per month)
None

internals.parameters.by(table=None, dims=None, **kwargs)
A value for each level of one or more stratifications, or of people’s own properties
Use it for a parameter that differs between groups, e.g. a higher transmission rate for children, or a death rate by age and sex.
With several dimensions as keywords, the value of a group is the product of its value in each. A table gives every combination directly: it has a column for each stratification (holding the labels of its levels) and a column of values.
A property of people that is not a dimension of the sim (e.g. sex, read from people.female, or a property such as urban) is read from each person, as agents: give its values by name (sex=dict(female=..., male=...)), or as a table. A column of numbers in a table holds the lower edges of bins (the last one open-ended), so a table by single year of age works as agents whatever the model’s age groups (a compartmental run needs bins whose edges are those of the groups, or coarser: a group split by a bin has no one value, and is refused); a row whose key is None gives the value for people with no value of the property, who otherwise get the mean over the levels.

Type
Description
Default

df / array

None

each dimension, and one value per level (a list, by position), or a dict of values by label (or, for one dimension, by lower bin edge if the keys are numbers, as in a table: ss.by(age={0: 0, 15: 0.3}))




A value may itself vary in time (ss.timeseries or ss.seasonal), in the keyword and table forms.
Arithmetic with a number, or with another ss.by over the same levels, gives an ss.by; anything else (e.g. tables by different bins, a count, or np.minimum(by, 1)) is an expression, worked out where it is used.



beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03])
beta = ss.by(age=[0.08, 0.05, 0.03], sex=[1.0, 0.8]) # One per age group and sex: the product

internals.parameters.timeseries(
    data,
    values=None,
    interpolation='step',
    period=None,
)
A value that varies in time, given at some times and interpolated between them
It can be used wherever a value or a function of the sim can: as a rate or a duration, as the amount of ss.modify(), or as the coverage or capacity of a delivery. Before the first time the first value is used, and after the last time the last, so a value that holds from before the sim needs no time of its own: give it at the first time you have. A bare time is read as the sim reads any (see ss.timeline): a calendar year if the sim has a calendar (a start that is a date or a year), however small, else a time in its unit from 0; a duration is a time after the start (e.g. ss.days(91), 91 days in; with no calendar, day 91, the same when the start is 0). A bare value is read in the module’s unit, as any other; to give the values a unit, put the series in a type (ss.peryear(ss.timeseries(...)), a series of rates per year), or give each value one.

Type
Description

A time is a date, a bare number (a calendar year in a sim with a calendar, e.g. 2030, and otherwise a time in the sim’s unit from 0), or a duration, that long after the start of the sim
required

list

None

'step'

None

internals.errors
Errors, warnings, and notes.
Most errors are Python’s own (ValueError, TypeError, a KeyError for a name that is not found); the few kept as classes here are those that code may want to catch by kind, e.g. ss.CapabilityError. A note is a line about something that was assumed or approximated: it is kept in sim.notes and printed when verbose is 1 or more (see ss.note()).

internals.dates.datedur(value=None, **kwargs)
A calendar duration, e.g. datedur(months=1): a thin wrapper of pd.DateOffset, used inside Starsim (as ss.dates.datedur)
Users write ss.months(1) or ss.years(1): a whole number of months or years added to a date is already a calendar offset, so dt=ss.months(1) steps a sim by calendar months; a datedur is what the timeline steps by.
Added to a date, it follows the calendar, so a month from 31 January is the end of February and a year from 1 March 2020 is 1 March 2021. It takes whole numbers of years, months, weeks, and days (as keywords), or one of: a pd.DateOffset, a dateutil.relativedelta, a number of years, or a duration in one of these units (e.g. ss.days(7)). As a number (.years, .days, or divided by another duration) it is approximate, as other durations are: a year is 365 days, and a month a twelfth of a year. The time between two dates (date - date) is ss.days, not a datedur.


ss.date('2020-01-31') + datedur(months=1) # 2020-02-29

title: internals.arrays
text:
internals.arrays
Arrays of agents’ values: states such as age or infection status, and the UIDs that index them
A state holds a value for every agent, and reads only the active ones, so code can use it like a NumPy array as agents are born and die. A few classes here stand in for them when a run has groups of people rather than agents (GroupAges, GroupAlive).
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




Arr
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.


BaseArr
An object that acts exactly like a NumPy array, except stores the values in self.values.


BoolArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for booleans.


BoolState
A boolean array being used as a state.


CatArr
A categorical state: one of a list of categories for each agent (e.g. a district, or a wealth quintile), read, compared and set by category


FloatArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for floats.


GroupAges
people.age in a compartmental run: one row per group, at the middle of its age group


GroupAlive
people.alive in a run without agents: one row per group of people, not one per person


IndexArr
A special class of Arr used for UIDs and RNG IDs; not to be used as a general integer array (for that, use IntArr)


IntArr
Subclass of ss.Arr with defaults for ints.


TimeArr
Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead


UIDArr
The UIDs of all agents (people.uid), which take no memory: a UID is the agent’s index, so raw is made when read


Unkept
A declared disease’s time of entering a state (ti_X) that is not kept, since the engine does not need it (see ss.Sim(keep_times=True))


Watch
The link from a state to the engine that keeps count of who is in it (BoolState.watch), which is told of


uids
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.





internals.arrays.Arr(
    name=None,
    dtype=None,
    default=None,
    nan=None,
    label=None,
    raw=None,
    skip_init=False,
    people=None,
    mock=None,
    columns=None,
    shared=False,
)
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.
In practice, Arr objects can be used interchangeably with NumPy arrays. They have two main data interfaces: Arr.raw contains the “raw”, underlying NumPy array of the data. Arr.values contains the “active” values, which usually corresponds to agents who are alive.
By default, operations are performed on active agents only (specified by Arr.auids, which is a pointer to sim.people.auids). For example, sim.people.age.mean() will only use the ages of active agents. Thus, sim.people.age.mean() is equal to sim.people.age.values.mean(), not sim.people.age.raw.mean().
Arr.raw includes agents who have died, and also has slots that are not people yet: room at the end for agents born later, which hold the array’s nan (NaN for an ss.FloatArr, not its default). So np.sum(arr.raw) can be NaN for a float array; to sum, count, or average over the people, use the array itself (arr.sum(), arr.mean()) or arr.values, and to read particular agents, index by UID (arr[uids]).
If indexing by an int, integer array, or ss.uids object, Arr.raw is used (i.e. the ints are treated as UIDs). If indexing by a full slice ([:]) or a boolean array, Arr.values is used. Arr objects can’t be directly indexed by a list, as this would be ambiguous about whether values or raw is intended. For example, if there are 1000 people in a simulation and 100 of them have died, sim.people.age[999] and sim.people.age[ss.uids(999)] both return the age of the agent with UID 999, whereas sim.people.age.values[899] returns the age of the last active agent.
Note on terminology: the term “states” is often used to refer to all ss.Arr objects, (e.g. in module.define_states()), whether or not they are BoolStates.

Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead
Stored as float32 step numbers, NaN for “never” (not set), so ti_I > 0 and (sim.ti - ti_I)*sim.t.dt give the right answer. due() gives whose time has come, with a time between steps rounded up or down at random in proportion (by each agent’s phase, as the agent engine rounds a dwell time: see ss.People.phase()), so it keeps its mean; isclose(sim.ti) gives whose time is taken at this step, and .years converts them to years. == and != raise, since a time between steps never equals a step: eq() is exact equality. For plain arithmetic on the times, compare them: e.g. ti_x < sim.ti + 0.5 is due at the nearest step, and ti_x <= sim.ti at the first step at or after it.
A declared state’s time of entering (ti_X) reads as the index of the step the move happened in, whatever kind of move it was (a progression at the step’s start, an infection by contact at its end), so ti_X.isclose(sim.ti) is “entered this step”. The engine keeps its own time of the move, which .raw gives (see shift). So the difference of two of them is not always a duration: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step and a scheduled move at the start of its step, so ti_I - ti_E of an SEIR reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays (e.g. np.mean(seir.E.stays), the mean latent period), which is built from the engine’s times.

self.ti_infectious[uids] = self.ti + dur # In steps

internals.arrays.uids()
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.
It exists so that indexing an ss.Arr with these reads those agents by UID, not by position.
For all practical purposes, behaves like a NumPy integer array. However, has additional methods uids.concatenate(), uids.remove(), and uids.intersect() to simplify common UID operations.
The following operators are supported:

+ / +=: if the RHS is a uids, concatenation (equivalent to uids.concatenate()); otherwise element-wise addition (e.g. uids([1,2]) + 1 → uids([2,3])). Concatenation preserves duplicates.
- / -=: set difference — equivalent to uids.remove(). Duplicate entries in the original will also be removed (uses np.setdiff1d internally).
| / |=: union (unique elements from both arrays). Note that duplicate entries in the original are removed (use + instead to keep them).
& / &=: intersection
^ / ^=: symmetric difference

Note: because uids is a subclass of np.ndarray, set-like in-place operators (+= with a uids RHS, -=, |=, &=, ^=) must return a new array and rebind the variable. However, += with a scalar or array RHS modifies the array in-place and preserves id(self).


a = ss.uids([1, 2, 3])
b = ss.uids([3, 4, 5])
a + b   # Concatenate: uids([1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5])

internals.arrays.Arr(
    name=None,
    dtype=None,
    default=None,
    nan=None,
    label=None,
    raw=None,
    skip_init=False,
    people=None,
    mock=None,
    columns=None,
    shared=False,
)
Store a state of the agents (e.g. age, infection status, etc.) as an array.
In practice, Arr objects can be used interchangeably with NumPy arrays. They have two main data interfaces: Arr.raw contains the “raw”, underlying NumPy array of the data. Arr.values contains the “active” values, which usually corresponds to agents who are alive.
By default, operations are performed on active agents only (specified by Arr.auids, which is a pointer to sim.people.auids). For example, sim.people.age.mean() will only use the ages of active agents. Thus, sim.people.age.mean() is equal to sim.people.age.values.mean(), not sim.people.age.raw.mean().
Arr.raw includes agents who have died, and also has slots that are not people yet: room at the end for agents born later, which hold the array’s nan (NaN for an ss.FloatArr, not its default). So np.sum(arr.raw) can be NaN for a float array; to sum, count, or average over the people, use the array itself (arr.sum(), arr.mean()) or arr.values, and to read particular agents, index by UID (arr[uids]).
If indexing by an int, integer array, or ss.uids object, Arr.raw is used (i.e. the ints are treated as UIDs). If indexing by a full slice ([:]) or a boolean array, Arr.values is used. Arr objects can’t be directly indexed by a list, as this would be ambiguous about whether values or raw is intended. For example, if there are 1000 people in a simulation and 100 of them have died, sim.people.age[999] and sim.people.age[ss.uids(999)] both return the age of the agent with UID 999, whereas sim.people.age.values[899] returns the age of the last active agent.
Note on terminology: the term “states” is often used to refer to all ss.Arr objects, (e.g. in module.define_states()), whether or not they are BoolStates.

if True, the array takes no memory per agent until a value is set (other than by its default, which must be a scalar): until then every agent has the default, and raw is a read-only view of it; if an Arr, the same with that array’s values (as people.slot reads people.uid)

For 2D arrays (i.e. if columns is supplied), arr[uids] returns an array of shape (len(uids), ncols), arr[uids, v] or arr[:, v] returns column v, and arr.col(v) returns column v as a 1D Arr. If the columns are named, v can also be a name, e.g. arr.col('mutant'), arr['mutant'], or arr.mutant. A scalar default fills every column, and a callable default should return an array of shape (n, ncols). Arrays with more dimensions are also supported via a tuple, e.g. columns=(2,3) gives a raw array of shape (len_tot, 2, 3).



# Create a standalone Arr for quick testing
age = ss.Arr('age', default=0, mock=5) # 5 = length if not supplying a real People object
age[:] = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
age.mean()  # Returns 40.0

# Use within a simulation
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=100).init()
sim.people.age.mean()  # Mean age of active agents

# Create a 2D array, e.g. immunity to each of 3 variants
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=3, mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 2] = 0.8 # Set immunity to variant 2 for agents 0 and 1
imm[ss.uids([0, 1])] # Returns an array of shape (2, 3)
(imm.col(2) > 0.5).uids  # Returns ss.uids([0, 1])

# Create a 2D array with named columns
imm = ss.FloatArr('imm', default=0, columns=['wildtype', 'mutant'], mock=5)
imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 'mutant'] = 0.8 # Same as imm[ss.uids([0, 1]), 1] = 0.8
(imm.col('mutant') > 0.5).uids  # Returns ss.uids([0, 1])

Times, as step numbers of the module’s timeline: when something happened or is due for each agent, e.g. a declared disease’s ti_X (when each entered state X) and ti_exit_X, as agents, and people.ti_dead
Stored as float32 step numbers, NaN for “never” (not set), so ti_I > 0 and (sim.ti - ti_I)*sim.t.dt give the right answer. due() gives whose time has come, with a time between steps rounded up or down at random in proportion (by each agent’s phase, as the agent engine rounds a dwell time: see ss.People.phase()), so it keeps its mean; isclose(sim.ti) gives whose time is taken at this step, and .years converts them to years. == and != raise, since a time between steps never equals a step: eq() is exact equality. For plain arithmetic on the times, compare them: e.g. ti_x < sim.ti + 0.5 is due at the nearest step, and ti_x <= sim.ti at the first step at or after it.
A declared state’s time of entering (ti_X) reads as the index of the step the move happened in, whatever kind of move it was (a progression at the step’s start, an infection by contact at its end), so ti_X.isclose(sim.ti) is “entered this step”. The engine keeps its own time of the move, which .raw gives (see shift). So the difference of two of them is not always a duration: an infection by contact happens at the end of its step and a scheduled move at the start of its step, so ti_I - ti_E of an SEIR reads one step longer than the latent period was. For the time people spent in a state, use the state’s stays (e.g. np.mean(seir.E.stays), the mean latent period), which is built from the engine’s times.


sim = ss.Sim(ss.SIR(), unit='day', stop=100, solver='abm').run()
sir = sim.diseases.sir
infected_today = sir.ti_I.isclose(sim.ti).uids
years = sir.ti_I.years # The year of infection of each agent (NaN if never infected)

# In a disease written as code
self.define_states(ss.BoolState('exposed'), ss.TimeArr('ti_infectious'))
self.ti_infectious[uids] = self.ti + dur # In steps
mask = self.exposed & self.ti_infectious.due() # Those whose time has come

internals.arrays.uids()
Class to specify that integers should be interpreted as UIDs.
It exists so that indexing an ss.Arr with these reads those agents by UID, not by position.
For all practical purposes, behaves like a NumPy integer array. However, has additional methods uids.concatenate(), uids.remove(), and uids.intersect() to simplify common UID operations.
The following operators are supported:

+ / +=: if the RHS is a uids, concatenation (equivalent to uids.concatenate()); otherwise element-wise addition (e.g. uids([1,2]) + 1 → uids([2,3])). Concatenation preserves duplicates.
- / -=: set difference — equivalent to uids.remove(). Duplicate entries in the original will also be removed (uses np.setdiff1d internally).
| / |=: union (unique elements from both arrays). Note that duplicate entries in the original are removed (use + instead to keep them).
& / &=: intersection
^ / ^=: symmetric difference

Note: because uids is a subclass of np.ndarray, set-like in-place operators (+= with a uids RHS, -=, |=, &=, ^=) must return a new array and rebind the variable. However, += with a scalar or array RHS modifies the array in-place and preserves id(self).


a = ss.uids([1, 2, 3])
b = ss.uids([3, 4, 5])
a + b   # Concatenate: uids([1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5])
a | b   # Union:       uids([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
a & b   # Intersect:   uids([3])
a - b   # Difference:  uids([1, 2])

solvers.agents
Not for the user: the agent engine: a declared model run as agents (abm)
It also holds the transmission that diseases written as code use, so that both give the same numbers.
Used with: agents; declared and coded modules

solvers.agents.Agents(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as agents
It exists so that a declared model can run with individuals, for what compartments cannot hold.
Each state that holds people is a boolean array over agents. A dwell time is sampled when an agent enters a state and the exit is scheduled; rates that depend on the state of the model are drawn each step, with competing rates out of one state resolved in a single draw; and contact-mediated transitions are drawn over the sim’s networks. States that are not people stay plain counts.

solvers.agents.Transmission(module, sim)
Transmission as agents, the same for a declared disease (Agents, for its transmissions) and one written as code (ss.Disease.transmit(rel_trans=..., rel_sus=...), through its engine, ss.solvers.Undeclared): who can transmit and be infected, with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (current_value()); who is infected over a network (over_network()); and who infected whom (first_infections())
Where the two differ, the caller says how:

Hazard or probability. over_network() takes the chance of an edge in the step, and scales its hazard by every other factor (the edge’s weight and acts, rel_trans, rel_sus, and the modifiers). A declared disease gives 1 − exp(−β·dt) from its rate, or, on a network with acts, works out a hazard per act (Agents.transmit_acts()); one written as code gives its beta as the probability in the step, converting a rate the same way (ss.Rate.to_prob()).
Order and attribution. The routes are taken in the order of sim.networks, and on each, p1 to p2 and then p2 to p1; someone reached by several is infected by the first (first_infections()), which is the source in the infection log. With strains, every strain is passed on in one pass, and someone reached by several is infected by one of them drawn at random, whose strain they take (pick_sources()), and then only if they are not protected against it (unprotected()): declared or written as code, by the same code.
Random numbers. Each edge’s is drawn by its source and target from the disease’s trans_rng, so the same disease, by the same name, gives the same edges the same numbers, declared or written as code; and so are the draws of who infects whom, and of protection, which are keyed by the step alone (step_draw()).

solvers.agents.Agents(module, sim, solver=None)
Runs a graph as agents
It exists so that a declared model can run with individuals, for what compartments cannot hold.
Each state that holds people is a boolean array over agents. A dwell time is sampled when an agent enters a state and the exit is scheduled; rates that depend on the state of the model are drawn each step, with competing rates out of one state resolved in a single draw; and contact-mediated transitions are drawn over the sim’s networks. States that are not people stay plain counts.

solvers.agents.Transmission(module, sim)
Transmission as agents, the same for a declared disease (Agents, for its transmissions) and one written as code (ss.Disease.transmit(rel_trans=..., rel_sus=...), through its engine, ss.solvers.Undeclared): who can transmit and be infected, with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (current_value()); who is infected over a network (over_network()); and who infected whom (first_infections())
Where the two differ, the caller says how:

Hazard or probability. over_network() takes the chance of an edge in the step, and scales its hazard by every other factor (the edge’s weight and acts, rel_trans, rel_sus, and the modifiers). A declared disease gives 1 − exp(−β·dt) from its rate, or, on a network with acts, works out a hazard per act (Agents.transmit_acts()); one written as code gives its beta as the probability in the step, converting a rate the same way (ss.Rate.to_prob()).
Order and attribution. The routes are taken in the order of sim.networks, and on each, p1 to p2 and then p2 to p1; someone reached by several is infected by the first (first_infections()), which is the source in the infection log. With strains, every strain is passed on in one pass, and someone reached by several is infected by one of them drawn at random, whose strain they take (pick_sources()), and then only if they are not protected against it (unprotected()): declared or written as code, by the same code.
Random numbers. Each edge’s is drawn by its source and target from the disease’s trans_rng, so the same disease, by the same name, gives the same edges the same numbers, declared or written as code; and so are the draws of who infects whom, and of protection, which are keyed by the step alone (step_draw()).

solvers.agents.Transmission.code_route(i, route, betas, rel_trans, rel_sus)
The transmission of a disease written as code along a single network (or other route): see ss.Disease.transmit()
On a network, each edge transmits with probability 1 − (1 − net_beta())^(rel_trans·rel_sus·modifiers), the modifiers being those of the network’s contacts and of rel_sus on the route (ss.modify(..., network=)) (see ss.Network.transmit()), as for a declared disease run as agents, by the same code (over_network()), with beta as the probability in the step. The modifiers of rel_trans and rel_sus (including products) are applied here.

expressions.attr(
    value,
    on=None,
    combine='last',
    init=None,
    name=None,
    label=None,
)
A value for each person: drawn at an event, recorded at an event, drawn once when the person is made (a trait), or derived
Which it is depends on value and on=: a distribution with on= is drawn when the event happens to someone; an expression (or the name of another attribute) with on= is recorded then, as it was just before the move; a distribution with no on= is a trait; and an expression, or a dict of one by state (states not listed give NaN), with no on= is derived, worked out when it is read. Attributes set on the same event are set in the order they are declared, and each sees the ones before it. As agents only.

title: networks
text:
networks
Networks and mixing pools: who meets whom, and so who can infect whom
A network holds the contacts (edges) between people, over which a disease spreads. Mixing pools (ss.MixingPool, ss.networks.MixingPools) and contact matrices (ss.contacts()) spread it between groups instead, without edges. These exist so that a model’s contacts are separate from its diseases, and one network can carry several diseases. In a compartmental run, a network is replaced by what it implies: contact rates, a matrix, or a model of partner change.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




BreastfeedingNet
A network from each mother to her infant while she breastfeeds, for transmission by breastfeeding


DegreeNet
Partnerships that form and dissolve, with a target number of partners at a time


DynamicNetwork
A network where partnerships update dynamically


MixingPool
Mixing between two groups of people (or everyone), without edges: used in place of a network


MixingPools
Mixing between groups of people, by a matrix of contacts between them: a mixing pool (ss.MixingPool) for each pair of groups, without edges


Network
A network of contacts (edges) between people, over which diseases spread, and the methods


PostnatalNet
A network from each mother to her infant after birth, for transmission after birth (e.g. by close contact)


PrenatalNet
A network from each pregnant woman to her unborn child, for transmission in pregnancy


RandomNet
Random connectivity between agents


Route
A way a disease spreads between people: the base class of networks and mixing pools


SexualNet
Sexual partnerships that form and dissolve, between two groups of people: by default, men and women

networks.DegreeNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    acts=_,
    who=_,
    between=_,
    memory=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Partnerships that form and dissolve, with a target number of partners at a time
The number of partners people have at any moment (n_contacts) is a target for the whole population, not a fixed number for each person: partnerships end at random, and people look for new ones at a rate that depends on how many they already have, chosen so that the distribution of the number of partners stays at the target. Everyone moves through it over time, as in EpiModel’s networks fitted to target statistics: this covers the same ground as a dyad-independent exponential random graph model (ERGM), with the terms for edges, degree, and mixing, but not terms such as triangles. The network starts at the target. In an open population, partnerships that end at a constant rate (dur a mean) end less often by as many as are ended by a partner leaving (dying), as EpiModel’s d.rate correction does, so they last as long as given on average; with any other distribution of durations, people look for partners more (or less) often, by a factor that keeps the mean number of partners at the target. Partnerships are not only sexual: people who share needles have partners too. For sexual partnerships, with an age of debut, see ss.SexualNet.
Each partnership can be between one person of each of two groups (between), e.g. a man and a woman, so a disease’s beta on it can differ by direction; each group can then have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With no target (the default), people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time.
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.





Name
Type
Description
Default




n_contacts
float/ss.Dist/ss.by/dict
if given, a target for the number of partners a person has at a time: a number, which is the mean of a Poisson (whose shape concurrency and max_contacts can change), or a distribution over whole numbers (e.g. ss.constant(1), for exactly one); or a number for each level of a property of people (ss.by(risk=[0.4, 1.6])), as EpiModel’s nodefactor; or one for each group of between, e.g. dict(fsw=3, client=0.5) (each partnership has one of each, so these should give the two groups about as many partners in all). By default, no target: at most one partner, pairing people who have none on every step
_


dur
float/ss.Duration/ss.Dist
how long partnerships last: a mean (they end at a constant rate), or a distribution; a bare number is in the sim’s unit (default: 10)
_


acts
rate/ss.Dist
if given, the number of acts per unit time in each partnership: a frequency such as ss.freqperweek(2) (or a rate, ss.perweek(2)), or a distribution of them drawn once for each partnership; a disease’s beta is then per act (see ss.peract)
_


who
Cond / str / func
if given, who takes part: a condition over people (e.g. ss.person.pwid), as for ss.Event(); nobody else is in the network
_


between
str / tuple
if given, who partnerships are between: 'mf', a man and a woman, so its directions are m2f and f2m and a disease’s beta on it is ss.peract(m2f=..., f2m=...), or one value for both; 'mm', two men, with one beta; or a pair of groups, each the name of a boolean property of people or of a level of a stratification, e.g. ('fsw', 'client'), whose directions are fsw2client and client2fsw (nobody can be in both)
_


concurrency
float
if given, the fraction of people with two or more partners at once; the distribution of n_contacts is adjusted to give it, keeping its mean
_


max_contacts
int
if given, nobody has more partners than this at once
_


match
dict
if given, the fraction of partnerships between people at the same level of a property of people (a stratification, or an attribute such as 'female'), e.g. dict(risk=0.8), as EpiModel’s nodematch; or of each of several, e.g. dict(risk=0.8, region=0.6)
_


memory
dur
how long it remembers partnerships that have ended, for contact tracing (see ss.DynamicNetwork)
_

dict
the same parameters, as a dict
None



The realized network is recorded in the results (mean_degree, concurrency, and match, or with several properties match_<name> for each), and net.check() compares it with the targets.



# EpiModel's introductory network: 175 partnerships among 500 people, 110 people with two or more partners, nobody with four or more, and partnerships lasting 50 steps
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, concurrency=0.22, max_contacts=3, dur=50)

# Most partnerships within a risk group, and over half within a region
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8, region=0.6))

# And four times as many partners in the high-risk group (with sim.stratify(risk=['low', 'high']))
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=ss.by(risk=[0.4, 1.6]), dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8))

# Needle sharing among people who inject drugs (a boolean property of people), with 20 injections a month in each partnership
needles = ss.DegreeNet(name='needles', who=ss.person.pwid, n_contacts=2, dur=ss.months(6), acts=ss.freqpermonth(20))

# Sex work, between female sex workers and their clients (boolean properties of people)
sw = ss.DegreeNet(name='sw', between=('fsw', 'client'), n_contacts=dict(fsw=5, client=0.5), dur=ss.months(1), acts=ss.freqperweek(1))

    source = {'0-15': ss.person.age < 15, '15+': ss.person.age >= 15},
    target = {'0-15': ss.person.age < 15, '15+': ss.person.age >= 15},
    n_contacts = [[2.4, 0.91], [0.49, 0.16]],  # Illustrative contact matrix: row i, the contacts of a person in target group i
)

sim.plot()

# Contacts that differ between people: a Poisson draw for each person, with the matrix as its mean

Transmission to a susceptible person s is 1 − (1 − p)^(rel_sus_s · Σ_j c_sj · trans_j), for the disease’s chance p over the step, s’s contacts c_sj with source group j, and that group’s mean infectiousness trans_j. This is exact for a force of infection proportional to the contacts and the mean infectiousness. For discrete contacts with random members of a group, it is a mean-field approximation: it uses the group’s mean infectiousness rather than that of the people met, which slightly overstates infection (by a relative p(1 − f)/2 when a fraction f of the group is infectious). It is exact when everyone in the group is equally infectious, and close when p is small.

networks.Network.transmit(rel_trans, rel_sus, edge_hazard, rng, prob=None)
The edges that transmit in a step, in each direction the network transmits in (p1 to p2, then p2 to p1 unless it is one way)
An edge from source to target transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[source]·rel_sus[target]·hazard), or prob() if it is given: each factor scales the hazard over the step, so a contact infects at most once in it, wherever a model puts an effect. Random numbers are drawn only for the edges that can transmit: with CRN, each edge’s number depends only on its source and target, so this gives the same result as drawing one for every edge. The beta is worked out only for the edges from someone infectious to someone susceptible, which are found for both directions in one pass over the edges, or, once the edges have stayed the same for a step (edge_index()), from the edges of the infectious (or the susceptible) alone, if they have few; either way they are in the order of the edges.

networks.RandomNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    who=_,
    dynamic=_,
    method=_,
    remove_self_loops=_,
    memory=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Random connectivity between agents
Each agent has a number of contacts (n_contacts), and the other end of each is drawn from the other agents’ contacts (method='fast', the default), so an agent’s chance of being picked is proportional to its own number of contacts. This keeps the mixing structure of risk-stratified networks (a small high-risk core with many contacts forms most of its edges with itself).
method says how the other end of each contact is drawn:

'fast' (the default): by sampling the contacts with replacement. The source side of each edge is exactly n_contacts, while the target side is Poisson-distributed with mean n_contacts, so agents have somewhat more variable numbers of contacts than with 'exact'; about 1.8x faster than 'exact'.
'exact': by shuffling the contacts (sampling without replacement), so each agent has exactly n_contacts contacts, if it is even: each agent starts half of its contacts and is the other end of as many, so an odd number is rounded at random to the even numbers either side for each agent (5 gives 4 or 6, 5 on average).
'uniform': uniformly from all eligible agents, regardless of their own n_contacts, as in Covasim v3’s random networks. This gives less variable numbers of contacts (e.g. with n_contacts=ss.poisson(20), a variance of about 15, rather than 30 for 'fast' or 20 for 'exact'), but loses the mixing structure above.
'safe': by giving each contact a random place on a line, from the agent’s own random numbers, and joining it to its nearest neighbor there. Adding an agent then changes only the contacts next to theirs, which suits scenario comparisons, but it is slower, and does not yet work within places.

Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die, unless dynamic=False: with any of these methods but 'safe', one death rewires almost every edge.
By default (dur=0), each contact lasts one step of the network: with dynamic=True (the default), the contacts are drawn again on every step, and with dynamic=False, once. With dur= above 0, each contact lasts that long, and the ones that end are replaced by new ones drawn at random. For partnerships formed toward a target number of partners, see ss.DegreeNet.

networks.SexualNet(
    pars=None,
    between=_,
    dur=_,
    debut=_,
    acts=_,
    participation=_,
    n_contacts=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Sexual partnerships that form and dissolve, between two groups of people: by default, men and women
A ss.DegreeNet between men and women (between='mf'), in which people take part after their debut (debut), if they do (participation, drawn at their debut). By default, people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time. With n_contacts, the number of partners people have at a time is a target instead (among people who take part, after their debut), as for ss.DegreeNet; with partnerships much longer than people’s time in the network, it takes a few decades to settle.
Each partnership is between one person of each of two groups (between): a man and a woman, two men, or e.g. a female sex worker and a client, and each group can have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With match=, a fraction of partnerships is between people at the same level of a property of people, such as a risk group.
Each partnership has a number of acts per unit time (acts), so a disease’s beta on it is a probability per act (see ss.peract), and the fraction of them in which a condom is used (condoms, 0 unless set, e.g. by a subclass in add_pairs()), which a modifier of the transmission on the network reads, e.g. ss.modify(hiv.infection, efficacy=0.8, frac=lambda net: net.edges.condoms, network='sexualnet').
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
For several types of partnership with their own rules, see STIsim; for partnerships that are not sexual (e.g. needle sharing), ss.DegreeNet.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

    matrix=None,

Mixing between groups from a contact matrix; returns ss.networks.MixingPools
A matrix, and what it is over:

a country’s, by name (ss.contacts('Kenya')), from starsim_data, by 5-year age group;
its own age groups, given by their lower edges (ss.contacts(matrix, ages=[0, 15, 65])), which need not be the model’s (it is regrouped to them);
the model’s own stratifications: its age groups (ss.contacts(matrix)), another one, by name (ss.contacts(risk=matrix)), or several together (ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])), for mixing that is not a product, e.g. men mix with women, and by risk differently for each sex;
nobody in particular: a number (ss.contacts(10)) is homogeneous mixing, with that many contacts per person per unit time (an ss.MixingPool of everyone).

Mixing that is a product over stratifications takes a matrix for each, by name (ss.contacts(age=..., area=...)): the contacts between two groups are the product of the entries for each. The matrix by age can have its own age groups here too (ss.contacts(age=..., area=..., ages=[0, 15, 65])).
What the matrix multiplies is said by the rate of the infection, with I_j and N_j the number infectious and the number of people in group j, and N everyone:

beta*I: the fraction of each group who are infectious, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N_j, with C the contacts of a person and β per contact (as for contact surveys);
beta*I.n: their number, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j, density-dependent (as in Lloyd & Jansen’s metapopulation);
beta*I.frac (or beta*I.n/N): their number over everyone, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N (as in Keeling & Rohani’s matrices, and WAIFW matrices).
a weighted count, beta*(ss.by(w)*I).n or beta*I.n_infectious: their number, each counted by its weight, β·Σ_j C_ij·w_j·I_j (for n_infectious, w_j is each group’s infectiousness).

So a textbook’s matrix goes in as the textbook gives it, with no rescaling. See the user guide’s page on population data for more.

sir.stratify(risk=['low', 'high'])
mixing = ss.contacts(risk=[[2, 1], [1, 8]])

home, school = ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school']) # Contacts a day, by 5-year age group
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=[home, school], stratify=dict(age=[0, 5, 18, 65]), unit='day', stop=100)

# A product: by age, then 90% of contacts within one's own area
mixing = ss.contacts(age=[[10, 3], [3, 5]], area=[[0.9, 0.1], [0.1, 0.9]], ages=[0, 18])

# Keeling & Rohani's Program 3.1: a matrix of rates per year on fractions of everyone, so the rate is I.frac
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(S >> I @ I.frac, I >> S @ ss.peryear(1), init_prev=0.001).stratify(risk={'high': 0.2, 'low': 0.8})
sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ss.contacts(risk=[[10, 0.1], [0.1, 1]]), unit='year', stop=15).run()

# Men mix with women, and the high-risk with each other more among men than among women: a matrix over sex and risk together
matrix = np.zeros((2, 2, 2, 2)) # [sex, risk, sex, risk], with sex ['female', 'male'] and risk ['low', 'high']
matrix[0, :, 1, :] = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.5, 1.5]] # Women's contacts with men
matrix[1, :, 0, :] = [[0.8, 0.5], [0.2, 2.0]] # Men's contacts with women
mixing = ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])

# Contacts that differ between people: lognormal, around a country's mean contacts a day
C = ss.data.contacts('Kenya')
mixing = ss.contacts(ss.lognormal(mean=C, std=C*0.5))

networks.fisher_yates_shuffle(arr, randvals)
In-place Fisher-Yates shuffle using precomputed uniform random values.
Equivalent to np.random.permutation (a uniform random shuffle), but ~1.3x faster for the large arrays used in network generation. randvals should be uniform on [0, 1) and the same length as arr.
Note: randvals is consumed in order (randvals[k] for the k-th swap), not indexed by position. This means that changing the array length (e.g. adding one agent) shifts every swap, so the shuffle is not random-number safe – matching ss.RandomNet(method='exact')’s intended behavior (see ss.RandomNet(method='safe') for the CRN-safe version).



networks.nb_transmit(src, trg, rel_trans, rel_sus, hazard, randvals)
Optimized transmission kernel: returns the (source, target) UIDs of transmitting edges.
Edge i transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[src]·rel_sus[trg]·hazard[i]): every factor scales the hazard in the step, so one contact infects at most once, whichever factor a model puts its effect in (see Network.transmit()). Fuses the gather/multiply/compare and the UID extraction into a single branchless pass. This avoids a full-length boolean temporary and two separate gather passes (trg[mask], src[mask]) – ~1.4x faster at typical transmission rates, more when transmission is common. UIDs are emitted in edge order, preserving CRN behavior.

networks.DegreeNet(
    pars=None,
    n_contacts=_,
    dur=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    acts=_,
    who=_,
    between=_,
    memory=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Partnerships that form and dissolve, with a target number of partners at a time
The number of partners people have at any moment (n_contacts) is a target for the whole population, not a fixed number for each person: partnerships end at random, and people look for new ones at a rate that depends on how many they already have, chosen so that the distribution of the number of partners stays at the target. Everyone moves through it over time, as in EpiModel’s networks fitted to target statistics: this covers the same ground as a dyad-independent exponential random graph model (ERGM), with the terms for edges, degree, and mixing, but not terms such as triangles. The network starts at the target. In an open population, partnerships that end at a constant rate (dur a mean) end less often by as many as are ended by a partner leaving (dying), as EpiModel’s d.rate correction does, so they last as long as given on average; with any other distribution of durations, people look for partners more (or less) often, by a factor that keeps the mean number of partners at the target. Partnerships are not only sexual: people who share needles have partners too. For sexual partnerships, with an age of debut, see ss.SexualNet.
Each partnership can be between one person of each of two groups (between), e.g. a man and a woman, so a disease’s beta on it can differ by direction; each group can then have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With no target (the default), people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time.
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

Type
Description
Default

float/ss.Dist/ss.by/dict
if given, a target for the number of partners a person has at a time: a number, which is the mean of a Poisson (whose shape concurrency and max_contacts can change), or a distribution over whole numbers (e.g. ss.constant(1), for exactly one); or a number for each level of a property of people (ss.by(risk=[0.4, 1.6])), as EpiModel’s nodefactor; or one for each group of between, e.g. dict(fsw=3, client=0.5) (each partnership has one of each, so these should give the two groups about as many partners in all). By default, no target: at most one partner, pairing people who have none on every step
_

how long partnerships last: a mean (they end at a constant rate), or a distribution; a bare number is in the sim’s unit (default: 10)
_

The realized network is recorded in the results (mean_degree, concurrency, and match, or with several properties match_<name> for each), and net.check() compares it with the targets.



# EpiModel's introductory network: 175 partnerships among 500 people, 110 people with two or more partners, nobody with four or more, and partnerships lasting 50 steps
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, concurrency=0.22, max_contacts=3, dur=50)

# Most partnerships within a risk group, and over half within a region
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=0.7, dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8, region=0.6))

# And four times as many partners in the high-risk group (with sim.stratify(risk=['low', 'high']))
net = ss.DegreeNet(n_contacts=ss.by(risk=[0.4, 1.6]), dur=50, match=dict(risk=0.8))

# Needle sharing among people who inject drugs (a boolean property of people), with 20 injections a month in each partnership
needles = ss.DegreeNet(name='needles', who=ss.person.pwid, n_contacts=2, dur=ss.months(6), acts=ss.freqpermonth(20))

# Sex work, between female sex workers and their clients (boolean properties of people)
sw = ss.DegreeNet(name='sw', between=('fsw', 'client'), n_contacts=dict(fsw=5, client=0.5), dur=ss.months(1), acts=ss.freqperweek(1))

networks.MixingPool(pars=None, source=_, target=_, n_contacts=_, **kwargs)
Mixing between two groups of people (or everyone), without edges: used in place of a network
Each person in the target group is exposed to the average infectiousness of the source group, times their number of contacts. With no edges, it suits mixing in which who meets whom does not matter person by person. For mixing between several groups by a contact matrix, see ss.contacts().
Every communicable disease transmits over it; a disease’s beta on it is the disease’s, by route (0 for one that does not spread here).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

import starsim as ss

# Set the parameters
mp_pars = dict(
    source = ss.person.male, # Only men are infectious
    target = None, # Everyone is susceptible
    n_contacts = ss.poisson(mean=4),
)

# Seed 5% of the male population
def p_init(sim, uids):
    return 0.05*sim.people.male[uids]

# Create and run the sim
sis = ss.SIS(init_prev=p_init)
mp = ss.MixingPool(**mp_pars)
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=sis, networks=mp)
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Transmission to a susceptible person s is 1 − (1 − p)^(rel_sus_s · Σ_j c_sj · trans_j), for the disease’s chance p over the step, s’s contacts c_sj with source group j, and that group’s mean infectiousness trans_j. This is exact for a force of infection proportional to the contacts and the mean infectiousness. For discrete contacts with random members of a group, it is a mean-field approximation: it uses the group’s mean infectiousness rather than that of the people met, which slightly overstates infection (by a relative p(1 − f)/2 when a fraction f of the group is infectious). It is exact when everyone in the group is equally infectious, and close when p is small.

networks.Network.transmit(rel_trans, rel_sus, edge_hazard, rng, prob=None)
The edges that transmit in a step, in each direction the network transmits in (p1 to p2, then p2 to p1 unless it is one way)
An edge from source to target transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[source]·rel_sus[target]·hazard), or prob() if it is given: each factor scales the hazard over the step, so a contact infects at most once in it, wherever a model puts an effect. Random numbers are drawn only for the edges that can transmit: with CRN, each edge’s number depends only on its source and target, so this gives the same result as drawing one for every edge. The beta is worked out only for the edges from someone infectious to someone susceptible, which are found for both directions in one pass over the edges, or, once the edges have stayed the same for a step (edge_index()), from the edges of the infectious (or the susceptible) alone, if they have few; either way they are in the order of the edges.

Random connectivity between agents
Each agent has a number of contacts (n_contacts), and the other end of each is drawn from the other agents’ contacts (method='fast', the default), so an agent’s chance of being picked is proportional to its own number of contacts. This keeps the mixing structure of risk-stratified networks (a small high-risk core with many contacts forms most of its edges with itself).
method says how the other end of each contact is drawn:

'fast' (the default): by sampling the contacts with replacement. The source side of each edge is exactly n_contacts, while the target side is Poisson-distributed with mean n_contacts, so agents have somewhat more variable numbers of contacts than with 'exact'; about 1.8x faster than 'exact'.
'exact': by shuffling the contacts (sampling without replacement), so each agent has exactly n_contacts contacts, if it is even: each agent starts half of its contacts and is the other end of as many, so an odd number is rounded at random to the even numbers either side for each agent (5 gives 4 or 6, 5 on average).
'uniform': uniformly from all eligible agents, regardless of their own n_contacts, as in Covasim v3’s random networks. This gives less variable numbers of contacts (e.g. with n_contacts=ss.poisson(20), a variance of about 15, rather than 30 for 'fast' or 20 for 'exact'), but loses the mixing structure above.
'safe': by giving each contact a random place on a line, from the agent’s own random numbers, and joining it to its nearest neighbor there. Adding an agent then changes only the contacts next to theirs, which suits scenario comparisons, but it is slower, and does not yet work within places.

Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die, unless dynamic=False: with any of these methods but 'safe', one death rewires almost every edge.
By default (dur=0), each contact lasts one step of the network: with dynamic=True (the default), the contacts are drawn again on every step, and with dynamic=False, once. With dur= above 0, each contact lasts that long, and the ones that end are replaced by new ones drawn at random. For partnerships formed toward a target number of partners, see ss.DegreeNet.

networks.SexualNet(
    pars=None,
    between=_,
    dur=_,
    debut=_,
    acts=_,
    participation=_,
    n_contacts=_,
    concurrency=_,
    max_contacts=_,
    match=_,
    **kwargs,
)
Sexual partnerships that form and dissolve, between two groups of people: by default, men and women
A ss.DegreeNet between men and women (between='mf'), in which people take part after their debut (debut), if they do (participation, drawn at their debut). By default, people who have no partner are paired on every step, so nobody has more than one at a time. With n_contacts, the number of partners people have at a time is a target instead (among people who take part, after their debut), as for ss.DegreeNet; with partnerships much longer than people’s time in the network, it takes a few decades to settle.
Each partnership is between one person of each of two groups (between): a man and a woman, two men, or e.g. a female sex worker and a client, and each group can have its own number of partners (n_contacts as a dict). With match=, a fraction of partnerships is between people at the same level of a property of people, such as a risk group.
Each partnership has a number of acts per unit time (acts), so a disease’s beta on it is a probability per act (see ss.peract), and the fraction of them in which a condom is used (condoms, 0 unless set, e.g. by a subclass in add_pairs()), which a modifier of the transmission on the network reads, e.g. ss.modify(hiv.infection, efficacy=0.8, frac=lambda net: net.edges.condoms, network='sexualnet').
A subclass that overrides step() forms its own partnerships: the base starts none for it, and has none of the parameters for forming them, only between.
For several types of partnership with their own rules, see STIsim; for partnerships that are not sexual (e.g. needle sharing), ss.DegreeNet.
Note: not CRN safe when people are born or die.

networks.contacts(
    matrix=None,
    ages=None,
    dims=None,
    name=None,
    study=None,
    layer='all',
    unit=None,
    **by_dim,
)
Mixing between groups from a contact matrix; returns ss.networks.MixingPools
A matrix, and what it is over:

a country’s, by name (ss.contacts('Kenya')), from starsim_data, by 5-year age group;
its own age groups, given by their lower edges (ss.contacts(matrix, ages=[0, 15, 65])), which need not be the model’s (it is regrouped to them);
the model’s own stratifications: its age groups (ss.contacts(matrix)), another one, by name (ss.contacts(risk=matrix)), or several together (ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])), for mixing that is not a product, e.g. men mix with women, and by risk differently for each sex;
nobody in particular: a number (ss.contacts(10)) is homogeneous mixing, with that many contacts per person per unit time (an ss.MixingPool of everyone).

Mixing that is a product over stratifications takes a matrix for each, by name (ss.contacts(age=..., area=...)): the contacts between two groups are the product of the entries for each. The matrix by age can have its own age groups here too (ss.contacts(age=..., area=..., ages=[0, 15, 65])).
What the matrix multiplies is said by the rate of the infection, with I_j and N_j the number infectious and the number of people in group j, and N everyone:

beta*I: the fraction of each group who are infectious, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N_j, with C the contacts of a person and β per contact (as for contact surveys);
beta*I.n: their number, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j, density-dependent (as in Lloyd & Jansen’s metapopulation);
beta*I.frac (or beta*I.n/N): their number over everyone, β·Σ_j C_ij·I_j/N (as in Keeling & Rohani’s matrices, and WAIFW matrices).
a weighted count, beta*(ss.by(w)*I).n or beta*I.n_infectious: their number, each counted by its weight, β·Σ_j C_ij·w_j·I_j (for n_infectious, w_j is each group’s infectiousness).

So a textbook’s matrix goes in as the textbook gives it, with no rescaling. See the user guide’s page on population data for more.

sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.05*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10), init_prev=0.01)
mixing = ss.contacts([[10, 3], [3, 5]], ages=[0, 18])
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=mixing, unit='day', stop=100).run()

sir.stratify(risk=['low', 'high'])
mixing = ss.contacts(risk=[[2, 1], [1, 8]])

home, school = ss.contacts('Kenya', layer=['home', 'school']) # Contacts a day, by 5-year age group
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks=[home, school], stratify=dict(age=[0, 5, 18, 65]), unit='day', stop=100)

# A product: by age, then 90% of contacts within one's own area
mixing = ss.contacts(age=[[10, 3], [3, 5]], area=[[0.9, 0.1], [0.1, 0.9]], ages=[0, 18])

# Keeling & Rohani's Program 3.1: a matrix of rates per year on fractions of everyone, so the rate is I.frac
S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(S >> I @ I.frac, I >> S @ ss.peryear(1), init_prev=0.001).stratify(risk={'high': 0.2, 'low': 0.8})
sim = ss.Sim(sis, networks=ss.contacts(risk=[[10, 0.1], [0.1, 1]]), unit='year', stop=15).run()

# Men mix with women, and the high-risk with each other more among men than among women: a matrix over sex and risk together
matrix = np.zeros((2, 2, 2, 2)) # [sex, risk, sex, risk], with sex ['female', 'male'] and risk ['low', 'high']
matrix[0, :, 1, :] = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.5, 1.5]] # Women's contacts with men
matrix[1, :, 0, :] = [[0.8, 0.5], [0.2, 2.0]] # Men's contacts with women
mixing = ss.contacts(matrix, dims=['sex', 'risk'])

# Contacts that differ between people: lognormal, around a country's mean contacts a day
C = ss.data.contacts('Kenya')
mixing = ss.contacts(ss.lognormal(mean=C, std=C*0.5))

networks.fisher_yates_shuffle(arr, randvals)
In-place Fisher-Yates shuffle using precomputed uniform random values.
Equivalent to np.random.permutation (a uniform random shuffle), but ~1.3x faster for the large arrays used in network generation. randvals should be uniform on [0, 1) and the same length as arr.
Note: randvals is consumed in order (randvals[k] for the k-th swap), not indexed by position. This means that changing the array length (e.g. adding one agent) shifts every swap, so the shuffle is not random-number safe – matching ss.RandomNet(method='exact')’s intended behavior (see ss.RandomNet(method='safe') for the CRN-safe version).



networks.nb_transmit(src, trg, rel_trans, rel_sus, hazard, randvals)
Optimized transmission kernel: returns the (source, target) UIDs of transmitting edges.
Edge i transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[src]·rel_sus[trg]·hazard[i]): every factor scales the hazard in the step, so one contact infects at most once, whichever factor a model puts its effect in (see Network.transmit()). Fuses the gather/multiply/compare and the UID extraction into a single branchless pass. This avoids a full-length boolean temporary and two separate gather passes (trg[mask], src[mask]) – ~1.4x faster at typical transmission rates, more when transmission is common. UIDs are emitted in edge order, preserving CRN behavior.

utils.standardize_data(
    data=None,
    metadata=None,
    min_year=1800,
    out_of_range=0,
    default_age=0,
    default_year=2024,
)
Standardize formats of input data
Input data can arrive in many different forms. This function accepts a variety of data structures, and converts them into a Pandas Series containing one variable, based on specified metadata, or an ss.Dist if the data is already an ss.Dist object.
The metadata is a dictionary that defines columns of the dataframe or keys of the dictionary to use as indices in the output Series. It should contain:

metadata['data_cols']['value'] specifying the name of the column/key to draw values from
metadata['data_cols']['year'] optionally specifying the column containing year values; otherwise the default year will be used
metadata['data_cols']['age'] optionally specifying the column containing age values; otherwise the default age will be used
metadata['data_cols'][<arbitrary>] optionally specifying any other columns to use as indices. These will form part of the multi-index for the standardized Series output.

If a configured column is not present in the data, a known synonym is used instead if one is available (see ss.utils.col_synonyms); for example, year data labeled “Time” (as in UN World Population Prospects data) is used for a data column configured as “Year”. title: diseases
text:
diseases
Diseases: the base class (ss.Disease), diseases with transmission written as code (ss.AgentDisease), the record of who infected whom (InfectionLog), and the textbook models (ss.SIR, ss.SIS, ss.SEIR)
ss.Disease exists so that one class can hold a disease declared from states and transitions, written as code, or both. A declared disease runs with any solver; ss.AgentDisease and other code that works on individual agents runs as agents.
Used with: agents and compartments; declared and coded modules





Name
Description




AgentDisease
A transmitted disease written as code, as agents: the plain array operations of an infection, each a method to override


BuiltAfterInit
Build what a disease declares in its __init__() (define_states(), define_transitions()) once that has finished


Disease
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both


InfectionLog
A record of who infected whom, and when: kept by a disease when an analyzer needs it (e.g. ss.infection_log), to trace chains of transmission


SEIR
An SEIR model: as ss.SIR, with an exposed (latent) state before people become infectious


SIR
An SIR model: susceptible, infected, and recovered, optionally with deaths from infection


SIS
An SIS model: people recover from infection and are susceptible again





diseases.AgentDisease(pars=None, strains=None, **kwargs)
A transmitted disease written as code, as agents: the plain array operations of an infection, each a method to override
Gives the susceptible, infected (and infectious, by default the same), rel_sus, rel_trans, and ti_infected states; seeds init_prev of the people at the start; and each step transmits from transmissibility() to susceptibility() over the sim’s networks (transmit()), counts the new cases in the infection result, and gives them their prognoses (set_prognoses()). A subclass overrides only what it needs: usually set_prognoses(), for what happens to those infected, and step_state(), for how their states change; those infected before birth (over ss.PrenatalNet) go to set_congenital() instead, which a disease with outcomes at birth overrides. Anything else is plain code on the arrays. The betas of the networks are route_betas(), which can be overridden too (e.g. by sex).
With strains=ss.Strains(...), each person carries one strain at a time (self.strain, the index of the strain of their current or last infection, -1 if none), which the disease’s code reads (e.g. in set_prognoses(), with strain_value() for a strain’s values). The strains are transmitted in one pass, each by those infectious with it at its rel_trans; each new case is infected by one of those who reached them in the step, at random, and takes their strain, unless protected against it (strain_sus(): protection from ss.immunity(due_to=<state>, protection=matrix) by the strain they had, or the disease’s own), as a declared disease’s strains are passed on.
An infection in a step happens at its end, so a course scheduled from it starts at the next step: schedule a move dur steps after it at self.ti + 1 + dur, in an ss.TimeArr, and take it when due(). The seeds are dated by the step before the first (self.ti is -1 while they are set), so they have the same course.
A disease that can be written as states and transitions is shorter declared (see ss.SIR), and runs with every solver.
