class SIR(ss.AgentDisease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(beta=ss.perday(0.05), init_prev=0.01, dur_inf=10)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('recovered'), ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

    def step_state(self):
        done = (self.infected & self.ti_recovered.due()).uids
        self.infected[done] = False
        self.recovered[done] = True

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + self.pars.dur_inf

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIR(), networks='random', unit='day', stop=100).run()

# With two strains, the second more transmissible; recovering from one protects fully against it, and partly against the other
class SIRS(SIR):
    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()
        self.susceptible[self.recovered] = True # Protected only by the immunity of their strain

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.recovered[uids] = False

strains = ss.Strains(['H1', 'H3'], rel_trans=[1, 1.5], immunity=ss.immunity(due_to='recovered', protection=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]))
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIRS(strains=strains, name='flu'), networks='random', unit='day', stop=100).run()
sim.diseases.flu.strain # The strain of each person's current or last infection

diseases.Disease(
    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    solver=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both
Declared from its states and transitions, no methods need to be defined, and the disease can be run with any solver (see ss.Sim):
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
The same disease can be declared in a class body (the class form), which can also add behavior by defining methods; ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are written this way.
A disease can also be written as code: a subclass that declares nothing, defines its per-agent arrays (define_states()), and changes them in its own step_state() and step(); it runs as agents. One class can mix the two, e.g. a declared natural history and a coded array that its step() updates after super().step() has taken the declared transitions. Each lifecycle method runs the declared part through the disease’s engine (which, for a disease that declares nothing, has nothing to run), so an override calls super() as for any module. ss.AgentDisease adds transmission written as code: transmit(rel_trans=..., rel_sus=...), the same array operation as a declared transmission’s (see transmit()).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

A disease’s own solver= is useful when one disease of a sim needs a different way of running as agents from the others:

ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep'): by steps, with rates applied over whole steps to those in the state at the start of the step, as code with ss.bernoulli() does; faster, and a little less exact when the step is coarse
ss.solvers.abm(step='events'): event by event, in continuous time
by default: the sim’s, if it names a step; else the class’s suggested_solver (e.g. suggested_solver = ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep') in the class body); else 'midstep' (see ss.solvers.abm() and ss.solvers.agent_solver())

The results are the number in each state (I), the flow along each transition by its name (infection, with its cumulative total as res.infection.cum), and the results and outcomes declared (e.g. active=(E + I).frac). Its infected states also give the results infected, the number in them, and prevalence, their fraction of everyone in the disease’s states, unless it defines its own: those of its force of infection (E and I in S >> E @ beta*I), or those it says are infected (infected = E + I + H, ss.State(infected=True), or ss.states('S E I H R', infected='E I H')).

sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)
ss.Sim(sir, stop=100).run().plot()

class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R   = ss.states(3)
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

# Written as code: a disease that is not transmitted
class Anemia(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(p_onset=ss.bernoulli(0.01))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('anemic', label='Anemic'))

    def step_state(self):
        self.anemic[self.pars.p_onset.filter()] = True

diseases.Disease.R0(matrix=False)
The basic reproduction number, from the next-generation matrix at the disease-free state
By definition it is in a population with no infection and no immunity: the people infected at the start are left out, and everyone else is taken to be in the first state (e.g. S), each group keeping its size, whoever starts immune (init=dict(R=0.9)). So where transmission is density-dependent (beta*I.n), R0 is for the population less the people seeded, which matters only when many are (half the people seeded halves it). If no transition links some states to the first (a chain of states for each host species), their people are in the state their own chain starts from. People filled by a constant inflow (births of a number a day) and counts that are not people (mosquitoes) are at their equilibrium, which the inflow and the rates out of them set (Λ/μ). The reproduction number at the start, with any immunity, is in the line a run prints as it starts, when it differs (R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)).
The model is laid out as an ODE: if the disease is in a sim, a copy of that sim is made with solver='ode', with its mixing and stratification; otherwise a sim with the disease alone, under homogeneous mixing, with the default number of people. Values that vary in time (a seasonal β) are taken at the start, so this is R0 at the start time. A sim runs a copy of the disease it is given, so the R0 of a sim’s model is sim.diseases.<name>.R0(); this matters where a count is a number rather than a fraction of the people (mosquitoes per person).
This is the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix. Where infection passes through a vector (people infect mosquitoes, which infect people), each passage is a generation, so R0 is the square root of the classical Ross–Macdonald value. Shedding into a reservoir that is a count (such as water) is not an infection, so there R0 is the number of people infected through the reservoir by one person.

diseases.Disease.Rt()
The reproduction number over the course of a run, as a result: the number one infectious person infects at each time point
This is R0 at the state of the run at each time point: the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix with the people in each state of each group as they were then (so fewer when some are immune), and the rates as they were then (so lower while an ss.modify() halves β). It falls below 1 as an outbreak peaks. As in R0(), the model is laid out as an ODE, a copy of the sim with solver='ode', stepped alongside the run; a run as agents is taken by the counts in each state of each group. A state with several compartments (the stages of a dwell time) is split among them as in the copy; and the copy is what an intervention triggered by the state of the run sees.


S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3*I, recovery=ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10), name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, total_pop=10_000, stop=150).run()
sim.diseases.sir.Rt().plot() # From 3 at the start, below 1 after the peak

diseases.Disease.transmit(
    transition=None,
    rel_trans=None,
    rel_sus=None,
    beta=None,
)
Who is infected in this step by transmission: by one of the disease’s declared transmissions (transition), or, as agents, from the transmissibility and susceptibility of each agent (rel_trans and rel_sus), over the sim’s networks and other routes
Declared. A declared disease’s transmissions are its transitions whose rate depends on contact with infectious people (e.g. S >> I @ beta*I). Override this to write one as code, and call super().transmit(transition) for what the solver would do, e.g. to add a route of its own or remove some of the cases. The engine calls it once a step for each transmission, and moves those it gives along that transition, counted in its flow. A disease with one transmission can leave out the argument (def transmit(self):); with several, transition says which (e.g. if transition.name == 'infection':). As agents, it gives the new cases’ UIDs (those not in one of the transition’s source states are not moved); as compartments, the number infected in each group (or one number), taken from the source states in proportion. Under the ODE, it is taken once a step, at the start, as a move of that many (as ss.move() from code is), so the ODE no longer integrates that transition within the step: give a rate (e.g. S >> I @ (lambda self, sim: ...)) to keep it exact. Anything that needs individuals (UIDs) raises an error in a compartmental run; if isinstance(self.sim.solver, ss.solvers.ode): can give each its own.
As array operations. With rel_trans and rel_sus, it is the same transmission as an operation that code calls, as agents (in a disease written as code, or in a declared one’s own code): each edge of a network from u to v transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[u]·rel_sus[v]·H), where H is the hazard of the network’s chance for the step (see ss.Network.transmit()), with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (so the disease says allow_modifiers = ('rel_sus', 'rel_trans')), and the draws of each edge from the disease’s trans_rng; other routes (e.g. a mixing pool) give their own (compute_transmission()). Someone reached by several is infected by the first, which is their source, recorded with the route in an ss.infection_log. Nobody is moved: the code that calls it says what happens to those infected.

diseases.AgentDisease(pars=None, strains=None, **kwargs)
A transmitted disease written as code, as agents: the plain array operations of an infection, each a method to override
Gives the susceptible, infected (and infectious, by default the same), rel_sus, rel_trans, and ti_infected states; seeds init_prev of the people at the start; and each step transmits from transmissibility() to susceptibility() over the sim’s networks (transmit()), counts the new cases in the infection result, and gives them their prognoses (set_prognoses()). A subclass overrides only what it needs: usually set_prognoses(), for what happens to those infected, and step_state(), for how their states change; those infected before birth (over ss.PrenatalNet) go to set_congenital() instead, which a disease with outcomes at birth overrides. Anything else is plain code on the arrays. The betas of the networks are route_betas(), which can be overridden too (e.g. by sex).
With strains=ss.Strains(...), each person carries one strain at a time (self.strain, the index of the strain of their current or last infection, -1 if none), which the disease’s code reads (e.g. in set_prognoses(), with strain_value() for a strain’s values). The strains are transmitted in one pass, each by those infectious with it at its rel_trans; each new case is infected by one of those who reached them in the step, at random, and takes their strain, unless protected against it (strain_sus(): protection from ss.immunity(due_to=<state>, protection=matrix) by the strain they had, or the disease’s own), as a declared disease’s strains are passed on.
An infection in a step happens at its end, so a course scheduled from it starts at the next step: schedule a move dur steps after it at self.ti + 1 + dur, in an ss.TimeArr, and take it when due(). The seeds are dated by the step before the first (self.ti is -1 while they are set), so they have the same course.
A disease that can be written as states and transitions is shorter declared (see ss.SIR), and runs with every solver.

class SIR(ss.AgentDisease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(beta=ss.perday(0.05), init_prev=0.01, dur_inf=10)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('recovered'), ss.TimeArr('ti_recovered'))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

    def step_state(self):
        done = (self.infected & self.ti_recovered.due()).uids
        self.infected[done] = False
        self.recovered[done] = True

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.ti_recovered[uids] = self.ti + 1 + self.pars.dur_inf

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIR(), networks='random', unit='day', stop=100).run()

# With two strains, the second more transmissible; recovering from one protects fully against it, and partly against the other
class SIRS(SIR):
    def step_state(self):
        super().step_state()
        self.susceptible[self.recovered] = True # Protected only by the immunity of their strain

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        self.recovered[uids] = False

strains = ss.Strains(['H1', 'H3'], rel_trans=[1, 1.5], immunity=ss.immunity(due_to='recovered', protection=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]))
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=SIRS(strains=strains, name='flu'), networks='random', unit='day', stop=100).run()
sim.diseases.flu.strain # The strain of each person's current or last infection

    *args,
    pars=None,
    strains=None,
    stratify=None,
    solver=None,
    _names=None,
    **kwargs,
)
A disease: states people are in and the transitions between them (declared), code, or both
Declared from its states and transitions, no methods need to be defined, and the disease can be run with any solver (see ss.Sim):
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
The same disease can be declared in a class body (the class form), which can also add behavior by defining methods; ss.SIR, ss.SIS, and ss.SEIR are written this way.
A disease can also be written as code: a subclass that declares nothing, defines its per-agent arrays (define_states()), and changes them in its own step_state() and step(); it runs as agents. One class can mix the two, e.g. a declared natural history and a coded array that its step() updates after super().step() has taken the declared transitions. Each lifecycle method runs the declared part through the disease’s engine (which, for a disease that declares nothing, has nothing to run), so an override calls super() as for any module. ss.AgentDisease adds transmission written as code: transmit(rel_trans=..., rel_sus=...), the same array operation as a declared transmission’s (see transmit()).
Note: CRN safe as agents.

A disease’s own solver= is useful when one disease of a sim needs a different way of running as agents from the others:

ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep'): by steps, with rates applied over whole steps to those in the state at the start of the step, as code with ss.bernoulli() does; faster, and a little less exact when the step is coarse
ss.solvers.abm(step='events'): event by event, in continuous time
by default: the sim’s, if it names a step; else the class’s suggested_solver (e.g. suggested_solver = ss.solvers.abm(step='wholestep') in the class body); else 'midstep' (see ss.solvers.abm() and ss.solvers.agent_solver())

The results are the number in each state (I), the flow along each transition by its name (infection, with its cumulative total as res.infection.cum), and the results and outcomes declared (e.g. active=(E + I).frac). Its infected states also give the results infected, the number in them, and prevalence, their fraction of everyone in the disease’s states, unless it defines its own: those of its force of infection (E and I in S >> E @ beta*I), or those it says are infected (infected = E + I + H, ss.State(infected=True), or ss.states('S E I H R', infected='E I H')).

S, I, R   = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01)
ss.Sim(sir, stop=100).run().plot()

# Class form: for when there is behavior that is not a transition
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R   = ss.states(3)
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

# Written as code: a disease that is not transmitted
class Anemia(ss.Disease):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(p_onset=ss.bernoulli(0.01))
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)
        self.define_states(ss.BoolState('anemic', label='Anemic'))

    def step_state(self):
        self.anemic[self.pars.p_onset.filter()] = True

diseases.Disease.R0(matrix=False)
The basic reproduction number, from the next-generation matrix at the disease-free state
By definition it is in a population with no infection and no immunity: the people infected at the start are left out, and everyone else is taken to be in the first state (e.g. S), each group keeping its size, whoever starts immune (init=dict(R=0.9)). So where transmission is density-dependent (beta*I.n), R0 is for the population less the people seeded, which matters only when many are (half the people seeded halves it). If no transition links some states to the first (a chain of states for each host species), their people are in the state their own chain starts from. People filled by a constant inflow (births of a number a day) and counts that are not people (mosquitoes) are at their equilibrium, which the inflow and the rates out of them set (Λ/μ). The reproduction number at the start, with any immunity, is in the line a run prints as it starts, when it differs (R0 = 15.2 (R = 1.52 at the start, with 10% susceptible)).
The model is laid out as an ODE: if the disease is in a sim, a copy of that sim is made with solver='ode', with its mixing and stratification; otherwise a sim with the disease alone, under homogeneous mixing, with the default number of people. Values that vary in time (a seasonal β) are taken at the start, so this is R0 at the start time. A sim runs a copy of the disease it is given, so the R0 of a sim’s model is sim.diseases.<name>.R0(); this matters where a count is a number rather than a fraction of the people (mosquitoes per person).
This is the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix. Where infection passes through a vector (people infect mosquitoes, which infect people), each passage is a generation, so R0 is the square root of the classical Ross–Macdonald value. Shedding into a reservoir that is a count (such as water) is not an infection, so there R0 is the number of people infected through the reservoir by one person.

diseases.Disease.transmit(
    transition=None,
    rel_trans=None,
    rel_sus=None,
    beta=None,
)
Who is infected in this step by transmission: by one of the disease’s declared transmissions (transition), or, as agents, from the transmissibility and susceptibility of each agent (rel_trans and rel_sus), over the sim’s networks and other routes
Declared. A declared disease’s transmissions are its transitions whose rate depends on contact with infectious people (e.g. S >> I @ beta*I). Override this to write one as code, and call super().transmit(transition) for what the solver would do, e.g. to add a route of its own or remove some of the cases. The engine calls it once a step for each transmission, and moves those it gives along that transition, counted in its flow. A disease with one transmission can leave out the argument (def transmit(self):); with several, transition says which (e.g. if transition.name == 'infection':). As agents, it gives the new cases’ UIDs (those not in one of the transition’s source states are not moved); as compartments, the number infected in each group (or one number), taken from the source states in proportion. Under the ODE, it is taken once a step, at the start, as a move of that many (as ss.move() from code is), so the ODE no longer integrates that transition within the step: give a rate (e.g. S >> I @ (lambda self, sim: ...)) to keep it exact. Anything that needs individuals (UIDs) raises an error in a compartmental run; if isinstance(self.sim.solver, ss.solvers.ode): can give each its own.
As array operations. With rel_trans and rel_sus, it is the same transmission as an operation that code calls, as agents (in a disease written as code, or in a declared one’s own code): each edge of a network from u to v transmits with probability 1 − exp(−rel_trans[u]·rel_sus[v]·H), where H is the hazard of the network’s chance for the step (see ss.Network.transmit()), with the modifiers and products on rel_trans and rel_sus applied (so the disease says allow_modifiers = ('rel_sus', 'rel_trans')), and the draws of each edge from the disease’s trans_rng; other routes (e.g. a mixing pool) give their own (compute_transmission()). Someone reached by several is infected by the first, which is their source, recorded with the route in an ss.infection_log. Nobody is moved: the code that calls it says what happens to those infected.

title: Tutorials
text:
Running the tutorials yourself
Install Starsim with pip install "starsim[jax]" (see installation). JAX is used for gradients and for fitting by NUTS in the user guide; the tutorials run without it (pip install starsim).
Download a tutorial as a Jupyter notebook from the “Jupyter notebook” link beside the page’s contents. The notebook has the Python code as cells; the R code is included as text.
Data files: T6 reads the reported cases from data/measles_cases.csv and data/measles_cases_after.csv. Save them in a folder called data beside the notebook. The other tutorials need no files.
To run all the tutorials at once, clone the Starsim repository, install it (pip install -e .), and open the files in docs/tutorials in Jupyter (jupyter lab): with jupytext installed, Jupyter opens the .qmd files directly, or run ./convert_notebooks there first to convert them.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
🧠0% 🤖100%
This page is a ten-minute tour of Starsim. It builds one model step by step: a simple epidemic, then the same epidemic with age groups, an intervention, data to fit it to, and many runs to show the uncertainty. Each step is a few lines of code, and each step says what the code means in the terms of an epidemiological model. The parameters are illustrative, not estimates for any particular disease or setting.
To follow along, install Starsim with pip install "starsim[jax]", then download this page as a Jupyter notebook from the “Jupyter notebook” link beside the page’s contents, and run its cells in order. You can also clone the Starsim repository and open docs/tour.qmd in Jupyter (with jupytext installed, Jupyter opens .qmd files directly).

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
An SIR model
In an SIR model, everyone is in one of three compartments: susceptible (S), infectious (I), or recovered (R). The model is the standard set of equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta \frac{S I}{N} \\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I \\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I
\end{aligned}
\]
where N = S + I + R is the population size. People move between the compartments along two transitions:

Infection, from S to I. Each susceptible person is infected at a rate of β times the fraction of people who are infectious, so the number infected per day is β S I / N (frequency-dependent transmission).
Recovery, from I to R. People stay infectious for 10 days on average, so they recover at a rate of γ = 1/10 per day.

In Starsim, the compartments are states, and each transition says where people move from, where they move to, and at what rate (after @):

import starsim as ss

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 0.3*I        # From S to I, at a rate of 0.3 times the fraction infectious
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)  # From I to R, after 10 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery)

A state in a rate, like I in 0.3*I, is the fraction of people in it. A duration, like ss.days(10), is the average time spent in a state before leaving it. Since the duration is in days, β = 0.3 is per day. Starsim writes out the same equations from the model:

sir.equations()

dS/dt = -beta * S * I / N
dI/dt =  beta * S * I / N - I / dur_I
dR/dt =  I / dur_I


The basic reproduction number is R0 = β × the duration = 0.3 × 10 = 3. To run the model, give it to a sim with how long to run for:

sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=ss.days(100))
sim.run()
sim.plot()

Sim: sir, 10,000 people, as an ODE, days 0 to 100
  sir: R0 = 3, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0032 s; sir: 9,309 infections; at most 3,036 infectious, on day 27









The sim says what it ran and what happened: 10,000 people (the default population) as an ODE, R0 = 3 as expected, and the size and timing of the peak. Since nothing in this model is about individual people, Starsim runs it as a deterministic compartmental model (an ODE). The same model can also be run as a stochastic model or as agents, as the last section shows.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
How the epidemic starts
By default, 1% of people start infected, and everyone else starts in the first state, S. The fraction that starts infected is init_prev, the initial prevalence:
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)  # 0.1% start infected
init_prev puts people in the state that an infection leads to: I here, but E in an SEIR model, where people are exposed before they are infectious. To start people in any state, give init (the fraction of people in each state) or init_n (the number of people in each):
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001, R=0.2))  # 0.1% infectious, 20% already immune
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_n=dict(I=10))         # 10 people infectious

Checking the model
Starsim fills in whatever the model leaves out: the population size, how long a state lasts beyond its average (here, exponentially distributed, as in an ODE), how people mix, and so on. describe() lists the whole model as Starsim has built it: every state, transition, and setting, with each value that Starsim chose itself marked as guessed, so that nothing is hidden:

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Age groups and contacts
Most respiratory infections spread differently between age groups. stratify() splits each state by age: here into three groups, with the fraction of the population in each. ss.contacts() says how much each group mixes with each other one: a contact matrix, in which row i, column j is the number of contacts a day that a person in group i has with people in group j. With contacts, β is the rate of infection per contact. The infectious period is a parameter too, dur_inf, so that it can be changed later. This model also has an outcome, cases: the infections that are reported, here one in five.

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(0.02, bounds=[0.005, 0.1]) # A parameter that can be fitted, between these bounds
dur_inf = ss.par(ss.days(10))            # The mean infectious period

infection = S >> I @ beta*I
recovery  = I >> R @ dur_inf
cases     = ss.outcome(0.2*infection) # One infection in five is reported
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, cases, init_prev=0.0001)
sir.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the fraction of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]])
pars = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=1e6, start='2025-01-01', stop='2025-07-01')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.sir.I.by('age').plot()

Sim: sir, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01
  sir: R0 = 2.82, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0017 s; sir: 907,069 infections; at most 262,517 infectious, on 2025-02-25









Every state and transition has a result of the same name (S, I, R, infection, recovery), and so does each outcome (cases). by('age') splits a result by age group, and select() picks one group, e.g. sim.results.sir.I.select(age='65+').

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Interventions
An intervention changes the course of the epidemic from some point on. Here are two, both starting on 1 February, as the epidemic grows towards its peak: vaccinating 80% of children under 15, who have the most contacts and so carry the most transmission, with a vaccine that cuts their chance of infection by 90%; and masks, which cut transmission by 40%:

vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.9, who=sir.age < 15, when='2025-02-01', coverage=0.8)
masks = ss.modify(sir.pars.beta, multiply=0.6, start='2025-02-01')

To compare them, make a sim for each scenario, and run them together with ss.parallel():

scenarios = {'No intervention': None, 'Vaccine': vaccination, 'Masks': masks}
sims = {}
for label, intervention in scenarios.items():
    sims[label] = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=intervention, **pars)

msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot(['sir.I', 'sir.cases'])

MultiSim: 3 runs of 3 scenarios (No intervention, Vaccine, Masks)
  Done in 0.21 s









msim.summarize() gives each result over the whole run (the total of a flow, such as infections, and the final value of a state) for each scenario; here, the infections:

msim.summarize('sir.infection')








value


scenario





No intervention
907,069


Vaccine
665,003


Masks
658,629







Each prevents about a quarter of the infections, and halves the peak or more. Since R0 is about 3 without them, two thirds of people are still infected in the end with either; what they do most is flatten and delay the epidemic, which matters for the number who are ill at once.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Data and fitting
A model is fitted by finding the values of its parameters that make its results match data. To try this where the right answer is known, make data from a model: run it with β = 0.025, and draw weekly counts of cases from it, with random noise as in real reporting. Real data never come from exactly the model being fitted, so here the data come from a slightly different one, in which the infectious period varies less from person to person (an Erlang distribution with 3 stages, rather than the exponential of the model). The noise is drawn with the true sim’s own random seed (rand_seed=2), not the default seed of the sims being fitted, since the noise in real data has nothing to do with the model’s.

truth = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(beta=0.025, dur_inf=ss.erlang(k=3, mean=ss.days(10))), rand_seed=2, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week')
data.head()

Sim: sir, 1,000,000 people, as an ODE, 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-01
  sir: R0 = 3.53, with 100 infectious at the start
  Done in 0.0021 s; sir: 954,833 infections; at most 488,276 infectious, on 2025-02-04

A forecast is made from the data so far. Here, the first four weeks of cases, up to 1 February, are the data, and the sim stops when they do. Data is matched to results by name: the column cases is compared with the result cases, and since the data is weekly, each row is compared with the total of the model’s cases over its week. sim.fit() then fits every parameter that has bounds (here, β) to every result that has data:

early = data[data.date < '2025-02-01']
sim = ss.Sim(sir, data=early, **(pars | dict(stop='2025-02-01')))
fit = sim.fit()
fit.plot()

the last row of the data on cases (2025-01-29) starts a period that ends after the run, so it is not compared with the results. Starsim labels each row of data on a flow by the start of the period it covers; if these data are labeled by its end (e.g. weeks ending on a date), subtract one period from their times; if not, run the sim to the end of that period.

The loss is 0.006244 at the best values and 0.9404 at the initial values









The plot shows the model’s cases with the starting value of β (before) and the fitted one (after), against the data. fit.pars has the values found:

fit.pars

sc.obj(beta=0.029112419344762594)


The fitted β is higher than the 0.025 the data was made with: the fitted model’s exponential infectious period gives a slower growth for the same β than the data’s less variable one, so it makes up for it with more transmission. A fit finds the values that make the model match the data, which are only the true values when the model is the true one.
fit.project() runs the fitted model on, here to 1 July, for the forecast; given all the data, its plot shows the cases that were still to come:

forecast = fit.project(stop='2025-07-01', data=data)
forecast.plot('sir.cases')








From the first four weeks alone, the forecast gets the timing and size of the peak about right.

title: A tour of Starsim
text:
Uncertainty and many runs
The ODE gives one answer: the epidemic as expected on average. A real epidemic varies by chance from one outbreak to the next, and more so in a small population or when there are few cases. To see this, run the fitted model in a town of 20,000, which starts with 2 infectious people (the same 0.01%), as a stochastic model, in which the number of people who move between states each day is random. solver='binomial' runs the same model this way (as a chain-binomial model), and n_runs=20 runs it 20 times, each with its own random seed:

town = ss.Sim(sir, pars=fit.pars, **(pars | dict(total_pop=20_000)))
msim = ss.parallel(town.new(solver='binomial'), n_runs=20)
msim.plot(['sir.I', 'sir.cases'])

In every run, nearly everyone in the town is infected, so the size of the epidemic hardly varies; what chance changes is when it happens. In these runs, the peak comes anywhere from 3 to 14 February, depending on how quickly the first few chains of transmission took off.
The model can also be run as agents, one for each person (solver='abm'), which is what a model needs when people differ in ways that compartments can’t hold, such as their contacts in a network. The tutorials show how, starting with T1.

text:
Next steps
